records.introduction_en: The Niagara Escarpment Biosphere Reserve in Ontario stretches 725 km from Lake Ontario, near Niagara Falls, to the tip of the Bruce Peninsula, between Georgian Bay and Lake Huron.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Niagara Escarpment represents the largest contiguous stretch of primarily forested land in south-central Ontario. The biosphere reserve shows the greatest topographic variability in southern Ontario, with habitats ranging over more than 430 m in elevation. These habitats include Great Lakes coastlines, cliff edges, talus slopes, wetlands, woodlands, limestone alvar pavements, oak savannahs, conifer swamps and many others. These habitats collectively support the highest level of species diversity among Canadian biosphere reserves. They include more than 300 bird species, 55 mammals, 36 reptiles and amphibians, 90 fish and 100 varieties of special interest flora. The Niagara Escarpment stretches 725 km along the entire eastern edge of the Bruce Peninsula, a globally significant area covering 1,700 km2. At the tip lies Bruce Peninsula National Park. Within the park, the escarpment forms the Georgian Bay shoreline and constitutes part of the core area of the biosphere reserve. The park contains an array of habitats, ranging from rare alvars to dense forests and clean lakes. Over 1,000-year-old cedar trees grow among the rugged cliffs. Along with Fathom Five National Marine Park, the Bruce Peninsula National Park facilitates access to the shores of Lake Huron, the fifth largest freshwater lake in the world.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Niagara Escarpment

records.introduction_en: Riding Mountain Biosphere Reserve is located in south-central Canada, about 300 km north-west of Winnipeg, Manitoba. It is situated at the junction of the grassland and boreal forest biomes. Forests cover most of the area and are dominated by aspen (Populus tremuloides).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Forests cover most of the area and are dominated by aspen (Populus tremuloides). Although grasslands occupy only 7,400 ha of the total 1,331,800 ha, they are considered of national importance since they exist as discrete units, and the rare climax rough fescue community represents the eastern extent of its range. Grasslands once occurred throughout southern Manitoba, but they have been transformed since European settlement in the late nineteenth century. The biosphere reserve also includes agricultural areas that used to be forests or grasslands. The forest ecosystem maintains many larger mammals, such as black bear (Ursus americanus), American bison (Bison bison), grey wolf (Canis lupus) and coyote (Canis latrans).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Riding Mountain

records.introduction_en: The Tsá Tué Biosphere Reserve is located in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The area is the homeland of the Sahtuto’ine, the ‘Bear Lake People’. It encompasses Great Bear Lake, the last large pristine arctic lake, and part of its watershed. Boreal forest and taiga cover much of the watershed and form the habitat of wildlife including muskox, moose and caribou. The only human residents of the site are the traditional First Nation Dene community of Délı̨nę, ‘where the water flows’. The community, almost all of whom are Sahtuto’ine, is located on the western shore of the lake. The community relies on harvesting wildlife and fish to supply most of its needs. The economy includes limited but increasing tourism, infrastructure development and self-government administration.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area includes Great Bear Lake, the largest lake lying entirely within Canada. Three eco-zones are represented in the watershed: the Taiga Plains in the west, the Taiga Shield to the south-east including the Camsell River drainage area, and the Southern Arctic eco-zone on the north-eastern rim of the lake. Within these eco-zones, lands can be further classified into nine eco-regions and a total of 22 eco-districts. Each of these smaller areas has a distinct combination of landforms, permafrost, soils, climate and biological communities that give them a unique character. The largely unpolluted waters of the biosphere reserve, its healthy fisheries and the presence of wildlife in strong numbers throughout the watershed together produce an ecosystem with a very high degree of ecological integrity. Species such as grizzly bear (Ursus arctos), barren ground caribou (Rangifer tarandus groenlandicus), moose (Alces alces andersoni) and muskox (Ovibos moschatus) are present in large numbers.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Tsá Tué

records.introduction_en: The largest municipality in the Philippines by land area, Sablayan stretches across Occidental Mindoro from mountain forests above 2,200 metres to coral reefs and open sea. At its marine heart lies Apo Reef Natural Park, the largest contiguous coral reef system in the Philippines, while its upland forests shelter the tamaraw (Bubalus mindorensis), a critically endangered dwarf buffalo found nowhere else on Earth. Of the estimated 465–493 individuals remaining, the majority live within this biosphere reserve.
records.name: Matibay na Bayan ng Sablayan

records.introduction_en: The Palawan Biosphere Reserve is a cluster of islands composed of one long main island and smaller island groups around it. The biosphere reserve includes the entire Province of Palawan, the westernmost province of the Philippines.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Known as the Philippines’ “last ecological frontier”, the biosphere reserve is an archipelago of the main island and more than 1,700 islands. It is endowed with rich natural resources and highly diverse flora and fauna on land and at sea. Based on the IUCN classification, it has 105 of the 475 threatened species in the Philippines. Of these 105 threatened species, 67 are endemic to the country, and 42 of those 67 are Palawan endemics. Its coastal and marine ecosystems include coral reefs with 379 species of corals, seagrass meadows with 13 species and mangroves with 31 species across 44,500 ha of mangrove forests, the highest remaining mangrove cover in the Philippines. It also harbours several marine mammals, including marine turtles, dugong and whale shark. Terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems are likewise diverse, including old-growth and second-growth tropical rainforest, karstic limestone areas, forest over ultramafic rocks, casuarinas and beach forest. These serve as habitats for freshwater fish, with a total of 18 Philippine endemics, amphibians, with 26 Philippine endemics, reptiles with 69 species, birds with 279 species, migratory birds, and terrestrial mammals with 58 species, of which 16 are Palawan endemics.
records.name: Palawan

records.introduction_en: The Benoué Biosphere Reserve is located on the Benoué river plain, at the foot of the Adamaoua plateau in northern Cameroon. Tropical woodland savannah and dry open forests are the major habitats. More than 300 bird species can be found in the area as well as several mammal species including elephants (Loxodonta africana), waterbuck (Kobus ellipsiprymnus), leopards (Panthera pardus), hippopotamuses (Hippopotamus amphibius) and vervet monkeys (Chlorocebus pygerythrus). The local population depends mostly on cotton, traditional cultivation, stock raising, hunting and fishing for its livelihood.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The highest peak in the area is Mount Garoua, with an elevation of 1,100 metres above sea level. Major ecosystems include tropical woodland savannah and dry open forests, which host wildlife associated with Sudano-Guinean vegetation. Among the most common flora are wild syringa (Burkea africana), Combretum glutinosum and Prosopis africana. The diversity of fauna at Benoué is high, with more than 300 bird species, including the white-crested turaco (Turaco leucolophus), Goliath heron (Ardea goliath) and Senegal coucal (Centropus senegalensis). Mammal species include the African wild dog (Lycaon pictus) and the western hartebeest (Alcelaphus buselaphus major). The reserve is also home to a small population of endangered West African lions (Panthera leo senegalensis) and possibly the last example of the critically endangered western black rhinoceros (Diceros bicornis longipes).
records.name: Benoué

records.introduction_en: Korup Rainforest Biosphere Reserve lies in Cameroon’s south-west region within the Guineo-Congolian zone, and is ecologically linked to Nigeria’s Cross River National Park. It is one of Africa’s oldest rainforests, over 60 million years old, recognised as a Pleistocene refugium, conserving exceptional biodiversity and maintaining wildlife corridors and genetic diversity. The reserve’s objectives are to support sustainable, low-carbon livelihoods and evidence-based management, conserve forest cover, tackle poaching and illegal trade, protect flagship species, and serve as a hub for research, monitoring and education.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set in the Guineo–Congolian biogeographical region of south-west Cameroon, the Korup Rainforest Biosphere Reserve forms an ecological continuum dominated by evergreen lowland forest. The landscape ranges from foothill and swamp forests to submontane outliers on granitic peaks such as Mt Yuhan (1,079 m). Embedded within a broader conservation landscape that includes Korup National Park, council and community forests, logging concessions, and forest reserves, it protects one of the wettest and most isolated remnants of the Atlantic Biafran forest. Recognised as one of Africa’s two Pleistocene refugia, the area exemplifies long-term habitat persistence in west-central Africa.Plant diversity and endemism are exceptionally high, with more than 30% of tree and shrub species endemic to Korup. Notable examples include the cassipourea tree (Cassipourea korupensis) and shrubs of the genus Chytranthus. On hilltops, where the forest canopy drops to approximately 10–15 metres, characteristic species include junglesop (Anonidium mannii) and waterberry (Syzygium staudtii).Faunal diversity is equally remarkable, with nearly a quarter of Africa’s primate species represented. These include the critically endangered Preuss’s red colobus (Piliocolobus preussi) and Cross River gorilla (Gorilla gorilla diehli), as well as the endangered Nigeria–Cameroon chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes ellioti) and drill (Mandrillus leucophaeus).The reserve performs vital ecological functions: its forests sequester and store carbon, regulate water cycles, stabilise soils, and maintain wildlife corridors that sustain genetic diversity across the wider landscape.
records.name: Korup Rainforest

records.introduction_en: The Belezma Biosphere Reserve is in the north-east of Algeria within the Batna Province. It lies on the slopes of the Belezma Range which forms part of a subrange in the Aurès Mountains. The biosphere reserve comprises a rich mosaic of habitats, including forests, thickets, lawns, cliffs, mountain foothills, rivers and mines. It also contains 5,315 ha of Atlas cedar, which represents almost one third of the cedar forests of Algeria. This tree is several hundred years old and is the flagship species of the Aurès region. Its wood is used for traditional crafts such as weaving and agriculture. The biosphere reserve also contains several historical and archaeological sites, including caves and tombs that represent traces left by ancient civilisations. Local people engage mostly in agricultural activities such as livestock and grain farming, administrative and commercial activities, as well as handicrafts.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Belezma Biosphere Reserve is the southernmost national park of the northern part of the country, and acts as a bulwark against the negative influences of desertification. The very rugged terrain throughout the biosphere reserve is formed by folds orientated south-west, west and north-east. These orientations provide a great variety of natural habitats. This mosaic of habitats consists of forest, maquis shrublands, lawns, cliffs, scree, mountains, rivers, caves and mines. The Belezma flora includes 650 identified plant species, including fungi, with 11 protected species. This represents around 20 per cent of the overall Algerian flora. It includes several rare plant species such as rosemary (Rosmarinus officinalis), dog rose (Rosa canina), globe daisy (Globularia alypum) and holly (Ilex aquifolium). More importantly, the Atlas cedar (Cedrus atlantica), a tree species endemic to North Africa, specifically Algeria and Morocco, is a protected species in Algeria by executive decree. The Atlas cedar, a majestic tree that is centuries old, is the emblematic species of the Aurès region. Its wood is used in traditional crafts such as weaving. The habitats of the cedar forests in the Belezma Biosphere Reserve are special and unique compared to other Algerian cedar forests. The biosphere reserve is considered to be one of the great nesting sites for birds of prey in the Aurès Mountains, mainly because of the tranquillity and diversity of the uninhabited areas. The diversity of the habitats allows the local fauna to thrive because of the rich food supplies. The biosphere contains a total of 655 animal species, including 26 mammal species, 112 bird species and 22 reptile species. There are also several rare animal species such as the Egyptian vulture (Neophron perc … [truncated]
records.name: Belezma

records.introduction_en: Gouraya Biosphere Reserve lies on the Mediterranean coast in the Kabylie region. It overlaps with the national park of the same name. The reserve occupies a mountainous massif that dominates the north-west of the town of Béjaïa, culminating at 672 metres at Fort Gouraya. It also includes a small calcareous massif in the western zone. The site contains a wetland, Lake Mézaïa, and a marine area located to the west of the Gulf of Béjaïa.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve features rich flora and fauna, as well as several historic and picturesque sites. Protected species include the tree spurge (Euphorbia dendroides) and prickly juniper (Juniperus oxycedrus). Aleppo pine (Pinus halepensis) forms a para-climax forest on the limestone of Mount Gouraya. Kermes oak (Quercus coccifera) and Ampelodesma mauritanica are the dominant species on the southern side of the massif. The northern side, with its sharp relief and imposing cliffs, hosts original plant communities unique to the Algerian coast. The forests and maquis contain troops of Barbary apes (Maccaca sylvanus) and other endangered mammals such as the jackal (Canis aureus algeriensis), wild cats (Felis sylvestris) and the Algerian hedgehog (Erinaceus algirus). The marine zone includes five mammals, of which four are of national importance: the sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus), short-beaked common dolphin (Delphinus delphis), bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus) and harbour porpoise (Phocoena phocoena). Forests are characterised by Aleppo pine (Pinus halepensis), olive trees (Olea europea), carob (Ceratonia silica), myrtle (Myrtus communis) and Pistacia terebinthus. The maquis features kermes oak (Quercus coccifera), Ampelodesma mauritanicum and Phyllirea media. Cliffs support species such as Asteriscus maritimus, Lotus cytisoides and Limonium gougetianum. The marine area includes marine algae such as Lithophyllum lichenoides, Cystoseira ercegovicii and C. mediterranea. The site also includes a freshwater lake.
records.name: Gouraya

records.introduction_en: The Geno Biosphere Reserve lies at the southern edge of the Zagros Mountains, close to the Persian Gulf and the Hara Biosphere Reserve. Mountain ranges reach 3,000 m above sea level and separate the warm, humid Persian Gulf from the arid deserts of central Iran. Vegetation and microclimatic conditions vary with elevation throughout the biosphere reserve, and the valleys contain several hot springs.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is formed by the Geno Mountains, which rise above the Persian Gulf plains. Shallow slopes and plains surround the reserve to the south and east, while low hills are found in the north and west. The climate is arid at lower elevations, becoming semi-arid and cold from 2,300 m above sea level. Endemic plant species include Zhumeria majdae, Wendelboi petrocephalus and Acacia tortilis. The reserve supports high bird diversity, including the bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus) and the see-see partridge (Ammoperdix griseogularis). Endangered mammals occur here as well, notably the leopard (Panthera pardus) and the grey wolf (Canis lupus).
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Geno

records.introduction_en: The Kavir Biosphere Reserve is located in the Anatolian Iranian Desert. The Kavir plain is composed mainly of flood plains and low mountain ranges. The reserve is characterised by salt and sandy lands with arid and semi-arid desert vegetation, and is inhabited by steppe communities.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Kavir Biosphere Reserve is located south-east of the megacity of Tehran and encompasses parts of the Great Salt Lake basin and Dasht-e-Kavir. The reserve represents a typical type of Central Asian steppe grassland classified as desert. The central zone contains the oldest Precambrian stones found, together with active and semi-active volcanoes. Two hundred and five plant species have been identified within the reserve, of which 35 are endemic. Based on studies, there are 31 mammal species, 131 bird species, 20 reptile species and only one amphibian, Bufo kavirehsis. The reserve served as an important habitat for the Persian zebra (Equus hemionus onager), but the species gradually became extinct due to hunting from the late nineteen-seventies onwards.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Kavir

records.introduction_en: The Miankaleh Biosphere Reserve is located in the south-eastern region of the Caspian Sea. Major habitats include wetlands, intertidal mud with sandy shores, and shallow marine waters. Forests, peatlands and agricultural areas are also present. Miankaleh was designated a Ramsar site in 1975. Local people earn their income from agriculture, horticulture and animal husbandry. Other livelihoods include handicrafts, carpet weaving, traditional poultry farming and tourism. Management challenges include overgrazing, illegal hunting and fishing, and deforestation, as well as the unplanned spread of villages.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Miankaleh Wildlife Refuge consists of two ecosystems, aquatic and terrestrial. The sand dunes, which are an essential part of the terrestrial ecosystem, slope gently from west to east along the Caspian Sea’s shoreline. Relative differences in altitude range from 3 m to 5 m across the Miankaleh Peninsula. The reserve is one of the richest and most invaluable geological regions situated along the Caspian Sea. A variety of ecosystems, wetlands and sand dunes exist in the area, hosting a diverse range of migrant water and land birds, reptiles, mammals and different types of flora communities found throughout the biosphere reserve. The reserve also serves as a major staging area for millions of migrant birds. Some species are listed in the IUCN Red Data Book of Threatened Animals, including the white-tailed eagle (Haliaeetus albicilla), the Dalmatian pelican (Pelecanus crispus) and the white-headed duck (Oxyura leucocephala). The Miankaleh wetland fulfils Ramsar Convention criteria as a result of the number and distribution of migrant water birds and the presence of spawning grounds, and nursery and migration paths of endemic and commercial fish.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Miankaleh

records.introduction_en: Stretching from mountain peaks to the Adriatic coast, the Skadar Lake Watershed Biosphere Reserve is one of Europe’s most biodiverse landscapes. At its heart lies Lake Skadar, the largest lake in the Balkans and a Ramsar wetland, whose waters support 281 bird species, representing 55% of all European bird species, including nesting colonies of the Dalmatian pelican.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: With 1,396 taxa recorded across its wetlands, karst gorges, riparian forests and coastal ecosystems, the biosphere reserve is a living mosaic of Mediterranean and Balkan biodiversity. In 2025, botanists discovered within its boundaries an entirely new genus (Petrolamium crnojevicii) one of the most significant plant discoveries in Europe in recent decades, a reminder that this landscape still holds secrets.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Skadar Lake Watershed

records.introduction_en: The Great Gobi Biosphere Reserve is one of the largest biosphere reserves in the world. Located in south-west Mongolia at the border with the People’s Republic of China, it represents the Central Asian deserts. Fenced off from the sea by the surrounding mountains, the Great Gobi has a highly continental climate.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve ranges from 850 to 2,695 metres above sea level and includes rare desert and mountain steppe vegetation. It provides habitat for many endangered species, including the snow leopard (Uncia uncia), Siberian ibex (Capra sibirica), wild Bactrian camel (Camelus ferus), Gobi bear (Ursus arctos gobiensis), Asiatic wild ass (Equus hemionus), argali wild sheep (Ovis ammon) and goitered gazelle (Gazella subgutturosa). Birds include the houbara bustard (Chlamydotis undulata), whooper swan (Cygnus cygnus) and ground jay (Podoces hendersoni). Reptiles include the sand boa (Eryx tataricus) and the bent-toed gecko (Cyrtodactylus). The Great Gobi was established as a national Strictly Protected Area in 1975 and was included in the World Network of Biosphere Reserves in 1991 as one of the largest, covering 5.3 million ha. The biosphere reserve is especially important for the wild camel, as it is one of the last three locations where this rare animal can be found.
records.name: Great Gobi

records.introduction_en: Rising to 1,993 metres, the highest point in mainland Portugal, Serra da Estrela is a landscape shaped by deep geological time. Its granite formations, glacial valleys and high-altitude peat bogs are among the most significant glacial legacies in southwestern Europe, formed some 30,000 years ago and now recognised as a UNESCO Global Geopark. The future Biosphere Reserve will give this territory a second UNESCO designation, and an integrated governance model that treats geological and biological heritage as a single story.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Mindoro pine, one of only two native pine species in the Philippines, grows in forests that are also home to the Alangan and Taubuid Mangyan peoples. Their ancestral knowledge systems and community-based conservation practices are inseparable from the landscape they have shaped for generations.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Serra Da Estrela

records.introduction_en: Nestled within the Upper Paraná Atlantic Forest, one of the most biodiverse and threatened ecosystems on Earth, the Sur del Alto Paraná Biosphere Reserve protects critical remnants of a forest that once blanketed eastern South America. Today only a fraction of the original cover remains, making every fragment vital.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve shelters the jaguar, tapir, black-fronted piping guan and endemic swift species, while its core areas (Ñacunday National Park and the Moisés Bertoni Scientific Monument) anchor a network of ecological corridors connecting Paraguay, Brazil and Argentina in the trinational Iguazú region.
records.name: Sur del Alto Parana

records.introduction_en: Baishuijiang Biosphere Reserve is located in Wenxian County, Gansu Province. One of its primary aims is the conservation of the giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca). Baishuijiang is among the regions with the highest panda populations in China. The area is also important for biodiversity as it spans a large elevation range, from evergreen broad-leaved forests to alpine meadows.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Situated at the junction of the Palaearctic and Oriental realms, Baishuijiang Biosphere Reserve includes three major floral regions: the China–Japan Forest Floral Region, the China–Himalayan Forest Floral Region and the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau Floral Region. The main part of the reserve lies in the eastern section of the Minshan Mountains, where deep-cut alpine valleys dominate. The terrain is higher in the north-west and lower in the south-east, mostly at an altitude of 1,500–3,100 m. The highest peak reaches 4,072 m above sea level, and the lowest point is 595 m. The other part of the biosphere reserve is an extension of the Western Qinling Mountains, a moderately dissected Zhongshan mountainous area. Forest covers 192,194.7 ha, accounting for 85.9 per cent of the total area. Effective ecosystem protection plays an important role in water conservation, soil retention and the prevention of debris flows. This underpins the ecological safety of the region. Over the last ten years, populations of giant pandas and other rare and distinctive plants and animals have been restored and increased. Twenty-eight ecological monitoring sites have been established, forming a more complete and standardised system for scientific research and monitoring.
records.name: Baishuijiang

records.introduction_en: Located at the south-west tip of Yunnan Province in south-west China, Xishuangbanna Biosphere Reserve borders Laos to the east and Myanmar to the west in the upper Mekong basin. It comprises the largest and most comprehensive tropical forest in China. Owing to its distinctive geography and climate, it contains the country’s richest biodiversity. Tourism, agriculture and fishing are the main economic activities.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Xishuangbanna Biosphere Reserve lies within Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture in southern Yunnan. It consists of five geographically separate sub-reserves: Mengyang, Menglun, Mengla, Shangyong and Man’gao, located from west to east across Menghai, Jinghong and Mengla. Together they form a large, integrated reserve focused on protecting tropical forest ecosystems and rare wildlife. The area is the largest tropical primitive forest in China, with a complete tropical forest ecosystem and rich biological resources. The reserve supports numerous rare wild animals and plants, including many threatened species. It holds China’s largest population of the Asian elephant (Elephas maximus indicus), with a relatively concentrated distribution. More than 90 per cent of China’s wild elephants occur in this region. Natural vegetation is divided into eight types: tropical rainforest, tropical monsoon forest, subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest, deciduous broad-leaved forest, warm coniferous forest, bamboo forest, shrubland and grassland, with 38 formations. There are 2,772 species of vascular plants in 1,003 genera and 212 families, including 262 fern species (90 genera, 40 families) and 2,510 seed-plant species (913 genera, 172 families). Recorded fauna comprise 102 mammal species, 400 bird species, 63 reptile species, 38 amphibian species and 100 fish species.
records.name: Xishuangbanna

records.introduction_en: Baotianman Biosphere Reserve lies at 360–1,830 m above sea level. In this large ecological space, strongly undulating terrain and diverse landforms create a range of bioclimatic environments. These encompass a full suite of typical warm-temperate natural landscapes, together with the climatic features of a transition zone. Land cover consists of residential areas, forest land and agricultural land.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Alpine wetlands and marshes occur within high-mountain forest areas. They vary in size and form unique forest habitats. Scattered across the landscape, they range from just over 10 square metres to several hundred square metres. Alpine wetlands and marshes play important roles in conserving species diversity, sequestering carbon, releasing oxygen and conserving water, as well as delivering other ecological functions. There are 105 species of rare and endangered plants, including 24 nationally key protected plant species. The reserve has rich animal resources, with 359 species of wild vertebrates from 83 families and 32 orders. Forty-one animal species are rare and threatened. The biosphere reserve also supports traditionally used species, along with fauna and flora resources of significant commercial value. For example, Fructus corni, a traditional medicinal herb, is the main source of nourishing medicines such as Liuwei Dihuang Pill; magnolia is a medicinal herb used for seasonings and cosmetics; and kiwifruit, a wild fruit distributed in the Funiu Mountains, provides raw materials for natural beverages and food.
records.name: Baotianman

records.introduction_en: The Changbaishan Biosphere Reserve is in the north-east of China on the border with the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. The topography consists of a basalt platform, basalt slope highlands and cone-like volcanoes. Ancient craters now form lakes, which are surrounded by sixteen mountains. The highest peak, Mount Changbai, rises 2,691 metres above sea level. At its summit are Heavenly Lake, hot springs and a waterfall. Small volcanoes stretch from the north-west to the south-east and delineate the border of the reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The temperate continental climate of the reserve is influenced by monsoons. Vegetation varies with altitude and includes deciduous forests, mixed coniferous–broadleaf forests with Korean pine (Pinus koraiensis), coniferous forests, dwarf-birch forests and alpine tundra. The flora combines European, Siberian and central Chinese elements and include 1,800 species of vascular plants. The biosphere reserve also provides habitat for the Northeast Asian tiger (Panthera tigris longipilis), the largest tiger subspecies in the world. Temperate and sub-polar broad-leaf forests or woodlands, and mixed mountain and highland systems, are the major ecosystem types. Examples of flora and fauna found in the reserve include Manchurian ash (Fraxinus mandshurica), tiger (Panthera tigris) and scaly-sided merganser (Mergus squamatus).
records.name: Changbaishan

records.introduction_en: Chebaling lies in south-eastern Shixing County, Guangdong Province, on the southern foothills of the Nanling Mountains. It protects subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest and forms the headwaters of the Hengdu and Zhangdongshui rivers, which feed the Beijiang system. The forest’s hydrological function supports irrigation on the Shixing Plain, known as the granary of northern Guangdong, while helping to stabilise soils and maintain downstream water quality. The site serves both as a conservation area and a hub for science and education, conserving species and ecosystems, securing water resources, and supporting carefully managed, sustainable use of natural resources.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve has a subtropical monsoon climate, with seasonal variation influenced by both continental and marine conditions. Numerous streams intersect the site: the Hengdu and Zhangdongshui rivers provide the main headwaters, flowing through the reserve and maintaining year-round discharge into the Beijiang system. The major ecosystem is subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest, with overall forest cover above 95%. The forest plays a key hydrological role. A lush canopy, rich understorey and favourable microclimates enable irrigation of over 300 hectares of adjacent dryland converted to paddy fields, and support irrigation across tens of thousands of hectares on the Shixing Plain. Local communities benefit directly from these water-regulation services. As a natural defence and water-conservation area for northern Guangdong, the forest helps stabilise soils, regulate runoff and sustain downstream water quality. Natural ecosystems also include shrub, bamboo and river habitats, while typical semi-natural systems occur in the surrounding landscape as agro-ecosystems, including dryland and paddy fields. The mountain–valley landform supports a mosaic of primary evergreen broad-leaved stands, secondary woodland and associated habitats, providing refuges for a wide range of flora, fauna and macrofungi. By maintaining intact forest cover and ecological processes, Chebaling underpins regional ecological security and the resilience of subtropical forest biota.
records.name: Chebaling

records.introduction_en: Dalai Lake Biosphere Reserve, in the far north-eastern part of China, covers grassland ecosystems and wetlands that are considered internationally important for migratory birds under the Ramsar Wetland Convention. The biosphere reserve is an ideal site for research on wetland ecosystems and bird migration, with many rare species present. This region is thought to be one of the places where traditional Mongolian culture originated.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve centres on a wetland complex formed by Hulun Lake, Buir Lake and the Wuerxun and Kelulun rivers. The territory spans grasslands, extensive wetlands and open-water areas, forming a diverse mosaic of habitats and natural landscapes characteristic of North China’s typical Stipa grandis–Leymus chinensis. Biodiversity is rich, with 42 nationally protected birds, around 18 of which are globally threatened. Key species include Mongolian gazelle (Procapra gutturosa) and great bustard (Otis tarda), as well as black stork, golden and eastern imperial eagles, Pallas’s fish eagle, red-crowned, Siberian and hooded cranes, and relict gull. The wetlands are an important staging site on the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, hosting thousands of little curlews in spring and autumn. Hulun Lake, the largest freshwater lake in northern China, supports a notable fish community including cold-water taxa such as Lota lota and Brachymystax lenok, northern sub-frigid species like Esox reicherti and Carassius auratus, and productive plain-river fishes such as Erythroculter mongolicus and Culter erythropterus. Dalai Lake Biosphere Reserve is a prime site for research on wetlands and bird migration, with active cooperation across the borders with Mongolia and the Russian Federation.
records.name: Dalai Lake

records.introduction_en: Situated in Guangdong Province in southern China, the Dinghushan Biosphere Reserve comprises low mountains and the hilly lands of the Dayunwu Mountain Range. The range runs from north-east to south-west, with Jilong Mountain its highest point. More than 20 peaks of this range are located within the reserve. Dinghushan was China’s first nature reserve and has played a significant role in the conservation of ecosystems over the last 40 years. The biosphere reserve is also known as a major Buddhist centre in South-East Asia.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The very humid climate in the area has enabled the growth of subtropical and tropical humid forests, which host a rich diversity of species. In contrast to the disturbed surrounding forests, the Dinghushan Biosphere Reserve comprises rare primary forests that are at least 400 years old. The geological structure is composed of sandy shale, thick sandstone and quartz sandstone. Many plant species, such as castanopsis (Castanopsis chinensis), grow on the predominantly lateritic red earth. Christmas camellia (Camellia semiserrata), which also grows in the reserve, is a species of commercial importance and is used to produce a special oil and tea. Endangered animal species include the silver pheasant (Lophura nycthemeta) and the Chinese pangolin (Manis pentadactyla aurita). About 2,110 higher plant species, 120 bird species, 38 mammal species and 20 snake species have been recorded within Dinghushan.
records.name: Dinghushan

records.introduction_en: Located in the north-easternmost part of China, this biosphere reserve covers 28,500 hectares in a typical hilly region known for its intact natural stands of Korean pine (Pinus koraiensis). This tree species is of world-wide interest for timber production and these forests constitute a valuable gene bank which should be protected, in spite of pressure to exploit the trees.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Most of the landscape types of original forests are tilia Korean pine trees, birch-Korean pine trees and spruce-fir Korean pine trees, which are 52.9% of total area of the Reserve. Forest landscapes are in a vertical distribution of mountain broadleaf Korean pine forest belt. There are totally 15 forest landscape types in the Reserve.
records.name: Fenglin

records.introduction_en: Foping Biosphere Reserve sits on the southern slope of the middle Qinling Mountains in Foping County, Shaanxi Province. Recognised as a national biodiversity demonstration base, it protects a high-value mountain ecosystem, home to emblematic wildlife including the giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca). Set where warm temperate and northern subtropical zones meet, it conserves montane forests and rich flora and fauna. The reserve aims to strengthen biodiversity conservation while ensuring sustainable use and fair sharing of benefits. It works with research partners to apply nature-based solutions to climate, food security and local development.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Foping Biosphere Reserve comprises a montane area with well-preserved primary forest above 2,200 metres. It forms a complete mountain-forest ecosystem where the northern subtropical and warm temperate zones meet. The reserve’s forests provide key services including water and soil conservation, nutrient cycling, carbon storage and oxygen release, air purification and biodiversity support. The site lies at the junction of the floras of northern, central and south-western China and hosts a significant number of wild plant species, including medicinal, aromatic and oil-bearing species. Fauna reflects the transition between the Oriental and Palaearctic realms, with complex communities and ancient lineages. Key rare and endangered species include the takin (Budorcas taxicolor bedfordi) and golden snub-nosed monkey (Rhinopithecus roxellana). Within the Qinling range, the Foping area supports one of the densest known giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca) subpopulations, reflecting the quality of the reserve’s relatively undisturbed forests which provide reliable food and secure cover, with strong conditions for long-term research and conservation.
records.name: Foping

records.introduction_en: The Qomolangma Biosphere Reserve extends from China’s border with Nepal in the south to the watershed between the Yaluzangbu River and southern Tibet in the north. Centred on Mount Qomolangma, rising 8,848 metres, it spans humid alpine systems, mountain forests, wetlands and semi-arid plateau grasslands shaped by both oceanic and continental glaciers. The reserve is a setting for hiking and scientific research. Objectives focus on conserving alpine, mountain forest and shrubland ecosystems and the natural habitats they support, including emblematic species such as snow leopard and Himalayan tahr.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Extending across the southern and northern sectors of the Himalayas, the Qomolangma Biosphere Reserve covers great altitudinal variation, displaying a clear shift from humid alpine systems to semi-arid plateau shrub–grassland. The main ecosystems are mountain forests in the southern Himalayas, grasslands in the northern Himalayas and wetlands, including marshes. Two glacier types are present: oceanic glaciers in the south and continental glaciers in the north. The reserve serves as a vast water reservoir, a biological gene pool and an ecological security barrier. It supplies hundreds of millions of cubic metres of water to downstream areas and contributes to climate change mitigation. Its defining feature is Qomolangma (Mount Everest), the world’s highest peak, rising 8,848 metres. The reserve’s complex terrain and diverse habitats support extraordinary biodiversity, with nationally protected species including snow leopard (Panthera uncia) and Himalayan tahr (Hemitragus jemlahicus), as well as Old World monkeys (family Cercopithecidae). Notable flora include Himalayan yew (Taxus wallichiana) and Himalayan spruce (Picea smithiana).
records.name: Qomolangma

records.introduction_en: Saihan Wula Biosphere Reserve lies in the mountains south of the Greater Khingan Range. The reserve brings together a forest and grassland transition with valley wetlands and is regionally significant for ecotonal biodiversity and the hydrological functions of its wetland corridors. Management follows a protection-first approach that targets illegal logging and poaching and strengthens fire prevention. The reserve works through co-management with local authorities and Gacha communities to limit grazing in agreed areas, restore degraded sandy grassland and expand tree cover in the transition area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set at the ecotone between East Asian broadleaved forests and the boreal conifer belt of the Greater Khingan Range, Saihan Wula forms a forest–grassland mosaic reaching 1,957 metres at Wulanba peak, the reserve’s highest point. Mountain forests dominate, with birch and aspen interspersed with remnant conifers such as Picea meyeri and Larix principis-rupprechtii. On sunny slopes, Quercus mongolica and apricot occur with Artemisia shrublands, while ridgelines support Manchurian rhododendron (Rhododendron dauricum) thickets. Grasslands range from silver spikegrass meadows on gentle slopes to sandy grassland that has developed after periods of degradation. Valley wetlands run through the hills in connected bands. Willow forests and shrubs (Salix rorida, S. rosmarinifolia and other Salix species) provide habitat structure, regulate flows, filter water and stabilise soils. In places, floodplains form broad wet meadows with large willows that develop natural tree cavities used by nesting birds. Habitats of special interest include rocky screes (unstable slopes of loose rock fragments) on upper slopes near the main ridge at about 1,800–1,850 metres, and sandy landscapes that are erosion-prone and prioritised for remediation. The reserve’s habitats support high diversity: wildlife includes well-preserved red deer (Cervus elaphus), Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx) and a diverse bird community, with records of species of high conservation concern such as Aquila clanga, Otis tarda and Grus grus.
records.name: Saihan Wula

records.introduction_en: Shankou Mangrove Biosphere Reserve comprises the eastern and western terrestrial and coastal waters of the Shatian Peninsula. It can be divided into the Yingluo Harbor district and the Dandou Sea.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is a marine wetland in the coastal transition zone, representative of Guangxi’s terraced coasts and mangrove-fringed shores. An indented shoreline interlaces land and sea, with hills running down to the water as embayments reach inland. Sheltered conditions and slow-moving waters favour the growth of mangroves. The highest peak in the reserve is Hongkan Ridge, with an elevation of around 30 m. The undulating coastal plain terraces are usually 10–20 m above sea level. There are three small seasonal streams and a number of small reservoir marshes in the reserve. Tidal creeks are well developed within the mangroves, with deep, fine muds, and a shellfish aquaculture belt runs along the embankment. The co-occurrence of mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass in one site is uncommon on China’s coast. The reserve supports nine species of true mangroves, five semi-mangrove species, 21 mangrove associates, two alien species, two seaweed species, 221 species of large benthic invertebrates and fish, 164 bird species and 273 insect species, underscoring its importance for biodiversity conservation.
records.name: Shankou mangrove

records.introduction_en: The Snake Island–Laotie Mountain Biosphere Reserve is in the western part of Dalian’s Lushunkou District and covers a total area of 9,072 ha. Its primary targets for protection are Agkistrodon shedaoensis, migratory birds and ecological environments.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Snake Island lies in the north-western part of the Bohai Sea. It covers 73 ha and hosts about 20,000 venomous pit vipers, Gloydius shedaoensis, a species endemic to the island. Gloydius shedaoensis feeds on small migratory birds, and its two peak periods of activity are synchronous with the migrations. Snake Island forms part of an independent island ecological system called the ‘Gloydius Shedaoensis-Migratory Birds Environment’. In 2004, Gloydius shedaoensis was listed in the China Red Data Book of Endangered Animals and categorised as ‘critically endangered’. Laotie Mountain is at the southern tip of the Liaodong Peninsula, facing the Yellow Sea to the west and the Bohai Sea to the east. It is an important node for bird migration, with over 10 million birds migrating through the area. Vegetation types include forest, brush, shrub-meadow and meadow. Records indicate 703 species of plants, 217 species of amphibians, 10 species of reptiles and 307 species of birds.
records.name: Snake Island-Laotie mountains

records.introduction_en: Tianmushan Biosphere Reserve is in Zhejiang Province in the eastern coastal region of China, about 230 km south-west of Shanghai. Also known as the ‘kingdom of big trees’, the biosphere reserve protects the most ancient wild communities of Ginkgo biloba.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The vegetation in the reserve is very rich, encompassing evergreen and deciduous broadleaved forest, bamboo forest, coniferous forests, marshes and aquatic vegetation. Its major habitats include subtropical evergreen broadleaf forest with Castanopsis sclerophylla, Cyclobalanopsis glauca and Schima superba. Subtropical evergreen and deciduous broadleaf mixed forest features Phoebe chekiangensis, Ginkgo biloba and Emmenopterys henryi. Coniferous forest includes Cryptomeria fortunei, Pseudolarix kaempferi and Pinus taiwanensis. Agroecosystems support rice, vegetables and maize. Forestry ecosystems include bamboo, mulberry, medicinal plants and tea (Camellia sinensis).
records.name: Tianmushan

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve lies in south-west China, in Sichuan Province, about 150 km from Chengdu. Great mountain ranges, rising from about 1,150 to 6,250 metres above sea level, traverse the reserve between its north-eastern and south-western boundaries. Soil variation is notable: successive elevation bands support different soil types, from yellow soils and mountain black-brown soils to mountain brown soils. This heterogeneity underpins the area’s rich biodiversity.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Approximately 4,000 plant species have been recorded in the various habitats of the reserve, which include evergreen forests, evergreen deciduous broadleaf forests and mixed coniferous and broadleaf forests. Specific examples include the dove tree (Davidia involucrate) and Larix mastersiana, a conifer species. Gastrodia elata, a herb in the Orchidaceae family, is among flora associated with traditional Chinese values and is used for medical purposes. Altogether, 96 mammal species, 300 bird species and 1,700 insect species live in Wolong. Thirty fauna species are under legal protection, including many endangered or vulnerable animals, such as the Chinese monal (Lophophorus lhuysii) and the giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca). The presence of the world’s largest giant panda population was one of the main reasons for the designation of the biosphere reserve. More than 100 giant pandas inhabit the area, representing around 10 per cent of China’s giant panda population.
records.name: Wolong

records.introduction_en: The reserve is located in the Xingkai Lake basin on the Sanjiang Plain, bordering the Russian Federation along the Songacha River in the east and Daxingkai Lake in the south. Wetland and forest ecosystems are the main habitats and function like a vast reservoir, providing 16 billion cubic metres of water. The reserve holds a leading position in species diversity and abundance, and supports rare, endangered and relict species. It is known for its agricultural and industrial output. Ecotourism has been supported and promoted in recent years.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Xingkai Lake Biosphere Reserve is located in Mishan City, Jixi City, in the south-east of Heilongjiang Province, 130 km from Jixi City and 35 km from Mishan City. To the west lies Mount Laoye of the Changbai mountain ranges, and to the east is the Sikhote–Alin Range in the Russian Federation. Its topography is higher in the north-west and lower in the east, with elevations ranging from 574 metres down to 68 metres. Most terrain units comprise the Muling–Xingkai alluvial plain and a low lacustrine plain, with small areas of low hilly land resulting from structural erosion of Fengmi Hill. Wetland and forest ecosystems act as a huge reservoir, providing 16 billion cubic metres of water. The wetland ecosystem also helps secure ecological barriers in the upper reaches of the Wusuli River. Wetland vegetation can be divided into five higher-level types, nine subtypes, 28 formation groups, 37 formations at the intermediate level and 57 associations at the basic level. The reserve has high species diversity and abundance, with rare, endangered and relict species, and covers almost all wetland species found on the Sanjiang Plain. There are 414 vertebrate species across six classes, 34 orders and 77 families. These include 40 species of mammals in six orders and 14 families, and 289 species of birds in 16 orders and 53 families. Reptiles comprise eight species in two orders and three families, amphibians comprise seven species in two orders and four families, cyclostomes (jawless fish) include two species in one order and one family, and there are 68 species of fish in seven orders and 15 families.
records.name: Xingkai Lake

records.introduction_en: The Yancheng Biosphere Reserve is located on the Sub-Huang Huai plain of northern China, within the Palearctic biogeographical region. The reserve consists of a coastal marsh wetland that extends up to 582 km and includes a variety of salt marshes. Tidal salt marshes account for over 80 per cent of the reserve’s area and contain the most salt-resistant flora species. In addition, two major rivers traverse the region: the Yellow River and the Yangtze River.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The combination of monsoon rains and a temperate climate in the north, together with a subtropical climate in the south, provides ideal natural conditions for the growth of unique flora in the reserve. Examples of common flora species include Aeluropus littoralis, blady grass (Imperata cylindrica), and common reed (Phragmites communis). Nineteen amphibian, 23 reptile and 381 bird species have been recorded in the Yancheng biosphere reserve. Furthermore, 14 species have been categorised as protected wildlife, including red-crowned crane (Grus japonensis), relict gull (Ichthyaetus relictus) and Chinese paddle fish (Psephurus gladius). Moreover, numerous estuaries in the reserve serve as breeding grounds and habitats for cetaceans and fish.
records.name: Yancheng

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve and its surroundings are characterised by a great diversity of habitats in a relatively small area, most of which are representative of the Pampas plains.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Mar Chiquita Biosphere Reserve and surrounding areas constitute an area of great faunal interest. From a biogeographical point of view, it is located in a transition area between the Subtropical Zone and the Patagonian Zone. It is also notable for the presence of estuary environments and a coastal lagoon, which make the area a unique biotope. The environmental heterogeneity of the zone is reflected in the diversity of fauna present in the area. Other than the lagoon, the dominant habitat is grassland, including espartillar grasslands and psammophytic (sand-loving) vegetation. It should be noted, in relation to the biological diversity of grasslands, that these environments have been identified as the type of ecosystem that will experience the greatest proportion of change globally due to changes in land use and climate change. The biosphere reserve has been declared a Valuable Rangeland Area for Argentina by the consensus of experts in the country, within the framework of the Rangeland Programme of the Argentine Wildlife Foundation. The biosphere reserve has also been declared an Important Bird Conservation Area through the AICA programme, coordinated by Aves Argentinas and within the framework of a project coordinated by BirdLife International. This designation recognises the entire reserve, not just the grasslands, and is based on the fact that the biosphere reserve is inhabited by a group of globally threatened bird species.
records.name: Mar Chiquito

records.introduction_en: The Ñacuñán Biosphere Reserve lies on the semi-arid plains at the foothills of the Andes in Mendoza Province, Argentina. Across its upland grasslands, shrubby steppe and open woodland, Prosopis flexuosa is particularly characteristic: it has long provided Indigenous communities with timber and food, and it creates microhabitats by altering microclimatic conditions, namely water availability, light and soils. Following sustained conservation efforts, formerly scarce fauna are now recorded more frequently, including foxes and the elegant crested tinamou (Eudromia elegans).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Ñacuñán Biosphere Reserve belongs to the warm desert and semi-desert biome, and to the Monte biogeographic province. It is located in central-east Argentina on an extensive intermontane plain at 540 m above sea level, formed by sediments derived from the weathering of mountain rocks. Aeolian and water processes are manifested in sandy loam soils and in dunes, depressions and temporary furrows that create undulations in the terrain. The climate is desert, warm temperate. Average annual rainfall is 330 mm, mainly in summer. High evapotranspiration gives a negative water balance. The dominant plant community is the open forest of carob tree (Prosopis flexuosa). The jarilla (Larrea) dominates the shrub layer, accompanied by a rich variety of grasses. Around 190 species of wildlife are found, either permanently or temporarily, in the reserve. Vulnerable species such as the land tortoise (Chelonoidis chilensis), the crowned eagle (Buteogallus coronatus) and the grey fox (Lycalopex griseus) are protected in the reserve. Maras (Dolichotis patagonum), iguanas (Tupinambis rufescens) and pumas (Puma concolor) are also protected. Many species have developed strategies to adapt to the desert such as living underground, being nocturnal and having physiological mechanisms to reduce water loss. The forest that was cut down in the early twentieth century to produce charcoal is now in full recovery.
records.name: Nacuñán

records.introduction_en: Located on the central axis of the eastern Pyrenees, in the north of Andorra, the Ordino Biosphere Reserve presents a good sampling of the mountain range’s biological diversity. Traditional agriculture and herding have shaped the landscape, which is dominated in part by forests of Scots pine, fir, sessile oak and hook pine. Notable for the protection of several rare and endangered species on the IUCN Red List, Ordino is home to the great tetra, emblematic of the Pyrenees, the bearded vulture and the Pyrenees lizard, and it is a hotspot for Lepidoptera, or butterflies. The main driver of economic development in the region has been tourism, which is highly dependent on the quality of the natural environment and the conservation of heritage.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This biosphere reserve is characterised by its forests of Scots pine, fir, sessile oak and hook pine. The region, located in the central Pyrenees mountains, boasts high biodiversity of flora and fauna. There are many endemic species, including the Pallars lizard (Iberolacerta aurelioi) and the Pyrenean desman (Galemys pyrenaicus). The region is diverse, from meadows where dense floral vegetation thrives to mountain peaks covered in snow.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Ordino

records.introduction_en: Situated in the Emirate of Fujairah, the biosphere reserve consists of a water catchment area in an arid climate that is part of the Hajar mountain range. The site hosts rich fauna and flora endemic to the Arabian Peninsula. It is one of the last places in the United Arab Emirates where traditional farming practices are still maintained.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The main landforms in the biosphere reserve are characteristic of the Hajar Mountains and include mountain ranges, wadi systems, and alluvial plains. The area’s distinctive geology has created a unique hydrogeological system, in which runoff water emerges as springs at the contacts between impermeable and permeable rock layers in several wadis.All nine freshwater habitat types found here, ranging from riffles and streams to waterfalls, are spring-fed. Water flows alternate between underground and surface pathways. The mountain ranges reflect the desert montane characteristics of the Hajar Mountains: they are dry, with little to no soil development due to high erosion rates, and support a sparse cover of native trees and shrubs. Even so, they provide suitable habitat for Arabian leopards and Arabian tahr, both of which were last recorded in the wild in the area.The wadi systems are relatively green. Where permanent water is present, corridors of lush vegetation cut through the dry, barren landscape. Most of the region’s biodiversity is concentrated in these wadis, which provide essential water and food resources and serve as movement corridors for wildlife. The alluvial plains are areas of sediment deposition that support plant growth. After winter rains, they can rapidly transform into grazing hotspots as grasses may cover these areas almost overnight.The only record of the bloody darter dragonfly (Crocothemis sanguinolenta) in the United Arab Emirates comes from the park. Key flora include the orchid (Epipactis veratrifolia) and wetland plants such as Typha spp. Other species include Garra barreimiae, the bar-tailed semaphore gecko (Pristurus celerrimus), the rock semaphore gecko (Pristurus rupestris), the Omani carpet viper (Echis omanensis), the blue-ta … [truncated]
records.name: Wadi Wurayah

records.introduction_en: Pilón-Lajas Biosphere Reserve lies on the far eastern spur of the Andes. It comprises mixed mountain and highland systems, low hills and Amazonian plains, covered by humid tropical forest, subtropical and tropical forest, forest on ancient alluvial terraces, and mountain and valley forest.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The variety of ecosystems, geomorphology and vegetation types supports a wide range of species. About 70 mammal species have been reported, including tapir (Tapirus terrestris), ring-tailed coati (Nasua nasua), spectacled bear (Tremarctos ornatus) and jaguar (Panthera onca). There are 338 bird species, including genera Ara, Aratinga, Pyrrhura and Brotogeris. Recent studies report great floristic diversity in the region.
records.name: Pilón-Lajas

records.introduction_en: The Beni Biosphere Reserve is located in the Department of Beni, at the convergence of three biogeographical zones: the Amazon, the Chaco and the Cerrado. It comprises diverse forest formations, including gallery forests and forest islands of deciduous trees, lowland dense forest, and open, middle-height forest with tajibo (Tabebuia spp.) and matorral formations including tuzeque (Machaerium spp.). Seasonally flooded savannas are also present.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: More than 100 mammal species, 500 bird species and over 2,000 vascular plant species have been recorded. Some are endangered, such as turtles (Podocnemis unifilis). Tropical forest is characterised by cohoo (Hura crepitans), mara (Swietenia macrophylla) and motacú (Attalea princeps). There are also gallery forests and forest islands of deciduous trees. Lowland dense forest is characterised by palo maría (Calophyllum spp.), guayabochi (Calycophyllum spruceanum) and chonta (Acrocomia spp.). Open, mid-height forest features tajibo (Tabebuia spp.), mapajo (Curatella americana) and Pseudobombax marginatum. Matorral formations include tuzeque (Machaerium spp.), and there are extensive savannas and agroecosystems.
records.name: Beni

records.introduction_en: The Salzburger Lungau & Kärntner Nockberge Biosphere Reserve provides a representative example of inner-alpine landscapes with high mountains and deep valleys. It is a richly structured landscape ranging from 600 m to 3,000 m above sea level and encompasses typical ecosystems of the Central Alps, such as mountain meadows and marshes with great biodiversity. The human inhabitants have profited from this biodiversity for millennia, currently primarily in the form of ecotourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Salzburger Lungau & Kärntner Nockberge is the largest biosphere reserve in Austria, covering an area across the provinces of Salzburg and Carinthia. The site is extremely diverse, ranging from marsh areas and alluvial forests in the valleys, to cultivated meadows and woodland areas at intermediate altitudes, and extending up to the glaciers of the alpine summit regions. A large proportion of the different types of vegetation native to both federal provinces can be found here. The mixed forests of the montane level are composed of deciduous and coniferous trees. In this region, the hillsides close to the valleys are covered by high montane spruce forests. These gradually give way to larch and Swiss pine with increasing height. Bogs, boulder piles, avalanche stretches, and rock steps often interrupt the dense coniferous forests of the subalpine level. Due to the geological conditions, a remarkable multiplicity of bogs has formed, particularly in the south-east of the Preber. These include the Ramsar-protected “Überling mires”, which, with 117 ha of oligotrophic bogland, is the largest bog complex in Austria. The biosphere reserve is a refuge and a home for many animal species, including the barbastelle bat (Barbastella barbastellus) and the whiskered bat (Myotis mystacinus), as well as predators such as badgers (Meles meles), lynx (Lynx lynx) and bears (Ursus arctos). In addition, bird species such as the eagle owl (Bubo bubo), the black woodpecker (Dryocopius martius) and the capercaillie (Tetrao urogallus) find food, such as insects, seeds and fruit, as well as nesting sites in the area.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Salzburger Lungau & Kärntner Nockberge

records.introduction_en: The Noosa Biosphere Reserve is in eastern Australia at the northern end of the south-east Queensland region. A combination of erosion, deposition of underlying geological formations, vegetation growth, sand erosion and aeolian transport has produced the area’s topography. The eastern part of the reserve comprises littoral rainforests, lake systems and coastal dune heaths. The western and north-western regions are mountainous, with elevations up to 450 metres. Inselbergs rising to 430 metres, such as Mount Cooroy, Mount Cooroora and Mount Cooran, dominate the western landscape. The reserve also features an extensive system of saline and freshwater lakes, heathlands and marshes.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The southern coastline of Noosa is dominated by sand dunes with different types of vegetation that rise over 100 metres. The biosphere reserve is characterised by rich vegetation in tall, open eucalyptus forests and melaleuca. Renowned for its large diversity in flora and fauna, it is globally recognised for its effective conservation approach. Approximately 1,365 species of higher flora have been identified across 63 distinct ecosystems, of which 10 are endangered, which cover around 13 per cent of remnant vegetation within the reserve. Endangered and vulnerable flora species include the shrub (Boronia keysii), the stringybark (Eucalyptus conglomerate) and the rainforest vine (Tecomanthe hillii). In addition, the Cooloola area contains the largest remaining area of vegetation growing on aeolian sands. Noosa is also home to the largest variety of amphibians, birds, snakes and bats in all Australia. Altogether, around 711 species of native fauna live within the reserve. These include 78 butterflies, 303 birds, 64 mammals and 30 amphibians, as well as 121 marine fish and 22 freshwater fish. The extensive lake and river system produces ideal conditions for the growth of mangroves and rainforest, which in turn provide numerous habitats for globally unique fauna species. In total, 30 fauna species are of international importance. Around 45 per cent of all resident and regular migratory birds in Australia live in Noosa. Moreover, wet sclerophyll forests contain the highest number of endangered or threatened reptile and mammal species. Sixty-six fauna species are rare and threatened, including the Cooloola sedge frog (Litoria cooloolensis), the little tern (Sterna albifrons sinensis) and the false water-rat (Xeromys myoides).
records.name: Noosa

records.introduction_en: Situated in the Ashanti Region of Ghana, Lake Bosomtwe is one of six meteoritic lakes in the world. The southernmost section of the site overlaps the northern section of the Bosomtwe Range Forest Reserve, creating a combination of forest, wetland and mountain ecosystems. The biosphere reserve sustains 35 tree species, including some used for timber. It is also home to a great diversity of wildlife and to local communities whose main economic activities are farming, fishing and tourism, as the lake is a major national tourist destination. The area is widely used for research, especially on climate change, as well as for environmental education for schools and universities.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Lake Bosomtwe is an important national cultural and natural site of particular relevance for international conservation. It is believed to be the result of meteoritic action about 1 million years ago, when a crater formed by the impact of an asteroid gradually filled with rainwater. It is the only natural lake in Ghana and one of six major meteoritic lakes in the world and is thus considered a unique national resource. The lake catchment spans two districts, Bosomtwe and Bosome-Freho, and consists of a mixture of three unique types of ecosystems – forests, wetlands and mountains – which contribute to the conservation of vital biodiversity.The major tree species are Terminalia (Terminalia spp, Funtumia spp), Ceiba pentandra, African oil palm (Elaesis guineesis), Senegalese evergreen (Trema senegalensis) and fig tree (Ficus spp).The only faunal species of serious importance for conservation purposes is the tree pangolin (Phataginus tricuspis). Other species found on the reserve include the western green mamba (Dendroaspis viridis), the marsh mangoose (Atilax paludinosus), the red-chested cuckoo (Cuculus solitaries), the white-crested hornbill (Tockus albocristatus) and the lesser spot-nosed monkey (Cercopithecus petaurista).
records.name: Lake Bosomtwe

records.introduction_en: The Mare aux Hippopotames Biosphere Reserve is located about 60 km north of Bobo-Dioulasso in Houet Province, south-west Burkina Faso. It is known for its freshwater lake (“mare”) with associated pools and marshes in the floodplain of the Volta Noire River, as well as for its gallery forests. The reserve contains a wide variety of biodiversity, especially near the lake after which it is named.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is characterised by a Sudanese climate with two distinct seasons, a dry season lasting eight months and a rainy season lasting four months. Vegetation includes forests, wooded savannah, and vegetation found on the ferruginous crust and in aquatic and flood areas. The forest forms corridors along the Mouhoun rivers (gallery forests), while a lake extends over 660 ha, serving as a principal attraction. Wild mammals include a population of hippopotamus (Hippopotamus amphibius), elephants (Loxodonta africana), West African crocodiles (Crocodylus suchus), large antelopes such as the sable antelope (Hippotragus niger), and numerous primates such as the patas monkey (Erythrocebus patas) and warthogs (Phacochoerus africanus africanus). Birdlife is represented by 160 species of waterfowl, mainly kingfishers, the white-faced whistling duck (Dendrocygna viduata) and the golden-breasted jacana (Actophilornis africanus). The lake itself hosts 34 species of fish, represented mainly by tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus), catfish and African knifefish (Gymnarchus niloticus). La Mare aux Hippopotames is also a Ramsar Wetland Site.
records.name: Mare aux Hippopotames

records.introduction_en: The Central Balkan Biosphere Reserve lies in central Bulgaria, extending along the Balkan Mountain Range. This range is the principal mountain system of both the Balkan Peninsula and Bulgaria, and forms an extension of the Alpine–Carpathian folds. Four major Bulgarian rivers have their sources within the reserve: the Tundzha, Vit, Osam and Stryama.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Central Balkan Biosphere Reserve is rich in endemic plant and animal species. Within its core and buffer zones there are 45 species of algae, 238 species of moss, 337 species of macromycetes and almost 1,700 species of higher plants. Of the park’s floristic wealth, 186 species are of conservation value, and 17 are recognised on the IUCN Red List. There are 98 endemic plant species. The list of higher plants that are also relicts comprises 101 species: 48 Tertiary relicts and 53 glacial relicts. The park ranks among the most important refuges of arctic-alpine elements in the high mountains of southern Europe. The populations of eight mammal species are of global conservation significance. These include the snow vole, the souslik, the lesser mole-rat, the edible dormouse, Bechstein’s bat and the Balkan chamois. Bird species of global significance include the semicollared flycatcher and the white-backed woodpecker. It is also a key territory for the restoration of large European vultures, namely the griffon vulture, cinereous vulture and bearded vulture, as well as the saker falcon.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Central Balkan

records.introduction_en: The Ouémé Lower Valley Biosphere Reserve is located on the south-eastern Atlantic shore of Benin. It is a biodiversity hotspot hosting ecosystems of the Dahomey Gap.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve contains a variety of ecosystems, including hydromorphic ecosystems, meadows, marshes, gallery forests and mangroves. These are key to preserving the natural environment of the region. The territory is divided into four distinct regions: the coast, the Valley of Ouémé, Pobè and the plateau.
records.name: Oueme Lower Valley

records.introduction_en: The Bantimurung Bulusaraung Biosphere Reserve lies in southern Sulawesi, Indonesia, and comprises three main landscapes: Bantimurung, Bulusaraung and Maros–Pangkep. The Maros–Pangkep karst is among the largest tower-karst systems in the region. Within the core area, Bantimurung Bulusaraung National Park is internationally known for its butterflies, with more than 250 recorded species. Communities such as the Makassar and Bugis have maintained their traditions for centuries. While nature- and culture-based tourism are well developed, agriculture, including paddy farming, dryland cultivation, livestock and fishing, remains the main livelihood.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve extends from flat and undulating plains to hilly and mountainous terrain, rising to around 1,565 m in the north-east. Hilly tracts include intrusive, sedimentary and karst ridges, with low-relief plains between tower-karst outcrops. The Maros–Pangkep Karst covers around 40,000 ha, and is one of Indonesia’s few tower-karst landscapes; its extensive caves, rich in stalactites and stalagmites, contrast with the country’s more widespread hill karst. Karst caves host obligate cave-dwelling fauna such as dim-eyed and blind fish (Bostrychus), blind cockroaches (Nocticola), the beetle Eustra saripaensis, cave crickets (Rhaphidophora) and cave mites (Trombidiidae). Three principal forest ecosystems occur supporting high biodiversity: forest on karst (over limestone), lowland forest and lower montane forest. About 710 plant species are recorded, including wanga palm (Pigafetta filaris), sugar palms (Arenga) and protected Sulawesi ebony (Diospyros celebica). The reserve’s forests provide essential ecosystem services, from carbon storage and local climate regulation to flood mitigation and water purification. Bantimurung Bulusaraung National Park, within the core area, is internationally renowned for butterflies: more than 250 species are recorded, including the endemics Papilio blumei and Papilio gigon, and the protected Troides haliphron and Cethosia myrina.
records.name: Bantimurung Bulusaraung - MA'RUPANNE

records.introduction_en: The Bromo Tengger Semeru-Arjuno Biosphere Reserve is located in the province of East Java and encompasses an active volcano, Mount Bromo at 2,392 m above sea level. There are 1,025 reported species of flora, of which 226 species are orchids and 260 are medicinal and ornamental plants. Plant families commonly found in this area include Fagaceae, Moraceae and Anacardiaceae. Some of the mammal species found in the core area are included in the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Livestock farming of cattle, goats, sheep, horses, rabbits and chickens contributes to the local economy. The main economic activity is tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Bromo Tengger Semeru-Arjuno Biosphere Reserve is located on Java Island in East Java and forms part of the Indo-Malayan region. The biosphere reserve lies in a mountainous area that includes the active volcano Mount Bromo at 2,392 m above sea level, as well as Tengger Semeru, Arjuno and Mount Welirang. The core area incorporates mountains with an altitude of over 1,000 m above sea level that are covered with tropical rainforest. Several types of terrestrial ecosystem are found in the reserve, including cultivated areas, secondary forest and primary forest. The primary forest includes lowland rainforest, mountain rainforest, desert, savannah and sub-alpine ecosystems. In addition, the reserve incorporates lakes, and aquatic and riparian ecosystems. The reserve is home to about 1,025 species of flora, including 226 species of the Orchidaceae family and 260 species recorded as traditional medicinal plants and ornamentals. An inventory of fauna recorded 158 species, consisting of 22 mammal species, of which 15 are protected, 130 bird species, of which 27 are protected, and six species of reptiles. Protected mammal species include the Sunda pangolin (Manis javanica), leopard (Panthera pardus), Malayan porcupine (Hystrix brachyura) and Indian muntjac (Muntiacus muntjak). Protected bird species include the Brahminy kite (Haliastur indus), spotted kestrel (Falco moluccensis), green peafowl (Pavo muticus), Javan kingfisher (Halcyon cyanoventris) and Sunda minivet (Pericrocotus miniatus).
records.name: Bromo Tengger Semeru-Arjuno

records.introduction_en: The Karimunjawa-Jepara-Muria Biosphere Reserve in Central Java, Indonesia, is located in the mountainous region surrounding Mount Muria. It is critical in preserving the biodiversity of the central region on the island of Java. It includes a large variety of ecosystems, including small islands and marine ecosystems, as well as lowland and mountain tropical rainforests.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Karimunjawa-Jepara-Muria’s core area is situated in its islands. The diverse marine ecosystem hosts about 69 hard corals and 15 sea cucumber species. Karimunjawa National Park is home to numerous nesting sites for sea turtles, including the hawksbill and green turtle. Marine species, from giant clams (known locally as kima) to bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops aduncus), are protected by law, helping to maintain a healthy marine biota. The lowland and mountain tropical rainforests range from sea level to 1,500 metres above sea level. These forests support a variety of life, with over 130 bird species recorded. The biosphere reserve surrounds Mount Muria, a dormant volcano. The Javan deer (Cervus timorensis) occurs in the forests and is protected by law.
records.name: Karimunjawa-Jepara-Muria

records.introduction_en: Wakatobi is an acronym for the four main islands of Wangi-Wangi, Kaledupa, Tomia and Binongko, which together with smaller islands comprise the Tukang Besi Archipelago at the south-eastern tip of Sulawesi. The archipelago is renowned for the diversity of its coral gardens. Wakatobi’s 3.4 million acres of islands and waters were declared a national park in 1996. The ethnically diverse human population aims to make the area a learning laboratory in fields such as fisheries and agriculture.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Wakatobi has diverse ecosystems with many marine and coastal species of seagrass, coral reefs, fish used both for consumption and for sale, seabirds, turtles, cetaceans and mangroves. There are about 590 fish species, 396 coral reef species, 22 major and 11 associate mangrove species, and 9 of the 12 seagrass species found in Indonesia. Rare and endangered species with protected status include the hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata), green turtle (Chelonia mydas), napoleon fish (Cheilinus undulatus), canary crab (Birgus latro), giant clams (Tridacna), trochus (Trochus niloticus), dugong (Dugong dugon), and dolphins including Delphinus delphis, Stenella longirostris and Tursiops truncatus. There are 85 marine bird species in Wakatobi, for example brown booby (Sula leucogaster plotus), Malaysian plover (Charadrius peronii) and common kingfisher (Alcedo atthis). Several cetacean species are also found in the area, including sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus), short-finned pilot whale (Globicephala macrorhynchus), killer whale (Orcinus orca), pygmy killer whale (Feresa attenuata), pantropical spotted dolphin (Stenella attenuata), rough-toothed dolphin (Steno bredanensis), Risso’s dolphin (Grampus griseus), bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus) and melon-headed whale (Peponocephala electra).
records.name: Wakatobi

records.introduction_en: The Central Amazon Biosphere Reserve is located in a vast region influenced by the Negro and Solimões rivers, which are tributaries of the Amazon River.
