It lies in the Amazon Plains–Guyana Shield transition area. Representative of the largest forest in the world, it comprises vast protected areas as well as smaller units that function as ecological corridors, maintaining the genetic flow of species between these different units.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Habitats include Amazonian floodplains with white-water rivers, lakes and floodplain forests. Characteristic species include Echinochloa polystachya, Oryza perennis, Pistia stratiotes and Eichhornia spp. Igapó forest occurs along black-water rivers and lakes, with species such as Acmanthera latifolia, Acosmium spp. and Agonandra spp. Upland forest is characterised by Aldina heterophylla, Brosimum potabile, Calophyllum angulare and Cariniana micrantha. Campinarana is an upland forest type characterised by Annona nitida, Anthurium spp., Borreria capitata var. tenella and Clusia columnaris. The ‘baixio’ forest includes Mauritia flexuosa, Mauritia aculeata, Oenocarpus bataua (syn. Jessenia bataua) and Iriartea exorrhiza. Agroecosystems include floodplain agriculture, and there is also river sand extraction and mining.
records.name: Central Amazon

records.introduction_en: The Barranca de Metztitlán Biosphere Reserve lies in eastern Hidalgo, at the junction between the Sierra Madre Oriental, a mountain range which runs along eastern Mexico, and the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt (Neovolcanic Axis), which crosses the country west to east. Cut by tributaries of the Pánuco River, the landscape spans 900–2,600 m above sea level and forms a distinctive canyon system recognised as a national conservation priority. The reserve’s priorities include conserving xerophilous scrub and its emblematic cacti by addressing overgrazing and illegal extraction. It also seeks to guide local production towards sustainable practice, improving agricultural standards in the Metztitlán Valley and developing ecotourism rooted in the area’s landscapes and cultural heritage.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Barranca de Metztitlán Biosphere Reserve comprises a mosaic of xerophilous scrub, tropical dry forest, submontane scrub, coniferous forest, grasslands and riparian vegetation. Its relief offers striking viewpoints over the canyon, the valley and the Metztitlán Lagoon, where on full-moon nights the moon appears to meet the water, giving Metztitlán its name, ‘Place of the Moon’. This natural reservoir is of regional economic and ecological importance and is designated a Ramsar Wetland of International Importance. It helps regulate the local climate and serves as a refuge for large numbers of migratory waterbirds including pelicans, cormorants, resident herons and ospreys. It is also a source of food and employment for the valley’s population and creates favourable conditions for agriculture in the valley. The reserve is recognised as a Pleistocene refuge for Mexico’s desert biota, with affinities to the Chihuahuan and Sonoran Deserts, and today it functions as a biological corridor for arid zones on the central plateau. Submontane scrub has been greatly reduced in Mexico due to land-use change and overgrazing, yet in the reserve it is well represented under favourable conditions and designated as a core zone. Fauna is diverse and includes 17 amphibians, most endemic to Mexico, with representative species including Rana spectabilis in the lagoon and rivers. Overall, the reserve shelters fragile arid-zone ecosystems of high biological, scientific, economic, social and cultural value, with its canyoned river basin and position between major landforms underpinning this richness.
records.name: Barranca de Metztitlán

records.introduction_en: The reserve is located in the physiographic province Llanura Costera del Golfo Sur and the subprovince Llanuras y Pantanos Tabasqueños. Topographic formations are dominated by a barrier plain along the coast, including beaches, and, above all, the coastal floodplain. These landscapes are formed by the mouths of the Grijalva and Usumacinta rivers.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve safeguards 569 identified species of flora in eight main associations, with both monocotyledons and dicotyledons in aquatic and terrestrial systems. Notably, hydrophilic communities occupy more than one third of the Centla swampy region. There are also medium-altitude and lowland sub-evergreen forests of black olive trees (Bucida buceras) and logwood (Haematoxylon campechianum). The most economically important species within these two associations are Spondias mombin, Tabebuia rosea, Lonchocarpus hondurensis, bitter angelim (Vatairea lundelii), gumbo-limbo (Bursera simaruba), guanandis (Calophyllum brasiliense), mahogany (Swietenia macrophylla) and cedar (Cedrela odorata). Mangroves grow where brackish water from the Gulf of Mexico enters, and the soils that support them contain large concentrations of organic matter and nutrients that sustain the marine species living among their roots. There are four species of mangroves: the red mangrove, the white mangrove, the black mangrove and the button mangrove. Regarding fauna, 52 species of fish, 68 species of reptiles, 27 species of amphibians, 104 species of mammals and 255 species of birds have been identified so far, including both migratory and resident species from aquatic and terrestrial habitats. The most representative birds include the jabiru stork, the maguari stork, the Páspaque, the ruddy ground dove (Columbina talpacoti), the muscovy duck (Cairina moschata), the black-bellied whistling duck, Podilymbus podiceps, the peregrine hawk and the ibis. The most important rivers in the reserve are the Grijalva and the Usumacinta. They discharge 90 million m³ of water annually, placing this hydrographical region seventh in the world. This discharge carries an average of 7.3 million m³ o … [truncated]
records.name: Pantanos de Centla

records.title_en: Alto Golfo de California y El Pincate
records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve comprises the Pinacate area, the Gran Desierto del Altar and the Bahía of Adair on the Gulf of California border. It is located in Sonora State in extreme north-eastern Mexico. Geological volcanic formations with craters, dunes, oases and beaches, and the diversity of plant associations, determine its distinctive landscape. In the transition and buffer areas, inhabitants live in ejidos, or communal properties, mainly engaged in agriculture, forestry, mineral extraction and cattle raising, located mainly in the coastal areas. One of the most important economic activities in the transition areas is the presence of international enterprises, maquiladoras, in San Río Colorado, which engage local residents living in the urban villages. The same economic model is to be implemented in the village of Sonoyta as an industrial park.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The variety of species in the zone ranges from marine through coastal to land species. Located in the coastal zone are flats, beaches and dune systems, granite sierras and volcanic shield communities. The land fauna of the reserve is diverse due to the varied mosaic of its vegetation, which ranges from that associated with wetland areas to more inhospitable sites found in the sandy areas of the great desert. The Colorado River is the main habitat for the hogfish (Lachnolaimus maximus). This location is one of the few places in North America where the fringe-toed lizard (Uma inornata) is distributed. It is also the western limit for the distribution of the Gila monster (Heloderma suspectum). Among the reptiles, the diamond rattlesnake, the coral snake, the chameleon and the desert tortoise are notable. Birdlife is well represented with at least 80 species of land and aquatic birds, both resident and migratory, which characterise the area with high diversity. The land mammals are mainly representative of the Sonora and San Bernardina biotic provinces. They include white-tailed deer, mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus), bighorn sheep (Ovis canadensis cremnobates), the pronghorn (Antilocapra americana), the javelina and the long-nosed bat, among others. Plant species include the saguaro cactus, the strawberry hedgehog cactus (Echinocereus engelmannii), the thorny biznaga cactus, the Mexican palo verde (Parkinsonia aculeata) and the ironwood tree, among many others. The marine species include the porpoise or vaquita (Phocoena sinus), protected by Mexican law as an endangered species, the totoaba and the Yuma clapper rail.
records.name: Alto Golfo de California y El Pincate

records.introduction_en: Located about 140 km off the Mexican coast, Arrecife Alacranes is the largest coral structure in the Gulf of Mexico. Its high biodiversity and strong fishing potential arise from the calcification of overlapping colonies of various coral species over thousands of years. The Arrecife Alacranes Biosphere Reserve contains five main vegetated islands: Isla Pérez, Isla Desertora, Isla Pájaros, Isla Chica and Isla Exterrada. Isla Pérez is the only inhabited island. Tides and storms have also endowed the area with notable cultural heritage, including stranded boats, lighthouses and buildings, some of which are historical monuments.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve comprises five sandy islands with dunes and mangroves. Most of the reef has formed through the calcification of overlapping coral colonies over millennia. The emergence of the islands, and their continual reshaping by storms and tides, determines vegetation distribution and cover. These landscapes provide important nesting sites for several bird species, including the sharp-shinned hawk (Accipiter striatus), peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus) and piping plover (Charadrius melodus). Thirty-four coral species occur on the reefs.
records.name: Arrecife Alacranes

records.introduction_en: Located at the south-eastern tip of the State of Quintana Roo on Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula, Banco Chinchorro Biosphere Reserve covers over 144,866 ha and contains a mosaic of open water, seagrass beds, mangroves, sand beaches and coral reefs. It is the largest platform-type reef complex in Mexico and, owing to its isolated position, retains well-preserved natural ecosystems.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Corals characterise the area and form a circular strip of coral islets, which constitute the morphological structure of Banco Chinchorro. Owing to this coral topography, together with irregular submarine relief and orientation, a great diversity of habitats coexists. Some 95 coral species have been inventoried. Only 0.4 per cent of the core area is terrestrial, and it is strongly influenced by the sea. The saline substratum allows only halophyte or coastal-dune vegetation and mangroves. The buffer area comprises the broad coral ring and an extensive marine zone to a depth of 60 m. Seagrass beds are abundant in the Cayo Norte zone and in the interior lagoon of Cayo Centro; they serve as reproduction and nursery refuges for ecologically and economically important species, notably the Caribbean lobster (Panulirus argus) and queen conch (Strombus gigas). There are three coral systems, Cayo Norte, Cayo Centro and Cayo Lobos, which form the three core areas.
records.name: Banco Chinchorro

records.introduction_en: Located within the Neotropical biogeographical region, the El Cielo Biosphere Reserve is situated in the Sierra de Cucharas, a mountainous chain derived from the larger Sierra Madre. It is one of the most ecologically rich and diverse places in Mexico. The reserve comprises 14 vegetation types, dominated by tropical sclerophyllous forest. Conservation of El Cielo’s ecosystems is essential, as they host a number of threatened plant and animal species, including the oso negro (Ursus americanus), jaguarundi (Herpailurus yagouaroundi), tigrillo (Leopardus wiedii), jaguar (Panthera onca), ocelote (Leopardus pardalis) and cabeza de viejo (Eira barbara).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve includes various transition ecosystems with characteristic temperate-zone elements. A principal aim is to protect montane cloud forest vegetation because of its species richness and its very limited national extent, covering only about 1 per cent of the country. Other vegetation types include sub-deciduous tropical forest, pine–oak forests and xerophyte shrubland, which contain threatened or endangered endemic species. Mammals recorded include Eira barbara, Panthera onca, Leopardus pardalis, Leopardus wiedii, Herpailurus yagouaroundi, Ursus americanus, Bassariscus astutus, Glaucomys volans and Odocoileus hemionus. Birds include Accipiter striatus, Ara militaris, Asio clamator, Atthis heloisa, Bubo virginianus, Crax rubra, Falco peregrinus, Otus asio, Oxyura dominica and Icterus graduacauda. Reptiles include Phrynosoma cornutum and Gopherus berlandieri, as well as species of the genus Crotalus. Plant species present include Ariocarpus agavoides, Astrophytum myriostigma, Ceratozamia kuesteriana, Zamia fischeri, Magnolia schiedeana, Encyclia cochleata, Laelia anceps, Laelia speciosa, Lycaste deppei and Ferocactus hamatacanthus.
records.name: El Cielo

records.introduction_en: Straddling the border between Poland and Belarus, this forest complex is one of the last remnants of primary mixed forests in Europe. It lies in the transition between the boreal and temperate zones.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Situated in the transition between the boreal and temperate zones, the biosphere reserve contains several tree species at the limits of their distribution. Norway spruce (Picea abies) reaches the southern limit of its northern range, and sessile oak (Quercus petraea) is at its north-eastern limit. Notable mammal species include European bison (Bison bonasus), wolf (Canis lupus) and lynx (Lynx lynx). This is the last large complex of old-aged European mixed primeval forests. It has benefited from effective long-term protection since the fifteenth century, preserving relict forest patterns and processes, and maintaining high biodiversity. Its location in the transition zone between Western European mixed hardwood and Eastern coniferous forest ecosystems makes it significant as a research site. It holds the largest natural population of European bison.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Belovezhskaya Pushcha

records.introduction_en: The Dimonika Biosphere Reserve is located in the central Mayombe mountain chain about 50 km from the Atlantic coast.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The central Mayombe mountain chain region has a hot, humid climate, combining tropical and oceanic traits. A lowland Guineo-Congolese rainforest dominates the biosphere reserve together with savannah vegetation. The area lies in the transition zone between semi-deciduous and evergreen forest. Of special scientific interest are various types of forest communities recolonising old areas of forest exploitation. The fauna within the biosphere reserve is diverse and varied.
records.name: Dimonika

records.introduction_en: The Seaflower Biosphere Reserve is an oceanic archipelago comprising coral banks, small islands and islets that form parts of atolls, features that are rare in the Caribbean Sea.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Given its oceanic island setting and the small size of the islands, the terrestrial fauna is diverse yet generally low in abundance, with a relatively high degree of endemism. Notable terrestrial species include the black crab (Gecarcinus ruricola), “shanky” (Gecarcinus lateralis) and the white crab (Cardisoma guanhumi), which are harvested and traded locally.
records.name: Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta

records.introduction_en: The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta Biosphere Reserve and National Park overlook the Caribbean coast of northern Colombia. Most of the reserve, 675,000 ha, lies in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, with the remaining 56,250 ha comprising Tayrona National Park.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area extends from the Caribbean coast, with well-preserved coral reefs, extensive beaches, and several bays and inlets, up into the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, which is independent of the Andean chain and rises to 5,775 m only 42 km from the coast. The snow-capped peaks, called 'tundra', are considered sacred. Vegetation ranges from sub-hygrophyte levels to snow levels and includes cloud forest and high barren plains. In Tayrona National Park, three main vegetation types are present: forest and matorral, dry forest and humid forest. Some areas are being modified by smallholder agriculture and cattle grazing, and by the extraction of high-value timber, especially in the coffee belt.
records.name: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve is situated in the easternmost part of Switzerland on the right bank of the Inn River, close to the Italian border. Ranging from 1,400 to 3,173 metres above sea level, the area comprises forests, alpine grasslands, bare rock and scree.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Engadine valley, on the biosphere reserve’s northern edge, is the only valley in Switzerland that drains into the Danube, and several plants usually found further east have probably spread via this valley.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Biosfera Engiadina Val Müstair

records.introduction_en: The Comoé Biosphere Reserve is located in the north-east of Côte d’Ivoire, between the Comoé and the Volta rivers. It comprises an interfluvial peneplain and a series of ridges and granite inselbergs rising up to 600 m.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area represents a transitional habitat from savannah to rainforest, normally found only further south. Open forests and savannah with Panicum and Ctenium, characteristic of the Sudano-Guinean zone, occupy about 90 per cent of the area, while gallery forests dominated by Cynometra vogelii and dense dry forests cover about 10 per cent. Among the endangered species in the area are the roan antelope (Hippotragus equinus) and the plant Datura, which is used for artificial colouring and carries a high value on the international market.
records.name: Comoé

records.title_en: Corredor Biológico Nevados de Chillán-Laguna del Laja
records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve lies in the northern part of Patagonia within the Central Chilean zone, a global biodiversity hotspot characterised by an abundance of endemic species. The biological corridor connects three core areas.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Nevados de Chillán and Río Polcura sites have been designated high priorities for biodiversity conservation in Chile owing to their rich fauna, particularly insects, and flora, high genetic diversity, and the presence of the South Andean deer (Hippocamelus bisulcus). Fauna comprises 155 species; floristic richness totals 355 species. Among invertebrates, conservation-priority species account for 37 per cent of those recorded. Laguna del Laja National Park was created by Supreme Decree No. 652 of 25 June 1958, the first park of its kind south of Santiago. It is located in the Andes, east of the city of Los Ángeles in the Biobío Region, between the slopes of the Antuco volcano, the Sierra Valley and the Laja River, at 976–3,585 metres above sea level. The park is under the custody and administration of the National Forestry Corporation.
records.name: Corredor Biológico Nevados de Chillán-Laguna del Laja

records.introduction_en: Los Argüellos is located in the northern centre of León Province and includes the municipalities of Vegacervera, Cármenes and Valdelugueros. The region has distinctive geomorphological features, with numerous caves, such as Valporquero, Llamazares and Barredo, of touristic and scientific interest.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Los Argüellos is an example of a Cantabrian mountain ecosystem where, for centuries, the population has made wise use of scant resources, shaping a unique landscape. The biosphere reserve includes geomorphological features of undeniable attraction, among them numerous caves, such as those of Valporquero, Llamazares and Barredo, of great touristic and scientific interest. The spectacular gorges of Vegacervera and Valdeteja, also shaped by water through completely different processes, occur alongside open valleys. In these valleys, friable material has given way to the excavation of watercourses. Vegetation is varied, ranging from alpine grasslands to an abundant series of endemic species, including endemic forests of Juniperus, and to oak groves of Quercus pyrenaica near the Mediterranean environment. Other ecosystems, such as sub-steppe areas of annual grasses, active highland peatbogs and tufa-forming springs, are noteworthy. The numerous caves and crannies are home to 15 of the 26 species of bats in the Iberian Peninsula. They are also used by many birds of prey and two characteristic vertebrates of Cantabrian mountain ecosystems: the grey partridge and the broom hare. The brown bear should also be mentioned, one of the most endangered species in the Iberian Peninsula.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Los Argüellos

records.introduction_en: This site is situated in the Province of Castilla y León and is characterised by the cooperative venture of four valley communities to promote tourism and new economic activities that are respectful of nature. Mining and hydraulic energy production are the main sources of revenue in the transition area. This biosphere reserve has great importance for the protection of the brown bear (Ursus arctos pyrenaicus).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Valley of Laciana is located near the headwaters of the River Sil in the Cantabrian Cordillera, to the north of the Province of León, bordering Asturias. The area has a wide range of altitudes, with the consequent richness of landscape and valuable habitats. These include limestone oak groves, rocky outcrops, mountain grasslands, birch groves, yew forests, scrubland, numerous rivers, and riparian forests in a good state of conservation. The mountain grasslands have traditionally been used by the transhumant sheep flocks from Extremadura and by cattle managed by the Asturian nomadic cowherds, known as vaqueiros de alzada. This has given rise to scrubland with broom and bilberry, and to grasslands suited to the broom hare, endemic to the Cantabrian Cordillera, and to the grey partridge. The area also supports large wild ungulates such as roe deer, chamois and red deer, and their main predator, the Iberian wolf. There are also endangered species such as the brown bear and the western capercaillie.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Valle de Laciana

records.introduction_en: The Alto Turia Biosphere Reserve is located along the middle course of the Turia River, which passes through the Valencian counties of El Rincón de Ademuz and La Serranía in the central-eastern part of the country. The Turia valley, which runs from north-west to south-east, is the main defining axis of the biosphere reserve. There are plans to develop trade in local products of recognised quality to drive sustainable development in the territory.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area lies within the Mediterranean biogeographic region and is characterised by very diverse soils and vegetation. Summers are hot and dry, subjecting the vegetation to significant water stress. Predominant arboreal species include Aleppo pine (Pinus halepensis), maritime pine (Pinus pinaster), holm oak (Quercus rotundifolia) and gall oak (Quercus faginea), as well as Spanish juniper (Juniperus thurifera). The shrub layer consists of kermes oak (Quercus coccifera), cade (Juniperus oxycedrus), common juniper (Juniperus communis), Phoenicean juniper (Juniperus phoenicea), common hawthorn (Crataegus monogyna) and strawberry tree (Arbutus unedo), among others. The main fauna include steppe birds, the Granada hare (Lepus granatensis) and the European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus). Along watercourses, the white-throated dipper (Cinclus cinclus) and the common midwife toad (Alytes obstetricans) can also be found. Endemic fauna in the reserve include the Catalan barbel (Barbus haasi) and the Valencia chub (Squalius valentinus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Alto Turia

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve is located in the Gulf of Cádiz and represents one of the most important protected areas in Spain. The core area is made up of Doñana National Park. The importance of Doñana lies in the variety of ecosystems it hosts and the high number of species it represents.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This is one of the most important wetland areas in the world and covers diverse landscape units. The coastal strip includes virgin beaches and chains of both static and migrating dunes. These alternate with forests of centuries-old pine trees and complex lagoon systems interconnected by the water table, as well as enormous estuary areas and marshlands influenced by tides. There are seasonally flooded grasslands such as the scrubland plains, and forests of age-old cork elms converted into grasslands. The “white mountain” areas have a predominance of rockrose, thyme and rosemary. In the “black mountain” area, the dark colour of the heather abounds. The most notable feature is the extraordinary wealth of fauna that makes Doñana a unique enclave where over 300 species of vertebrates have been identified. It is estimated that some 6 million birds pass through the reserve annually on their migratory flyways, due to its strategic location between Europe and Africa. Doñana is also one of the last refuges for endangered species such as the Iberian lynx and the Spanish imperial eagle.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Doñana

records.introduction_en: The Gerês–Xurés Transboundary Biosphere Reserve is located in the westernmost region of the Iberian Peninsula. The hilly terrain includes two major peaks: Nevosa at 1,556 m and Fontefría at 1,559 m. A continuous mountain range includes the Peneda, Amarela, Xurés, Quinxo and Santa Eufemia mountains, which are encircled by tributaries of the Rivers Limia and Minho. Other major rivers that cross the biosphere reserve are the Vez, Homem and Cávado. The natural landscape is divided into plateaux and glacial valleys, notably the Homem and Vez, the wide valley of the Lima River and steep slopes. In general, the hydrographic network extends through narrow, deep valleys, creating almost rectilinear trajectories.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve has a rich and distinctive diversity of flora with more than 800 taxa, including many Lusitanian and Iberian endemisms. Endemic Lusitanian–Galician species include, among many others, Armeria sampaioi and climbing corydalis (Ceratocapnos claviculata). Records of Iberian endemic species comprise more than 100 taxa, approximately 50 per cent of which are limited to the north-west of the Iberian Peninsula. The distribution areas of several vascular plants are closely linked to this territory, effectively forming a fingerprint of the biosphere reserve. Many species of vascular flora are included on protection lists at European, national or regional level. The Gerês–Xurés Transboundary Biosphere Reserve is also the home range of yellowbeard iris (Iris boissieri), Veronica micrantha and butcher’s-broom (Ruscus aculeatus). More than 300 taxa of bryophytes occur in this territory, comprising four taxa of hornworts, 227 taxa of mosses and 86 taxa of liverworts. Nearly 250 vertebrate species and more than 1,000 invertebrates have been recorded. Examples of common fauna include the southern smooth snake (Coronella girondica), the Eurasian eagle-owl (Bubo bubo), the Iberian wild goat (Capra pyrenaica), the Iberian desman (Galemys pyrenaicus), the golden-striped salamander (Chioglossa lusitanica) and the Iberian wolf (Canis lupus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Gerês

records.title_en: Las Sierras de Béjar y Francia
records.introduction_en: The Las Sierras de Béjar y Francia Biosphere Reserve is in the east of the Iberian Peninsula, specifically in the south-east of Salamanca Province. In the west of the reserve lies the site of Cuidad Rodrigo and the Sierra de Gata. The reserve’s topography is marked by mountain ranges that traverse the area from the north-east to the south-west. These ranges have steep slopes and large gaps, and divide into two sub-plateaux in the centre. The higher altitudes reach up to 2,425 m at La Ceja. The lowest mountains reach 360 m at Soto Serrano. The two major rivers, the Duero in the north and the Tajo in the south, intertwine within the reserve and create hydrographic basins of high geographical and geological value. During the Ice Age, many flora species were isolated within Las Sierras de Béjar y Francia. After the glaciers melted, these endemic and rare species became of great phytogeographical importance.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Las Sierras de Béjar y Francia is influenced by a Mediterranean climate, although Atlantic winds and rainfall also affect the area. Together with the altitudinal differences, this uncommon combination of climatic influences fosters the development of rare and globally unique species. The major ecosystem type is Mediterranean deciduous woodland. The Sangusín River valley lies in the west of the reserve, with abundant oak forests and meadows that provide ideal conditions for livestock farming. In addition, the Cuerpo de Hombre River flows through the south of Las Sierras de Béjar y Francia, forming a valley where chestnut trees flourish. Characteristic flora includes European alder (Alnus glutinosa) and narrow-leaved ash (Fraxinus angustifolia). Pyrenean oak (Quercus pyrenaica) is distributed throughout most of the region and accounts for 24 per cent of all flora. Meadows, which represent 22 per cent of the vegetation, cover a large area of the reserve. Fauna such as the Mediterranean painted frog (Discoglossus pictus), European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) and whiskered bat (Myotis mystacinus) also live within Las Sierras de Béjar y Francia. Tench (Tinca tinca) is of great commercial value. The biosphere reserve also contains the Iberian lynx (Lynx pardinus), one of the rarest and most endangered species in Western Europe.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Las Sierras de Béjar y Francia

records.introduction_en: Las Ubiñas–La Mesa is located in the heart of the Cantabrian Range in the Principality of Asturias. It encompasses old-growth forest in pristine condition with high biodiversity. The biosphere reserve plays an important role in attracting or maintaining rural inhabitants.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The complicated geomorphology of this area, the wide variety of lithological substrates and various human uses have produced a large variety of vegetation and habitats, with significant species richness in both flora and fauna. The area is rich not only in the number of different species but also in rare or threatened species. Among the highly threatened plant species are the Centaura de Somiedo (Centaurium somedanum), which thrives on rocky limestone slopes, and the water-starwort (Callitriche palustris), found in some mountain lakes in the area of Quiros and Lena. Tree species with specific management plans for their conservation include yew (Taxus baccata), holly (Ilex aquifolium) and holm oak and its subspecies (Quercus ilex and Quercus rotundifolia). The biosphere reserve has eighteen wildlife species that are protected at the regional level, which account for more than half those listed for the whole Asturian territory. The brown bear (Ursus arctos) and the western capercaillie (Tetrao urogallus) are flagship species of the Cantabrian Mountains and are classified as endangered at both regional and national levels. This area represents one of their last refuges.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Las Ubiñas-La Mesa

records.title_en: Los Valles de Omaña y Luna
records.introduction_en: The region of Valles de Luna y Omaña is in the north-west of León Province in northern Spain, including the municipalities of Sena de Luna, Barrios de Luna, Soto y Amío, Murias de Paredes, Riello and Valdesamario. Elevations exceed 2,000 m in the south-west, in the Sierra de la Cañada mountain complex. Omaña is surrounded by mountain chains that mark the contact between the Cantabrian mountain range and the Montes de León. The region includes the Luna and Omaña rivers, which give rise to a succession of fertile valleys and narrow passages.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The regions of Omaña and Luna are the result of a farming system established during the Middle Ages, which remained in operation until the mid twentieth century. This system, associated with each settlement, included land allocated to grasslands, woods to supply timber, and croplands. The high mountain landscapes in the extreme north, west and south of the reserve are noteworthy for their high ecological value. Landscapes shaped by human and livestock activities are scattered throughout Omaña. The reserve harbours many singular fauna species, and for some this is the limit of their southern distribution. There are seriously endangered species such as the brown bear and the western capercaillie, and species endemic to Cantabria such as the broom hare. There are also species endemic to Spain, such as the Iberian desman, and singular species such as the grey partridge, the wolf and large populations of trout with very specific characteristics adapted to mountain watercourses. In general, bird, mammal, amphibian and reptile communities are widely and richly represented. The area has considerable and interesting flora, with numerous species endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It conserves examples of deciduous and marcescent forests in excellent condition. Notable are the birch groves, considered unique in the Iberian Peninsula, and the vast Quercus pyrenaica groves, along with clumps of another species of oak, Quercus orocantabrica, described in 2002. Also of interest are the riparian forests, combined with traditional agro-systems in a mosaic of outstanding landscape and cultural value.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Los Valles de Omaña y Luna

records.introduction_en: The main characteristic of the Menorca Biosphere Reserve is the diversity typical of Mediterranean island ecosystems. Notable habitats include gullies, caves and wetlands made up of ponds, lagoons and marshes, as well as dune systems, coasts and islets. Some 220 species of birds and 1,000 species of plants have been recorded, including 60 endemic species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This island has very flat landforms, with the highest altitude at Mount Toro (358 m). Although seasonally flowing torrents and ravines predominate, two low-discharge courses of permanent water are of special ecological interest. The climate is Mediterranean sub-humid, with a mean annual temperature of some 17 °C and mean annual rainfall ranging from 450 to 650 mm. Frequent and very strong winds have an impact, especially on the north coast. The well-conserved rural landscape is dominated by an agroforestry mosaic, comprising a wide mesh of dry walls, enclosed fields and country houses. Coves, cliffs and beaches are found along the coast, which remain largely untouched across most of the island. The flora includes endemic species such as peonies and diverse thorny shrubs forming cushions, known locally as socarrell, Launaea cervicornis. Among the fauna, there are large colonies of seabirds gathering in S’Albufera des Grau, such as the European shag, and an abundance of birds of prey such as the booted eagle and the red kite.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Menorca

records.title_en: Río Eo, Oscos y Terras de Buron
records.introduction_en: The Río Eo, Oscos y Terras de Burón Biosphere Reserve is located on the border of Asturias and Galicia in the north-west of Spain. The River Eo is the largest river in the reserve, and many others such as the Navia, Porcía and Miño flow through the area. The valleys have fertile soils, and agricultural farms are situated along their length. Pico Busbeirón, at 1,286 m, is the highest peak and forms part of hills that approach the main axis of the Cantabrian Mountains. The coastal area is primarily characterised by cliffs over 30 m high, formed by a combination of climate dynamics, eustatic changes and complex orogenic processes.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The River Eo encompasses thirty habitat types, while the mainland has more than twenty-five. Deciduous forests and swamps, with the Schreiber’s green lizard (Lacerta schreiberi), are the major ecosystem types within the reserve. Coastal ecosystems can be categorised into three zones: littoral, grassland and vegetated. Each zone has a different structure and habitat size varies due to natural factors such as tides, winds and other abiotic influences. Forest covers around 40 per cent of the area, while agricultural land makes up 33 per cent. Characteristic flora include English oak (Quercus robur), tormentil (Potentilla erecta) and the perennial bulbous plant (Narcissus asturiensis), which is native to the area. Common fauna include the slow worm (Anguis fragilis), black-throated loon (Gavia arctica), Eurasian oystercatcher (Haematopus ostralegus) and Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Río Eo, Oscos y Terras de Buron

records.introduction_en: The Montseny Biosphere Reserve and National Park are located between the Mediterranean and Eurosiberian–Pyrenaic regions in the Mediterranean Sclerophyll Province. It is the highest part of the Catalan coastal range.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Montseny is a northern massif, isolated from the Catalan pre-coastal cordillera. It includes extraordinary diversity in its flora and fauna because it lies in the transition zone between the Mediterranean and Atlantic regions. Forests of cork oak, holm oak, beech, chestnut, pine and even fir are very well conserved. These give way to vast grasslands in the highlands. The numerous watercourses are bordered by riparian forests of aspen, willow, hazelnut and ash trees. Among the fauna, alongside other Mediterranean species, are species characteristic of Central European ecosystems, such as the edible dormouse, the European green lizard and the Aesculapian snake. High-mountain species include the Pyrenean brook salamander and the European common frog. The entomological fauna is also very varied, with a rich diversity of butterfly species.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Montseny

records.title_en: Os Ancares Lucenses y Montes de Cervantes, Navia y Becerrea
records.introduction_en: Os Ancares Lucenses e Montes de Cervantes, Navia e Becerrea Biosphere Reserve lies among the upper elevations of the Cantabrian Mountains in the north-west of Spain, in Galicia. Its isolated location limits many endemic flora and fauna species to the reserve. The site lies between the Euro-Siberian and Mediterranean biogeographic regions, which results in highly complex biodiversity. Os Ancares Lucenses forms part of the Eastern Sierras de Galicia, and its steep relief is surrounded by irregular valleys and rivers with strong currents, such as the Río Navia. The foothills of the Serra dos Ancares have a fairly regular morphology with gently undulating hills. Finally, Mustallar, 1,924 metres high, Penalonga, 1,842 metres high, and Corno Maldito, 1,847 metres high, are the highest peaks in the biosphere reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Geographic isolation caused by complex orographic features has preserved a high-quality natural environment that contains endangered fauna, including the brown bear (Ursus arctos), considered a priority species. Among invertebrates, species of great importance include crayfish, Austropotamobius pallipes, and the Quimper snail (Elona quimperiana). Endangered amphibians and reptiles include the gold-striped salamander, Chioglossa lusitanica, the west Iberian painted frog (Discoglossus galganoi), the Iberian rock lizard (Iberolacerta monticola) and the Iberian emerald lizard (Lacerta schreiberi). Different mountain levels host a wide variety of forest types. Birch forests, dominated by Betula alba, occupy the highest parts of the shady slopes, at 1,400–1,700 metres. Forests containing Pyrenean oak are found mainly on sunny slopes, between 500 and 1,000 metres. These species, together with common hazel (Corylus avellana), are the most common in the biosphere reserve’s forests. The common holly tree (Ilex aquifolium) is of particular interest, since it is rarely seen in the Cantabrian Mountains and Galicia.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Os Ancares Lucenses y Montes de Cervantes, Navia y Becerrea

records.title_en: Real Sitio de San Ildefonso-El Espinar
records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve of Real Sitio de San Ildefonso–El Espinar is on the north-western slope of the Sierra de Guadarrama, within the Iberian Central System, in the south of the province of Segovia, 50 kilometres from Madrid.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve occupies a large cirque, a bowl-shaped depression, that opens to the north over the Segovia plains and includes the highest peaks of the Guadarrama mountain range. Vegetation on the northern slope of the Guadarrama mountain range is characterised by coarse grasses and scrub formations adapted to the area’s extreme weather, together with pine and oak, and alluvial grasslands that are optimal for livestock. Some of Spain’s most emblematic wildlife species, listed as endangered, are found here. These include the imperial eagle, black stork and black vulture, a large colony of roosting griffon vultures, and different species of chough, and migratory birds such as the eagle and black kite.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Real Sitio de San Ildefonso-El Espinar

records.title_en: Ribeira Sacra E Serras Do Oribio E Courel
records.introduction_en: Located in Galicia, at the mountainous north-western tip of the Iberian Peninsula, the biosphere reserve is a place of great natural beauty, enriched by strong cultural heritage. The River Miño meanders at the bottom of the vertiginous Sil canyons, in a landscape of valleys, tertiary depressions and scrubland foothills, creating a diversity of microclimates.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve now encompasses a UNESCO Global Geopark and six Natura 2000 sites, constituting a unique haven for biodiversity that harbours 1,214 species of vascular flora, 52.7 per cent of the floristic diversity of Galicia, and 277 species of fauna. The site is the westernmost extension of the ecological corridor formed by biosphere reserves in the Cantabrian Mountains and protected areas along the European Atlantic coast.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Ribeira Sacra E Serras Do Oribio E Courel

records.introduction_en: The Urdaibai Biosphere Reserve is located in the Euro-Siberian region, on the Bay of Biscay coast in the north of the Iberian Peninsula. The territory is characterised by a hydrographic basin that culminates in a large salt marsh, and by a coastal landscape of high, sheer cliffs and capes.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is located in a river basin that drains into an estuary of the Cantabrian Sea, forming marshlands with a wide intertidal area, in a region with a temperate ocean climate. The mean annual rainfall and temperature are 1,400 mm and 14 °C respectively. Natural vegetation is a mosaic of lush forests, scrublands and moorlands, together with anthropic conifer vegetation, meadows and croplands. It includes a varied zoological community associated with the different environments. Urdaibai, which means “river of the boars” in Euskera, reflects the abundance of this animal. The marshlands are critical for birdlife, both as a nesting area and as a stopping or wintering site. The coastal wetlands are also a natural nursery of great importance for many marine species that spend their first years in this area.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Urdaibai

records.introduction_en: The Tejo/Tajo International Transboundary Biosphere Reserve is located in the western part of the Iberian Peninsula, shared between Spain and Portugal, with the Tajo River as its main axis. The area is characterised by sharp relief and low altitudes. Vegetation consists largely of cork oak formations and patches of scrub, as well as cultivated areas and pastures. The fauna is typically Mediterranean and includes many rare species. Among the most important are the Iberian imperial eagle (Aquila adalberti), Bonelli’s eagle (Aquila fasciata), the black stork (Ciconia nigra), the black vulture (Aegypius monachus), and the otter (Lutra lutra). Livestock and forestry are the main sources of income for the small population of the reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area of the biosphere reserve is characterised by sharp relief and low altitudes. The vegetation consists largely of sclerophyllous and cork oak formations and abundant patches of scrub, as well as cultivated areas, extensive pastures and open stand formations. Among the most significant plant taxa are different species of orchids. The fauna is typically Mediterranean and includes a large number of threatened or endangered taxa, some of which are endemic to the peninsula. Among the most important species are the Iberian imperial eagle (Aquila adalberti), Bonelli’s eagle (Aquila fasciata), black stork (Ciconia nigra), black vulture (Aegypius monachus), Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus), great bustard (Otis tarda), otter (Lutra lutra) and green lizard (Lacerta schreiberi), along with the extensive fauna of the Mediterranean rivers.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Tejo/Tajo Internacional

records.introduction_en: The Baconao Biosphere Reserve lies on Cuba’s south-eastern edge and encompasses the Sierra de la Gran Piedra, east of Santiago de Cuba. The reserve brings together terrestrial and marine ecosystems, including extensive caves and caverns that host one of Cuba’s most diverse cave faunas. The reserve’s objectives are to strengthen landscape-scale environmental management by reducing agricultural, forestry and fisheries pressures, restoring key habitats and connectivity, and controlling invasive species, while building local capacity and governance for sustainable resource use.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve spans a coastal–montane landscape on Cuba’s south-eastern edge. To the north, the Farallones de Santa María del Loreto form dramatic cliffs with populations of endemic Melocactus; along the southern fringe, isolated limestone plateaux and hills step down in marine terraces to the sea. Coastal vegetation includes xeromorphic woodland and microphyllous semi-deciduous forest with sea grape thickets and scattered mangroves. Together, mangroves and reefs buffer storm impacts, moderate coastal inundation and support climate regulation. Marked geological and climatic gradients underpin high ecosystem and species diversity. Terrestrial systems range from coastal dry forest through mesophilous semi-deciduous and evergreen forest to montane rainforest. Forests along this gradient support soil formation, maintain nutrient cycles and regulate flows and quality of available water, underpinning clean water supply. Plant diversity is notable, with hundreds of fern species and over 1,900 flowering plants, alongside a wide variety of animals and high endemism across flora and fauna. Forty-eight butterfly species are recorded, including rare, charismatic species such as Calisto sibylla, Anaea cubana and the endemic Parides gundlachianus.
records.name: Baconao

records.introduction_en: The Cuchillas del Toa Biosphere Reserve is located in the Greater Antilles in north-eastern Cuba and covers the mountain region of Sagua–Baracoa in Alejandro de Humboldt National Park. It extends across 208,305 ha, of which 6,013 ha is marine. Cuchillas del Toa is considered one of the principal centres of biodiversity and endemism in Cuba and the insular Caribbean. Habitats range from rainy mountain forests and cloud forests to xerophytic matorral and complex coastal vegetation with mangroves and coral reefs.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The karstic system of the Great Cave of the Moa Headlands is one of the five natural monuments in the country and one of the major cave systems in eastern Cuba. Biodiversity is high in both flora and fauna. There are 928 endemic species reported, including the genera Podocarpus and Dracaena, considered ‘botanical jewels’ among the most primitive lineages. Vertebrates such as the royal carpenter (Campephilus principalis), the caguarero sparrowhawk (Chondrohierax wilsonii) and the almiquí (Solenodon cubanus) are also considered highly endangered species. Some of the world’s smallest mammal species are found in the reserve.
records.name: Cuchilla del Toa

records.introduction_en: The youngest and only volcanically active island in the south of the Cabo Verde archipelago, the Fogo Biosphere Reserve culminates at an altitude of 2,829 metres. It is home to various indigenous species, including rare birds and reptiles.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Fogo Biosphere Reserve is located to the west of Senegal in the western Atlantic Ocean. It forms part of the Cabo Verde archipelago and consists of Fogo Island and the surrounding marine space. The region hosts a wealth of native vegetation, including the endemic cowtongue (Echium vulcanorum), a flowering plant used for medicinal and dietary purposes. The biosphere reserve supports many terrestrial species, including the rare López-Jurado's half-toed gecko (Hemidactylus lopezjurado). The coastal skies are home to Fea’s petrel (Pterodroma feae), an endangered seabird of the region. Marine ecosystems host the short-beaked common dolphin (Delphinus delphis) and mackerel scad (Decapterus macarellus).
records.name: Fogo

records.introduction_en: The Bílé Karpaty (or White Carpathians) Biosphere Reserve is an area of hills and uplands in the north-west of the Carpathian massif on the border with Slovakia. It represents a cultural landscape with rich biodiversity and traditional land-use systems. Extensive species-rich orchid meadows covering 4,000 ha, near-natural deciduous forests, old orchards and solitary fruit trees are integral to the Bílé Karpaty landscape.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is a low-mountain area along the Czechia–Slovakia border. It is particularly valued for species-rich grasslands, which cover more than 4,000 ha and host many orchids and other rare plants, attracting a large number of insects. Its high biodiversity is attributed to its position, where Carpathian and Pannonian species meet, combined with long-term sustainable grassland management by local people. Meadow orchards are a significant part of the landscape and its biodiversity, hosting a wide range of old and local fruit cultivars. Other important habitats include old-growth beech forests and oak–hornbeam forests. The area is rich in traditions and living folklore.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Bílé Karpathy

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve lies in the western part of the Middle Bohemian range, about 16 km west of Prague. It comprises a wide variety of broad-leaved and mixed coniferous forest ecosystems, grasslands, pastures, valley meadows and agricultural land. The core area is used for hunting. In the buffer and transition zones, activities include logging, timber processing, charcoal production, manufacturing and light industry, stone extraction and tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Křivoklátsko is a predominantly forested region of the Central European highlands. Sixty-two per cent of the total area is broad-leaved and mixed coniferous forest, and the site has high species diversity, with about 1,800 vascular plant species and 84 native tree and shrub species. The major landscape feature is the Berounka River valley, which forms a network of deeply cut canyons, narrow floodplains, terraces, steep slopes and cliffs. These landforms provide a wide range of habitats for plants and animals. Geological diversity, including variation in parent rocks and soils, adds to microclimatic differences and, in turn, to overall biodiversity. Historical human settlement has also shaped the area: its past use as royal hunting grounds helped limit deforestation and other impacts. Today the landscape is a mosaic of small villages, agricultural land, silvicultural plots and forests.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Krivoklátsko

records.introduction_en: Situated in South Moravia, about 35 km south of Brno and adjacent to the Austrian and Slovak borders, the area is dominated by the Pavlov Hills, whose limestone cliffs and steep slopes support steppe, forest and grassland. A considerable part of the landscape has also been converted to arable land and vineyards.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The north-eastern part of the biosphere reserve lies in the flat alluvium of the Dyje River. This area is now mostly agricultural, with remnants of floodplain meadows and forests. The southern and eastern parts are characterised by arable land. The largest Central European expanse of hardwood alluvial forests and continental floodplain meadows, about 8,000 ha, is preserved in the triangle between the town of Břeclav, the village of Týnec and the confluence of the Morava and Dyje rivers. The central part of the reserve comprises a depression occupied by fishponds, which are shallow artificial lakes. The core area corresponds to zone 1 of the Pálava Protected Landscape Area, together with smaller protected areas outside this zone. The buffer zone consists of zone 2 of the Pálava Protected Landscape Area and mainly forested areas outside it. The transition area comprises zones 3 and 4 of the Pálava Protected Landscape Area and mainly agricultural land beyond.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Lower Morava

records.introduction_en: The Berchtesgadener Land biosphere reserve lies in the Berchtesgaden Alps, 150 km south-east of Munich on the border with Austria, and forms part of the Northern Limestone Alps. It is the only alpine biosphere reserve in Germany. It covers alpine landscapes and their foothills with lower areas. Elevation ranges from 380 to 2,700 metres above sea level. The reserve therefore encompasses riparian, submontane, montane and subalpine forests, as well as alpine and lowland meadows. Small-scale agriculture gives the landscape its characteristic features. The core area and buffer zone are identical with Berchtesgaden National Park, which includes the famous Lake Königssee. Local communities depend greatly on tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Berchtesgadener Land Biosphere Reserve comprises a typical section of the Northern Limestone Alps, including the pre-Alps such as the Berchtesgaden Alps and the Chiemgau Alps, and the young moraine landscape of pre-alpine hills and bogs. Geological diversity, high relative relief with peaks in the south over 2,700 metres above sea level and valleys in the north around 400 metres, and a wealth of glaciological formations create a mosaic of biotope types within a small area. Accordingly, the reserve includes submontane, montane and subalpine forests and alpine meadows. The core area and buffer zone are identical with Berchtesgaden National Park, which includes the famous Lake Königssee. Major habitats and land-cover types include submontane, montane and subalpine forests with mountain pine (Pinus mugo), larch (Larix decidua), sycamore (Acer pseudoplatanus) and Norway spruce (Picea abies). Alpine limestone grasslands occur alongside distinct plant communities in rock crevices and on rocky debris. Oligotrophic lakes and running waters are present. Grassland farming is widespread, and forestry systems use spruce, larch, beech and fir. The area supports many fauna and flora species of European relevance, with some interlinking of populations. The 2010 site extension added further important species, including corncrake (Crex crex), Eurasian curlew (Numenius arquata), scarce fritillary (Euphydyras maturna) and southern damselfly (Coenagrion mercuriale). The Bavarian Alps are home to around 45–50 breeding pairs of golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Berchtesgadener Land

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve covers Germany’s largest pond region. It extends approximately from Kamenz in the west to the Neisse River in the east. The area is characterised by striking habitat diversity within a small area, with ponds lying alongside sandy dunes. Its position at the transition from Atlantic to continental climate also helps explain the rich species diversity.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Oberlausitzer Heide- und Teichlandschaft Biosphere Reserve has been shaped by human use for more than three millennia since the Bronze Age. Alongside original habitats, this has created cultural ecosystems and increased species and habitat diversity. The created pond-and-watercourse system is an outstanding landscape feature. The core area largely comprises the few near-natural habitats that remain, such as bogs, carr woodlands and dune pine forests, together with adjacent forests and heathlands. The biosphere reserve’s post-mining landscape is unique in Germany: due to the lack of post-mining remediation here, soil formation and natural succession can take place unhindered. In accordance with the Biosphere Reserve Ordinance, the core area is a strict nature reserve and its protection regime precludes any human activity. The buffer zone contains most of the pond ecosystems which, in their cohesion, complexity and species richness, are also unique among German biosphere reserves. This zone also includes near-natural and largely near-natural woodlands, heaths and meadows. Tailor-made management and maintenance regimes prioritise species and biotope conservation objectives and aim to preserve and increase existing species diversity. The buffer zone, like the core area, is designated as a nature conservation area, Naturschutzgebiet–NSG, and is protected by law from any deterioration in its ecological status. Improved, conservation-oriented management methods and the marketing of near-natural produce are intended to create alternative income sources for land users. The biosphere reserve provides suitable habitat for many rare and protected species from a wide range of climatic regions. To date, more than 5,200 species of flora and fauna have been identified … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Oberlausitzer Heide- und Teichlandschaft

records.introduction_en: The transregional Flusslandschaft Elbe is Germany’s largest inland biosphere reserve. The five federal states, or Länder, each hosts a different share of the biosphere: Saxony-Anhalt, Brandenburg, Lower Saxony, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Schleswig-Holstein. The reserve is representative of the glacial valleys of the northern German older moraine landscape. This centuries-old cultural landscape contains numerous, spatially connected river and alluvial features and corresponding near-natural habitats. The integrated protection of a major river alluvial system across five Länder within a single biosphere reserve is unique in Germany.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The region’s topography is shaped by the Elbe River and its tributaries. The other main landscape unit is the intermittently flooded alluvial plain. In the lowlands of Lower Saxony, near the north-western border of the reserve, the alluvial plain grades into tide-influenced marshlands. Away from the surviving alluvial plain are lowlands with peatlands, extensive areas of talsand and dune systems. Higher-lying areas consist of glacially formed ground moraines and moraine ridges. The biosphere reserve lies in the central European temperate climate region and, under the Köppen–Geiger system, is classified as a temperate oceanic climate. Geologically, the valley bottom of the Elbe glacial valley was formed during the last northern inland glaciation and consists primarily of sandy glaciofluvial deposits. Scouring by the Elbe in the post-glacial period produced lower river terraces. These terraces structure the glacial-valley lowlands and can reach widths of more than 50 km. At the edge of the valley, sand drift and deposition over several thousand years have formed expansive inland dune systems. The lower river terraces delimiting the floodplain contain groundwater gley soils, locally showing fen peat formation, as well as brown earths and podzols that developed above the groundwater level. Owing to the transition from oceanic to continental climate and the diversity of sites, the biosphere reserve hosts more than 1,300 plant species, of which approximately 400 are listed in the IUCN Red List of endangered ferns and flowering plants. The most characteristic plants occur in aquatic habitats, reflecting the area’s variety of waters. The rich mosaic of habitats also supports unusually large populations of fauna with continental, Atlantic, boreo-alpine and boreal d … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Flusslandschaft Elbe

records.introduction_en: The Thuringian Forest is one of the longest-running biosphere reserves in Germany. When designated in 1979, it was called Vessertal Biosphere Reserve and covered 1,384 ha. It was later expanded to over 225,000 ha. It represents a typical section of the central European Mittelgebirge ridge in the Thuringian Forest, one of the country’s largest contiguous forest areas. Because of its forest wealth and traditional land use, the area is of great importance for the preservation of biological diversity, as demonstrated by the occurrence of 193 species of ferns, flowering plants, fungi and lichens, as well as 245 animal species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve forms part of the deciduous-forest biome within the Central European forest province of the Palaearctic regnum. Forest ecosystems dominate, totalling 28,204.8 ha, or 83.7 per cent. Despite the prevalence of conifer-dominated stands, there is considerable diversity in forest communities and in the intensity of human use. As one of Germany’s 30 biodiversity hotspots (Federal Biodiversity Programme), it is home to various endemic species, such as the mountain lead beetle (Oreina alpestris polymorpha) and the red alga (Lemanea rubra).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Thuringian Forest

records.introduction_en: The West Estonian Archipelago Biosphere Reserve is situated in the eastern Baltic Sea and comprises the islands of Saaremaa, Hiiumaa, Vormsi and Muhu, as well as numerous islets and marine areas. Located in the transition zone between temperate coniferous and broad-leaved forests, terrestrial habitats include pine forests, mixed spruce and deciduous forests, juniper and coastal meadows, swamps and peat bogs. Alvar forests (spruce, pine or birch on limestone plains with thin soils) are of particular interest.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The West Estonian archipelago lies in the southern part of the boreal forest zone of the Northern Hemisphere, where the south-taiga subzone transitions into a spruce–hardwood subzone. Phytogeographically, Estonia belongs to the Euro-Siberian region of the Holarctic realm. The islands primarily represent ecosystems formed on coastal features from different developmental phases of the Baltic Sea over the last ten thousand years. The distinctive features and diversity of nature on the West Estonian islands are shaped by their geographical position, the young age of the area, lime-rich soils and centuries of human activity. A long, intricate coastline includes both low and dune beaches, and low bays with small islets and holms. Millennia of land use have influenced the structure of forests, meadows, arable land and pastures, producing a mosaic landscape and diverse nature. Terrestrial habitats include pine forests, mixed spruce and deciduous woodlands, juniper and coastal meadows, swamps and peat bogs. Alvar forests (spruce, pine or birch on thin-soiled limestone plains are especially notable. Parts of the area are designated as wetlands of international importance under the Ramsar Convention. Efforts have been made to re-establish viable populations of the critically endangered European mink (Mustela lutreola) on Saaremaa and Hiiumaa.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: West Estonian Archipelago

records.introduction_en: The Yasuní Biosphere Reserve is located in the Amazon region, in Napo Province in northern Ecuador. The dominant ecosystem is humid tropical rainforest, part of the upper Amazon basin. The Yasuní Biosphere Reserve is recognised as one of the most biodiverse areas per square metre on the planet.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: In terms of plant formations, the most diverse dicot family is Fabaceae, with species such as balsam (Myroxylon balsamun), mahogany (Platymiscium stipulare) and guabas (Inga), among others. Next is the family Annonaceae, with canopy and sub-canopy species in the genera Crematosperma, Guatteria, Porcelia and Rollinia. Other recorded genera include Brosimum, Ficus and Perebea in the Moraceae, as well as Pourouma and Cecropia in the Cecropiaceae. The most abundant and diverse monocots are anthuriums, palms, orchids and ferns. Primary forests host a wide variety of epiphytes, climbers, lianas, mosses, lichens and fungi that constitute a gene bank of potential value, though they remain little known. The family Araceae is among the most important and diverse, with several genera such as Anthurium, Chlorospatha, Dieffenbachia and Urospatha. The mammalian fauna is represented by 204 species (11 orders and 31 families). 80 per cent of species are nocturnal. Only the large mammals, with extensive home ranges, use the forest as a whole. Bats are the most abundant and show a great variety of habits, from primitive insectivores such as Myotis to blood-feeding species such as Desmodus rotundus. There are only three endemic species: a gnome fruit-eating bat (Dermanura gnoma) and two arboreal spiny rats (Proechimys quadruplicatus and Proechimys simonsi). Recorded species include rodents, such as agoutis, pacas and mice, and carnivores such as felids, foxes and coatis. Species present include the agouti (Dasyprocta fuliginosa), white-lipped peccary (Tayassu pecari), collared peccary (Pecari tajacu), deer (Mazama), paca (Cuniculus paca), capybara (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris), Amazonian tapir (Tapirus terrestris), nine-banded armadillo (Dasypus novemcinctus), puma (Puma conco … [truncated]
records.name: Yasuni

records.introduction_en: Omayed Biosphere Reserve represents a variety of habitats, biological communities, land-use patterns and human settlements in Egypt’s Mediterranean coastal desert. It serves as a site that reflects the region’s ecological diversity alongside human activities and land management.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: There are five main habitat types in the reserve: coastal dunes, inland ridges, saline depressions, non-saline depressions and an inland plateau. The area lies within a warm desert and semi-desert ecosystem. Coastal calcareous dunes feature Ammophila arenaria, Euphorbia paralias and Pancratium maritimum. Inland ridges with shallow skeletal soils are characterised by communities of Thymellaea and Gymnocarpus decadrum, or by associations of Plantago albicans and Asphodelus microcarpa. Saline marshy depressions are dominated by Salicornia fruticosa, Cressa cretica and Atriplex halimus. Non-saline depressions and the inland plateau include species such as Artemisia monosperma and Hammada elegans in calcareous soils. Shallow, degraded soils support Anabasis articulata and Hammada scorpia. Saline soils host Suaeda pruinosa and Salsola tetrandra. Land uses include pasture, fig plantations and agroecosystems. Environmental constraints include land degradation, habitat fragmentation, overgrazing, loss of biodiversity, soil salinisation and over-exploitation of mineral and groundwater resources. The area is undergoing a marked transformation from natural rangelands to agricultural land, particularly following the extension of an irrigation canal and expanded networks from the Nile. The availability of irrigation water has reshaped local livelihoods and created land-tenure conflicts due to rising land prices.
records.name: Omayed

records.introduction_en: Non-sedentary inhabitants use the biosphere reserve’s natural resources for livestock transhumance, charcoal production, the collection of medicinal plants, quarrying and small-scale cultivation.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: In the downstream wadi system, vegetation is frequently flooded, with extensive shrub groves of Tamarix, Heliotropium supinum and Glinus lotoides. Above the flood zone, vegetation is dominated by xerophilic species such as Salsola baryosma and Acacia ehrenbergiana. In the upstream wadi system, the vegetation is dominated by Balanites aegyptiaca, Salvadora persica, Acacia raddiana and A. tortilis. Agroecosystems include vegetables, cereals and fodder crops.
records.name: Wadi Allaqi

records.introduction_en: Situated on Guadeloupe Island in the Caribbean Sea, this biosphere reserve comprises two geographically separate sites. Basse-Terre consists of tropical forest in the west of the island, overlooked by the active volcano La Soufrière (1,467 m). The forest, uninhabited today, is home to more than 300 species of trees and shrubs despite centuries of human impact that decimated numerous species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Grand Cul-de-Sac Marin, a vast 15,000 ha bay between Basse-Terre and Grande-Terre, includes coral reefs, mudflats, seagrass beds and mangrove forests, as well as freshwater swamp forests and marshes. In the lagoon, seafloor meadows provide habitat for turtles and teem with fish. Giant sponges, soft corals, urchins and fish are widespread. The mangroves host many sedentary and migratory birds, including pelicans, terns, moorhens, ducks, herons and kingfishers. Parts of the biosphere reserve also form a Ramsar site, designated in 1993.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Archipel de la Guadeloupe

records.introduction_en: The Dordogne River and its basin form one of the six major watersheds of the Adour–Garonne, covering about 24,000 km². The Dordogne is an emblematic river draining central France and providing important ecosystem services to the region.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Dordogne rises on the flanks of Puy de Sancy (1,658 m) near Mont-Dore, at the confluence of the Dore and the Dogne. Its catchment measures roughly 280 km at its longest and 150 km at its widest. The river crosses a variety of landscapes and functions, from mountains and hydropower reaches to broad meanders, before meeting the Garonne at the Bec d’Ambès, north of Bordeaux, to form the Gironde estuary, the largest in Europe. Given its size, the basin spans two main biogeographical regions with a transitional zone between them. The continental region to the east is characterised by temperate coniferous forests; the Atlantic region to the west (Aquitaine) by temperate deciduous forests. Between them lies a transition influenced by both climates and by the shift from mountainous headwaters to the alluvial lowlands at the river mouth, supporting a mix of temperate coniferous and deciduous forests as well as Mediterranean woodlands and scrub. The Dordogne basin hosts rich biodiversity of national and European significance. It supports 39 fish species and is especially valuable as the last refuge for all major diadromous fishes of western Europe.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Bassin de la Dordogne

records.introduction_en: Located in Île-de-France, about 70 km south-east of Paris, this biosphere reserve comprises temperate deciduous forest, mainly oak, Scots pine and beech, together with heathlands, open rock areas and several wetlands. The forest lies on an ancient marine sandbank, locally overlain by sandstone, which itself rests on Brie limestone and green marl where springs arise. Soil diversity is high, helping to explain the exceptional botanical richness: more than 5,800 plant species have been recorded. The reserve contains two habitats of community interest listed under the EU Habitats Directive: Northern Atlantic wet heaths with Erica tetralix, and forests of slopes, screes and ravines (Polystico-Corylenion).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve’s 20 core areas include Northern Atlantic wet heaths with Erica tetralix and forests of slopes, screes and ravines (Polystico-Corylenion). The core and buffer zones correspond to the administrative unit of the Forêt de Fontainebleau, managed by the Office national des forêts. The transition area lies principally within the Parc naturel régional du Gâtinais français and also includes surrounding communes, among them the town of Fontainebleau.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Fontainebleau et du Gâtinais

records.introduction_en: Mont Ventoux, at 1,909 metres above sea level, lies between the Alpine massif to the north and the Mediterranean massifs to the south. Its varied relief creates a mosaic of microclimates and habitats. Owing to its intermediate position and slope orientation, the mountain hosts exceptional floristic and faunal richness. The summit is notably rich in flora, with about sixty rare species. The surrounding area supports a wide variety of trees, notably beech and juniper
records.ecological_characteristics_en: In the heart of calcareous Provence, at the crossroads of the Alps, the Massif Central and the Rhône Valley, the Mont Ventoux Biosphere Reserve offers a natural and cultural synopsis from the Alps to the Mediterranean. This isolated mountain is a centre of passage and contact, with its peak showing a curious phenomenon of biological telescoping. Natural habitats and species of Mediterranean and Alpine origin occur side by side in a distinctive way. This rich biodiversity poses important challenges for nature conservation. Over 1,200 plant species have been identified, some endemic to Ventoux, including Acis fabrei and Silene petrarchae. More than 1,400 butterfly species are recorded, around 30 per cent of those found in France. Over 120 nesting bird species occur, including the golden eagle, peregrine falcon, Sardinian warbler and boreal (Tengmalm’s) owl. Following reintroduction and population reinforcement, large fauna such as chamois, red deer, mouflon and roe deer are also present.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mont Ventoux

records.introduction_en: Located along the French–German border, the Vosges du Nord and the Pfälzerwald share three defining natural features: water, sandstone and forests. Sandstone outcrops characterise the broad forest belt, where beech, oak and pine are managed. Springs, streams and lakes are found throughout the humid valleys.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Parc naturel régional des Vosges du Nord in France was designated a biosphere reserve in 1988, and Germany’s Pfälzerwald Nature Park in 1992. The two parks then prepared the creation of a transboundary biosphere reserve, achieved in 1998. The objective is to develop methods for the sustainable management of natural resources and to establish a renewed relationship between people and the environment, advanced through research and education with the participation of local communities. The two units cooperate to establish long-term monitoring of water and air, create strictly protected forest reserves, and maintain the lynx (Lynx lynx) population. The presence of lynx, peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus) and bog arum (Calla palustris) receives significant attention from a nature conservation perspective.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Vosges du Nord

records.introduction_en: Kafue Flats is a vast floodplain set midway along the Kafue River in south-central Zambia. The landscape is generally flat, with floodplain and swamp zones that are inundated annually as the river overflows its banks in the rainy season. Lochinvar and Blue Lagoon National Parks form the core protected areas, with the Kafue Flats Game Management Area around them as a buffer. Recognised as a Ramsar Wetland of International Importance, the site is noted for waterbirds and for the emblematic Kafue lechwe, endemic to the Kafue Flats. The biosphere reserve aims to conserve biodiversity and natural resources, promote research and education on ecosystem conservation, and recognise cultural practices and peaceful coexistence between different groups of people and between people and wildlife.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Kafue Flats lie within the Afrotropical realm and a wetland biome. Low-lying terrain between roughly 950 and 1,000 metres above sea level, created by past faulting into a shallow basin, is reshaped each year by the rise and fall of the Kafue River. During the rains, the river floods, filling marshes and shallow lagoons, then retreats to leave rich pasture and feeding grounds. The landscape is a mosaic of open floodplain grasslands, reedbeds and papyrus, seasonally wet termitaria grasslands, and slightly higher woodlands. Floodplain grasslands support deep-water grasses such as wild rice, hippo grass and burgu millet, with reedbeds and papyrus in swampier zones.
