Slightly higher ground carries Kalahari, mopane and munga woodlands with characteristic trees adapted to drier conditions. The Flats are an Important Bird Area and designated Ramsar wetland. They support large numbers of resident and migratory waterbirds. Notable birdlife includes the wattled crane (Grus carunculatus), grey crowned crane (Balearica regulorum), slaty egret (Egretta vinaceigula), lappet-faced vulture (Torgos tracheliotos) and Chaplin’s barbet (Lybius chaplini). The Kafue Flats are the only home of the endemic Kafue lechwe (Kobus leche kafuensis), a wetland antelope that follows the receding waters to graze new growth. Other mammals include plains zebra, African buffalo, reedbuck, sitatunga, hippopotamus and greater kudu.
records.name: Kafue flats

records.introduction_en: Chimanimani Biosphere Reserve lies in the Eastern Highlands on the Zimbabwe–Mozambique border. Steep mountain relief supports a range of ecosystems from montane moist forests and grasslands to drier lowland systems. Set within the Eastern Afromontane biodiversity hotspot, Chimanimani hosts high levels of endemism and is one of the few places in Zimbabwe where small remnant patches of low- and mid-altitude moist forest persist alongside high-elevation habitats. The reserve’s principal objectives include conserving ecosystems and species, strengthening the district’s resilience to climatic shocks and stresses, and promoting sustainable socio-economic development.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Chimanimani Mountains support a steep environmental gradient, with altitude ranging from around 300 m in the Rusitu River valley to over 2,400 m on Mt Binga, the range’s highest peak. This relief drives marked climatic contrasts with hotter, drier lowlands and cooler, moister highlands, underpinning six key biodiversity areas rich in endemic plants. Vegetation spans three ecoregions across distinct biomes: tropical moist forests, savanna woodlands, and montane grasslands and shrublands. Montane thickets and grasslands perform important root-binding functions that are crucial to both soil and water conservation.Floral diversity is high, with endemics including the Chimanimani Mountains violet, and medicinal plant species harvested by local communities, such as the pepper-bark tree (Warburgia salutaris) and Aloe chimanimaniensis. The range also provides vital habitats for birdlife, including the bearded vulture, Cape eagle-owl and purple-crested turaco. Long-term research and monitoring are undertaken in the reserve with regional universities and national institutions, in partnership with community members. Key monitoring activities track vegetation condition and deforestation, catchment health, surface and groundwater, and the status of key wildlife groups, supporting biodiversity conservation, climate adaptation and watershed management.
records.name: Chimanimani

records.introduction_en: The Kafa Biosphere Reserve is located in the Kafa Zone of Ethiopia, approximately 460 km south-west of Addis Ababa. The Bonga National Forest Priority Area (NFPA) partly forms the southern boundary of the biosphere reserve, while the eastern boundary follows Adiyo Woreda. The Gojeb River and the Gewata–Yeba (Boginda) NFPA form the northern boundary. Kafa is the birthplace of wild Arabica coffee and contains close to 5,000 wild varieties of the plant in this biodiversity hotspot.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: From a biodiversity perspective, the biosphere reserve supports a wealth of plant, animal and invertebrate species. It also contributes to the conservation of avifaunal diversity, providing habitat for numerous bird species. The Alemgono Wetland System and surrounding area are particularly important breeding habitats for wattled crane (Grus carunculatus), black-crowned crane (Balearica pavonina), Abyssinian longclaw (Macronyx flavicollis) and Rouget’s rail (Rougetius rougetii). Saylem Woreda forms the northern part of the biosphere reserve, and the western boundary constitutes the Gesha NFPA. The Kafa Zone contains more than 50 per cent of Ethiopia’s remaining montane forests and is the centre of origin and genetic diversity of wild Coffea arabica.
records.name: Kafa

records.introduction_en: The Lake Tana Biosphere Reserve is located in the Amhara National Regional State, approximately 563 km north-west of Addis Ababa in north-western Ethiopia. The biosphere reserve comprises Lake Tana, the country’s largest lake and the main source of the Blue Nile, which provides important ecosystem services. The area is a biodiversity hotspot, internationally known as an Important Bird Area, and is of global importance for agricultural genetic diversity. It is characterised by a high heterogeneity of land uses and natural ecosystems.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Lake Tana is Ethiopia’s largest freshwater body, accounting for 50 per cent of the country’s inland waters, and is the source of the Abbay (Blue Nile) River. The biosphere reserve is an important fish resource and is home to up to 67 fish species, about 70 per cent of which are endemic. The Barbus species of Lake Tana constitute the only remaining intact assemblage of large cyprinid fish in the world. Numerous wetlands fringe the lake; some are among the largest and most ecologically important in Ethiopia and the Horn of Africa and form part of the Central Ethiopian Wetland Complex. Dominated by papyrus and Typha stands, these wetlands provide breeding, nesting and feeding grounds for large bird populations and supply animal fodder, domestic water, building material, fuel and food for local communities. The biosphere reserve is part of the Eastern Afromontane Biodiversity Hotspot and comprises four terrestrial and three freshwater Key Biodiversity Areas. More than 217 bird species have been recorded. High abundances qualify areas around the lake as a Ramsar site. Many Palaearctic migrant waterbirds depend on the lake for feeding and resting, including common crane (Grus grus), black-tailed godwit (Limosa limosa) and ruff (Calidris pugnax). Few patches of original forest and montane ecosystems remain, with high plant endemism of global importance. Indigenous trees include Sesa (Albizia gummifera), Birbira (Millettia ferruginea) and Wanza (Cordia africana). The region is a gene centre for indigenous crops such as noug (Guizotia abyssinica) and teff (Eragrostis tef). Wild coffee (Coffea arabica) occurs naturally, especially on the Zegie Peninsula. Four major wetland ecosystem types have been identified: riverine freshwater wetlands, lacustrine freshwater wetl … [truncated]
records.name: Lake Tana

records.country_title_en: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
records.introduction_en: Located in the Irish Sea, the Isle of Man has a coastline featuring cliffs, stacks, islets and long beaches, while the hills hold important peat reserves and are deeply cut by wooded glens in the east. Grasslands, pools and wetlands cover the coastal plain to the north of the island. The marine environment is rich in biodiversity and harbours large populations of European eel, Atlantic cod and basking sharks, among others. The surrounding sea is harvested for shellfish. In the countryside, farming centres on sheep and cattle livestock and includes arable areas. The island has been a popular tourist destination since the late nineteenth century and has seen notable development in services and manufacturing over recent decades.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Isle of Man lies in the centre of the Irish Sea and includes a varied coastline of cliffs, stacks, central hills, islets and long beaches. The hills hold important peat reserves and are deeply cut by wooded glens in the east. The coastal plain in the north contains pockets of unimproved grassland, pools and wetlands, including the Ballaugh Curragh Ramsar site. The biosphere reserve extends into the Irish Sea and encompasses all of the Isle of Man’s territorial waters. The seabed supports rich and varied biodiversity, including horse mussel and Sabellaria reefs, and maerl and seagrass beds, many of which are protected within the Ramsey Bay Marine Nature Reserve. The island has a small number of terrestrial mammals, including eight species of bats (Microchiroptera), stoats (Mustela erminea), feral polecat ferrets (Mustela lutreola, Mustela putorius), introduced or reintroduced brown and mountain hares (Lepus europaeus and Lepus timidus) and hedgehogs (Erinaceus europaeus). Native amphibians are believed to be limited to one species, the common frog (Rana temporaria). Terrestrial reptiles are represented by the common lizard (Lacerta vivipara). Marine mammals regularly occurring around the Isle of Man include Risso’s dolphins (Grampus griseus), the common dolphin (Delphinus delphis) and the bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus), basking shark (Cetorhinus maximus) and minke whales (Balaenoptera acutorostrata), with other whale species visible on rare occasions.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Isle of Man
records.country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

records.introduction_en: Situated in the Province of Turku and Pori in south-western Finland, this biosphere reserve comprises terrestrial and marine habitats, including coniferous forests, wood meadows, heaths, rocky meadows, rocky or sandy islets, arable land, seashores and open sea. It represents a coastal environment of small islands in the Baltic Sea. Island societies are small in scale, and people who have lived there for generations maintain close contact with the sea and nature. Traditional livelihoods such as fishing and agriculture are becoming less profitable, and the population has declined markedly since the beginning of the last century.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Special habitats include old-growth forest, cultural landscapes, moors, herb-rich forests and marine seagrass meadows, which have a patchy distribution. The mosaic archipelago consists of 6,500 islands larger than 0.5 ha and is unique worldwide. Post-glacial land uplift is a key factor shaping the archipelago’s topography and scenery; the current rate is four to five millimetres per year. The bedrock in the Archipelago Sea area is a remnant of the ancient Svecofennides mountain chain and forms a peneplain, consisting mainly of granite, gneiss and schist, with small, local limestone occurrences.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Archipelago Sea Area

records.introduction_en: And Atoll lies in the Federated States of Micronesia, within the Caroline Islands tropical moist forests ecoregion. The oceanic islands and surrounding reefs of this region form one of the world’s most biologically diverse seascapes. And Atoll comprises a ring of low, narrow, forested islets around an enclosed lagoon, with steep outer reef slopes and a navigable southern reef pass that drains the lagoon on the falling tide. And Atoll is Pohnpei’s most biologically diverse and least disturbed atoll, ranked the island’s number one Marine Area of Biological Significance and one of 24 priority action areas in the ecoregional plan under the National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan. The reserve seeks to model sustainability by harmonising local economic activity with the atoll’s slower-changing ecology, offering an example for Micronesia and the Pacific, and enabling enduring livelihoods without loss of ecological diversity, complexity or function.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: And Atoll is biologically and topographically representative of most atolls in the Federated States of Micronesia. It encloses a lagoon reaching about 40 m in depth, and supports rich biodiversity. Ecosystems include the atoll forest–beach strand complex along sandy and coralline shorelines, with shrubs, herbaceous and woody species, and an extensive nearshore marine system comprising intertidal areas, sandy and coralline lagoons, channels and reefs. The lagoon contains seagrass beds and mangrove forests on islets. Mangroves help protect the islets and shorelines from storm activity, and collect sediments and pollutants that would otherwise wash into the marine environment. Several emblematic sites underscore the atoll’s conservation value. Wolouna islet remains one of the region’s few relatively intact seabird rookeries, hosting approximately 600 pairs of black noddies (Anous minutus). The atoll also provides important nesting grounds for marine turtles. The main channel into the lagoon is known as a spawning and aggregation site for three reef groupers: squaretail coralgrouper (Plectropomus areolatus), brown-marbled grouper (Epinephelus fuscoguttatus) and camouflage grouper (Epinephelus polyphekadion). It is also one of the few places in the Pohnpei area with notable aggregations of grey reef shark (Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos) and barracuda (Sphyraena forsteri). Surrounding reefs hold the only healthy populations of giant clams in Pohnpei, notably bear paw clam (Hippopus hippopus) and small giant clam (Tridacna maxima).
records.name: And Atoll

records.introduction_en: Uninterrupted human presence since the Neolithic Age has left Asterousia, in the southern part of Crete, with a rich archaeological heritage. Scattered settlements sit within a mountainous landscape of natural and semi-natural habitats, alongside areas of high ecological value hosting over half of the island’s animal and plant species. Asterousia Mountain Range is the southernmost mountainous area of Europe.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Asterousia Mountain Range Biosphere Reserve is located on Crete, the largest of the Greek islands. The island runs 260 kilometres in length and features four large mountain ranges. The biosphere reserve lies in the southernmost area of the island and includes the highest peak, Kofinas, which rises to 1,231 metres. Over these peaks, rare and iconic avifauna such as the Bearded Vulture, Griffon Vulture, Golden Eagle and Bonelli’s Eagle can be seen. Fifty per cent of all animal and plant species recorded on Crete are found within this biosphere reserve, making it an important area for biodiversity in the Mediterranean.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Asterousia Mountain Range

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is situated on the eastern part of mainland Greece and covers the eastern limestone foothills and the summit of Mount Olympus, rising to 2,914 metres above sea level. The landscape comprises maquis and Mediterranean sclerophyll shrublands, beech and oak woodlands, pine (Pinus nigra) forests, montane grasslands and alpine areas. The biosphere reserve is managed as a national park, and there are no settlements within the area. As in much of the Mediterranean, it was formerly subject to heavy grazing and timber extraction. Today, local communities use the buffer zone for grazing, hunting, gathering herbs and wood extraction. Tourism is the main economic activity. Many visitors, both national and foreign, come to this centre of Greek mythology, where Homer wrote of the twelve Greek gods and their palaces on Mount Olympus.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The region of the park is mountainous, with Mount Olympus, the highest mountain in Greece, standing out from the surrounding area. In the north and east, alluvial plains ascend gradually to around 300 metres, and from there the foothills rise steeply. Deep valleys, especially in the east and north, dissect the massif. The reserve consists of coniferous woodlands and forests between 500 and 1,700 metres. The main type of vegetation is black pine (Pinus nigra). Meadows and various montane grasslands occur where forest has been removed. Mediterranean maquis covers the foothills of Mount Olympus. A total of 104 species of birds, including seven species of woodpecker, and 32 species of mammals have been recorded across the reserve’s ecosystems. Several animal species are endangered or threatened with extinction, including Geoffroy’s bat (Myotis emarginatus), the chamois (Rupicapra rupicapra), the bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus) and the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mount Olympus

records.introduction_en: The Maya Biosphere Reserve in the Petén region of northern Guatemala, together with the Maya Forest of Belize and Mexico, represents one of the largest areas of tropical forest north of the Amazon and the northernmost tropical forest in the Western Hemisphere. It is also the site of three contiguous UNESCO biosphere reserves: the Maya Biosphere Reserve in Guatemala, and the Calakmul and Montes Azules Biosphere Reserves in southern Mexico. The reserve has seven core areas, comprising four national parks and three wildlife reserves with lowland and mid-elevation forests, inundated savannas, small stands of pine, caves and rocky habitats, lakes and lagoons, rivers, wetlands and remnant mangrove forests. The multiple-use zone consists of tropical forest managed for the sustainable harvest of xate palms, chicle gum, allspice and timber.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Although other sites in Guatemala may have greater biodiversity per unit area, the Maya Biosphere Reserve is a place of major importance for species conservation in the country. Studies conducted by various scientists have placed it among Guatemala’s most significant areas for biological diversity; estimates suggest up to 2,800 species of vascular plants, around 34 per cent of the national total. Timber species of high commercial value include mahogany (Swietenia macrophylla), cedar (Cedrela odorata), santa maría (Calophyllum brasiliense), pucté (Bucida buceras), danto (Vatairea lundellii), malerio (Aspidosperma stegomeris), manchiche (Lonchocarpus castilloi) and ronrón (Astronium graveolens). Non-timber species include allspice (Pimenta dioica). The reserve is also noted for faunal richness. Recorded taxa include seven scorpion species, five tarantula species, 40 species of coprophagous beetles, 112 ant species and 535 butterfly species. The reserve also has at least 41 species of fish, 33 amphibians, 106 reptiles, 513 birds and 122 mammals. Amphibians represent about 20 per cent of Guatemala’s total, reptiles 41 per cent, birds 71 per cent and mammals 64 per cent. Of the mammals, at least 60 species are bats, representing 55 per cent of the country’s recorded bat fauna.
records.name: Maya

records.introduction_en: Aggtelek National Park lies in the Gömör–Torna Karst region, an area rich in unique natural and cultural assets. It is the first Hungarian national park dedicated to the protection of abiotic values, surface landforms and caves. The subterranean natural treasures, namely the caves of the Aggtelek Karst and the Slovak Karst, were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1995. One of the most celebrated treasures is Baradla Cave, the largest and most magnificent cave in Hungary. Excavations in and around the cave have shown that it has sheltered people for more than 7,000 years.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: About three million years ago, the caves of the karst began to evolve. More than 1,200 caves are known in the karst today. The underground world is largely untouched, with many different rock and mineral formations. About 500 taxa of cave-dwelling animals live permanently or temporarily in the caves, several occurring only in the Aggtelek Karst. Of the 39 bat species in Europe, 28 can be found in the karst, though not all are cave-dwelling. The area is characterised by outstanding species richness, with about 8,000 animal species recorded. Owing to its geological setting, both species typical of high mountains, such as the European lynx (Lynx lynx), the Eurasian pygmy owl (Glaucidium passerinum) and Bielzia coerulans, and species preferring dry, warm habitats, such as the matriarchal katydid (Saga pedo) and the rock bunting (Emberiza cia), can be seen. The diversity of habitats has also produced an extremely rich butterfly fauna.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Aggtelek

records.introduction_en: Like most other Hungarian biosphere reserves, Lake Fertő Biosphere Reserve is a typical first-generation site designated mainly for conservation. Its designation predated the establishment of Lake Fertő National Park, later extended to form the Fertő–Hanság National Park covering the whole Fertő–Hanság wetland basin, and it was a major driver of nature conservation along the Iron Curtain. The area behind the Iron Curtain was a near-abandoned no-man’s-land between Hungary and Austria. It remained largely intact for nearly forty years and was entered only by border guards and a few licensed civilians for reed management, limited fishing and hunting, and, exceptionally, birdwatching or other research. Outstanding natural values, especially nesting and migratory bird fauna, developed in the undisturbed, extensive reed habitats. After the political changes of 1990 and the end of the Iron Curtain, a new local nature conservation body was established to oversee the site: the Lake Fertő National Park.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area is a saline lake with extensive reedbeds, saline meadow and xerophilous oak forest associations occur in its surroundings. Lake Fertő is the second largest lake in Hungary and the fifth in Europe. Its area is 309 km², of which 75 km² lies in Hungary. The lake sits in a depression of the Kisalföld region that connects to the deeper Hanság basin to the east. The original surface of its basin was created by sediments of an ancient, naturally desalinating lake during the late Pliocene, later shaped by wind, with the ancient Danube and Lajta rivers depositing layers of gravel and clay. Most of the core zone lies in the central parts of the reed belt and the very sensitive alkaline swards. A key aim in designating the core zone was to preserve the high diversity of several biotope types, including the westernmost occurrences of characteristic alkaline steppe-like associations in the Carpathian Basin, alongside plant and animal species representing the flora and fauna of the Alps. The core zone includes small open-water surfaces within the reedbeds (locally known as “internal lakes”), the untouched central reed areas, the alkaline swards, and the steppe meadow of the Szárhalom Forest with its relict species.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Lake Fertö

records.introduction_en: Located just south-west of the city of Killarney in south-west Ireland, Kerry Biosphere Reserve, formerly Killarney, comprises the mountains and woodlands surrounding Lough Leane and nearby smaller lakes, as well as moorlands, parks and gardens.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Much of the natural woodland has been cleared, but the remaining fragments include the most extensive areas in the country. Owing to differing geology across the biosphere reserve, three main woodland types can be distinguished: woods of sessile oak (Quercus petraea) with holly (Ilex aquifolium) in the understorey on sandstone; a yew (Taxus baccata) wood growing on almost bare limestone; and carr forest dominated by Alnus glutinosa along the north-east shore of Lough Leane and in other poorly drained areas. Present human impacts and uses include conifer afforestations, lake eutrophication and tourism activities. Additional human influences include past introductions of alien species, which have affected the natural ecosystems of Killarney. The most notable of these introduced species are Rhododendron ponticum and sika deer, which overgraze the woodland floor and pose a potential threat to the genetic integrity of the native red deer.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Kerry

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve encompasses a mosaic of ecological systems that represent the Mediterranean Basin’s version of the global ‘evergreen sclerophyllous forests, woodlands and scrub’ ecosystem types.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The region is primarily hilly, with an average altitude of 300 m and a maximum altitude of 400 m above sea level. A cross-section from south-east to north-west reveals a syncline between the Carmel Hills and the Hills of Um El Fakhem. A transect from south-west to north-east reveals an asymmetrical landscape. From the water divide eastwards, the land descends steeply to the Yizrael Valley, and westwards it slopes gently towards the sea. Consequently, the streams flowing east, which drain into the Kishon River, are short with sharp inclines. The streams flowing west, which drain into the Mediterranean Sea, are long with a gentle gradient.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Megiddo

records.introduction_en: The Achanakmar–Amarkantak Biosphere Reserve is the most dramatic and ecologically diverse landscape in the states of Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh, India. It is one of the less developed and least disturbed areas in both states, and it encompasses most of the original natural and cultural features.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Achanakmar–Amarkantak Biosphere Reserve is located at the junction of hill ranges, with topography ranging from high mountains to shallow valleys and plains. Moist deciduous forests constitute 63 per cent of the area. The biosphere reserve is very rich in flora and fauna due to its tropical moist deciduous vegetation, which covers the majority of the area, and tropical dry deciduous vegetation in its southern part. Minimally disturbed landscapes, endemism and genetic variation further enhance its diversity. It has nearly 1,498 plant species belonging to 799 plant genera, including thallophytes, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms. There are three endemic and 282 regionally rare species, and 39 different categories of globally threatened floral species. In animals, there are 327 species belonging to 256 genera of invertebrate and vertebrate fauna, besides many taxonomically undescribed species. The biosphere reserve is home to 67 threatened faunal species, belonging to various categories of global threat as per IUCN 2001 categorisation, such as the four-horned antelope (Tetracerus quadricornis), Indian wild dog (Cuon alpinus), sarus crane (Grus antigone), Asian white-backed vulture (Gyps bengalensis) and sacred grove bush frog (Philautus sanctisilvaticus). The geology of the area is unique and varied, ranging from schists and gneisses with granite intrusions to sandstones, shales, limestone, basaltic lava and bauxite. The soil varies in composition and texture from sandy to loamy clays, generally light brown to brownish, with olive-green clay in some places. Red soil, due to the presence of iron oxide, is porous and fertile. Alluvial soil occurs on the banks of numerous streams in the tract, and black cotton soil in many areas. Togeth … [truncated]
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Achanakmar-Amarkantak

records.introduction_en: Great Nicobar is the southernmost island of the Nicobar Islands archipelago. It covers 103,870 ha of tropical evergreen forest ecosystems. The island hosts rich biodiversity, including around 650 species of angiosperms, ferns, gymnosperms and bryophytes, among others. In terms of fauna, over 1,800 species are recorded, some endemic to the area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve contains a wide spectrum of ecosystems, including tropical wet evergreen forests, mountain ranges and coastal plains. Mount Thullier reaches 642 m. The region is noted for high biodiversity, with about 650 species of angiosperms, ferns, gymnosperms, bryophytes and lichens. Plant diversity includes rare and endemic species such as the tree fern Cyathea albosetacea and the orchid Phalaenopsis speciosa. A total of 14 mammal species, 71 bird species, 26 reptiles, 10 amphibians and 113 fish have been reported. Many endemic and endangered fauna occur here: to date, 11 mammals, 32 birds, seven reptiles and four amphibians are considered endemic. Notable endemic and/or threatened species include the crab-eating macaque, Nicobar tree shrew, dugong, Nicobar megapode, serpent eagle, saltwater crocodile, marine turtles and reticulated python.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Great Nicobar

records.introduction_en: The Gulf of Mannar, endowed with three distinct coastal ecosystems (coral reefs, seagrass beds and mangroves) is considered one of the world’s richest regions from a marine biodiversity perspective. It is known for its unique biological wealth and is a storehouse of marine diversity of global significance. The gulf’s 4,223 species of plants and animals, ranging from primitive to higher forms, make it one of the richest coastal regions in India. Most of the islands have luxuriant mangrove growth on their shorelines and in swampy areas. The sea bottom of the inshore area around the islands is carpeted with seagrass beds, which serve as an ideal feeding ground for the dugong (Dugong dugon), an endangered herbivorous marine mammal. Highly productive fringing and patch coral reefs surround the islands and are often referred to as an underwater tropical rainforest and a treasure house for marine biodiversity, particularly ornamental marine fishes. The occurrence of these specialised ecosystems makes the Gulf of Mannar a unique large marine ecosystem in the Indian subcontinent.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The islands have irregular outlines, with spits and partially enclosed bays, and often higher sandy beach ridges enclosing areas of mudflats and standing water within the bay. They are made up of sand structures with gravel and coral boulders. Seagrass beds serve as nursery and spawning grounds for diverse biota and provide habitat for macroalgae and microalgae as epiphytes. This habitat is the feeding ground for a large endangered marine mammal, the dugong (Dugong dugon), and also sea turtles. This area is also the last refuge of an invertebrate, the unique living fossil Balanoglossus, which links vertebrates and invertebrates. It is also important for crustaceans, molluscs, echinoderms, fishes, turtles and other mammals.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Gulf of Mannar

records.introduction_en: Panna Biosphere Reserve falls within the biogeographic zones of the Deccan Peninsula and the biotic province of the Central Highlands. It comprises effectively protected and minimally disturbed areas. Land uses include forests, agriculture, waterbodies, settlements and wastelands, providing ample scope for research and management. The reserve is habitat to various rare and endangered species. Panna National Park has also been declared the Panna Tiger Reserve. In addition, the entire area of Panna National Park and three parts of the Gangau Sanctuary have been notified as a Critical Tiger Habitat.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Panna Biosphere Reserve encompasses Panna National Park, three sections of the Gangau Sanctuary (sections I, III and IV), and the reserved and protected forests of the North Panna Forest Division. The Panna Tiger Reserve is one of the most important sites in the North Central Highlands for protecting the Bengal tiger (Panthera tigris tigris). Two other cat species occur: the caracal (Caracal caracal) and the jungle cat (Felis chaus). The avifauna is rich, with over 280 species recorded. The Ken River is a notable place to see the Indian paradise flycatcher (Terpsiphone paradisi). The site is characterised by forests, seasonal vegetation, aquatic habitats and marshy vegetation.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Panna

records.introduction_en: Aya, in the eastern part of Japan’s southern Kyushu Island, harbours one of the country’s largest remaining lucidophyllous forests. The forest has high biodiversity and includes many indigenous species. Forest therapy and traditional recycling-based agriculture in Aya Town are an ecotourism draw to the Aya Biosphere Reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Aya Biosphere Reserve consists of a plateau containing high-relief mountains over 600 m, low-relief mountains at 200–400 m, and shirasu (deposits of volcanic ash and sand), as well as a flat alluvial plain around the confluence of the Ayakita and Ayaminami rivers. It lies near the centre of Miyazaki Prefecture in south-eastern Kyushu, where the Kyushu Central Mountains meet the Miyazaki Plain. Lucidophyllous forests within the biosphere reserve consist of many species endemic to Japan. In East Asia these forests are distinctive, lying at the boundary between two floras, one formed mainly by tropical evergreen trees and the other by temperate deciduous trees, a pattern that dates to the Cretaceous Period (about 143–65 million years ago). Forests account for 88 per cent (12,839 ha) of the total area of the biosphere reserve, of which about 16 per cent (2,330 ha) are natural lucidophyllous forests and about 25 per cent (3,675 ha) are secondary lucidophyllous forests. A total of 1,033 botanical species, 145 fungal species, 70 avian species and 19 mammal species have been identified in the biosphere reserve. The area around Aya Town marks the southern limit of habitat for the Japanese serow and golden eagle.
records.name: Aya

records.introduction_en: Although it is only about one hour from Tokyo, Minakami Biosphere Reserve is rich in valuable natural heritage. The site includes the central divide of the island of Honshu, formed by a mountainous backbone reaching 2,000 metres in elevation, including the Tanigawa mountain range. Significant environmental differences between the eastern and western slopes, as well as between the mountainous and lowland areas, create distinct biological and cultural diversity. The main activities are agriculture and tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Gunma Prefecture is located in the centre of Japan. Minakami Biosphere Reserve comprises the entire area of Minakami Town, the northernmost part of Gunma Prefecture. Adjacent areas belong to neighbouring Uonuma City, Minamiuonuma City and Yuzawa Town, all in Niigata Prefecture. The total area is 91,368 ha, over 90 per cent of which is forest. The altitude ranges from about 300 to 2,000 metres above sea level. The Tone River, which has the largest basin area in Japan, originates on Ominakami-yama in the northernmost part of Minakami Town. It supports the lives and livelihoods of 30 million people in the Tokyo metropolitan area. The mountain ridges on the borders of Gunma and Niigata Prefectures form the central divide, where air masses over the Pacific and the Sea of Japan collide. This area experiences some of the heaviest snowfall in the world. In addition to steep rock faces and bare rock, accumulated winter snow forms distinctive landforms such as nivation hollows, floodplains, river terraces and periglacial features. Glacial marks from the Ice Age are also present despite elevations of only about 2,000 metres above sea level, which is relatively low for such features. The unique landforms and geology, together with the distinct climate, foster ecosystems where rare and diverse fauna and flora persist. This includes endemic species such as the alpine plant Hosobahina-usuyukisou.
records.name: Minakami

records.introduction_en: Shiga Highland Biosphere Reserve is in the central part of Honshu, Japan, spanning five municipalities in two prefectures: Yamanouchi Town and Takayama Village in Nagano Prefecture, and Nakanojo Town, Kusatsu Town and Tsumagoi Village in Gunma Prefecture. The core area and buffer zone overlap Joshin’etsukōgen National Park. The volcanic lake of Mt. Shirane is reputed to be the most acidic lake in the world, with a pH of 0.8.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Shiga Highland Biosphere Reserve comprises mountains formed by volcanic activity, and valleys, river terraces and alluvial fans shaped by rivers. Forests cover the surface layers of the mountains and valleys, while habitats, paddy fields, fields and orchards are spread across the river terraces and alluvial fans. Mt. Shirane, in the south-east of the buffer zone, is an active volcano, and vegetation influenced by ongoing volcanic activity occurs around it. Deciduous broad-leaved forests extend below about 1,600–1,700 m above sea level. Areas altered by humans are covered by secondary forests of deciduous broad-leaved trees, planted coniferous forests or bamboo thickets. Paddy fields, fields and orchards are concentrated around river terraces, alluvial fans and hills below 800 m above sea level, where volcanic hot springs emerge in many places. In the rural zone, the typical Japanese satoyama landscape can be seen, comprising human-managed secondary forests and pastoral land. Many mammals inhabit the area, including the Japanese macaque (Macaca fuscata), Japanese dormouse (Glirulus japonicus), Asian black bear (Ursus thibetanus) and stoat (Mustela erminea). Birds include the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos), coal tit (Periparus ater) and olive-backed pipit (Anthus hodgsoni).
records.name: Shiga Highland

records.introduction_en: The Appennino Tosco-Emiliano Biosphere Reserve is located in the Tuscany and Emilia-Romagna regions of north-central Italy. It covers the Tuscan-Emilian Apennine ridge from Passo della Cisa to Passo delle Forbici, which marks the geographical and climatic boundary between continental and Mediterranean Europe. The area contains close to 70 per cent of the total species present in Italy, including 122 species of birds, amphibians, reptiles, mammals and fish, as well as a wide variety of flora comprising at least 260 aquatic and terrestrial plant species. The main economic activity in the reserve is agriculture. Recreational activities and tourism also represent important economic resources for residents, as well as for tourists and second-home owners.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Apennines mountain range forms the backbone of the Italian peninsula. The reserve is located in the Northern Apennines and is typical of this mountain region. It also constitutes a focal point of the continental–Mediterranean climatic boundary which, together with geological heritage and other factors, has given rise to a complex ecological and cultural patchwork that underlies the evolution of the landscape. Floral biodiversity is rich and significant, with at least 260 aquatic and terrestrial plant species of community and regional conservation interest. These include several endemic species such as Primula apennina, Vicia crusnae, Saxifraga etrusca and Aquilegia alpina. Almost 70 per cent of the species found throughout Italy, over 2,000 in total, inhabit the reserve. These include 122 bird species, invertebrates, reptiles, fish, mammals and amphibians, such as the spectacled salamander (Salamandrina terdigitata) and crested newt (Triturus cristatus). Species of particular conservation interest include the wolf (Canis lupus), golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos) and hermit beetle (Osmoderma eremita).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Appennino Tosco-Emiliano

records.introduction_en: Located in the coastal belt of southern Latium, the state-owned forest of Circeo lies within Circeo National Park, a larger protected area that safeguards high-diversity environments of ecological, hydrogeological and faunal interest. It comprises a lowland forest on a series of continental dunes, three coastal lakes, marshy areas and the calcareous massif of Mount Circeo, at 541 metres above sea level, as well as agricultural fields and pastures. The Circeo Biosphere Reserve partly overlaps Circeo National Park and includes a Ramsar site. The area is a popular destination for tourists due to its proximity to Rome, which results in pressure on the ecosystem, especially the coastal dunes. Another challenge for biosphere reserve management is eutrophication and water pollution of coastal lakes caused by urban sewage and agricultural activities. The national park provides environmental education activities, and an ecomuseum presents key information for visitors.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is almost uninhabited and is characterised by dense forest cover, with deciduous oak forest featuring Mediterranean species. It represents the only example of lowland forest dominated by deciduous oaks in Italy. It includes a coastal landscape with wide lowland areas that were formerly characterised by the Pontine wetlands and the large Terracina forests, some of which still survive. Internal lagoons and retrodunal lakes are separated from the sea by a recent sand-dune belt over an area of 25 km. The main formation in the area is mesophilous oak forest, including small, periodically flooded depressions with hygrophilous vegetation. Artificially reforested patches are also present, consisting of stone pine (Pinus pinea) and Eucalyptus. Forty species of mammals have been reported, including 14 bat species and wild boar (Sus scrofa). Over 280 species of birds occur, including migratory species. There are 16 species of reptiles, eight species of amphibians, 50 species of fish and an unknown number of terrestrial, marine and freshwater invertebrates.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Circeo

records.introduction_en: The Julian Alps are a region in the Southern Limestone Alps, where north-eastern Italy meets Slovenia. The Slovenian Julian Alps Biosphere Reserve, which includes Triglav National Park, was designated in 2003. The biosphere reserve constitutes an important Alpine corridor, notably for large carnivores as well as birds. The area is also a meeting place of the Latin and Slav worlds, with millennia of cultural interaction testified by its multitude of dialects, settlement methods, and agricultural and artistic practices.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The specific biological nature of the biosphere reserve is determined by several factors. Its biogeographical location, elevation gradient and abundant rainfall are particularly relevant. From a biogeographical point of view, following the Udvardy classification system, the biosphere reserve is situated within the ‘Central European Highlands’ biogeographical province. It is in close proximity to the ‘Balkan Highlands’, and not far from the ‘Middle European Forest’ and the ‘Mediterranean Sclerophyll’. With respect to the Habitats Directive (Directive no. 92/43/EEC), the area is located on the border between the Alpine and continental regions, and it shows significant traces of the influence of the Mediterranean region. Species in the area include brown bears, lynxes, otters and wildcats.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Julian Alps

records.introduction_en: The site lies in central Italy at the confluence of two river systems, with the Tiber to the east and the Paglia to the west. It consists of an extensive forested area and is an important natural pool of fauna, flora and mushroom species in and around an ancient, extinct volcano. These natural resources allow for activities compatible with sustainable development.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Monte Peglia Reserve and surrounding area are characterised by a relatively compact, elliptical system of hills encircled on three sides by the Tiber to the east and the Paglia to the west. To the north, the hills extend beyond the area of the Municipality of San Venanzo and join the plain of Lake Trasimeno. From a topographical viewpoint, the area features one particularly significant hill, Monte Peglia, situated in the southern part of the reserve. A series of comparatively lower hills occupies the central–northern area. The ecosystem consists of an extensive forested area in which the great variety of flora remains intact. Habitats are well preserved, and original biotic communities can still be found. The area forms an important natural pool of fauna, flora and fungi that have developed in the area of the ancient, extinct volcano.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Monte Peglia

records.introduction_en: Located in northern Italy, the Monte Grappa Biosphere Reserve encompasses the Monte Grappa Massif and its surrounding foothills. Set at the junction of biogeographical regions, it typifies the dynamics of the Eastern Italian Prealps and links the Po Valley with the Eastern Dolomites. The reserve conserves a rich mosaic of landscapes, ecosystems and biodiversity including 24 Natura 2000 habitat types, while fostering research, education and sustainable development. The reserve works to improve community well-being through green and circular economy approaches and corporate social responsibility, and counter long-term depopulation by engaging young people in safeguarding local values.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set on a faulted massif, Monte Grappa presents the main features of the Eastern Italian Prealps. Snow-capped ridges and alpine meadows rise above the Veneto and Po Valley plains, with the Piave River to the east and the Brenta to the west. Mountain, hill and high-plain areas, together with a dense drainage network, support a rich habitat mosaic ranging from broadleaf forests and chestnut groves to mountain-pine slopes and arid meadows. This diversity supports many species and has driven local speciation, resulting in high endemism. Endemics include the butterfly Parnassius apollo grappensis and beetles such as Duvalius breiti, Orotrechus gracilis, Trechus gracilitarsis, Leptusa montsiggrappae and Liparus grappensis. Pastures, woods and meadows support well-differentiated vegetation types, including dry grasslands dominated by Bromus erectus, grasslands with Brachypodium caespitosum, and nutrient-rich pastures. Notable fauna include roe deer, chamois and the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Monte Grappa

records.introduction_en: The Po Grande Biosphere Reserve lies within the central tract of the River Po, in a basin that has been significantly affected by human activities. The Po is the longest river in Italy, with the highest water discharge in the country, and one of the largest in Europe. Cultural diversity is very high in the biosphere reserve, whose establishment complements two recently created biosphere reserves along the Po River: Po Delta (2015) and Collina Po (2016).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The River Po ecosystem is a mosaic of ecological systems that include the riverbed and its branches, marginal wetlands and oxbow lakes, fluvial islands, riparian forests, hygrophilous meadows and hunting valleys, and agrarian and land reclamation territories. In terms of biodiversity, the central section of the River Po is occupied by a complex network of Rete Natura 2000 sites (RN2000) that include all main natural and semi-natural areas and habitat types of the central Po Valley. The area is dominated by two arboreal genera: willow, mainly the white willow (Salix alba), and poplar (Populus), predominantly white (Populus alba), but also black (Populus nigra) and hybrids with North American species. These are heliophilous, colonising species able to renew themselves, even en masse, on newly formed sandy bars that create new riverbeds. Over time they are destined to be replaced by more stable forest formations, such as oak–elm forests, where the bar stabilises over many decades.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Po Grande

records.introduction_en: The Selve Costiere di Toscana Biosphere Reserve lies along the Mediterranean coast of Italy, west of Pisa between Viareggio and Livorno, in Tuscany. The reserve is rich in biodiversity, comprising natural and semi-natural plain habitats, including dunes, wetlands, mesophytic woodlands and pinewoods, and agricultural zones with hedges. These habitats contain rare species that have disappeared from most of Italy and the wider Mediterranean region. Plain woodlands that are rare elsewhere in Italy cover extensive areas of the reserve. The main economic activities are fishing, agriculture (including organic agriculture and autochthonous breeding) and tourism, in particular bathing establishments.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve includes natural and semi-natural plain habitats such as dunes, wetlands, mesophytic woodlands and pinewoods, alongside agricultural zones with hedges. These habitats contain rare species that have otherwise disappeared from much of Italy and the Mediterranean region. The protection of dune environments is one of the main goals of the biosphere reserve. The coastal dunes are of particular interest due to the presence of sand-consolidating pioneer flora, endemic species and highly specialised animal species. The dunes are connected with inland habitats through multiple symbiotic relationships, notably the protection they provide to woods against strong sea winds. The wetlands can extend for several hundred hectares, for example the Massaciuccoli marsh and Lame di Fuori, and ensure the reproduction of numerous rare bird species such as the purple heron (Ardea purpurea), the great bittern (Botaurus stellaris) and the cattle egret (Bubulcus ibis). Further inland, vast tracts have been historically used for agriculture and were developed over past centuries from swamp areas. The flora in these areas follows the rhythm of soil tillage, cultivation management, animal breeding and other agricultural activities.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Selve Costiere di Toscana

records.introduction_en: Located in Sardinia, this biosphere reserve covers more than 140,000 ha. It presents mountainous areas to the west and a flat strip to the east, with rivers and coastal areas. The reserve comprises 17 municipalities, between the provinces of Olbia-Tempio and Nuoro.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area is in the north-east of Sardinia and its boundaries are established by the drainage basin of the Rio Posada and the massifs that surround it, from Montalbo to the Alà mountains and Monte Nieddu. In some respects, the territory in the reserve embodies recent radical changes in the relationship between the coast and the interior of the island. Sardinia is one of the main biodiversity hotspots in the Mediterranean, with high levels of endemism. There are 183 endemic plants that are exclusive to the island and 91 endemic plants in the Sardinian-Corsican-Tuscan Archipelago biogeographic province. In addition, 121 taxonomic units of the Sardinian flora are endangered according to IUCN criteria or included in lists of special attention, such as the list of the most threatened species of the Mediterranean islands. As for the fauna, the biosphere reserve is home to mouflons (Ovis musimon), wildcats (Felis silvestris), Sardinian partridges (Alectoris barbara), Sardinian hares (Lepus capensis), pine martens (Martes martes), western or purple swamphens (Porphyrio porphyrio) and wild boars (Sus scrofa).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Tepilora, Rio Posada and Montalbo

records.introduction_en: Bordering the Dead Sea at 416 metres below sea level, the Mujib Biosphere Reserve surrounds Wadi Mujib, a deep canyon that cuts through the rugged highlands and drains into the Dead Sea. It is home to rich biodiversity, including 300 plant species and numerous resident and migratory birds.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is located in the central highlands of the southern part of the Jordan Valley. It lies between Wadi Zarqa Ma’in to the north and Wadi Shegeig to the south. The western boundary follows the Dead Sea Road, the lowest depression on Earth, 420 metres below sea level. The reserve comprises a system of mountains and wadis extending from the Rift Valley escarpment to the shores of the Dead Sea. The escarpment drops abruptly from the edge of the gently undulating, basalt-capped highland plateau and the rain-fed wheat fields at the heart of the ancient kingdom of Moab. Altitude and rainfall decrease from east to west. At higher altitudes, the escarpment is formed of rounded, relatively smooth spurs and promontories that descend gently westwards and are dissected by numerous steep but smooth-sided valleys. At lower altitudes, the terrain is more broken and uneven. Cliffs occur at all levels and are largest and most impressive at the lowest altitudes, especially at the terminal gorge of Wadi Mujib just before it reaches the Dead Sea, and where Wadi Hidan cuts through the basalt outcrop.
records.name: Mujib

records.introduction_en: Kiunga Biosphere Reserve lies at the northern end of Kenya’s coastline and comprises a chain of low islands and shoals. The vegetation consists mainly of shrubs, with some areas of mangrove forest, while the coastal strip has sandy beaches and dunes that are a key source of clean water for nearby communities. The site is known for hosting a high number of seabirds, marine turtles and the dugong. The reserve’s main purpose, as defined by the area’s stakeholders, is to conserve and protect marine and coastal forest species, especially the threatened sea turtles, dugong, Coastal topi, wild dogs and elephants along with their associated habitats for the benefit of present and future generations. Management objectives focus on ecological conservation, tourism development and community partnership.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Kiunga brings together coastal forests, mangroves, grasslands, seagrass beds and coral reefs in a single land–sea mosaic. Vegetation ranges from mangrove forests on the coast, to shrub communities with savanna-type grasses further inland. Critical habitats include extensive mangrove forests, seagrass meadows that provide feeding grounds for green turtles (Chelonia mydas), hawksbill turtles (Eretmochelys imbricata) and dugongs (Dugong dugon), and coral reefs that underpin fisheries and are also a key visitor attraction. The reserve maintains important ecological connectivity between coastal and inland habitats, allowing a wide range of species to move between foraging and refuge areas. Rivers are essential to this connectivity; the Mangai River is the only perennial source of freshwater in the Dodori corridor. Land allocation decisions for hotel construction along the coast have raised concerns for the reserve’s sand dunes, and putting in place measures to address this is a core focus of the reserve, in collaboration with Kenya Water Resources management and the county government.
records.name: Kiunga

records.introduction_en: Malindi–Watamu Biosphere Reserve is part of the marine protected areas of the Kenyan coast. It comprises marine and coastal ecosystems, including coral reefs and associated ecosystems such as seagrass beds and mangrove forests, which are crucial for the livelihoods of coastal people and for the national economy. Coral reefs provide food and income to coastal communities and deliver other goods and services of strategic importance to the national economy, including tourism, fisheries and coastal protection.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Malindi–Watamu Biosphere Reserve is located on the coast of Kenya, about 100 km north of Mombasa. Notable physical features include rock platforms, cliffs and sandy beaches. Mida Creek comprises tidal mudflats with fringing mangrove swamps within the biosphere reserve area, and includes coral reefs and seagrass beds. The region has important biodiversity assets as an Important Bird Area, for both migrating and resident species. It has coral reef and fish assemblages of high conservation value, including Red List species and endemics. Seagrass beds and inshore rockpool habitats provide nursery areas and offer as yet unassessed blue carbon benefits. The mangrove forest hosts the widest range of mangrove species on the East African coast. The area also lies on major cetacean migration routes, warranting good marine stewardship to ensure their safe passage.
records.name: Malindi-Watamu Arabuko Sokoke

records.introduction_en: Mount Elgon was designated as a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 2003. It lies about 300 km north-west of Nairobi and extends into two counties, Trans Nzoia and Bungoma. Mount Elgon is the main contributor to the major rivers that drain into Lake Victoria, and it has a radial drainage pattern.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Mount Elgon ecosystem is one of Conservation International’s 35 biodiversity hotspots. It forms part of the eastern and central Afromontane hotspots that encompass several widely scattered but biogeographically similar mountain ranges in eastern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, from Saudi Arabia and Yemen in the north to Zimbabwe in the south. The main part of the hotspot’s 1,017,806 km² is made up of ancient block massifs, notably the Eastern Arc Mountains and Southern Rift, the Albertine Rift and the Ethiopian Highlands, as well as the volcanic highlands of Kenya and Tanzania. The biosphere reserve is a major water reservoir for adjacent areas. The major tree species and land cover types in the lower zones include Juniperus procera and Cassipourea malosana. Higher-altitude zones are dominated by bamboo (Arundinaria alpina) and a mosaic of bamboo and Podocarpus milanjianus. At higher altitudes, rainfall also supports Hagenia abyssinica and Hypericum revolutum, along with grass and moorland zones. In areas with plentiful rainfall, especially on the windward side, Elgon teak, giant camphor and other hardwoods thrive. Species found exclusively on Mount Elgon and rarely elsewhere include giant groundsel and giant lobelia. The biosphere reserve also hosts endemic wildlife such as the river frog, the side-striped chameleon, the marine viper, the king mole rat and the mole shrew. Other wildlife present includes giant forest hogs, leopards, eland, buffalo, duiker, an antelope species, and colobus monkeys.
records.name: Mount Elgon

records.introduction_en: Mount Kulal’s ecosystem captures moisture in the form of mist and rain and provides important hydrological services for northern Kenya. The mountain has a volcanic origin: lava fields define the surrounding landscape, and its sides are steep and often cut by deep canyons. The presence of a peak as high as Mount Kulal in one of the driest regions of East Africa makes it unique topographically and contributes to the particular ecosystem services that the mountain and its forest provide to the region. Historically, the biosphere reserve was a major habitat for elephants (Loxodonta africana) and black rhinoceroses (Diceros bicornis), which were plentiful until 1976; however, these species have now been exterminated by poaching.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Mount Kulal Biosphere Reserve has three main habitat types: the mountain-top habitat; the flanks, gorges and valleys; and the surrounding flatlands. All are niches for unique biodiversity. The most prominent components are the terrestrial flora and fauna, and the fish of Lake Turkana. Lake Turkana, to the west of Mount Kulal, harbours a great variety of aquatic animals, including crocodiles, hippos, fish and birds. It is also an important waterbird site. A total of 84 bird species, including 34 Palearctic migrants, have been recorded in and around the shores of Lake Turkana. In addition, 23 aquatic bird species, including goliath heron and African skimmer, breed on the shores of the lake. There are many other species of fauna, including reptiles such as the venomous saw-scaled viper, night adder, puff adder and cobra, as well as lizards. Scorpions and other invertebrates are also common. Birds are considered a major asset within the Mount Kulal Biosphere Reserve and attract significant interest, including the endemic Kulal white-eye (Zosterops kulalensis).
records.name: Mount Kulal

records.introduction_en: The Gochang Biosphere Reserve is in the south-west of the country and comprises forest, coastal and freshwater ecosystems. The tidal flats are major stopover sites for migratory birds, especially longbills and plovers.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve includes the forest ecosystem of Mt Seonun Provincial Park, the coastal ecosystem of Gochang and the Buan Tidal Flats Ramsar site, and the freshwater ecosystem of Dongrim Reservoir. Dongrim Reservoir is a wildlife protection area designated by the Ministry of Environment and a well-known habitat for migratory birds. The reserve also includes Ungok Wetland, a lowland mountain wetland. The Gochang and Buan tidal flats are of particular significance as a stopover for migratory birds. Among the birds that inhabit the reserve, several species are of national and international importance. Resident and migratory birds such as stork, black-faced spoonbill, spoonbill, black swan, whooper swan, Saunders’s gull, bean goose, goshawk and oystercatcher highlight the area’s importance as bird habitat.
records.name: Gochang

records.introduction_en: Shinan Dadohae is an island archipelago in the south-west of the Republic of Korea. It includes terrestrial and marine areas as well as large tidal flats that host diverse species and serve as resting places for rare migratory birds. Traditional forms of fishing, such as hand fishing, and salt production are still practised.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The temperate evergreen broadleaf forest is dominated by Castanopsis cuspidata, silver magnolia and camellia. Herbaceous plants include Ardisia japonica and Hedera rhombea, along with Saeri trees and Kalopanax pictus. Dune vegetation includes Ischaemum anthephoroides, Zoysia macrostachya, Vitex rotundifolia, Calystegia soldanellaand Messerschmidia sibirica, with a colony of Carex kobomugi on Jeungdo Island. Species such as Phragmites communis and Vitex rotundifolia are distributed throughout the dunes. On some uninhabited islands, evergreen coniferous forest persists, with colonies of Japanese black pine dominating seashores and hillsides. Insects such as Graphium sarpedon and Papilio protenor occur in these forests and in coastal dunes. The tidal flats are dominated by reed and Phragmites communities in wetland areas. Along the coast, various saltmarsh plants form halophyte communities. The intertidal zone hosts many organisms, and the surface of the flats is important habitat for diatoms and plankton; owing to complex ecological circulation and food chains, many shells and other invertebrates are found here. With Jangdo Island High Moor and Jeungdo Tidal Flat, the biosphere reserve includes two Ramsar sites.
records.name: Shinan Dadohae

records.introduction_en: The Alakol biosphere reserve covers 193 089 hectares. It is located in the desert zone of Eurasia in the central part of the Alakol inter-mountain depression and lies on the Central Asian–Indian bird migration route. The wetlands of the reserve are of global significance as a habitat and as a nesting site for water birds.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve encompasses the Alakol–Sasykkol lake system and is situated at the margins of the Alakol Depression, bounded by the Tarbagatai Ridge to the north, Dzhungarian Alatau to the south, and Barlyk Ridge to the east and south-east. The reserve lies along the Central Asian–Indian bird migration route and is recognized as a wetland of global importance, serving as a key habitat and aggregation site for waterbirds.Inscribed on the Ramsar Convention’s List of Internationally Important Wetlands in 2009, the reserve provides nesting habitat for 203 bird species out of the 342 recorded. More than half of these nesting species (110) are waterbirds, including 22 rare or endangered species listed in the Red Data Books of Kazakhstan and by the IUCN. Notable species include the Dalmatian pelican (Pelecanus crispus), Eurasian spoonbill (Platalea leucorodia), greater flamingo (Phoenicopterus roseus), and ferruginous duck (Aythya nyroca). Across the main and buffer zones, 269 bird species have been recorded, of which 110 are waterbirds, particularly abundant during spring and autumn migrations.The reserve also supports 678 species of higher plants and 25 species of aquatic flora, including two species listed in the Red Data Book of Kazakhstan: Tulipa kolpakowskiana and Tulipa brachystemon. Approximately 40% of the floristic diversity in the reserve consists of economically important species. The main plant associations are represented by five primary types—desert, meadow, marsh, tugai, and underwater—along with two additional types occurring in fragments: shrub and large-leaved forest.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Alakol

records.introduction_en: The Ak-Zhayik Biosphere Reserve is situated on the plains of the southern part of the Caspian Depression at an elevation of −27 m. The area is a single territory divided by the Ural River and adjacent to the coast of the Caspian Sea. The waters of the Caspian Sea are not included in the biosphere reserve’s total area. Ak-Zhayik mainly encompasses the wetlands of the Ural River delta and adjacent territories along the Caspian Sea coast, on one of the largest bird migration routes. This route stretches from Eurasia across the Caspian and Black seas towards Eastern Africa, making the area a concentration site for over 240 migrating bird species. The marshy depression is partitioned by a system of delta channels with banks overgrown by dense vegetation, and the sea reaches a depth of up to 2 m.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve lies in the desert zone and the subzone of steppified northern deserts. It includes various aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. Virgin steppe, coastal ecosystems with high reed thickets, shallow lakes, meadows and shrub thickets along rivers are all present in Ak-Zhayik. The area is characterised by low plains with saline meadows, solonchaks, solonetz and extensive wetlands. The main vegetation is represented by six types: desert, meadow, marsh, forest, shrubs and water-submerged. The wetlands of Ak-Zhayik are situated on one of the largest bird migration routes. Of the migratory birds, 110 are waterbirds, including 18 specially protected species. The biosphere reserve is therefore a nesting site for approximately 70 waterbirds, eight of which are specially protected natural objects. The rare bird Pelecanus crispus occurs here, with a population of more than 600 nesting pairs, accounting for 12 per cent of the global population. In total, 292 bird species are recorded in the Ural River delta and adjacent sea coast, with up to 3 million birds during migration. The site is the last untouched area of wild nature in the region. It serves as a refuge for many species of wild fauna and flora, especially sturgeon fish, which have recently been threatened with complete extinction. There are 48 mammal species recorded in Ak-Zhayik. The aquatic parts of the site are currently the only protected territories for conservation of endemic relict species such as the Caspian seal (Pusa caspica). In terms of flora, the area contains 229 species of higher plants. Among these, seven species are relict in the Potamogetonaceae family, and four species are rare and specially protected in the Salicaceae family. There is also a group of medicinal plants of 10 … [truncated]
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Ak-Zhayik

records.introduction_en: The Barsakelmes Biosphere Reserve is located in the Sahara–Gobi Desert zone of the Aral Sea basin. The Aral Sea region is a priority area for wetland conservation, with several bird migration routes converging over the region. The territory of the biosphere reserve is a valuable site for the preservation of biodiversity in the Aral Sea, which includes approximately 2,000 species of invertebrates, 30 mammal species, 178 bird species and 20 reptile species. The reserve also encompasses four archaeological sites that form part of the nomadic Kazakh heritage of the Silk Roads.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The core zone of the Barsakelmes Biosphere Reserve has been under state protection since 1939, when the Barsakelmes State Nature Reserve was established within the limits of Barsakelmes Island. At that time, the island was situated near the central part of the Aral Sea and covered an area of 18,000 ha. At the end of the twentieth century, shrinkage of the Aral Sea exposed a large area of marine plain around Barsakelmes that linked the island with the mainland. The dried bottom of the Aral Sea subsequently became an arena for the establishment of flora, fauna and unique ecosystems. This territory constitutes the world’s only natural “laboratory” for observing natural desert ecosystems in their initial stages under conditions of climate change. The unique flora of Barsakelmes reflects regional botanical diversity typically found in Turanian deserts. Widely distributed zonal vegetation types include Artemisia terrae-albae, Anabasis salsaand Haloxylon aphyllum, which serve as examples of undisturbed vegetation. There are 12 species of reptiles, 178 bird species and 27 mammal species in the area. Among the mammals, special attention should be paid to herbivorous rodents and ungulates. Two species of jerboa – the five-toed pygmy jerboa (Cardiocranius paradocus) and the dwarf fat-tailed jerboa (Pygeretmus pumilio) – are native inhabitants of the island. The main protected animal species are ungulates such as the saiga antelope (Saiga tatarica), the onager (Equus hemionus) and the goitered gazelle (Gazella subgutturosa). The Syrdarya Delta is an official Ramsar Wetland Site.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Barsakelmes

records.introduction_en: Situated in the inter-montane basin of Ili, in the southeast of Kazakhstan, this biosphere reserve unites the canyon-like valley of the Charyn river with relict ash forest, deserts and steppes typical of Central Asia. The floristic diversity includes some 1,000 species of higher vascular plants. The fauna is rich and diverse. While agriculture has long been the main economic activity in the region, tourism has been developing for several years alongside cattle breeding and horticulture.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The territory of the Charyn Biosphere Reserve is located in the basin of the Charyn River. It represents a unique biogeosystem in the central part of the Ili intermontane basin in southeast Kazakhstan, encompassing both the canyon valley and adjacent desert areas.The floristic diversity of the reserve includes about 1,000 species of higher vascular plants, belonging to 426 genera and 90 families, representing approximately 18% of Kazakhstan’s flora. The fauna is equally diverse, with hundreds of species present, including endangered and vulnerable species such as the goitered gazelle (Gazella subgutturosa) and Pallas’ cat (Otocolobus manul).
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Charyn

records.introduction_en: Covering some of the least disturbed ecosystems in the southern Western Altai, Markakol lies close to the border with China. It encompasses unique and characteristic mid-mountain taiga and high-mountain alpine landscapes of the temperate steppe ecoregion of Eurasia. These are home to various endemic species, including the rare and endangered snow leopard and the stone marten. Most inhabitants earn their livelihoods from animal husbandry and tourism, though the latter is in decline.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Markakol Basin is a unique geobiosystem of the southern Altai. It brings together the aquatic zone of the second-largest lake in eastern Kazakhstan, with its ichthyofauna and ornithofauna, benthic bed and plankton, and hydrophyte and hygrophyte flora, and the terrestrial flora and fauna of the ridges surrounding the lake, diverse in origin, distribution and ecology. The floral diversity of the Markakol Reserve includes some 700 higher plant species from 75 families. This diversity reflects the region’s location at the junction of the Kazakh steppes, the semi-deserts of Central Asia and the taiga forests of southern Siberia, as well as the mountain relief and varied climatic conditions. The reserve preserves a unique gene pool of endemic subspecies of fish, including the Markakol lenok (Brachymystax lenok) and the Siberian grayling (Thymallus arcticus), both salmon-like fishes, as well as subspecies of minnow (Gobio gobio) and char (Noemacheilus barbatulus).
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Markakol

records.introduction_en: The Kanneliya–Dediyagala–Nakiyadeniya Biosphere Reserve lies in the southern Wet Zone of Sri Lanka and forms a connected forest complex between the Gin Ganga and Nilwala Ganga river catchments. It is recognised nationally for exceptional species richness and endemism, with long-standing cultural and socio-economic value for surrounding communities. The core area covers natural dense forest in Kanneliya, while the Dediyagala and Nakiyadeniya forests form a continuous natural buffer. The reserve works to conserve biodiversity, support sustainable livelihoods and provide a platform for research, education and training.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Kanneliya–Dediyagala–Nakiyadeniya Biosphere Reserve is a connected rainforest landscape in Sri Lanka’s southern Wet Zone. It comprises three adjoining forest blocks – Kanneliya, Dediyagala and Nakiyadeniya – that together form a single protected complex. The reserve lies on the upland between the Gin Ganga and Nilwala Ganga, both flowing to the south coast. The climate sustains mature wet evergreen rainforest with a multi-layered, species-rich canopy. Dipterocarps – tall, dominant tropical trees – are a defining feature. Set within the Southern Lowland Hills floristic region, the forest is an outstanding centre of plant diversity. Fauna includes several Sri Lankan endemics; rare endemic amphibians such as Ichthyophis glutinosus which occurs in shaded stream and leaf-litter habitats. The forested uplands act as the headwaters for both rivers, supporting agriculture, industry and coastal ecosystems downstream. Several studies of the forest complex have underlined its exceptional biodiversity importance.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Kanneliya-Dediyagala-Nakiyadeniya

records.introduction_en: Žuvintas lies in the southern part of the Middle Lithuanian Lowlands in south-eastern Lithuania and brings together lakes, wetlands, mires, peat bogs and pine stands. The area is nationally important as Lithuania’s oldest protected site and is internationally recognised for wetlands that serve as a migratory corridor for waterbirds and a significant peatland carbon sink. Management priorities centre on restoring natural water regimes, recovering priority meadow, fen and bog habitats, and promoting environmentally friendly farming in the buffer and wider catchment.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Žuvintas Biosphere Reserve is a wetland landscape shaped by glaciation and sustained by intact hydrological processes. Ecosystems range from raised bog and transitional mire to fen, reed bed, sedge swamp and three shallow lakes that feed the Dovinė River. Floating reed islands edge Lake Žuvintas, Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) grows on the drier hummocks and black alder (Alnus glutinosa) anchors the wet hollows. These peatland and wetland habitats store carbon, regulate water and filter sediment, reducing downstream flood peaks and helping to maintain water quality across the catchment. The continuity of habitats supports movement of wildlife across open water, peatland and woodland, and functions as an important migratory corridor on the East Atlantic flyway. Biodiversity is notable, with high conservation significance. Mammals include European beaver (Castor fiber) and river otter (Lutra lutra) alongside globally threatened birds such as aquatic warbler (Acrocephalus paludicola) and ferruginous duck (Aythya nyroca). Plant and fungal diversity is high, with characteristic Sphagnum communities and nationally important Fennoscandian deciduous swamp woods and alluvial forests that contribute to long-term carbon storage and microclimate regulation. Long-standing protection and international recognition under Ramsar, Natura 2000 and Important Bird Area networks testify to the site’s ecological value.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Žuvintas

records.introduction_en: Located on the north-west coast of Madagascar, this biosphere reserve contributes to the conservation of three specific habitats: dry semi-deciduous forest, mangrove forest and coral reefs. The forest is one of the few remaining patches of dry littoral forest on the west coast of Madagascar. The outer coral reef, about 5–10 km west of the Radama Islands, protects an ancient coral reef on its western side, forming Madagascar’s slope. The Bay of Sahamalaza, which can reach a depth of 20 m, includes a large area of mangrove.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Sahamalaza-Iles Radama Biosphere Reserve contains a diversity of habitats and ecosystems. The marine ecosystem comprises coral reefs, seagrass beds, steep reefs, sandy-muddy seabeds and mudflats. It contains 216 species of corals and invertebrates, 168 species of fish, and three species of marine mammals, including dolphins and whales. The reserve also contains mangroves covering an area of 10,000 ha. The eight species of mangroves known to Madagascar are represented. The mangroves are inhabited by mangrove crabs, fish and shellfish exploited by the local population. This habitat is ecologically important for the conservation of five threatened bird species, including the Madagascar sea-eagle (Haliaeetus vociferoides). The third ecosystem is the low, dry coastal forest, covering 11,100 ha and hosting locally endemic lemur species in danger of extinction, such as Eulemur macaco flavifrons and Hapalemur sahamalazensis.
records.name: Sahamalaza-Iles Radama

records.introduction_en: Located in the south-west of Morocco, this biosphere reserve covers a vast intramontane plain, bordered by the High Atlas and Anti-Atlas Mountains and open to the Atlantic in the west. The area is known for its endemic species, the argan (Argania spinosa), which is important for conservation, research and socio-economic development. Argan oil has multiple uses in cooking, medicines and cosmetics. The trees are also used as fuelwood for cooking and heating.
