records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Arganeraie denotes the argan forest and its ecosystem, which is globally unique for its resilience in arid conditions and the biodiversity it sustains. The region is home to rare endemic flora, including the Moroccan lotus (Lotus maroccanus) and Selaginella balansae. The biosphere reserve also features species such as the caracal (Caracal caracal) and the Barbary sheep (Ammotragus lervia). The latter is considered vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. Recently, climate change has resulted in long periods of drought followed by heavy rain and floods.
records.name: Arganeraie

records.introduction_en: Situated in the central Atlas Mountains, the Atlas Cedar Biosphere Reserve is home to 75 per cent of the world’s Atlas cedar tree population. The region contains a wealth of ecosystems, and mountain peaks reaching up to 3,700 m provide critically important water resources. Fruit plantations, modern agriculture and tourist activities have replaced semi-nomadic pastoral traditions, but they are taking a toll on scarce water resources. The local Berber culture is particularly strong in this area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Atlas Cedar Biosphere Reserve is home to the Atlas cedar (Cedrus atlantica) and accounts for 75 per cent of the total global Atlas cedar tree population. In addition to the Atlas cedar and other cedars, green oak (Quercus rotundifolia) and maritime pine (Pinus pinaster) occur in the forests. The High Atlas section to the south of the reserve has peaks reaching up to 3,700 m, which provide the region with critically important water resources. The main ecosystem is the Haute Moulouya plain, an arid steppe at 1,500 m. The region is home to the last surviving examples of the Maghreb leopard (Panthera pardus). Other mammals inhabiting the area include the Barbary macaque (Macaca sylvanus), the serval (Leptailurus serval), Cuvier’s gazelle (Gazella cuvieri) and the lesser kestrel (Falco naumanni). The area encompasses Ramsar sites: Lake Afennourir; Aguelmams Sidi Ali–Tifounassine; and Lacs Isly–Tislite.
records.name: Atlas Cedar

records.introduction_en: The Intercontinental Biosphere Reserve of the Mediterranean is the first intercontinental reserve declared by UNESCO. The reserve includes a marine corridor and establishes a framework for communication and collaboration between two continents with different conditions: Europe and Africa. It extends between southern Andalusia and northern Morocco, forming an open arc towards the Mediterranean and interrupted by the Strait of Gibraltar. The uniqueness of this natural and socio-cultural crossroads, where Atlantic influence is a determining factor, is exemplified by its main axes: mountains, water, Spanish firs and Andalusian culture, as well as the environmental and socio-economic complementarity between its northern and southern sections.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The physical and natural foundation of the biosphere reserve is the large and rugged Bético-Rifeña (Betic Rif) mountain range, which extends through Andalusia and northern Morocco. Elevations range from 2,170 metres in Jbel Lakraay to over 500 metres in the Strait of Gibraltar. These shared natural conditions extend across both shores. The mountain ranges, with their abrupt reliefs, hold a large amount of water, which has generated diverse environments. This diversity is reflected in more than 2,000 species of flora and fauna, with important endemism such as the Spanish fir, the black juniper and the cedar. In addition, the Strait plays a major role in the migrations of European and African birds, with a rate of 1,000 birds per hour, and in the transit of different species of cetaceans, as well as in constructions of biotic origin such as coral.
records.name: Intercontinental BR of the Mediterranean

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve lies in the West African savanna, approximately 200 km north-west of Bamako in western Mali. The 918,000 ha area, also designated as a national park, comprises two biogeographic zones: the Sudano-Guinean zone in the south and the Sahelian zone in the north.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve includes shrub savanna dominated by Combretum, grading into Isoberlinia savanna woodland in the south. The Baoulé River is fringed by dense riverine forest. While vegetation in the south shows few signs of degradation, vegetation in the north is suffering from the effects of drought. Clearing for agriculture is also a major threat. The area once supported many large mammals, but their populations have been heavily reduced by hunting pressure and competition from livestock. In the protected areas, essential elements of biodiversity have been preserved to some extent. Following several initiatives, numbers of various species have stabilised or increased, including elephants, lions and hyenas.
records.name: Boucle du Baoule

records.introduction_en: Addu Atoll, the southernmost atoll of the Maldives, lies north of the Chagos Archipelago in the central Indian Ocean. Made up of a complex formation of seven individual reefs, this biosphere reserve hosts significant wetland ecosystems, including mangroves, freshwater ponds and brackish lakes (kilhis). Coral reefs play an important role, buffering the atoll from storms and erosion and providing habitat for diverse marine life and seabirds. The biosphere reserve aims to apply ecosystem-based approaches to atoll management and to develop plans and actions for sustainable development by conserving and restoring the country’s environmental assets and pursuing carbon neutrality.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Addu Atoll consists of 30 islands arranged around a semi-enclosed lagoon, forming a distinctive heart shape. Habitats include coral reefs, reef passes, lagoons, seagrass beds, sandbanks, mangroves and wetlands. The northern end of Hithadhoo, the main administrative district of Addu City, is especially diverse, with significant sites such as Eadhigali Kilhi, one of the largest wetlands in the Maldives, and Ranin Hanaa Fengan’da, a natural freshwater lake, alongside several mangrove communities, shallow marine waters and well-preserved reefs. Coral reefs buffer these low-lying islands from storms and erosion and support rich marine life. In Addu Nature Park, humphead parrotfish, napoleon wrasse, hawksbill turtles and eagle rays are commonly observed. Seagrass and mangroves act as important carbon sinks, while wetlands mitigate flooding during heavy monsoon rains and provide feeding, breeding and roosting sites for migratory and endemic birds, including the Maldivian pond heron (Ardeola grayii phillipsi), the Maldivian waterhen and the great egret (Egretta alba modesta). Key pressures include reef habitat loss from land reclamation and disturbance associated with poorly managed diving and increasing visitation. Close approaches, anchoring on reefs, trampling and litter can stress turtles, seabirds and reef manta rays and degrade sensitive sites.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Addu Atoll

records.introduction_en: The Fuvahmulah Biosphere Reserve is in the southern Maldives. Covering approximately 1,300 ha, it is the country’s only single-island administrative atoll. It hosts highly diverse coral ecosystems with healthy habitats and distinctive coral-sand beach formations. The atoll is notable for its single-island setting and shallow bowl form.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Fuvahmulah is known for remarkably diverse coral ecosystems and varied biodiversity across coral reefs, mangroves and wetlands (locally, kilhi). The reef systems support significant populations of sharks, mainly tiger, thresher and whale sharks. Fish diversity is particularly high, with more than 1,200 species recorded. The biosphere reserve is also important for migratory birds, with over 167 species recorded, five of which are endemic. Hard underlying bedrock on the outer rim consists chiefly of hardened coral and sand conglomerates. The island surface forms a very shallow bowl with two water bodies at medial low points, creating two small linked sub-catchments. These water bodies Bandara Kilhi and Dhandi Magu Kilhi are surrounded by marshes under thick layers of peat and mud. Coconut palms, trees and shrubs grow around the marshes, which are dominated by Cladium and an unidentified fern species suspected to be an exotic invasive introduced in the twentieth century. Because there is no lagoon between the outer reef edge and the beaches, strong wave action affects the island from all sides. These oceanic conditions have produced the famous Thoondu, an area of fringing reef extending from the island’s northern point, and a pebble beach with unique, glossy small pebbles not seen elsewhere in the Maldives.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Fuvahmulah

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is located on Mauritius, an island in the Indian Ocean. It is important for conserving the last remaining fragments of the island’s endemic vegetation, namely tropical evergreen forest.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: About 25 per cent of Mauritius’s flora and fauna is endemic to the island. However, with the invasion of alien species, indigenous nature is at high risk. As part of Black River Gorges National Park, the biosphere reserve fosters in situ conservation through human intervention, including weeding of exotic species and trapping introduced macaques. It also supports ex situ conservation, such as plant propagation and captive breeding of birds.
records.name: Black River Gorges-Bel Ombre

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve, a major site for chimpanzee research, includes Gombe National Park, forest reserves and part of Lake Tanganyika. Faunal species present in the area include African elephants, ornate frogs and eight primate species. Its flora includes a species discovered in, and named after, Gombe, Pleiotaxis gombensis. The biodiversity of Lake Tanganyika includes over 300 fish species, 250 bird species and reptiles such as the water cobra and the Tanganyika water snake.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The core area of the reserve has exceptional natural, scenic, cultural and social attributes. It falls within tropical savannah and woodland vegetation and the Albertine Rift systems of mountain ecosystems. It is rich in a variety of ecosystems within its boundaries. The combination and variety of landforms and vegetation types create a uniquely scenic landscape that is both diverse and ecologically complex. In the core zone, Gombe National Park, the main species of conservation interest is the eastern subspecies of chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii), which, like all chimpanzee subspecies, is classified by IUCN as endangered. According to a 2015 survey, around 85 per cent of chimpanzees are found in the buffer zone and some areas of the transition zone. Other taxa present include terrestrial mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and plants. Other key species found in the buffer and transition zone include Pterocarpus angolensis, Milicia excelsa and Isoberlinia scheffleri. Under CITES, Isoberlinia scheffleri is categorised as vulnerable. Large mammal species include African elephants (Loxodonta africana).
records.name: Gombe Masito Ugalla

records.introduction_en: Rocky assemblages of various ages shape the land texture in Huatulco. The relief is mountainous in the southern portion, with valleys running perpendicular to the coast.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The terrestrial area includes rounded hills, isolated hills, dunes, escarpments, cliffs, mangroves, wetlands, savannah, lowland deciduous vegetation and riparian vegetation. The marine area includes bays, beaches, islands, and kelp and coral communities. The biosphere reserve covers territory recognised as national land, managed by the National Fund for Tourism.
records.name: Huatulco

records.introduction_en: These reserve lies where three water bodies converge: the California Current, the current from the coast of Costa Rica, and the waters of the Gulf of California, as described by Wyrtki in 1965.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Marieta Islands are an archipelago comprising two larger and two smaller islands. They are located where three water masses converge: the California Current, the Costa Rican Coastal Current and the waters of the Gulf of California. This convergence has enabled a habitat where marine species characteristic of the Mexican central and south Pacific cohabit with those from the Gulf of California and the Pacific coast of Baja California. The islands are notable for their rich bird and fish fauna. They are a fundamental part of the reproductive processes of endangered species such as the humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) and the olive ridley (Lepidochelys olivacea). They also harbour the largest nesting colonies in Mexico of the brown booby (Sula leucogaster), the bridled tern (Sterna anaethetus) and the brown noddy (Anous stolidus), and, for the Pacific, the laughing gull (Larus atricilla).
records.name: Islas Marietas

records.introduction_en: Islas Marías Biosphere Reserve is a remote Pacific archipelago off western Mexico. The reserve’s constituent islands run north-west to south-east and rise from sea level to about 640 metres, with rugged volcanic landforms on land and productive tropical waters offshore. Long isolation over more than eight million years has produced a notable set of Mexican endemics. The reserve’s objectives focus on conserving and restoring dry tropical forests, crassicaule scrub and the mangroves of María Magdalena and María Cleofas, together with surrounding reefs and pelagic waters. Carefully managed, science-based use is enabled and capacity is built through coordinated research, monitoring and environmental education.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve brings together a full land–sea system. On land, vegetation includes tropical deciduous and subdeciduous forests and subtropical crassicaule scrub with shrubs up to four or five metres tall, interspersed with shrubby cacti. Mangroves occur on María Magdalena and María Cleofas, while coastal dunes and cliff communities add further habitat diversity. The marine environment spans pelagic waters, reefs, and rocky and sandy intertidal zones and supports coral communities, reef fish, sharks, rays, turtles and marine mammals. The archipelago serves as a refuge, nesting and feeding site for large seabird colonies and shelters many protected species. Notable endemics include the Tres Marías yellow-headed parrot (Amazona oratrix tresmariae), the Islas Marías raccoon (Procyon insularis) and the Tres Marías rabbit (Sylvilagus graysoni). Marine turtles present include the hawksbill (Eretmochelys imbricata), the olive ridley (Lepidochelys olivacea) and the black turtle (Chelonia agassizii). Plant taxa under protection include mangrove species such as Rhizophora mangle, Avicennia germinans and Conocarpus erectus, as well as Guaiacum coulteri and the endemic Bursera arborea. Hurricanes, tropical storms and droughts shape vegetation dynamics and coastal habitats, and help explain the marked seasonality of the tropical dry system.
records.name: Islas Marias

records.introduction_en: Cozumel Island lies off south-east Mexico and encompasses diverse marine and terrestrial ecosystems rich in amphibian and reptile species. The main terrestrial ecosystems are medium semi-deciduous forest and mangroves. The Isla Cozumel Biosphere Reserve forms part of the world’s second-largest reef system, the Mesoamerican Reef, which is home to 1,192 marine species. Tourism is the most developed sector on the island, which includes close to 40 Maya archaeological sites.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The principal terrestrial ecosystems are medium semi-deciduous forest and mangroves. Medium semi-deciduous forest is rare elsewhere in the state of Quintana Roo and hosts a substantial proportion of species endemic to the island. Marine ecosystems make up a significant portion of the reserve, which is part of the Mesoamerican Reef. With its diverse marine and terrestrial ecosystems, the area is rich in amphibians and reptiles and is home to more than 1,000 marine species, including the anhinga (Anhinga anhinga), Atlantic bluefin tuna (Thunnus thynnus), Caribbean sharpnose puffer (Canthigaster rostrata) and hawksbill sea turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata). It is also home to three endemic species that the IUCN considers Critically Endangered: the Cozumel raccoon (Procyon pygmaeus), Cozumel thrasher (Toxostoma guttatum) and Cozumel harvest mouse (Reithrodontomys spectabilis). The area includes two Ramsar sites: Parque Nacional Arrecifes de Cozumel and Manglares y Humedales del Norte de Isla Cozumel.
records.name: Isla Cozumel

records.title_en: Laguna Madre y Delta del Rió Bravo
records.introduction_en: Laguna Madre lies on the coastal plain of the Gulf of Mexico, about 120 km west of Ciudad Victoria, the state capital. Recognised internationally as a Ramsar site and as an Important Bird Area, it features in national priority maps for terrestrial, marine and inland waters. The reserve’s objectives are to conserve its hypersaline lagoon–delta system by safeguarding freshwater inflows and tidal exchange, protecting mangroves and seagrass meadows, and aligning local livelihoods with ecological zoning and long-term monitoring.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Together with Laguna Madre in Texas, United States, this is the largest hypersaline coastal wetland in North America and one of seven worldwide. It harbours a high diversity of species and ecosystems because it is situated between the Nearctic and Neotropical regions. The influence of the Carolinian and Caribbean marine provinces creates diverse soils, climates, rainfall regimes and levels of relative humidity. Key habitats include extensive seagrass meadows, mangroves, intertidal marshes (ciénegas) and freshwater systems, alongside the Tamaulipan matorral (desert shrubland). The landscape includes the deltas of the Bravo, San Fernando and Soto la Marina rivers, long barrier islands and coastal dune systems; hydrologically it sits between the Bravo–Conchos and San Fernando–Soto la Marina basins. This region marks the northern limit along the Gulf of Mexico for tropical vegetation, including mangroves, and lowland and midland forests. Two of Mexico’s most important nesting sites for Kemp’s ridley (Lepidochelys kempii) occur here. The area also serves as a natural corridor for migratory aquatic birds, as it lies along the Gulf migratory route, the continent’s most important for birds of prey. It is essential for the survival, mating, breeding or resting of 450 bird species. Notably, 36 per cent of the world population of the redhead duck converges here, as well as the largest winter population of migratory waterfowl arriving in Mexico. It is considered the best-conserved habitat in the Gulf of Mexico, functioning as a biological corridor for species such as jaguar, ocelot, and puma.
records.name: Laguna Madre y Delta del Rió Bravo

records.introduction_en: Covering 30,500 ha and located within the Guadalajara Metropolitan Area, La Primavera Biosphere Reserve plays an important environmental role in the region, including refilling groundwater reserves and absorbing carbon dioxide. Depending on the location of its forested areas, there is a wide diversity of ecosystems spanning two floristic provinces.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The region includes two floristic provinces: the Sierra Madre Occidental and the Sierras Meridionales (Volcanic Axis), the so-called belt of fire. It lies in the Mesoamerican Mountain Region and is formed by the confluence of two major realms, the Nearctic and the Neotropical. The area contains critical habitats for representative flora and fauna, serving as a genetic reservoir and biological corridor among the region’s natural systems, including the canyon of the Santiago River, Cerro Los Bailadores, El Tepopote, Cerro de Tequila, Sierra de Navajas and Cerro Viejo. It is crucial for maintaining biodiversity and genetic heritage, and for promoting the continuity of evolutionary processes. It also constitutes a living laboratory for scientific research and environmental education. The area is home to 205 resident and migratory bird species, as well as 49 reptile and amphibian species. Recent studies have identified nine endemic species from Jalisco within the reserve.
records.name: La Primavera

records.introduction_en: Set in the central and eastern sector of the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, Los Volcanes Biosphere Reserve covers the southern Sierra Nevada and the Sierra de Río Frío east of Mexico City. The landscape rises to 5,452 metres and is dominated by the volcanoes Iztaccíhuatl, Popocatépetl, Telapón and Tláloc. The site includes the long-protected Izta-Popo Zoquiapan National Park and retains pockets of glacial ice and alpine meadows on Iztaccíhuatl. The reserve’s purpose is to conserve this high-altitude transition landscape while safeguarding water and other ecosystem services for millions of people living downstream, through community-led restoration, sustainable livelihoods and research-driven management.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The site’s importance arises from its location within the Transverse Volcanic Axis in its central–eastern sector, which forms the biogeographical boundary between the Nearctic and Neotropical regions. It includes a pronounced ecosystem gradient driven by altitude, favouring high species richness and the presence of endemic species. Ecosystems include pine, sacred fir (Abies religiosa) known locally as oyamel, and high-mountain grasslands. Popocatépetl is among the most active volcanoes globally. Geological formations, including hills, volcanic cones and slopes, are of volcanic origin, with a predominance of basalt and andesitic rocks. Altitude ranges from 2,589 m to 5,452 m above sea level. Ecological processes here are tightly linked to water. Forests and high-mountain grasslands regulate runoff, stabilise slopes and feed infiltration to the aquifers that supply the Valleys of Mexico, Puebla and Cuernavaca. Ravines and contrasting wet and dry gullies create fine-scale habitat variation that supports pine, oyamel and tussock communities within short distances. The massif holds notable endemism and species of conservation concern, with emblematic fauna such as the volcano rabbit (Romerolagus diazi) and rich fungal diversity in cool, shaded belts. In this live volcanic setting, young substrates support natural disturbance and soil renewal. In parallel, restoration in degraded belts is improving native cover and hydrological function.
records.name: Los Volcanes

records.introduction_en: The protected area includes a portion of the Sierra Madre Oriental at its northern extremity. Its elevation, configuration and geographical interconnections support a great variety of plants and animals representative of the Chihuahuense Desert and the Sierra Madre Oriental itself. Especially notable are communities typical of mesophilic forests in the area, survivors from geological periods when this part of the country was cooler and more humid, approximately 10,000 years ago.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: From a physiographic standpoint, the Sierra del Carmen is an island, consisting of a very high mountain massif rising out of desert plains. It lies at the convergence of three physiographic regions: in the west, the Chihuahua Desert; in the south-east, the Tamaulipas thorny scrubland; and the central region of Coahuila plains. This setting creates a variety of natural environments in a relatively small area, ranging from riparian ecosystems at 500 m above sea level, to the Chihuahua desert plains and the typical thorny scrubland of Tamaulipas rosette vegetation, to grasslands and oak and juniper chaparral at 1,500 m above sea level. Above 2,000 m, there are oak and pine forests, and forests dominated by Pseudotsuga and Abies. It is a refuge for migratory species of Neotropical and Nearctic birds, as well as birds of prey. It harbours the golden eagle, the peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus), the black bear (Ursus americanus), the white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) and the mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus). It also supports small endemic and relict mammals such as the grey shrew, moles, opossums, armadillos, squirrels, beavers (Castor canadensis), the North American porcupine and the kit fox (Vulpes macrotis), among many others. On the chalkstone hills, healthy populations of candelilla (Euphorbia antisyphilitica) can be found.
records.name: Maderas del Carmen

records.introduction_en: The Calakmul Biosphere Reserve, located at the base of the Yucatán Peninsula, is the largest forest reserve in Mexico. It comprises 723,185 ha of protected land with some 52 ejidos, or local communities, in its buffer zone. It is not an untouched forest, as shown by the remnants of Mayan cities abandoned in AD 900. It consists of a tropical humid forest ecosystem covered with evergreen tropical humid forest, semi-deciduous forest with low temporarily flooded forest, thorn forest and tropical deciduous forest.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is characterised by its size, good state of conservation and continuity with other regions in the Yucatán Peninsula, Chiapas, Guatemala and Belize. It is considered the largest forest mass in Mexico and, together with the forests of Guatemala and Belize, the second-largest remnant forest in Latin America after the Amazon. Its great species diversity reflects regional heterogeneity. Despite limited landform variation, there are high- and medium-altitude sub-evergreen moist forests, medium-altitude sub-deciduous dry forests with a predominance of holywood lignum-vitae (Guaiacum sanctum), lowland deciduous forests and savannahs. This group of forests harbours Mexico’s largest populations of fauna and flora. It includes charismatic or flagship species of biological and ecological importance for the region, such as the jaguar, the puma, the tapir, the white-lipped peccary, the howler monkey and the spider monkey, the king vulture and the ornate hawk, together with mahogany, cedar and ciricote trees. There are also endemic species of economic and ecological importance for the region, such as the ocellated turkey (Meleagris ocellata) and the grey brocket deer. According to Galindo-Leal in 1999, 90 per cent of the amphibian species and over 50 per cent of the reptile species reported for the peninsula are found in the region. For birds, over 360 species have been recorded, and the area is also an important geographical zone for Neotropical migratory species, according to Galindo-Leal in 1999 and Berlanga and Wood in 2001.
records.name: Region de Calakmul

records.introduction_en: The Sierra La Laguna Biosphere Reserve is the most important reproduction site for Mexico’s and Latin America’s main hummingbird species, such as Costa’s hummingbird (Calypte costae) and Xantus’ hummingbird (Hylocharis xantusii), the latter endemic to the region. It comprises the dry forests of Baja California, and its temperate woods are home to biodiversity of global significance. The site is essential for the local population: it is the most important hydrological reservoir in the region and, according to Mexico’s National Water Commission, six basins form from Sierra La Laguna. Its 42 native mammal species represent 70 per cent of the fauna found in southern Baja California. It is also very important for resident and, especially, migratory birds.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is a vegetation “island” amid arid surroundings, which has led to a substantial level of endemism. Its dry forests are mostly covered with pine–oak and oak woodlands, with adjacent low and medium deciduous forest, an important area for tropical species. Endemic plants include palo extraño (Ilex brandegeana) and manzanita (I. californica). The main reproduction site for the hummingbirds for which Sierra La Laguna is known takes place between August and October. Of almost 50 mammal species found in the region, roughly 40 per cent are endemic, such as Osgood’s mouse (Peromyscus gratus). Preserving the region is critical for securing safe water sources for the local population. Located on the fringes of a desert with low precipitation (0–400 mm annually), the regional average is 700 mm.
records.name: Sierra La Laguna

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve lies in the Dnieper basin within the Polesie mixed forest zone, on the border with Ukraine. It covers low-lying, sparsely populated forested landscapes on the left bank of the Desna River in the Bryansk Region. The area is regionally significant for its extensive floodplain wetlands and old-growth ash–oak forests, which support major spring migrations of waterbirds and sustain key hydrological functions. The reserve’s main aims include conserving genetic resources, ecosystems and landscapes, providing a platform for research, long-term monitoring and environmental education, and supporting sustainable development by maintaining traditional land use and developing ecotourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Nerusso–Desnianskoe–Polesie Biosphere Reserve brings together a broad spectrum of regional ecosystems, forming a coherent forest–wetland landscape in the Nerussa–Desna lowlands. These include pine, pine–oak, oak and spruce–broadleaved forests, wetlands, meadows, lakes and rivers. Habitat complexity arises from natural disturbance and land use legacies, and this underpins species richness. Rivers create oxbows, side channels and swamp patches, while spring floods move sediments and periodically reshape the floodplain. A mosaic of natural and replanted forest, drained peat, logged areas, meadows and pasture at different recovery stages adds further structural variety. The Desna and Nerussa floodplains are of particular note, providing roosting, feeding and breeding grounds for large congregations of waterfowl, with more than 90,000 migrating waterbirds in spring. They host breeding populations of regionally rare species such as great white egret (Egretta alba), mute swan (Cygnus olor) and greylag goose (Anser anser). Large tracts of old-growth floodplain forest also lie along the Nerussa River, where ash–oak communities predominate along with extensive stands of bear’s onion (Allium ursinum), a rare and protected species of the region. Floodplain forests play an important role in the hydrological balance of the Nerussa River, functioning as natural filters during spring floods.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Nerusso-Desnianskoe-Polesie

records.introduction_en: Lake Elton Biosphere Reserve is located in the south-eastern part of the East European Plain, within the Caspian lowlands in the Russian Federation. Lake Elton is a hypersaline lake and the largest in Europe. It is also among the deepest situated, at 16 m below sea level, and one of the most saline lakes in the world. People live in 14 rural settlements and herder posts in the biosphere reserve, with seasonal variations almost doubling human presence in the area. The lake is important to nomads and their livestock, the only remaining agricultural activity in the area. It is also important to numerous mammals and birds, including cranes, some of which belong to threatened species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The specific features and uniqueness of the biosphere reserve arise from its geographical location and the presence of particularly valuable, almost undisturbed natural landscapes. It lies in the transitional zone between Europe and Asia, on the boundary of two biomes, steppes and deserts, several biogeographic regions and historic distribution areas of many plant and animal species. The area is also crossed by several global migration routes of many bird species protected under the Convention on Wetlands (1971), the Bonn Convention on Migratory Species of Wild Animals (1979) and the Agreement on the Conservation of African–Eurasian Migratory Waterbirds (2012). These routes include the Black Sea–East Mediterranean Flyway, the West Asian–East African Flyway and the Central Asian Flyway. Annually, the Lake Elton area is traversed by 1.5–2 million waterbirds. These include globally rare species such as the red-breasted goose (Branta ruficollis), lesser white-fronted goose (Anser erythropus), common pochard (Aythya ferina), white-headed duck (Oxyura leucocephala) and sociable lapwing (Vanellus gregarius). It is also traversed by 15,000–20,000 common cranes (Grus grus). Lake Elton covers more than 15,000 ha. It is among the deepest situated, at 16 m below sea level, and one of the most saline lakes in the world, at 200–500 per cent. It is characterised by extreme habitats with a specific biotic composition and valuable reserves of balneological resources.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Lake Elton

records.introduction_en: Darvinskiy Biosphere Reserve is situated on a peninsula in the north-west of the Rybinsk reservoir on the Volga River. The biosphere reserve comprises bogs, marshes and inundated pine forests. The fauna and flora are typical of the southern taiga. Rare birds that nest in the area include the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos) and osprey (Pandion haliaetus). Elk (Alces alces), brown bear (Ursus arctos) and wild boar (Sus scrofa) find refuge in the biosphere reserve. Due to the operation of nearby hydroelectric stations, the water level changes, which affects near-shore habitats.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The territory of the reserve forms a single natural system. It brings together typical ecosystems of the central parts of low-lying flat watersheds, including high- and intermediate bogs, and ecosystems of well-drained coastal areas occupied by coniferous and mixed forests. It also includes a low, periodically flooded terrace, where amphibious communities of the temporarily submerged zone have developed. The specific feature of the territory is the convergence of the central parts of the submerged watersheds with the coastal strip of a large water body. As a result of the Mologa–Sheksna lowland being submerged by the waters of the Rybinsk reservoir, a vast area of temporary submergence was formed, including coastal land and temporarily submerged areas. This area became the site of the highest concentration of biodiversity.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Darvinskiy

records.introduction_en: Great Volzhsko-Kamsky Biosphere Reserve consists of four units: Raifa Forest, Sarali Land between Rivers, Spassky Insular Archipelago and Sviyazhsky Wetland Area. Each unit has a core area, buffer zone and transition area. All units are located in close proximity to the Volga and Kama rivers.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The territory of the biosphere reserve is distinguished by high biodiversity. The diversity of biotopes, along with good feeding and protective conditions, underpins the high productivity of plant and animal populations. A total of 900 species of higher plants, 58 species of mammals, 114 species of nesting birds, 13 species of amphibians and reptiles, 49 species of fish and around 2,800 species of invertebrates have been recorded across the biosphere reserve units. Among them are 80 vertebrate species, 30 plant species and seven mushroom species that are regionally endangered. Three plant species, two mushroom species and nine vertebrate and invertebrate species are listed in the Red Data Book of the Russian Federation.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Great Volzhsko-Kamsky

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is located in the southernmost European part of the Russian Federation and covers mountain ranges of the western part of the Greater Caucasus. The designated area comprises a variety of natural ecosystems, about 80 per cent of ecosystem types of the Greater Caucasus.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve represents distinctive ecological belts that change with altitude, from subtropical up to glacial and nival zones, and it offers high species endemism. Within the biosphere reserve, two biogeographical provinces meet, which increases species diversity. The northern slopes belong to the Kuban biogeographical province and the southern slopes to the Colchic province. The faunistic diversity is rich, including the leopard (Panthera pardus ciscaucasica), brown bear (Ursus arctos), lynx (Lynx lynx) and Caucasian deer (Cervus elaphus maral).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Kavkazskiy

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is a conservation, research and eco-educational institution of federal significance. Its purpose is to preserve and study the natural course of natural processes and phenomena and the genetic diversity of the plant and animal world. It also preserves and studies individual plant and animal communities, as well as the typical and unique ecological systems of the Middle Volga region that represent the entire ecosystem of the eastern part of Europe.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The ecological systems of the Middle Volga complex biosphere reserve form a diverse mosaic characteristic of the temperate zone of European Russia. This area includes difficult-to-reach slopes of the Zhiguli Mountains with unique vegetation formations, notably relict steppe pine forests on limestone ridges and rocky steppes with elements of narrow-local endemic flora and subendemic entomofauna. In addition, various deciduous and mixed forests on the plains, meadow and forest-steppe biocenoses, and fragments of steppe formations including feather-grass communities are found across the reserve. The reserve also has rich aquatic and semi-aquatic ecosystems of substantial area. All ecosystems of the biosphere reserve are, to a greater or lesser extent, affected by human impact. The impact is minimal across most of the Zhiguli reserve territory and the conservation areas of Samarskaya Luka National Park.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Middle-Volga Integrated

records.introduction_en: Located in the Southern Urals, this biosphere reserve is covered with mixed coniferous and broad-leaved forests, mixed coniferous small-leaved forests and mountain taiga spruce–fir forests. Mountain ranges, with summits from 800 m to 1,178 m, and mountain valleys are interconnected by boulder streams. The western part of the reserve is low altitude, while the eastern part alternates between sloping mountain ridge elevations and depressions with lakes and deeply incised swampy valleys. The main objective is to transition from extractive industries to a sustainable development model based on biological natural resource management, tourism and the rehabilitation of landscapes scarred by mining.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve territory is characterised by both unique and typical ecosystems of the Southern Urals. The biomes typical for the Southern Urals occupy the largest areas, including coniferous broad-leaved forests, mountainous boreal spruce–fir forests, secondary mixed coniferous small-leaved forests and light coniferous pine woods. A smaller area is occupied by ecosystems associated with elements of the Southern Urals that reflect landscape and geomorphological variation characteristic of the biosphere reserve. The vertebrate fauna comprises 56 species of mammals, 188 species of birds, six species of reptiles, eight species of amphibians and 22 species and breeds of fish. There are 188 bird species, including 159 nesting within the biosphere reserve, 18 passage migrants and 10 wintering species. A vast invertebrate fauna amounts to more than 7,500 species, according to expert evaluation by specialists. A large number of animals in the biosphere reserve are huntable species, including mallard (Anas platyrhynchos), capercaillie (Tetrao urogallus), hazel grouse (Tetrastes bonasia), Eurasian woodcock (Scolopax rusticola), mountain hare (Lepus timidus), Eurasian beaver (Castor fiber), muskrat (Ondatra zibethicus), European pine marten (Martes martes), American mink (Neovison vison), red fox (Vulpes vulpes), wild boar (Sus scrofa), moose (Alces alces) and brown bear (Ursus arctos). Fish resources include common bream (Abramis brama), chub (Leuciscus cephalus), asp (Aspius aspius), white bream (Blicca bjoerkna), crucian carp (Carassius carassius), common nase (Chondrostoma nasus), gudgeon (Gobio gobio), ide (Leuciscus idus), common dace (Leuciscus leuciscus), common minnow (Phoxinus phoxinus), adult roach (Rutilus rutilus), northern pike (Esox lucius), bur … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mountainous Urals

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve is located in the south-east of Rostov Region. The natural conditions of the territory, which lies in the valley of the Kuma–Manych depression and on the spurs of the Salo–Manych ridge, are, in general, typical of the southern European part of Russia. The reserve’s territories have long been used with varying intensity. The activities of the administration of the reserve are aimed at preserving the natural diversity of the core zone, and at the sustainable development of the buffer zone and the zone of co-operation. In the protected zone of the reserve, ecologically adapted agricultural technologies are being implemented. The area has great potential for the development of many types of tourism, and for recreation and sport fishing.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The territory of the biosphere reserve is represented by two dominant zonal types of vegetation on dark chestnut soils in complex with salt marshes. These are moderately dry fescue–feather grass steppe with temperate xerophilous motley grass, and dry fescue–feather grass steppe with desert-steppe motley grass and semishrubs. Small areas of intrazonal character support plant communities of the turf–cereal–wormwood semidesert type on light chestnut soils with salt marshes. On the plateau of the spurs of the Salo–Manych ridge are presented fundamental features, as well as meadow steppes and mowing meadows, pastures and arable land. The ecosystem diversity of the reserve is determined by the presence of a large number of species of living organisms. The flora includes about 460 species of higher vascular plants. The vertebrate fauna consists of 270 species. These include 31 mammals and more than 219 birds, including sedentary, nesting, migratory and regularly visiting species. There are also three amphibians, nine reptiles and 16 fish. Among this species diversity, of particular interest are species identified as needing special protection. These include seven plant species, 32 bird species and eight insect species included in the Red Book of Russia.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Rostovsky

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is located in the north-west of the Smolensk Region and is notable for its diversity of glacial landscapes within a relatively small territory. In addition to end moraines, long sandy ridges and glacial lowlands, there are 35 picturesque lakes of glacial origin. Other habitats include bogs, marshes and virgin coniferous and broad-leaved forests.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is located in the north-west of the Smolensk Region and belongs to the Casblanca–Zapadnodvinskogo sandrovo–morenoa district. The park has 35 lakes, many of which are designated as natural monuments. Most of the lakes belong to the Przhevalskaya group, numbering about 20 water bodies and confined to the marginal deposits of the glacier. Nearly a quarter of the area is covered by all types of swamps, including upland, transitional and lowland, with occasional keys and splaviny. The territory is surrounded by 16 small rivers and by streams that are 3–4 orders of magnitude lower. The largest watersheds are in the southern and western parts of the park, between the pools of Else, Hobzy and Polovyi. The total length of watercourses in the park is about 700 km. Most of the rivers and streams of the park are on the watershed of the plateau occupied by forests. Forests cover three quarters of the national park, or 74 per cent, and are dominated by secondary forests. The zonal fir forest type occupies less than 25 per cent of the forested area and largely comprises complex spruce forest with an admixture of broad-leaved trees, along with preserved old spruce forests of the first class. Meadows occupy less than 1 per cent of the territory and are mostly of anthropogenic origin, having arisen on abandoned fields, logging areas or quarries. Within the biosphere reserve, 345 species of vertebrates inhabit the area. The mammals are represented by a complex of species whose origins are associated with adjacent natural areas of the taiga, deciduous forests, forest-steppe and steppe. There are 37 species of fish and lampreys. The invertebrate fauna includes over 2,000 species. The territory is included in the List of Key Ornithological Territories of R … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Smolensk Lakeland

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is divided from south to north by the Yenisey River, with the Siberian lowland to the west and the more elevated Siberian Plateau to the east. The river is 2–3 km wide, while the valley extends over 8–10 km. The glacial plain in the west is characterised by swamps and slow rivers, while rivers to the east are steep and swift. The biosphere reserve contains representatives of all taiga ecosystems of Central Siberia. The flora is typical of the middle taiga sub-zone, with Pinus sibirica and Larix as predominant species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The upper parts of the plateau are forest-free and dominated by mountain tundra and golets, bare rocky caps with sparse alpine or tundra vegetation. About 40 species of mammals live in the area, including sable (Martes zibellina), elk (Alces alces), bear (Ursus arctos), badger (Meles meles), otter (Lutra lutra) and lynx (Lynx lynx). The harsh climate of Siberia has always limited people’s development in the region. The core area is entirely free from human modification.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Tzentralnosibirskii

records.introduction_en: Taimyrsky Biosphere Reserve is located in the northern Siberian lowlands on the Taimyr Peninsula. The site is a cluster biosphere reserve with three core areas, one of which covers part of Lake Taimyr. Each has a relatively narrow surrounding buffer zone, and all are protected collectively as the Taimyr State Reserve. The area is a highly important breeding site for birds in the northern part of the East Atlantic flyway. The biosphere reserve covers pristine tundra and steppe habitats, as well as the northernmost forest communities with larch and dwarf birch.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: In the greater part of the area, the relief is flat. The contemporary surface was formed mostly by intermittent glaciations and marine transgression events during the Quaternary period, and subsequently by alluvial activity of numerous rivers. The terrain therefore features well-pronounced, relatively flat plain landscapes of marine origin, including lacustrine–lagoon systems, hilly–ridge moraine ranges and lake-covered, flat lacustrine–alluvial troughs. The entire area lies in the continuous permafrost zone, whose thickness is up to 500 m. The biosphere reserve is home to reindeer, muskox, polar foxes and snowshoe rabbits, as well as polar bears, walrus, ringed seals and white whales. It is an important nesting place for over 80 species, such as the black-throated diver, the white-fronted goose and the Siberian duck. The area is a summer breeding ground for the Laptev Sea walrus (Odobenus rosmarus laptevi), which is currently in the WWF Red Data Book.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Taimyrsky

records.introduction_en: Ubsunorskaya Kotlovina lies in the Republic of Tuva on the Russia–Mongolia border. It forms the Russian part of the Uvs Lake Depression Transboundary Biosphere Reserve, together with Mongolia’s Uvs Nuur Basin Biosphere Reserve. This is a key cross-border region linking the Siberian taiga with the Mongolian steppe, and supporting joint biodiversity conservation and community-based ecotourism. The reserve’s purpose is to keep ecosystems and species intact by using clearly marked core areas, with buffer zones concentrating human use outside the cores. This approach supports pastoral livelihoods and carefully managed tourism in line with sustainable development.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set in the Altai–Sayan ecoregion, the reserve spans a continuous gradient from wind-shaped desert sands and dry steppe through mountain taiga and alpine meadows to permanent snow and glaciers near 4,000 metres on Mongun-Taiga, the site’s highest area. At the arid extreme, Tsugeer Els is among the world’s most northerly sand deserts, with dunes ranging from bare and shifting to forms stabilised by Caragana and other desert plants. Within these sands, Tore Khol is a rare freshwater lake ringed by damp meadows and sedge marshes, creating an oasis for water and riverside birds. Further east, Yamaalyg’s granite steppe rises into the Sengilen range at Ular, where open tundra and high ground shelter snow leopard (Panthera uncia) and argali (Ovis ammon), with marmots on the slopes and ptarmigan overhead. On the south side of the East Tannu-Ola, mixed mountain forests and meadows hold wide-ranging mammals such as brown bear (Ursus arctos) and Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx). Around Uvs Nuur and Orucku Shynaa, lakes, marshes, river floodplains and reed beds connect into a broad wetland complex that functions at a regional scale as breeding, feeding and staging habitat for waterbirds, including grey geese and bay ducks.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Ubsunorskaya Kotlovina

records.introduction_en: Valdaiskiy Biosphere Reserve is located in the Valdai Highlands, the main watershed of the Russian plain, including the source of the River Volga, in the north-west of the country. The core area and buffer zones are made up of Valdaiskiy National Park. The relief is hilly and includes hill-moraine glacial relief with different forms of glacial morphology such as moraine banks and ridges, and lifting cones.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area includes characteristic ecosystems of the southern sub-zone of the Eastern European taiga. For centuries the area has been exposed to human activities of variable intensity. The native forests, typical and unique bogs, and lake and river ecosystems are mixed with former agricultural landscapes, especially areas of regenerating clear-cut forest. The biosphere reserve has to ensure protection of flora and fauna of forest and wetland ecosystems, as well as different forms of traditional land use. The flora encompasses more than 750 species of vascular plants and 126 moss species, including rare and endangered species. There are about 50 mammals and more than 180 bird species.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Valdaisky

records.introduction_en: Vodlozersky Biosphere Reserve is in the extreme north-west of the country. Mid-latitude and northern taiga landscapes are preserved here, and all kinds of terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems typical of this zone are represented, including boreal coniferous forests with spruce (Picea abies and P. obovata) and pine (Pinus sylvestris), as well as mires, lake ecosystems and river ecosystems.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve lies in the biogeographical region of boreal coniferous forests, at the junction of the northern and middle taiga subzones. According to regional geobotanical zoning, more than 80 per cent of the reserve belongs to the Vodlozersky and Onegoretsky areas of middle taiga forests. Spruce–moss forests of the myrtillus type prevail here, and sphagnous pine and spruce forests are also widely distributed. The flora of the reserve contains Eastern European and Eastern European–Siberian types, including Larix sibirica, Trisetum sibiricum, Rubus humulifolius, Atragene sibiricaand Aconitum septentrionale. In the northern part of the reserve, vegetation is characteristic of the White Sea northern-taiga forest zone, where sparse Paris quadrifolia, myrtillus and moss–cladina type spruce forests prevail. Large waterlogged areas are an important condition for the life and reproduction of hydrophilous animals. They play an international role in bird nesting and migration.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Vodlozersky

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve in the Province of Apayao is divided into two distinct regions. The Upper Apayao has rugged terrain with towering peaks, plateaux and valleys. The Lower Apayao features flatlands with rolling hills and plateaus. Stretching 180 km, the Apayao River serves as a vital watershed and nurtures 18 tributaries across the province. Recognised for its ecological significance, Apayao harbours the Apayao Lowland Forest Key Biodiversity Area, which has high levels of endemism and serves as a refuge for critically endangered species such as the Philippine eagle (Pithecophaga jefferyi).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Apayao contains one of the Philippines’ last remaining lowland forests, and the Apayao Lowland Forest is one of Northern Luzon’s 12 globally recognised Key Biodiversity Areas. The site has a globally high level of endemism, including 18 Philippine endemic plants listed as threatened and two tree species listed as critically endangered by the IUCN. It is also home to the critically endangered Philippine eagle (Pithecophaga jefferyi), indicating a healthy dipterocarp forest and the presence of prey species.
records.name: yApayaos

records.introduction_en: Corvo is the smallest of the Azorean islands, located in the extreme north-west of the archipelago. The biosphere reserve encompasses the entire emerged land area of the island and a surrounding marine zone, covering a total area of 25,853 ha. It includes landscapes and biological values of great regional, national and international importance. When the Azores Islands were discovered, they were uninhabited, and no Indigenous population is known to have existed. The current population is the product of several centuries of settlers and a miscellany of various ethnic groups.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The rich mosaic of ecological systems of significant interest in the Corvo Island Biosphere Reserve is associated with high biological diversity. The reserve is home to a wide range of species of European and regional relevance. With regard to its flora, Corvo Island has 93 registered endemisms, featuring the largest proportion of endemisms in the archipelago. Among the botanical species recorded on this island are 19 species listed in Annex II of the European Union Habitats Directive, three of which are priority, and two species listed in Annex IV of the same Directive. There are also eight bryophyte species listed on the European Red List of Bryophytes. One of them, Echinodium renauldii, is currently considered one of the most threatened bryophytes in the world. It is relevant to note that Corvo Island possesses the highest density of rare or endangered species, as well as endemic species, per km² in the whole Autonomous Region of the Azores.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Corvo Island

records.introduction_en: The Fajãs de São Jorge Biosphere Reserve covers the entire island of São Jorge, the fourth-largest island in the Archipelago of the Azores. Its highest elevation is Pico da Esperança at 1,053 m. The island’s rugged coastal cliffs form a unique landscape of highland meadows, peat bogs and scrubs. The combination of high altitude and coastal ecosystems has resulted in a wealth of endemic terrestrial flora. It is also home to diverse invertebrates, terrestrial arthropods, molluscs and bird species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: São Jorge Island has a unique landscape consisting of remarkable geological, environmental and cultural assets. Due to its elongated shape, the island has an extensive coastline, the third-longest in the Azores Islands. Its hilly configuration results from rocky cliffs, mainly on the north side, which create a steep landscape. The coastline is occasionally interspersed with flat areas known as fajãs, including detritic and lavic fajãs, which are a distinctive feature of the island. The highlands of São Jorge are extremely windy and humid, with high levels of rainfall and frequent fogs, even during the summer season. In combination with the island’s orographic features, this strong hydrological potential sustains large wetland areas of local and regional importance. In terms of biodiversity, São Jorge Island hosts a significant number of endemic animal and plant species across several groups, including mammals, birds, molluscs, arthropods, vascular plants and bryophytes. Faunal species include the little egret (Egretta garzetta), Azores wood pigeon (Columba palumbus azorica), sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) and short-beaked common dolphin (Delphinus delphis). The area of the biosphere reserve also includes two Ramsar sites: the São Jorge Central Plateau/Pico da Esperança and the Fajãs of Caldeira de Santo Cristo Lagoon and Cubres Lagoon at São Jorge.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Fajas de Sao Jorge

records.introduction_en: The Gerês–Xurés Transboundary Biosphere Reserve is located in the westernmost region of the Iberian Peninsula. The hilly terrain includes two major peaks: Nevosa at 1,556 m and Fontefría at 1,559 m. A continuous mountain range includes the Peneda, Amarela, Xurés, Quinxo and Santa Eufemia mountains, which are encircled by tributaries of the Rivers Limia and Minho. Other major rivers that cross the biosphere reserve are the Vez, Homem and Cávado. The natural landscape is divided into plateaux and glacial valleys, notably the Homem and Vez, the wide valley of the Lima River and steep slopes. In general, the hydrographic network extends through narrow, deep valleys, creating almost rectilinear trajectories.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve has a rich and distinctive diversity of flora with more than 800 taxa, including many Lusitanian and Iberian endemisms. Endemic Lusitanian–Galician species include, among many others, Armeria sampaioi and climbing corydalis (Ceratocapnos claviculata). Records of Iberian endemic species comprise more than 100 taxa, approximately 50 per cent of which are limited to the north-west of the Iberian Peninsula. The distribution areas of several vascular plants are closely linked to this territory, effectively forming a fingerprint of the biosphere reserve. Many species of vascular flora are included on protection lists at European, national or regional level. The Gerês–Xurés Transboundary Biosphere Reserve is also the home range of yellowbeard iris (Iris boissieri), Veronica micrantha and butcher’s-broom (Ruscus aculeatus). More than 300 taxa of bryophytes occur in this territory, comprising four taxa of hornworts, 227 taxa of mosses and 86 taxa of liverworts. Nearly 250 vertebrate species and more than 1,000 invertebrates have been recorded. Examples of common fauna include the southern smooth snake (Coronella girondica), the Eurasian eagle-owl (Bubo bubo), the Iberian wild goat (Capra pyrenaica), the Iberian desman (Galemys pyrenaicus), the golden-striped salamander (Chioglossa lusitanica) and the Iberian wolf (Canis lupus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Xurés

records.introduction_en: The Arrábida Biosphere Reserve extends across the municipalities of Palmela, Sesimbra, and Setúbal, bordering the River Sado. It is distinguished by remarkable geological formations, unique flora, and diverse landscapes of ecological, cultural, and scenic value. The Reserve encompasses habitats ranging from rugged coastal cliffs to forested slopes and has a long tradition of human activity, including fishing, agriculture, livestock farming, beekeeping, wine and cheese production, and tourism. Its designation seeks to integrate ecosystem conservation with sustainable economic and cultural practices, while promoting research, education, and public awareness. By aligning natural and human systems, the Reserve reinforces local identity and contributes to the global network of Biosphere Reserves as a model of sustainable development.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Biosphere Reserve is recognized as a biodiversity hotspot where Euro-Atlantic, Mediterranean, and Macaronesian influences converge, forming a rich mosaic of habitats. Its varied terrain creates diverse microclimates that support approximately 1,400 plant species—around 40% of Portugal’s flora—including rare endemics such as Convolvulus fernandesii and Euphorbia pedroi. Key habitats include oak (Quercus spp.) forests, Mediterranean scrub, calcareous rocky grasslands, and orchid-rich semi-natural grasslands, many of which are of national and European conservation importance.The marine environment further enhances the reserve’s significance, with more than 2,000 species of fish, crustaceans, and molluscs protected within the Professor Luiz Saldanha Marine Park. Terrestrial fauna comprises around 200 vertebrate species, along with numerous invertebrates, some of them endemic. The common bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus), together with rare crustaceans and molluscs, is among the emblematic species benefiting from these protections.Together, the terrestrial and marine ecosystems make Arrábida an area of exceptional ecological value, shaped by natural processes and centuries of human activity.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Arrábida

records.introduction_en: The Bosque Mbaracayú Biosphere Reserve is located in the upper basin of the Jejui River, which is home to a complex ethnic and cultural mosaic. Its inhabitants are Paraguayan and Brazilian smallholder farmers, Indigenous communities, and urban populations.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Bosque Mbaracayú Biosphere Reserve is the first designated in Paraguay. It corresponds to a biodiversity hotspot within the continental part of the Mata Atlántica biological corridor. It is a tropical humid forest ecosystem that includes low-altitude, medium-altitude and inundated Atlantic semi-deciduous forests, savannas with palm trees, dry forests, tropical savannas and pasture lands. The area is home to 89 mammal species, 19 of which are threatened, such as the jaguar (Panthera onca) and the puma (Puma concolor). Low-altitude Atlantic forest is characterised by Astronium fraxinifolium, Aspidosperma polyneuron, Tabebuia heptaphylla and Albizia hassleri. Medium-altitude Atlantic forest is dominated by Copaifera langsdorfii, Syagrus romanzoffiana and Cedrela. Inundated Atlantic forest is dominated by Gomidesia palustris and Calyptranthes concina. Savannas with palm trees include Butia paraguayensis, Acrocomia hassleri and Syagrus, alongside dry forest, tropical savanna, pasture lands and agroecosystems.
records.name: Bosque Mbaracayú

records.introduction_en: Located in the east of the country, the Itaipu biosphere reserve covers a surface area of over a million hectares. It comprises semi-deciduous subtropical forest, also known as the Upper Paraná Atlantic Forest. This is one of the most important ecosystems for the conservation of biological diversity on a global scale, because of the large number of endemic species, the richness of species and its original forest cover. It is home to large predators such as pumas (Panthera onca), as well as large herbivores such as tapirs (Hydrochaeris hydrocheris).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve comprises semi-deciduous subtropical forest, also known as the Upper Paraná Atlantic Forest. This forest forms part of the Global 200 list of ecoregions identified by the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), the global conservation organisation, as priorities for conservation. The Atlantic Forest is one of the most important ecosystems for the conservation of biological diversity on a global scale. This is due to its high number of endemic species, overall species richness and the scarcity of original forest cover following the accelerated destruction of the habitat for agricultural purposes. The Upper Paraná Atlantic Forest is home to vertebrates including large predators such as harpies (Harpia harpyja) and crested eagles, jaguars (Felis concolor) and pumas (Panthera onca). It also supports large herbivores such as tapirs (Hydrochaeris hydrocheris), species of deer (Mazama) and two species of peccaries (Tayassu).
records.name: Itaipu

records.introduction_en: Nui Chua Biosphere Reserve is set on Viet Nam’s south-central coast, in Ninh Thuan province. It brings together a large land–sea area that includes semi-arid coastal landscapes and adjacent marine waters. Notable features include extensive, highly diverse coral reefs, rich, ecologically linked seagrass beds, and sea turtle nesting beaches. The site represents the country’s tropical dry forest ecosystem and forms part of the globally important Annamite ecoregion. The reserve’s purpose is to create harmony between people and nature, guided by the principle: “conservation for development, development for conservation.”
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set along a section of the Nam Truong Son Range, the reserve’s topographical structure brings together forest, marine and semi-desert areas within one landscape. The semi-arid zone of Ninh Thuan and Phan Rang is considered the driest in Viet Nam and hosts unique vegetation, sea turtle nesting beaches and extensive coral reefs. The reserve hosts precious and rare fauna of international significance including the black-shanked douc (Pygathrix nigripes), Cao Van Sung lizard (Cyrtodactylus caovansungi) and silver-backed chevrotain (Tragulus versicolor). Endemic flora includes Isotrema nuichuaense, Calamus nuichuensis and Aspidistra ventricosa. The underwater ecosystem is equally rich. Shallow coastal waters hold vast coral reefs with complex morphological and structural types and include more than 300 reef-forming species, with ecological links to neighbouring seagrass beds. Nui Chua’s protected waters lie between high-biodiversity areas from Nha Phu Lagoon, Nha Trang Bay and Thuy Trieu Lagoon in the north to Hon Cau–Vinh Hao in the south. Every year sea turtles arrive to lay eggs on many of the reserve’s beaches. Aquatic ecosystems in the reserve provide essential benefits: regulating water flow, reducing soil erosion and flood risk, and supporting hydropower and irrigation for local people and the wider province.
records.name: Nui Chua

records.introduction_en: The Can Gio Mangrove Biosphere Reserve is located in the coastal district south-east of Ho Chi Minh City. The reserve provides opportunities to advance environmental protection across a continuum of habitats, from coastal areas to the boundaries of Ho Chi Minh City, the largest industrial city in Viet Nam. The mangrove forest hosts the highest diversity of mangrove plant species, mangrove-dwelling invertebrates, and mangrove-associated fish and shellfish species in the sub-region. It is regarded as the green lungs of the city.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Can Gio mangrove forest developed from a comparatively recent brackish swamp, with soil foundations created by the Saigon and Dong Nai rivers. Its development depends on high precipitation and a dense network of rivers interweaving the area. These rivers provide a rich and plentiful supply of alluvium in the estuarine regions. The soil in Can Gio has formed through a combination of clay alluvial depositions, vitriolic processes and a brackish water table. Can Gio encompasses diverse habitats including mangroves, wetlands, salt marshes, mudflats and seagrasses. The ecosystem functions as the green lungs of Ho Chi Minh City, absorbing carbon dioxide and other polluting agents on a daily basis. The mangroves contain a high diversity of flora and fauna. Notable mangrove species include Rhizophora apiculata, Thespesia populnea and Acanthus ebracteatus. A high number of faunal species occur in the biosphere reserve, including the king cobra (Ophiophagus hannah), the saltwater crocodile (Crocodylus porosus), the spot-billed pelican (Pelecanus philippensis) and the fishing cat (Felis viverrina).
records.name: Can Gio mangrove

records.introduction_en: The Cu Lao Cham–Hoi An Biosphere Reserve is located in central Viet Nam and consists of two core areas: the World Cultural Heritage Site of Hoi An and the Cu Lao Cham archipelago. The archipelago is renowned for marine species, including corals, molluscs, crustaceans and seaweed. The islands contain mountainous areas and rainforest ecosystems strongly influenced by seasonal monsoons. The Cultural World Heritage Site of Hoi An is an ancient trading port that bears witness to the fusion of Vietnamese and European cultures.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Topographical formations of maritime–marsh origin lie to the east of the township of Hoi An, in the villages of Cam Chau, Cam An and Cam Thanh, and stretch along the coast south of the Thu Bon River running past Trung Phuong, Duy Xuyen district. The most typical are deposits found at Cam Chau. They reach a maximum height of 0.8–1.2 m and comprise black, muddy sediment indicating the presence of organic matter. These deposits provide evidence of ancient seas that receded, leaving swamps and marshes that gradually filled up. They are approximately 2,000 years old. There are two core areas where long-term conservation focuses on preserving land and seascape diversity. The objective is to conserve ecosystems, habitats, species and genetic resources intact, and to prevent disturbance by human populations. The corridor between the two core areas is considered the ecological buffer zone and transition area linking the river mouth, Cua Dai, and the archipelago. This zone contributes substantially to the recovery of marine ecosystems in the area. The area boasts very rich biodiversity. According to research, there are 947 kinds of creatures living around the marine area of the islets, including 178 species of fish, 122 species of seaweed, 134 species of coral, 144 species of shellfish and 25 species of crustacean, as well as many other marine species. Characteristic fish species include the coral grouper (Epinephelus coralicola), bumphead parrotfish (Bolbometopon muricatum) and the endangered humphead wrasse (Cheilinus undulatus), along with angelfishes (Pomacanthidae).
records.name: Cu Lao Cham - Hoi An

records.introduction_en: Kon Ha Nung is located in the highlands of central Viet Nam, often referred to as the ‘Roof of Indochina’. The highest peak reaches over 1,700 m. Two nationally protected sites serve as the core areas of the biosphere reserve: Kon Ka Kinh National Park and Kon Chu Rang Nature Reserve. Both are located in Gia Lai Province.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is characterised by high biodiversity and is home to rare species, such as the grey-shanked douc (Pygathrix cinerea). This endemic primate of Viet Nam is classified as Critically Endangered, with only about 1,000 individuals in the wild. Kon Chu Rang Nature Reserve forms part of the Kon Tum Plateau Endemic Bird Area and has been recognised as one of the most important bird zones in Viet Nam.
records.name: Kon Ha Nung Highland

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is situated in the depression of the East African Rift Valley in the Lake Manyara Basin in northern Tanzania. Below the rift wall, perennial springs in the north support a groundwater forest, characterised by Trichilia roka and Croton macrostachyus, and the yellow fever tree (Acacia xanthophloea). Riverine habitats, swamps, woodland and alkaline grasslands also characterise the area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is rich in a variety of environments within its boundary. The combination and variety of landforms and vegetation types create a unique scenic landscape that is both diverse and ecologically complex. These provide a range of habitats and harbour an exceptional diversity of living organisms that are important for ecosystem services. The principal features of the core area are Lake Manyara, floodplains and associated grasslands, riverines, groundwater forest, escarpment, Acacia woodlands, lakeshore, swamp, Marang’ forest and the hot water springs. All these provide a variety of habitats and harbour an exceptional diversity of living organisms of special attraction for tourism. Lake Manyara, at 220 ha, lies in the southernmost part of a chain of saline lakes of the Rift Valley. These lakes are very diverse in their formation, water quality, animal life and appearance. The lake is also an important bird area and habitat for some 2 million flamingos, and birdlife totalling over 380 species. In terms of fauna, Lake Manyara National Park has what is possibly the greatest biomass density (weight per area) of mammals in the world.
records.name: Lake Manyara

records.introduction_en: Irati Biosphere Reserve is located within the mid-mountain expanse of the western Pyrenees. It encompasses the picturesque valleys of Salazar and Aezkoa in the north-eastern reaches of Navarre.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: A haven for biodiversity, the biosphere reserve has expansive beech and beech–fir forests; its beech forest is the second largest in Europe.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Irati

records.introduction_en: Located in the central Yinshan Mountains of Inner Mongolia, the Daqingshan Biosphere Reserve protects one of the richest biodiversity hotspots of the region. It contains a unique mosaic of forests, shrubs, and grasslands bridging the North China forest and Mongolian Plateau grassland systems. Historically situated on the ancient “Tea Horse Road,” the reserve is also a cultural crossroads linking China with Mongolia, Russia, and Europe.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve harbors 1,179 species of higher plants, eight of them endemic to the Yinshan Mountains (four exclusive to Daqingshan). It also records 300 vertebrate species and 1,804 arthropod species. Among them are globally threatened species: the critically endangered yellow-breasted bunting (Emberiza aureola), the endangered great bustard (Otis tarda), steppe eagle (Aquila nipalensis), and Przewalski’s horse (Equus ferus). Vegetation displays distinct vertical zonation: grasslands on the north slopes, and on the south slopes a full sequence from grasslands to shrubs, forests, and subalpine meadows.
records.name: Daqingshan

records.introduction_en: Perched high in the trans-Himalayan region of northern India, the Cold Desert Biosphere Reserve spans across the stark landscapes of Himachal Pradesh’s Lahaul–Spiti district. With altitudes from 3,300 to 6,600 m, it encompasses Pin Valley National Park and the Kibber and Chandratal Wildlife Sanctuaries. Glacial valleys, alpine lakes, rugged high-altitude deserts, and windswept plateaus make it one of the coldest and driest ecosystems in UNESCO’s World Network of Biosphere Reserves.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Cold Desert harbors 732 vascular plant species, including 30 endemics and 157 near-endemics of the Indian Himalayas. Vegetation includes hardy alpine grasses, medicinal herbs, willow-leaved sea-buckthorn (Hippophae salicifolia), Himalayan birch (Betula utilis), and Persian juniper (Juniperus polycarpos). Fauna includes the snow leopard (Panthera uncia), Himalayan ibex (Capra sibirica), blue sheep (Pseudois nayaur), Himalayan wolf (Canis lupus chanco), and rich avifauna such as the Himalayan snowcock (Tetraogallus himalayensis) and golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos daphanea).
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Cold Desert

records.introduction_en: Along Madagascar’s remote western coastline, the Tsimembo Biosphere Reserve blends dry deciduous forests, lush floodplains, intricate mangroves, and Ramsar Wetlands of International Importance within the ecologically vital Tsimembo–Manambolomaty Complex. This mosaic of habitats forms one of the island’s most threatened yet vital ecosystems, providing refuge for remarkable biodiversity and sustaining the livelihoods of local communities.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve encompasses a unique combination of dry deciduous forests, wetlands, mangroves, and lake systems that support exceptional biodiversity. It is home to more than 115 bird species, including the critically endangered Madagascar fish eagle (Haliaeetus vociferoides) and the Madagascar or Humblot’s heron (Ardea humbloti). The dry forests shelter eight lemur species, such as Decken’s sifaka (Propithecus deckenii), rare orchids, iconic baobab trees, and numerous endemic reptiles and amphibians, including the Madagascar big-headed turtle (Erymnochelys madagascariensis). Wetlands and lakes serve as critical fish nurseries, supporting aquatic biodiversity and local fisheries. These ecosystems also provide key ecological services such as water regulation, carbon storage, and coastal protection.
records.name: Tsimembo

records.title_en: Lac du Bourget, between the Rhône and the Alps
records.introduction_en: The Lac du Bourget Biosphere Reserve is situated between the Jura and the Alps, and contains France’s largest natural lake. At the confluence of oceanic, alpine, and Mediterranean influences, it integrates wetlands, alluvial forests, alpine meadows, and bocage farmland. Recognized as a Ramsar Wetland of International Importance, the reserve protects a unique ecological and cultural landscape where biodiversity, heritage, and human activity are deeply intertwined.
