records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve hosts more than 6,100 recorded species of plants and animals across 43 areas of ecological interest and four Natura 2000 sites, with 35% of the territory under legal protection.Notable species include Arctic char (Salvelinus alpinus), European pond turtle (Emys orbicularis), white-clawed crayfish (Austropotamobius pallipes), great naiad (Najas marina), scarce large blue butterfly (Phengaris teleius), depressed darter (Sympetrum depressiusculum), yellow-bellied toad (Bombina variegata), tall violet (Viola elatior), Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx), golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos), stag beetle (Lucanus cervus), and drooping star-of-Bethlehem (Ornithogalum nutans).Many species are listed on the French IUCN Red List.Its ecosystems regulate water cycles, store carbon, and buffer floods, providing vital ecological services to surrounding communities.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Lac du Bourget, between the Rhône and the Alps

records.title_en: Marshes and Tides between the Loire and the Vilaine
records.introduction_en: The Marshes and Tides between the Loire and the Vilaine Biosphere Reserve, located between the Loire and Vilaine rivers on France’s Atlantic coast, is a unique territory where freshwater marshes, peatlands, bocage landscapes, salt marshes, coastal dunes, estuaries, and marine ecosystems interconnect. This rich mosaic of habitats supports exceptional biodiversity, including numerous protected species, while also sustaining traditional human activities such as livestock grazing, fishing, salt production, reed harvesting, and tourism. Shaped over centuries by the interplay between people and water, the reserve embodies a living heritage where natural and cultural values are deeply intertwined. Today, it aims to reconcile biodiversity conservation with sustainable economic development, particularly in the face of climate change, urbanization, and ecological pressures, making it a model territory for balance between human activities and the preservation of natural ecosystems.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve harbors exceptional ecological richness, with a mosaic of wetlands, salt marshes, bocage landscapes, coastal dunes, estuaries, and marine areas that sustain a wide range of habitats and species. The Brière and Brivet marshes alone cover nearly 20,000 hectares and serve as major breeding, migratory, and wintering grounds for waterbirds, including rare and protected species such as the Eurasian bittern (Botaurus stellaris), black tern (Chlidonias niger), and bluethroat (Luscinia svecica), as well as mammals like the European otter (Lutra lutra).The area also supports 24 species of fish and functions as a critical growth zone for the critically endangered European eel (Anguilla anguilla). The Guérande and Mès salt marshes add further ecological value, providing habitat for rare plants such as Tolypella salina and supporting important bird populations.Altogether, the reserve represents a biodiversity hotspot of national and international importance, where natural processes and centuries of traditional human practices have co-created unique ecological conditions.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Marshes and Tides between the Loire and the Vilaine

records.introduction_en: Located in the southeastern Peloponnese, the Mount Parnon – Cape Maleas Biosphere Reserve covers mountains, forests, wetlands, and islands. Almost a quarter of the biosphere reserve is marine waters. From the cedar forests of Parnon, the only natural stands in Europe, to the petrified forest of Agios Nikolaos, the Evrotas Delta, lagoons, gorges, and the turquoise coves of Elafonisos, it presents a mosaic where geology, biodiversity, and culture have coexisted for millennia.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve shelters over 800 plant species, including 75 Greek endemics and 14 found exclusively within the reserve. Its habitats range from cedar (Cedrus spp.), black pine (Pinus nigra), chestnut (Castanea sativa), and oak (Quercus spp.) forests to wetlands, dunes, caves, and rocky coastlines.The fauna includes the endangered Mediterranean monk seal (Monachus monachus), golden jackal (Canis aureus), golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos), Eleonora’s falcon (Falco eleonorae), loggerhead sea turtle (Caretta caretta), and the critically endangered European eel (Anguilla anguilla). Wetlands such as Moustos Lagoon and the Evrotas Delta are crucial for migratory birds, including the eastern imperial eagle (Aquila heliaca) and greater spotted eagle (Clanga clanga).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mount Parnon – Cape Maleas

records.introduction_en: Located in the westernmost part of Papua, Indonesia, the Raja Ampat Biosphere Reserve spans across roughly 610 islands, atolls, and takas, of which only 34 are inhabited. This vast archipelago lies at the heart of the Coral Triangle, one of the planet’s most important marine biodiversity hotspots. Its landscapes and seascapes combine mangroves, white and black sand beaches, rainforests, and some of the richest coral reefs on Earth, forming a globally significant socio-ecological mosaic.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The marine environment of Raja Ampat covers ten core marine areas. Terrestrial habitats include lowland and montane rainforests as well as protected wildlife reserves. The reefs host over 75% of all known coral species, more than 1,320 species of coral reef fish, and five rare or endangered species of sea turtles, including the hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata). Around 60% of coral reefs are in good to excellent condition, and the region supports mangrove forests, seagrass meadows, deep reef systems, and unique coastal ecosystems that together underpin one of the highest concentrations of marine biodiversity on Earth.
records.name: Raja Ampat

records.introduction_en: Situated south of the World Heritage Site Mount Kinabalu, the Crocker Range Biosphere Reserve forms a chain of mountains with no distinct peaks in western Sabah. The rocky topography consists of mountains, hills and small basins dissected by deep river valleys. Elevation ranges from 6 m to 2,076 m above sea level. The area receives around 3,000 mm of precipitation per year and is home to a wide array of endangered species. The biosphere reserve encompasses rich biodiversity and a tropical hill–montane landscape.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Crocker Range ecosystem mainly contains hill and lower montane tropical forests from central to northern Borneo. It spans various altitudinal vegetation types, from lowland–hill forest below 300 m to cloud forest above 1,500 m. The core area consists of the Crocker Range Park and three legally protected forest reserves. Here, undisturbed hills are dominated by lower montane tropical forest. The core area is covered by natural vegetation, is ecologically connected to the buffer zone and is surrounded by it. In the buffer and transition zones, natural hills with lower montane tropical forest, secondary forest, hill paddy, rubber plantations and palm-oil plantations are all under observation. Despite the limited number of floristic studies in the Crocker Range, six permanent plots (50 m × 50 m) for ecological monitoring have been established, with an inventory of more than 300 plant species as of August 2011. Two endemic Rafflesia species are found in the Crocker Range. A total of 737 plant species have been recorded in Trus Madi, the reserve’s eastern vicinity. In terms of fauna, species recorded in Crocker Range Park and its surrounding area include 101 mammals, 259 birds, 47 reptiles, 63 amphibians and 42 freshwater fish. The Crocker Range is also the habitat of several endangered species, such as the orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus), sun bear (Helarctos malayanus) and clouded leopard.
records.name: Crocker Range

records.introduction_en: Located on Penang Island in Malaysia’s Indo-Malayan region, the Penang Hill Biosphere Reserve brings together urban, agricultural and natural landscapes, and safeguards one of Malaysia’s last coastal rainforests. The reserve aims to protect the island’s natural environment while supporting sustainable development. Long-standing ties between hill and sea are maintained through community stewardship, responsible tourism and careful land–sea management.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Penang Hill Biosphere Reserve encompasses a gradient of ecosystems, from coastal lowland and hill dipterocarp forest to mangroves, wetlands, sandy beaches and coral reefs. It contains Malaysia’s only meromictic lake – a rare system with two unmixed layers, freshwater above and seawater below – which supports rich biodiversity. The range of habitats within the reserve sustains endemic and threatened fauna including the Irrawaddy dolphin (Orcaella brevirostris) and the Sunda pangolin (Manis javanica). The reserve’s beaches are regular nesting sites for endangered sea turtles.The reserve is a key site for research, monitoring and environmental education on forest ecosystems. Biodiversity is monitored through annual census walks led by the Department of Wildlife and National Parks, in collaboration with universities and other local research institutions.
records.name: Penang Hill

records.introduction_en: Almost all of the reserve is wetland, comprising the freshwater lake, Tasik Chini, and its feeder rivers. The landscape also includes a moderately steep hill, Chini Hill (Bukit Chini), and the Tasik Chini State Park Reserve Fores
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The freshwater lake, together with its drainage basin and the gazetted Tasik Chini State Park, including Bukit Chini (641 m), contains habitats endemic to Tasik Chini that occur only in this area. Other species characteristic of the extreme lowlands may also be present and are of considerable conservation interest due to diminishing lowland habitats elsewhere in Peninsular Malaysia. The natural freshwater lake within the reserve also provides economic benefits. Of the two natural lakes in Peninsular Malaysia, Tasik Chini is the second largest and is located about 100 km from Kuantan, the state capital of Pahang. With the construction of a barrage on the only river that drains the lake, the Sungai Chini, Tasik Chini remains flooded even during the drier season, supporting year-round ecotourism.
records.name: Tasik Chini

records.introduction_en: Located in the centre of the country, the site comprises a mosaic of savannas, depressions, pits and sand dunes. The fauna is diverse and includes large mammals such as the dorcas gazelle, the pale fox and the golden jackal. The population of the reserve belongs to two main ethnic groups, the Tuaregs and the Peuls, and the main activity is pastoralism with a nomadic lifestyle.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Located in a climatic transition zone between the Sahel and the Sahara, the Gadabédji Biosphere Reserve represents, in part, the characteristic ecosystem of the Sahelo-Saharan biogeographical region. It is particularly important for the conservation of Saharan wildlife, as it is rich in pasture and provides natural habitat for wildlife. Home to migratory birds and several sedentary species such as the ostrich, it is populated by several species of gazelles and jackals, and other large mammals such as giraffes and oryx. It is also located on the edge of the seasonal migration zones of the addax, a rare wild animal that still inhabits the Ténéré Desert. Twenty-three wildlife species have been counted, the most important of which are ostriches (Struthio camelus), oryx (Oryx algazella), dama gazelle (Nanger dama), dorcas gazelle (Gazella dorcas) and giraffe (Giraffa camelopardalis peralta). Today, however, most of these species have disappeared from the area, with the exception of the dama gazelle, whose numbers were seriously threatened by the years of crisis experienced between 1990 and 2008.
records.name: Gadabedji

records.introduction_en: Located in the Sudan–Sahelian zone of Nigeria, in the Lake Chad basin, the biosphere reserve encompasses Nigeria’s first Ramsar site, the Bade Nguru Wetland. It also includes the Baturiya Game Reserve, a former community forest.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The seasonal rising of the Hadejia and Jama’are rivers floods lowlands and uplands in the states of Bauchi and Kano, as well as the Jos Plateau, home to many resident and migratory bird species. The region is recognised globally as important for bird conservation. A total of 377 bird species have been recorded in the biosphere reserve, according to BirdLife International (2019). Two species of global conservation concern, Circus macrourus and Gallinago media, winter occasionally in the biosphere reserve. Numbers of overwintering Aythya nyroca have declined considerably in recent years. The wetlands are extremely important for waterbirds, both for breeding species and for wintering and passing Palearctic waterbirds, while the surrounding areas hold significant numbers of species of the Sahel and Sudan–Guinea savannah biomes.
records.name: Hadejia Nguru Bade

records.introduction_en: Oban Biosphere Reserve is located in Cross River State in the south-eastern corner of Nigeria, encompassing the Oban Forest Reserve, the Cross River National Park and the Obudu Plateau.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Oban is an important watershed, with hills rising above 500 m and one peak reaching approximately 1,000 m. The Oban Hills once formed part of a lowland rainforest refugium during the last glacial period. The area is an internationally recognised biodiversity hotspot and a centre of species richness and endemism, particularly for primates, amphibians, butterflies, fish and small mammals. The biosphere reserve harbours a significant portion of Nigeria’s remaining tropical rainforest, with 1,568 plant species, of which more than 80 per cent are endemic. It is crucial in protecting megafauna such as the critically endangered Cross River gorilla, the Nigeria–Cameroon chimpanzee, the forest elephant and many other rare and endangered species. Oban is also one of the richest and most ornithologically diverse sites in the country.
records.name: Oban

records.introduction_en: Ometepe Island Biosphere Reserve is located in the south-west of Nicaragua in the country’s neotropical zone. Two imposing volcanoes, Maderas and Concepcion, define the topography of the reserve. Maderas is located in the east of the reserve and rises to 1,394 metres. Concepcion, which is still active, is found in the north-east and rises to 1,610 metres. The volcanoes are separated by the Istian isthmus, formed by the eruption of lava millions of years ago. Ometepe Island is surrounded by Lake Nicaragua, the largest freshwater lake in Central America, while the River San Juan traverses the length of the reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The major ecosystem types on Ometepe Island are wetlands and tropical rainforests characterised by Spanish cedar (Cedrela odorata) and Guarea grandifolia. The fog forests in the biosphere reserve have the highest conservation value in Nicaragua. The different mountain elevations host a variety of distinctive species, and the numerous craters serve as ideal habitats for rare species. The humid subtropical climate and fertile soils enable the growth of rare and endemic species.Characteristic flora include Ardisia costaricensis, Terminalia oblonga (guayabón) and Picramnia antidesma in the family Picramniaceae. Fauna of commercial use include Boa constrictor, paca (Agouti paca) and tayra (Eira barbara). Volcan Maderas National Park is home to endangered fauna, including the yellow-naped parrot (Amazona auropalliata), white-headed capuchin (Cebus capucinus) and smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata).
records.name: Ometepe Island

records.introduction_en: The Río San Juan Biosphere Reserve is composed of seven protected areas and adjacent territories. The biosphere reserve encompasses a variety of ecosystems representative of tropical humid forests and wetlands, tidal marsh, coastal lagoons and estuaries, which are important shelters for rare or threatened animals and plant genetic resources of the Mesoamerican tropics.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve hosts a large number of flora and fauna species, including endemic, rare, threatened and endangered species. Emblematic fauna includes the jaguar (Panthera onca), tapir (Tapirus bairdii), manatee (Trichechus manatus), harpy eagle (Harpia harpyja), green macaw (Ara ambiguus), sawfish (Pristis perotteti) and American crocodile (Crocodylus acutus). Aquatic fauna is represented by freshwater sharks such as the bull shark (Carcharhinus leucas) and two sawfish species, Pristis pectinata and P. perotteti. Their special osmotic adaptation to freshwater conditions is unique worldwide and is of great scientific interest.
records.name: Río San Juan

records.introduction_en: This agricultural river landscape in the Meuse valley, in the south-eastern part of the Netherlands, has been shaped by continuous interaction between people and nature. The site is used for hay meadows and includes the oldest and largest network of natural hedges in the Netherlands. The landscape comprises a mosaic of small agricultural fields enclosed by hedges, sand dunes, forests, lakes, wet meadows and reed beds. The plan is to use the biosphere reserve as a laboratory for sustainable development and tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve represents a variety of valuable landscapes formed by geological, geomorphological, cultural and historical processes. These landscapes, rich in cultural heritage, natural areas and valuable habitats, are of great importance for the biological and cultural diversity of the area. Besides the finely meshed network of hedges, characterised by high biodiversity and special species, valuable habitats such as xeric sand calcareous grasslands and lowland hay meadows, and vegetation associations such as Quercetea robori-petraeae, Koelerio-Corynephoretea and Nardetea are also present in the area.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Maasheggen

records.introduction_en: The Kempen-Broek Biosphere Reserve is part of a transboundary area that straddles the border between Flanders in Belgium and the Netherlands. Once-expansive wetlands have been transformed into farmland since the nineteenth century, but the area retains remnants of its marshes, punctuated by ponds, open marshlands and bog forests. Villages and towns are scattered on higher ground. Diverse bird species flourish across varied landscapes. The area constitutes an important open space with high landscape and biodiversity value.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The region is renowned as one of the Netherlands’ prime habitats for dragonflies. Its stream valleys feature meadows and fields, while the higher elevations are mostly used for agriculture. Towards the north, vast expanses of moorland and inland dunes preserve intriguing prehistoric sites. Due to its rich biodiversity, the area has an important role in the conservation of habitats and species in the Netherlands.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Kempen-Broek

records.introduction_en: La Amistad Biosphere Reserve and National Park lie in the foothills and mountains of the Cordillera de Talamanca, between the mountain ranges of Panama and Costa Rica.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Cordillera de Talamanca is the highest and wildest non-volcanic mountain range in Central America. It was formed by orogenic activity, which created the land dividing the Pacific and Caribbean Oceans. Of the 20 life zones of Costa Rica, at least eight occur in the park, from lowland tropical wet rainforest to cloud and paramo forests. Most of the main crest lies within the montane rainforest life zone. It is characterised by mixed oak forest, including the largest tracts of virgin forest in Costa Rica. On high peaks along the ridge over 3,000 metres above sea level, there are frequent stands of paramo, swamps and cold marshes. The paramo on Mt. Kamuk contains the richest and most varied vegetation in the entire Talamanca Range. Signs of tapirs (Tapirus terrestris), possibly of a species as yet unrecorded for Costa Rica, are abundant near the Panamanian border. Puma (Felis concolor), ocelot (F. pardalis), jaguarondi (F. yagouaroundi), Central American squirrel monkey (Saimiri oerstedii) and Geoffroy's spider monkey (Ateles geoffroyi) are found within the biosphere reserve.
records.name: La Amistad

records.introduction_en: Located in the provinces of Satipo and La Convención in central Peru, Avireri Vraem ranges from 280–6,271 m in altitude. It hosts 12 ecosystems across three ecoregions: the Amazonian rainforest at the foot of the Andes, the Yungas on steep mountain slopes with montane and cloud forests, and the Andean region in the heights of the Andes mountain range. The biosphere reserve establishes a link between Peru’s Oxapampa Ashaninka Yanesha and Manu biosphere reserves.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is home to 257 endemic fauna species, 307 endemic and endangered flora species, and 115 endangered fauna species listed on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species.
records.name: Avireri Vraem

records.introduction_en: Located in Peru’s Central Andes, the Bicentenario–Ayacucho Biosphere Reserve spans a diverse Andean landscape that includes the historic Pampa de Ayacucho. This high-altitude plain, protected as a Historical Sanctuary, was the site of the decisive 1824 battle that secured Peru’s independence from Spanish rule. Celebrated for harbouring the world’s largest population of Puya raimondii, known locally as “titanka”, the reserve is rooted in Quechua culture and communal stewardship. Its objectives are to conserve biodiversity and cultural heritage, foster agroecological and nature-based development, and serve as a living laboratory for research, monitoring, education and demonstration.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set in Peru’s Central Andes, the reserve forms a connected mountain landscape of high-elevation headwaters, or upper catchments, and inter-Andean valleys. Its core zone unites the Pampa de Ayacucho Historical Sanctuary and the Bosque de Puya Raimondi Titankayocc Regional Conservation Area, established to safeguard Puya raimondii and home to the largest known population of this iconic high-Andean plant. Beyond the core, the reserve encompasses Andean shrublands, humid puna grasslands, seasonally dry inter-Andean forests, high-elevation wetlands (bofedales), and relict woodlands of Polylepis, Escallonia and other mid-Andean trees.These ecosystems underpin vital services. Native woody vegetation – Puya, Polylepis, Escallonia and cacti – contributes to carbon storage, soil stability and the scenic values that drive nature-based tourism. Puna grasslands and bofedales at the headwaters regulate water for downstream communities and provide dry-season forage for llama, alpaca and vicuña. Aquatic health is tracked using indicator species such as the Andean water frog Telmatobius jelskii (“karia”) and native Orestias killifish (“chocce”) in cold, high-altitude streams, springs and wetlands. Valleys and ridgelines maintain habitat connectivity. Faced with pressures including recurrent fires, land-use change, overgrazing, altered hydrology and fuelwood extraction, the reserve offers strong opportunities for research, environmental education and climate-resilient management.
records.name: Bicentenario-Ayacucho

records.introduction_en: Chitral Bashkar Garmchashm Biosphere Reserve lies in Chitral District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, in north-west Pakistan, bordering Afghanistan to the north and west. The Hindu Kush landscape here includes glaciers and mountain ranges, with several peaks reaching over 7,000 m. Culturally, it is home to the distinctive Chitral heritage, including endangered Indo-Aryan languages such as Kalasha and Kalasha-mun. The reserve’s objectives are to conserve temperate and subtropical mountain ecosystems and their biodiversity, foster sustainable development, particularly nature- and culture-based ecotourism and associated livelihoods, and to provide logistic support for environmental education, training, research and monitoring in collaboration with local institutions.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set within the highest and most dense section of the Hindu Kush range, the site spans steep mountains, deep valleys, alpine pastures and glaciers. At the junction of two Asian biogeographic regions, it supports a wide range of habitats, including juniper and deodar cedar (Cedrus deodara) forests alongside extensive cold-desert and dry-alpine zones. Iconic mountain fauna include the Kashmir markhor, Siberian ibex, Ladakh urial and snow leopard – all protected species of conservation concern.Notable Hindu Kush glaciers within the reserve include Chiantar (33.8 km long) and Upper Tirichmir (29 km long), with other long tongues such as Atrak (29 km long) and Darban-Udren (24 km long). Their meltwaters feed the Laspur system, including high-altitude lakes across the Bashkar–Laspur landscape that act as reservoirs for the River Laspur and provide refuge for migratory birds along the Indus flyway. Between Bumburet and Rumbur lies Lake Bahuk – a turquoise, glacier-fed lake at around 4,000 m in an amphitheatre of peaks with a well-known view of Tirich Mir, regarded by the Kalash people as a holy lake and as the resting place of fairies. Glacial surge and retreat, and shifts in the nival/sub-nival (snowline) zones, play a key ecological role in watershed regulation and flood and drought mitigation, while associated erosion, weathering and sediment transport shape valleys and soils.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Chitral Bashkar Garmchashm

records.introduction_en: Situated in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province, Pakistan, the Gallies Biosphere Reserve lies within the moist-temperate Western Himalayan Temperate Forests ecoregion. Its rugged, precipitous slopes form small side valleys and varied aspects, supporting habitats from subalpine meadows and moist temperate forest to subtropical pine. Home to unique flora and fauna, including many endangered and threatened species, it is among the best-preserved areas of the Western Himalayas. The ecoregion is recognised in the Global 200 as among those most crucial to conserving global biodiversity. The reserve’s core purpose is the conservation and sustainable management of this ecosystem, alongside provision for scientific research, education and recreation.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Ranging from 1,050–3,027 m, from Lahur Kass to Miranjani, the reserve spans subalpine meadows, moist-temperate forest across the ridges, and subtropical pine at lower elevations. The forest complex – among Pakistan’s best-preserved moist-temperate stands – features blue pine (Pinus wallichiana), yew (Taxus wallichiana), horse chestnut (Aesculus indica) and native oaks (Quercus). Flagship wildlife includes leopard (Panthera pardus), koklass and Kalij pheasants (Pucrasia macrolopha, Lophura leucomelanos), and the Kashmir flying squirrels (giant and small; Petaurista petaurista, Eoglaucomys fimbriatus).The site sits within the Western Himalayan Temperate Forests ecoregion, recognised in the Global 200 and preserving features typical of the Sino-Japanese region. These forests store carbon, stabilise steep slopes and regulate climate and water. As Galiyat’s “water tower”, streams draining the area supply drinking and irrigation water to Rawalpindi, Islamabad, Abbottabad, Haripur, Mansehra and Attock.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Gallies

records.introduction_en: Lal Suhanra Biosphere Reserve and National Park is situated on the north-west edge of the Cholistan Desert in the Punjab Province of Pakistan. This arid landscape is relatively flat and interspersed with sand dunes. The dunes extend up to 1,000 ha and reach 4 m in height, and some are unstable.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Lal Suhanra Biosphere Reserve and National Park is situated on the north-west edge of the Cholistan Desert in the Punjab Province of Pakistan. This arid landscape is relatively flat and interspersed with sand dunes. The dunes extend up to 1,000 ha and reach 4 m in height, and some are unstable. The biosphere reserve is crossed by the dried-up bed of the Hakra River and comprises Patisar Lake and irrigated land. The lake (1,935 ha) was originally built as a water reservoir and used to be an important wetland and a wintering site for many waterfowl. Today, the lake supports extensive reed beds and submerged and floating aquatic vegetation, and it has therefore lost its habitat function for most birds. Subtropical thorn forest includes Calligonum polygonoides, Calotropis procera, Capparis decidua, Prosopis cinerariaand Tamarix aphylla. The Lesser Cholistan Desert is characterised by Crotalaria burhia, Ziziphus mauritiana, Haloxylon recurvum and Aerva javanica. Irrigated plantations include Acacia nilotica, Dalbergia sissoo, Eucalyptus camaldulensis, Prosopis cineraria, Tamarix aphylla, Capparis decidua and Salvadora oleoides. Freshwater wetlands include Eichhornia crassipes, Hydrilla verticillata, Nelumbo nucifera, Nymphaea lotus, Phragmites karka and Typha domingensis.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Lal Suhanra

records.introduction_en: Most of the biosphere reserve is covered by oak–lime–hornbeam forest, Tilio-Carpinetum, a high-value forest habitat for nature protection in the temperate zone. The majority of forest habitats protected by law on both sides of the border exhibit a primeval character, which gives the biosphere reserve exceptional value. Moreover, a great deal of dead wood present in each habitat type provides a very specific and unique microhabitat for numerous species, most of them endangered, threatened or rare. Despite relatively good knowledge of Europe’s biological diversity, new species of fungi or invertebrate fauna are discovered in the Białowieża Forest almost every year.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Białowieża Forest is also home to the whole range of ungulates present in Poland, with the exception of mountain species, large predators such as the lynx and the wolf, and typical forest-dwelling birds. The forest has a large population of woodpeckers. Among these, the white-backed woodpecker and the three-toed woodpecker, both typical of old and natural tree stands, are particularly interesting.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Bialowieza

records.introduction_en: Located in the European lowlands north-east of Warsaw, and parallel to the valley of the Vistula River, this biosphere reserve is characterised by a high diversity of lowland habitats. Dune belts are separated by swamp areas, with a mixture of forest types that include bog-alder forest, ash–alder floodplain forest, pine–oak mixed forest, and low oak–lime–hornbeam forest. The abundance of natural habitats enabled the successful reintroduction of elk (Alces alces), European beaver (Castor fiber) and lynx (Lynx lynx). The core area of the biosphere reserve includes strictly preserved areas within the administrative boundaries of Kampinos National Park.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve lies in an ice-marginal valley, with a maximum width of 16 km and a total length of 35 km, parallel to the Vistula River. Its borders are defined by the Vistula River to the north, the Bzura River to the west, the watershed between the river basins of the Utrata River and the Lasica Channel to the south, and the urban areas of Warsaw to the east. The Lasica Channel is the central watercourse of the biosphere reserve. The area shows high variability in relative altitude, and basic ecosystem types occur in parallel belts. The biosphere reserve is located in the transitional zone between the Atlantic and continental climate zones. This results in a high diversity of temperatures and precipitation. The climate also differs markedly from surrounding areas and is strongly diverse within its boundaries.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Puszcza Kampinoska

records.introduction_en: Situated along the southern Baltic coast between Leba and Rowy, this biosphere reserve focuses on the protection of coastal aeolian processes and mobile sand dunes, which are among the most active and extensive around the Baltic Sea.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Baltic Sea activity and other geomorphological processes create sandbars that separate lakes from the sea. The mobile dunes can reach more than 30 m above sea level. The Slowinski wetlands are of high importance in the Baltic Sea region as a breeding and stopover area for many bird species. Within the biosphere reserve, there are at least 25 bird species listed in Annex I of the European Union Birds Directive, of which 15 are listed on the Polish national Red List, including Aegolius funereus, Asio flammeus, Botaurus stellaris and Philomachus pugnax. It was designated a Ramsar site in 1995. The biosphere reserve comprises a series of vegetation zones created by natural succession, extending from the coastline towards the mainland. The system includes pioneer and initial sand communities, as well as coastal coniferous forests with crowberry.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Slowinski

records.introduction_en: The Tatra Mountains are the highest mountains in the long Carpathian range, which stretches from Slovakia into Romania via Hungary, Poland and Ukraine. The territory of the biosphere reserve covers two national parks on each side of the political boundary between Poland and Slovakia. This transboundary biosphere reserve features karst topography with dolomites and limestone, canyons and waterfalls, a dwarf pine belt, alpine meadows, lakes and rocky peaks. The tourism sector provides the principal form of employment, as does forest management.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The main objective of the reserve is to protect the alpine character of the highest range in the Carpathian mountain chain. The Tatras encompass five climatic zones and include plants from lower montane forests, subalpine forests, dwarf mountain pine, alpine grasslands and sub-nival habitats. Natural features within the reserve include karst topography with dolomites and limestone, canyons and waterfalls, a dwarf pine belt, alpine meadows, lakes and rocky peaks. Among the nearly 1,300 species of plants in the Tatras, the most valuable are 27 endemic and sub-endemic species. There are also numerous relics of Pliocene and glacial flora. Plant species include the European beech (Fagus sylvatica), mountain pine (Pinus mugo), highland rush (Juncus trifidus) and Oreochloa disticha. Numerous animal species are found in the reserve, including the largest European predators: the European brown bear (Ursus arctos arctos), the Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx) and the European wolf (Canis lupus lupus). High-altitude species such as the marmot (Marmota marmota), the snow vole (Chionomys nivalis) and the chamois (Rupicapra rupicapra) can also be found. Since 2000, the chamois population has increased by almost 850 due to the efforts of the Tatra Chamois Rescue Project.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Tatra

records.introduction_en: The Rocky Mountains Biosphere Reserve is located on the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains along the Continental Divide, 100 km north-west of Denver in Colorado. The biosphere reserve and national park is managed for nature conservation, environmental education and public recreation.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Three vegetation zones are represented within the altitudinal range of 2,328–4,345 m above sea level. The upper montane forest is characterised by ponderosa pine (Pinus ponderosa), shrublands, meadows and grasslands. The subalpine forest zone comprises mainly Engelmann spruce (Picea engelmannii) and fir (Abies lasiocarpa). The alpine tundra includes open stands of grasses, sedges, dwarf flowering plants and willows. Early meat and sport hunting drastically reduced large ungulate populations in the area. Wapiti (Cervus elaphus), reintroduced in 1913–14, has increased to a winter herd of about 1,500. Mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus) is now common, and about 350 bighorn sheep (Ovis canadensis) utilise the high-elevation ranges. Some species, however, such as grizzly bear (Ursus arctos), pronghorn (Antilocapra americana) and bison (Bison bison) never recovered.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Rocky Mountains

records.introduction_en: Big Bend Biosphere Reserve lies in the eponymous big bend of the Rio Grande in western Texas, United States of America. It is one of three biosphere reserves in the Chihuahuan Desert, alongside Jornada (United States) and Mapimí (Mexico). The landscape is marked by the Chisos Mountains rising above the desert and three deep canyons carved by the Rio Grande. The biosphere reserve’s objectives focus on deepening ties with surrounding communities to advance the site’s core functions. Through outreach, distance-learning and on-site collaboration, the reserve works to bridge geographic isolation and become a familiar local partner. Education and communication programmes support co-designed conservation, sustainable livelihoods and shared research and monitoring.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Big Bend Biosphere Reserve is a prime example of the Chihuahuan Desert region, enclosed on the west, south and east by the Rio Grande, which forms the U.S.–Mexico boundary and cuts three major canyons. The landscape is defined by the Chisos Mountains, rising several thousand feet above the desert floor. Four major vegetation zones occur, largely determined by elevation: shrub desert with succulents and open shrubs such as creosotebush (Larrea divaricata); grasslands with yucca, sotol (Dasylirion leiophyllum) and native grasses; woodlands of pinyon pine (Pinus cembroides), oak (Quercus) and juniper (Juniperus); and the narrow Rio Grande floodplain with cottonwood (Populus acuminata), reeds and willows. The fauna underscores the site’s conservation value, particularly along the river corridor. The Rio Grande holds the only known location for the endemic Chihuahuan shiner (Notropis chihuahua). The endemic fish Gambusia gaigei also occurs near the river. Two land snails are also endemic to Big Bend: Humboltiana edithae and Holospira yucatensis.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Big Bend

records.introduction_en: The Cascade Head Biosphere Reserve and Experimental Forest is situated 136 km south-west of Portland on the Pacific Coast. The Experimental Forest was established in 1934 for scientific studies of typical coastal Sitka spruce (Picea sitchensis) and western hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla) forests found along the Oregon Coast. Since then, the forest stands have been used for long-term studies, experimentation and ecosystem research.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Ecosystems represented in the biosphere reserve are very diverse. Two major prairie headlands jut out into the Pacific Ocean. The recently restored Salmon River estuary provides a critical juncture between fresh and salt water, and maintains staging areas for upstream spawning migrations of anadromous fish, as well as rearing areas for juveniles and smolts. The forested ecosystems include very productive young and mature, 150-year-old, stands of Sitka spruce–western hemlock and Douglas fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii) forests, with riparian areas and stream banks dominated by red alder. Spotted owl, marbled murrelet, coho salmon and Oregon silver spot butterfly are four federally listed endangered species that occur in the biosphere reserve.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Cascade Head

records.introduction_en: Crown of the Continent Biosphere Reserve and National Park, formerly known as Glacier until its renaming in 2017, is situated in north-western Montana in the northern Rocky Mountains, adjacent to the Canadian Waterton Biosphere Reserve. In 1932, Glacier and Waterton Lakes National Park were designated as Waterton–Glacier International Peace Park to celebrate the longstanding peace between the two nations. Glacier and Waterton have both been designated as biosphere reserves and as a single World Heritage Site.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Crown of the Continent ranges from 985–3,150 m in elevation and straddles the continental divide in the North American Rocky Mountains. Habitat variations include grasslands, conifer and deciduous forests, lakes, wide glacial valleys and steep alpine zones. There are approximately 1,270 vascular plant species, 272 bird species, 23 fish species and 63 mammal species. Threatened or endangered species include grizzly bears, Canada lynx, grey wolves and bull trout. Glacier National Park is surrounded by National Forest Service wilderness areas to the south and west, the Blackfeet Indian Reservation to the east, and Waterton Lakes National Park and Crown Forest Lands to the north in Canada. These lands collectively make up the protected lands in the Crown of the Continent ecosystem. The park sustains great biodiversity and intact land connectivity, allowing for species migration. It is a pristine laboratory for scientific studies of global climate change, snowpack, natural wildfire processes, species migration and population estimates, and water and air quality. Research includes ecosystem and species impacts of adjacent human activities such as energy development, resource use, fire management, invasive species control, and human population and economic growth. The park has a wealth of baseline data collected over the past 100 years.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Crown of the Continent

records.introduction_en: The Golden Gate Biosphere Reserve is a partnership of 13 protected areas in the greater San Francisco Bay area. It extends through the central California coastal region from the Bodega Research Reserve in the north to Jasper Ridge in the south. It also includes the Farallon Islands, Angel Island and Alcatraz within the San Francisco Bay.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Golden Gate Biosphere Reserve is situated on both sides of the San Andreas Fault. Each side has a completely different type of bedrock, and the western side of the rift is moving northward. Habitats in the biosphere reserve are diverse. They include mixed evergreen, redwood, Douglas fir, Bishop pine and oak forests, and woodlands and savannas, as well as coastal scrub and chaparral. Coastal dune and coastal strand habitats, tide pools and kelp forests, and grasslands and marshes are also present. The associated fauna is also rich, with cougars, tule elk, California sea lions, elephant seals, many shorebirds and the California red-legged frog.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Golden Gate

records.introduction_en: Isle Royale Biosphere Reserve and National Park is a remote island archipelago situated in the north-western part of Lake Superior in Michigan. The park offers outstanding opportunities for research in a remote ecosystem where human influences are limited.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Isle Royale Biosphere Reserve is world-renowned for its long-term wolf (Canis lupus) and moose (Alces alces) predator–prey study. Vegetation is mainly boreal conifer and northern hardwood forest. In the cooler, wetter areas near Lake Superior, balsam fir (Abies balsamea), white spruce (Picea glauca) and Betula papyrifera dominate the mature forest. Sugar maple (Acer saccharum) and yellow birch (Betula alleghaniensis) dominate the warmer, drier sites in the interior of the biosphere reserve. The area’s waters contain the most productive native fishery and genetically diverse trout populations in Lake Superior.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Isle Royale

records.introduction_en: The Jornada has served as a field research laboratory since its establishment in 1912. The varied scientific activities on the range throughout this century have led to important discoveries about desert ecosystems. These findings have underpinned principles of land management with application around the globe. This region is probably the most extensively studied desert on earth.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Jornada Biosphere Reserve is one of three biosphere reserves representing the Chihuahuan Desert, alongside Big Bend Biosphere Reserve in western Texas and Mapimí Biosphere Reserve in Mexico. The area extends from the crest of the San Andres Mountains, which are dominated by shrub woodlands, to the Jornada Plains, which are characterised by semi-desert grasslands. Twenty-two different soil types are present on the Jornada Plain. These soils have almost no humus or organic matter, and there is little change in texture between surface soil and subsoil. Lime content is high in all soil types. Through time, lime from the soil and from calcareous dust has leached downward and been deposited at the depth to which rainfall normally penetrates, from a few inches to several feet. This zone of lime accumulation, or caliche layer, is often so thick and dense that penetration by water or roots is severely limited.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Jornada

records.introduction_en: Set in the southern Sierra Nevada of California between the San Joaquin and the Owens valleys, the Sequoia-Kings Canyon Biosphere Reserve covers dramatic mountain terrain cut by the Kern, Kaweah and Kings rivers. The reserve is significant for intact, connected habitats and range-edge biodiversity within the southern Sierra Nevada ecoregion. Its objectives focus on safeguarding naturally-functioning mountain ecosystems, supporting long-term research and monitoring, and providing education and nature-based recreation that benefit neighbouring communities.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Sequoia-Kings Canyon Biosphere Reserve brings four of the world’s five biomes into close proximity across a dramatic vertical relief reaching about 4,000 metres: aquatic, grassland-savanna, forest and tundra. Lower slopes carry oak woodland with blue oak (Quercus douglasii) and interior live oak (Q. wislizenii), with chaparral shrubland dominated by Adenostoma fasciculatum and Arctostaphylos viscida. Mid-elevations hold mixed conifer forest with white fir (Abies concolor), ponderosa pine (Pinus ponderosa), red fir (Abies magnifica) and montane meadows. Upper zones support subalpine forest and meadows, krummholz and true alpine habitats. Granitic and karst geology has produced extensive cave systems that support specialised subterranean fauna alongside diverse aquatic and terrestrial communities. Botanical diversity is high with some 120 plant families and 2,175 species; the reserve is home to giant sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum), the largest tree on Earth. Low fragmentation by roads and settlement allows movement between neighbouring habitat belts and maintains ecological connectivity where major Californian ecological zones meet. Across the Sierra Nevada, environmental changes are altering biological and hydrogeologic systems, and the Sequoia-Kings Canyon Biosphere Reserve feels these pressures. Trends include reductions in glacial mass, reduced snowpack at lower elevations, increased conifer mortality, denser forests and shrublands linked to altered fire regimes, and range shifts in small mammals.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Sequoia-Kings Canyon

records.introduction_en: This cluster biosphere reserve is in south-east California and comprises four management units: Death Valley National Monument, Joshua Tree National Monument, the Santa Rosa Mountains Wildlife Management Area and Anza Borrego Desert State Park.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Death Valley, the principal feature of the biosphere reserve, encompasses a substantial part of the northern Mojave Desert. Its extreme altitude range, from 86 m below sea level to 3,368 metres above sea level, results in a large diversity of features at the northern edge of this biogeographic region. Rugged, sparsely vegetated mountains border a north–south-oriented valley and are incised by numerous deep rocky canyons that terminate in huge alluvial fans. Lower and middle elevations are dominated by shrubs such as creosote bush (Larrea divaricata), sagebrush (Atriplex), Mormon tea (Ephedra) and blackbrush (Coleogyne ramosissima). Trees include Utah juniper (Juniperus osteosperma) and one-needle pine (Pinus monophylla). Joshua Tree National Monument, east of Los Angeles, straddles the transition area between the Mojave and Colorado Deserts. It is known for its Joshua tree (Yucca brevifolia) woodlands, a typical feature of the Mojave Desert, which is higher, moister and slightly cooler. There are also characteristic species of the lower Colorado Desert, including Washingtonia.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mojave and Colorado Deserts

records.introduction_en: The University of Michigan Biological Station and Biosphere Reserve is located at the northern tip of the Lower Peninsula of Michigan, on the southern shore of Douglas Lake. Since its establishment in 1909, the biological station has continually served as an instructional and research centre for students and scientists from around the world.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is located in the northern hardwood forest ecosystem. It comprises forests of beech–maple and successional stages of aspen, oak and pine on the better-drained soils. Moister habitats have spruce, fir and cedar forests. Wetlands include bogs, fens, swamps, marshes and numerous lakes.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Obtawaing

records.introduction_en: Situated in the Eastern Carpathians, the Carpathian Biosphere Reserve encompasses foothill oak groves, mountain beech, mixed and spruce forests, pine–alder alpine elfin woodland, subalpine and alpine meadows, and upland rocky–lichen landscapes. The biosphere reserve protects the largest massif of virgin beech forests in Europe, the Uholsko-Shyrokoluzhanskyi massif, as well as the Valley of Narcissi. Since 28 June 2007, it has formed part of the serial UNESCO World Natural Heritage site within the Ukrainian–Slovak nomination “Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians”.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Carpathian Biosphere Reserve plays a significant role in biodiversity conservation in the region, and its know-how and capacity allow it to fulfil this function. It covers all the natural–climatic zones of the southern macro slope of the Ukrainian Carpathians, from the Transcarpathian lowland up to the alpine belt at 180–2,061 m above sea level, and fully represents the region’s landscape and biological diversity. Slightly disturbed and practically undisturbed pre-montane oak forests, mountain beech, mixed and pure spruce forests, and subalpine meadows with pine–alder crooked woodland and rocky–lichen landscapes are found here. Viable populations of large carnivores such as wolf, lynx and bear are well preserved. In total, 3,022 plant species are recorded, of which 1,353 are higher vascular plants. There are 315 vertebrate animal species, including 66 mammals, 195 birds, nine reptiles, 14 amphibians, 29 fishes and one cyclostomatous species, as well as about 15,000 invertebrates protected within the biosphere reserve. The most well-preserved Carpathian ecosystems are represented here, providing shelter for many rare and endangered plants and animals. In all, 197 plant species, including fungi, and 248 animal species are listed in the Red Book of Ukraine, the European Red Lists, the International Red Book and other conservation lists valid in Ukraine.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Carpathian

records.introduction_en: Located in the north-western part of Serbia, Backo Podunavlje Biosphere Reserve covers 176,635 ha and extends over the alluvial zones of the central Danube plain. It consists of remnants of historic floodplains and human-made landscapes shaped by agriculture and settlements. The floodplain includes alluvial forests, marshes, reed beds, freshwater habitats, alluvial wetlands and flood-protected forests. The main activities are agriculture, forestry and industry.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve encompasses the largest conserved floodplain complex in the upper course of the Danube River in Serbia, and one of the largest floodplains along the middle section of the Danube. It is surrounded by traditional villages and settlements. The area combines ecological conditions at the contact zone between the Central European and South-Eastern European forest zone with steppes. It also has characteristic hydrological dynamics. Together with complex, centuries-long human influences, these factors have produced very rich and specific diversity of landscapes, habitats and species. Primary habitats include alluvial forests, Pannonian salt steppes and salt marshes, mesotrophic standing waters, natural eutrophic lakes and muddy river shores. They also include alluvial wetlands, wet meadows, sand deposits, river islets, sand shores, floodplains, oxbows, abandoned riverbeds and meanders. The floodplain hosts rich fauna, notably Bechstein’s bat (Myotis bechsteinii), otter (Lutra lutra) and red deer (Cervus elaphus). One Prime Butterfly Area exists in the biosphere reserve: Gornje Podunavlje. In total, 156 taxa of butterflies have been recorded in this area. The floodplain is also very important as a fish spawning site.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Backo Podunavlje

records.introduction_en: Juzur Farasan Biosphere Reserve is a remote archipelago of more than 170 islands and islets formed from uplifted fossil coral reef in the Red Sea. The two main islands, Farasan al Kabir and As Saqid, are surrounded by shallow waters less than 11 metres deep, natural submerged ridges and fringing coral reefs with mangrove stands, seagrass meadows, salt marsh and extensive algal communities. The reserve’s long-term goal is to protect its terrestrial and marine ecosystems and the unique species they host, to sustain and improve ecosystem services, and to support the well-being of island communities through sustainable development.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The islands lie on the Arabian continental shelf where shallow seas and seasonal currents drive highly productive ecosystems. Reef flats and slopes host hard corals such as Porites, Platygyra, Acropora and Stylophora, and soft corals including Xenia. Mangroves occur on at least fifteen of Juzur Farasan’s northern islands. The islands host rich marine life, including reef fishes, pelagic species, manta rays (Manta birostris) and whale sharks (Rhincodon typus), along with dugong (Dugong dugon) and two marine turtles that are common in the area, the green turtle (Chelonia mydas) and the hawksbill (Eretmochelys imbricata). Ecosystem services are wide ranging. Reefs and macroalgal communities recycle nutrients and provide richly productive habitat, while winter currents bring nutrient-rich waters that attract plankton feeders and underpin fisheries. Seagrass and mangroves stabilise coasts, trap sediments and support nurseries for commercially valuable fish, shrimp and pearl oysters, sustaining both biodiversity and local livelihoods. On land, over half of the surface is subtropical desert with ancient reef pavements, shallow soils and pockets of denser scrub in gullies and silt pans. Characteristic plants include Acacia ehrenbergiana, Salvadora persica and Capparis sinaica. The Farasan idmi gazelle (Gazella arabica farasani) represents the largest wild population in Saudi Arabia, and uses broken coral ridges and acacia groves for forage and shelter. The islands lie on a major migration flyway and hold important breeding colonies of Goliath heron (Ardea goliath), pink-backed pelican (Pelecanus rufescens) and crab plover (Dromas ardeola), with regionally significant numbers of Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus).
records.name: Juzur Farasan

records.introduction_en: Located in north-western Saudi Arabia within the Al Ula region, the Harrat Uwayrid Biosphere Reserve lies in the hot desert biome of the Middle East and Western Asia. It is set among towering sandstone mountains, a lush oasis valley and ancient cultural heritage sites dating back thousands of years. Key objectives include rebalancing the fragile desert ecosystem by reintroducing native flora and fauna and addressing recent human impacts; strengthening knowledge through targeted, interdisciplinary research on ecosystem functions and traditional land uses; and improving data on geological formations and landscape features. In parallel, it aims to raise local awareness and build a sense of ownership that secures long-term community support.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set in the hot desert biome of the Middle East and Western Asia, Harrat Uwayrid is the largest of five nature reserves in the AlUla region. The landscape combines features of the Arabian Desert and Palearctic bioregions and forms a mosaic of habitats, from open gravel plains and water-draining wadis to high-altitude rocky slopes and traditional date palm groves. Vegetation falls broadly into four types: deserts and scarcely vegetated areas; dwarf shrublands; woodlands and xeromorphic shrublands at higher elevations; and wadi communities.The reserve is home to globally critically endangered fauna, notably the Arabian leopard, and supports Arabian gazelle populations, alongside several endemic plant species. Characteristic plants include Sinai thyme (Thymus decussatus). The reserve’s ecosystems provide essential services that sustain local livelihoods and bolster long-term landscape resilience including climate moderation, water purification, and soil and flood control.
records.name: Harrat Uwayrid

records.introduction_en: Located in north-central Saudi Arabia, the Imam Turki Bin Abdullah Biosphere Reserve covers nearly 5% of the country. Declared protected by Royal Decree in 2018, it encompasses vast desert, steppe, basaltic plateaus, wadis, and Acacia savannahs, making it one of the Kingdom’s most significant conservation landscapes.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve harbors 41 mammal species, including the Sand Gazelle (Gazella marica), Arabian Oryx (Oryx leucoryx), and Caracal (Caracal caracal). Avifauna includes the Asian Houbara (Chlamydotis macqueenii, Vulnerable [VU]), Steppe Eagle (Aquila nipalensis, Endangered [EN]), and Eastern Imperial Eagle (Aquila heliaca), as well as endemic species such as the Arabian Green Bee-eater (Merops cyanophrys) and Arabian Lark (Eremalauda eremodites). The reserve also supports 30 reptile species, including the Egyptian Spiny-tailed Lizard (Uromastyx aegyptiaca, Vulnerable [VU]), alongside diverse desert-adapted flora.
records.name: Imam Turki Bin Abdullah

records.introduction_en: Blekinge Archipelago includes most of the coastal areas and archipelagos of Blekinge in the south-east of Sweden. The biosphere reserve comprises granite coastlines and an accompanying archipelago with a variety of islands and islets. The area is marked by rich natural and cultural heritage, and by strong local commitment to maintaining the region’s social and economic dynamics through innovative thinking and entrepreneurship. This development goes hand in hand with energy-efficient and environmentally friendly technologies. Municipalities and universities are carrying out joint research on the sustainable use of coastal resources.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The many shallow and highly desalinated bays, lagoons and estuaries along the coast are important spawning and nursery areas for several fish species. They are also internationally significant stopping and overwintering grounds for several seabird species. The area’s importance for fish and birds has led to Ramsar designations, including Mörrum River and Pukavik Bay, and three separate areas within the Blekinge Archipelago. Threatened oak-living species in the area include the stag beetle (Lucanus cervus), the hermit beetle (Osmoderma eremita), the warted oak polypore (Inonotus dryadeus), the lacquered bracket (Ganoderma resinaceum) and the lichen (Lecanographa illecebrosa). The unique wealth of species in the Mörrum River is equally important for the preservation of biological diversity. A genetically unique strain of salmon (Salmo salar) is crucial for the presence of salmon in the whole southern Baltic Sea and is therefore of high economic value. The shallow, partly fresh and brackish coves are valuable spawning and growth areas for fish such as northern pike (Esox lucius), European perch (Perca fluviatilis) and Atlantic herring (Clupea harengus). These coves are of significant ecological and economic value. They are simultaneously of great importance for several species of stopping and overwintering seabirds. The shallow coves also host the alga Baltic stonewort (Chara horrida), which is endemic to the Baltic Sea.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Blekinge Archipelago

records.introduction_en: Samba Dia Biosphere Reserve is located on the Atlantic coast within the West African woodland savannah. The flat plain lies only 5–10 m above sea level and contains one of the best remaining stands of the once widespread Borassus aethiopum communities. In addition to these palm stands, there are populations of Acacia seyal, Combretum glutinosumand Anogeissus leiocarpus.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The coastal zone forest is dominated by Borassus aethiopum, with Acacia seyal, Combretum glutinosum and Anogeissus leiocarpus. The Sahelo-Sudanian savannah is characterised by Acacia seyal, A. senegal, A. albida, Borassus flabellifer and Detarium microcarpum. Agroecosystems are also present.
records.name: Samba Dia

records.introduction_en: Located in the eastern part of the country, this biosphere reserve includes the largest preserved complex of floodplains in Slovenia. Here, the interweaving of natural factors and human presence has created an exceptional cultural riverine landscape. The main sources of income for residents are agriculture, industry, forestry and tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: According to the classification of the EU’s Natura 2000 network, the biosphere reserve lies within the Continental Biogeographic Region. The area contains rivers with muddy banks with Chenopodion rubri and Bidention vegetation, alluvial forests with black alder (Alnus glutinosa) and common ash (Fraxinus excelsior), and watercourses from plain to montane levels with Ranunculion fluitantis and Callitricho-Batrachion vegetation. It also includes hydrophilous tall-herb fringe communities in the plains and at montane to alpine levels, and lowland hay meadows with meadow foxtail (Alopecurus pratensis) and great burnet (Sanguisorba officinalis). Riparian mixed forest features pedunculate oak (Quercus robur), European white elm (Ulmus laevis) and ash (Fraxinus). There are natural eutrophic lakes with Magnopotamion or Hydrocharition-type vegetation, molinia meadows on calcareous, peaty or clayey-silt-laden soils, and Illyrian oak–hornbeam forest. It encompasses a large number of habitat types important at national and international levels in the Continental Biogeographic Region and in Europe, particularly wetlands and floodplain forests. Due to complex ecological conditions, the core area is a mosaic of well-preserved characteristic habitats of the middle sections of dynamic river floodplains, which demonstrates its high ecological value. Owing to these conditions and low-intensity management, the core area contains very old stands of floodplain forests, especially white willow, common oak and black and white poplar. The buffer zone comprises a wide variety of habitats. These include wetlands, agricultural land with significant areas of natural vegetation, transitional woodland–scrubs, natural grasslands, a mosaic of agricultural landscapes with fragmented plots, w … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mura River

records.introduction_en: The territory of the biosphere reserve is bounded by the Savinja and Sotla rivers. It is a colourful mosaic between the Alpine and Pannonian worlds, resulting in a unique landscape. Hills, ravines, gorges, rock outcrops, karst hollows, caves and abysses, waterfalls, springs and meanders, along with numerous fossil remains, meadow orchards and dry meadows, form a natural environment that is home to exceptional plant and animal species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area is one of the most important nature conservation areas in Slovenia in terms of biotic diversity. The landscape is an extraordinary mosaic of pre-Alpine mixed forest, upland meadows, meadow orchards and flatlands along the Sotla River. Numerous torrential ravines, streams, springs, tufa waterfalls and other waterfalls, swamps, oxbows, backwaters and gravel banks provide exceptional and increasingly rare habitats for unusual animal and plant species. These species have great importance not only within the framework of the area, but are also extremely important for the wider European region.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Kozjansko & Obsotelje

records.introduction_en: Doi Chiang Dao Biosphere Reserve lies in Chiang Dao District, Chiang Mai Province, in northern Thailand. The reserve is situated where the towering limestone massif rises within the Upper Ping River Basin. Spanning an altitudinal range from low valleys to a unique subalpine zone in Thailand, it protects an exceptional continuum of evergreen and deciduous forests, wetlands and karst caves. The reserve aims to safeguard the unique sub-alpine and forest ecosystems and the headwaters of the Ping, build its role as a hub for scientific study and learning, and support local livelihoods through carefully managed nature-based tourism and certified good agricultural practice.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: With a significant altitudinal range, the reserve supports seven main ecosystem types: subalpine vegetation, hill evergreen forest, dry evergreen forest, lower montane coniferous forest, mixed deciduous forest, dry dipterocarp forest and wetlands. Wetlands include natural streams, swamps, springs and marshes alongside man-made paddy fields, ponds and reservoirs. The subalpine zone is unique in Thailand and shows floristic continuity with the Himalaya and southern China. Botanical diversity exceeds 2,000 plant species, around a fifth of Thailand’s flora, and the site is recognised as an Important Plant Area. Notable threatened flora in the core zone include four endangered orchids: Paphiopedilum bellatulum, Papilionanthe biswasiana, Sirindhornia pulchella and Vanda coerulea. At least thirty endemic plants are recorded, including Trachycarpus oreophilus and Impatiens chiangdaoensis. Faunal interest includes three IUCN-listed threatened turtles and tortoises: big-headed turtle (Platysternon megacephalum), elongated tortoise (Indotestudo elongata) and impressed tortoise (Manouria impressa). Steep karst topography, with horseshoe limestone ridges, lapies and sinkholes, shapes a distinctive hydrology. Rainwater rapidly percolates to feed extensive caves, notably Tham Luang Chiang Dao, and underground streams such as Huai Nalu and Mae Pha. These headwaters contribute to the Ping River, sustaining flows to Chiang Dao and Chiang Mai and, via the Chao Phraya system, to the central plains. The reserve therefore plays an important role in water regulation and catchment resilience.
records.name: Doi Chiang Dao

records.introduction_en: Declared as a biosphere reserve in 1997, the Ranong Biosphere Reserve is situated 650 km south of Bangkok along the Andaman coast of the isthmus of Thailand. The reserve incorporates a range of diversified natural and disturbed habitats, including mangrove forests, tropical evergreen forests, open sea, seagrass beds, and urban and agricultural land. Mangroves are the most representative ecosystem within this biosphere reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This biosphere reserve covers about 30,000 ha, of which 40 per cent is marine area. It consists of a narrow coastal plain characterised by many waterways and mangrove forests that reach out to the sea towards seagrass beds at a depth of 10 m. The Njao area and Laem Son National Park are contiguous to Ranong, and hence there is a continuum of protected habitats going from the mountain ecosystem down to the coast and sea. Within the reserve, over 300 species of fauna have been identified, including the dugong (Dugong dugon), and more than 50 species of mangroves. The Ranong Biosphere Reserve currently exists as the largest continuous stand of mangroves within Thailand and is an important nexus for mangrove-related research regionally.
records.name: Ranong

records.introduction_en: The Tatra Mountains are the highest mountains in the long Carpathian range, which stretches from Slovakia into Romania via Hungary, Poland and Ukraine. The territory of the biosphere reserve covers two national parks on each side of the political boundary between Poland and Slovakia. A variety of natural features are represented within this transboundary biosphere reserve, including karst topography with dolomites and limestone, canyons and waterfalls, a dwarf pine belt, alpine meadows, lakes and rocky peaks. The tourism sector provides the principal form of employment, as well as forest management.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The main objective of the reserve is to protect the alpine character of the highest range in the Carpathian Mountain chain. The Tatras cover five climatic zones including plants from lower montane forests, subalpine forests, dwarf mountain pine, alpine grasslands and sub-nival. A variety of natural features are represented within this reserve, such as karst topography with dolomites and limestone, canyons and waterfalls, a dwarf pine belt, alpine meadows, lakes and rocky peaks.Among the nearly 1,300 species of plants in the Tatras, the most valuable are 27 endemic and sub-endemic species. There are also numerous relics of Pliocene and glacial flora. Plant species include the European beech (Fagus sylvatica), the mountain pine (Pinus mugo), the highland rush (Juncus trifidus) and theOreochla disticha.Numerous animal species are found in the reserve, including the largest European predators: the European brown bear (Ursus arctos arctos), the Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx) and the European wolf (Canis lupus lupus). High-altitude species such as the marmot (Marmota marmota), the snow vole (Chionomys nivalis) and the chamois (Rupicapra rupicapra) can also be found. Since 2000, the Chamois population has increased by almost 850 due to the efforts of the Tatra Chamois Rescue Project.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Tatra

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve is a broken hilly area, mainly at altitudes of about 450 metres above sea level, with two permanent rivers. The mountain range within the biosphere reserve forms a watershed that divides the Central African and Sudanese hydrographic systems.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Dominant tree species are Terminalia brownii, Combretum, Anogeissus leiocarpusand Isoberlinia doka. Endangered woodland and plain mammalian species include the elephant (Loxodonta africana) and the giraffe (Giraffa camelopardalis).
records.name: Radom

records.introduction_en: Ichkeul Biosphere Reserve lies about 25 km south-west of Bizerte in northern Tunisia and comprises a wooded massif (Djebel Ichkeul) and a brackish water body (Lake Ichkeul). The reserve is a major stopover and wintering area for birds and is designated as a Ramsar Site. The Ichkeul Biosphere Reserve’s key objectives include restoring marshes and safeguarding bird habitats, managing land-use needs with local communities, and grounding decisions in long-term research, monitoring and education.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Ichkeul brings together a lake, surrounding marshes and the Djebel Ichkeul massif in a single wetland–mountain system. The lake basin is Quaternary alluvium, with marshes fringing the shores, while the Djebel mountain is Triassic–Jurassic limestone. The climate is typically semi-arid and vegetation is dominated by characteristic Mediterranean species. Seasonal freshwater inflows and the sea connection shape the site’s ecology, causing salinity and water levels to fluctuate through the year and driving aquatic plant growth and waterbird abundance. Ichkeul wetland is one of the most important sites in the Mediterranean for wintering Palaearctic waterfowl, with records of up to 300,000–400,000 birds present at one time. Habitats include aquatic meadows, marshes, cliffs and scrub. Notable groups are ducks and geese, coots, waders, herons and egrets, storks, spoonbills and flamingos. Raptors recorded include peregrine and kestrel, Bonelli’s eagle and short-toed snake eagle. Plant life of note includes Potamogeton pectinatus, Scirpus maritimus and orchids (Ophrys, Orchis).
records.name: Ichkeul

records.introduction_en: The Camili Biosphere Reserve is located in north-east Türkiye in the Colchic sub-region of the Euro-Siberian phytogeographic area. Mountains surround Camili on three sides, and the Georgian border forms the northern edge of the reserve. The topography of the north-west side of the Camili Biosphere Reserve is characterised by the Karçal Mountains, at 3,415 m above sea level, while three main valleys are found within the reserve: Uğur–Maral, Efeler and Düzenli.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The main ecosystem types in the Camili Biosphere Reserve are boreal coniferous forests and temperate deciduous forests. Tree species include black alder (Alnus glutinosa), oriental spruce (Picea orientalis), Caucasus lime tree (Tilia rubra caucasicus) and sessile oak (Quercus petraea). In addition, the Camili basin forms part of the Karçal Mountains Important Plant Area, one of the 122 most important botanical sites identified by WWF in Türkiye. The basin is also the only region where the Caucasus bee has remained untouched and genetically pure, making it one of the world’s three most important bee species. The Camili Biosphere Reserve lies on an important bird migration route on the east side of the Black Sea, where two Important Bird Areas (IBA) are identified: the Eastern Black Sea Mountains IBA and the Karçal Mountains IBA. Bird species common to the reserve include the common blackbird (Turdus merula), coal tit (Parus ater) and common raven (Corvus corax). There is also a large population of bark beetles that threaten regional forest ecosystems in Camili. Lastly, some fauna species in the reserve are categorised as endangered, including the Caucasian salamander (Mertensiella caucasica) and the European tree frog (Hyla arborea).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Camili

records.introduction_en: The North-East Tobago reserve is located in the south-east Caribbean Sea in Trinidad and Tobago. The reserve encompasses a large marine and terrestrial area. Included in this reserve is one of the oldest legally protected tropical forests, the Tobago Main Ridge Forest Reserve, created in 1776. A total of 1,774 species are protected in this reserve, with 83 on the IUCN Red List, 41 endemic species, 13 EDGE criteria species, 48 international migratory CMS criteria species and 120 CITES criteria species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere’s 19 distinct habitat types are home to globally unique and endangered species. The avifauna is distinct. Two species of avifauna stand out in this region: the charismatic Trinidad motmot (Momotus bahamensis) and the less conspicuous Tobago greenlet (Hylophilus insularis). Both of these species are endemic. However, the highest faunal endemism is found among the herpetofauna, which include three snakes, one lizard and four frogs. This reserve is home to one of the last remnants of a dry tropical forest in the Caribbean. The Tobago Main Ridge Forest Reserve is the oldest legally protected tropical forest and has been protected since 1776.
records.name: North-East Tobago

records.introduction_en: At 4,000 km², Mount Elgon has the largest volcanic base in the world. Located on the Uganda–Kenya border, it is also the oldest and largest solitary volcanic mountain in East Africa. Its vast form, 80 km in diameter, rises more than 3,000 m above the surrounding plains. The mountain’s cool heights offer respite from the hot plains below, and the higher altitudes provide a refuge for flora and fauna.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Mount Elgon National Park is home to more than 300 species of birds, such as Jackson’s Francolin and Black-collared Apalis. Among those limited to just a few mountains in eastern Uganda are the Black-shouldered Kite and Tacazze Sunbird. Mount Elgon is one of the few places in Uganda where the endangered Lammergeyer can be seen, soaring above the caldera and Suam Gorge. The area also supports a variety of wildlife, including rock and tree hyraxes, blue monkeys, elephant, buffalo, Defassa waterbuck, oribi, bushbuck, duiker, forest hog, bush pig, leopard, civet and serval cats, spotted hyena, aardvark and several rodent species.
records.name: Mount Elgon

records.introduction_en: The name of this biosphere reserve reflects the fact that Venezuela’s most important headwaters and initial tributaries of the Orinoco River are located here. The Orinoco is the main and most abundant body of water in the country, on which most land-use planning programmes of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela are based.
