In this area, the hydrographic basins of the Orinoco River and the Amazon River are interconnected through the Casiquiare Branch, a hydrographic phenomenon of great scientific interest.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is one of the tropical forest areas with the least intensity of intervention. Despite deficiencies in baseline information about biology and ecology, a high level of biological diversity and endemism is evident. There are no fewer than 4,000 species of vascular plants, with some 500 endemic species, which so far have not been fully inventoried. The presence of the tonina (Inia geoffrensis), the giant water dog (Pteronura brasiliensis), the Orinoco caiman, the arrau turtle (Podocnemis expansa) in danger of extinction, and the danto (Tapirus terrestris), among others, has been reported. However, the official lists are not systematised to date.
records.name: Alto Orinoco-Casiquiare

records.introduction_en: The terrain comprises mountains with severe to moderate slopes. The maximum slope exceeds 70 per cent in some areas, especially in the north and north-east, as well as on the western side. The rock ratio ranges between 50–90 per cent. There are bare and semi-bare rocks. The highest elevation above sea level is 2,200 metres, in the north-east boundary of the area near Azzan Mountain. The lowest elevation above sea level is 200 metres on the south-west side near Wadi Alaswad.
records.name: Bura’a

records.introduction_en: The Cape Winelands Biosphere Reserve is in the Western Cape Province of South Africa, approximately 40 km east of Cape Town. The reserve extends northwards from the Kogelberg Biosphere Reserve in the south, along the Cape Fold Belt Mountain Chain and adjoining valleys that constitute the Cape Winelands. It incorporates key portions of the registered Cape Floral Region Protected Areas World Heritage Site. The area is characterised by a mosaic of diverse ecosystems and physiographic environments, and a range of land uses and human settlement patterns associated with the renowned Cape Winelands viticultural landscape. It includes an array of historic towns, hamlets and farmsteads.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The topography is characterised by diverse features ranging from the high Cape Fold mountains and deep valleys to rolling hills and open plains. The mountain complex that forms the core of the biosphere reserve results from the meeting of two axes of the Cape Fold Belt Mountain Chain and provides a range of habitats and landscape features. The area lies within the Cape Floristic Region, or Cape Floral Kingdom, which is the smallest of the world’s six floral kingdoms. The Cape Floristic Region sustains 20 per cent of the total number of plant species found on the African continent. It has five endemic and two near-endemic plant families, and 988 plant genera containing nearly 9,000 species of vascular plants. Main vegetation types in the region include fynbos, succulent Karoo and renosterveld. A high species richness of birds, mammals, frogs, reptiles and insects is found in the fynbos biome. Bird species typical of the Cape mountains include the hamerkop (Scopus umbretta) and the Cape eagle-owl (Bubo capensis). Medium-sized species occurring in the area include the leopard (Panthera pardus), the caracal (Caracal caracal), and the klipspringer (Oreotragus oreotragus). Smaller animals include the baboon (Papio ursinus), the honey badger (Mellivora capensis) and the striped polecat (Ictonyx striatus). South Africa has the highest tortoise diversity in the world. The Western Cape in particular is home to one of the world’s top 25 endangered turtles. The endangered geometric tortoise (Psammobates geometricus) is endemic to the renosterveld of the area. The Cape Winelands Biosphere Reserve forms part of the Cape Floral Region, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
records.name: Cape Winelands

records.introduction_en: Kogelberg Biosphere Reserve was the first South African biosphere reserve and is situated in the Western Cape Province about 40 km from Cape Town. It covers 103,629 ha, of which more than 80 per cent is mountainous landscape that ranges from high mountain peaks and deep valleys to gentle hills and lower mountain slopes. The remaining area consists of a gently rolling coastal plain and a marine area of about 24,500 ha, with a mostly rocky coastline and sandy beaches and estuaries.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Over 80 per cent of the Kogelberg Biosphere Reserve is a mountainous landscape. It varies from rugged terrain in the core area, with high mountain peaks and deep valleys, to gentle hills and lower mountain slopes. The marine environment forms part of the warm temperate south coast and is subject to nutrient-upwelling events that support a highly productive and diverse marine community. The area constitutes the floristic heart of the Cape Floral Kingdom, the smallest of the world’s floral kingdoms, and provides habitats for approximately 1,600 plant species. An estimated 150 taxa are endemic to the area and characteristic of the Fynbos biome. Fynbos is the predominant vegetation type and includes both montane and coastal forms. Characteristic Cape flora includes the Proteaceae, Ericaceae, Restionaceae and Bruniaceae. An area on the coast near Betty’s Bay provides habitat for a small colony of the jackass penguin (Spheniscus demersus). This species is listed in both the South African Red Data Book and the World Checklist of Threatened Birds. Other animals include the leopard (Panthera pardus), greater flamingo (Phoenicopterus ruber) and the endangered Cape platanna (Xenopus gilli).
records.name: Kogelberg

records.introduction_en: Vhembe Biosphere Reserve is located in the north-east of South Africa near the borders with Botswana, Mozambique and Zimbabwe. The reserve includes the northern part of Kruger National Park, Mapungubwe National Park and World Heritage Site, several provincial nature reserves, two recognised centres of biodiversity and endemism, Soutpansberg and Blouberg, and the Makgabeng Plateau, which contains more than 1,000 rock art sites. The area has a relatively large and rapidly growing human population with a high unemployment rate, which has a severe negative impact on natural resources that are harvested in an unsustainable manner.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Vhembe Biosphere Reserve includes Mapungubwe National Park and the Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape World Heritage Site, the Makgabeng Plateau with its outstanding concentration of San rock art, and the Blouberg and Soutpansberg mountain ranges with their remarkable biological diversity and endemism. It also encompasses the semi-arid Limpopo River Valley with its unique floristic and faunal composition, and the subtropical northern part of the Greater Kruger National Park with its high diversity of ecosystem types and species, vast floodplains and associated unique habitats and species. The reserve comprises three biomes, namely savannah, grassland and forest, with four bioregions that are home to 23 different vegetation types or biotopes. Eight of these biotopes are endemic to South Africa. The area also constitutes a biogeographical node that includes the Kalahari and Lowveld bioregions, which are characterised by temperate and tropical climatic conditions. These zones feature a wide range of ecologically important interactions that need to be protected to ensure conservation viability. The area has a rich biodiversity that includes 250 species of butterfly, 44 species of amphibians, 140 species of reptiles, 542 species of birds and 152 species of mammals. These include the Maquassie musk shrew (Crocidura maquassiensis), the yellow golden mole (Calchochloris obturirostris), the eland (Taurotragus oryx), the rufous hairy bat (Myotis bocagei) and the Sykes monkey (Cercopithecus albogularis). The Vhembe Biosphere Reserve includes a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape, and a Ramsar site, the Makuleke Wetlands.
records.name: Vhembe

records.introduction_en: The Kempen-Broek Biosphere Reserve is part of a transboundary area that straddles the border between Flanders in Belgium and the Netherlands. Once-expansive wetlands have been transformed into farmland since the nineteenth century, but the area retains remnants of its marshes, punctuated by ponds, open marshlands and bog forests. Villages and towns are scattered on higher ground. Diverse bird species flourish across varied landscapes. The area constitutes an important open space with high landscape and biodiversity value.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The region is renowned as one of Belgium’s prime habitats for dragonflies. Its stream valleys feature meadows and fields, while the higher elevations are mostly used for agriculture. Towards the north, vast expanses of moorland and inland dunes preserve intriguing prehistoric sites. Due to its rich biodiversity, the area has an important role in the conservation of habitats and species in Flanders.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Kempen-Broek

records.introduction_en: The Al Jabal Al Akhdar Biosphere Reserve, located in the Sultanate of Oman, is a mountainous ecosystem of global ecological and cultural significance. Located in the Western Hajar Mountains, it features high-altitude juniper forests, fertile valleys, terraced agriculture, and diverse wildlife, including endemic and endangered species such as the Arabian Tahr. The Biosphere Reserve integrates natural and cultural heritage, with local communities practicing traditional agriculture, pastoralism, and craft industries that have shaped the landscape for centuries.Its zoning ensures the protection of sensitive ecosystems while supporting sustainable human use. Management involves government bodies, local communities, research institutions, NGOs, and the private sector working together to balance environmental protection with social and economic progress.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Al Jabal Al Akhdar Biosphere Reserve is defined by rugged mountains, deep valleys, and varied geological formations. Peaks exceeding 2,400 meters are interspersed with fertile wadis, including Wadi Bani Kharus, Wadi Mistal, Wadi Bani Habib, and Wadi Al Ain, which support terraced agriculture through the traditional falaj irrigation system. Evergreen mountain forests dominated by juniper and wild olive trees, pastoral lands, wetlands, and unique caves create habitats for species such as the Arabian Tahr, Arabian Wolf, and Egyptian Vulture. Seasonal water flows and diverse soils further contribute to biodiversity and sustainable agricultural practices. The reserve provides critical ecosystem services: provisioning services such as food, water, and medicinal plants; regulating services including climate moderation, erosion control, and water purification; cultural services through ecotourism and heritage preservation; and supporting services that maintain biodiversity and soil fertility. This integration of natural and human-modified landscapes demonstrates ecological sustainability combined with cultural and economic benefits.
records.name: Al Jabal Al Akhdar

records.introduction_en: Straddling Oman’s Eastern Hajar Mountains, the Sirrin Biosphere Reserve safeguards the rugged natural habitat of the endangered Arabian tahr (Arabitragus jayakari), a species found nowhere else in the world. Its steep mountains, winding valleys, and freshwater springs form a dramatic karstic terrain that integrates biodiversity conservation with cultural heritage and community-led development. Fully protected core areas are complemented by sustainable use zones in the buffer and transition areas, guided by a clear management plan.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve encompasses steep mountain slopes, deep wadis, freshwater springs, and karstic formations characteristic of the Eastern Hajar Mountains. It provides essential habitat for Arabian tahr (Arabitragus jayakari), Arabian gazelles (Gazella arabica), Arabian wolves (Canis lupus arabs), red foxes (Vulpes vulpes), Blondheim’s foxes (Vulpes cana), and over 400 plant species, including 14 endemic or nationally threatened species. These ecosystems form a unique arid mountain landscape that supports both high biodiversity and ecological processes adapted to harsh climatic conditions.
records.name: Sirrin

records.introduction_en: Located on Iceland’s west coast, the Snæfellsnes Biosphere Reserve is a landscape of striking contrasts, encompassing volcanic peaks, lava fields, wetlands, grasslands, coastal cliffs, and the iconic Snæfellsjökull glacier. Known as “Iceland in a nutshell,” the biosphere reserve contains over 70% of Iceland’s flora, shaped by three active volcanic systems and centuries of human interaction. It represents a living example of how natural processes and cultural heritage intertwine in a dynamic subarctic environment.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Snæfellsnes hosts approximately 330 species of wild flowering plants and ferns, including rare Arctic–alpine specialists as well as endemic lichens and mosses. Its diverse ecosystems provide important breeding and feeding grounds for seabirds such as the Atlantic puffin (Fratercula arctica), Arctic tern (Sterna paradisaea), black-legged kittiwake (Rissa tridactyla), and white-tailed eagle (Haliaeetus albicilla).Coastal waters support grey seals (Halichoerus grypus) and harbour seals (Phoca vitulina), while mineral-rich springs, rivers, and wetlands sustain native freshwater fish populations. Volcanic landscapes and glaciers further contribute to the peninsula’s remarkable ecological diversity in the North Atlantic.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Snæfellsnes

records.introduction_en: Located on the southern slopes of the Greater Caucasus, the biosphere reserve sweeps across one of the world's most significant biodiversity hotspots, from lowland river valleys at 245 metres to alpine peaks rising above 3,600 metres.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This dramatic altitudinal range sustains a mosaic of broad-leaved forests, subalpine grasslands and high-mountain ecosystems, home to 48 mammal species including brown bear, wolf, lynx and the Dagestan tur. With over 1,000 plant species, it harbours one sixth of Azerbaijan's entire flora.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Great Caucasus

records.introduction_en: The Québec City Biosphere Reserve is an example of a predominantly urban biosphere reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Bordered by vast forests, crossed by 1,400 kilometres of waterways and dotted with 80 lakes and extensive wetlands, the territory sustains remarkable biodiversity within a dynamic urban landscape. The St. Lawrence River runs through it all, a vital migratory corridor for birds and fish, and a historical living thread connecting the Laurentian highlands to the sea.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Québec City

records.introduction_en: A short distance from Vancouver, the Átl’ka7tsem/Howe Sound Biosphere Reserve encompasses fjord and islands, over 218,723 ha, of which 16 per cent are marine areas. This mountainous coastal ecosystem, with a great altitudinal range influenced by the Pacific Ocean, is home to high levels of biodiversity. It supports some 721 native terrestrial animal species, including grizzly bears, wolverines and bald eagles. It also sustains thousands of marine species, including living glass sponge reefs that were long thought to have gone extinct 40 million years ago. Átl’ka7tsem, pronounced At-Kat-sum, is the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh/ Squamish word for paddling up the Sound. First Nation people have prospered in the region since time immemorial.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The rich mosaic of ecological systems found in south-western British Columbia is among the richest in Canada. It arises from the region’s topographical diversity, with an elevation range from sea level to almost 3,000 metres within a relatively short distance. Its close proximity to the moderating effects of the ocean and its location among the most southerly latitudes in the country also contribute. These factors together create a dramatic range in climate, from Canada’s mediterranean climate of warm, dry summers and mild, wet winters along the coastal lowlands, to the wettest climatic conditions in the country on higher west-facing slopes. This contrasts with the extreme cold and heavy snow conditions at the highest elevations. Within the boundaries of the reserve are the iconic geographies of Sea to Sky Country: coastal communities, rugged shorelines, forested islands, rich estuaries, cascading waterfalls, dormant volcanoes, alpine lakes and peaks, and tumbling glaciers. After more than 30 years of restoration, there are promising signs of recovery; whales, dolphins and pink salmon have returned, and the estuary is once again a rich, productive ecosystem that is recognised internationally as an Important Bird Area.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Átl'ka7tsem/Howe Sound

records.introduction_en: The Lac Saint-Pierre Biosphere Reserve is a vast territory that has been home to many communities for generations. At its biogeographical centre lies Lake Saint-Pierre, a fluvial expansion of the St Lawrence River formed as the Champlain Sea retreated at the end of the last ice age.The lakeshore and archipelago host distinctive wetland ecosystems recognised under the Ramsar Convention. The area includes North America’s largest heronry and is one of the continent’s key stopovers for migratory birds. Human activities include commercial shipping along the waterway that crosses the lake and its archipelago, and extensive agriculture across much of the landscape.Together with the proximity of one of Quebec’s largest cities, these factors make managing the reserve, balancing people and nature, particularly challenging.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The St Lawrence River traverses the Lac Saint-Pierre Biosphere Reserve from end to end: from Lavaltrie to Trois-Rivières on the north shore, and from Sorel-Tracy to Deschaillons-sur-Saint-Laurent on the south shore. Although much of the territory bears signs of human use, many areas remain wild and provide important refuges for wildlife. The lake’s archipelago comprises nearly one hundred islands, making it the largest archipelago in the St Lawrence River and a stronghold for great blue herons. Completing a comprehensive assessment of the reserve’s ecosystems is a priority, and surveys have already covered several highly productive areas. At present, information on ecosystems is concentrated on the lakeshore, which supports much of the region’s biodiversity and has attracted most research. Over 500 plant species are estimated to occur here, about 50 of which have legal protection in Quebec and Canada. Recorded fauna include 290 bird species, 90 fish species, 61 invertebrate taxa, 40 mammals, 16 amphibians and 12 reptiles. At least eight invasive alien species have been identified around the lake.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Lac Saint-Pierre

records.introduction_en: The Long Point Biosphere Reserve is in southern Canada on the shores of Lake Erie. The area comprises a rich mosaic of ecological systems associated with erosion-deposit sand spit formations around the Laurentian Great Lakes, as well as some of the largest remaining forest tracts in Carolinian Canada. The variety of habitats supports a rich flora and fauna, including a waterfowl staging area and a migration stopover of continental importance for land birds.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Long Point is one of Canada’s iconic landscapes, with a sand spit that extends 40 km into Lake Erie. It is the largest erosion-deposit formation in the Great Lakes. It was created by water-borne sediments swept eastward and deposited in part along an underwater glacial moraine. Habitats on and around Long Point include woodlands, sand dunes and bluffs, marshes, ponds, meadows, beaches and lakeshore. The complex is the largest biophysical formation of its kind in the Laurentian Great Lakes of North America. Inner Long Point Bay covers approximately 78 km2 between the spit and Lake Erie’s north shore. The Inner Bay is a diverse sport fishery and a continentally important staging area for migratory waterfowl. Immediately adjacent to the coastal reserve is a distinctive terrestrial area of temperate Carolinian broadleaf forests, conifer plantations, oak savannas and diverse agroecosystems. Recorded among the flora and fauna in the reserve and surrounding region are 1,384 species of plants, 370 species of birds, 102 species of fish, 46 species of mammals, 34 species of amphibians and reptiles, and 91 species of butterflies. These include American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius), American badger (Taxidea taxus), Acadian flycatcher (Empidonax virescens) and channel darter (Percina copelandi). The Long Point Biosphere Reserve has been recognised as a Ramsar site and as a globally significant Important Bird Area by Bird Life International. It is the oldest continuously operated bird observatory in North America.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Long Point

records.introduction_en: Located in the Pacific coastal lowlands of Mexico, La Encrucijada Biosphere Reserve comprises two lagoon systems that host a wide variety of ecosystems, including mangroves, marshes, forests, coastal dunes and palms. It spans six municipalities in the state of Chiapas. With a rich variety of species, the area is also a fundamental resting place for migratory birds.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: La Encrucijada is characterised by extensive mangroves, with patches of seasonal deciduous forest and lowland deciduous forest. Plant associations include tulares, popal and zapotonales, together with floating and submerged vegetation, palms and coastal dune vegetation. Eleven major rivers flow into the reserve, forming fresh- and saltwater lagoons, mangroves and tula swamps. Biological diversity and richness are high and include wildlife such as jaguars (Panthera onca), crocodiles and alligators, spider monkeys (Ateles fusciceps), and turtles. More than 300 bird species occur, including around 100 migratory species, as the ecosystem is a vital wintering and breeding ground.
records.name: La Encrucijada

records.introduction_en: Mapimí Biosphere Reserve sits where the states of Durango, Chihuahua and Coahuila meet in northern Mexico. The area lies in a closed basin ringed by low mountain ranges running roughly north–south, within the Bolsón de Mapimí basin. Mapimí is a representative Chihuahuan Desert landscape and a key stronghold for the endemic Bolson tortoise (Gopherus flavomarginatus) and other arid-adapted fauna.Its objectives include restoring soils and grasslands, strengthening biological monitoring and species conservation, consolidating organic beef production and regenerative ranching, developing rural tourism circuits, and sustaining research and training in biology, conservation and sustainable production.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is representative of northern Mexico’s desert ecosystems within the Chihuahuan Desert, notable for endemism and a dominance of macrophyllous shrub species that give a desert scrub physiognomy. Vegetation is characterised by rosette desert scrub dominated by maguey (Agave asperrima), creeping prickly pear (Opuntia rastrera) and other crassicaule species, as well as microphyllous, mostly spineless scrub, especially creosote bush (Larrea tridentata). Large expanses of natural grassland are common, dominated by tobosa grass (Hilaria mutica). Desert scrub and grasslands provide nutrient cycling, carbon capture and habitat provision. The reserve supports fauna adapted to arid conditions. Characteristic species include mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus), Bolson tortoise (Gopherus flavomarginatus), coyote (Canis latrans), bobcat (Lynx rufus) and puma (Puma concolor). Current monitoring focuses on migratory grassland birds, golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos), Bolson tortoise, vegetation and soil erosion.
records.name: Mapimí

records.introduction_en: The natural protected area belongs to the physiographic province of Eje Volcánico Transversal, which marks the extreme south of the Mexican Altiplain and separates it from the Balsas depression. It is a discontinuous mountain system, deeply dissected by strong tectonic processes, composed of a group of mountain ranges and hills that take up 77 per cent of the total surface, grouped in the south-centre portion, and separated by small intermountain valleys, 12 per cent, and plains, 6 per cent. It comprises five types of vegetation: sacred fir forests, characterised by the predominance of sacred fir (Abies religiosa), which constitute the characteristic habitat of the monarch butterfly (Danaus plexippus), pine–fir forests, pine forests, oak forests and cedar forests.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is located in a region where conservation of the natural heritage is a challenge because of its unique physical, geomorphological, climatic, hydrological and biogeographic features. This is especially true because every year millions of monarch butterflies (Danaus plexippus) complete their migratory cycle here, migrating from Canada and the United States. The mountains in the region are mainly covered by oak forests up to 2,900 m, pine–oak and pine forests between 1,500 and 3,000 m, and sacred fir, Abies religiosa, at an altitude of 2,400–3,600 m above sea level. Other, less represented, associations are the cedar and juniper forests, and the grasslands. It is an important catchment area for rainfall, feeding numerous water bodies in the States of Michoacán and Mexico. It is also the habitat of various endemic species from the centre of the country, notably Pinus martinezii, Ambystoma ordinarium and Regulus calendula. As it is a transition zone between the Nearctic and Neotropical regions, attached to the Southern Sierras Province of the Mesoamerican Mountain Region, it hosts enormous biodiversity due to the convergence of flora and fauna from both biogeographical regions. Partial studies have reported 198 species of vertebrates, 493 species of vascular plants and about 100 species of fungi.
records.name: Mariposa Monarca

records.introduction_en: Montes Azules is located in the Selva Lacandona region in the state of Chiapas in south-east Mexico, between the Lacantún and Lacanjá rivers. It comprises 331,200 ha within the forestry protection area of the Lacandona Forest, designated in 1978. It is one of the largest humid tropical forests in Mexico and Central America, with areas of pine forest at higher altitudes and montane rainforest. The reserve’s main challenge is to improve living conditions for local communities, especially Indigenous peoples, by promoting ecologically sustainable food production, agroforestry and small-scale cattle farming while respecting local traditions and practices.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve marks the northernmost distribution boundary for many biota originating from the Pleistocene refuges of Polochic (Guatemala) and Chiriquí (Panama). It contains the greatest concentration of biodiversity in Neotropical Mexico. It includes 20 per cent of the country’s plant diversity (around 4,300 species), 25 per cent of its bird species (345 species), and 27 per cent of its mammals (114 species). Among invertebrates, butterflies alone number about 800 diurnal species, representing 44 per cent of Mexico’s total. The reserve contains about 500 tree species. In the past, the forest was exploited for chicle and mahogany but was not substantially altered. Forest clearing and fires are recognised threats, as they can destroy habitat for the hundreds of species in the region. The area supports over 390 bird species (almost 50 per cent of Mexico’s total), 116 mammal species, and reptiles such as the Morelet’s crocodile (Crocodylus moreletii); it also hosts the northern tamandua (Tamandua mexicana) and the currently Vulnerable white-lipped peccary (Tayassu pecari).
records.name: Montes Azules

records.introduction_en: Located at the eastern end of the Yucatán Peninsula, the Ría Lagartos Biosphere Reserve encompasses key wetlands recognised by the Ramsar Convention. It features mangroves, small estuaries, coastal lagoons, marshes and savannah that are home to many species and serve as nesting sites for some. In the past decade, the reserve has stabilised numbers of various endangered species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area is fundamental for the conservation of several species. Its marshes are the only nesting site for the Caribbean pink flamingo (Phoenicopterus ruber ruber) and an important nesting site for turtles, including the critically endangered hawksbill sea turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata) and the green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas). The wetlands also host a substantial number of rare, vulnerable and endangered species, such as Rhyncholaelia digbyana. It is an important resting place for migratory birds, including the black-necked stilt (Himantopus mexicanus), which winters in the region.
records.name: Ría Lagartos

records.introduction_en: This is one of the two regions in the country with a considerably large stretch of highland and medium-altitude forest characteristic of the Mexican humid tropics. Its importance stems from its size, biological diversity, and ecological and geological relevance.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The site has a complex and varied cave system of karstic origin. Its karst aquifers are considered to be “the reserve for the Third Millennium”, with a very high-quality area located in the canyon of the La Venta River due to its isolation and the limited pressure from human settlements. A total of 712 plant species have been described, with numerous species of economic importance, including timber trees and medicinal, edible and ornamental plants. Notable trees include mahogany (Swietenia macrophylla), Mexican cedar (Cedrela odorata), sapodilla (Manilkara zapota) and Mexican yam (Dioscorea composita). A total of 584 terrestrial vertebrate species have been reported: 24 amphibians, 58 reptiles, 395 birds and 107 mammals. These represent 48.5 per cent of Chiapas’s vertebrates and 23.23 per cent of the country’s vertebrates.
records.name: Selva El Ocote

records.introduction_en: Considered one of the most important protected areas in western Mexico for its rich natural resources, extent and environmental role in the region, Sierra de Manantlán is highly biodiverse and provides a secure water source. It has 13 vegetation types, which provide refuge for 64 per cent of all species in the state of Jalisco and 25 per cent of Mexico’s mammal species. A major goal of the reserve is to promote alternative productive diversification for agrarian communities in ecotourism, sustainable forest management, agriculture and handicrafts.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Sierra de Manantlán Biosphere Reserve lies at the transition between the Nearctic and Neotropical realms. It encompasses parts of the Sierra Madre del Sur, with a wide range of altitudes, climates and soils. It features both tropical rainforests and mountain pine woods, in a diversity of landscapes that support hundreds of species. The region is home to over 350 bird species, some of which are at risk of extinction, such as the military macaw (Ara militaris) and the lilac-crowned parrot (Amazona finschi). It also contains a variety of endemic species, including 13 reptiles and several wild crop relatives. Discovered in the 1970s, the wild maize (Zea diploperennis) helped raise awareness of the need to create a biosphere reserve in the following decade.
records.name: Sierra de Manantlán

records.introduction_en: The Veracruzano Coral Reef System National Park (NPVRS) is located in the State of Veracruz, opposite the municipalities of Veracruz, Boca del Río and Alvarado, at an altitude of 0 m above sea level. The total area is approximately 52,238 ha, and the site is around 2.7 km at its widest from the coast to the open sea, on the continental shelf. NPVRS borders to the north-west with the Lobos–Tuxpan Coral Reef System, located in front of the Lagoon of Tamiahua and Tuxpan, Ver., and to the east with the Campeche and Yucatán Coral Reef System (Gutiérrez et al., 1993).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Veracruz Coral Reef System comprises flats, islands and reefs located on the inner part of the continental shelf, rising from a depth of close to 40 m. The area regulates the climate and acts as a barrier against waves and storms. The biosphere reserve harbours resident, transitory and migrant fish. The latter cross the area as part of their annual migratory routes, such as the Atlantic Spanish mackerel (Scomberomorus maculatus) and the king mackerel (Scomberomorus cavalla). The importance of the coral reef system arises from its relevance for fisheries. Among the pelagic species of commercial interest are the tarpon (Megalops atlanticus), the crevalle jack (Caranx hippos), the horse-eye jack (Caranx latus), the bar jack (Caranx ruber), the jurel (Caranx cirus), the permit (Trachinotus falcatus) and the Atlantic bonito (Sarda sarda). Of the species living on the seabed, those of interest include the black grouper (Mycteroperca bonaci) and the scamp (M. phenax), the red snapper (Lutjanus campechanus), the goliath grouper (Epinephelus itajara), the snappers Lutjanus jocu, L. griseus and L. analis, and the flounders Bothus lunatus and B. ocellatus. Commercial catches in the area comprise 89 species of fish, four species of shark, two species of ray, one species of lobster and two species of octopus. The taxonomic position of some of these species, and ecological and fisheries information, may be consulted in Jiménez et al.
records.name: Sistema Arrecifal Veracruzano

records.introduction_en: The protected area of Sierra de Álamos–Río Cuchujaqui lies within the geographical provinces of the Western Sierra Madre and the Northwest Coastal Plain. It consists of an elevational gradient of vegetation, from tropical deciduous forest, also called lowland deciduous forest, to the Sierra Madre evergreen forest, or pine–oak forest. The Sierra de Álamos runs parallel to the coast of the Pacific Ocean and is crossed by numerous deep gullies excavated by rivers that flow into the Pacific. This is the case of the Cuchujaqui River, a tributary of the Río Fuerte. The area hosts key species such as the puma (Puma concolor), jaguar (Panthera onca) and ocelot (Leopardus pardalis). There is abundant riparian forest of Taxodium mucronatum, as well as a wide range of soils and geology. The region of Álamos is known for the confluence between the northern limits of many tropical species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This biosphere reserve is located in an enclave in one of the municipalities harbouring the most biodiversity in the state of Sonora. It has mixed plant communities, such as deciduous tropical forest, also called lowland deciduous forest, the Sinaloa thorny shrubland, and the evergreen Sierra Madre Forest composed of pine and oak forests. It contains extraordinary biological wealth, with approximately 1,200 species of plants in 566 genera and 148 families (Rzedowski, 1991). In terms of fauna, the area contains approximately 557 species of vertebrates. Because of this biological diversity, the area is considered very rich at both state and national level (Rzedowski, 1991). Notable flora includes Guaiacum coulteri, the palm Brahea, the cycad Dioon tomasellii and the magnolia Magnolia pacifica. Vertebrates include the Gila monster (Heloderma suspectum), the beaded lizard (Heloderma horridum), the Álamos mud turtle (Kinosternon alamosae), the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos), the hummingbird (Amazilia violiceps), the great blue heron (Ardea herodias), the eared quetzal (Euptilotis neoxenus) and the freshwater shrimp Macrobrachium. Mammals also present include the jaguar (Panthera onca), ocelot (Leopardus pardalis) and otter (Lontra longicaudis).
records.name: Sierra de Alamos - Rio Cuchujaqui

records.introduction_en: The Tehuacán-Cuicatlán Biosphere Reserve lies within a complex system of mountain ranges and valleys that generate great biodiversity and varied ecosystems. The region has played an important role in the development of agriculture in Mesoamerica.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is bound on the west by the Sierra Mixteca, and on the east by three mountain ranges: the Sierra Zongolica in the north, the Mazatec Sierra in the middle, and the Sierra de Juárez in the south. The most prominent ranges – the Sierra Zongolica and the Sierra Mazatec – are characterised by karst topography cut by deep canyons. One of the most exceptional ecological features is the columnar cactus forest, which holds one of the highest concentrations of columnar cacti in the world. In this central portion of the country, 45 of the 70 species reported in Mexico occur. These species are the dominant component in nine plant communities, most of them endemic to Tehuacán-Cuicatlán. The area also contains xeric scrub, tropical deciduous forest, pine forest, pine–oak forest and cloud forest. Among vertebrates, the reserve has 18 fish species and 27 amphibian species, a high diversity compared with the deserts of North America and Australia. It also has 85 reptile species, of which 20 are endemic, and 338 bird species, of which 16 are endemic. Owing to its endemic, threatened and rare floristic species, the site is often described as a global biodiversity hotspot.
records.name: Tehuacan-Cuicatlan

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve covers 100 km of the north-east shore of Lake Baikal and extends 45–80 km inland to the western slope of the Barguzinskiy mountain range. Barguzinskyi Biosphere Reserve overlaps with the Lake Baikal World Heritage site. Situated in south-east Siberia, Lake Baikal, at 3.15 million hectares, is the oldest and deepest of the world’s lakes. It is about 25 million years old and reaches 1,637 metres at its deepest point.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Its age and isolation have produced one of the world’s richest and most unusual freshwater fauna that is of exceptional value to evolutionary science. With its outstanding variety of endemic animals and plants, Lake Baikal is one of the most biologically diverse lakes on earth. Main habitats of the biosphere reserve include lacustrine terraces with larch (Larix dahurica), coniferous forests with pine (Pinus sibirica), spruce (Picea obovata) and fir (Abies sibirica), and thickets of dwarf pine (Pinus pumila). There is also tundra dominated by Kobresia, and lichen-covered rocks and cliffs. Hot springs recall a warmer climate in the past, with relict species such as violets (Viola). The fauna is characteristic of the taiga. There are 39 species of mammal recorded, including pika (Ochotona hyperborea), Siberian chipmunk (Eutamias sibiricus), marmot (Marmota baibacina), flying squirrel (Pteromys volans), fox (Vulpes vulpes) and brown bear (Ursus arctos).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Barguzinskyi

records.introduction_en: The Astrakhanskiy Biosphere Reserve is situated about 90 km from the town of Astrakhan, in the Volga delta. This is the largest inland delta in Europe and is predominantly a freshwater riverine wetland complex with permanent and seasonal lakes and riverine floodplains. The area is a Ramsar site, as its wetlands support up to 750,000 waterfowl during mild winters.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The lower part of the Volga delta features channels, creeks and alluvial islands, including shallow lakes. It also includes shallow bays, known as “kultuks”, which form a transition zone between the delta and the fore-delta. Freshwater wetlands occur alongside riverine forests dominated by Salix alba and Salix triandra. Shrublands with Tamarix ramosissima and Rubus caesius include Carex acutiformis. Grasslands are dominated by Phragmites australis and Typha angustifolia. Permanently flooded areas, such as shallow “kultuks” and the fore-delta, are covered by emergent vegetation. A particular feature is the presence of lotus (Nelumbo nucifera), a common species of the tropics that here reaches its northernmost distribution. This species increased in distribution from 3.5 ha in the 1930s throughout the entire Volga delta to several thousand hectares in the biosphere reserve in the 1980s.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Astrakhanskiy

records.introduction_en: Bashkirskiyi Ural Biosphere Reserve is located on the western slopes of the southern Urals and has a variety of landscapes, from mountain river gorges to mountain steppes, meadows, floodplains and reservoirs. It is also home to significant archaeology and cultural traditions and hosts a growing tourism industry.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Karst processes are widespread throughout the biosphere reserve. There are 166 known caves, some of which are internationally unique, including Shulgan-Tash (Kapova), Novomuradymovskaya Cave and Sumgan Cave, the greatest downwarping cave in Europe. In addition to underground forms, surface karst forms are also common, including craters, ponors, bridges, canyons and cave-in lakes. The high biodiversity is due to limited human impact, diverse landforms, a complex history of vegetation formation during the Pleistocene and Holocene, and the junction of two major forest biomes from Europe and Siberia. There are more than 1,650 plant species, of which 34 are endemic, and over 2,000 animal species. The biosphere reserve includes the Bielsko–Nugush interfluve and Uryuk, two ornithological territories of European importance. The biosphere reserve plays an especially important role in preserving rare animals, plants and ecosystems of two forest biomes, European nemoral broad-leaved forests and hemiboreal light coniferous forests of Siberian type, which are situated at the boundary of their areas. The site contains five different protected areas, including national parks and forestry districts.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Bashkirskiyi Ural

records.introduction_en: Situated about 170 km south-west of Ulan-Ude, Baikalskyi Biosphere Reserve comprises parts of the south shore and water bodies of Lake Baikal as well as contiguous forests.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The south of the reserve is cut off from the northern part by the flat-topped Khamar-Daban range, which runs on an east–west axis. From its highest point at Sokhor Mountain, 2,323 metres, the range slopes precipitously down to Lake Baikal. Given these changes in altitude, vegetation in the biosphere reserve varies greatly. Sphagnum bogs and forests of poplar (Populus) and the willow-like Chosenia macrolepis occupy low-lying areas. River valleys contain bird cherry (Prunus padus), rowan (Sorbus aucuparia) and alder (Alnus glutinosa). The northern slopes of the mountains have taiga of Korean pine (Pinus koraiensis), spruce (Picea), cedar (Pinus sibirica) and fir (Abies sibirica). The southern slopes are covered with mixed larch (Larix sibirica) and pine (Pinus) forests, which give way to steppe vegetation on the foothills. At higher altitudes there is cedar elfin woodland and mountain tundra with shrubs such as Rhododendron parvifolium. The high-altitude meadows support thickets of dwarf Siberian pine (Pinus pumila) and birch (Betula middendorfii). A total of 37 mammal species and 260 species of birds have been recorded.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Baikalskyi

records.introduction_en: The Commander Islands Nature and Biosphere Reserve is situated on the boundary between the north-western Pacific Ocean and the Bering Sea, to the east of the Kamchatka Peninsula on the Commander Islands. The islands are covered by mountain tundra and motley-grass meadows, with extensive wetlands, a long coastline and Russia’s largest protected marine zone. The flora and fauna of the Commander Islands, the westernmost point of the Commander–Aleutian island arc that stretches for more than 2,000 km, are notable for an unusual combination of species of Asian and American origin. The coastal ecosystems are unique for their diversity of marine mammals and birds.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The flora and fauna of the Commander Islands are notable for an unusual combination of species of Asian and American origin. The coastal ecosystems are unique because of the diversity of marine mammals. Nowhere else in Russia is there such a concentration of marine birds and mammals within such a small area. Within the territory of the islands and in coastal waters there are 432 species and subspecies of vascular plants, more than 150 species of algae, 37 species of mammals, more than 215 species of birds and 216 species of fish. More than 50 species, subspecies and forms of plants and animals are included in the IUCN Red List and Red Book Russia, some of them being island endemics. The ecosystems of the territory and shelf waters of the Commander Islands are of Asian and global conservation significance because of their good condition.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Commander Islands

records.introduction_en: Kenozersky Biosphere Reserve in Arkhangelsk Region, in the north-west of the country, includes virgin taiga forest and mixed pine–spruce forest ecosystems. The site is a globally important migratory bird habitat and contains unique swamp and forest ecosystems.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Kenozersky Biosphere Reserve corresponds to Kenozero National Park. It supports bird species typical of the middle taiga as well as those of deciduous forest and steppe zones. Numerous birds inhabit the northern or southern limits of their natural distribution. Many birds of prey are recorded in the area, such as buzzard, goshawk, hen harrier and marsh harrier. Cultural landscapes play an important role in sustaining high biodiversity levels in this protected area. Natural–geographical features and centuries of history have created conditions for the existence of a variety of plant and animal species. A total of 534 plant species are recorded in the area, of which 53 are rare or endangered, including many orchid species. The fauna includes many typical taiga species such as wolf, brown bear, glutton, elk, lynx, otter, marten and mink.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Kenozersky

records.introduction_en: Consisting of 11 islands, the Far East Marine Biosphere Reserve lies off the continental coast south of Vladivostok, where boreal and subtropical currents meet in the Sea of Japan. The coastal areas combine rocky abrupt capes, small peninsulas and bays, with coniferous and deciduous forests inland. The reserve sits at the crossing of the spring and summer migration routes of birds between Siberia and Japan and between the Arctic and China. Over 300 bird species, including some of the rarest representatives of the avifauna, can be observed here.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Almost all the landscapes of southern Primorsky Krai are represented in the reserve. These include subtropical and boreal forests, broadleaf and coniferous forests, wetlands and steppes, rocks, warm-water sandy coves and cold-water depths of the Sea of Japan, as well as streams, lakes and brackish-water lagoons. Nowhere else in the world is such a unique diversity of geological structures and soils concentrated on such a small area of reserved islands and continental coast. The variety of habitats and environmental conditions underpins the rich biological diversity of the reserve. More than 3,000 species of invertebrates and vertebrates, both marine and terrestrial, are represented. The region is the richest in Russia in terms of the number of bird species, with some 340; the site is a major location along the East Asian flyway. The fauna of terrestrial mammals on Bolshoi Pelis Island is poor. Large mammals such as sika deer, roe deer, fox and raccoon dog have been observed, although records are sporadic. Among murines, the Striped Field Mouse, Korean Field Mouse and Common Vole permanently inhabit the island. Among bats, the Brown Long-eared Bat and Savi’s Pipistrelle occur. Among amphibians, the Mongolian Toad and Japanese Tree Frog are present, and among snakes, the Asian Keelback and Dione Ratsnake. The Spotted Seal, previously almost completely extirpated in southern Primorsky Krai, has returned to the islands as a permanent habitat. The southernmost population of this species lives in Peter the Great Bay, and about 80 per cent of the population aggregates in the reserve during the summer season.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Far East Marine

records.introduction_en: Kedrovaya Pad is the oldest Russian reserve, created in 1916 and located in the extreme south of the Russian Far East, not far from the borders with China and Democratic People's Republic of Korea. Two main mountain ridges, Gakkelevsky and Sukhorechensky, at around 400 metres above sea level, characterise the relief and form a river valley.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The environment in this region has suffered damage from human activities, especially forest fires. Kedrovaya Pad is the only area still in its original condition and is the only example of south Ussuri taiga. The coniferous–broadleaf forests of Kedrovaya Pad Biosphere Reserve combine elements of the northern taiga and subtropical forests, but in this area southern flora predominates. The overlap of southern and northern species of plants and animals explains the high biodiversity, with many endemic and relict species of the Far East. These include the Amur tiger (Panthera tigris altaica), the Amur leopard (Panthera pardus orientalis) and the Himalayan black bear (Ursus thibetanus). Although it covers only 0.1 per cent of Primorsky Province, a significant number of animal and plant species can be found here. The biosphere reserve contains 900 of the 2,000 vascular plant species found in Primorsky. The location of Kedrovaya Pad at the southern tip of Primorsky Krai places it in the path of warm, humid air masses from the Philippines. As a result, the frost-free period stretches an extra two months in comparison with nearby areas. The mountainous relief also plays a significant role in creating microclimates within the biosphere reserve and provides conditions for specific species present only in Kedrovaya Pad and neighbouring areas. For example, the headwaters of the Gakkelevsky Stream are protected from the sea by a mountain ridge. Here, the number of sunny days each year can be up to three times greater than in the central regions of the reserve. For this reason, sun-loving plants like melons and tomatoes grow well in regions just a few kilometres from areas where they cannot grow at all.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Kedrovaya Pad

records.introduction_en: The landscape of Kologrivsky Forest in the north-eastern part of the Russian Plain includes areas influenced by human activities as well as undisturbed southern taiga ecosystems. These comprise pine forests, spruce forests, small-leaved forests, marshes, meadows and water bodies. Over 1,000 species of flora and fauna are recorded in the biosphere reserve, including four plant and 13 animal species on the Red List of Threatened Species of the Russian Federation. That list also includes birds nesting in the reserve, among them the willow ptarmigan (Lagopus lagopus rossicus), osprey (Pandion haliaetus), eagle owl and azure tit (Parus cyanus). Eco-tourism is a strategic activity for sustainable development in an area with high unemployment.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve, located in the north-west of Kostroma Region, is a centre for preserving landscapes and the genetic diversity of the Kologriv, Manturovo, Neya, Chukhloma and Parfenyevo municipal districts. The core includes the State Nature Reserve Kologrivsky Forest, which consists of two clusters, the Kologriv and Manturovo parts. The woodland is typical southern taiga, among the oldest in central Russia, and has not been influenced by human activities. Species of flora and fauna unable to survive in commercial forests thrive here because young trees, old trees and deadwood occur together. The biosphere reserve is characterised by autochthonous dark coniferous forests, the only surviving ones in the southern taiga. This woodland shows near-optimal regeneration, energy efficiency and a balanced structure. It has an optimal ratio between the biota and the abiotic environment, which underlines the need for special conservation. Twenty lichen species are common indicators of old-growth forests and are disappearing elsewhere because of tree felling and air pollution. Species that indicate environmental quality include lung lichen (Lobaria pulmonaria) and several species of Bryoria and Usnea. The avifauna, comprising 78 species, is mainly forest birds that dwell in the tree layer, shrubs and herb layer. Small areas of shrubs alternating with meadows, wasteland and forest roads, similar to forest–meadow habitats in the Kologrivsky site, are inhabited by 16 species that use freshly cut areas. Meadows and tall herbage support 21 species. Swampy areas with small water bodies are used by 13 species. Habitats with rivers and streams host 30 species, most of which are waterfowl or sandpipers. Some birds nesting in the reserve are on the Red List of the Russian … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Kologrivsky Forest

records.introduction_en: Located on the border with Finland, the site comprises the Kostomukshsky Reserve and contains one of the oldest intact north taiga forests in north-west Russia. The north taiga forests are essential for the reproduction of many bird species. The local population lives from forestry, agriculture, fishing, hunting and gathering non-timber forest products.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is located on the eastern side of the Western-Karelian Upland. Maximum absolute elevations range from 250 to 290 metres above sea level. The terrain is rugged, with relative elevation ranging from 20 to 100 metres. The biosphere reserve displays a wide range of typical and unique north taiga ecosystems. Forests that have never been clear-cut are well managed. Lower-intensity selective cutting has occurred only along river banks, lake shores and near old villages. This is notable for northern Europe, where few extensive forests have survived. The biosphere reserve is located within one such forest. The reserve also includes peat bog and freshwater White Sea ecosystems typical of the north taiga. The biosphere reserve is home to over 1,200 animal species. Mammal fauna shows typical north taiga features. Common animals of the subzone are squirrel, marten, wolverine, brown bear and forest reindeer, which form comparatively large populations because their biotopes are well preserved. Bird fauna displays a typical north taiga pattern: northern species make up 39 per cent, while species of southern origin account for only 21 per cent of nesting birds. Total bird population density is 179 pairs per square kilometre, an average figure for the north taiga. The nesting grounds are in the centre of the White Sea–Bothnia watershed. High taiga bird species diversity is due to the high conservation quality of aboriginal ecosystems. Increased nesting densities have been recorded for many taiga aboriginal species, including brambling, rustic bunting, parrot crossbill, waxwing, grey-headed chickadee, Siberian jay, three-toed woodpecker, black woodpecker, boreal owl, great grey owl, goldeneye, whooper swan, bean goose, black-throated diver and lesser bl … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Metsola

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is situated approximately 240 km south of the city of Pechora, on the western slopes of the Northern Ural Mountains.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The site represents the West Eurasian taiga. Habitats include virgin coniferous forests and, at higher altitudes, subalpine scrub woodlands, meadows, tundra and bare rock areas. The biosphere reserve includes important winter-feeding sites for elk and reindeer. It also provides spawning, growth and fattening grounds for salmon (Salmo salar).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Pechoro-llychskiy

records.introduction_en: Set in eastern Russia’s Zabaykalsky Krai, about 25 kilometres north of the Mongolian border, Sokhondinskiy Biosphere Reserve centres on Mount Sokhondo, an isolated massif trending south-west to north-east, with elevations from roughly 900 to 2,500 metres. The reserve lies at the junction of two biogeographical regions, the East Siberian taiga and the Mongolian-Manchurian steppe, creating a pronounced transition from forest to steppe that rises into subalpine and alpine belts. The reserve’s objectives are to uphold strict non-intervention in the core, regulate resource use in the buffer, and use the transition zone to study interactions between people and nature and to model sustainable land management.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set in the highest part of the Khentey-Chikoy Highlands, Sokhondinskiy spans a compact sequence from mountain steppe through birch and larch on the lower and mid-slopes to mossy taiga and, above the treeline, to alpine tundra. The massif is Jurassic granite, shaped into dome-like summits with glacial terraces, cirques, moraines and broad fluvioglacial plains. In the valleys, willow thickets line waterlogged floodplain oxbows. This structural variety underpins a clear biogeographical transition: the reserve lies where the East Siberian taiga meets the Mongolian-Manchurian steppe, with strong ecological gradients reinforced by a strongly continental climate. Several habitats stand out for conservation importance, including Daurian-Manchurian mountain steppe on drier exposures, extensive cedar and larch taiga across the main forested belt, and a set of high-mountain lakes and mineral springs. Taiga forests support large carnivores and ungulates, with brown bear (Ursus arctos) and Eurasian red deer (Cervus elaphus) characteristic, while open steppe and wetland edges host raptors and other steppe and wetland birds. The site also supports specialist carnivores of regional conservation interest, including Pallas’s cat (Otocolobus manul).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Sokhondinskiy

records.introduction_en: This cluster biosphere reserve is situated on the northern slopes of the Greater Caucasus Range in the upper Teberda Valley. It is a typical mountainous region, with elevations largely above 2,000 m.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Teberdinsky tract is situated on the northern slopes of the Greater Caucasus Range, in the upper Teberda Valley. It is a typical mountainous region, with 83 per cent of the area lying higher than 2,000 m above sea level. More than 100 glaciers are known in the reserve, covering 10 per cent of its area. The largest glaciers are located in the Greater Caucasus Range. The reserve presents an interconnected ecological network of montane ecosystems, from pine and dark conifer forests to alpine tundra, with river valleys and upland lakes. The area supports natural habitats that are significant for the conservation of biological diversity, including habitats of rare and endangered species of great scientific and conservation importance. Notable species include the West Caucasian goat (Capra caucasica), chamois (Rupicapra rupicapra), Anatolian leopard (Panthera pardus), and Caucasian otter (Lutra lutra). The area supports breeding grounds of rare raptors, including the griffon vulture (Gyps fulvus), peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus), bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus) and golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos). It includes portions of migratory routes of birds and a reintroduction site of the Caucasian wisent (Bison bonasus), the most important large mammal of the region. This is an intraspecies hybrid morphologically identical to the animals that once roamed here.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Teberda

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is located about 550 km south of Moscow, close to the Ukrainian border. Situated in the Pontian Steppe biogeographic region, the area comprises meadow steppes with vast floristic diversity, with up to 80 species per square metre. The Tsentral'nochernozem Biosphere Reserve takes its name from its soil type, the so-called chernozem, which is a black and very fertile soil. Today, pristine steppe ecosystems are rare. All major steppe zones of Europe and America’s prairies have been transformed into agricultural land due to their highly productive soil.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve includes a mosaic of all natural ecosystems of Kursk Region. Plakorny meadow, or northern steppes, including Streletsky and Kazatsky, survived only thanks to the creation of the reserve, and they occupy 0.1 per cent of Kursk Region. It is important in preserving the biological diversity of the region. As of 31 December 2013, there were 7,531 species of living organisms in its territory, of which 227 species of animals, plants and mushrooms are included in the Red Data Book of Kursk Region, which makes up 67 per cent of the total. The region is home to 23 bird species, nine species of insects, nine species of vascular plants and two species of mushrooms included in the Red Data Book of Russia.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Tsentral'nochernozem

records.introduction_en: Tsentral’nolesnoy Biosphere Reserve is located in Kalinin Oblast’, about 280 km north-west of Moscow.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is typical of the moraine landscape of the Central Russian Plain, with southern-taiga forest and extensive oligotrophic sphagnum bogs that include elements of hypoarctic flora. Among the 51 mammal species are the beaver (Castor fiber), the wolf (Canis lupus) and the brown bear (Ursus arctos).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Tsentral'nolesnoy

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve is located in the valleys along the banks of the Ugra and Zhizdra rivers and their tributaries. It is characterised by the vast biodiversity of lakes, unique meadows and diverse forest ecosystems. The territory is dominated by complex multilayered pine forests, green moss forests and complex spruce forests. In the transition zone, there are relatively large rural communities, with a significant proportion of summer cottages owned by residents of Moscow and major cities of the Moscow, Kaluga and Tula regions.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve territory lies within the Eastern European phytogeographical region and at the junction of the subzones of mixed deciduous and coniferous forests, known as subtaiga, and deciduous forests. The area plays a key role in conserving natural and cultural landscapes in the catchments of the Ugra, Zhizdra and Oka rivers. The biosphere reserve also includes main Important Bird Areas (IBAs) of international significance, as well as one of the few remaining old-growth broadleaf woodlands in European Russia. The area is home to various endangered species, such as Alburnoides bipunctatus rossicus, Cottus gobio, Gavia arctica arctica, Ciconia nigra, Pandion haliaetus, Circus macrourus, Haliaeetus albicilla, Aquila clanga and Aquila pomarina, among others.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Ugra

records.introduction_en: The Visimskiy Biosphere Reserve is located in the forests of the central Ural Mountains north-west of Yekaterinburg. Situated on the natural border between Europe and Asia, the site plays a significant role in maintaining the ecological balance of the region.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The territory of the Visimskiy State Reserve lies on the dividing ridge of the Ural Mountains. It extends from north to south for 25 km and from east to west for 38 km. A geographical border of Europe and Asia passes through the reserve. The main part of the reserve is in Europe on the western slope of the Middle Urals in the upper tributaries of the River Chusovaya, namely the Sulem, Daria and Shishim rivers, which belong to the Volga–Kama basin. The smallest is the eastern part of the reserve, which belongs to the dividing ridge area where the River Vogulka begins. The Vogulka is a left tributary of the Tagil that belongs to the Ob basin. The virgin southern-taiga mountainous spruce–fir forests, notably Picea obovata and Abies sibirica, represent the most characteristic ecosystem in the region. Visimskiy also includes human-derived meadows, known locally as yelan, and secondary forests. The climate is temperate continental in the western part and more severe, cooler and wetter in the east. This pattern is due to the high altitudes of the Ural Mountains. The main features of the local climate include persistent winter inversions and summer temperature inversions, which are temperature disruptions.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Visimskiy

records.introduction_en: The Berlengas Biosphere Reserve includes a group of small islands and rocks, and the city of Peniche on the mainland.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve includes the Berlengas archipelago, the city of Peniche on the mainland, and a marine corridor between the archipelago and Peniche. The main conservation concerns in the reserve are located in the Berlengas archipelago, which consists of a group of islands and coastal reefs in three groups: Berlenga Island and associated reefs, Farilhões and Estelas. The geology and geomorphology of the archipelago do not favour the formation of aquifers or perennial watercourses, and the vegetation is mainly herbaceous. Most of the rocky substrate is in the form of steep cliffs sparsely covered with vegetation, which shelter important seabird nesting colonies. The archipelago is situated 5.7 miles off the mainland, in a region characterised by two important geomorphological structures, Cabo Carvoeiro and the Nazaré Canyon. These two formations have a significant influence on the physical environment and ecological features of the region, since they interact with the circulation associated with coastal upwelling, intensifying primary production in the ecosystem.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Berlengas

records.introduction_en: The Castro Verde Biosphere Reserve is in southern Portugal, in the hinterland of the Baixo Alentejo region, on the long, extensive plains of the Beja district, in the heart of the Campo Branco. The extensive and level surface of Castro Verde is dominated by open, continuous fields where cereal crops, fallows, natural grasslands and fields with leguminous plants prevail. With gently sloping relief around 200 m above sea level, this agricultural matrix is interrupted occasionally by old olive groves and recent vineyards, sporadic trees, either standing alone or in small groups, patches of shrubby or arboreous natural vegetation, and freshwater wetlands. Of the faunal species, a structured and diverse bird community of around 200 species stands out. The mining complex of Neves-Corvo, one of the major massive sulphide mineral deposits of the Iberian Pyrite Belt, operating since 1988, stands out as a major employer, involving a community of about 2,200 workers between the surface and the extraction wells.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Castro Verde Biosphere Reserve holds the most important cereal steppe area of Portugal. It is one of the most representative cereal steppe, or pseudo-steppe, landscapes of the Iberian Peninsula and Europe. Cereal steppe or pseudo-steppe is one of the most threatened rural landscapes of the Mediterranean region. The area has a predominantly flat territory with a sub-humid to dry ombroclimate. It is mostly in the thermomediterranean level, and in some places reaches the mesomediterranean level. The list of plant species present in the reserve includes trees and shrubs with plain, leathery and persistent leaves, such as holm oak and cork oak, which are confined to sparse montado areas, especially of holm oak. The oleander (Nerium oleander) is mainly present near the few steep valleys where humidity is still present. There are aromatic plants such as lavender (Lavandula), thyme (Thymus) and rosemary (Lavandula stoechas). The area has a high degree of endemism in its flora, with 11 Iberian and Mediterranean endemisms. There is also the presence of two rare Lusitanian endemisms, Linaria ricardoi and Armeria neglecta, unique species in the world that occur only in the region where the biosphere reserve is located, Alentejo. Of the faunal species, a structured and diverse bird community of around two hundred species stands out. These include steppe birds such as great bustard (Otis tarda), black-bellied sandgrouse (Pterocles orientalis) and Montagu’s harrier (Circus pygargus). The fauna also includes eight Iberian endemisms. Among these is the emblematic Iberian imperial eagle (Aquila adalberti), one of the most endangered birds of prey in Europe and one of the rarest in the world. The low human presence and the presence of the wild rabbit (Oryctolagus cunicul … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Castro Verde

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve covers the entire terrestrial area of Flores Island in the Azores Archipelago, as well as the oceanic area extending approximately 4.8 km from the coast. Flores Island is the emergent surface of a seamount located near the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, originating from volcanic activity that began less than 10 million years ago.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Flores Island has the highest number of endemic species per unit area in the archipelago, surpassed only by Corvo. This reflects its great biodiversity and relatively unaltered vegetation areas. The high central plateau, with an average altitude of 600–700 m above sea level, is the island’s major topographic feature. In this area are some of the most important natural habitats of the island, such as the high-altitude peatlands. These habitats also play a major role in the island’s hydrological systems and in the landscape features of Flores Island. The coast is mostly high cliffs, islets and coastal caves formed by continuous maritime erosion. The coastal zone is the breeding area for several marine bird species. Notably, the roseate tern (Sterna dougallii) has, in the Azores, around 40 per cent of its total population nesting in the coastal zone of Flores Island.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Flores Island

records.introduction_en: The Meseta Ibérica Transboundary Biosphere Reserve lies along the northern border of Spain and Portugal. It includes a wide variety of landscapes, orographic features and land uses. Altitudes range from 100 m to 2,000 m above sea level. The area contains many flagship species, some of which have been the subject of conservation projects, such as the black stork (Ciconia nigra), Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus), Bonelli’s eagle (Aquila fasciata), Eurasian eagle-owl (Bubo bubo), European otter (Lutra lutra) and Iberian wolf (Canis lupus signatus). The area also includes built heritage dating back to Roman times and the Middle Ages. The remains of forts, castles and walled enclosures in localities bear witness to frequent wars between Spanish and Portuguese kingdoms during the Middle Ages. The cultural heritage is notable in the architecture, customs, traditions and folklore.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is in the north-west of Spain and the north-east of Portugal. It has an average altitude of 823 m, with large variations across the area. Altitudes range from 100 m to 2,000 m above sea level. The biosphere reserve is well irrigated, with a number of dams and reservoirs. With more than 3,400 million cubic metres, the region has the third highest water storage capacity in Spain, second only to the Province of Badajoz and the Province of Cáceres. On the Portuguese side, the area supports a wide diversity of landscapes. The district is known for its climatic contrasts, described locally as nine months of winter and three of heat, and for its rugged geomorphology. Diversity is the watchword for the biodiversity of the Meseta Ibérica Biosphere Reserve. The most abundant forests are formed by Pyrenean oak and turkey oak. There are also interesting stands of holly and yew. Birch and alder are abundant along the riverbanks, where streams descend from the summits to the lagoons within the biosphere reserve. At higher altitudes, forest gives way to thickets of escabonales, cambronales and heaths. The Meseta Ibérica is among the most important areas for wildlife at national and European levels. A very significant part of the Spanish and Portuguese terrestrial fauna is represented here. Around 250 species of vertebrates are recorded, and there is also high richness and diversity of invertebrates. Many species are endangered. Flagship species include the black stork (Ciconia nigra), Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus), Bonelli’s eagle (Aquila fasciata), Eurasian eagle-owl (Bubo bubo), European otter (Lutra lutra), Iberian wolf (Canis lupus signatus), Bocage’s wall lizard (Podarcis bocagei) and Seoane’s viper (Vipera seoanei).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Meseta Iberica

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve was the first in the Madeira Archipelago. The site features rich fauna and flora with a high degree of endemism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Madeira Island has very steep relief, and the coastal area is almost entirely composed of steep sea cliffs and some cliff deposits formed by the retreat of the cliffs due to oceanic abrasion. In the centre of the island, a mountain massif rises in several peaks above 1,600 m, cut by numerous basaltic dykes and veins. In the eastern part of the massif, there is an extensive plateau with an average altitude of 1,550 m. Hills and valleys link the coast to the central massif, formed by the weathering of bedrock by water. This geomorphological complexity creates a wide range of heterogeneous bioclimatic conditions. These conditions support diverse native climatophilous broadleaf vegetation and unique habitats. Notable examples include Macaronesian coasts with endemic vegetation, the Mediterranean laurel forest of the Canary laurel, the temperate laurel forest of the Madeira laurel, and high-altitude heathlands. The biosphere reserve covers the entire onshore area of the municipality of Santana. It also includes the adjacent marine area down to the 200 m isobath.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Santana Madeira

records.introduction_en: The Tejo/Tajo International Transboundary Biosphere Reserve is located in the western part of the Iberian Peninsula, shared between Spain and Portugal, with the Tajo River as its main axis. The area is characterised by sharp relief and low altitudes. Vegetation consists largely of cork oak formations and patches of scrub, as well as cultivated areas and pastures. The fauna is typically Mediterranean and includes many rare species. Among the most important are the Iberian imperial eagle (Aquila adalberti), Bonelli’s eagle (Aquila fasciata), the black stork (Ciconia nigra), the black vulture (Aegypius monachus), and the otter (Lutra lutra). Livestock and forestry are the main sources of income for the small population of the reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area of the biosphere reserve is characterised by sharp relief and low altitudes. The vegetation consists largely of sclerophyllous and cork oak formations and abundant patches of scrub, as well as cultivated areas, extensive pastures and open stand formations. Among the most significant plant taxa are different species of orchids. The fauna is typically Mediterranean and includes a large number of threatened or endangered taxa, some of which are endemic to the peninsula. Among the most important species are the Iberian imperial eagle (Aquila adalberti), Bonelli’s eagle (Aquila fasciata), black stork (Ciconia nigra), black vulture (Aegypius monachus), Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus), great bustard (Otis tarda), otter (Lutra lutra) and green lizard (Lacerta schreiberi), along with the extensive fauna of the Mediterranean rivers.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Tejo/Tajo Internacional

records.introduction_en: This large biosphere reserve contains important national parks in Paraguay, such as Defensores del Chaco, Médanos del Chaco and Teniente Agripino Enciso, and other protected areas, including Cerro Cabrera, Río Negro National Park and the Cañada El Carmen Reserve. It also includes a single urban centre on the Paraguay River, Bahía Negra.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The El Chaco Biosphere Reserve, in northern Paraguay, features highly diverse dry-forest ecosystems, which support a great diversity of mammals, birds, reptiles and other fauna. Some species are considered threatened, such as the guanaco, jaguar, tapir and the giant armadillo. The territory shares similar areas with its Chaco neighbours, the Argentinean Chaco and the Bolivian Chaco, with whom it maintains a fluid exchange. Located in the biosphere reserve’s core area, Río Negro National Park is also a Ramsar Site, designated in 1995.
records.name: El Chaco

records.introduction_en: Cat Ba Biosphere Reserve is an archipelago located in northern Viet Nam adjacent to the Ha Long Bay World Heritage site.
