It is internationally renowned for its limestone karst geomorphology and provides one of the best examples in the world of a fengcong and fenglin karst landscape invaded by the sea. The 366 limestone islands include landforms, caves and cave deposits that provide evidence of a long history of erosion and landscape evolution.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Cat Ba Biosphere Reserve is considered part of the Indochinese rainforest biogeographical province. It includes tropical humid forests, wetlands, mangroves and coral reef ecosystem types. The northern coastal region of Viet Nam has a humid, tropical monsoon climate with distinct wet and dry seasons. The area suffers from a high frequency of typhoons, with 28 per cent of all typhoons impacting the Vietnamese coastline appearing in this area. There are 2,026 species found in the biosphere reserve, including 199 phytoplankton and 89 zooplankton. The flora and fauna also include 75 forms of seaweed, 23 types of mangrove and 160 corals. There are 475 zoobenthonic organisms and 119 fish, three seagrasses, 142 species of terrestrial fauna and 741 plants. Many species are endemic and rare, the most significant being the globally important golden-headed langur (Trachypithecus poliocephalus), restricted in range to Cat Ba Island, the largest of the 366 islands, and found nowhere else in the world. The hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata) found in the Cat Ba region is inscribed on the IUCN Red List, while the seahorse (Hippocampus) is also rare and threatened. Mangroves and seagrasses on Cat Ba function as nurseries for life in the bay and as protective buffers for local inhabitants from storm surges and typhoons driven by climate change and sea-level rise.
records.name: Cat Ba

records.introduction_en: The Langbiang Biosphere Reserve is located in Lam Dong Province. Regional biodiversity is high and includes many endangered species listed on international red lists. The core area contains a biodiversity corridor that maintains the integrity of 14 tropical ecosystems in the east of southern Viet Nam and across Viet Nam in general. It also provides habitat for numerous wildlife species, including several classified as rare and endangered, such as the sun bear (Helarctos malayanus). Agriculture, forestry and fishery are the main sources of employment for local communities. Among cultivated crops, flowers, coffee and tea generate the strongest regional revenue.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is in the northern part of Lam Dong Province in the Central Highlands of Viet Nam. It is one of four national biodiversity centres. The altitude ranges from 650 metres to nearly 2,300 metres. Several different forest systems occur, including middle-mountain evergreen forest, coniferous broad-leaved mixed forest, primeval forests, high-mountain dwarf forest, mossy forest, bamboo and savannah. The reserve also contains precious trees around 1,000 years old, which are being researched by members of the Tree Ring Lab at the Lamont–Doherty Earth Observatory of Columbia University in New York. The reserve is characterised by rich vegetation, including Krempf’s pine (Pinus krempfii) forest ecosystems and dwarf forest on hilly topography, which is distributed over 60 per cent of the total forest area. The reserve includes 1,940 plant species belonging to 825 genera and 180 families, of which 64 are listed in the Viet Nam Red Data Book and 34 are of high conservation value. Plant species play important roles in conservation and pharmaceutical use. They include two critically endangered species, agarwood (Aquilaria crassna) and the spotted orchid (Gastrochilus calceolaris), and three globally endangered species, dong nai mango (Mangifera dongnaiensis), white meranti (Shorea roxburghii) and Cinnamomum balansae. Overall, 89 species of mammals, 247 species of birds, 46 species of reptiles, 46 species of amphibians, 30 species of fish and 335 species of insects have been recorded within the reserve. These include five globally critically endangered species: the Indochinese tiger (Panthera tigris corbetti), black-shanked douc (Pygathrix nigripes), yellow-cheeked gibbon (Nomascus gabriellae), Indian bison (Bos gaurus) and Indochinese silvered leaf monkey (Trac … [truncated]
records.name: Langbiang

records.introduction_en: The waters around the islands are considered some of the best fishing grounds in the southwestern region of Viet Nam of which the most important resources are squid and cuttlefish.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve has three core zones that overlap with three national parks and one nature reserve. These areas include parts of the Mekong River basin, Phu Quoc Island and several protected marine areas, some of which host coral reefs. The reserve contains various tropical forest ecosystems. These include primary and secondary forests with dominant Dipterocarpaceae families, and limestone and karst forests with dominant species of Trestonia mergvensis and Dacrydium pierrei. There are also seasonally flooded forests dominated by Melaleuca cajuputi, mangrove ecosystems including Rhizophora, Aegiceras, Bruguiera and Avicennia, especially Lumnitzera rosea, as well as coastal mudflats, lakes and coral reef and seagrass ecosystems. There are 89 hard coral species, 19 soft corals, 125 coral reef fishes, 132 molluscs, 32 echinoderms and 62 seaweed species. The seagrass beds are important for foraging marine turtles and support a population of the globally threatened dugong (Dugong dugon). They also provide habitat for the scaly clam (Tridacna squamosa), the trochus shell (Trochus niloticus), and the Critically Endangered hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata) and green turtle (Chelonia mydas).
records.name: Kien Giang

records.introduction_en: Set along Tanzania’s south-eastern coast, the Rufiji–Mafia–Kibiti–Kilwa (RUMAKI) Biosphere Reserve is a largely low-lying marine–coastal seascape of coral reefs, seagrass meadows, mangrove forests and open waters centred on Mafia Island and the crescent-shaped Rufiji Delta. It includes Tanzania’s first marine protected area – Mafia Island Marine Park – and neighbours the Swahili stone-town ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara. RUMAKI’s objectives are to conserve mangroves and the Mafia–Songosongo reef–seagrass complex, foster community-led fisheries and low-impact ecotourism for resilient livelihoods, and underpin management with research, monitoring and education.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: A coastal–marine system of exceptional richness, the RUMAKI Biosphere Reserve brings together coral reefs, seagrass beds, mangroves, intertidal flats, sandbanks and deeper offshore waters. It is recognised as the most biologically productive and diverse marine area in Tanzania and East Africa. At its heart lies the largest contiguous mangrove block on the Eastern Africa seaboard – the Rufiji Delta Mangrove Forest Reserve – alongside far-reaching reef systems around Mafia and Songosongo, part of which is designated as a Ramsar site.Marine and coastal habitats here support a nesting population of 80–100 female green and hawksbill turtles. The shoreline and wetlands provide important stopovers for Palearctic migratory birds and other waders, and dolphins are recorded year-round between Kitutia and Mange reefs. The area is nationally important for prawn fisheries and for pelagic fisheries that target open-water species, and it harbours vulnerable and endangered wildlife, including an aggregation of over 100 whale sharks (Rhineodon typus) and a small remnant population of dugong (Dugong dugon).Ecological functions are very significant within the reserve: seagrass meadows are highly productive nurseries that also store carbon; mangrove forests buffer coastal communities from storms, erosion and tsunamis; and flowering, diverse plant species sustain beekeeping and honey production – a direct link between ecosystem health and coastal livelihoods.
records.name: Rumaki (Rufiji-Mafia-Kibiti-Kilwa)

records.introduction_en: The Serengeti–Ngorongoro biosphere reserve includes Serengeti National Park and the Ngorongoro Conservation Area in northern Tanzania. It supports about 1.5 million wildebeest, 900,000 Thomson’s gazelle and 300,000 zebra. Topis, giraffes, black rhino, antelopes and primates are also well represented. The large herbivores support five main predator species, including lions, leopards, cheetahs, spotted hyenas and wild dogs. The reserve is also home to the Indigenous Maasai people, alongside a fast-growing tourist industry.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The plains of the Serengeti are mostly formed by crystalline rocks overlain by volcanic ash, with numerous rock outcrops known as kopjes. The open plain rises to the crater highlands, comprising volcanic massifs reaching up to 3,587 metres above sea level. The Ngorongoro Crater is a giant caldera, some 16–19 km in diameter, with the floor lying 400–600 metres below the rim. A variable climate and diverse landforms have resulted in several distinct habitats. Serengeti’s undulating plains are covered in grass, but turn almost to desert during periods of severe drought. Some woodlands are found along the rivers. More elevated areas are covered by scrub and heath, with remains of montane forest, notably on the upper slopes within the Ngorongoro Conservation Area. The Serengeti and Ngorongoro regions are known for vast herds of ungulates that migrate following the water supply. The most common are the Thomson’s gazelle (Gazella thomsoni), wildebeest (Connochaetes taurinus), zebra (Equus burchelli), Grant’s gazelle (Gazella granti) and buffalo (Syncerus caffer). The accompanying predators include lion (Panthera leo), leopard (Panthera pardus), cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus), jackal (Canis aureus and Canis adustus) and wild dog (Lycaon pictus). There is a noteworthy black rhinoceros (Diceros bicornis) population.
records.name: Serengeti-Ngorongoro

records.introduction_en: The Zambezi valley is part of Region 54 of the African Terrestrial Ecoregions. It consists of Riverine, and terrestrial ecosystems unique to the subcontinent.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Among threatened species found in the valley are the black Rhino (Diceros bicornis), the painted wild dog, (Lycaon pictus) and the Nyala (Tragelaphus angasii). The flora consist of Colophospermum/Combretum/Terminalia woodland and the Zambezi riparian forest. At Mana Pools, it comprises the only flood plain ecosystem left in the Middle Zambezi.
records.name: Middle Zambezi

records.introduction_en: In the heart of the Dominican Republic, the Madre de las Aguas Biosphere Reserve spans across 11 provinces and 35 municipalities. Shaped by the Cordillera Central, its varied topography includes plateaux and cascading waterfalls. The reserve contains four distinct ecosystems and harbours 88 bird species, 20 of which are endemic and 17 are under threat. The Sparrowhawk (Buteo ridgwayi) is classified as Critically Endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The region features plateaux, intramontane valleys, waterfalls, gorges and canyons, and an exceptional hydrographic network of more than 700 watercourses covering the island’s eight main watersheds. Its four ecosystems are subtropical broadleaf rainforests, subtropical dry broadleaf forests, subtropical coniferous forests and montane grasslands and shrublands. It is one of the most important sites in the country for bird conservation: 88 species have been recorded, of which 20 are endemic and 17 are threatened, notably the Sparrowhawk (Buteo ridgwayi), categorised as Critically Endangered by IUCN, while six others are protected under CITES.
records.name: Madre de las Aguas

records.introduction_en: This picturesque landscape in the Veneto region of north-eastern Italy is defined by 81 volcanic hills, including Monte Venda, rising amidst thermal spas and plains with olive groves and vineyards. Endowed with a diverse array of flora and fauna endemic to the Veneto plain, the biosphere reserve has established partnerships with universities and a comprehensive management framework.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Euganean Hills, or Colli Euganei, are of volcanic origin. The region fosters sustainable agriculture and ecotourism while ensuring participatory governance, laying the groundwork for harmonious coexistence between human economic activities and environmental preservation.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Colli Euganei

records.introduction_en: The Khomyn Tal Biosphere Reserve, situated in the Great Lakes Basin of western Mongolia, extends across desert and arid steppes, mountain ranges, sand dunes, lakes, and rivers. It brings together key conservation zones, including a national park, a local protected area, and an internationally recognized Important Bird Area, creating a vital ecological corridor for migratory ungulates and endangered species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The core area contains two sections. The Seer Mountains are dedicated to the reintroduction of the Przewalski’s Horse (Equus ferus przewalskii), while the Khomyn Tal plain supports populations of Mongolian gazelle (Procapra gutturosa), Saiga antelope (Saiga tatarica), Black-tailed gazelle (Gazella subgutturosa), and the elusive snow leopard (Panthera uncia). The steppe ecosystem is dominated by Stipa, Artemisia, Caragana, and feather grass communities, which sustain rich biodiversity and provide essential habitat for more than 250 bird species, including globally threatened species such as the great bustard (Otis tarda) and the lesser kestrel (Falco naumanni). The varied topography and sand deposits also support endemic plants and desert-adapted mammals of the Central Asian steppe.
records.name: Khomyn Tal

records.introduction_en: Situated on both the northern and southern slopes of the Qinling Range in Shaanxi Province, Zhouzhi Biosphere Reserve straddles the boundary between China’s northern temperate and northern subtropical zones. This mountain range forms the watershed between the Yangtze and Yellow River basins and is a vital geographic and climatic divide. The biosphere reserve is 96% forested and serves as an ecological bridge between major biogeographic regions, while also sustaining cultural traditions and thriving local economies.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Zhouzhi Biosphere Reserve harbors over 3,630 species of wild flora and fauna. Its forests span distinct vertical zones, creating a rich diversity of habitats. Iconic species include the Qinling Panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca qinlingensis), Golden Snub-nosed Monkey (Rhinopithecus roxellana qinlingensis), and Golden Takin (Budorcas bedfordi). Twelve species are classified as critically endangered or endangered on the IUCN Red List, and 64 are endemic to China. The Qinling Mountains play a crucial role as a climatic and ecological barrier, supporting both temperate and subtropical communities. Forest ecosystems regulate water for the Yangtze and Yellow rivers, store carbon, and sustain soil stability, making the area a key ecological security zone for central China.
records.name: Zhouzhi

records.introduction_en: The Ajloun Biosphere Reserve, located in northern Jordan, is a vital ecological and cultural site recognized for its role in biodiversity conservation, sustainable development, and environmental education. Situated within the Mediterranean biogeographical zone, the reserve is dominated by evergreen oak forests that provide essential habitats for diverse flora and fauna, including globally threatened species such as Iris bismarckiana and Iris atropurpurea. It is also designated as an Important Bird Area (IBA), serving as a key nesting and stopover site for migratory birds along the African-Eurasian Flyway. These ecosystems make Ajloun a crucial refuge for species survival and a cornerstone of national conservation efforts. Beyond its ecological value, the reserve supports local communities through socio-economic initiatives that link cultural heritage with sustainable practices. Small enterprises such as the Soap House, Biscuit House, and Calligraphy House, together with ecotourism facilities like accommodations, restaurants, and adventure activities, create alternative livelihoods while strengthening the connection between conservation and community well-being. Managed by the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature (RSCN), the reserve also serves as a hub for education, research, and training, ensuring that Ajloun fulfils its role as a model biosphere reserve where conservation, development, and knowledge sharing are integrated.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Ajloun Biosphere Reserve, located in Jordan’s northern highlands, spans elevations from 700 to 1,100 meters. Its Mediterranean climate, combined with its fertile soils and varied topography of valleys, wadis, and mountains, make Ajloun one of Jordan’s most ecologically rich areas. The reserve lies within the Mediterranean biogeographical zone and is dominated by evergreen oak (Quercus coccifera) forests, complemented by species such as Palestinian pistachio, strawberry tree, hawthorn, and buckthorn. It is also home to 15 nationally endangered orchids and diverse wildlife, including mammals such as the golden jackal, red fox, wildcat, and Persian squirrel; reptiles such as the European chameleon and Palestinian viper; and numerous migratory and resident birds, from the hoopoe to the short-toed eagle. This ecological richness underscores Ajloun’s significance as a biodiversity hotspot.
records.name: Ajloun

records.introduction_en: Located in Madagascar’s Alaotra Mangoro region, the Mantadia Biosphere Reserve covers humid tropical forest, wetlands, riparian zones, and regenerating landscapes. It connects Analamazaotra and Mantadia National Parks through the Kalanoro Forest Corridor, creating a vital ecological bridge for one of the island’s most celebrated rainforest ecosystems.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The core areas protect intact primary forest that harbors exceptional biodiversity. The biosphere reserve is home to 14 lemur species, including the indri (Indri indri), diademed sifaka (Propithecus diadema), and black-and-white ruffed lemur (Varecia variegata). It also contains 113 bird species, 51 reptiles, 84 amphibians, and 388 recorded plant species, of which 329 are endemic. Critically endangered plants such as Breonia madagascariensis and rare amphibians like Mantella aurantiaca highlight the site’s global ecological importance.
records.name: Mantadia

records.introduction_en: The Kinabatangan Biosphere Reserve, located in Sabah on the island of Borneo, follows the Kinabatangan River, one of Malaysia’s longest waterways. It links the Heart of Borneo’s mountainous headwaters to the Lower Kinabatangan Segama Wetlands, a Ramsar site of international importance. The reserve integrates forests, wetlands, and community landscapes into one of Southeast Asia’s most dynamic conservation corridors.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve protects a remarkable mosaic of tropical ecosystems, including lowland dipterocarp forests, peat swamps, mangroves, heath forests, ultramafic forests, limestone forests, and extensive wetlands. It harbors 127 species of mammals, 315 species of birds, 100 reptiles, and 33 amphibians, of which 64 are globally threatened. Notable species include the Bornean orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus), Bornean pygmy elephant (Elephas maximus borneensis), proboscis monkey (Nasalis larvatus), sun bear (Helarctos malayanus), and clouded leopard (Neofelis nebulosa). The area is recognized as one of the world’s most important strongholds for riverine biodiversity.
records.name: Kinabatangan

records.introduction_en: Located in Cabo Delgado Province in the north of the country, the site consists of 11 islands. It combines marine parks and a freshwater system, including the Montepuez River and Lake Bilibiza, a bird sanctuary. The islands support 3,000 floral species, of which 1,000 are endemic. They also support a rich fauna that includes 23 species of reptiles, 447 species of birds and 46 species of terrestrial mammals, including four of the Big Five: elephant, lion, buffalo and leopard. There are also eight species of marine mammals, including whales and dolphins. The main economic activities are fishing, animal husbandry, tourism, arts and crafts, and sea transport.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: According to Udvardy’s classification of the world’s biogeographical provinces, published in 1975, the biosphere reserve forms part of the Afrotropical ecological realm and, within it, the miombo forest biogeographical region. The area also includes marine and terrestrial habitats, including mangroves, seagrass meadows and coral reefs. In the marine environment, there are 52 coral species and 140 mollusc species, including threatened taxa such as Charonia tritonis, Cypraecassis rufa, Cassis cornuta and Tridacna squamosa. Five marine turtle species occur: loggerhead (Caretta caretta), green (Chelonia mydas), leatherback (Dermochelys coriacea), hawksbill (Eretmochelys imbricata) and olive ridley (Lepidochelys olivacea). All are included on the IUCN Red List. The terrestrial part of the biosphere reserve features five main types of vegetation cover: three distinct types of miombo woodland (open miombo woodland, dense miombo woodland and Velloziaceae–miombo woodland), coastal thicket (scrubland), open forest and grassland, including acacia grassland, riparian forests and mangrove forest. As for land fauna, the biosphere reserve includes species of worldwide importance, including four of the Big Five: elephant (Loxodonta africana), buffalo (Syncerus caffer), lion (Panthera leo) and leopard (Panthera pardus), with significant populations of African wild dogs (Lycaon pictus). There are records of 46 species of medium- to large-sized mammals, of which six are endangered and 13 are protected by law in Mozambique. A total of 447 bird species can be found, of which at least one species, the ground hornbill (Bucorvus leadbeateri), is endangered, and 12 others are protected by law in Mozambique.
records.name: Quirimbas

records.introduction_en: The Aïr and Ténéré Biosphere Reserve is located in the Agadez region in northern Niger and covers almost 24 million hectares. It contains the volcanic rock massif of the Aïr and the Saharan desert of Ténéré. The flora comprises about 300 higher plant species, while the fauna boasts an outstanding variety of wild animals, including three threatened antelope species. The area is renowned for numerous archaeological and prehistoric sites, with rock engravings indicative of ancient human settlements. Today, Tuareg nomads constitute the largest population within the reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is one of the driest zones in the country and encompasses two geographic regions. Aïr is a mountainous massif of crystalline and volcanic rocks and shows traces of early metalworking. Ténéré is made up of Quaternary sands (fine alluvium, disc-shaped sands of aeolian origin and moving sand dunes). The flora comprises about 300 higher plant species. Several species persist from the humid period of the Holocene, including olive baboon (Papio anubis), patas monkey (Erythrocebus patas), and Cape dassie (Procavia capensis), as well as carnivores such as caracal and hyena. Other species such as Loder’s gazelle (Gazella leptoceros), dama gazelle (Gazella dama), white antelope (Addax nasomaculatus) and ostrich (Struthio camelus) are in a precarious situation due to low population numbers. The Aïr and Ténéré Natural Reserves have been inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List.
records.name: Aïr et Ténéré

records.introduction_en: The ‘W’ Region Biosphere Reserve is the first transboundary biosphere reserve in Africa. The Niger component of the ‘W’ complex was designated a biosphere reserve in 1996. After a long process of study and consultation, and strong support from the concerned national authorities, the reserve was extended to Burkina Faso and Benin in 2002. The ‘W’ Region Transboundary Biosphere Reserve takes its name from the double bend of the Niger River and today covers more than 3 million hectares. The biosphere reserve straddles the borders of the Soudano-Guinean, Sudanese and Sahel biogeographic regions and is home to wide and varied biodiversity. The ‘W’ Region also constitutes a barrier against the advance of desertification from the north. The area hosts one of the largest populations of ungulates in West Africa and comprises wetlands of international importance recognised under the Ramsar Convention. People have occupied the area since the Neolithic period and have contributed to the development of the present landscape. Wild plant species continue to play an important role in traditional land use and agriculture. For all these reasons, parts of the biosphere reserve are inscribed on the World Heritage List.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is located in the transition zone between the Sudanese region and the forested Guinean region. It includes shrub and tree savannahs and gallery forests along watercourses. The climate is tropical, with an average annual rainfall of between 500 mm and 800 mm. Average temperatures range between 31.2 °C and 10.7 °C for January, the coldest month, and 44 °C and 26 °C for May, the hottest. The reserve hosts rich and varied fauna, including 114 species of fish and over 367 species of birds, amid landscapes of great natural beauty. More than 70 species of mammals can also be found, including the West African manatee (Trichechus senegalensis), African elephant (Loxodonta africana), aardvark (Orycteropus afer) and caracal (Caracal caracal). Threatened species include the cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) and the last population of West African giraffe (Giraffa camelopardalis). The riparian part of the reserve, 3,500 ha, includes some of the most important permanent humid zones in West Africa. It incorporates three Ramsar sites: Site du Complexe W in Benin, Dallol Bosso in Niger and Parc National du W in Burkina Faso.
records.name: W Region

records.introduction_en: In the coastal evergreen rainforest along the Gulf of Biafra, Okwangwo lies in the north of Cross River National Park, on the edge of the Cameroon Highlands between the Cross and Sanga rivers. This combination of river systems underpins a unique wealth of biodiversity.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Faunal species in the area include African elephant (Loxodonta africana), African buffalo (Syncerus caffer nanus) and bushpig (Potamochoerus porcus pictus), as well as the critically endangered Cross River gorilla (Gorilla gorilla diehli). The fauna of the Okwangwo Forest Reserve is highly diversified because of its position on the edge of the Cameroon Highlands between the Cross and Sanga rivers. It contains some of the most extensive areas of relatively undisturbed tropical moist forest remaining in Nigeria and lies within the Lower Guinea faunal region. Species typical of the Guineo-Congolian forest occur, including elephant, African buffalo and bushpig. The reserve also supports many narrowly distributed plants and animals from the Cross River in Nigeria to the Sanga River in Cameroon, together with the island of Bioko, including the giant otter shrew (Potamogale velox), angwantibo (Arctocebus calabarensis), drill (Mandrillus leucophaeus), Preuss’s guenon (Cercopithecus preussi) and chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes). The Okwangwo Division has richly diverse flora, with about 1,545 species representing 98 plant families recorded. There are 280 recorded bird species, including the vulnerable grey-necked rockfowl (Picathartes oreas), which breeds in the Mbe Mountains, the golden greenbul (Calyptocichla serinus), which is rare in Nigeria, and the grey parrot.
records.name: Okwangwo

records.introduction_en: Bosawas is a meeting point between the fauna of North and South America. It hosts an enormous diversity of vertebrate and invertebrate organisms. It is located in north-eastern Nicaragua and is bordered to the north-west by the Republic of Honduras, to the west by the departments of Jinotega and Nueva Segovia, to the south by the South Caribbean Autonomous Region, and to the east by the North Caribbean Autonomous Region.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The tropical forest is the richest biome on the planet, and estimates indicate that 13 per cent of known species worldwide can be found in Bosawas. There is a significant number of quetzals. The arboreal composition of the reserve’s forests does not present significant changes because of high humidity levels. This is a positive factor for biodiversity conservation. Scientific studies carried out by MARENA (2011) indicate that “in the core areas of the reserve the forests show an excellent state of conservation, surrounded by an area with intervened areas”. Six kinds of forests can be found in the biosphere reserve.
records.name: Bosawas

records.introduction_en: The Darién Biosphere Reserve, National Park and World Heritage site is in the province of Darién, east of Santa Fe and the Gulf of San Miguel. It covers the region adjacent to the Colombian border and includes parts of the Pacific coast. This reserve is a unique site that forms the bridge between the two continents of the Western Hemisphere.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve comprises raised folds and high mountains, with the most extensive lowland tropical forest on the Pacific coast in Central America. It contains a wide range of habitats, including sandy beaches, rocky coasts, mangroves, freshwater marshes, palm-forest swamps, and lowland and upland moist tropical forest. Darién forests have been characterised by scientists as the most diverse ecosystems of tropical America and are still relatively undisturbed. It is one of the greatest natural heritages of the Central American region, with four of the nine ecoregions and seven of the thirteen life zones identified in the country. The Darién region also contains three eco-floristic zones and four identified endemic hotspots in Panama.
records.name: Darién

records.introduction_en: The Huascarán Biosphere Reserve is located in the department of Ancash, north of Lima, in the central-west region of Peru. Its altitude ranges from 1,020–6,768 m at Mount Huascarán and encompasses 11 habitat types, from tropical desert scrub to Andean tundra. The Cordillera Blanca, an Andean mountain range within the biosphere reserve, is considered the world’s most extensive tropical cordillera and hosts numerous glaciers and 296 lakes. The population is mostly ethnic Andean mestizo and is mainly engaged in agriculture and livestock-rearing. The region also contains mining concessions and has a commitment to tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Cordillera Blanca is the most extensive tropical ice-covered mountain range in the world, with the largest concentration of ice found in Peru. Peru’s highest peak, Mount Huascarán (6,768 m), is located in the Cordillera Blanca. The area contains a variety of formations, including sub-alpine wet páramo, alpine and nival pluvial tundra, and moist montane forest formations in the majority of ravines. The soils of the Huascarán Biosphere Reserve are alluvial, colluvial–alluvial and glacio-fluvial, with residual material soils and anthropogenic soils. Glaciation is a major element in the geomorphology and hydrology of the area. It is estimated that around one-quarter of the volume of glacial ice in the cordillera may have disappeared since the late nineteen-sixties, an ongoing process that will likely transform the landscape of the reserve. The Huascarán National Park, which lies within the reserve, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Glaciers extend for approximately 180 kilometres, from Nevado Tuco in the south to the vicinity of Nevado Champara in the north, and cap a series of imposing mountains. Around 296 lagoons have also been identified within the limits of the biosphere reserve. Among the most representative vegetation are Polylepis forests and the Queen of the Andes (Puya raimondii), known for its giant flower spike. Fauna represented in the area includes the northern viscacha (Lagidium peruanum), Andean fox or culpeo (Lycalopex culpaeus), spectacled bear (Tremarctos ornatus), Andean white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus peruvianus), taruca (Hippocamelus antisensis) and Andean condor (Vultur gryphus).
records.name: Huascaran

records.introduction_en: The Manu Biosphere Reserve is situated in the departments of Cusco and Madre de Dios in south-eastern Peru. Its lowest point lies at 300 m, and its highest point, the summit of Apu Kañahuay, reaches 3,800 m. The reserve includes 19 habitat types and is among the most diverse places for birds in the world, with 860 identified species. There are numerous settlements of native communities, including the Matsigueka, Yine, Harakmbut and Quechua.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Manu Biosphere Reserve is the largest rainforest reserve in the world. Its altitude ranges from 3,800 m at the top of Apu Kañahuay down to 300 m, where the Manu River converges with the Alto Madre de Dios. Predominant plant formations are highland punas, then a transition belt of woody scrubland followed by low montane forest. Below this altitude lies montane rainforest and, finally, tropical moist forest or lowland forest stretching along the great Amazon plains. Manu is considered to be among the sites with the highest biodiversity in the world. Over 3,000 plant species have been identified. Fauna is similarly impressive, with over 1,000 vertebrate species observed, including at least 200 species of mammals and more than 800 species of birds. Recorded mammals include the giant otter (Pteronura brasiliensis), giant armadillo (Priodontes maximus), emperor tamarin (Saguinus imperator) and brown-throated sloth (Bradypus variegatus). Thirteen primate species and eight felids are present, including the jaguar (Panthera onca), cougar (Puma concolor) and the elusive and endangered Andean mountain cat (Leopardus jacobita).
records.name: Manu

records.introduction_en: The Oxapampa–Ashaninka–Yanesha Biosphere Reserve is in the Department of Pasco in central Peru. It contains the last undisturbed ecosystems in the country’s central jungle. Its position between the Amazon forest lowland and the montane cloud forest results in high diversity of flora and fauna, and a marked altitudinal range of 300–4,500 m at Nevado de Huaguruncho. The reserve is composed of native communities including Yánesha, Asháninka and Ashéninka, descendants of European settlers of Austro-German and Swiss origin, and communities from the Andes, coastal areas and the Amazonian jungle. These communities engage mainly in agriculture and livestock rearing, although logging and handicraft development have gained importance in recent years.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Oxapampa–Ashaninka–Yanesha Biosphere Reserve is representative of the Peruvian Upper Amazon Forest region in the Tropical Andes and is situated within the biogeographic province of the Tropical Yungas. The area has a high concentration of fauna and flora with restricted distributions, and a wide diversity of zones and transitional areas. The transition from Amazon low forest to montane cloud forest, combined with uneven physiographic characteristics and high rainfall, has produced a complex range of flora that includes epiphytes, lianas, grasses, shrubs and trees. Examples of the rich wildlife include the Andean cock-of-the-rock (Rupicola peruvianus), white-lipped peccary (Tayassu pecari), South American tapir (Tapirus terrestris), spectacled bear (Tremarctos ornatus), jaguar (Panthera onca) and harpy eagle (Harpia harpyja), the largest predator of treetop fauna and an indicator of the integrity of several ecosystems. The frog Ctenophryne barbatula is found only in the reserve.
records.name: Oxapampa-Ashaninka-Yanesha

records.introduction_en: Pakistan’s largest juniper forest is located in this reserve. The forest ecosystem is of inestimable value for biodiversity conservation. It is also of great ecological significance, providing local, regional and global benefits.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is home to the largest area of juniper forest (Juniperus excelsa) in Pakistan, covering about 110,000 ha. It is believed that the forest is the second largest of its kind in the world. The juniper tree species found here are of global significance because of their advanced age and slow growth rate. The junipers of Ziarat are among the oldest living trees in the world. Although no dendrological study has yet been conducted, one estimate suggests the age of a mature tree can exceed 1,500 years. Local people refer to the trees as living fossils, and this remarkable longevity allows research into past weather conditions in the region. This makes the species of special significance for climate change and ecological studies. The juniper forest ecosystem of Ziarat provides a habitat for endangered wildlife species and supports a rich diversity of plant species. Because of its rich biodiversity, the different areas of the ecosystem have been assigned protected status, including wildlife sanctuaries and game reserves. The mountain ranges, including Khalifat Mountain, consist of a core habitat reportedly hosting several globally important wild species, among them the Suleman markhor, urial, black bears and wolves. The forests also serve as a habitat for other species, including the Afghan pika, foxes, jackals and several species of migratory birds. Various anthropological factors such as illegal hunting, human habitation and livestock grazing have encroached on wildlife habitats, leading to their fragmentation.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Ziarat Juniper forests

records.introduction_en: The Babia Gora Biosphere Reserve is the second-highest mountain massif in Poland and is situated in the Beskid Mountains. Its highest peak reaches 1,725 m above sea level and forms a watershed between the Baltic Sea and the Black Sea basins.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Four habitats, changing with altitude, are represented in the biosphere reserve: the lower forest belt, up to 1,150 m; the upper forest belt, up to 1,390 m; the dwarf pine belt, up to 1,650 m; and the alpine belt, up to 1,725 m. The biosphere reserve was extended as a result of the periodic review in 2000. It now includes a state forest oriented to near-natural forest management, as well as inhabited areas.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Babia Gora

records.introduction_en: This transboundary biosphere reserve lies in the Central European biogeographical region and is characterised by boreal coniferous forests and temperate deciduous forests. West Polesie plays a critical role at the junction of biogeographical regions, migratory pathways and cultural landscapes.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The West Polesie Biosphere Reserve contains numerous lakes (several dozen in Belarus, 62 in Poland and 28 in Ukraine) alongside marshes, meadows, and swamp and lake complexes with distinctive flora and fauna. These include rare and endangered species listed in the Red Books of Belarus, Poland and Ukraine, as well as international Red Lists. The region lies at the meeting point of different biogeographical zones, where many species occur at the edge of their ranges, including relict boreal, Atlantic, eastern-continental and Pontian species. West Polesie is home to the globally endangered aquatic warbler (Acrocephalus paludicola). It is also a breeding area for European endangered birds, including the marsh sandpiper (Tringa stagnatilis) and the Eurasian crane (Grus grus). The area is an important crossing point for migratory birds: north to south flyways, notably the White Sea, Baltic and Mediterranean route, intersect with east to west latitudinal routes in West Polesie. Two endemic plant species occur in the region, Silene lituanica and Festuca polessica, as well as four rare orchid species. The West Polesie Biosphere Reserve expands opportunities for biodiversity conservation in Europe and helps mitigate boundary effects for migrating animals such as wolves, elk and European bison.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: West Polesie

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is situated on the coast of the north-western part of the Florida Peninsula, within the Apalachicola River floodplain. It comprises Apalachicola Bay, which is one of the most productive estuarine systems in the northern hemisphere.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Located along the curve of the Florida Panhandle, the reserve encompasses 234,715 acres of diverse marine and terrestrial habitat. The reserve boundaries include 52 miles of the lower river and its associated floodplain, most of Apalachicola Bay, two barrier islands, part of a third, and several small out-parcels. In the Central Gulf Coastal Plain ecoregion, there are typical estuarine and coastal formations, including river channels, sloughs, backwaters, bay islands and swamp hardwood forests. The Apalachicola Basin has the highest species density of amphibians and reptiles in all of North America north of Mexico.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Apalachicola

records.introduction_en: Situated west of Los Angeles, the Channel Islands Biosphere Reserve represents one of the last examples of natural Mediterranean ecosystems in North America and some of the few remaining natural southern California coastal ecosystems. Characteristic features are coastal sage scrub communities on the islands and exceptionally pristine tide pools on the marine terraces surrounding them.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Eight islands are encompassed within this biosphere reserve, which offers one of the last examples of natural Mediterranean ecosystems in North America and some of the few remaining natural southern California coastal ecosystems. The area’s major terrestrial ecosystem type is evergreen sclerophyllous woodland, with a coastal and marine component. Characteristic features are coastal sage scrub communities on the islands. Marine sanctuary waters cover 1,128 square nautical miles, extending from mean high tide to 6 nautical miles offshore of San Miguel, Santa Rosa, Santa Cruz, Anacapa and Santa Barbara islands. Warm and cool currents support a great variety of flora and fauna, including giant kelp, fish and invertebrates, marine birds, pinnipeds and cetaceans. The sanctuary’s secluded, relatively undisturbed waters also provide full- or part-time homes for several endangered species, including blue, humpback and sei whales, southern sea otters, the California brown pelican and the California least tern.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Channel Islands

records.introduction_en: The Champlain–Adirondack Biosphere Reserve straddles the border of north-central New York and north-western Vermont, with Lake Champlain, the sixth largest lake in the United States, and the Adirondack and Green Mountains as its central natural features.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Champlain–Adirondack Biosphere Reserve includes extensive temperate coniferous and deciduous forests, as well as large numbers of lakes, bogs and freshwater wetlands. It comprises the largest protected area in the eastern United States. The single most important ecosystem service is related to watershed values. Lake Champlain is the sixth largest lake in the United States, with its headwaters in the Green Mountains and Adirondack Mountains. Overall, the biosphere reserve contains ecologically healthy populations of approximately 200 species of birds, 58 mammal species, 35 species of reptiles and amphibians, 1,400 plant species and 20,000 species of invertebrates. Eastern timber wolves and mountain lions have been extirpated.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Champlain-Adirondak

records.introduction_en: The Congaree Biosphere Reserve comprises the last vestiges of old-growth bottomland hardwood forest in the eastern United States. It lies in the gently undulating to flat floodplain of the Congaree River and represents a range of natural ecosystems typical of this vast coastal region.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is located in the gently undulating to flat floodplain of the Congaree River and represents a range of natural ecosystems that are typical of this vast coastal region. The area also hosts several endangered animal species, including the red-cockaded woodpecker, American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis) and bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Congaree

records.introduction_en: Denali Biosphere Reserve and National Park is situated in south-central Alaska, centred on the Alaska Range, which separates the coastal lowland from the interior. Denali includes Mount McKinley, the highest peak in North America, which towers 4,800 metres above the surrounding landscape, as well as the Denali fault system, the largest crustal break in North America.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The landscapes and ecosystems of Denali National Park and Preserve are influenced by geological history, earth movements, climate, the advance and retreat of glaciers, permafrost, wildland fire and water flow. One of the major influences on Denali’s ecosystems is the Alaska Range, a massive wall of rock, glacial ice and snow running from south-west to north-east across the park’s 2.4 million hectares. It towers above and separates the Kuskokwim and Tanana river basins to the north from the Susitna River lowlands to the south. This mountain barrier creates two major climate zones in the park and dramatic elevation differences. Denali lies within the northern boreal forest biome. The park’s ecosystems range from lowlands with taiga forests, braided glacial stream floodplains and meandering sloughs to subalpine woodlands, meadows and scrub tundra of willow, alder and dwarf birch. They also include alpine low-shrub tundra slopes and unvegetated steep peaks, including Denali, also called Mount McKinley, at 6,194 metres. Nearly one third of Denali consists of high, glaciated mountains and bare rock outcrops. The upper limit of plant growth is about 2,290 metres. Vertebrate species include 39 mammals, such as grizzly (brown) bear, grey wolf, caribou, moose and Dall’s sheep. There are 168 birds, including 116 documented breeding species, 14 fish, no reptiles and one amphibian, the wood frog. Plant diversity includes 754 vascular plant species, with eight tree species, and approximately 600 species of mosses, lichens and liverworts.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Denali

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve in south-eastern Alaska consists of two units, Glacier Bay and Admiralty Island. Glacial advance and retreat, occurring since the mid-Miocene, have shaped the area’s landscape. The latest episode of ice recession began only 200 years ago, and the ice within Glacier Bay has withdrawn about 95 km during this period.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Plant succession has led to the establishment of pioneer plants closest to the glacier, including lichens, moss, alder, willow, soapberry and cottonwood. More mature forest associations occur at some distance, notably western hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla) and Sitka spruce (Picea sitchensis). Admiralty Island comprises one of the greatest remaining blocks of productive old-growth temperate rain forest in the world. Other plant communities found in both units include shrublands, freshwater marshes and subtidal meadows.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Glacier Bay-Admiralty Island

records.introduction_en: The Guanica Forest Biosphere Reserve is located in the south-west part of Puerto Rico. It is considered the best-preserved subtropical forest and the best example of dry forest in the world. The ecosystem and vegetation systems identified in the reserve include the full sequence of vegetation succession for a coastal tropical dry forest, from coastal shrubs to evergreen and cactus forests.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Guanica Biosphere Reserve encompasses a mosaic of ecological systems. Over nine forest types have been identified at the core zone, and it is considered by many experts as the most pristine subtropical dry forest in the world. It is a critical habitat for a range of species that are endemic and endangered.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Guanica

records.introduction_en: Situated in Kentucky, the Mammoth Cave Area Biosphere Reserve encompasses a karst system characterised by complex underground watercourses and a multilayered cave system with distinctive fauna and mineralisation features. It is also significant culturally, as prehistoric peoples explored the caves, extracted minerals, used them for shelter, and cultivated the surrounding surface area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Mammoth Cave Area Biosphere Reserve covers 909,328 acres in six counties within the Pennyroyal Plateau biogeographic region. This part of Kentucky features rolling hills, caves and widespread karst topography. These conditions have enabled the development of the world’s most extensive cave system. The fauna of Mammoth Cave is among the most diverse cave-dwelling wildlife known, with more than 130 animal species regularly occurring within the cave system. The park also has one of the highest levels of subterranean biodiversity worldwide, with 41 species of cave-adapted organisms.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mammoth Cave Area

records.introduction_en: The New Jersey Pinelands Biosphere Reserve is situated in the urbanised north-eastern United States and consists of a mosaic of upland, wetland and aquatic environments. Wildfires have favoured a pygmy forest of pitch pine (Pinus rigida), blackjack oak and scrub oaks.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The New Jersey Pinelands Biosphere Reserve’s wetlands provide suitable habitats for most of the rare and endangered plant and animal species of the region. The region’s expansive forests provide habitat for 39 species of mammals, 299 species of birds, 59 reptile and amphibian species, and 91 fish species. Forty-three animal species are listed as threatened or endangered. The biosphere reserve also contains approximately 12,000 acres of globally rare pitch pine–shrub oak, large swathes of Atlantic white cedar swamps, intermittent ponds, acid-water aquatic and wetland plants and animals, as well as a fire-adapted landscape.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: New Jersey Pinelands

records.introduction_en: The Virginia Coast Biosphere Reserve is one of the last coastal wildernesses on the East Coast of the United States of America. It is also one of the most important migratory bird stop-over sites in North America. The reserve manages and protects the 1,250-acre seaside farm known as Brownsville Preserve and 45,000 acres of natural landscape. These holdings include 14 barrier and marsh islands, multiple mainland tracts, and a seascape that is being successfully restored with eelgrass, oysters and soon, bay scallops.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Wilderness barrier islands are among the rarest habitats on the eastern seaboard. Beach-nesting birds, including piping plovers, enjoy excellent nesting success, with rates among the highest on the East Coast. Salt marshes, seagrass beds and oyster reefs are among the most diverse, productive and resilient marine habitats on Earth, and they are thriving at the Virginia Coast Biosphere Reserve.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Virginia Coast

records.introduction_en: The Yellowstone–Grand Teton Biosphere Reserve area anchors a broader geography known as the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. The biosphere, at 1,067,380 ha, is the heart of a mosaic of public and private lands that encompasses ecologically valuable protected areas and vibrant western communities. Its diversity and natural wealth include hydrothermal features, wildlife, vegetation and lakes, as well as geological wonders such as the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone River and the Grand Teton, and culturally significant landmarks such as the Miller Ranch.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Yellowstone–Grand Teton biosphere area is incredibly diverse. At its core, the biosphere has an array of flora and fauna, with about 1,386 native plant taxa, 11 species of amphibians, 10 species of reptiles, 341 species of birds, 81 species of mammals and 19 species of fishes. A key value of the biosphere area is the conservation of large assemblages of wildlife across a vast landscape. It has some of the largest elk herds in North America, the largest free-roaming wild herd of bison in the United States, and one of the few grizzly populations in the contiguous United States. The biosphere area supports intact native predator–prey–scavenger communities that move, migrate and disperse across a vast landscape. These communities are subject to a full suite of natural selection factors, including competition, disease, predation and substantial environmental variability. The biosphere is home to glaciers, wetlands, numerous mountains, hundreds of lakes and thousands of kilometres of flowing waters that historically contained 12 species of native fish, including the largest inland population of cutthroat trout in the world. Additionally, the biosphere reserve contains one of the most geologically dynamic areas on Earth. From high peaks and glaciers to earthquakes and shallow magma, the biosphere attracts scientists from around the world. The area contains more than 79 peaks higher than 10,000 feet and about 10,000 hydrothermal features, and it hosts the largest concentration of active geysers in the world. It is one of the few places in the world where active travertine terraces are found. It is also the site of many “stands” of petrified trees formed 45–50 million years ago.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Yellowstone - Grand Teton

records.introduction_en: The Danube Delta Biosphere Reserve is a labyrinth of water and land shared between Romania and Ukraine. It is made up of countless lakes, channels and islands at the end of a 2,860 km long river. The Danube Delta is the largest European wetland and reed bed, and constitutes Europe’s largest water purification system. The area is particularly well known for its abundance of birdlife, with 312 important bird species, many of which use the delta as an important stopover and breeding area. About 90 fish species are present, including populations of sturgeon (Acipenser). The delta is also one of the last refuges of the European mink (Mustela lutreola), the wildcat (Felis silvestris), the freshwater otter (Lutra lutra) and the globally threatened monk seal (Monachus monachus). The Danube Delta is home to a rich mix of Bulgarian, Gagauz, Lipovan, Moldovan, Russian, Turkish and Ukrainian people, scattered around the delta in small villages. The main economic activities in the biosphere reserve are fishing, hunting, reed harvesting, livestock raising and subsistence agriculture, as well as tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Danube Delta is Europe’s largest wetland and reed bed, and functions as its most important water purification system. The delta has wet soils that are temporarily covered with water, with plants adapted to living in wet conditions. The Danube Delta also includes fixed and mobile sand dune areas, home to psamophilic plants. Grassland ecosystems are located on higher parts of riverine bars and on the edges of reed beds, adjacent to coastal bars. The water ecosystems of the reserve are very diverse. They include the freshwater ecosystems of watercourses, limans and numerous lakes and bays, and brackish water ecosystems in the delta of the Kiliya Arm. The freshwater ecosystems give the reserve rich biodiversity. There are 312 bird species, including the glossy ibis (Plegadis falcinellus), the purple heron (Ardea purpurea), the white-tailed eagle (Haliaeetus albicilla) and the largest population of great white pelicans (Pelecanus onocrotalus) in Europe. Fish species include the sterlet (Acipenser ruthenus), small sturgeon, the thornback ray (Raja clavata) and the spined loach (Cobitis danubialis). Other animals living in the Danube Delta include the meadow viper (Vipera ursinii), the European mink (Mustela lutreola), the harbour porpoise (Phocoena phocoena) and the common bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus). The biosphere reserve incorporates four Ramsar wetland sites: the Danube Delta in the Romanian part and Kyliiske Mouth, Kugurlui Lake and Kartal Lake in the Ukrainian part. The Danube Delta is also inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Danube Delta

records.introduction_en: Desnianskyi Biosphere Reserve is located in the middle reach of the Desna River, one of the largest branches of the Dnipro River, in the Eastern Polesie Region. It presents the characteristic landscape types of the eastern Polesie Lowland. These include rivers and lakes, extensive floodplains, bogs, transition mires and fens. The area also includes real, peaty and swampy grasslands, and pine, broad-leaf and mixed forests, including floodplain forests.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Within the area there is preservation of landscapes, ecosystems, species and genetic diversity that are characteristic of the Eastern Polesie Region. The territory is important for conserving floodplain natural complexes in the Desna River basin, as well as pine and oak–pine forests. The flora consists of more than 800 species of vascular plants, and the dendroflora comprises more than 60 per cent of all tree species of the Eastern Polesie Region. There are 20 species listed in the Red Book of Ukraine. Ninety species of the 340 vertebrate species are protected. In particular, 11 species belong to the European Red List, 34 species belong to the IUCN Red List, and 39 species are included in the Red Book of Ukraine. The black stork (Ciconia nigra), grey crane (Grus grus), short-toed eagle (Circaetus gallicus), lesser spotted eagle (Aquila pomarina), booted eagle (Hieraaetus pennatus), capercaillie (Tetrao urogallus), Tengmalm’s owl (Aegolius funereus) and pygmy owl (Glaucidium passerinum) nest in the reserve. The corncrake (Crex crex), which is endangered at the global level, is quite common. In addition, migration routes for a number of birds such as geese, ducks, sandpipers and gulls, and for mammals such as bears and lynxes, are located within this territory. Within the reserve, more than 1,300 invertebrate species are recorded. Osmoderma eremita and Formica polyctena are included in the IUCN Red List. Osmoderma eremita, Hirudo medicinalis, Formica polyctena, Formica rufa and Myrmeleon formicarius are included in the European Red List. Species listed in the Red Book of Ukraine include Acherontia atropos, Anax imperator, Aromia moschata, Bombus muscorum, Calopteryx virgo, Catocala sponsa, Limenitis populi, Lucanus cervus, Nymphalis xanthomelas, Papilio mach … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Desnianskyi

records.introduction_en: Askaniya-Nova Biosphere Reserve represents the Black Sea southern-steppe biogeographic province. It is situated 60 km south-east of the town of Kakhovka, close to the Black Sea. Within this area, the Festuca and Stipa steppe ecosystem has been conserved like an island in the Dnieper–Molochnoe lowland, which otherwise has intensive land use practices.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Major habitats include feather grass steppe dominated by Stipa lessingiana, S. ucrainica and S. capillata, together with fescue (Festuca sulcata) and crested hair grass (Koeleria cristata). There are festucetae communities with Festuca valesiaca, Crinitaria villosa and Stipa ucrainica. Slopes support stipetae associations with species such as Stipa capillata, S. ucrainica and Festuca valesiaca. Dales have elytrigetae communities supporting Elytrigia pseudocaesia, Bromopsis inermis and Poa angustifolia. Wet meadows include Beckmannia eruciformis, Alopecurus pratensis and Juncus gerardii.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Askaniya-Nova

records.introduction_en: The East Carpathians Biosphere Reserve is a transboundary mountain reserve in Central Europe that encompasses areas of significant value for biodiversity conservation. It covers the western edge of the East Carpathians, stretching across Poland, Slovakia and Ukraine. The European mountain areas of the reserve are among the few that retain well-preserved native flora and fauna. In particular, the mixed Carpathian forest provides suitable conditions for large mammals such as the European bison (Bison bonasus). Population density varies, from vast wild spaces on the Polish side to relatively densely populated areas in the Ukrainian part, with cultivated valleys, hay meadows, pastures and deciduous forest. Forestry remains the main local economic activity.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The East Carpathians Biosphere Reserve is located in Western Bieszczady, the southern part of which is known as Bukovske Hills. Primeval forest fragments in this area have been preserved up to the present day. Large portions of the territory comprise forest and non-forest ecosystems, accompanied by numerous plant communities growing in semi-natural rural areas. Four distinct vegetation types are found within the biosphere reserve: beech forest (Fagetum sylvaticae), beech–fir forest (Fageto-Abietum), dwarf-shrublands with green alder (Alnetum viridis), and a belt of treeless poloniny–subalpine meadows dominated by Prata subalpina. The mixed Carpathian forest provides suitable conditions for large mammals such as the European brown bear (Ursus arctos), the European bison (Bison bonasus), the Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx) and the European wolf (Canis lupus). Over 100 species of birds live in the area, including the black stork (Ciconia nigra) and the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos). The reserve also contains several sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List, including the Wooden Tserkvas of the Carpathian Region in Poland and Ukraine, and the Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians in Slovakia and Ukraine.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: East Carpathians

records.introduction_en: The Roztocze Transboundary Biosphere Reserve is located in the Roztocze region in Poland and Ukraine, a natural and cultural borderland near the European Union border. It lies in the immediate vicinity of Lviv in Ukraine and Zamość in Poland, cities inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Roztocze has potential for dynamic development because of its scenic location and rich natural and cultural heritage. The Ukrainian part, called Roztochya, was designated a biosphere reserve in 2011.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The varied relief and complex geological structure are reflected in the tremendous diversity of living nature. The area of the biosphere reserve is not homogeneous. Loess areas are located in the west and are characterised by the highest density of ravines per 1 km² in Poland. Tomaszów Roztocze, known as Roztocze Tomaszowskie, features limestone hills cut by river valleys in the southern marginal zone, forming deeply cut valleys with topographic thresholds. Rava Roztocze, known as Roztocze Rawskie, is an area of wooded hills, mineral waters and good weather, with many sunny days. Roztocze is an ecological corridor of European importance, a narrow land connection linking the Polish Highlands with Podolia, enabling the movement of plants and animals. As a result of this, and its location at the Carpathian arc, plant species of three geographical areas occur in this region. The region is an important natural boundary. The north-eastern limit of the geographical range of beech, fir, spruce and sycamore runs through the region. Heterogeneous forests are the main resources of the region, including in particular the Carpathian beech forest and fir forest. Mammals of Roztocze are represented by 66 species, including three considered extinct (one confirmed, two unconfirmed), and four alien invasive species. The most interesting mammals are bats, including the barbastelle, greater mouse-eared bat, Bechstein’s bat and Alcathoe bat, as well as fat dormouse, forest dormouse, lynx and wolf. The most important refugia of mammals in Roztocze are natural forests located mainly in protected areas. The avifauna of the region includes species of high nature conservation value such as ferruginous duck, black stork, honey buzzard, lesser spotted eagle, Ural owl, boreal owl, gre … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Roztochya

records.introduction_en: This transboundary biosphere reserve is located in the Central European Biogeographical Region and is characterised by boreal coniferous forests and temperate-zone deciduous forests. West Polesie plays a critical role at the juncture of biogeographical regions, migrational pathways and cultural landscapes.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set on the south-west edge of the East European Plain, the reserve sits at the meeting point of boreal coniferous and temperate broadleaf forests. Pine woods with bilberry and green moss occur alongside sedge-dominated mires, as well as fens and occasional oligotrophic bogs. Rivers, canals and ponds wind through and connect the lowland hollows. Twenty-eight lakes form one of the largest lake systems in Europe, created mainly by fluvioglacial processes. Lake Svitiaz is the deepest natural lake in the country at 58.4 metres; its water is fresh, clear and well oxygenated. The deeper lakes of the complex maintain stable levels through water from aquifers, while the shallower peat-fringed lakes are sustained by rainfall and groundwater. These bodies of water deliver essential ecological benefits, supplying oxygen for aquatic wildlife through the winter and supporting high biological productivity of plants and animals. Near-shore vegetation is diverse, including floating and submerged plants such as Aldrovanda vesiculosa and Lemna minor, alongside water-lily communities. The region lies at the meeting point of two major migration routes, and tens of thousands of waterbirds use the lakes in spring and autumn. Western Polesie is a core area for the globally threatened aquatic warbler (Acrocephalus paludicola), with further species of European concern including Haliaeetus albicilla, Milvus milvus and Lutra lutra.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Shatskyi

records.introduction_en: The Ngaremeduu Bay Region lies on the west coast of Babeldaob Island, the largest island of Palau in the South Pacific. The biosphere reserve corresponds to the Ngaremeduu Conservation Area and incorporates the largest estuary in Micronesia, freshwater marshes, Pandanus, grass and shrub savannah, one of the largest stretches of mangroves on the small Pacific islands, and extensive coral reefs and seagrass beds.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Ngaremeduu Bay Region lies on the west coast of Babeldaob Island, the largest island of Palau in the South Pacific. The biosphere reserve corresponds to the Ngaremeduu Conservation Area and incorporates the largest estuary in Micronesia, freshwater marshes, Pandanus, grass and shrub savannah, one of the largest stretches of mangroves on the small Pacific islands, and extensive coral reefs and seagrass beds. The area is among the richest in biodiversity in Micronesia, with a wide range of marine and terrestrial species. Reef habitats support approximately 220 species of stony corals, and when soft corals are included, the total number of coral species can exceed 100 per site. The stretches of mangroves include 44 per cent of Palau’s mangrove forest and comprise 18 mangrove species. Ngaremeduu Bay also provides habitat for several endangered and threatened species, including the dugong, the saltwater crocodile and sea turtles.
records.name: Ngaremeduu

records.introduction_en: The suite of ecotypes in the Al Reem Biosphere Reserve is representative of those found across much of the arid, desert-like Middle East biogeographic region. The varied habitat types between higher limestone mesas and low-lying sabkha plains encompass all but a few of the key Middle Eastern desert ecotypes. The varied forms of land use within the reserve create a complex mosaic of ecological systems. The reserve encompasses open gravel plain grazing pastures interspersed with water-draining wadis, numerous point-source irrigated crop farming operations, traditional Arabian village communities, a limited distribution of commercial and industrial operations, wildlife management and breeding centres, archaeological ruins, traditional artisanal fishing communities, date palm plantations and semi-nomadic animal husbandry.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve constitutes a single land management unit. The landscape is generally flat to undulating, with some prominent hills and the stark-relief mesas of the Zekreet peninsula. Land elevation ranges between 0 m and 60 m above sea level. Saline, swampy mudflats are common along the coastal areas, while rocky elevations and gravel plains are mostly found in the inland parts of the reserve. Notable features include elevated limestone formations along the west coast, known as the Dukhan anticline, under which lies the Dukhan oil field. The reserve has no rivers, and other than occasional rainfall, the primary source of fresh water is fossil groundwater. Surface water is very limited and may be seen in depressions and wadis only for a short time after good winter rainfall. At present, the reserve is home to a breeding centre for native gazelles and oryx. It has also pioneered reintroduction programmes in the country. The reserve offers unparalleled research opportunities for sustainable development and use of arid lands. Potential investigations include the use of saline water for irrigation of halophytes as animal fodder, zonation for sustainable grazing, camel farming and culturally sensitive tourism, among others.
records.name: Al Reem

records.introduction_en: Kristianstads Vattenrike is the oldest of Sweden’s biosphere reserves. Established in 2005, it includes two thirds of the municipality of Kristianstad in Skåne, the southernmost of Sweden’s provinces. This rich cultural landscape is endowed with almost every type of natural habitat to be found in Sweden. The majestic River Helge å is a central feature. Fed by streams from the ridges and plains, it expands into Lakes Araslövssjön and Hammarsjön before reaching the Baltic Sea in Hanöbukten Bay. The river is fringed by wetlands and seasonally flooded grasslands, but there are also leafy forests and dry sandy arable lands within the reserve. Such variety creates numerous habitats for animals, plants and fungi. The species-rich reserve, covering less than two tenths of one percent of the area of Sweden, is a refuge for some 20 percent of the nation’s red-listed species! Work in Kristianstads Vattenrike Biosphere Reserve is predicated on broad local support and cooperation with local, regional, national and international stakeholders: associations, local authorities, government ministries, schools, entrepreneurs and landowners. A Consultation Group promotes dialogue and collaboration among landowners, authorities and organisations to support the various projects, each designed to serve as an example to inspire others. The overall long-term objective of Vattenriket’s activities is to create a shift in attitude towards economic, ecological and social sustainability.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Helge Å River with its lakes and wetlands is of international importance (River Helge Å Ramsar Convention Site) and flows through the centre of Kristianstads Vattenrike. Other habitats with particularly high natural values are ancient broadleaf forests, sandy grasslands with a long tradition of a rotation system of cultivation and fallow, eelgrass beds in Hanöbukten Bay and sand dune areas along the coast. Around 40 areas in the biosphere reserve are included in the EU's Natura 2000 network and there are also around 40 nature reserves. The biosphere reserve is one of the foremost areas in Sweden in terms of species richness as well as the presence of threatened species. According to the biosphere reserve's latest survey, there are 947 red-listed species in the biosphere reserve, 417 of which are threatened (CN, EN and VU). Several of these species have a particularly high conservation value as their main distribution is within the biosphere reserve. The Biosphere Office works broadly and innovatively to benefit species and recreate habitats. In close dialogue with landowners and land users, we make use of local knowledge and develop new methods to conserve important natural values. We work on projects that span nature conservation measures, research, education, public activities and communication. Wetland construction is a clear example of adaptive co-management, in discussion and collaboration with landowners. By integrating biosphere expertise into planning processes, we also contribute to more sustainable development in which biodiversity, outdoor recreation and ecosystem services are taken into account.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Kristianstads Vattenrike

records.title_en: Lake Vänern Archipelago and Mount Kinnekulle
records.introduction_en: The Biosphere Reserve comprises part of the drainage basin of Lake Vänern, the largest lake in Sweden and the third largest lake in Europe.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Biosphere Reserve comprises part of the drainage basin of Lake Vänern, the largest lake in Sweden and the third largest lake in Europe.In the western part of the area lies Hindens rev, a five-kilometre-long glacial moraine that extends into the lake. Hindens rev forms part of the so-called Middle Swedish Ice Marginal Zone, created by the retreating inland ice approximately 10,000 years ago.In the central part of the biosphere reserve rises Mount Kinnekulle, Västergötland’s highest plateau mountain, along with Mount Lugnåsberget, one of the smallest plateau mountains in the country. The area also contains boulder ridges and sand ridges. Southwest of Mount Kinnekulle lies Skebykärret, the only species-rich, highly calcareous fen outside the region’s main limestone-rich area.The land south and southwest of the plateau mountains consists mainly of relatively flat cultural landscape dominated by agriculture. Large contiguous forest areas are found in the archipelago as well as in the southern and eastern parts of the reserve.Along the 350-kilometre shoreline of Lake Vänern, there are numerous sites with extensive reed beds and rich birdlife. The largest continuous reed bed is located at Lake Dättern in the southwestern part of the area. The islands and skerries of the archipelago feature wide sandy beaches and dunes, rocky shores, pine forests growing on flat rock, and bilberry-rich spruce forests. Torsö, the largest island in Lake Vänern, includes an important wetland area.The reserve contains five rivers. The two largest, Tidan and Lidan, discharge into Lake Vänern at the two largest population centres, Lidköping and Mariestad. The three smaller rivers — Friaån, Sjöråsån, and Mariedalsån — flow through the agricultural landscape before emptying into Lake Vänern.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Lake Vänern Archipelago and Mount Kinnekulle

records.introduction_en: The Nedre Dalälven area has a varied landscape with a wide range of ecosystems linked to local habitats. These include a large river with bays, lakes, tributaries, waterways, rapids, ravines, microhabitats in farmland, river meadows, shore grasslands, productive forest lands, old-growth forest, freshwater swamp forest, broadleaf deciduous forest and grazing lands. The Nedre Dalälven lies in the borderland between the European broadleaf deciduous forest region, with a large proportion of hardwood trees, and the northern coniferous forest region.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: A large part of the core area consists of Färnebofjärden National Park, known for its great biodiversity. The vegetation differs widely across the park. The south features coniferous forests and marshes with a northern character. The north has richer vegetation with a large proportion of hardwood trees, primarily oak and lime. The fauna is diverse, and Färnebofjärden is known for its rich birdlife. Over a hundred species of birds regularly breed here, including all seven Swedish woodpecker species, Ural owl, osprey and whooper swan. Mammals include strong populations of elk, roe deer, hare and marten. Other mammals found in the area include lynx, beaver, otter and bear. Wolf and wolverine pass through the area. Several rare and threatened insect species live in dead and dying trees, including the cinnabar-red flat bark beetle (Cucujus cinnaberinus), Ceruchus chrysomelinus, the hairy pine borer (Tragosoma depsarium) and Acanthocinus griseus.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Nedre Dalälven River Landscape

records.introduction_en: Located in central Sweden, the Voxnadalen Biosphere Reserve encompasses the catchment of the River Voxnan. Extensive boreal woodlands cover much of its north-west, while the more populated south-east features open farmland. The site hosts engineering, hydro energy and high-tech companies, and it is home to 274 nationally endangered species of flora and fauna, as well as 16 that are internationally threatened. Local authorities have introduced policies prioritising the preservation of several species, including wolves (Canis lupus) and wolverine (Gulo gulo), and their habitats. The site is notable for its Decorated Farmhouses of Hälsingland, inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2012.
