The site will seek to explore and demonstrate collaborative approaches to sustainable development on a regional scale.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve lies in the region of the northern boreal needleleaf forests, in the border zone between the southern boreal zone, an area with low hills and river valleys, and the mid-boreal zone. The latter zone is typical of northern Sweden, with high hills and undulating mountainous terrain and outcrops of primary rock. Due to the size of the area, its topography (51–686 metres above sea level) and its location, it extends over four Swedish plant hardiness zones (zone IV–VII). This range helps explain the rich variation in the landscape’s vegetation. Woodland covers 80–90 per cent of the biosphere reserve, most of it production forest. Conifers such as pine (Pinus sylvestris), spruce (Picea abies) and deciduous trees including birch (Betula pendula and B. pubescens), aspen (Populus tremula), willow (Salix caprea), rowan (Sorbus aucuparia) and alder (Alnus incana) are the predominant trees. Within the biosphere reserve, 274 species have been observed that are nationally red-listed in ArtDatabanken, the Swedish Species Information Centre, and 16 species that are internationally red-listed in IUCN.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Voxnadalen

records.introduction_en: In southern Sweden, Storkriket Biosphere Reserve spans some of the country’s most species-rich landscapes. Its mosaic of farmland, forests, wetlands, lakes, grasslands, and historic towns supports an exceptional concentration of biodiversity — with 15,600 recorded species, including 22% of Sweden’s nationally red-listed species, within only 0.25% of the nation’s land area. Shaped by centuries of human stewardship and unique geology, Storkriket is both an ecological hotspot and a dynamic cultural landscape.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve encompasses a diverse range of habitats, including wetlands, lakes, forests, agricultural land, grasslands, coastal zones, and urban green spaces. These environments support approximately 15,600 recorded species, among them the Scandinavian red deer (Cervus elaphus elaphus), hooded sunburst lichen (Xanthomendoza fallax), golden-gilled bolete (Phylloporus pelletieri), Batavian sand bee (Andrena batava), and common spadefoot (Pelobates fuscus).The reserve is home to 18 of Sweden’s 19 bat species, while its wetlands and lakes serve as crucial breeding grounds for amphibians and waterfowl. The white stork (Ciconia ciconia), once extinct in Sweden, has been successfully reintroduced to the area, and today around 50 nesting pairs thrive within the reserve.The region also harbors a remarkable diversity of mosses, lichens, and fungi, many of which are nationally rare and protected. Its ecosystems provide essential services such as water filtration, carbon storage, pollination, and food production, making it one of Sweden’s most important reservoirs of biodiversity.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Storkriket

records.introduction_en: Situated in the Delta of the Senegal River, this transboundary biosphere reserve presents few variations in altitude, but owes its diversity to its vast hydrographic network, which is divided into several basins. The landscape is very diverse and includes floodplains fed by water from natural or artificial rising of the river (through hydraulic works), backwaters, lakes, and by the sea. Continental and coastal dunes slightly mark the relief. The floodplains are deprived of vegetation in the dry season. The importance of the area with regards to conservation can be perceived through the great variety of protected areas that have been designated here. Migratory birds find refuge in the delta and more than 350 species have been recorded in the 'Oiseaux du Djoudj' National Park with a bird population of over 3 million individuals from November to May.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The core areas of the biosphere reserve include national parks and natural reserves that form part of the national network of protected areas, such as the ‘Oiseaux de Djoudj’ National Park (Senegal), which is both a UNESCO World Heritage site and a Ramsar Wetland, as well as Diawaling National Park and the Chat TBoul Reserve (Mauritania), both designated as Ramsar Wetlands. The buffer zones are managed according to the statutes that govern the core areas, except for the Gandon Forest (Senegal), which is classified as a Community Natural Reserve.The transition area comprises public or state-owned land, as well as private property. Within the delta, the agricultural landscape is dominated by irrigated rice cultivation and sugarcane farming. Livestock rearing, fishing, and the harvesting of natural resources are also important human activities in the region.
records.name: Delta du Fleuve Senegal

records.introduction_en: Located in a well-watered area along the banks of the Gambia River in south-eastern Senegal, the gallery forests and savannahs of Niokolo-Koba National Park contain a great diversity of ecosystems and very rich fauna. Species include the Derby eland, the largest of the antelopes, chimpanzees, lions and leopards. The park also supports a large population of elephants, as well as many birds, reptiles and amphibians.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Located in the Sudano-Guinean zone, Niokolo-Koba National Park is characterised by a group of ecosystems typical of this region. Watered by large waterways, including the Gambia, Sereko, Niokolo and Koulountou, it comprises gallery forests, savannah grass floodplains, ponds and dry forests, which are either dense or with clearings. It also contains rocky slopes and hills, and barren Bowés. This remarkable plant diversity justifies the presence of rich fauna. Notable species include the Derby eland, the largest of African antelopes, chimpanzees, lions and leopards. There is also a large population of elephants, as well as many species of birds, reptiles and amphibians.
records.name: Niokolo-Koba

records.introduction_en: The Julian Alps are a region in the Southern Limestone Alps, where north-eastern Italy meets Slovenia. The Slovenian Julian Alps Biosphere Reserve, which includes Triglav National Park, was designated in 2003. The biosphere reserve constitutes an important Alpine corridor, notably for large carnivores as well as birds. The area is also a meeting place of the Latin and Slav worlds, with millennia of cultural interaction testified by its multitude of dialects, settlement methods, and agricultural and artistic practices.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The specific biological nature of the biosphere reserve is determined by several factors. Its biogeographical location, elevation gradient and abundant rainfall are particularly relevant. From a biogeographical point of view, following the Udvardy classification system, the biosphere reserve is situated within the ‘Central European Highlands’ biogeographical province. It is in close proximity to the ‘Balkan Highlands’, and not far from the ‘Middle European Forest’ and the ‘Mediterranean Sclerophyll’. With respect to the Habitats Directive (Directive no. 92/43/EEC), the area is located on the border between the Alpine and continental regions, and it shows significant traces of the influence of the Mediterranean region. Species in the area include brown bears, lynxes, otters and wildcats.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Julian Alps

records.introduction_en: Situated in northern Thailand, this biosphere reserve comprises one of the most populated mountain areas in the country and encompasses the watershed of Thailand’s second-largest city, Chiang Mai. Five natural ecosystems are represented in Mae Sa–Kog Ma: moist evergreen forest, hill evergreen forest, coniferous forest, mixed deciduous forest and dry dipterocarp forests.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Mae Sa-Kog Ma Biosphere Reserve conserves a compact mountain watershed with a clear altitudinal sequence of ecosystems: hill evergreen forest dominates the upper slopes, grading into mixed deciduous and dry dipterocarp forests, with riparian corridors along streams and valley floors. Characteristic trees include Castanopsis and Quercus–Lithocarpus in hill evergreen stands, Afzelia xylocarpa in mixed deciduous forest, upper-slope mosaics of Pinus kesiya and P. merkusii, and emblematic dipterocarps such as Shorea siamensis and Dipterocarpus obtusifolius on drier foothills. Pine plantings have been used strategically to rehabilitate previously degraded areas, creating mixed stands that now host diverse understorey species. The reserve experiences a humid monsoon climate, with a marked rainy season (May–November), a drier period (December–April), and mean annual rainfall near 1,900 mm. This hydrological regime underpins year-round flow in several perennial tributaries of the Mae Sa River and supports high plant richness recorded across the main forest types. As a natural buffer for Chiang Mai’s hinterland, the forested slopes and catchment geology help moderate run-off, reduce erosion and maintain perennial flows, securing dry-season water for farms and households across the Mae Sa basin.
records.name: Mae Sa-Kog Ma

records.introduction_en: Huay Tak Teak Biosphere Reserve is located in Lampang Province, northern Thailand. The core area is dominated by stands of teak (Tectona grandis) interspersed with trees of mixed deciduous forest. Huay Tak Teak Biosphere Reserve is part of Tham Pha Thai National Park, designated for the protection and conservation of native flora and fauna.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Huay Tak Teak Biosphere Reserve uniquely represents pristine mixed deciduous forests dominated by an intact stand of teak (Tectona grandis) in Thailand. It is now recognised as a gene bank for teak in Thailand. Lignite deposits underground indicate that flora and fauna were once abundant. Moreover, cave paintings dated to 2,500–3,000 years ago signify the importance of a civilised early human society. Rough terrain surrounded by thick forests hindered licensed timber extraction in the past. Most parts of the core area remain undisturbed. Six types of natural forest exist in the area: pine forest, hill evergreen forest, dry evergreen forest, moist evergreen forest, mixed deciduous forest and dry dipterocarp forest.
records.name: Huay Tak Teak

records.introduction_en: Lubombo is the first biosphere reserve in the Kingdom of Eswatini. The country is landlocked, bound by South Africa to the north, west and south, and by Mozambique to the east. The Lubombo region is the largest of Eswatini’s four administrative regions, representing 34.24 per cent of the country’s area, yet it has the second-smallest population. Biodiversity is high, including important populations of globally threatened species such as the black rhinoceros (Diceros bicornis). The regional economy is driven mainly by sugarcane growing and processing: all the country’s sugar mills are located in the Lowveld part of Lubombo, making a major contribution to national GDP.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Lubombo Biosphere Reserve spans parts of three biomes: Lowveld savannah, forests of the Lubombo Plateau, and the riparian zone. Although existing protected areas are relatively well placed to capture biodiversity variation, growing threats affect both these reserves and remaining natural areas across the landscape. Lubombo is a highly endemic zone, with Lubombo ironwoods (Androstachys johnsonii), Lubombo cycads (Encephalartos lebomboensis), and a recently described Barleria species – Barleria lebomboensis – underlining the need for systematic survey and research. The landscape also includes indigenous forests such as the Jilobi Forest, which has high species diversity. The ecosystem provides habitat for distinctive fauna, some endemic to a region stretching from northern KwaZulu-Natal to southern Mozambique and south-eastern Zimbabwe, such as the suni (Nesotragus moschatus zuluensis). Threatened species such as the leopard (Panthera pardus) and other Near Threatened wildlife occur here; conserving them would constitute a significant contribution to Eswatini.
records.name: Lubombo

records.introduction_en: The Polana Biosphere Reserve is situated in central Slovakia within the Western Carpathians. It is a mountain landscape with diverse topography that reflects a complex geological history of volcanic activity, faulting and erosion. The vegetation is characterised by the common occurrence of both thermophilous and mountain plant species, reflecting changes in elevation, alternating rock and soil types, the influence of slope aspect, and the region’s outlying position south of the main West Carpathians arc.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Polana is one of the greatest European former volcanoes, at approximately 2,500 m above sea level, and it is the highest volcanic mountain range in Slovakia. The highest altitude is 1,458 m above sea level, and the lowest is 460 m above sea level. The Polana Biosphere Reserve is characterised by the common occurrence of both thermophilous and mountain plant species. Forest covers almost 85 per cent of the reserve, with a slight majority being coniferous forests, and the rest deciduous. Many of these forests have the character of primeval forest. The forest system is very diverse, ranging from oak forests to spruce forests growing on andesites. These spruce forests are well known for their southernmost occurrence within the Western Carpathians and cover the highest part of the mountain range. There are about 1,220 species of higher plants in the area, and it is also rich in lichens and mosses, of which 80 species fall into categories of protection, threat and rareness. The variety and species richness of the fauna reflect the environmental diversity of the Polana Biosphere Reserve. There are many biogeographically outstanding and biosociologically significant animal species, whose rare populations are often endangered and thus strictly protected. The invertebrate fauna includes several Carpathian endemic species. The fauna is particularly species rich in beetles, butterflies, reptiles and birds, as well as large predators including wolf (Canis lupus), Eurasian brown bear (Ursus arctos arctos) and lynx (Lynx lynx). The avifauna is exceptionally rich, with 174 species of birds recorded. In consideration of the occurrence of endangered and rare bird species, Polana has been recognised as an Important Bird Area in Slovakia.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Polana

records.introduction_en: Situated adjacent to the Aggtelek Biosphere Reserve in Hungary, Slovenský kras in southern Slovakia is a karst landscape that comprises almost the full range of karst phenomena found in temperate climates. A series of plateaux at 400–900 metres above sea level are surrounded by steep slopes that descend to basins, valleys and gorges. More than 700 caves are recognised in the 60,000 ha karst area, which is shared with Hungary. In 1995, the Caves of Aggtelek and Slovak Karst were designated as a World Heritage site.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Situated adjacent to the Aggtelek Biosphere Reserve in Hungary, Slovenský kras in southern Slovakia is a karst landscape that comprises almost the full range of karst phenomena in temperate climates. It consists of a series of plateaus at 400–900 metres above sea level, surrounded by steep slopes that descend to adjacent basins, valleys and gorges. More than 700 caves are recognised in the 60,000 ha karst area, which is shared with Hungary. Carpathian oak–hornbeam forests are characterised by Carpinus betulus and Quercus petraea. Mixed oak forests are dominated by Quercus petraea, Carpinus betulus, Fagus sylvatica and Fraxinus excelsior. Xerothermophilous oak forests feature Cornus mas, Quercus petraea, Quercus cerris and Cerasus mahaleb. Beech forests include Fagus sylvatica, Acer platanoides, Acer pseudoplatanus and Tilia cordata. The shrub layer includes Cornus mas, Acer campestre, Corylus avellana, Crataegus monogyna, Rosa canina, Ligustrum vulgare, Cerasus mahaleb, Sorbus aria and Sorbus torminalis. Limestone rock walls and rock cracks support Asplenium trichomanes, Asplenium viride and Moehringia muscosa. Grasslands and grass meadows are present across the site. There are underground brooks and lakes, as well as caves, caverns and chasms. Fields host Adonis aestivalis, Anagallis foemina and Caucalis platycarpos. Orchards and vineyards are also found.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Slovak Karst (Slovenský Kras)

records.introduction_en: The Lajat Biosphere Reserve is located on the Lajat Plateau in Sweida Governorate, in the southernmost corner of Syria on the border with Jordan. It covers 12,038 ha at elevations from 600 to 900 m above sea level. The site supports extremely diverse biological wealth and encompasses some of the most striking landscapes of Sweida Province. Basaltic undulating hills, interspersed with black pumice or pozzolan high cones, are unparalleled in the country and the region, and they contrast sharply with the varied semi-arid landscapes elsewhere in the reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: These basaltic habitats support, in their fissures and cracks, open woodlands of Atlas mastic tree (Pistacia atlantica), bitter almond (Amygdalus communis), wild almond (Amygdalus korschinskii), olive (Olea europaea), tanner’s sumach (Rhus coriaria) and azarole (Crataegus azarolus), with an understorey of Capparis spinosa, Ononis, Atraphaxis and the endemic Iris aurantiaca.
records.name: Lajat

records.introduction_en: The Djebel Bou-Hedma Biosphere Reserve and National Park is situated 85 km east of Gafsa along the southern Tunisian mountain ranges that are extensions of the Saharan Atlas. It consists of a limestone and marl mountain range with some travertine deposits and a gypsum and salt alluvium plain.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The vegetation of Bou-Hedma features typical Mediterranean semi-arid elements of Tunisia, including plant communities along permanent and seasonal watercourses, as well as steppe communities resulting from degraded juniper forests. It is especially noted for relicts of pre-Saharan savanna, notably Acacia raddiana forests. The fauna is characteristic of the Sahara and arid Mediterranean regions, and includes elements that have disappeared elsewhere in Tunisia. Endangered species include the addax antelope (Addax nasomaculatus), Struthio camelus australis and Gazella dama mhorr.
records.name: Djebel Bou-Hedma

records.introduction_en: Djebel Chambi Biosphere Reserve is located in west-central Tunisia, and is centred on Jebel El Chaambi, the country’s highest peak at 1,544 m. The massif supports characteristic North African montane vegetation with stands of Aleppo pine, holm oak and Phoenician juniper. The area is one of the last refuges for Cuvier’s gazelle. The reserve’s management focuses on protecting wild flora and fauna and on reducing negative human impacts, aiming to counter pressures such as overgrazing and the effects of drought by improving livelihoods in the buffer zone and transition area through integrated development projects.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve lies in a semi-arid climate. Main habitats carry montane slopes with holm oak (Quercus ilex), Stipa and Cotoneaster nummularius. Elsewhere, Aleppo pine (Pinus halepensis) forest mixes with holm oak, Phoenician juniper (Juniperus phoenicea), rosemary (Rosmarinus officinalis) and Globularia alypum. Steppe communities dominated by Stipa tenacissima occupy exposed ridges and plateaux, while agro-ecosystems with cereals are found at lower elevations. Geologically, Djebel Chambi forms part of the Tunisian Dorsal, the eastern continuation of the Atlas Mountains. Bedrock is predominantly limestone, with harder Triassic units in the east and softer Lower–Middle Cretaceous limestones elsewhere. Fossil oyster beds are exposed in several places, attesting to the massif’s marine origins. Species of particular conservation interest include Cuvier’s gazelle (Gazella cuvieri), Barbary sheep (Ammotragus lervia), striped hyena (Hyaena hyaena) and African wildcat (Felis lybica).
records.name: Djebel Chambi

records.introduction_en: Îles Zembra et Zembretta Biosphere Reserve lies in the Gulf of Tunis, about 15 km from the Port of Sidi Daoud. The two namesake islands of Zembra and Zembretta are small and steep, formed mainly of Oligocene sandstone and marl. Zembra rises to 435 m above sea level with a single main valley running south to the shore. The climate is Mediterranean with mild winters, and strong north-west winds in autumn and early winter. The reserve’s objectives are to conserve and rehabilitate fragile island ecosystems and to monitor terrestrial and marine components over time across the site.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Despite their compact size, the islands support rich herbaceous and woody vegetation, with about 230 recorded plant species. Characteristic woody plants include olive and Phoenician juniper, and maquis, a dense evergreen Mediterranean shrubland, where mastic, strawberry tree, dwarf palm and Phlomis are common. Salt-tolerant plants line the coast, including Atriplex patula, Erodium maritimum and Salicornia arabica. The monk seal (Monachus monachus) is a priority species on the islands and a focus of protection and rehabilitation. Zonation in the reserve includes terrestrial core areas around the summit observatory, Cathedral Rock and Oued Zitoun, with a marine core that extends 1,500 m around Zembra. Site management guards and monitors nesting areas and tracks changes in fauna.
records.name: Iles Zembra et Zembreta

records.introduction_en: Lower Amudarya State Biosphere Reserve in Uzbekistan is located in the northern part of the lower reaches of the Amudarya River, south-east of the former coast of the Aral Sea. The site contains one of the largest areas of natural tugai in Central Asia. From a global perspective, tugai is a unique and threatened ecosystem.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area provides important habitat for plant and animal life and contains the highest biodiversity in the desert regions of Central Asia. The natural vegetation is composed of tugai, a form of riparian forest or woodland endemic to Central Asia. It is also the natural and protected environment of the threatened Bukhara deer (Cervus hanglu bactrianus), which is included on the IUCN Red List.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Lower Amudarya State

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve covers the south-western end of the Chatkal'skiy Range in the western Tien-Shan Mountains. Covering altitudes between 1,110 and 4,000 metres above sea level, Mount Chatkal Biosphere Reserve has high habitat and species diversity. Habitats include mountain steppes, mountain forests, rocky areas, alpine meadows, river valleys and floodplain forests.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: About 1,300 types of plants grow in the reserve, and the vegetation cover is extremely diverse. Over 57 per cent of the territory is covered with arboreal and shrubby coenoses. Woodland is sparse and low, with many open areas. Closed stands of juniper (Juniperus), apple trees (Malus), cherry plum (Prunus), birches (Betula), willows (Salix), poplars (Populus) and walnut trees (Juglans regia) are seen only on restricted sites favourable for growth on slopes, and more often in valleys. The prevailing tree species is Zerafshan juniper (Juniperus serawchanica). It occupies 24 per cent of the area. About one third of the territory has 100 per cent cover. More than half is covered with vegetation by over 80 per cent. A wide ecological range of herbaceous vegetation determines the diversity of botanic groupings. The fauna of the reserve includes four species of fish, two species of amphibians, 11 species of reptiles, 176 species of birds and 33 species of mammals. The IUCN Red List includes the following animals as being under threat of extinction: the snow leopard (Uncia uncia), Menzbier marmot (Marmota menzbieri) and wood sleepyhead (Dryomys nitedula). Bats include the greater and lesser horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus ferrumequinum and Rhinolophus hipposideros) and the three-coloured myotis (Myotis emarginatus). Among birds, the black vulture (Aegypius monachus), lesser kestrel (Falco naumanni), brown pigeon (Columba eversmanni) and white-winged woodpecker (Dendrocopos leucopterus) are included.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Mount Chatkal

records.introduction_en: The Garden Route Biosphere Reserve is a highlight of the plant biodiversity of the Cape Province. Its diverse wildlife includes large mammals such as elephants, rhinos and buffalo. It is home to plateau forest, and shrubs and herbs relevant to Indigenous groups such as the Khoisan people. It includes the Tsitsikamma Marine Protected Area, Wilderness Lake Ramsar site, Garden Route National Park and two World Heritage Sites, the Nelson Bay Cave and the Langkloof Valley.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Garden Route Biosphere Reserve falls within a biodiversity hotspot, the Cape Floristic Region, which is the smallest yet most diverse biodiversity hotspot in the world. Parts of this area, including Garden Route National Park and Nelson Bay Cave on Robberg Nature Reserve, have also received global recognition. They have been incorporated as UNESCO World Heritage Sites due to unique, endemic and spectacular biodiversity and palaeo-anthropological significance. In the eastern section of the biosphere reserve there are numerous areas of wetland adjacent to the region’s rivers and on the coastal platform. These wetlands are extremely sensitive to disturbances such as agricultural activities and development. They accommodate high species diversity and fulfil natural water purification and flood retention roles. The Knysna basin is a key topographical feature of the area because it is responsible for the Knysna Estuary, ranked first in the country for its conservation importance. The area is central to the South African fishing industry and supports a wide diversity of marine mammals and seabirds. It also supports deep-water and open-ocean fish and shellfish. Almost the entire Garden Route Biosphere Reserve forms part of the natural habitat of the African elephant, black rhinoceros and Cape buffalo. It therefore serves an important role in the conservation of large mammals.
records.name: Garden Route

records.introduction_en: The Waterberg Biosphere Reserve is in the Bushveld district of the Limpopo Province of South Africa. As the name implies, the Waterberg serves as a water reservoir for this arid region. The area consists of low mountain ranges and escarpments with poor soils and a relatively low level of economic activity. Vegetation is dominated by veld types characteristic of mountainous savannah areas, creating rich biodiversity with more than 5,500 species of plants. The area has been inhabited for hundreds of thousands of years and is one of the most important San rock art areas in South Africa. Tourism is the major source of income. People also practise cattle raising and crop production, and are increasingly switching from game farming to eco-tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Waterberg Mountain Range is one of three major mountain ranges in the Limpopo Province. There are four main drainage rivers in the area: the Lephalala, Mokolo, Matlabas and the Mogalakwena. These rivers, together with numerous lesser rivers and streams, form a major water catchment for the Limpopo basin. The Waterberg Biosphere Reserve represents a considerable area of the savannah biome of Southern Africa. The savannah biome, or wooded grasslands, has rich biodiversity with more than 5,500 species of plants, 43 per cent of which are endemic to Southern Africa. The area is characterised by seven vegetation types: Central Sandy Bushveld, Limpopo Sweet Bushveld, Makhado Sweet Bushveld, Roodeberg Bushveld, Waterberg Mountain Bushveld, Waterberg–Magalies Summit Sourveld and Western Sandy Bushveld. At least 18 threatened or scarce plant species, 11 bird species, four reptile species, four species of fish, one butterfly species and 18 mammals occur in the Waterberg Biosphere Reserve. All are considered of the utmost importance for biodiversity conservation. Red Data List species include the white-backed night-heron (Gorsachius leuconotus), the Cape vulture (Gyps coprotheres), the aardvark (Orycteropus afer), the brown hyaena (Parahyaena brunnea) and the critically endangered black rhinoceros (Diceros bicornis). The Nylsvley Nature Reserve in the south-east of the reserve is a recognised wetland and a registered Ramsar site.
records.name: Waterberg

records.introduction_en: The Kruger to Canyons Biosphere Reserve is in the north-east of South Africa. It encompasses Kruger National Park and other national and provincial nature reserves, such as the Blyde River Canyon Nature Reserve. Three Southern African biomes occur in the biosphere reserve: grasslands, Afromontane forests and the savannah of the lowveld. The area has a high level of biodiversity, with especially strong plant endemism on mountaintops. Land use includes gold, phosphate and copper mining, plantation forestry with exotic species, and extensive cultivation of subtropical fruits and vegetables.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The core areas include a large portion of South Africa’s world-renowned Kruger National Park, home to many iconic savannah species, including the Big Five. The Kruger to Canyons Biosphere Reserve also forms part of the Great Limpopo Transfrontier Conservation Area, a conservation landscape linking South Africa, Mozambique and Zimbabwe that covers approximately 3.5 million ha. It is one of the largest conservation areas in the world. Some of the best-known landmarks in the Kruger to Canyons biosphere region lie along the Mpumalanga Escarpment and form part of the Panorama Tourism Route, including Mariepskop, the Blyde River Canyon, Bourke’s Luck Potholes, the Three Rondawels, God’s Window and Graskop. This area is also considered a Strategic Water Source Area, generating a disproportionate amount of water for lower-lying regions. Major rivers in the region include the Olifants, Blyde and Sabie rivers. The Kruger to Canyons Biosphere extends over 2.5 million hectares and is home to a wide diversity of South African species, including 75 per cent of birds, 80 per cent of birds of prey, 72 per cent of mammals and 50 per cent of frogs. Three main vegetation biomes are represented within the biosphere reserve: savannah, Afromontane forests and threatened grasslands.
records.name: Kruger to Canyons

records.introduction_en: The Magaliesberg Biosphere Reserve is located in South Africa between the cities of Pretoria and Johannesburg to the east and Rustenburg to the west. The reserve lies at the interface of two great African biomes, the Central Grassland Plateaux and the sub-Saharan savannah, and retains remnants of a third, the Afromontane forest. The rich biodiversity includes floral species such as Aloe peglerae and Frithia pulchra, and faunal species such as the forest shrew (Myosorex varius) and sable antelope (Hippotragus niger). A total of 443 bird species occur here, representing 46.6 per cent of total bird species in the southern African sub-region. The area is characterised by remarkable scenic beauty and unique natural features. The reserve also forms part of the Cradle of Humankind World Heritage Site, which encompasses cultural heritage and archaeological sites dating back 4 million years. The area faces high levels of unemployment and poverty. The main economic activities are agriculture, mining, urban development and tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve includes a variety of landscapes, including slopes, cliffs, crests, kloofs, rivers, wetlands and valleys. Although the area covers a diverse geological zone, it consists mainly of the Magaliesberg mountain complex, which comprises two geological formations: the Transvaal System and the Bushveld Igneous Complex. These formations contain the richest platinum and platinum-group minerals in the world, and their varied topography hosts 14 different vegetation types. The reserve contains four important habitats. The Moot Plains Bushveld is characterised by open to closed, low and often thorny savannah dominated by various species of acacia. The Gold Reef Mountain Bushveld consists of rocky hills and ridges with denser woody vegetation. The Northern Afrotemperate Forest comprises low, relatively species-poor forests of afromontane origin. The Marikana Thornveld is characterised by open Acacia karroowoodlands occurring in valleys, slightly undulating plains and some lowland hills. A total of 90 indigenous mammal species have been recorded in the Magaliesberg Biosphere Reserve, including the klipspringer (Oreotragus oreotragus), sable antelope (Hippotragus niger), leopard (Panthera pardus) and brown hyena (Hyaena brunnea). The bird diversity in the area is exceptional. In total, 46.6 per cent of the bird species recorded in the southern African sub-region are found in the reserve. These include the Cape vulture (Gyps coprotheres), secretary bird (Sagittarius serpentarius), great white pelican (Pelecanus onocrotalus), martial eagle (Polemaetus bellicosus) and African grass-owl (Tyto capensis). The reserve contains the Cradle of Humankind World Heritage Site.
records.name: Magaliesberg

records.introduction_en: Located in the north of the country, this biosphere reserve comprises a unique freshwater ecosystem that includes the Molemane, Molopo and Marico river systems. The ecosystem features wetlands and a dolomitic system, which form a valuable part of South Africa’s natural heritage. The savannah and grassland areas support vulnerable plant species such as Searsia maricoana. Endemic fauna includes 73 species of mammal, such as the African elephant, the black rhinoceros and the lion. The main economic activities are subsistence agriculture, livestock, game ranching and tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The most noteworthy environmental characteristic of the area is the dolomitic aquifers that underlie much of the reserve and give rise to three river systems: the Marico River, the Molopo River and the Molemane River. The Molemane River feeds into the Klein-Marico River, the “Small” Marico River, which later feeds into the Marico River, outside the Marico Biosphere Reserve boundaries. The Marico River, in turn, feeds into the Limpopo River, which serves four countries in total: South Africa, Botswana, Zimbabwe and Mozambique. As the Marico River is one of the cleanest and healthiest rivers in South Africa, it plays a significant role in supplying water to the Limpopo river systems. The reserve covers parts of two biomes, the savannah and the grassland biomes, encompassing sections of five bioregions and a total of seven vegetation types. It has a high representativity of biodiversity compared to the surrounding area.
records.name: Marico

records.introduction_en: Stretching along the north bank of the Gambia River and adjoining Senegal’s Delta de Saloum Biosphere Reserve, Niumi includes extensive mangroves along the coast and riverbanks. Downstream, striking red limestone formations punctuate tropical forest and open savannah woodland. The reserve safeguards some of West Africa’s last relatively pristine mangrove forests, alongside the Bao Bolong Wetland Reserve and state forests. It also encompasses a Ramsar site and the UNESCO World Heritage site of Kunta Kinteh Island, which was a key site of the transatlantic slave trade. Key livelihoods include farming and fisheries. It is the first biosphere reserve designated in The Gambia.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve hosts a mix of terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems including woodlands and wooded grasslands, savanna, gallery forests, permanent marine waters and mangroves, that underpin regional ecological processes. Biodiversity is high across flora and fauna, with habitats for marine mammals, reptiles, amphibians and protected tree species. There are an estimated 80 mammal species (out of 117 nationally), over 500 bird species, around 70 fish species, and numerous reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates. The area has been the focus of many scientific studies.
records.name: Niumi

records.title_en: Archipel des Sept Frères – Ras Siyyan – Khor Angar – Godoria
records.introduction_en: The Archipel des Sept Frères – Ras Siyyan – Khor Angar – Godoria Biosphere Reserve is situated at the confluence of the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. It protects an extraordinary marine crossroads where warm tropical waters meet nutrient-rich cold upwellings that contains one of the most biodiverse seascapes on Earth. Its mosaic of coral reefs, seagrass beds, volcanic islands, mangroves, and desert landscapes makes it a biodiversity hotspot of global significance.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve harbors over 970 recorded species, including 12 marine mammals, four globally threatened marine turtles, more than 520 reef fish species, and 238 coral species (32 of them threatened).Ras Siyyan, Khor Angar and Godoria, its three mangrove systems, are the largest and most diverse in Djibouti. The area is also one of the world’s most important raptor migration corridors, with 85,000–245,000 birds of prey passing annually. Iconic species include dugong (Dugong dugon), whale shark (Rhincodon typus), and sooty falcon (Falco concolor).
records.name: Archipel des Sept Frères – Ras Siyyan – Khor Angar – Godoria

records.introduction_en: Straddling the border between Albania and Montenegro, the Shkodër Lake Biosphere Reserve encompasses one of Southeast Europe's most ecologically and culturally significant landscapes. At its heart lies Lake Shkodër, the largest freshwater lake in the Balkans and a Ramsar wetland of international importance. Nestled within a mosaic of wetlands, forests and agricultural lands, the biosphere reserve stretches from the Adriatic coast to mountain peaks above 2,000 metres.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: A hub of freshwater ecosystem research, the biosphere reserve shelters over 280 bird species, including the Dalmatian pelican, as well as mammals, including the Balkan lynx. The biosphere reserve will support biodiversity conservation, the study of wild relatives of crop species and medicinal plants and sustain genetic resources critical for agriculture.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Shkodër Lake

records.introduction_en: Located in south-eastern Europe on the Balkan Peninsula, the Albanian component of the Ohrid-Prespa transboundary biosphere reserve combines water bodies with surrounding mountain relief. Flat areas border the outer limits of the territory, which stretches across Albania and North Macedonia.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Ohrid–Prespa Transboundary Biosphere Reserve encompasses a significant range of ecological systems, from mountainous areas around the three lakes to temperate subtropical forests at lower altitudes around the water basins. Together, the Ohrid and Prespa lake system is one of the largest of its kind in Europe. Both lakes are of special value at national and international levels because of their geological and biological uniqueness.Lake Ohrid is famous for over two hundred endemic species, including diatoms, oligochaetes, leeches, poriferans, triclads, molluscs, ostracods and fish. Five of the endemic species are restricted to micro-ecosystems within the lake. Ten of the lake’s 17 fish species are endemic, including the Ohrid trout (Salmo letnica) and belvica (Acantholingua ohridana). There is also a unique, endemic forest community composed of Pinetum peuces, Paeonian Grecian juniper woods, Helleno-Moesian Quercus frainetto forests, and south-western Moesian fir–beech forests.The Prespa region hosts original biotopes vital for preservation. These include extensive deciduous forests of Ostryo-Carpinion orientalis, evergreen box–juniper shrublands, evergreen coniferous forests consisting of 12 m-high Juniperus foetidissima and Juniperus excelsa, and the important endemic vegetation species of Ezerani.The protection of mammals is also crucial in the transboundary biosphere reserve. Notable species include the Balkan mole (Talpa stankovici), Balkan lynx (Lynx lynx martinoi), grey wolf (Canis lupus) and brown bear (Ursus arctos). The Balkan lynx is an exceptionally rare species of very high symbolic value. As for bird species, the Dalmatian pelican (Pelecanus crispus) is the reserve’s flagship species. In the Prespa region there are over 260 species of birds … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Ohrid-Prespa

records.introduction_en: Encompassing the entire island and its Exclusive Economic Zone, the Aruba Island Biosphere Reserve forms an integrated land-sea system of high conservation value. Within its 180 square kilometres of land, Aruba harbours 14 distinct ecosystems, from xeric shrublands and dry forests to mangroves, coral reefs and seagrass beds.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: These ecosystems are home to over 2,400 species of flora and fauna, including 34 endemic species. With more than 20 species of sharks and rays, the island sits at the heart of the Caribbean Islands Biodiversity Hotspot and serves as a vital steppingstone for migratory birds, sea turtles and marine mammals.
records.name: Aruba Island

records.introduction_en: Situated some 80 km east of Quebec City, Charlevoix Biosphere Reserve borders the Saint Lawrence River. Extending from 5 m to 1,150 m above sea level, the area comprises agricultural areas, river ecosystems, estuarine tidal marshes and flats, coniferous and mixed forests, stunted vegetation known as krummholz, and mountain tundra ecosystems.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Maple forests include paper birch (Betula papyrifera), alder (Alnus) and elm (Ulmus), with an understorey of sumac (Rhus typhina), Acer pensylvanicum and Cornus alternifolia. Mixed fir (Abies) forest features Corylus cornuta, Sambucus pubens and Taxus canadensis. Boreal forests up to an altitude of 300 m include fir and spruce (Picea). Estuarine tidal marsh and flats are dominated by Scirpus americanus meadows, including Zizania palustris, Sagittaria cuneata and S. latifolia. Tundra includes ericaceous zones consisting of Kalmia and Ledum groenlandicum. The stunted vegetation community, or krummholz, includes Picea mariana and Abies balsamea. Agroecosystems include cereals, fruits and legumes, and the area also contains river ecosystems. Animal species in the area include beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas), wolf (Canis lupus), boreal woodland caribou (Rangifer tarandus caribou), North American cougar (Puma concolor couguar) and blue whale (Balaenoptera musculus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Charlevoix

records.introduction_en: The Clayoquot Sound Biosphere Reserve is situated on Vancouver Island, on the west coast of British Columbia. A diverse range of ecosystems lies within the biosphere reserve boundaries, including temperate coastal rainforest, ocean and rocky coastal shores. Nine of the large, forested valleys remain untouched by logging or other industrial development. The area’s temperate rainforest, lakes, rivers and alpine peaks provide habitats for a vast array of species, a significant number of which are endangered or rare. As development increasingly fragments forest and alpine ecosystems and reduces biodiversity in coastal rainforests, this biosphere reserve provides a refuge and a centre for the natural dispersion and re-establishment of species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The primary habitat of the reserve is temperate rainforest in the coastal western hemlock zone, which covers 85 per cent of the terrestrial component and extends to altitudes of about 900 m. This habitat is dominated by large trees, including western hemlock, western red cedar, amabilis fir, western yellow cedar, Sitka spruce, pine, Douglas fir, yew and red alder. There are approximately 300 vertebrate species, including the American black bear (Ursus americanus), cougar (Puma concolor couguar), American mink (Neovison vison) and grey wolf (Canis lupus). The second most common habitat, covering 12 per cent of Clayoquot Sound above 900 m, is temperate rainforest in the mountain hemlock zone. Dominant trees include mountain hemlock, western yellow cedar and amabilis fir. Fewer species are found at such high altitude, but some are shared with the lower elevations. The marine component of Clayoquot supports mudflats, beaches and estuaries. The reserve contains the largest cover of eelgrass on the west coast of Vancouver Island. Grey whales (Eschrichtius robustus), orcas (Orcinus orca), humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae) and a variety of other whale, dolphin and porpoise species are common. Steller’s sea lion (Eumetopias jubatus) and the California sea lion (Zalophus californianus) are also found in the reserve. Commercial aquaculture of native salmon species and introduced Atlantic salmon, oysters and scallops constitutes a significant economic activity.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Clayoquot Sound

records.introduction_en: The landscape of the Manicouagan Uapishka Biosphere Reserve is dominated by the Saint Lawrence River to the south and the Manicouagan reservoir to the north. Together they form a circle visible from great distances, even from space. They are linked by a web of rivers that flow through vast woodlands.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Manicouagan Uapishka Biosphere Reserve is a testament to some of the most powerful phenomena the Earth has ever known. It was shaped by erosion over millions of years and other forces including the collision of a huge meteorite, the crushing passage of glaciers and an ancient sea that smoothed the land. The impact of the meteorite formed the crater and circular lake that characterise this biosphere reserve. The hinterland of the Manicouagan–Uapishka area consists of a vast dry plateau. Its surface is formed by hills ranging between 400 m and 600 m, separated by rectilinear valleys. It is surrounded by the Groulx Mountains massif, which is characterised by about 30 mountains over 1,000 m in height. The salt marshes of the Manicouagan Uapishka reserve are among the most productive habitats on the planet, acting as important resting places for more than 200 migratory birds. Fauna characteristic of boreal forests in the area includes the vulnerable boreal woodland caribou (Rangifer tarandus), cougar (Puma concolor), least weasel (Mustela nivalis), short-eared owl (Asio flammeus) and golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos). Threatened species include the wolverine (Gulo gulo) and the beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Manicouagan Uapishka

records.introduction_en: Located about 32 km east of Montreal, Mont Saint-Hilaire is a steep-sided circular formation rising some 250 m above the Saint Lawrence plain. It is one of the last remnants of old-growth deciduous forest in Quebec and hosts many rare and endangered species. The biosphere reserve lies near a major urban region. Increasing urban development around Mont Saint-Hilaire, together with a growing number of visitors, has multiplied human disturbances and fragmented the forest, which once covered the entire Richelieu Valley. Tourism and agriculture are important contributors to the economies of the five towns that form part of the transition area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Mont Saint-Hilaire Biosphere Reserve is a Monteregien hill rich in natural beauty and cultural interest. It is located in a peri-urban area that hosts exceptional flora and fauna, and contains unique minerals. The forest of Mont Saint-Hilaire has never been exploited commercially and is of remarkable quality. It contains mainly maples and beech trees, some of which are 400 years old. Over 600 species of vascular plants grow on the hill, over 30 of which are either endangered or vulnerable. The forest of Mont Saint-Hilaire also hosts numerous mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians. About 30 species of mammals are found in the reserve. Some can be seen on the roadside, lakes and hilltops, such as the grey squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis), eastern chipmunk (Tamias striatus) and raccoon (Procyon lotor). The biosphere reserve is also a notable site for birdwatchers, as 200 species have been recorded, representing 60 per cent of all species present in south-western Quebec. This diverse wealth has inspired many artists, painters, poets and storytellers, and it continues to inspire the residents of this rural and urban territory.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mont Saint Hilaire

records.introduction_en: The Frontenac Arch Biosphere Reserve is situated in south-eastern Ontario at the intersection of terrestrial and riverine ecosystems. The area comprises islands and islets of the Saint Lawrence River, which serve as stepping stones for migrating plants and animals. The Frontenac Arch is an important land bridge linking the habitats of the Algonquin and Adirondack Park regions.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Frontenac Arch is the name given to an ancient ridge of granite that sweeps across the Saint Lawrence River, forming a corridor between the Canadian Shield and the Adirondack Mountains. Where the ridge intersects with the Great Lakes and the Saint Lawrence River, it forms the Thousand Islands. The topography of the biosphere reserve is rugged, with steep, rocky slopes and ridges typical of the Precambrian Shield. These alternate with moist forest or wetland valleys inland, and with rocky promontories in the Saint Lawrence River (the Thousand Islands). First Nations call the Frontenac Arch the ‘backbone of the mother’ – Mother Nature’s spinal column. Five separate forest regions meet at the crossroads of the Frontenac Arch and the Saint Lawrence River, creating a rich ecosystem of plant, insect and animal species that is renowned as the most biodiverse region in Canada. It has a long and rich cultural heritage and serves as the gateway through which the Saint Lawrence River flows into Canada. Characteristic species of the area include the pitch pine (Pinus rigida), the least bittern heron (Ixobrychus exilis), the great blue heron (Ardea herodias), the osprey (Pandion haliaetus), the common loon (Gavia immer), the bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) and the pine warbler (Dendroica pinus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Frontenac Arch

records.introduction_en: The Waza Biosphere Reserve is located in the Chad depression in the extreme north of Cameroon. The area is characterised by low relief without permanent rivers, with rocky outcrops around Waza village rising to over 500 metres. Lake Chad once covered part of the area, while today the Yaéré floodplains with perennial grasses are vital to the carrying capacity of the Waza region. The fauna is rich and varied, with large numbers of giraffes (Giraffa camelopardalis), elephants (Loxodonta africana), aardvarks (Orycteropus afer) and warthogs (Phacochoerus aethiopicus). Many animals move to the Yaéré plains towards the end of the dry season.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Waza Biosphere Reserve is located in a region bound to the south by the Yagoua-Limani dunes, representing the ancient limit of Lake Chad. It has a semi-arid climate with three seasons: a rainy season from June to October, a cold dry season from November to February, and a warm dry season lasting from March to June. The vegetation comprises open combretaceous shrub savannah, Anogeissus leiocarpus woodland on sandy soil, Lannea humilis open grass savannah and Acacia seyal tree savannah on black clay soils that are saturated with water in the rainy season. The latter vegetation type is slowly spreading as the area gradually dries out. The Yaéré floodplains with perennial grasses are vital to the carrying capacity of the Waza region. The fauna is rich and diverse, including elephants (Loxodonta africana), spotted hyenas (Crocuta crocuta), leopards (Panthera pardus) and more than 300 bird species, such as the Nubian bustard (Neotis nuba), great white pelican (Pelecanus onocrotalus) and marabou (Leptoptilos crumenifer). Several threatened or endangered species are also found in the reserve, including the korrigum (Damaliscus korrigum korrigum), pale fox (Vulpes pallida) and the last population of Kordofan giraffes (Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum). The reserve also contains the Waza Logone Floodplains Ramsar Site.
records.name: Waza

records.introduction_en: Nestled in the Ouarsenis mountain range of central-western Algeria, the Theniet El Had Biosphere Reserve is home to one of the country's best conserved cedar forests, and the only natural cedar grove in western Algeria.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Dominated by the Atlas cedar, an endemic North African tree increasingly threatened by climate change, the biosphere reserve rises above 1,300 metres into a supramediterranean landscape of rare ecological richness.
records.name: Theniet el Had

records.introduction_en: The Tassili N'Ajjer biosphere reserve is located in the south-eastern part of the Algerian Sahara, close to the borders with Niger and Libya. The site hosts a rich inventory of fauna, and significant archaeological, historical, cultural and geological features, hence its designation as a national park and World Heritage Site. Ancient cave paintings and rock engravings of large fauna, such as hippopotamus and buffalo, are of international importance.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Tassili plateau, at 1,500 to 1,800 metres above sea level, forms part of the Ordovician and Devonian sandstone layer surrounding the Precambrian crystalline massif of the Hoggar. The plateau is hyper-arid, but there are sub-arid microclimates suitable for the survival of relict fauna and flora. Mountains support a relict flora with elements of Mediterranean, Sudano-Deccan and Saharo-Sindian species, such as tarout cypress (Cupressus dupreziana), wild olive (Olea laperrini) and myrtle (Myrtus nivellei). Wadis traverse the plateau. After rainfall, permanent or temporary waterholes, known as gueltas, form. River-bed habitats include Trianthema pentandra, Silene kiliana, Lupinus pilosus and Convolvulus fatmensis. Humid valleys include riverine species such as Typha, Juncus and Phragmites, and aquatic species such as Chara, Myriophyllum and Potamogeton. Rocky and sandy habitats include Mesembryanthemum gaussenii, Pseuderucaria clavata and Acacia scorpioides. Agroecosystems and pastureland are also present.
records.name: Tassili N'Ajjer

records.introduction_en: Taza Biosphere Reserve lies on the Mediterranean coast in the Kabylie region. It is characterised by spectacular cliffs, beaches, mountains and valleys. It is also noted for the Barbary ape (Macaca sylvanus), an endangered species of monkey and the only macaque primate in North Africa.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Taza Biosphere Reserve corresponds to the Taza National Park, which aims to improve the local economy in harmony with the natural environment. In particular, it seeks to conserve certain natural resources that are unique and special at the regional and even international levels. These include the Guerrouch area with its gall oak (Quercus faginea) formations and the Kabylie nuthatch (Sitta ledanti), a small, rare sparrow endemic to the Babors Region and Algeria, which attract many students and researchers. The single largest extension of gall oak in Algeria can be found in the biosphere reserve and its surroundings. Cork oak (Q. suber) formations are also common; although it is not a rare species in Algeria, cork is socio-economically important in the Jijel Province, as it is one of the main export products. The Djebel Taounart Mountain is a privileged site for many raptors such as vultures, falcons and eagles, as well as for mammals. The presence of picturesque landscapes and sites, pedestrian paths, scenic areas and caves has encouraged decision-makers to promote the areas in the buffer zone for tourism and research, and for the development of certain low-impact rural activities.
records.name: Taza

records.introduction_en: The Tlemcen Mountains Biosphere Reserve spans nearly 100,000 hectares in the province of Tlemcen in north-west Algeria. Characterized by rich biodiversity and a semi-arid climate, it includes the Tlemcen National Park. The reserve also encompasses important archaeological sites, cultural landmarks, and caves. Its inhabitants engage in agriculture, particularly livestock rearing and grain farming, as well as administrative, commercial, and artisanal activities.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve lies within a semi-arid zone, marked by karst topography, cliffs and caves. It is situated on the Lalla Setti plateau, overlooking the city of Tlemcen. The area supports a diverse flora, with over 1,130 species, including 40 protected species. Notable examples include the Montpellier maple (Acer monspessulanum) found in the Tassermramet forest, the Atlas pistachio (Pistacia atlantica), the Terebinth pistachio (Pistacia terebinthus), the green oak (Quercus) and the thuya (Thuja articulata). Wildlife species in the region include the common genet (Genetta genetta), the griffon vulture (Gyps fulvus) found in the mountains of Chouly, and the Eurasian bittern (Botaurus stellaris), which inhabits the Oued Khemis area.
records.name: Tlemcen Mountains

records.introduction_en: The Arasbaran Biosphere Reserve is situated in northern Iran at the border with Armenia and Azerbaijan, in the Caucasus Iranian Highlands. The reserve encompasses mountains, high-alpine meadows, semi-arid steppes, rangelands and forests, rivers and springs. Arasbaran is the territory of one of the country’s oldest tribes, the Qaradagh or Arasbaran tribe. Economic activities in the biosphere reserve consist mainly of agriculture, animal husbandry, horticulture, apiculture, handicrafts and tourism, while business activities are concentrated in urbanised areas.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Arasbaran is a high mountainous region, with elevations ranging from 256 m to 2,896 m above sea level. The area encompasses part of the Caucasus Mountains and features diverse natural landscapes, including highlands, steep valleys, high and steep mountainsides, forest lands, and agricultural, mountainous and river rangelands. The vegetation of Arasbaran is of particular importance within the country because of its uniqueness. In general, there are 48 mammal species, 215 bird species, 29 creeper species, five amphibian species and 17 fish species occupying different habitats of the reserve. Over 1,000 plant species found in the reserve survived the ice age and can be considered living fossils of the past.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Arasbaran

records.introduction_en: The Arjan and Parishan Biosphere Reserve is situated in the Zagros Mountains in the Caucasus–Iranian Highlands, and encompasses terrestrial as well as aquatic habitats. Significant elevational differences throughout the reserve result in a rich diversity of flora and fauna. People living in the area derive their livelihoods from agriculture, animal husbandry and carpet sewing, and, in the transition area, from industry.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Arjan and Parishan Biosphere Reserve has two entirely different climates and elevations ranging from 800–2,400 m. This has resulted in diverse living conditions and habitats throughout the area, which include the Zagros forests in the central and southern parts, the Miyankotal highlands and the Arjan and Parishan wetlands. The presence of two wetlands provides a wide variety of aquatic fauna and flora to the biotic community of the reserve. Recent studies carried out in Fars Province identified 2,253 species of flora and 398 species of fauna, including 60 mammal species, 43 fish species, 41 creeper species and four amphibian species, in the area. The biosphere reserve has been listed as a Ramsar site, meeting the ecological and biodiversity criteria of this universal convention.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Arjan

records.introduction_en: Dena is home to a vast range of plant species and several endangered and endemic mammal species. Oak species dominate the highlands, while pistachio and almond are common at lower elevations.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Dena Biosphere Reserve is located in the Central Zagros Mountains of Iran, with a general slope of more than 60 per cent. On mountaintops where temperature changes are most common, a fall in temperature to around –25 °C in winter is possible. Snow is common throughout the ranges in that season, and some higher peaks remain snow-covered throughout the year. The region contains globally significant ecosystems, species and genetic biodiversity. The area is characterised by extreme topographical and climatic conditions, which have led to a striking diversity of ecosystems and habitats over a small geographical area. Dena is home to a vast range of plant species and several endangered and endemic mammal species. Oak species dominate the highlands, while pistachio and almond are common at lower elevations, and hackberry, walnut and pear trees are scattered throughout this ecoregion. A variety of animal life, such as brown bear, eagles, wolves and various wild cats, including caracals, lynxes and leopards, as well as wild goats, have long made their homes in the region. Many large rivers, including the Karun, Dez and Karkheh, originate from the area, flowing into the Persian Gulf and the Oman Sea. Scenic waterfalls, pools and lakes add beauty to the mountainous landscape.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Dena

records.introduction_en: The Golestan Biosphere Reserve is located in northern Iran and forms part of the Caucasus–Iranian Highlands, situated between the sub-humid and semi-arid Caspian regions. The area includes temperate rainforest, cold-winter and semi-deserts, and mixed mountain and highland systems. A wide variety of habitats and rich biodiversity can be found in the reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Golestan Biosphere Reserve is a mountainous region located in the eastern Alborz. The landscape varies from dry, rocky mountains, valleys and foothills to mountainous forests and mountainous steppes, and to flat, dry plains in the east. The mountainous area is divided into northern and southern halves by a valley through which the Madar Su River flows. Although the reserve is in the western part of the Hyrcanian forests, its climate is strongly influenced by humidity and western winds from the Caspian Sea. Mountain rainfall increases the humidity of the area. The reserve has a wide variety of habitats, producing a unique diversity of fauna and flora. It hosts 150 species of birds, 54 species of reptiles and amphibians, eight species of large carnivores including the leopard (Panthera pardus) and the brown bear (Ursus arctos), and more than 1,366 plant species, of which 30 are endemic.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Golestan

records.introduction_en: The Hara Biosphere Reserve is located in the Mehran River delta in the south of Iran. It lies near the Strait of Khuran between Qeshm Island and the Persian Gulf, and is a key biodiversity site because of its Avicennia mangrove ecosystem.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The core area of the reserve is a marine zone. Major topographic features include a wetland with a series of small islands, known locally as mud hills, mangrove forests, tidal marshes and shallow coves. The reserve also hosts the largest Avicennia mangrove ecosystem along the Persian Gulf shoreline. Sea snakes use the aquatic habitats in Hara for feeding, breeding and subsistence. A species of xerophilous snake, Echis carinatus, occurs on the northern coast of the region, and the critically endangered hawksbill sea turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata) is found in the coastal waters of the reserve. The Strait of Khuran, in which the reserve is located, is a Ramsar site. It provides habitat for the pelican (Pelecanus crispus) during the winter months and is a regular feeding place for the green turtle (Chelonia mydas), both globally threatened species.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Hara

records.introduction_en: The Tang-e-Sayad & Sabzkuh Biosphere Reserve is located in the south-east of Chahar-mahal and Bakhtiari province in the Islamic Republic of Iran. Land subsidence, geological activity and melting ice caps have formed several wetlands in the area, which are inhabited by rare fauna such as the wildcat (Felis silvestris) and the lebetine viper (Vipera lebetina). Research shows that 22 fish species are found in the Karun River, including the pike barb (Esox niger) and the Mesopotamian catfish (Silurus triostegus). The river runs through the area. During the cold season, bushlands in the area welcome migratory birds such as the white stork (Ciconia ciconia) and the greater flamingo (Phoenicopterus roseus).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The main landscape of the reserve is highly distinctive in the height and density of its plant cover. According to research conducted in the area, every hectare is 180 times more valuable than average in Iran in terms of plant richness and wildlife diversity. The region is mountainous, with waterfalls, wetlands and abundant springs. These function as a permanent basin for the Karun River, the largest river in Iran. Various oak species cover the highlands, while wild pistachio and almond dominate the lowlands. Lote, walnut and pear trees are also scattered across the reserve. Depending on habitat conditions, oak–mastic and other combinations of tree or shrub species, such as hackberry, hawthorn and Arjan, occur alone or in groups that constitute the forest areas. More than 450 plant species can be found in the reserve. The variety of ecosystems sustains a valuable fauna. These include 27 mammal species such as the Syrian brown bear (Ursus arctos syriacus) and the striped hyena (Hyaena hyaena). There are 147 bird species, including the greater flamingo (Phoenicopterus roseus) and the white stork (Ciconia ciconia). The reserve hosts 26 reptile and amphibian species, such as the snake-eyed lizard (Ophisops elegans). It also supports 24 fish species, including the Mesopotamian catfish (Silurus triostegus). The Choghakhor Wetlands were designated a Ramsar Wetland Site.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Tang-e-Sayad & Sabzkuh

records.introduction_en: Set in the south-eastern Dinaric Alps, the Tara River Basin is a high-mountain landscape of plateaux, glacial lakes and some of Europe’s deepest river gorges. The Tara Canyon extends for about 80 kilometres and reaches 1,300 metres at its deepest point, carving through limestone to create a dramatic river–canyon system of outstanding natural beauty. Its canyons, karst springs and linked lake–river networks support varied habitats and species. The site focuses on protecting the integrity of the river and canyon, maintaining water quality, and conserving the alpine and subalpine ecosystems that define the basin. Long-running research on rivers, mountain lakes and fauna underpins conservation and guides sustainable use across the landscape.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Rising from 433 to 2,522 metres, the biosphere reserve spans an alpine to subalpine gradient that brings together alpine forests, swift rivers and high lakes with heath, transition mires, bogs and screes. Across this terrain, natural eutrophic lakes sit alongside alpine rivers and a mosaic of alpine and subalpine heathland. High ground holds sub-Arctic willow scrub (Salicetum appendiculata montenegro) and alpine calcareous grasslands, while pioneer communities colonise exposed rock. Forests are varied and extensive. Along rivers, relict alluvial stands of Alnion glutinoso-incanae persist. Upslope, Mediterranean pine includes the endemic black pine (Pinus nigra illyrica) and broad belts of beech. At higher elevations the canopy shifts to Pinus heldreichii with other Pinetea communities. At the heart of the site, the Tara River runs for roughly 150 kilometres from the Komovi area to its confluence with the Piva River near Šćepan Polje, fed by numerous tributaries, glacial lakes and powerful karst springs. This river has carved one of Europe’s great canyons, with depths exceeding 1,300 metres in places. The Tara River Canyon is recognised for exceptional aesthetic value and the abundance of paleoendemics, neoendemics and relict populations, making it a stronghold for specialised cliff and scree flora such as Edreianthus glisicii, Amphoricarpos autariatus and Daphne malyana. Forest and canyon systems support capercaillie (Tetrao urogallus), hazel grouse (Tetrastes bonasia) and a suite of raptors, owls and falcons. Cold, well-oxygenated waters hold salmonids including huchen (Salmo hucho), brown trout (Salmo trutta morpha fario) and grayling (Thymallus thymallus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Tara River Basin

records.introduction_en: The Mongol Daguur steppe and wetland territory comprises mainly low-mountain landscapes that support a variety of flora and fauna. The area is rich in biodiversity, encompassing Daurian and Manchurian flora and fauna, and has natural resource potential.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Mongol Daguur Biosphere Reserve provides nesting and breeding grounds for globally endangered species, such as the white-naped crane, and many rare or critically threatened birds use the steppe as migratory stopover sites. Situated at the eastern tip of Mongolia and bordering Russia, the biosphere reserve ecosystem has a distinct transboundary character.
records.name: Mongol Daguur

records.introduction_en: Onon–Balj Biosphere Reserve lies in north-eastern Mongolia at the southern edge of the Siberian taiga, spanning the Daurian steppe and the Onon–Balj river basin. A continuum of peatlands, wetlands and rivers supports major waterbird concentrations and forms part of the East Asian–Australasian Flyway. The reserve abounds in culturally important areas, including sites linked to Chinggis Khan (c. 1162–1227) and long-used common grazing lands for nomadic herders. The biosphere reserve’s core objectives include conserving the forest–steppe and riverine corridor, safeguarding threatened species and cultural heritage, and strengthening community-led, climate-resilient livelihoods through research, education and adaptive co-management.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set at the southern edge of the Siberian forest, where boreal coniferous forest gives way to the Daurian steppe, the Onon–Balj biosphere reserve spans the Onon and Balj river basin. The landscape is shaped by moderate mountains and a dense hydrological network of the Onon and its major tributaries, with mineral springs, and fresh and saline lakes. Major ecosystems include forest, grassland and freshwater habitats, arranged along a clear altitudinal transition from the Khentii mountain range through taiga (boreal coniferous forest) to steppe (temperate grassland).The Khurkh Khuiten Ramsar Site, in the reserve’s buffer zone, together with the Onon–Balj and Ulz river basins and surrounding wetlands, harbours one of the largest breeding populations of White-naped Crane (Antigone vipio) worldwide – over 400 breeding pairs. With a global population estimated between 3,700 and 4,500 mature individuals (IUCN Red List, 2018), the species is classed as Vulnerable due to habitat loss and other pressures. Wetlands are a defining ecological asset in the reserve, regulating and mitigating floods, improving water quality, and providing spawning and nursery areas for fish and breeding habitat for waterfowl. These systems are increasingly vulnerable to climate warming, livestock overgrazing and changing land-use practices.
records.name: Onon Balj

records.introduction_en: The Uvs Nuur Basin is the northernmost of the enclosed basins of Central Asia. It takes its name from Uvs Nuur Lake, a large, shallow and very saline lake that is important for migrating birds, waterfowl and seabirds. The site is made up of twelve protected areas representing the major biomes of eastern Eurasia.The Uvs Nuur Basin is one of the key areas of the Altai–Sayan Ecoregion, included in the Global 200 list of virgin or little-modified ecoregions of the world. The northern part of the basin is located in the Russian Federation on the territory of three administrative districts, or kozhuuns, of the Republic of Tuva. The southern part lies within Uvs aimag of Mongolia. The geographical position and climate of the Uvs Lake depression are marked by exceptional contrast due to its position in the centre of Asia, its relatively high altitude and its distinctive relief. The highest point of the territory is the peak of the Turgen Mountain Range, and the lowest point is Uvs Lake. The lake’s water is the remnant of a huge saline sea that covered a much larger area several thousand years ago.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Uvs Nuur Basin and its surroundings boast extraordinary landscape diversity, ranging from cold desert and steppe to floodplain forests and diverse wetlands, fixed sand dunes and even tundra. The basin is characterised by mixed mountains and highland systems with a total size of 70,000 km². The lake is the largest in Mongolia. It is 84 km long and 79 km wide. It covers 3,350 km² at 759 m above sea level, with an average depth of 6 m. The biosphere reserve serves as a significant scientific site for studying the evolution of the environment from the Ice Age to present day, due to remnant glaciers, Pleistocene ice sheets and numerous glacial lakes. The diverse landscape is inhabited by a rich diversity of species, including locally endemic plants and endangered species such as the snow leopard. Apart from the main lake, Uvs, the basin comprises several smaller lakes. As these lakes lie to the north of other inland seas of Central Asia, they are important places for waterfowl migration. With its reed beds and river deltas, the basin provides significant nesting and resting areas for 215 migratory water bird species. Notable examples are the white-headed duck (Oxyura leucocephala) and the swan goose (Anser cygnoides), both of which are endangered and included on the IUCN Red List. There are also many other nationally and globally threatened flora and fauna species, including the endemic fish Oreoleuciscus potanini, Oreoleuciscus pewzowi and Oreoleuciscus humilis.
records.name: Uvs Nuur Basin

records.introduction_en: Home to the oldest and largest karst formation in Asia, the Phong Nha-Ke Bang Biosphere Reserve encompasses 515,830 hectares of limestone mountains, ancient cave systems and pristine tropical forests in central Viet Nam. In 2025, together with Hin Nam No National Park in Lao PDR, it became the first transboundary UNESCO World Natural Heritage site in Southeast Asia.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Its forests shelter 2,954 vascular plant species, including 172 endemic to Viet Nam, and 1,399 animal species.. Three Important Bird Areas and the convergence of northern and southern floristic zones make it one of the most biodiverse corners of Southeast Asia.
records.name: Phong Nha - Ke Bang

records.introduction_en: The Bogeda Biosphere Reserve is located in the eastern region of the Tianshan Mountains. Local residents call the area the Sangong River Valley, named after one of the largest rivers in the region, which originates from Bogeda Peak. Five major landscapes are distributed throughout the northern and southern areas of the biosphere reserve: ice–snow belts (5,445–3,100 metres above sea level), alpine and sub-alpine meadow belts (3,100–2,500 metres above sea level), forest belts (2,500–1,600 metres above sea level), steppe belts (1,700–900 metres above sea level) and sand desert dunes (460–3,300 metres above sea level). The topography consists of a middle mountain belt, low mountain erosion hills and alluvial areas. Tianchi Lake is the only natural lake in the region and lies adjacent to the Sangong River.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Bogeda Biosphere Reserve is situated within the temperate continental arid climate zone. Different habitat types range from snowy landscapes to meadows, steppe and sand dunes, providing ideal conditions for a rich biodiversity. Alpine and sub-alpine landscapes with Koresia capilliformis and perennial herbaceous plants cover approximately 80 per cent of the area. The low plain lingo halophyte vegetation desert zone contains flora such as Suaeda physophora and Halostachys caspica. Characteristic fauna includes the black stork (Ciconia nigra), the long-legged buzzard (Buteo rufinus) and the eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx). However, numerous endangered or threatened animal species in the biosphere reserve struggle for survival, including the eurasian hobby (Falco subbuteo) and the black-tailed gazelle (Gazella subgutturosa). The region is also home to species of commercial or traditional importance, such as Cistanche salca, which grows in desert habitats and is used in traditional Chinese medicine.
records.name: Bogeda

records.introduction_en: Located in southern China, in Guizhou Province, Fanjingshan lies within the Chinese subtropical forest biogeographic region. The reserve has mountainous terrain, and its main peaks form part of the Wuling Mountain Range. Elevation ranges from 480 m to 2,570 m above sea level.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The climate in Fanjingshan is humid with mid-subtropical monsoons. The biosphere reserve is known for its large protophyte forests, the only well-preserved primitive forest ecosystem at this latitude in the world. Many endangered species, such as Rhinopithecus brelichi, depend on this complex forest ecosystem. The largest area of dove tree (Davidia involucrata) occurs in Fanjingshan. Abies fanjingshannensis is endemic to the region. Subtropical and temperate rain forests, as well as mixed mountain and highland systems, are the main ecosystems in the reserve.
