The area is home to populations of the endemic golden monkey (Rhinopithecus brelichi). The biosphere reserve has focused on research activities since its establishment in 1986 and has made notable advances in research on the ecology, domestication, reproduction and habitats of the golden monkey. Other fauna in the reserve includes the clouded leopard (Neofelis nebulosa).
records.name: Fanjingshan

records.introduction_en: The Hanma Biosphere Reserve encompasses a significant part of the boreal forest, or taiga, found in China. The reserve covers a range of forest and wetland ecosystems rich in biological diversity, including many endangered and rare species. Human ecological disturbance is minimal, resulting in abundant natural resources and high-quality local vegetation and ecology. The cold-temperate coniferous forest is among the best-preserved forest systems in China and is of significant scientific value. Local wetlands include swamps dominated by Larix gmelinii and wetlands dominated by Carex. They have retained their original natural landscapes and wetland functions. The biosphere reserve plays an important role in protecting water and rare wildlife resources, ensuring water purification and maintaining the ecological balance of the Heilongjiang area and the Jiliuhe River.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve lies at high elevation within the environs of Zhongshan Mountain on the western part of the main ridge of the northern Greater Khingan Mountains in Inner Mongolia. The surrounding mountains form a flat valley stretching north to south for 56 km, 32 km in width. The reserve includes a wide variety of wetlands covering more than 20,000 ha. These include river wetlands, lake wetlands, marsh wetlands, forest swamps, bush swamps and herbaceous swamps. It also forms part of a light-needled coniferous forest ecosystem within tundra mountains, with features typical of forests in the northern Greater Khingan Mountains. The main vegetation types are taiga and coniferous forest, including elfin Pinus pumila and Pinus sylvestris. Typical species include the Siberian salamander (Salamandrella keyserlingii), wolverine (Gulo gulo), moose (Alces alces cameloides), Siberian musk deer (Moschus moschiferus), sable (Martes zibellina) and great grey owl (Strix nebulosa), along with other near-Arctic animals of vital significance for China.
records.name: Hanma-Huzhong

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve lies on the southern slopes of the Minshan Mountains, within the transition area between the Sichuan Basin and the Qinghai–Tibet plateau. The altitude ranges from about 2,000 to 4,700 metres above sea level. The natural landscape includes snow-capped peaks, numerous waterfalls, forests, mountain streams and lakes. Lakes, waterfalls and travertine (calcareous-sinter) terrace-and-cascade karst landforms of Jiuzhaigou are rare worldwide. The population is primarily Tibetan, with Han and Qiang communities also present. Tourism is the principal industry.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Located in the south-east of the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau, Jiuzhaigou lies in the transition zone where the Tibetan Plateau descends sharply into the Sichuan Basin. With terrain higher in the south and lower in the north, it marks the fore-slope of China’s stepped topography, with towering peaks and deeply incised valleys. Jiuzhaigou’s waterscape is its most celebrated feature: numerous lakes of varying size and shape, waterfalls and cascades of different heights and widths, surface brooks and rivers, and underground streams together form a connected water system. The aesthetic value of this exuberant waterscape is internationally rare. A total of 3,634 species of flora and fauna have been recorded (excluding lichens and soil animals), including 3,553 native species and 81 cultivated or unintentionally introduced species, 419 algae, 203 fungi and 2,007 vascular plants. Invertebrates number 693 species (71 zooplankton, 45 benthic invertebrates, 539 insects and 38 other terrestrial invertebrates). Vertebrates total 313 species (two fish, six amphibians, four reptiles, 223 birds and 78 mammals).
records.name: Jiuzhaigou Valley

records.introduction_en: Niubeiliang Biosphere Reserve hosts typical representative fauna and flora for the Qinling Mountains. The relatively undisturbed natural forests have recorded the highest biodiversity in the eastern Qinling Mountains. Residents in the transition zone have developed innovative land-based industries in cooperation with research institutions, which are also active in scientific research and monitoring.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Niubeiliang Biosphere Reserve lies in the subalpine zone and is predominantly mountainous. Niubeiliang (2,802 m) is the highest peak in the eastern Qinling Mountains. The reserve’s southern slopes are cut by ravines and cliffs, while the upper northern slopes form platforms with gentler gradients within the Qinling fold–fault zone. The area supports a typical temperate, broad-leaved mixed mountain forest. Forests cover more than 94 per cent of the reserve, which spans three administrative counties: Chang’an, Ningshan and Zhashui. It provides habitat for many endangered and rare species, including the golden takin (Budorcas taxicolor bedfordi) and the dwarf musk deer (Moschus berezovskii), and serves as an important reservoir of genetic diversity. It is also a valuable reference site for vegetation research and conservation. A total of 950 seed-plant species have been recorded, including 71 medicinal plants, 110 oil-bearing and aromatic plants, 60 fibre plants, 84 starch- and sugar-producing plants, and 63 tanning plants. Fauna documented to date include 60 mammals, 124 birds, seven amphibians, 20 reptiles and seven fish. The region is a key water-conservation area for Xi’an and for southern Shaanxi Province.
records.name: Niubeiliang

records.introduction_en: Xilin Gol Grassland forms the main body of Inner Mongolia’s natural grassland and is one of the four great grassland regions in China. It is the most representative temperate true steppe, composed of bunch and rhizome grasses, including Stipa and Leymus chinensis. It is also the most intact part of the eastern Asia subregion of the Eurasian steppe region, with high value for conservation and scientific research.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve features landforms of hills, downlands, valleys, grassland, lava terraces and aeolian sandy lands, with grassland the most important. Xilin Gol is a mosaic of four ecosystems: typical grassland developed over chestnut soils under a semi-arid climate; meadow grassland distributed over chernozems with a semi-humid climate; sandy-land forests distributed over grasslands; and valley wetlands. The Xilin River, Zhagesitai Nor Lake and other waterbodies are dotted across the rolling grassland. These multiple and complex ecosystems, and the rich fauna and flora, form a world-class temperate grassland community that naturally combines grasslands, forests, rivers, lakes and sandy lands. It is an ideal site for study and long-term monitoring of grassland ecosystems. There are 280 vertebrate species in 164 genera, 65 families and 27 orders recorded in the reserve. These include, within the reserve and its surroundings, 198 bird species in 105 genera, 42 families and 17 orders: 37 resident species, 126 summer visitors, 35 passage migrants and one wintering species. There are 50 mammal species in 35 genera, 14 families and six orders, with rodents the most numerous at 22 species. The fauna also includes 10 reptile species in six genera, four families and two orders; six amphibian species in three genera, three families and one order; and 16 fish species in 15 genera, two families and one order.
records.name: Xilin Gol

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is part of the eastern extension of the Tibetan plateau ranging from 2,200 to 6,032 m a.s.l. The area is not only noted for its high biological diversity, but also for its associated cultural values as three sacred mountains are located within the area. The local inhabitants observe the custom of revering nature and preserving the environment of the sacred mountains. The Kangba-Tibetan ethnic group accounts for 90% of the total population of the biosphere reserve, which practise shamanism or adhere to five different sects of Tibetan Buddhism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Located in the south of Ganzi Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, the east of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and the middle of Hengduan Mountains, the Biosphere Reserve borders Muli county of Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture in the southeast, Xiangcheng county and Zhongdian county of Yunan in the west and Litang county in the north. In the east part of the reserve, three mountains are straight into the sky, which are Xiannairi in the north with an elevation of 6300 m, and Yangmaiyong and Chanodnj in the south and east respectively with the same elevation of 5958 m. They are known as holy snow-capped mountains in the west Tibetan areas of China. The higher mountain natural ecosystems are predominated by icy peaks, snowcapped mountains, glaciers, broad valleys, virgin forests and plateau meadows have been kept in this region.Endowed with distinctive landscapes, the reserve has vascular plants of 1126 species from 431 genera in 120 families and 291 species of vertebrata, including beasts of 69 species, birds of 197 species, reptiles of 5 species, amphibians of 10 species and fishes of 10 species. Attention is given to the protection of some 20 rare animal species in the area, including leopards, black bears, Asian golden cats, golden pheasants etc. There are 2 kinds of plants (Sorolepidium glaciale Christ and Isoetes) and 12 kinds of animals including 6 kinds of beasts and 6 kinds of birds under first-grade state protection, as well as 7 plants and 42 kinds of animals under second-grade state protection. 29 Chinese endemic species in the region include 15 kinds of beasts, 11 kinds of birds, plus 2 kinds of amphibians.
records.name: Yading

records.introduction_en: The Valdés Biosphere Reserve encompasses the Patagonian steppe, hill plains and plateaux, and Argentine Sea eco-regions. It is home to significant biodiversity, including highly fragile terrestrial and marine ecosystems whose conservation is crucial to addressing the vulnerabilities of key species. Both the Patagonian steppe eco-region and the Argentine Sea are recognised as important sites and are inscribed on WWF’s Global 200 list.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Patagonian steppe includes temperate grasslands, characterised by high fragility and a cold, dry climate with constant winds. These grasslands can absorb and store carbon, contributing to the fight against climate change. The biosphere reserve is also of botanical interest, as it hosts numerous endemic species, including families such as Brassicaceae, Cactaceae, Fabaceae, Oleaceae and Verbenaceae, among others. An emblematic endemic mammal is the Patagonian hare (Dolichotis patagonum). A key impact associated with human activities in this eco-region is desertification, which affects certain parts of the area and diminishes the capacity of ecosystems to provide ecological services such as carbon sequestration and the supply and regulation of water. The Argentine Sea eco-region is characterised by cold‑temperate waters and relatively low biodiversity compared with tropical environments, and presents species with a high biomass. The eco-region is among the most productive in the world. The Patagonian region in particular produces abundant phytoplankton, at a rate about three times higher than the world average. The coastal marine environment faces various anthropogenic threats, including degradation, overexploitation of resources, the introduction of new species, physical changes to the coastal zone, pollution and mass tourism. Even so, the marine coastal areas remain suitable habitats for the feeding and reproduction of many species of birds and marine mammals. Bodies of water, such as the Golfo Nuevo and San José, function as crucial sites for the reproduction of species such as the southern right whale (Eubalaena australis). The Valdés Biosphere Reserve incorporates the Peninsula Valdés Natural Protected Area, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in … [truncated]
records.name: Valdés

records.introduction_en: Argentina’s Valdivian Forest represents the easternmost remnants of the temperate rainforests shared with Chile. It covers approximately 2.33 million hectares along the eastern slope of the North Patagonian Andes, with 57% of this area included within a biosphere reserve. These forests are designated for conservation due to their high ecological integrity and strong habitat connectivity. Their primary goal is to preserve the long-term integrity and functioning of the Valdivian ecoregion at a landscape scale. At the same time, the biosphere reserve promotes the sustainable use of natural resources both inside and outside protected areas, emphasizing equity, active community participation, respect for cultural diversity, and improved coordination among the organizations managing the territory.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Andino Norpatagónica Biosphere Reserve comprises a narrow strip of high mountain environments, temperate forests, grasslands and sub-Andean steppes. Together, these form one of the most important remnants of well-conserved temperate forests on the planet. These environments play a key role in the protection of high basins. They define the eastern limit of the distribution of many of the most representative species of the ecoregion, including Nothofagus, Fitzroya, Austrocedrus and Araucaria. They also constituted refuges during the last glaciation. The reserve maintains an area of great environmental integrity and key importance for the conservation of the region as a whole, as well as the genetic variability of many of its relevant species. The area is home to endangered endemic species, such as the social tuco tuco (Ctenomys sociabilis), Challhuaco frog (Atelognathus nitoi), larch (Fitzroya cupressoides) and pehuén (Araucaria araucana). It is also home to species threatened with extinction, such as the huemul (Hippocamelus bisulcus) and huillín (Lontra provocax).
records.name: Andino Norpatagonica

records.introduction_en: Located in the southern part of the Río de la Plata estuary in Argentina, the Parque Costero del Sur Biosphere Reserve is a swampy region that comprises pampa grasslands, swamps, wetlands and dry forests. More than 200 bird species find refuge and food in the tala forests of the region, which is also home to mountain cats and ocelots. It is representative of the Pampas, the fertile lowlands that cover several regions of Argentina, Uruguay and Brazil. Tourism and livestock production are the most important economic activities.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is located at the intersection of two geosystems, the river and the Pampas. It features a great diversity of ecological niches and faunal populations. Due to its fertile soil, most of the Pampas has been degraded by agriculture, making the biosphere reserve one of the last original and preserved areas. It has different kinds of terrain, including grasslands, flooded and unflooded swamps, wetlands and forests, which are home to the marsh deer (Blastocerus dichotomus), currently considered vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. In addition, the tala forests (Celtis ehrenbergiana) are an important resting and feeding place for migrating and local birds. Their biological importance lies in the fact that Celtis ehrenbergiana is accompanied by a great variety of other tree, shrub, climbing and grass species that provide shelter for mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and insects.
records.name: Costero del Sur

records.introduction_en: With altitudes that can reach almost 6,000 metres above sea level, the Laguna Blanca Biosphere Reserve features a typical arid Andean landscape, with a saline lake in a main depression and surrounding rocky formations. It is located in the province of Catamarca, in the north-west of Argentina. Its creation in 1979 aimed at the conservation of the vicuña, which was endangered due to poaching. This goal led to the development of sustainable handling strategies, including reviving the Chaku, an ancient Inca practice of capturing, shearing and releasing vicuñas. In Laguna Blanca’s transition areas, residents are mostly public servants or workers in the developing tourism industry.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Laguna Blanca Biosphere Reserve is located in the north of the Belén Department and in the south-east of the Antofagasta de la Sierra Department, in the province of Catamarca. It is biogeographically situated in the Puna and High Andes ecoregion, between 3,000 metres above sea level in the depression south of the reserve and 5,912 metres above sea level at Cerro Galán. The climate is cold, dry and windy, with scarce seasonal rainfall of less than 250 mm per year.The area has a tectonic origin and is surrounded by mountain ranges, 3,200–5,500 metres above sea level, whose predominant direction is north–south. The lower areas are occupied by lagoons, and Laguna Blanca is the largest, at approximately 3,450 ha.Across the Puneñas and Altoandinas ecoregions, vegetation comprises shrubby and grassy steppes with low cover and patches of bare soil. In wetland-associated sectors—lagoons, streams and plains, or bofedales—vegetation is dominated by grasses such as chillaua (Festuca scirpifolia) and white grass (Cortaderia spp.). Sedges (Cyperaceae), such as Scirpus atacamensis, and rushes such as Juncus depauperatus can form continuous cover, creating key habitats with high concentrations of biodiversity. Rocky areas support notable cacti in the genera Denmoza, Maihueniopsis, Lobivia and Opuntia.The reserve contains a range of environments and high biodiversity. Characteristic mammals include the vicuña (Vicugna vicugna).
records.name: Laguna Blanca

records.title_en: Laguna Oca y Herraduras del Río Paraguay
records.introduction_en: The Laguna Oca del Río Paraguay Biosphere Reserve is located in Formosa Province in northern Argentina. The natural vegetation of the reserve comprises gallery forests, wetlands and savannas along the meanders and oxbow lakes of the Paraguay River. The gallery forests are densely structured, present high biodiversity and have abundant epiphytes, lianas and orchids.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Laguna Oca del Río Paraguay Biosphere Reserve is located on the flood plain of the Paraguay River and includes a portion of the Chaco plains. The most important woody species include species of the genus Prosopis, such as the white carob tree (Prosopis alba), the black carob tree (Prosopis nigra) and espinillo (Prosopis affinis). Species of the genus Tabebuia are present, including the palo cruz (Tabebuia nodosa), and in smaller quantity the paratodo (Tabebuia aurea). Other trees include tatané (Chloroleucon tenuiflorum) and quebrachillo (Aspidosperma triternatum). There are also specimens of the caranday palm (Copernicia alba) in a dispersed form. Among the bush species, the churqui (Acacia caven) and the aromito (Acacia aroma) are significant. Among the herbaceous species are those of the Poaceae family. The most important include espartillo (Elionurus muticus), paja boba (Paspalum intermedum) and paja brava (Panicum prionitis). Near Payaguá Island and Laguna Verde, almost pure manduvira (Cynometra bauhiniaefolia) forests have been found, with specimens that show good conformation. Good regeneration has been observed in those environments. Probably the largest number of species in one group corresponds to the group of insects with ants standing out as the main biomass of primary consumers in the region. Among the vertebrates, there are more than 50 species of fish, 40 of amphibians, 50 of reptiles, 300 of birds and 70 of mammals. Within the group of reptiles and amphibians, notable species include the black caiman (Caiman yacare), yacaré overo (Caiman latirostris), false chameleon (Polychrus acutirostris), cururú toad (Rhinella schneideri), Chaco climbing frog (Hypsiboas raniceps), Chaco snout frog (Scinax acuminatus), spotted-breasted frog (Scinax n … [truncated]
records.name: Laguna Oca y Herraduras del Río Paraguay

records.introduction_en: The Patagonia Azul Biosphere Reserve is located in the south of the country on the coast of Chubut Province. The reserve encompasses a coastal area with the greatest biodiversity on the Argentine coastline. It includes important breeding, feeding and migration sites for different species of birds and mammals.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve comprises a coastal area with the greatest biodiversity on the Argentine coastline. It includes important breeding, feeding and migration sites for different species of birds and mammals. For example, Punta Tombo hosts the largest colony of Magellanic penguins (Spheniscus magellanicus) in the world, accounting for almost 40 per cent of the global population. The area also constitutes a representative sample of the Patagonian steppe, the Patagonian south-west Atlantic, and plains and plateaus. The specific geographical characteristics, combined with numerous inaccessible areas and more than fifty islands, have resulted in pristine areas that protect the essential biodiversity of this region of Patagonia.
records.name: Patagonia Azul

records.introduction_en: Sitting on the banks of the Río de la Plata in the north-eastern part of Buenos Aires Province in Argentina, the Pereyra Iraola Biosphere Reserve is located between the municipalities of La Plata and Berazategui. As the last protected area of the original riverside ecosystem, it has the province’s greatest biological diversity. This includes endangered bird species such as the burrito colorado (Laterallus leucopyrrhus). The area is also known for its medicinal plants and aquifers. The reserve is the largest public space in Greater Buenos Aires. It serves as a nearby leisure site with activities that include hiking, cycling and birdwatching. Family farming provides a living for people who live in the reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Pereyra Iraola Biosphere Reserve is located in the heart of one of Latin America’s biggest urban areas, Greater Buenos Aires. It is one of the last remains of the original riverside ecosystem, which, in other areas, has been destroyed or completely modified by heavy urbanisation. It is home to hundreds of species that are unique to the region, particularly birds. Almost 70 per cent of all avifauna in the province can be found in the reserve, with 288 species, including the endangered burrito colorado. In terms of floristic biodiversity, the region is rich in native trees such as the tala (Celtis tala), sauco (Sambucus australis) and espinillo (Acacia caven), as well as ferns and grasslands.
records.name: Pereyra Iraola

records.introduction_en: In the Andes of Argentina’s San Juan Province, the San Guillermo Provincial Reserve was established in 1972 to protect the vicuña (Vicugna vicugna), which was then at risk of extinction. The area encompasses three contrasting ecoregions—High Andean, Puna, and woodland—and supports the largest populations of vicuña and guanaco (Lama guanicoe) in Argentina, both of which are currently increasing.The landscape forms a striking mosaic of deserts, high-altitude grasslands, and thorny shrublands in warmer lowland valleys. Beyond its importance for biodiversity conservation, the reserve plays a key role in securing sustainable water supplies for downstream communities. Local livelihoods are based mainly on mining, with tourism playing a smaller role.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Andes is the largest mountain range in the world, extending from Venezuela to the southern parts of Argentina and Chile. The San Guillermo Biosphere Reserve, in the western part of Argentina, is part of the largest arid ecosystem in South America, with a complete ensemble of native fauna and flora. The region is known for its populations of vicuñas (Vicugna vicugna) and guanacos (Lama guanicoe). It is also home to a wealth of species, such as the Suri Cordillerano (Pterocnemia pennata), the puma (Puma concolor) and the highly endangered Andean Mountain cat (Leopardus jacobita). In the higher areas of the biosphere reserve, the landscape comprises deserts and grasslands, while thorny bushes thrive in the somewhat warmer lowlands.
records.name: San Guillermo

records.title_en: Apolobamba National Natural Area of Integrated Management
records.introduction_en: The Apolobamba National Natural Area of Integrated Management Biosphere Reserve is located 160 km north-west of La Paz, and its western boundary follows the border with Peru. Situated in the higher parts of Bolivia, it encompasses a mosaic of ecological formations, including high plateau, tundra, high cordillera, mountains and lakes. These include the headwaters of the River Euichi and River Turiopa, additional lakes, and a permanent snow zone. The variety of habitats and ecological formations makes the reserve of exceptional importance for scientific research. The main goal is to protect natural, cultural, historical and anthropologic values through the sustainable management of natural resources with local participation and scientific support.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Apolobamba Cordillera is the principal mountain range, accompanied by the Cololo massif. East of the cordillera, formations of the Yungas type develop, with their typical plant associations. On the high plateau and tundra, the fauna includes camelids such as the vicuña (Vicuña vicugna) and the alpaca (Lama pacos). In the cordillera and at the heads of valleys, deer (Odocoileus) and the spectacled bear (Tremarctos ornatus) can be found.
records.name: Apolobamba National Natural Area of Integrated Management

records.introduction_en: Located in southeastern Austria, the Unteres Murtal Biosphere Reserve borders the Mura River Biosphere Reserve in Slovenia. The area is of significant natural, historical, and cross-border importance due to its location along the Slovenian border and its role within the European Green Belt.Following the Danube floodplains, it contains Austria’s second-largest alluvial forest along a major river.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The natural area known as the “Lower Mura Valley” lies in the south-eastern foreland of Styria. The region is characterised by a history of intense volcanism, forming part of a volcanic arc that extends from Slovenia to the Carpathian Arc. This activity occurred in two distinct phases differing in age, chemistry and origin, and is linked to subsurface extensional tectonics. In the Styrian volcanic region, rock units formed over the past 16 million years are exposed at the surface. The Mura River forms the border with Slovenia for approximately 40 km and, together with the adjoining floodplain forests, shapes the landscape. Through interactions among abiotic and biotic factors, it creates a mosaic of valuable land uses and habitats. Water-dependent habitats such as alluvial forests, swamps, ponds and wet meadows are found mainly along the Mura and its tributaries. Agricultural and forestry areas, together with settlements, characterise the more favourable sites for human use. The area is characterised by high biodiversity, particularly in water-bound flora and fauna. The reserve is home to almost 50 fish species, 14 of which are of European importance. It also supports a large number of amphibians and bird species, many of which are of European importance and appear on the IUCN Red List. Species present include the otter (Lutra lutra), Danube salmon (Hucho hucho) and kingfisher (Alcedo atthis).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Unteres Murtal / Lower Mura Valley

records.introduction_en: Six villages within a single alpine valley form the Grosses Walsertal Biosphere Reserve, situated in the western part of Austria. The valley is a prime example of a living cultural landscape. Since its occupation by the Walser people in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, a system of highly adapted mountain farming, pasture and extensive forestry has been developed.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Forests, meadows, ravines, springs, streams, hills, cliffs, mountain tops, alpine pastures and karst formations are all present in the reserve. Owing to its geological and morphological variety, the whole Grosses Walsertal valley forms a single, extensive biotope rich in flora and fauna. The valley’s mountain meadows contain many herbs, gentians and orchids. Ninety per cent of the Grosses Walsertal Biosphere Reserve comprises natural and cultivated landscapes. Core zones cover 8,165 acres (17 per cent) of the reserve. In the Grosses Walsertal valley these are the nature conservation areas of Gadental and Faludriga–Nova, the River Lutz, the Kirschwald–Ischkarnei area, the Tiefenwald moor region and Rote Wand (literally ‘Red Wall’), the highest mountain in the valley. The zoning did not introduce new regulations, as each of these areas already had special protective status under nature conservation law. Cultivation zones cover 32,942 acres (69 per cent) and are primarily mountain forests, alpine pastures and traditionally managed mountain meadows.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Grosses Walsertal

records.introduction_en: The Wienerwald Biosphere Reserve covers an undulating landscape between the Northern Alps and the Pannonian Basin, to the west of the city of Vienna. On the eastern slopes of the Wienerwald there is a geological rupture zone with hot springs. The area also features impressive marine terraces of a former sea. The limestone part of the Wienerwald is characterised by steep and rugged limestone and dolomite rock formations, as well as sharply cut gullies.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Wienerwald is an important biodiversity hotspot in Europe. Diverse habitats developed due to the meeting of different biogeographical and climatic regions, differing geological conditions and considerable altitude variation, and, last but not least, human influence. The habitats in the open-land cultivated area are of outstanding international importance. Vast meadows and pastures, the result of centuries of cultivation, dominate large parts of the region. Dry grasslands are particularly characteristic. There are also a few unimproved grasslands on moist and wet sites, including moor grass meadows and calcareous fens. Ancient vineyards and fruit orchards, areas dominated by agriculture, rich water sources and numerous structural elements enrich the landscape diversity of the Wienerwald. Large areas are contiguously wood covered, at more than 60 per cent. The dominant tree species is beech (Fagus sylvatica). However, there is more to the Wienerwald than beech forests. It is home to 25 different types of forest vegetation. Austria’s largest forests of downy oak (Quercus pubescens) and sub-Mediterranean pine forests with the endemic Austrian pine (Pinus nigra) at the easternmost edge of the region are of European significance.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Wienerwald

records.introduction_en: The Fitzgerald Biosphere Reserve is located between Bremer Bay and Hopetoun on the south coast of Western Australia. It comprises upland plains and a marine plain that is deeply incised by several rivers, creating large valleys and tablelands. A chain of small, isolated peaks runs close to the coast, forming the distinctive Barren Ranges. The highest peak reaches 450 metres above sea level. Rugged coastal cliffs occur where the quartzite ranges meet the ocean. Sand dunes, inlets, rivers, swamps and lakes also occur on the gently sloping marine plain, and they dry up in summer. There is a rich diversity of plant species in the park and surrounding areas, including dry sclerophyllous woodland, coastal woodlands and heath. The reserve contains over 250 rare or geographically restricted plant and animal species, many of which are little known. Of the 2,000 vascular plant species native to this area, around 75 per cent are endemic. Human impacts within the reserve are mainly related to tourism and the development of visitor facilities.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Fitzgerald Biosphere Reserve lies on the southern edge of the Yilgarn Block and the adjoining Albany–Fraser Province. The bedrock of the northern edge of the biosphere reserve forms part of an ancient crustal segment known as the Yilgarn Craton. Granite and gneiss are the predominant rock types, with minor enclaves of altered sedimentary and mafic igneous rock. Skeletal soils are associated with granite exposures, and there are extensive areas of shallow loamy sand. The region boasts huge diversity in plant species, including rare wet sclerophyll forest, with thick, leathery leaves, as well as dry sclerophyll forests, coastal woodlands and scrub. It also includes several major river systems, lakes and swamps, and remnants of biologically important woodlands and shrublands belonging to the wheatbelt. The region ranks among the most important areas for plant biodiversity in the world and contains over 800 rare and threatened plant and animal species, many of which are little known. Of the 5,000 or so vascular plant species native to this area, 79 per cent are endemic. Environments within the upland plains are important for threatened terrestrial mammal and bird species. Examples of endangered species include the western ground parrot (Pezoporus wallicus fusciventer), Carnaby’s black cockatoo (Calyptorhynchus latirostris) and the dibbler (Parantechinus apicalis). Other animal species include the western quoll (Dasyurus geoffroii), the quenda (Isoodon obesculus fusciventer), the tammar wallaby (Macropus eugenii), the mallefowl (Leipoa ocellata) and the peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus).
records.name: Fitzgerald

records.introduction_en: The Great Sandy biosphere reserve lies in the South East Queensland bioregion in eastern Australia. Renowned for its cultural and ecological significance, it contains the Great Sandy Strait, a Ramsar-listed wetland, and Fraser Island, a UNESCO World Heritage site. The reserve includes the largest sand island and coastal sand mass in the world.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve has a volcanic hinterland, with Mount Mothar the highest point at 450 metres above sea level. Six major river systems flow through Great Sandy: the Noosa, Mary, Susan, Burrum, Isis and Cherwell. The area is home to the world’s richest and tallest rainforest growing on sand; however, efforts to expand agricultural land threaten this forest. Ecosystem development processes are evident throughout the reserve. The dune systems overlap and pass through diverse stages, reflected in the variety of plant species. In addition, about 2,843 plant species occur within the reserve. This diversity reflects Great Sandy’s location in the McPherson–Macleay Overlap Zone, noted for high endemism and genetic diversity. Examples of rare and threatened plant species include southern penda (Xanthostemon oppositifolius) and ball nut (Floydia praealta). Characteristic species include sandpaper fig (Ficus coronata) and fringed wattle (Acacia fimbriata). Although sandy soils are nutrient-poor, a range of sand-based forests occur, including mangrove, eucalypt, riparian rainforest and dry rainforest. Satinay and turpentine dominate many forests. Altogether, 96 regional ecosystems are distributed across the reserve. The area provides habitat for 49 per cent of Australia’s bird species, and 40 per cent of the world’s perched lakes occur within Great Sandy. Fauna recorded include the gummy shark (Mustelus antarcticus) and white-bellied cuckoo-shrike (Coracina papuensis). The Woongarra Coast hosts the most southerly coastal fringing coral reefs on the eastern Australian mainland and supports significant fish habitat. Hervey Bay has high biodiversity, including rare marine fauna, coral reefs and seagrass beds, and is a key habitat for humpback whales.
records.name: Great Sandy

records.introduction_en: Located in South-east Queensland, a short distance from Brisbane, the area features a picturesque coastline, dunes and beaches. It also includes extensive waterways and wetlands, as well as a range of mountains in the hinterland. Home to two First Nations, the Kabi Kabi and Jinibara peoples, the biosphere reserve sustains a highly valued natural environment and rich biodiversity, particularly in the 2,585 km2 terrestrial and marine protected areas. The reserve supports both traditional and cutting-edge economic activities, with strong food, agribusiness and tourism sectors.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: With a subtropical climate and a long coastal strip, the Sunshine Coast is a region where two climate zones meet and overlap. Tropical habitats that extend southwards intermingle with temperate habitats extending northwards. This creates a unique region that showcases the landforms and rich biodiversity of both climate zones, and enhances the overall biological diversity of the area. The natural environment is a living network of landforms and catchments, wetlands and waterways, terrestrial ecosystems, coastal foreshores and marine waters. It includes the smallest lichen on Mount Coolum and the tallest eucalypt in the hinterland. It ranges from the humble brush turkey to the striking Richmond birdwing butterfly, and from the rarely seen water mouse to the towering Glass House Mountains. It also includes the internationally recognised Pumicestone Passage under the Ramsar Convention.
records.name: Sunshine Coast

records.introduction_en: Songor Biosphere Reserve lies on Ghana’s south-eastern coast at the mouth of the Lower Volta, where the river meets the Gulf of Guinea. A shallow, brackish lagoon sits at its centre, linked by creeks to low islands and the estuary. This river–lagoon–sea setting supports large numbers of migratory waterbirds on the East Atlantic flyway and important nesting beaches for marine turtles. The reserve aims to conserve habitats and species; integrate wildlife management with local use; and develop education, research, tourism and recreation across its conservation, development and logistic functions.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The site comprises a shallow, brackish lagoon and intertidal mudflats linked by creeks to the Lower Volta estuary and a chain of low islands. Seaward, lie a broad sandy beach and a narrow dune, and landward, coastal savannah with mangroves on the floodplains. Twice-daily tides, the regional Guinea Current and twice-yearly upwelling (cooling surface waters to around 25 °C) shape the coastal system and boost fish productivity, while the river mouth forms a brackish transition that serves as spawning and nursery habitat. As a Ramsar Wetland of International Importance on the East Atlantic flyway, Songor supports large numbers of migratory waterbirds and records Ghana’s highest counts of terns (seabirds in the gull family, Laridae). Beaches and islands provide nesting sites for olive ridley (Lepidochelys olivacea), leatherback (Dermochelys coriacea) and green turtle (Chelonia mydas). The river–estuary system also supports West African dwarf crocodile (Osteolaemus tetraspis) and Nile crocodile (Crocodylus niloticus). Mangroves filter pollutants, cycle nutrients and stabilise shorelines, reinforcing the productivity of the lagoon and nearshore fisheries.
records.name: Songor

records.introduction_en: Located in the West African savanna region of south-eastern Burkina Faso, the Arly Biosphere Reserve is part of the Afrotropical dry forest biome. Set in an ancient peneplain with diverse landscapes ranging from grassy plains and shrubland to gallery forests and seasonal waterways, it harbours areas of striking beauty including sites where baobab and shea trees grow in distinctive clusters. The reserve’s primary objectives are to restore and sustainably manage wildlife and habitats, strengthen transboundary migration corridors, and support socio-economic partnerships that benefit both biodiversity conservation and local livelihoods.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Arly Biosphere Reserve lies on the peneplain of an ancient massif, about twenty metres above the Niger River valley. Its landscape is shaped by the Pendjari and Arly rivers, with Voltaic sandstone outcrops – exposed sandstones of the Volta Basin that form low cliffs and benches – visible along the main watercourses. A network of tributaries and nearly 40 seasonal or permanent ponds sustain a rich mosaic of habitats, including wetlands with aquatic meadows, gallery forests, dry open forests, wooded and shrubby savannas, grasslands, and bowé – bare, iron-rich lateritic crusts where vegetation is sparse. This hydrological system, reinforced by groundwater from the Volta basin, ensures year-round ecological connectivity and underpins the reserve’s habitat diversity. The reserve is a stronghold for emblematic and threatened species including the cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus), African elephant (Loxodonta africana), lion (Panthera leo), leopard (Panthera pardus) and lappet-faced vulture (Torgos tracheliotos). It also supports threatened native trees including karité shea (Vitellaria paradoxa), afzelia (Afzelia africana) – a valuable savanna hardwood – and African mahogany (Khaya senegalensis). The wetlands provide crucial stopover and feeding grounds for Palearctic migratory birds, and hold Ramsar designation as a Wetland of International Importance. The reserve contributes to long-term conservation through its role in the transboundary W–Arly–Pendjari complex shared by Benin, Burkina Faso and Niger, and in the wider African biosphere reserve network.
records.name: Arly

records.introduction_en: Ouzounboudjak Biosphere Reserve is situated in Strandzha Mountain on the left bank of the Rezvaya River, at the Turkish border. Located about 20 km from the Black Sea, the climate has maritime influences.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve was established in 1956 to protect the specific flora and vegetation represented by Pontic, Mediterranean and central European ecological types. The area was declared a biosphere reserve in 1977. It comprises forests with more than 200-year-old oaks (Quercus polycarpa and Quercus frainetto) and beeches (Fagus orientalis). The understorey includes Rhododendron ponticum, Daphne pontica, blueberry (Vaccinium arctostaphylos) and Mespilus germanica. In Europe, some of these species occur naturally only in the Strandzha Planina area. The rich fauna includes wild boar (Sus scrofa), roe deer (Capreolus capreolus), wild cat (Felis silvestris), badger (Meles meles), red fox (Vulpes vulpes) and pine marten (Martes martes), while wolves (Canis lupus) occasionally come from Turkey.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Ouzounboudjak

records.introduction_en: Chervenata Stena Biosphere Reserve is characterised by a complex of unique natural values, including relief, altitude, composition of basic rocks, and soil and climatic conditions. These determine the richness of the flora, mycota, fauna and natural habitats, represented by a significantly high percentage of protected, endemic and relict species. As a result, the biodiversity of the reserve has high conservation significance at national, European and global levels.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve includes 15 habitat types listed under the EU Habitats Directive, five of which are EU priority habitats: petrifying springs with tufa formation, Tilio-Acerion ravine forests, alluvial alder and ash woods (with Alnus glutinosa and Fraxinus excelsior), eastern white oak woods, and sub-Mediterranean black pine forests. Eight species of mammals, excluding bats, are included in the Red Data Book of the Republic of Bulgaria, with the following national IUCN categories. Four species are endangered: Ursus arctos, Rupicapra rupicapra, Martes martes and Felis silvestris. Four species are vulnerable: Vormela peregusna, Lutra lutra, Spermophilus citellus and Canis lupus.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Tchervenata sténa

records.introduction_en: Stretching across the alluvial plain, and the delta and riverbank areas of the Mono River, this biosphere reserve comprises a mosaic of landscapes and ecosystems consisting mainly of mangroves, savannah, lagoons, floodplains and forests, including sacred forests. The reserve’s inhabitants are mostly engaged in small-scale agriculture of oil palm and coconut palms, pasture, forestry and fishing.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Recognised under the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, the Mono River delta on the Benin–Togo border supports diverse habitats including rivers, lakes, wetlands, savannah, gallery forest, mangroves and beaches, and a rich fauna including hippopotamuses, manatees, whales and many species of waterfowl. The biosphere reserve also has various species that are endemic to the Dahomey Gap, such as the white-throated guenon (Cercopithecus erythrogaster). Critically endangered species include the hawksbill sea turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata) and the leatherback sea turtle (Dermochelys coriacea).
records.name: Mono

records.introduction_en: Located in north-western Benin, the Pendjari Biosphere Reserve lies at the interface of the Sahel and Sudanian zones, offering a unique ecological corridor between West Africa’s drylands and its more humid regions. The reserve encompasses a largely flat peneplain, interspersed with riverine flood zones and low mountain chains. It plays a vital role in conserving the region’s landscapes, species, and genetic resources, while supporting ecological resilience and local livelihoods through sustainable resource use.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Pendjari’s landscape is defined by an array of savannas and forest formations. Elevation ranges from 150 to over 500 metres, with seasonal flooding along the Pendjari River and two main geological zones divided along a northeast–southwest axis. To the north, the terrain is composed of schist and sandstone of the Volta Basin, while the southern sector is dominated by Buem Series formations –sandstone, jasper and schist – that run parallel to the Atakora quartzite range. Pendjari’s vegetation is characteristic of the Sudanian zone, comprised of grassy, shrubby and wooded savannas, as well as open forest with a herbaceous layer dominated by grasses. The Bondjagou Forest within the reserve is of particular conservation importance, hosting six plant species listed as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List: Cordyla pinnata, Afzelia africana, Garcinia livingstonei, Kigelia africana, Raphia sudanica, as well as Thunbergia atacoriensis, a species endemic to Benin found only in this forest. As part of the transboundary W–Arly–Pendjari ecosystem, the reserve forms a major wildlife corridor linking protected areas across Benin, Burkina Faso and Niger. Along the Pendjari River, floodplains, semi-permanent watercourses and ponds sustain seasonal wetlands that buffer high flows and offer dry-season refuges.
records.name: Pendjari

records.introduction_en: The Belambangan Biosphere Reserve is located in East Java Province and incorporates three national parks, Alas Purwo, Baluran and Meru, and one nature reserve, Kawah Ijen. The reserve comprises terrestrial and marine ecosystems featuring karst landscapes and savannah. It includes different forest types, notably alpine and subalpine, upper, dry and lower montane, lowland, coastal and mangrove. The site also features seagrass beds and coral reefs. The main economic activities are agriculture and horticulture, as well as agroforestry, notably teak and mahogany.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Belambangan Biosphere Reserve is in East Java Province on Java Island and forms part of the Indo-Malayan region. It lies within Banyuwangi Regency, Situbondo, Bondowoso Regency and Jember Regency in East Java, and includes the mountain areas of Ijen and Mount Raung. The core area is covered with tropical rainforest at altitudes from 0 to 1,000 m above sea level. The reserve includes both terrestrial and marine ecosystems such as karst landscapes, savannah, alpine and subalpine forest, montane forest, lowland bamboo forest, coastal forest and seagrass beds. Mangroves are also present, and coral reef ecosystems are found in the buffer zone. More than 300 fish species have been identified. The reefs are dominated by coral species of the genus Acropora. The region is a biodiversity hotspot with many faunal species, including the banteng or Javanese wild bull (Bos javanicus), Christmas frigatebird (Fregata andrewsi), green peafowl (Pavo muticus) and the endangered Javan leopard (Panthera pardus). In addition, four species of sea turtle nest on the south and east coast of Alas Purwo National Park: olive ridley (Lepidochelys olivacea), leatherback (Dermochelys coriacea), hawksbill (Eretmochelys imbricata) and green turtle (Chelonia mydas).
records.name: Belambangan

records.introduction_en: Bukit Batu is a peatland area in Sumatra that features sustainable timber production and two wildlife reserves. These reserves are home to the Sumatran tiger, elephant, tapir and sun bear. Research activities in the biosphere reserve include the monitoring of flagship species and in-depth study of peatland ecology. Initial studies indicate good potential for sustainable economic development that uses flora and fauna to support inhabitants’ economic welfare.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Recognised as part of the Sumatra peat swamp ecoregion, Giam Siak Kecil–Bukit Batu has a unique habitat and plays a significant role in sustaining populations of rare, endangered and endemic species. About 189 plant species, from 113 families and 59 genera, are recorded in this area. Twenty-nine of these plant species are categorised as protected under CITES Appendices I and III. Nine protected species recorded in this area include: red costulata (family Apocynaceae); nyatoh (Ganua motleyana), family Sapotaceae; tiger orchid (Grammatophyllum speciosum), family Orchidaceae; daaropara (Knema), family Myristicaceae; mengris (Kompassia malaccensis), family Mimosaceae; pitcher plants (Nepenthes), family Nepenthaceae; suntai (Palaquium leiocarpum), family Sapotaceae; and balam (Palaquium burckii), family Sapotaceae. The core area is dominated by peat swamp forest. Recorded plant species here include ramin (Gonystylus bancanus), nyatoh (Palaquium leiocarpum), durian burung (Durio carinatus), meranti bunga (Shorea teysmanniana) and punak (Tetramerista glabra). Several key animal species are recorded in the core area and are listed as protected and endangered under CITES Appendix I. These include two birds (the great hornbill (Buceros bicornis) and Mycteria cynerea), four mammals (the sun bear (Helarctos malayanus), Malayan tapir (Tapirus indicus), Sumatran elephant (Elephas maximus) and Sumatran tiger (Panthera tigris sumatrae)), two reptiles (the false gharial (Tomistoma schlegelii) and estuarine crocodile (Crocodylus porosus), and one endangered fish species (the Asian bonytongue or arowana (Scleropages formosus).
records.name: Giam Siak Kecil - Bukit Batu

records.introduction_en: Situated between Flores and Sumbawa in Indonesia, the Komodo Biosphere Reserve and National Park is renowned for its population of about 5,000 giant lizards, also called Komodo dragons (Varanus komodoensis). They exist nowhere else in the world and are of significant interest to scientists studying the theory of evolution. In addition to Komodo Island, the biosphere reserve encompasses the islands of Rinca and Padar, as well as numerous islets. It also includes one of the world’s richest marine environments with coral reefs.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is situated in a transition zone between Australian and Asian flora and fauna habitats. Terrestrial ecosystems include open grassland, woodland savannah, tropical deciduous monsoon forest, mangroves and quasi cloud forest. The marine area constitutes 70.2 per cent of the biosphere reserve and is characterised by a combination of strong currents, coral reefs and islets, which make navigation around the islands in Komodo National Park difficult and dangerous. Komodo has one of the world’s richest marine environments. It includes more than 260 species of reef-building coral, 70 species of sponge, ascidians, marine worms, molluscs, echinoderms and crustaceans, as well as cartilaginous fishes and more than 1,000 species of bony fishes. Marine reptiles include green turtle and hawksbill turtle, and marine mammals include dolphins, whales and dugongs. Notable species of high commercial value include sea cucumbers, Napoleon wrasse (Cheilinus undulatus) and groupers. The number of terrestrial animal species is important from a conservation perspective, as some species are endemic. The Komodo dragon (Varanus komodoensis) is among the world’s largest reptiles. It can reach more than 3.6 metres in length and weigh more than 90 kg. In 1991, Komodo National Park was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site to protect the Komodo dragon. Many of the mammals are Asiatic in origin, including deer, pigs, macaques and civet, while several reptile and bird species are Australian. These include the orange-footed scrub fowl (Megapodius reinwardti), the lesser sulphur-crested cockatoo and the friarbird.
records.name: Komodo

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve and national park is situated on the Tanjung Peninsula in the south of Borneo and covers the swampy alluvial areas between Kumai Bay and the Seruyan River. Covering a total area of 415,040 ha, Tanjung Puting has a large diversity of forest ecosystems, including lowland forest, freshwater swamp forest, tropical heath forest (locally called kerangas), peat swamp forest, mangrove forest and coastal forest.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve comprises a wide spectrum of ecosystems such as remnants of dryland dipterocarp forests, peripheral mixed swamp forests, peat swamp forests, mangrove and coastal beach forests, and secondary forests. Tanjung Puting National Park was established by the Dutch colonial government in the nineteen-thirties for the protection of the orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus) and proboscis monkey (Nasalis larvatus). Today, these animals are the main tourist attractions, although the number of visitors is still modest. Iron wood (Eusideroxylon zwageri) and ramin (Gonystylus bancanus) are among the plant species of high importance from a conservation point of view. Tanjung Puting Biosphere Reserve harbours many species of wildlife. Other primates found in the area include the long-tailed macaque (Macaca fascicularis), pig-tailed macaque (Macaca nemestrina), agile gibbon (Hylobates agilis), grey gibbon (Hylobates mulleri) and red leaf monkey or maroon langur (Presbytis rubicunda rubida). Other notable mammals and species of conservation concern include the sun bear (Helarctos malayanus), sambar deer (Cervus unicolor), mouse deer (Tragulus javanicus klossii) and wild pig (Sus barbatus). The clouded leopard (Neofelis nebulosa) and leopard cat (Prionailurus bengalensis borneoensis) have also been recorded. Reptiles include the estuarine crocodile (Crocodylus porosus) and false gharial (Tomistoma schlegelii). A rich avifauna is present, with more than 200 species recorded, including the endangered and rare storm stork (Ciconia stormii), many kingfishers, hornbills, the oriental darter and herons. This area also harbours a number of interesting fish species, including a globally endangered species, the Asian bony-tongue (Scleropages formosus), locally called the ar … [truncated]
records.name: Tanjung Puting

records.introduction_en: Located in Central Java in the Indo-Malayan region, the biosphere reserve spans 254,877 ha. It is home to Gunung Merapi National Park, Gunung Merbabu National Park and Sermo Wildlife Reserve, each critical in protecting various endemic Javanese species. The Java–Bali montane forest type at the site protects the biodiversity of the Indo-Malayan region, as well as a limestone formation in the Menoreh area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The tropical forest of the Merapi Merbabu Menoreh Biosphere Reserve is part of the Java–Bali montane forest type. It plays an important role in biodiversity conservation in the Sundaland region, as well as in conserving limestone (karst) formations in the Menoreh part of the reserve. The core areas are dominated by montane forest and karst and are recognised as supporting a significant water reservoir that supplies the buffer zone and transition area. They also play an important role in controlling floods. These core areas harbour several protected, threatened and endemic flora and fauna. At least 48 species are recorded across these categories: nine mammals, 35 birds, two fish, one amphibian and one insect. Notable examples include the long-tailed macaque (Macaca fascicularis), the leopard (Panthera pardus) and the black-winged starling (Acridotheres melanopterus).
records.name: Merapi Merbaru Menoreh

records.introduction_en: The biosphere includes Lombok Island, part of the Lesser Sunda Islands. It consists of relatively flat coastal areas and hilly and mountainous areas. The highest peak is Mount Rinjani, the second-highest volcanic mountain in Indonesia at 3,726 metres above sea level. The area has a very high level of biodiversity, comprising various types of forest vegetation, including savannah forest and mountain and lowland rain forest, about 40 per cent of which are primary forests. The inhabitants’ main sources of revenue come from horticulture such as vegetables and fruits, cereal crops such as rice, animal husbandry including cows, goats and chickens, and the cultivation of coffee and cacao.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is a lowland area extending from the coast to hilly and mountainous terrain, with elevations ranging from 0 m to 3,726 m above sea level. Slopes are classified as gentle at 0–15 per cent, moderate at 15–25 per cent, sloping at 25–40 per cent, and steep at more than 40 per cent. A relatively sloping area located in the south and north-east lies at an altitude of 0–1,500 m above sea level at the foothill of Mount Rinjani. The highest peak is Mount Rinjani at 3,726 m above sea level. Adjacent mountains are separated by vast valleys and deep ravines, with steep and rocky slopes. In the western valley of Mount Rinjani lies Segara Anak Lake at 2,100 m above sea level, with waters rich in sulphur. In the middle of Segara Anak Lake, the “new volcano” called Mount Barujari at 2,376 m has risen. The volcano is still active, and the last eruption occurred in 2009. The reserve is a habitat for various important flora and fauna species of the Lesser Sunda and many other species adapted to the unique mountain tropical ecosystem of Lombok Island. The core area houses at least 19 species of mammals, 8 species of reptiles, 5 species of amphibians, 154 species of birds, 20 insect species, 447 species of trees, 59 species of ferns, 117 species of mushrooms, 55 species of orchids, 28 species of lianas and 6 species of rattans.
records.name: Rinjani Lombok

records.introduction_en: Saleh–Moyo–Tambora (SAMOTA) comprises five major ecosystems: small islands; a coastal area of mangrove; coastal, lowland and mountain forests; and savannah. Its core area plays an important role in conserving the region’s biodiversity. The buffer zone and transition area have agricultural potential for the production of fruit and vegetables, as well as rice, coffee and cacao, and for animal husbandry. The beauty of the Tambora Mountains has tourist potential, while Sumba Island communities attract cultural tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The three areas that comprise the Biosphere Reserve feature a great deal of biological diversity. In Saleh Bay, for instance, dugong species can be found in the mangrove habitat, as well as dolphins. In Moyo, there are 30 bird species, nine of which are protected. These include small crested yellow cockatoos (Cacatua sulphurea), orange-footed scrubfowl (Megapodius reinwardt), horned cikukua (Philemon boceroides), honey sriganti (Nectarinia jugularis), elegant pitta (Pitta elegans), parrots (Gracula religiosa), Halcyon chloris, Haliastur indus. In addition to various species of birds in Moyo and Satonda Island, there are several other species of animals such as timor deer (Cervus timorensis), wild boar (Sus), Macaca fasicularis and reticulated python (Python reticulatus). The Tambora National Park area has a high diversity of plant species. Vegetation is distributed across three forest ecosystem types, ranging from seasonal forests to tropical rainforests and savannah forests. Dense vegetation cover forms a solid ecosystem, giving the Tambora National Park region a strategic role as a life-support system to ensure the continuity of ecological functions in the region.
records.name: SAMOTA

records.introduction_en: Togean Tojo Una-Una Biosphere Reserve is located in the centre of the world’s coral reef triangle, which has the highest diversity of coral species globally. The biosphere reserve’s local population consists mainly of fishermen living in the transition area’s main settlements around the city of Ampana.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Togean Tojo Una-Una Biosphere Reserve lies in the centre of the world’s coral reef triangle, which has the highest diversity of coral species in the world. As an archipelago, the flora in the core area is grouped into terrestrial and aquatic flora. Lowland forests cover part of the land area of the Togean Islands. The composition of forests and oceans in the Togean Islands is considered unique because the islands lie on the Wallacea Line and the Weber Line, which influences their biodiversity. Based on a field survey and a study by a 2004 Integrated Team throughout the Togean Islands, 363 species of flora were recorded. Terrestrial flora on Togean Island includes palapi (Heritiera javanica), ironwood (Intsia bijuga), siuri/ranggu (Koordersiodendron pinnatum), uru (Magnolia vrieseana), flakes (Elmerrillia) and several species of Dipterocarpaceae, such as Shorea, Dipterocarpus and Hopea. In opened forest areas, species found include soap tree (Alphitonia excelsa), cananga tree (Cananga odorata), kadam (Anthocephalus chinensis), jackapple (Alstonia spectabilis), Mallotus, Macaranga, yellow cheesewood (Nauclea orientalis) and crima/bintuang (Octomeles sumatrana). There are 33 species of aquatic flora. Mangroves include Rhizophora, Avicennia, Ceriops and Excoecaria, Asiatic mangrove (Rhizophora mucronata), perepat (Sonneratia alba), api-api hitam (Avicennia alba), Scyphiphora, Pemphis, ketapang (Terminalia catappa), thatch screwpine (Pandanus tectorius) and sea hibiscus (Hibiscus tiliaceus). Mangrove monitoring by the National Park Office in the Togean Islands in 2013 showed that Rhizophora mucronata was the most dominant species across various vegetation levels. Other aquatic flora recorded include seven seagrass species. Turtle grass (Thalassia hemprichii) an … [truncated]
records.name: Togean Tojo Una-Una

records.introduction_en: The Atlantic Forest is one of the seven moist forest areas of the Neotropics and the second largest after the Amazonian rain forest. It covers around 90,000 km² along 3,000 km of the Atlantic coast, spanning 17 different Brazilian states. Although the remaining Atlantic Forest, about 10 per cent of the original vegetation, is rather homogeneous, the social diversity is very high. It includes large urban centres, including Rio de Janeiro, Florianópolis and São Paulo, as well as many small traditional communities, small-scale fishers and forest extractive groups.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The remnants of the Atlantic Forest are associated with secondary forests, forming a unique ecosystem stretching more than 3,000 km parallel to the coast and comprising Serra Mantiqueira, Serra Geral and Serra do Mar. These very rare Atlantic Forest remnants, and associated ecosystems such as mangroves, salt marsh scrublands, sand spits and upland grasslands, are under pressure from the most highly populated areas in the country. The Mata Atlântica Biosphere Reserve is a biodiversity hotspot. Estimates indicate that 55 per cent of tree species and 39 per cent of mammal species are endemic to this region. It is home to 15 per cent of Brazilian primates, including the golden lion tamarin (Leontopithecus rosalia) and jaguar (Panthera onca).
records.name: Mata Atlântica

records.introduction_en: Greater São Paulo comprises 39 municipalities over an area of 805,300 ha. Covering only one thousandth of the country’s territory, it is densely populated. In this context, the São Paulo Green Belt Biosphere Reserve provides numerous environmental services to the region, securing safe water sources, stabilising the climate and filtering polluted air.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Mostly covered with dense ombrophilous forests, the area is home to various species of the Brazilian Atlantic Forest, which is a biodiversity hotspot. Local authorities are mapping natural ecological corridors to allow these species to move, such as the black howler (Alouatta caraya) and the cougar (Puma concolor). Various birds also occur, such as the tawny-browed owl (Pulsatrix koeniswaldiana).
records.name: Sao Paulo City Green Belt

records.introduction_en: The Cuatrociénegas Biosphere Reserve consists of a small valley locally known as a bolson, an arid basin in mountainous areas where rainwater does not reach the sea on the surface. These wetlands are home to over 800 plant species and about 360 animal species, some of which are critically vulnerable or endangered. Its gypsum dune sites have among the highest levels of endemism in the world. The pozas (pools) awe visitors with their beautiful shades of blue.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is an arid zone with around 500 water bodies of varied shapes and blue hues, surrounded by mountains where unique regional species have developed. Since the creation of the biosphere reserve, several projects have promoted the conservation of wetlands, habitats and soils, among other priorities. In its water bodies, known as pozas, there are 33 endemic species and stromatolites. The colour of the water varies from deep blue to turquoise. The site also hosts significant resources such as gypsum outcrops, which form the second-largest dune field in the Americas and provide habitat for various endemic species. The area is recognised by the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) for its biodiversity.
records.name: Cuatrociénegas

records.introduction_en: El Triunfo is situated in the mountains of the Sierra Madre de Chiapas in the south of the state of Chiapas, in generally steep and mountainous terrain. The reserve forms the boundary between two of the largest hydrological regions of the state: the Pacific coast and the Grijalva–Usumacinta River. As a primary Pleistocene refuge, and due to its location in the Sierra Madre de Chiapas, it is considered an endemic area for different groups of plants and animals. El Triunfo is the most diverse evergreen cloud forest in Mexico and one of the most important sites for bird migration. It is covered with evergreen seasonal forest, montane rainforest and lower montane rainforest, which contain a higher proportion of endemic plants. A number of threatened mammalian species can be found in the reserve, namely Geoffroy’s spider monkey, margay, jaguar and puma.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The El Triunfo Biosphere Reserve protects 10 of the 19 types of vegetation reported for the state of Chiapas, including two of the most endangered ecosystems in Mexico, the cloud forest and the rainforest. El Triunfo’s cloud forest is one of the most extensive remnants in the country and contains the greatest diversity of tree species in North and Central America. The Sierra Madre de Chiapas, where El Triunfo is located, is one of the regions in the country that receives the most rainfall. The dense forest cover acts like a sponge, absorbing moisture from rain and dense mist, and makes a high contribution to the rivers that irrigate the Pacific coastal plain and the state’s Central Depression. Knowledge of the flora in the biosphere reserve remains incomplete, but 977 species have been reported. Regarding fauna, there are 548 terrestrial vertebrate species, representing 45 per cent of those reported for Chiapas and 22 per cent of those reported for Mexico. Twenty-two species of amphibians have been recorded, comprising 23 per cent of those recorded for Chiapas and 7.5 per cent of those for the country. As for reptiles, 63 species are known, corresponding to 32 per cent of those known for Chiapas and 9 per cent of those reported for the country. One hundred and twelve species of mammals have been recorded, which is 56 per cent of those for Chiapas and 23 per cent of those for Mexico. In general, invertebrates have been the least studied group in the reserve. For the Sierra Madre de Chiapas, 588 species of daytime Lepidoptera butterflies have been identified, corresponding to 49 per cent of those identified for Chiapas.
records.name: El Triunfo

records.introduction_en: La Sepultura Biosphere Reserve comprises a range of ecosystems and natural habitats that represent major biogeographic regions, alongside traditional forms of local land ownership that determine different uses for management and conservation. The main ecological system, owing to its extent and biodiversity, is lowland deciduous or dry tropical forest, distributed in the lower parts of both strands of the sierra.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve contains a range of ecosystems and natural habitats representing important biogeographical regions, together with local traditional forms of land allocation that involve different uses in managing and preserving the site. These include lowland deciduous forest (tropical dry forest), midland sub-evergreen forest (evergreen tropical forest), and midland sub-deciduous and mixed pine–oak–Liquidambar forests. Relict ecosystems are also present, such as montane cloud forest or evergreen cloud forest, cloud shrubland or high-altitude páramo, and pine savannah. It harbours more than 90 migratory bird species, six palm species of global economic importance, four cicada species and various orchids. Notable trees include Ulmus mexicana, Manilkara zapota, Triplaris melaenodendron, Cedrela odorata, Liquidambar styraciflua, Haematoxylum brasiletto and Croton guatemalensis. There are five feline species: oncilla, jaguarundi, ocelot, jaguar and puma. Other mammals include spider monkey, tapir, brocket deer and tamandua anteater. Birds include grey hawk, Swainson’s hawk, solitary eagle, king vulture, peregrine falcon and various psittacids. Parrots include the white-fronted parrot and yellow-naped parrot. Reptiles include boa, rattlesnake, coral snake, green iguana and black iguana.
records.name: La Sepultura

records.introduction_en: On Colombia’s northern Pacific coast in the Chocó department, the Tribugá–Cupica–Baudó Biosphere Reserve spans a marine–coastal zone and a continental zone that extend from coastal mangroves to a coastal mountain range – the Serranía del Baudó – forming a crucial passage for species moving between Central and South America. The reserve’s objectives include maintaining ecological connectivity, protecting mangroves, strengthening sustainable fisheries, and advancing collaborative research and monitoring to underpin community-led, sustainable development. Beyond its role as a centre of endemism and biodiversity, the reserve also supports cultural identity and ancestral knowledge.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Steep coastal landforms and the rugged Serranía del Baudó create a pronounced sea-to-mountain gradient across the reserve. Topography and hydrology generate a continuum of habitats, from tropical rainforest and mangroves to rocky and sandy shores, estuaries, and coastal waters with patchy coral formations. This diversity of ecosystems underpins high biodiversity. Coastal wetlands function as important stopover sites for migratory birds and provide key habitat for four marine turtles: the black turtle (Chelonia agassizii), hawksbill (Eretmochelys imbricata), leatherback (Dermochelys coriacea), and olive ridley (Lepidochelys olivacea). Rocky reefs (“riscales”) support several seabird species and shelter fish. Isolated coral colonies also occur, including Pocillopora spp., Porites spp., and Pavona varians.Mangroves in the Ensenada de Tribugá function as nurseries, with coastal currents transporting larvae and fry towards Utría National Natural Park. Together, the terrestrial and marine systems sustain a coastal–marine corridor across the Tropical Eastern Pacific, reflected in designations such as the Chocó–Darién hotspot, the Chocó–Manabí Conservation Corridor, and the Important Bird Area at Utría.
records.name: Tribugá-Cupica-Baudó

records.introduction_en: The El Tuparro Biosphere Reserve and National Park is located in the eastern plains of Colombia in Vichada Department, a flat area bound by the Orinoco River to the east, the Tomo River to the north, and the Tuparro and Tuparrito rivers to the south. The landscape undulates with a series of small valleys, major rivers and streams. Some areas are seasonally flooded during parts of the year.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: About 85 per cent of the area is covered with natural grass savanna dominated by plume grass. Woodlands occur along watercourses and host a range of tree species. Especially notable are the morichales and the mirití palm areas. Mammals of the savanna include white-tailed deer, giant armadillo, small savanna armadillo, tapir and dog fox. Peccaries, pumas, jaguars and different species of monkeys inhabit the woodlands. Noteworthy birds include guans, curassows, screamers, eagles and ducks. Giant otters, capybaras, Orinoco crocodiles, caiman and turtles are found along the river margins. The rivers abound with fish, including piranha and electric eel.
records.name: El Tuparro

records.introduction_en: The Yangambi Biosphere Reserve is situated within the Congo River Basin west of the City Kisangani in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Yangambi Biosphere Reserve lies within the Congo River Basin. Vegetation ranges from climax forests dominated by Brachystegia laurentii and monodominant stands of Gilbertiodendron dewevrei to semi-deciduous formations (including Scorodophloeus zenkeri) and secondary forests (often with Pycnanthus angolensis and Fagara macrophylla). Marshland forests are present, and valley forests along the Congo and its tributaries include wet meadows, flood vegetation and island forests. Post-agricultural secondary regrowth and other degraded secondary formations are also widespread. Notable fauna includes the forest elephant (Loxodonta africana cyclotis), river hog (Potamochoerus porcus) and monkeys (Cercopithecus), which are among the most threatened species.
records.name: Yangambi

records.introduction_en: Basse-Lobaye Biosphere Reserve lies in the south-west of the Central African Republic, bound by the Mengui and Lobe rivers to the west, the Lotemo to the east, the Kinga–Lombo–Lotemo road to the north and the border with the Republic of the Congo to the south. The reserve’s objectives are to conserve the forest–savanna mosaic and its Sudano–Guinean fauna, regulate wildlife use through recognised customary rights, sustain local livelihoods within ecological limits, and develop research, training and monitoring to inform adaptive management.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve lies in a permanently hot, humid zone. Vegetation is dominated by semi-deciduous humid forest with Ulmaceae, Sterculiaceae, Meliaceae and Sapotaceae. Beyond the humid forest, the wider landscape includes extensive tracts of dense and open dry forest, wooded savannas across much of the area, edaphic savannas along the main watercourses and areas of plantation regrowth at different stages. Fauna is characteristically Sudano–Guinean. Duikers are the most numerous large mammals, followed by primates such as guenons, colobus and mangabeys. Chimpanzee and forest elephant are present but rare. Carnivores include leopard, civets, genets and mongooses, and notable snakes include Bitis species, mambas, cobras and pythons. The site is of great scientific importance because it brings together well-studied Central African humid forests and the continent’s now-scarce dense dry forests, which here persist in sizeable, relatively intact tracts. This combination offers a rare opportunity for comparative research within a single conservation complex.
records.name: Basse-Lobaye

records.title_en: Complexe des Aires Protégées du Nord-Est de la République Centrafricaine
records.introduction_en: The Protected Area Complex of Northeast Central African Republic Biosphere Reserve lies in the north-east of the Central African Republic, in the transition zone between the Sahelian area to the north and the humid Equatorial area to the south. It marks the meeting point of the Congo, Lake Chad and Nile basins and is significant for the pivotal role it plays in regional ecological connectivity. The celebrated Manovo-Gounda Saint-Floris National Park World Heritage site is located at the heart of the reserve, recognised for its diversity of habitats that include Sudano-Guinean woodland savanna and flood plains. The main objective of the biosphere reserve is to preserve landscapes, ecosystems, terrestrial and aquatic biodiversity, and to generate incomes at the level of local communities.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve covers a wide range of natural zones that include dry forest with river corridors lined by gallery forest, and broad floodplains. Its size and connectivity at the junction of the Congo, Lake Chad and Nile basins make it an important corridor between major protected areas, supporting the movement of large mammals such as the elephant, hippopotamus, giraffe, Derby eland and lion.Floodplains, residual pools and small shaded streams create a gradient of wetland habitats that underpin exceptional biodiversity. The dense Chari–Logone river system provides roughly 95% of the Chari River’s annual contribution to Lake Chad – a large lake at the junction of Nigeria, Niger, Chad and Cameroon. This hydrological network is crucial for fish migration and productivity, and offers a dry-season refuge for large numbers of fauna. The reserve lies within the Sudanian regional centre of endemism and is recognised for its role in water regulation, carbon sequestration and buffering against land degradation and desertification pressures.
