Its designation as a biosphere reserve marked an important step for conservation and sustainable development in the Central African Republic.
records.name: Complexe des Aires Protégées du Nord-Est de la République Centrafricaine

records.introduction_en: The Taï Biosphere Reserve is located on the border with Liberia in the south-west of Côte d’Ivoire, about 200 km south of Man and 100 km from the coast. It represents one of the last remnants of the primary tropical forest of West Africa.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Within the biosphere reserve, there is a gradation from north to south, with the southern third being the moistest and richest area, especially in leguminous trees. This humid tropical forest has a high level of endemism. Its floral diversity and the occurrence of several threatened monkey species are of great scientific interest. Dense evergreen forest includes species such as the palm Eremospatha macrocarpa, ebony (Diospyros mannii), Parinari chrysophylla, Chrysophyllum perpulchrum and Chidlowia sanguinea on poorer soils. Dense evergreen Sassandrian forest is dominated by water-demanding species such as ebony (Diospyros) and Mapania. Swamp forest includes Gilbertiodendron splendidum, alongside agroecosystems.
records.name: Taï

records.introduction_en: The Araucarias Biosphere Reserve has continental climatic characteristics, with large summer temperature oscillations. Rainfall varies between 2,000 and 3,000 mm a year, and winter snowfall can reach up to 2 m in some areas.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The prevailing climate in the Conguillio sector is warm temperate, with fewer than four dry months. In the Alto Biobio sector, an icy climate predominates because of the altitude, with marked steppe characteristics. Observed forest formations include Araucaria Forest associated with steppe containing Chusquea. This habitat is exclusive to this region of the country and occurs only in the Alto Biobio sector. The fauna is typical of steppe environments. Pure Araucaria forests, and Araucaria associated with lenga beech (Nothofagus pumilio), N. dombeyi and Antarctic beech (N. antarctica), host a rich amphibian fauna, reptiles, birds and mammals, and various groups of invertebrates.
records.name: Araucarias

records.title_en: Bosques Templados Lluviosos de los Andes Australes
records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve corresponds to a section of the Valdivian eco-region, as defined by WWF in 2006. Compressed into a narrow north–south belt with pronounced latitudinal and altitudinal gradients, it presents varied climatic, hydrological and soil conditions and, consequently, a high diversity of species and ecological processes.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve contains four of the eleven biogeographical subregions recognised for the ecoregion: Andean Araucaria Forests, Mixed Nothofagus Forests, Andean Larch Forests and Aysén Coastal Forests. Several conifers are listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), including Fitzroya cupressoides, Araucaria araucana and Pilgerodendron uviferum; the first two are designated as Natural Monuments. The area was identified by Dinerstein et al. (1995) among 238 ecoregions, out of some 800 worldwide, hosting particularly outstanding and representative biodiversity.
records.name: Bosques Templados Lluviosos de los Andes Australes

records.introduction_en: The territory of the biosphere reserve is located in the Coquimbo Region in northern Chile. The region is one of the most biodiverse in the country, with 3,429 plant species, excluding varieties, of which 1,605, or 46 per cent, are entirely endemic to this area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This biosphere reserve represents dwarf coastal cloud shrubland composed of succulents and thorny shrubs, typical of Chile’s arid and semi arid Mediterranean type vegetation. Biomes present include river and estuary at the mouth of the Limarí River, coastline, semi-arid sclerophyll shrubland and evergreen relict forest. The evergreen relict forest is hygrophilous, featuring species characteristic of southern Chile, over 1,000 km away, such as olivillo (Aextoxicon punctatum) and winter’s bark or canelo (Drimys winteri). The native flora comprises 440 species, of which 266 are endemic to Chile; ten are listed as endangered and eighty-four as vulnerable.
records.name: Fray Jorge

records.introduction_en: La Mancha Húmeda Biosphere Reserve comprises Tablas de Daimiel National Park, which forms the core area, the Alcázar Lake, and Lagunas de Ruidera National Park, which is a refuge for aquatic birds.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This is a gently rolling plain at 600 to 700 m above sea level, characterised by Tertiary deposits and a great number of wetlands. These arise from the seasonal flooding of rivers such as the Guadiana, Cigüela, Záncara and Riánsares, and from numerous upwellings of the Manchego aquifer in depressions known locally as “eyes”. Tablas de Daimiel National Park is noteworthy, as is the complex of fifteen staggered lagoons that comprise Lagunas de Ruidera National Park. The boundaries of the reserve are imprecise, as they cover the maximum extension of the wetlands during the rainy season at the time the biosphere reserve was declared. Irregular rainfall, characteristic of a Mediterranean climate, makes its surface area very variable. The aquifer is over-exploited for irrigation, exceeding the level of natural replenishment by rainfall. An attempt is being made to compensate for this through the implementation of the Special Plan for Alto Guadiana. Typical lagoon vegetation includes wetland plants such as Mediterranean tall rush, blue sedge, yellow flag and many other reeds and sedges, together with small woodlands of water-loving trees such as tamarisk, willow and aspen. The concentration of thousands of Anatidae and other waterfowl gives this area special value. Notable species include pochards, lesser scaup and red-crested pochards, which feed in the vast flooded grasslands in these shallow waters.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mancha Húmeda

records.introduction_en: Babia Biosphere Reserve is located in the Castilla y León autonomous region of northern Spain, covering the municipalities of Cabrillanes and San Emiliano that form the region of Babia. It is an additional component of the future multi-unit Gran Cantabrica Biosphere Reserve extending across the Cantabrica Mountains.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Babia region is a mountain ecosystem where conservation of natural resources and their use have been excellently combined. The reserve is delimited by two high and rugged mountain ranges, with crests above 2,000 m in most of its area, lying in an east–west direction. Between them is the wide, flat valley of the Luna and Sil rivers, at 1,300 to 1,100 m above sea level. Through extensive stock-raising over the centuries, human activities have shaped the outstanding landscape. There are woody formations of beech, birch and oak, which indicate the existence of a tree cover that once extended across most of the territory. Meadows and grasslands grow on formerly forested land, enabling present human communities to subsist by basing their economy on stock-raising. Interspersed among abundant scrubland are areas of abandoned grasslands that are progressively being recolonised by the original forest. There are also alpine and subalpine formations, including rocky outcrops, quarries and crags, where productive use is practically impossible. The biological diversity of Babia is apparent in the number of interesting endemic species of flora and fauna found in the territory. It harbours unique species of fauna, notably the endangered Cantabrian brown bear, the grey partridge and the broom hare, an endemic Cantabrian species. There are numerous birds, a wide representation of bat species and well-conserved rivers that host rich fish populations. The flora is of undoubted interest, with numerous endemic Iberian species such as Saxífraga babiana and Centaurea janeris babiana.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Babia

records.introduction_en: Muniellos Biosphere Reserve is located in north-western Spain, in the south-westernmost part of Asturias Province.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This reserve includes various watersheds with steeply sloping landforms that become gentler in the lower-lying valleys. The climate reflects conditions typical of the extreme west of the Cantabrian Cordillera, with high rainfall that increases considerably with altitude. Muniellos is remarkable for its rich forests, as it is home to what is the largest and probably best conserved oak forest in Western Europe. It includes almost virgin communities of flora and fauna that in the past were dominant in most of the Cantabrian Cordillera. In addition to pedunculate oak, the drier areas harbour xerophyllous sessile oak forests with a stratum where alder buckthorn, mountain ash, whitebeam, hazelnut and holly flourish. In the humid, shady areas, a dense herbaceous stratum develops, and the dominant oak is accompanied by birch, ash and maple trees. The abundance and diversity of fungi, mosses and lichens, some of which are extremely sensitive to even slight air pollution, reflect the purity of the environment, making Muniellos seem like a huge, enchanted forest. The magnificent beech groves, including those of Hermo Monastery, give way in the higher areas to sub-alpine vegetation and lagoon systems such as those of the Cueto de Arbás, reflecting the glacial shaping of these mountain landforms. Although hard to observe because of the dense vegetation, large species of Atlantic European fauna, now extinct in most of the continent, live in the biosphere reserve. These include the brown bear and the wolf, which feeds on the abundant wild boar, deer and chamois. Birds are represented by over one hundred species, among them the rare western capercaillie.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Muniellos

records.title_en: Cuencas Altas de los Rios Manzanares, Lozoya y Guadarrama
records.introduction_en: Cuenca Alta del Río Manzanares Biosphere Reserve includes a regional park in midland and highland mountain areas. These are dominated by Mediterranean forests of evergreen oak (Quercus ilex ballota) and ash (Fraxinus angustifolia), dehesas or forested grasslands, mainly reafforested pine forests with Pinus pinaster, Pinus pinea, Pinus sylvestris, Pinus nigra and Pinus uncinata, and grasslands.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is located on medium- and high-altitude mountains with valleys and rocky areas on granite and gneiss. The Pedriza de Manzanares is a spectacular geological landscape. It is dominated by strongly eroded granite formations of enormous, capriciously shaped blocks known as berruecos, with Mediterranean vegetation of aromatic plants including thyme, lavender, Spanish lavender, rosemary and Cistus (rockroses). Among the tree formations are oak and ash groves, juniper and pine groves, and, at higher altitudes, Cytisus oromediterraneus scrubland. All this reflects a continental Mediterranean climate, with mean annual rainfall between 450 mm in the lower areas and 2,000 mm at higher altitudes. Among the fauna, Iberian endemic species are to be found such as the marbled newt and the Iberian frog. The Santillana Dam, which has been declared an internationally important wetland, is a wintering place for aquatic birds. These include winter populations of black-headed gulls and summer stork colonies.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Cuencas Altas de los Rios Manzanares, Lozoya y Guadarrama

records.introduction_en: The Gran Canaria Biosphere Reserve covers 43 per cent of the central and south-western land area of the island of Gran Canaria, in addition to a wide marine strip. The island is geologically ancient, at about 14.5 million years, and a history of volcanic construction and destruction have resulted in a geographical area that encompasses the oldest part of the island. Biodiversity across ecosystems is very high, with an outstanding degree of endemism among invertebrates and unique species of birds and reptiles, as well as great floristic diversity on large cliffs. In addition to ecosystems ranging from peaks to beaches and marine areas, the Gran Canaria Biosphere Reserve includes valleys under agricultural and traditional use, an intricate set of steep ravines, and geological landmarks of great interest.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: From the geological standpoint, the Gran Canaria Biosphere Reserve is of exceptional value for understanding the formation and evolution of ocean islands. Geological and lithological variety results in an abrupt landscape with steep slopes, incised ravines, large rocky massifs, cliffs that rise to more than 1,000 metres above sea level, and prominent crests and isolated rocks. Gran Canaria is characterised by great biological diversity. Its geographical isolation, together with the variety of available ecological niches, has favoured speciation processes that have produced numerous endemic species. Wide climatological variation across the island’s elevations and slopes, with an annual average of 22 °C, and other variables, shapes the distribution of vegetation. This creates a series of bioclimatic floors ranging from coastal xeric scrub to subalpine vegetation, passing through thermophilous forest and Canary pine forest, as well as remnants of recovering monteverde, namely laurisilva and evergreen forests. This area can be considered of vital importance for biological conservation and evolution.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Gran Canaria

records.introduction_en: The Intercontinental Biosphere Reserve of the Mediterranean is the first intercontinental reserve declared by UNESCO. The reserve includes a marine corridor and establishes a framework for communication and collaboration between two continents with different conditions: Europe and Africa. It extends between southern Andalusia and northern Morocco, forming an open arc towards the Mediterranean and interrupted by the Strait of Gibraltar. The uniqueness of this natural and socio-cultural crossroads, where Atlantic influence is a determining factor, is exemplified by its main axes: mountains, water, Spanish firs and Andalusian culture, as well as the environmental and socio-economic complementarity between its northern and southern sections.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The physical and natural foundation of the biosphere reserve is the large and rugged Bético-Rifeña (Betic Rif) mountain range, which extends through Andalusia and northern Morocco. Elevations range from 2,170 metres in Jbel Lakraay to over 500 metres in the Strait of Gibraltar. These shared natural conditions extend across both shores. The mountain ranges, with their abrupt reliefs, hold a large amount of water, which has generated diverse environments. This diversity is reflected in more than 2,000 species of flora and fauna, with important endemism such as the Spanish fir, the black juniper and the cedar. In addition, the Strait plays a major role in the migrations of European and African birds, with a rate of 1,000 birds per hour, and in the transit of different species of cetaceans, as well as in constructions of biotic origin such as coral.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Intercontinental BR of the Mediterranean

records.introduction_en: The Marismas del Odiel Biosphere Reserve is located in the Province of Huelva, at the mouth of the Odiel River. It is also a Ramsar site and a Special Protection Area for birds.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The site comprises tidal marshes scattered with islands, bordered by many streams, beaches and dune systems. Ongoing erosion and sedimentation processes give rise to rapid morphological changes. The Mediterranean climate is moderated by the ocean, with mean annual rainfall slightly above 500 mm. Wetland vegetation is dominated by halophilous species adapted to the high salt content of the soil. There are also strips of Italian stone pine and Spanish juniper. The area has an extraordinary wealth of birdlife, including the grey heron, the purple heron, the western marsh harrier and the spoonbill. One third of the whole European nesting population of spoonbills is found in Marismas del Odiel. After Doñana, with which it maintains a continuous link due to proximity, Marismas del Odiel is considered the second most important wetland area for waterfowl in Spain based on the diversity of species recorded.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Marismas del Odiel

records.title_en: Mariñas Coruñesas e Terras do Mandeo
records.introduction_en: The Mariñas Coruñesas e Terras do Mandeo Biosphere Reserve is located on the Cantabrian–Atlantic coast of Galicia, to the north-west of the Iberian Peninsula. The territory consists mainly of two large river basins belonging to the rivers Mero and Mandeo, and includes other small coastal watersheds.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The main natural elements of the biosphere reserve are the river corridors, which are crucial for the conservation of habitats and species. These areas sheltered humid subtropical species, including Culcita macrocarpa, Woodwardia radicans and Vandenboschia speciosa, during the cold periods of the Quaternary, and facilitated the expansion of these and other species into higher-altitude areas during warmer periods. The river corridors also include much of the country’s representative natural forests. These are home to many unique species, many of which are threatened or endemic. In Galicia, these forests are popularly known as fragas, notably with Quercus robur and Quercus pyrenaica. The biosphere reserve also has more than 17,000 ha of shrubland, which is home to a wide diversity of flora and fauna, including endemic, rare and endangered relict species. It also contains a wide variety of coastal habitats, including estuaries, marshes, streams, shallow bays, reefs, cliffs, swamps, coastal lagoons, dunes, coastal meadows and halophyte forests. These areas are excellent refuges for birds, invertebrates and kelp species.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mariñas Coruñesas e Terras do Mandeo

records.introduction_en: The Meseta Ibérica Transboundary Biosphere Reserve lies along the northern border of Spain and Portugal. It includes a wide variety of landscapes, orographic features and land uses. Altitudes range from 100 m to 2,000 m above sea level. The area contains many flagship species, some of which have been the subject of conservation projects, such as the black stork (Ciconia nigra), Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus), Bonelli’s eagle (Aquila fasciata), Eurasian eagle-owl (Bubo bubo), European otter (Lutra lutra) and Iberian wolf (Canis lupus signatus). The area also includes built heritage dating back to Roman times and the Middle Ages. The remains of forts, castles and walled enclosures in localities bear witness to frequent wars between Spanish and Portuguese kingdoms during the Middle Ages. The cultural heritage is notable in the architecture, customs, traditions and folklore.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is in the north-west of Spain and the north-east of Portugal. It has an average altitude of 823 m, with large variations across the area. Altitudes range from 100 m to 2,000 m above sea level. The biosphere reserve is well irrigated, with a number of dams and reservoirs. With more than 3,400 million cubic metres, the region has the third highest water storage capacity in Spain, second only to the Province of Badajoz and the Province of Cáceres. On the Portuguese side, the area supports a wide diversity of landscapes. The district is known for its climatic contrasts, described locally as nine months of winter and three of heat, and for its rugged geomorphology. Diversity is the watchword for the biodiversity of the Meseta Ibérica Biosphere Reserve. The most abundant forests are formed by Pyrenean oak and turkey oak. There are also interesting stands of holly and yew. Birch and alder are abundant along the riverbanks, where streams descend from the summits to the lagoons within the biosphere reserve. At higher altitudes, forest gives way to thickets of escabonales, cambronales and heaths. The Meseta Ibérica is among the most important areas for wildlife at national and European levels. A very significant part of the Spanish and Portuguese terrestrial fauna is represented here. Around 250 species of vertebrates are recorded, and there is also high richness and diversity of invertebrates. Many species are endangered. Flagship species include the black stork (Ciconia nigra), Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus), Bonelli’s eagle (Aquila fasciata), Eurasian eagle-owl (Bubo bubo), European otter (Lutra lutra), Iberian wolf (Canis lupus signatus), Bocage’s wall lizard (Podarcis bocagei) and Seoane’s viper (Vipera seoanei).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Meseta Iberica

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve comprises the Ordesa y Monte Perdido National Park, with an 18 per cent nucleus zone, and the Viñamala Hunting Reserve. It includes the Ordesa Valley, a canyon with vertical walls formed by successive Quaternary glaciations, and the valley of the Arazas River, which joins the Ara River and has many waterfalls. Located in the central Pyrenees, it is one of the best examples of mountain ecosystems shaped by erosion and glacial formations. It is home to unique species of flora and fauna of regional and international importance, many with some degree of threat, whose conservation is essential for maintaining biological diversity, especially in the core area of the Ordesa y Monte Perdido National Park.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve includes Pyrenean valleys and siliceous mountains in the north-west, and limestone mountains in the south and east. Peaks reach 3,355 m at Monte Perdido. Glaciations have modelled the landforms, creating deep U-shaped valleys, cirques and lakes excavated by ice, locally known as ibones. The limestone massifs also contain labyrinths of caves and galleries opened by water, a karst system. The most famous are the sinkholes in the Escuaín canyon, considered among the deepest in Europe. The climate varies with altitude and orientation, ranging from continental sub-Mediterranean zones in the lower parts to a boreal-alpine climate in the highlands. Vegetation is distributed in altitudinal layers, from oak groves to mosses and lichens in the highest areas near the perpetual snows. The intermediary layers are covered by a succession of oak, beech, fir and European black pine, mixed with birch, European yew, aspen, ash and willow. Plant diversity is very high, with more than 2,000 recorded species. Among the fauna, species of high value include the bearded vulture, the Pyrenean frog, the Pyrenean desman, the snowy partridge, the capercaillie and the black woodpecker.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Ordesa-Viñamala

records.introduction_en: Ponga Biosphere Reserve is located in Asturias, in the eastern centre of the Cantabrian Mountains, and encompasses the administrative territory corresponding to the municipality of Ponga. It is an area with a complex relief combining middle and high mountains, with steep slopes and incised fluvial valleys. The forests of Ponga are home to many faunal species, including the brown bear (Ursus arctos arctos). The area has a small population and contains a rich cultural heritage with several archaeological remains.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is a remote area of sparsely populated mountains and forests on the northern slopes of the Cordillera Cantábrica, in Asturias. The chain of mountains is known as the Cordal de Ponga. The area is known for its steep terrain, with altitudes between 213 m and 2,142 m above sea level. The deep green valleys climb to vertiginous peaks, passing through extensive beech forests on their way. The majority of the vegetation consists of mixed deciduous woodlands composed of species such as sycamore, alder, ash, chestnut, oak and hazel. The region contains many faunal species, including the endangered brown bear (Ursus arctos arctos) and the western capercaillie (Tetrao urogallus), emblematic species of the Cantabrian mountain range. Other faunal species include grey wolf (Canis lupus), golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos), Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus) and European tree frog (Hyla arborea).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Ponga

records.introduction_en: The Sierra Nevada is the highest mountain chain in the Iberian Peninsula, with higher elevations found only in the Alps.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This biosphere reserve includes the inner mountain nucleus of the Cordillera Penibética, which contains the Spanish peninsula’s highest peaks, such as the Mulhacen peak at 3,482 m. The steep mountain slopes are a reflection of its past, shaped by glacial erosion. The dominant climate is continental Mediterranean. There are strong variations in mean annual rainfall, ranging with altitude between 350 and 1,600 mm. The vegetation includes vast stretches of grasslands and high-mountain scrubland, as well as pine, juniper, and deciduous and sclerophyllous forests. The Sierra Nevada has extraordinary value for its numerous unique and endemic species of flora, with over 1,700 different species recorded, 64 of which are endemic. Notable examples include wormwood (Artemisia granatensis), monkshood (Aconitum) and stavesacre (Delphinium staphisagria). There are also numerous endemic invertebrates and emblematic high-mountain species, such as the mountain goat, the wallcreeper (Tichodroma muraria) and the royal eagle.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Sierra Nevada

records.introduction_en: The geographical position of this biosphere reserve near both the Mediterranean and the Atlantic coast, including the Strait of Gibraltar, together with the altitude of its mountains, results in a humid Mediterranean climate in Sierra de las Nieves. The area consists of an extensive limestone mountain landscape with rocks and lithologies belonging to the Betica Mountain Range.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve includes limestone and peridotite mountains in the eastern sector of the Ronda hills with steep slopes that give way to very deep valleys, and a profusion of gullies, ravines and precipices. The karstic modelling of these mountains has created an abundance of caves and sinkholes, including one with a freefall of 1,100 m that is the third deepest in the world. The Mediterranean climate, influenced by humid ocean air, has given rise to all Mediterranean bioclimatic layers and their associated vegetation. There is a notable presence of 3,000 ha of pinsapar, dominated by Spanish fir (Abies pinsapo), together with forests of Portuguese oak, holm oak, cork oak and pine. Characteristic fauna in these high and medium-height mountains includes populations of mountain goat, roe deer and wild boar, and birds of prey such as the royal eagle, Bonelli’s eagle, the booted eagle and the peregrine hawk.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Sierra de las Nieves

records.introduction_en: Somiedo comprises alpine ecosystems on the peaks, up to 2,100 metres above sea level, and the high ridges of the Cantabrian range. Slopes are covered by beech woods, green oak or Pyrenean oak, and swift-flowing streams run through the meadows that line the bottoms of the U-shaped glacial valleys.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Somiedo is characterised by abrupt landforms, with steep slopes ranging from 400 m in the extreme north to more than 2,100 m for some peaks along the southern divide. It belongs to the temperate humid climate domain. The transition between limestone and siliceous Asturias, together with differing lithology, strong tectonic folding, and the modelling of fluvial, glacial and karstic erosion, has created unique landscapes. These include glacial cirques and lacustrine complexes such as that of Saliencia, lakes such as Valle Lake, vertical dips, folds, hanging terraces and ravines. The plant cover is diverse and distinctive, with over 1,200 taxa of vascular plants, approximately half the flora of Asturias. Of the 73 trees and shrubs autochthonous to Asturias, 65 species are found in the biosphere reserve. Meadows and grasslands cover a vast expanse as a result of human use of the territory. Deciduous beech, oak and birch forests are noteworthy, as are diverse types of scrubland with common wire-weed, heather, Erica, gorse and broom. Somiedo harbours one of the most important Cantabrian populations of brown bears. There are also stable reproductive families of wolves. In the rocky areas the chamois finds refuge, while the forests are home to roe deer and red deer. Among the birds, notable species include the royal eagle and the Egyptian vulture as a migratory species, along with species linked to Atlantic forests such as the middle spotted woodpecker and the western capercaillie.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Somiedo

records.introduction_en: The Terres de l’Ebre Biosphere Reserve is located in north-eastern Spain and covers three regions: Baix Ebre, Montsià and Terra Alta. Sand plains, marshes, deltas, mountains and valleys with alluvial deposits from the River Ebro basin characterise this remarkable landscape. The estuary of the River Ebro forms the Delta del Ebro, one of the most important wetland areas in the western Mediterranean. Terres de l’Ebre includes large relief formations surrounded by steep slopes, plateaux and the mightiest river of the peninsula. Four mountain ranges mark the topography of the reserve, including the extensive massif Macizo dels Ports, which stretches to the foothills of the north-eastern Iberian Cordillera, and Las Sierras de Cardó y de Tivissa, which dominate the western regions. The highest peak in the biosphere reserve is El Montcaro at 1,447 m.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Altogether, six different landscape areas have been recorded in the Terres de l’Ebre Biosphere Reserve, each incorporating various habitats. The Delta del Ebro provides ideal hypersaline habitats for Limoniastrum and Zygophyllum, as well as beach groves and Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) forests with one-flowered wintergreen (Moneses uniflora). The Delta del Ebro is also home to 19 species protected under European, Spanish and Catalan wildlife legislation. The hydrographic network of Terres de l’Ebre is structured into four basins. The main basin forms part of the River Ebro and accounts for over 90 per cent of the reserve’s area; it is complemented by secondary rivers, streams and gullies. The four basins are the Cuenca del Ebro, Cuenca del Río Sénia, the basins of Calafat and Golfo de Sant Jordi, and the basins of Sierra del Montsià. In addition, 12 endemic taxa of flora were recorded within the biosphere reserve, including Thymus willkommii and Antirrhinum pertegasii. Furthermore, Atropa baetica, common moonwort (Botrychium lunaria) and common cotoneaster (Cotoneaster integerrimus) are among the 29 species present in isolated populations.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Terres de l’Ebre, Catalonia

records.introduction_en: Located in the Cabriel River basin in eastern Spain, the Valle del Cabriel Biosphere Reserve is characterised by a diversity of landscapes, including mountains, rock formations shaped by the confinement of fluvial channels, agricultural use in alluvial plains, salt marshes and lagoons. The area retains a rich cultural heritage, including Villar del Humo, part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula World Heritage site. The inhabitants of the Cabriel Valley have adapted to their environment by employing unique, ancient sustainable practices based on agricultural activity, livestock and water use. These practices have helped them conserve their specific tangible and intangible cultural heritage.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve lies in the Cabriel River basin in the autonomous communities of Castilla-La Mancha, Valencia and Aragón. The area is characterised by significant landscape diversity, including mountainous areas, rock formations formed by the confinement of fluvial channels, agricultural zones of the alluvial plains, salt marshes and lagoons. The climate is variable, with rainfall of 400–1,200 mm and average annual temperatures of 7–17 °C. Lithological and soil variability, together with altitudinal range from 340 m above sea level in the south to over 1,800 m in the north, has produced high ecosystem diversity. Most of the site has a Mediterranean climate, while the northern mountains are more temperate. Fluvial channels cross the area and function as a network of links not only for raw materials but also for ideas and customs. They also act as ecological corridors connecting the whole territory and enabling the distribution of vegetation and fauna. Vegetation includes Iberian gypsum vegetation (Gypsophiletalia) and karstic calcareous (basiphilous) grasslands of the Alysso–Sedion albi. It also includes Mediterranean pine forests of endemic black pines, endemic Juniperus forests, and pre-steppe areas of gramineous species and annuals of Thero–Brachypodietea. In relation to fauna, 249 species of vertebrates have been identified, of which 154 are birds, 47 mammals, 20 reptiles, 19 inland fish and nine amphibians.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Valle del Cabriel

records.introduction_en: The Agua y Paz (Water and Peace) Biosphere Reserve lies in northern Costa Rica, largely within the Costa Rican sector of the San Juan River Basin. The landscape is defined by mountain ranges including the Miravalles, Tenorio, Arenal, Chato and Platanar volcanoes, and broad plains that host lakes, flooded forests and swamps. The reserve strengthens habitat connectivity between the Cordillera Volcánica Central Biosphere Reserve in Costa Rica, and Indio Maíz Biological Reserve in Nicaragua, complementing the San Juan–La Selva Biological Corridor. The biosphere reserve fosters a shared regional identity and strengthens integrated water-resource management and the sustainable use of natural resources.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set within the Pacific ‘Ring of Fire’, the Agua y Paz Biosphere Reserve partially includes the Guanacaste, Tilarán and Central Volcanic ranges. Marked by numerous volcanic formations, the reserve has rich biodiversity. Vegetation around Tenorio Volcano includes jícaro danto (Parmentiera valerii), endemic to Guanacaste, whose trunk-borne flowers and fruits are a principal food for tapir. The Monteverde area holds exceptionally high orchid diversity, among the highest recorded globally, with more than 500 species. A defining feature is the extent of lowland tropical moist forest, under-represented in the national protected-area system, alongside a wide variety of wetlands at landscape scale, including lakes, lagoons, floodplains, inundated forests and swamps. The Caño Negro wetland is designated as a Ramsar Wetland of International Importance. These habitats support species of national importance such as the great green macaw, manatee and jaguar (Panthera onca). West of the Río Frío, a palustrine wetland with yolillo palm forest and seasonally flooded zones provides vital connectivity between Caño Negro National Wildlife Refuge and Los Guatuzos Wildlife Refuge in Nicaragua. This sector contains the last remnants of marillal in Costa Rica and Central America, an endangered ecosystem protected under national biodiversity laws, but it is highly threatened by drainage and fires.
records.name: Agua y Paz

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is located in the central highlands, about 60 km north-west to the city of San José. The Cordillera Volcánica Central reserve is one of the richest in both natural resources and cultural heritage. On its long axis there are several volcanic cones with their still well formed craters.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve comprises four national parks, including Poás and Irazú volcanoes, each rising over 3,000 metres above sea level and both still active. It also includes two forest reserves, six protected zones and a national monument. Marked variation in its physical characteristics has fostered high biological diversity, with life zones ranging from tropical wet and rain forests to semi-páramos. At the highest volcanic peaks only small patches of vegetation remain, generally in riverbeds. Here, several oak species occur, alongside trees in the Escallonaceae, Cornaceae (dogwoods) and Magnoliaceae (magnolias) families. The topography is very steep and dissected, with a wide altitudinal range. There are many streams, waterfalls and several lakes. Major land-cover types include premontane rainforest, tropical humid forest, lower montane rainforest and montane rainforest.
records.name: Cordillera Volcánica Central

records.introduction_en: The Buenavista Biosphere Reserve is situated on the northern coast of Cuba, in parts of the Villa Clara, Sancti Spíritus and Ciego de Ávila provinces, covering a total surface area of 313,502 ha. The larger marine part includes coral reefs and rocky and sandy beaches, while the terrestrial part comprises evergreen microphyllous coastal and subcoastal forest, mangrove forest and matorral.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The diversity of geographical regions is reflected in a wide variety of terrestrial, coastal and marine areas of high ecological sensitivity, high biodiversity and notable genetic resources. Floristic, faunistic, speleological and landscape value adds to this significance. The reserve is important for its fauna, as habitat heterogeneity has enabled high species richness. Species use the area for refuge, feeding and reproduction, as well as for stopovers during migrations. In total, 873 species have been inventoried, across 627 genera and 282 families. Endemism is a significant zoogeographic component, with 176 endemics recorded to date. The reserve has eleven core areas in two national parks, Caguanes and Santa María Key, and two faunal refuges west of Santa María Key and Las Loras Key. These core areas contain outstanding natural, historical and cultural values, including 35 archaeological sites and caves bearing rock art.
records.name: Buenavista

records.introduction_en: Set at the western tip of Cuba, the Guanahacabibes Peninsula Biosphere Reserve lies on a low karst plain at sea level. It is bound by the Gulf of Guanahacabibes to the north, the Yucatán Channel to the west and Bahía de Corrientes and the Caribbean Sea to the south. The peninsula serves as a major migratory corridor for birds. Its reefs, among the best-conserved and most diverse in the Greater Caribbean, sit alongside shores that host nesting beaches for three threatened sea turtles. The reserve works with local communities to safeguard ecosystems and endemic species, while supporting low-impact livelihoods and fostering research, long-term monitoring and environmental education.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set on a young karst plain, the reserve forms a rich land and sea mosaic with a pronounced dominance of marine–coastal systems and tropical dry forest. Habitats include semi-deciduous and evergreen forest on limestone outcrops, coastal and subcoastal xeromorphic scrub, and upper-shore vegetation on sand and rock, together with mangroves, coastal lagoons and other wetlands. Offshore, coral reefs and seagrass meadows are extensive and among the best-conserved and most diverse in the Greater Caribbean. Flora and fauna are notable for endemism and rarity. Characteristic plants include Amaranthus minimus, the rare shrub Vitex guanahacabibensis and the columnar cactus Harrisia taetra. Cave systems support rich subterranean life with 14 bat species and the only known living population of the Cuban greater funnel-eared bat (Natalus primus). Birds are the most diverse terrestrial vertebrates in the reserve, with endemics including the Cuban tody (Todus multicolor), the Cuban green woodpecker (Xiphidiopicus percussus) and the bee hummingbird (Calipte helenae), the smallest bird in the world. The peninsula functions as an active migratory corridor for birds, with thousands stopping over or spending the winter. The coastline hosts nesting populations of three threatened sea turtles, the loggerhead (Caretta caretta), green turtle (Chelonia mydas) and hawksbill (Eretmochelys imbricata).
records.name: Península de Guanahacabibes

records.introduction_en: The Sierra del Rosario Biosphere Reserve is located in the eastern part of the Guaniguanico mountain range, between the provinces of Pinar del Río and Havana in Cuba, where both the north and south coasts can be seen. The reserve has a complex geological structure, with a wide diversity of rocks that produce different soils which, in part, help determine floral endemism in its landscape.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The little orchid (Bletia purpurea), considered a symbol of the reserve, is found here. Some parts of the range have exposures of serpentine rock and, in these areas, grassland and thorny xeromorphic thickets and shrublands replace forest. While special features remain and natural systems are regenerating, and while an ecological field station is present, Sierra del Rosario has nevertheless lost much of its natural forest cover. However, semi-deciduous forests, cuabales, hummocks (mogotes) and secondary forest regeneration species, such as the royal palm and yagruma, are still present. Its tropical dry and deciduous forests are home to several endemic species, notably reptiles such as the Cuban boa (Chilabothrus angulifer).
records.name: Sierra del Rosario

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve, designated a Protected Landscape Area at the national level and covering 70,000 ha, is located largely in the shallow Trebon Basin in South Bohemia near the Austrian border. The region has been shaped by human activity for more than eight centuries. This semi-natural landscape comprises 460 artificial fishponds and lakes constructed in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and it is now the centre of the Czech fish-farming industry. The Třeboň fishponds and Třeboň peatlands, which form part of the core area of the biosphere reserve, are Ramsar sites designated in 1990 and 1993, respectively.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Trebon Basin Biosphere Reserve is a flat or slightly undulating region near the Austrian border that has been modified by human activity for more than eight centuries. A specific feature is an extensive system of fishponds – shallow artificial lakes ranging from 0.1 to 500 ha. There are 460 fishponds interconnected by canals and ditches, and 13 per cent of the biosphere reserve is covered by waterbodies. Most of the fishponds were built in the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries. Important ecosystems include a range of wetlands, notably fishpond littoral zones with reed and sedge belts, marshes, alder and willow carrs, wet meadows, floodplain forests, and various types of mires including peat bogs and acidic fens. The Lužnice is the main river axis of the reserve. Forests cover 50 per cent of the territory. Notable landscape features include fishpond dams and dykes, man-made canals and dykes, open sandpits, human settlements and historical landmarks. The reserve is an important bird area, especially for waterbirds during nesting and migration.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Trebon Basin

records.introduction_en: About an hour’s drive from Berlin’s city centre, this sparsely populated landscape of lakes, forests and low hills is a leader in organic agriculture. Within the biosphere reserve are a UNESCO World Heritage site, the ancient beech forest of Grumsin, and the famous monastery ruins at Chorin, a prime example of Gothic brick architecture. Around 15,000 years ago, the last ice age shaped the area, creating a landscape of unique character and outstanding beauty that accommodates a wide variety of biotopes and habitats. It is one of the largest protected areas in Germany.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Schorfheide within the Schorfheide–Chorin Biosphere Reserve is one of Germany’s largest forests. Without human influence, about 90 per cent of the biosphere would still be woodland. However, severe overuse in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries created extensive open landscapes, so today only about half the territory is forested. The remainder comprises arable land, grasslands, perennial crops, lakes, settlements, moors and swamps. The diversity of inland waters is outstanding at the national level. Endangered species such as whitefish, beaver (Castor fiber) and otter (Lutra lutra) occur throughout the reserve. Sixteen of the 22 bat species recorded in Germany live here. Nearly every village still has its own breeding pair of white stork. Several reptile and amphibian species threatened elsewhere in Germany occur in high numbers, including the fire-bellied toad (Bombina bombina) and great crested newt (Triturus cristatus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Schorfheide-Chorin

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve is situated in the south-eastern part of Rügen, Germany’s largest island. Within its 22,800 ha, almost all coastal forms of the southern Baltic Sea can be found.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The landscape was formed by glaciers of the last glacial period, which ended nearly 10,000 years ago. Today, the biosphere reserve includes areas of ground and terminal moraine hills deposited during the last glaciation, and Holocene depositional features such as sand bars. Inland waters are shallow, broken by peninsulas, small islands and hooked spits. Moraine areas are dominated by Baltic beech forests with Fagus sylvatica and Quercus robur. These areas also include the most productive agricultural lands, as well as pastures, low-productivity grasslands and coastal vegetation of brackish waters. Salt meadows and salt-reed beds occur mainly in shallow bays. These bays are very important for thousands of resting waterbirds, mainly in winter. Steep coasts and natural beaches are typical formations along the Baltic shore. More than 800 plant species occur in the biosphere reserve, nearly 200 of which are on Red Lists. In recent years, the waters around Rügen have again hosted a small colony of grey seals (Halichoerus grypus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: South-East Rügen

records.introduction_en: Located along the French German border, the Vosges du Nord and the Pfälzerwald share three defining natural features: water, sandstone and forests. Sandstone outcrops characterise the broad forest belt, where beech, oak and pine are managed. Springs, streams and lakes are found throughout the humid valleys.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Parc naturel régional des Vosges du Nord in France was designated a biosphere reserve in 1988, and Germany’s Pfälzerwald Nature Park in 1992. The two parks then prepared the creation of a transboundary biosphere reserve, achieved in 1998. The objective is to develop methods for the sustainable management of natural resources and to establish a renewed relationship between people and the environment, advanced through research and education with the participation of local communities. The two units cooperate to establish long-term monitoring of water and air, create strictly protected forest reserves, and maintain the lynx (Lynx lynx) population. The presence of lynx, peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus) and bog arum (Calla palustris) receives significant attention from a nature conservation perspective.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Pfälzerwald / Vosges du Nord

records.title_en: Wadden Sea and Hallig Islands of Schleswig-Holstein
records.introduction_en: The Wadden Sea along the North Sea coast is one of Germany’s few remaining large-scale natural landscapes. It is protected as a national park, and its global uniqueness has been recognised through designation as a UNESCO World Heritage site. The tidal flats and creeks, salt marshes and sandbanks are largely preserved in their original state. The Wadden Sea has the highest bird numbers in Europe. Three UNESCO biosphere reserves encompass the entire German Wadden Sea, located in Hamburg, Lower Saxony and Schleswig-Holstein. In 2016, they established a cooperation agreement to pave the way towards a unified biosphere reserve. The Wadden Sea along the coast of the federal state of Schleswig-Holstein is one of the largest national parks in Europe and was designated a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 1990. The designation includes an extension to cover the Hallig islands, five small inhabited islands without protective dykes.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Wadden Sea is a wetland consisting mainly of tidal mudflats and tidal creeks, as well as salt marshes and sandbanks. Only specialised species thrive in this extreme habitat, exposed to the dynamics of the tides. These occur in large numbers, including marine mammals such as harbour seal, grey seal and harbour porpoise. The Wadden Sea is also an important feeding area for migrating birds and a breeding and wintering site for over two million birds per year. The biosphere reserve includes an EU Important Bird Area and an EU Flora-Fauna-Habitat Area in its core zone. The International Maritime Organization has designated this part of the reserve a Particularly Sensitive Sea Area, and the Ramsar Convention recognises it as a Wetland of International Importance. UNESCO World Heritage status was achieved in 2009. The Hallig islands (Halligen) are a unique phenomenon: ten small, permanent islands formed of peat and mud, only a few of which have protective summer dykes. Since 2005, the five Halligen of Gröde, Hooge, Langeneß, Nordstrandischmoor and Oland have formed the biosphere reserve’s transition area. The remaining Halligen were already within the national park and biosphere reserve and belong to the core areas.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Wadden Sea and Hallig Islands of Schleswig-Holstein

records.introduction_en: This site forms part of the Wadden Sea on the North Sea coast, about 40 km north of the city of Bremerhaven in the Land of Hamburg. The Wadden Sea (Wattenmeer) extends from Ho Bay in Denmark to the Dutch island of Texel. With its sands and mudflats, salt marshes and dunes, it is the largest unbroken system of tidal sand and mudflats in the world. Its high biological productivity, which underpins the site’s worldwide significance for biodiversity, and its strong natural dynamics make it of extraordinary natural value. The inscription of the Dutch and German protected areas of the Wadden Sea on UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2009 underlined its global importance.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Situated near the mouth of the Elbe River, the site represents an estuarine system that provides habitat for harbour seal (Phoca vitulina) and a large diversity of birds and fish. The nutrient-rich waters of the Elbe support high biomass production and are important for fish spawning. The site includes sand and mudflats with channels, islands and salt marshes. It is designated as a National Park, Ramsar site and EU Special Protection Area for wild birds.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Waddensea of Hamburg

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve includes La Selle in Haiti (designated in 2012) and Jaragua–Bahoruco–Enriquillo in the Dominican Republic (designated in 2002). The two reserves are linked ecologically across a political and administrative frontier. Their joint designation supports more coherent environmental management.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: On the Haitian side, the biosphere reserve is located in the Massif de la Selle, which contains Haiti’s highest peak, Pic la Selle (2,684 m), and the second most biodiverse region of the country after the Massif de la Hotte. These two mountain ranges form the southern peninsula of the island of Hispaniola, known for its high level of endemism. Most endemic species are flowering plants; around 16 per cent are endemic to this specific region. The Dominican side includes three biogeographic regions in the Caribbean: the Hoya del Lago Enriquillo, the Sierra de Bahoruco and the Procurrente de Barahona. It comprises a wide variety of natural ecosystems, from tropical highlands to karstic terraces with coastal and marine areas, islands and cays, with rich biodiversity and important regional endemism. The area has rich faunal diversity, including the brown pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) and the West Indian manatee (Trichechus manatus). Isla Beata and the Los Frailes cays host an enormous variety of marine birds, with some 107 bird species recorded. Some 67 reptile species are reported across the reserve. Geologically, the area has a wide variety of igneous and sedimentary rocks dating to the Late Jurassic, around 140 million years ago.
records.name: Jaragua-Bahoruco-Enriquillo

records.introduction_en: Chocó Andino de Pichincha Biosphere Reserve lies in northern Ecuador, in Pichincha Province, north-west of Quito. Elevation ranges from 360–4,480 m above sea level. Together with the Amazon and Galápagos, its biodiversity and endemism have helped make Ecuador a recognised biodiversity hotspot. The Chocó Andino region spans two critical ecoregions: the humid forest lowlands of the Chocó–Darién (extending from Panama into western Ecuador) and the Northern Andean Mountain Forests.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area extends from the outer foothills of the western Andean cordillera to its inner foothills, encompassing the humid forests of the Chocó–Darién and the Northern Andean Mountain Forests. Natural fragmentation of the western moist forests has driven rapid evolution and high endemism. Around 10,000 plant species have been reported, about 2,500 of which are endemic. The region is considered a biodiversity hotspot. The reserve is home to some 270 mammal species, 210 reptiles, 200 bird species and 130 amphibians. Notable fauna include the spectacled bear (Tremarctos ornatus), Ecuadorian mantled howler (Alouatta palliata aequatorialis), pacarana (Dinomys branickii) and olinguito (Bassaricyon neblina), as well as endemic species such as the Chocó toucan (Ramphastos brevis), Pichincha rocket frog (Hyloxalus toachi) and speckle-faced parrot (Pionus tumultuosus).
records.name: Chocó Andino de Pichincha

records.introduction_en: The Archipiélago de Colón–Galápagos Biosphere Reserve lies in the eastern Pacific Ocean, 970 km off mainland Ecuador. The equator crosses the Wolf and Ecuador volcanoes on Isabela Island. The archipelago comprises 13 large islands of more than 10 km², six medium-sized islands of 1–10 km², and a further 215 smaller islands, along with rocky outcrops only a few square metres in size. Native, endemic and unique flora and fauna make the Galápagos Islands one of the most exceptional places on Earth. In recognition of their importance, the islands were designated a Natural World Heritage site in 1976, a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in 1984, and a Ramsar Site in 2001.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Situated on the Galápagos submarine platform, the islands consist of 13 major islands formed by volcanic processes around 4 million years ago. Most are the summits of volcanoes, with some rising more than 3,000 metres from the Pacific Ocean floor. The largest islands typically comprise one or more gently sloping shield volcanoes capped by craters or calderas. The terrain commonly features uplifted marine lava flows. The influence of several major surface and subsurface current systems gives Galápagos a diverse flora and fauna, with representatives of the Indo-Pacific, Panama and Peru biogeographic provinces. The geographic and historical isolation of Galápagos has produced high biodiversity and endemism. In 2015, more than 2,900 marine species were reported, 18.2 per cent of them endemic. Over 45 endemic bird species, 42 endemic reptiles, 15 endemic mammals and 79 endemic fishes occur in Galápagos, coexisting alongside the local population. The islands also support a rich variety of endemic plants, around 500 species across vascular plants, bryophytes and algae. Among the most emblematic species of Galápagos National Park are the giant tortoises (Geochelone elephantopus), which give the archipelago its name. Historically there were 14 tortoise species, but human predation in the eighteenth century by pirates and whalers drove three to extinction. Recurrent eruptions of La Cumbre volcano on Fernandina Island have also eliminated species on that island. All reptile species in Galápagos are endemic, with the exception of two marine turtles. They include giant tortoises (Geochelone elephantopus), land iguanas (Conolophus subcristatus and C. pallidus) and marine iguanas (Amblyrhynchus cristatus). More than 250 non-native species have been introduced, occurring … [truncated]
records.name: Galápagos

records.introduction_en: Situated in the south-west of Ecuador, this biosphere reserve includes a wide range of ecosystems, from high mountains to coastal and marine areas along the Pacific. It includes Las Cajas National Park and the Quimsacocha National Recreational Area, which play an important role in water provision and regulation.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve has four major ecosystem types: páramo, montane forest, cloud forest and mangrove. The páramo ecosystem is composed mainly of tufted, or bunch, grasses, mostly between 3,000 and 4,000 metres above mean sea level. At its lower limit are ceja andina shrubs in the transition between highland montane forest and páramo, and cultivated fields where Andean Forest has been cleared. Dominant genera include Calamagrostis and Festuca. The montane forest ecosystem is among the most diverse in the world. It performs important ecological functions, including water harvesting and erosion control, yet is also fragile: steep slopes make it highly vulnerable to accelerated erosion during heavy rain. These forests extend along the western slope of the Andes, ranging from roughly 300–450 metres up to about 3,000 metres above mean sea level. Cloud forest occurs on the western flank of the Andes. It has highly irregular relief with steep slopes, producing pronounced topographic variability across an altitudinal gradient of about 2,200–2,900 metres above mean sea level. High rainfall and humidity with persistent haze are characteristic. Waters drain into creeks and streams that feed major water systems of the western region. The mangrove ecosystem comprises tidal areas with water-level fluctuations of up to about 5 metres. Depending on the location, it may be permanently flooded or subject to twice-daily tides. This gradient in flood level and salinity influences vegetation structure and composition. On the Pacific coast, tidal variation is greater than in the Caribbean, so mangroves extend far into river deltas. This dynamic drives intense succession, often resulting in near-monospecific communities.
records.name: Macizo del Cajas

records.introduction_en: Among the most biodiverse areas in the Neotropics, the biosphere reserve covers 1,140,080 ha across the provinces of Loja and Zamora Chinchipe, including 10 cantons and 48 parishes. Its core zone includes three SNAP (National System of Protected Areas) sites: Podocarpus National Park, Yacuri National Park and Cerro Plateado Biological Reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve’s flora comprises 4,191 plant species, representing almost 25 per cent of Ecuador’s recorded flora within only 4 per cent of the national territory. Endemism is high, with 211 endemic plant species. The reserve is home to about half of Ecuador’s bird species within the same 4 per cent of national territory: 629 species are recorded, 55 of which fall within one of the country’s endemism zones. For larger mammals such as the Andean bear (Tremarctos ornatus), the reserve forms the largest contiguous block of habitat available for the species across its range within the Northern Andes Ecoregional Complex (CEAN).
records.name: Podocarpus-El Condor

records.introduction_en: The Sumaco Biosphere Reserve lies about 100 km south-east of Quito in western Napo province. There are numerous watercourses in the area, including the Suno, Coca, Pitayacu and Pusuno rivers. Sumaco Volcano (3,900 m above sea level) is a relatively isolated peak to the east of the main Andean range. The reserve spans a wide range of ecosystems, from tropical highlands–Andean páramo to the tropical Amazon plains.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve comprises a mosaic of natural areas and agricultural production. Land cover spans from non-intervention forests in the core zone to intensive uses such as cultivation in the transition zone, with intermediate covers including natural and intervened forests, shrub and herbaceous vegetation, grasslands and crops. The core and buffer zones are the principal sources of biological diversity conservation, with representative examples of the country’s tropical rainforest and Amazon region, supporting research and education, and maintaining habitats of singular importance. In the transition zone, large tracts of natural forest remain, enabling use through the maintenance of traditional practices and the sustainable use of resources.
records.name: Sumaco

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve covers an area of 110,882 ha in a biogeographic region characterised by rolling topography reaching a maximum height of 369 metres, a humid subtropical climate with over 1,000 mm annual rainfall, and a predominance of subtropical grasslands.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is located on the east side of the Cuchilla de Haedo among the headwaters of rivers that flow into the River Tacuarembó. It also contains recharge areas of the Guarani Aquifer, one of the largest reserves of fresh water on the planet. The landscape is characterised by quebradas, or ravines and gorges, situated between high embankments of the basaltic coasts of the Cuchilla. This biosphere reserve comprises a mosaic of ecosystems, including a primary forest with subtropical jungle in the quebradas, which represent the southernmost vestige of the ‘Atlantic Forest’ environment. Quebradas forests occur in depressions and present various types of vegetation. In the deeper areas, trees reach up to 25 metres in height, with abundant undergrowth of ferns, orchids and Piperaceae, as well as epiphytes, including Bromeliaceae, Orchidaceae and Cactaceae. The average density is approximately 350 trees per hectare. The subtropical jungle of the quebradas is one of the main attractions of the biosphere reserve. The region of the Cuchilla de Haedo functions as a biological corridor for tropical species entering Uruguayan territory, and represents the southernmost point for the presence of such fauna in Latin America. Rare amphibians and reptiles in the area include the Uruguayan frog (Hyla uruguaya), the toad of Devincenzi (Melanophryniscus devincenzii) and the South American rattlesnake (Crotalus durissus). More than 150 bird species have been identified in the quebradas, such as the buff-necked ibis (Theristicus caudatus), the bicoloured hawk (Accipiter bicolor) and the yellow-headed caracara (Milvago chimachima), among others, all of which are rare in other parts of the country. The other important habitat of this biosphere reserve, the pampa biom … [truncated]
records.name: Bioma Pampa-Quebradas del Norte

records.introduction_en: Located in the south of the Massif Central, this biosphere reserve offers striking, contrasting landscapes, from the limestone plateaux of the Causses, to the granite massifs of Mont Aigoual and Mont Lozère, to the schist slopes of the Cévennes. These features reflect geological, topographical and climatic diversity, as well as centuries of human activity, including agriculture and grazing.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Cévennes Biosphere Reserve and National Park encompasses varied landscapes: limestone causses, the granite massifs of Aigoual and Mont Lozère, and the schist mountains of the Cévennes. Long human presence since the Neolithic, combined with the area’s geology, has shaped its current biological richness. Habitats include beech, oak, pine and fir forests, Mediterranean scrub, high-altitude grasslands, rivers and peatlands. The region’s diversity depends on continued rural activity. As agriculture has declined, grazing pressure has fallen and many previously open areas and grasslands are being encroached by woody vegetation. The biosphere reserve therefore supports rural livelihoods through maintenance contracts for farmers, grants to restore farm buildings, the conservation of traditional breeds (notably Aubrac cattle and Raïole sheep), product labelling, the restoration of long-abandoned chestnut groves, and the management of hunting and forestry. The reserve is twinned with the Montseny Biosphere Reserve in Catalonia, north-eastern Spain, and cooperates closely on research, training and education.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Cévennes

records.introduction_en: Situated in the Tuamotu Archipelago, about 360 km north-east of Tahiti, this biosphere reserve comprises seven low-lying coral islands and atolls: Aratika, Fakarava, Kauehi, Niau, Raraka, Taiaro and Toau. They differ markedly in size, shape, population, activities, and whether their lagoons are open or closed to the ocean. This diversity makes the Commune de Fakarava Biosphere Reserve unique. Closed systems include Taiaro, with a hypersaline lagoon, and Niau, with a brackish lagoon. Open systems include Fakarava, which has the largest pass in French Polynesia at 1,600 metres wide.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve offers a great diversity of landscapes including coral formations, seagrass (phanerogam) beds and kopara ponds formed by living cyanobacteria, algae, bacteria and their accumulated organic matter. The reserve also contains primary forests of ‘Puatea’ (Pisonia grandis), coconut groves and other vegetation typical of French Polynesian atolls. Beyond the coral-reef communities, the reserve hosts notable flora and fauna, including rare, protected and endemic species. The Tuamotu kingfisher or ‘Koteuteu’ (Todiramphus gambieri niauensis) is entirely endemic to Niau Atoll. Taiaro is a ring-shaped atoll built upon an ancient volcano that subsided as the Pacific seafloor drifted. Today only the coral rim, forming a 5 km-wide barrier, is visible. Unlike the world’s other atolls, Taiaro’s inner lagoon is completely closed and therefore exhibits exceptional, little-studied characteristics.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Commune de Fakarava

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve comprises three inhabited islands, Ouessant, Sein and Molène, as well as the Molène archipelago, which consists of around twenty smaller islands, together with the waters between them. All the major ecosystems of the Atlantic biogeographical region are represented across island, coastal and marine environments, the latter including beaches, cliffs with Atlantic coastal vegetation, heathlands and grasslands.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Located off the coast of Brittany, the Îles et Mer d’Iroise Biosphere Reserve includes a marine park, the island of Sein, numerous small rocky islands and islets, and open marine areas to a depth of about 20 m, with strong currents and a high tidal range. It is significant for biodiversity, encompassing varied habitats for more than 300 seaweed species, large seabird colonies, and populations of the basking shark (Cetorhinus maximus) and grey seal (Halichoerus grypus). Ouessant rises to just 60 m in altitude; its landscape comprises sheep-grazed meadows latticed with stone walls and numerous hamlets. Habitats include islands, marine waters with sandy bottoms, marine algal communities dominated by Fucus spiralis, F. vesiculosus and Laminaria digitata, gravel and rocky bottoms with Zostera seagrass beds and Laminaria and kelp communities. There are sandy and pebble beaches (featuring Beta maritima and Crambe maritima), rocky coasts and islets, coastal marshlands and coastal grasslands. Terrestrial environments include dry moorlands, improved pasturelands and scrub with ferns and willows, along with mesotrophic backwaters.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Iles et Mer d'Iroise

records.introduction_en: Located in north-west Corsica, this biosphere reserve follows the Fango Valley watershed. The Fango is a mountain torrent that flows into the Gulf of Galéria. The reserve extends from the Mediterranean Sea up to 2,556 metres above sea level.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Altitudinal zones are clearly expressed in this strongly Mediterranean valley, with evergreen broadleaf forest and Mediterranean maquis. At the river mouth, a biologically rich mosaic supports notable birdlife, amphibians and reptiles. The Fango’s holm oak groves are ancient stands where evergreen oak remains dominant. The steep, rocky landscapes of the upper valley are home to Corsican mouflon, bearded vulture or lammergeier, and golden eagle.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Falasorma-Dui Sevi

records.introduction_en: The Gorges du Gardon Biosphere Reserve is in the Gard department of southern France. The landscape is typically Mediterranean, with scrub, evergreen oak, the Gardon River and cliffs. It harbours endangered and protected species such as Egyptian vulture, Bonelli’s eagle and woodcock orchid.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Situated in the Mediterranean biogeographical region, one of 34 global biodiversity hotspots, the reserve features vegetation typical of holm oak and kermes oak, forming part of the lower meso-Mediterranean scrub mosaic. The climate is characteristically Mediterranean, with low, erratic summer rainfall, hot dry summers and mild winters in the plains, making the area a significant reservoir of biodiversity. Domestic diversity is notable, reflecting producers’ efforts to preserve traditional varieties. More than 900 animal species have been identified, of which 202 are nationally protected by ministerial decree and 280 appear on the IUCN Red List. These include 151 bird species, with many rarities such as Bonelli’s eagle (Aquila fasciata); 49 mammals, including Eurasian beaver (Castor fiber); and 13 amphibians and 14 reptiles, such as ocellated lizard (Timon lepidus). Flora is equally rich, with 531 species recorded, eleven protected nationally, two regionally and seven on the global IUCN Red List.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Gorges du Gardon

records.introduction_en: In 1997, the Parc naturel régional du Luberon, established in 1977, became part of the biosphere reserve network. It is bordered to the south and east by the synclinal fold of the Durance, one of the largest rivers south-east of the Rhône that feeds important wetland habitats. The site comprises Mediterranean plains and hills irrigated by several rivers with irregular, torrential flow regimes, including the Calavon, Largue and Lauzon. East–west-oriented Provençal ranges dominate, with Alpine influence, notably the Luberon massif (1,125 m) and the Vaucluse Mountains (1,256 m).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Contiguous with the Mont Ventoux Biosphere Reserve to the north, the area consists of two mid-altitude chains: the Luberon and the Vaucluse. A long history of settlement has created a human-modified landscape and a mosaic of habitats with rich biodiversity. Traditional land-use methods that shaped this landscape have largely been abandoned, with marked effects on fauna and flora. Areas of major biological value have been identified and protected, including holm oak forests (Quercus ilex), Aleppo pine woodlands (Pinus halepensis), beech groves, garrigue shrublands, dry grasslands and riverine woodlands.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Luberon-Lure

records.introduction_en: The Mont-Viso Biosphere Reserve is a glacial cirque between the Alpine mountains and the Mediterranean. Surrounded by river valleys and high-altitude lakes, the area enjoys a dry, sunny climate.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Mont-Viso encompasses a mosaic of ecosystems, from the arid, rocky landscapes of the high altitudes of the Monviso massif (up to 3,841 m), to unusual forest ecosystems hosting, among others, Pinus cembra. The Alevè forest, extending along the western Alps, is the reserve’s most distinctive and intact area. Along the Po River a continuum of riparian environments can be followed from its springs at Pian del Re (2,020 m) to the municipality of Casalgrasso and downstream towards the Province of Torino, all shaped by the river’s permanent flow. Important ecosystems occur along the river and its small tributaries, hosting endemic species of conservation value. Notable fauna include Salamandra lanzai, Coronella austriaca, Parnassius apollo, Callimorpha quadripunctata, Tetrao tetrix and Mustela erminea. Noteworthy flora include Primula hirsuta, Veronica allionii and Juncus triglumis. The biosphere reserve contains areas recognised by international conservation frameworks such as Natura 2000 and Important Bird Areas.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mont-Viso

records.introduction_en: Located in the west of the country, this biosphere reserve includes afromontane forests in one of the most fragmented and threatened regions in the world. The landscape includes several wetlands and marshes. On higher ground, above 1,000 metres, vegetation is dominated by ferns and bamboo, while lower areas are covered with palm trees. This biodiverse region includes about 550 plant species, 33 mammal species and 130 bird species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area is characterised by rolling topography and steep slopes at higher altitudes and is highly dissected by small streams that drain into the Gilo, Akobo and Alwero rivers. Areas below 1,000 m above sea level are relatively flat. The landscape is dotted with many small wetlands and marshes. Highland wetlands are dominated by ferns, grasses and bamboo, while lowland wetlands are dominated by palms. Lowland woodlands are often characterised by clusters of lowland bamboo thickets. The biosphere reserve supports diverse plant and animal species and is important for conserving the genetic diversity of many useful plants, notably ensete (Ensete ventricosum) and yam (Dioscorea bulbifera). Over 130 bird species have been recorded. Characteristic mammals include the leopard (Panthera pardus), caracal (Caracal caracal), colobus monkey (Colobus guereza) and anubis baboon (Papio anubis).
records.name: Majang Forest

records.introduction_en: The Sheka Forest Biosphere Reserve includes forest, bamboo thickets, wetlands, agricultural land, rural settlements and towns. It covers a distinct biogeographic unit extending from cold, very wet highlands to hot lowland areas. The diverse resident population is committed to the sustainable use of forests through the production of wooden items and non-timber forest products.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Sheka Forest, part of the south-west highlands forests of Ethiopia, is important for the conservation of Afromontane vegetation types, especially Afromontane rainforest and alpine bamboo thickets. Afromontane forest has long been considered one of the most threatened ecoregions in the world. The area is rich in plant and animal life: over 300 higher plant species, 50 mammals, 200 birds and 20 amphibians occur across the biosphere reserve’s habitats. There are many endemic species, at least 55 plants and 10 birds, and 38 threatened species of flora and fauna. Characteristic Afromontane rainforest trees include Pouteria adolfi-friederici, Syzygium guineense, Polyscias fulva, Olea welwitschii, Diospyros abyssinica, Manilkara butugi and Cordia africana. A discontinuous canopy of smaller trees (under 10 m) includes Allophylus abyssinicus, Chionanthus mildbraedii, Clausena anisata, Coffea arabica and Deinbollia kilimandscharica. Native coffee is characteristic of the understorey. The shrub layer includes Acanthus eminens, Dracaena fragrans, Lobelia giberroa and Senecio gigas. Lianas and scrambling shrubs are numerous. Epiphytes are common and include Canarina abyssinica, Scadoxus nutans, Peperomia tetraphylla, Asplenium sandersonii and Loxogramme lanceolata, as well as various orchids and mosses. In the Afromontane and transitional rainforests, animals range from diverse invertebrates occupying niches from soil to high canopy, to vertebrates including amphibians, reptiles, birds, and small and large mammals. Common forest mammals and birds include porcupine, grivet (Chlorocebus aethiops), blue monkey (Cercopithecus mitis), De Brazza’s monkey (Cercopithecus neglectus), baboon, African buffalo, lion, leopard, African civet (Civettictis civetta), Ethiopian hare … [truncated]
records.name: Sheka

records.introduction_en: The Yayu Biosphere Reserve lies in the Illubabor Zone of Oromiya Regional State, in south-western Ethiopia. The area is drained by small rivers such as the Geba, Dogi, Saki and Sese, which discharge into the Baro River, a major tributary of the Nile.
