The reserve contains landscape elements of regional, national and international importance – principally forest, agricultural land, wetlands and grazing land – and forms part of the Eastern Afromontane Biodiversity Hotspot and internationally significant Important Bird Areas. The area is also of cultural and historical significance, with archaeological and ritual sites, caves and waterfalls.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve plays a key role in conserving natural and cultural landscapes. It forms part of the Eastern Afromontane Biodiversity Hotspot and includes Important Bird Areas of international significance. Notably, it contains one of the last remaining fragments of montane rainforest with wild coffee (Coffea arabica) populations. The core areas and buffer zone are recognised as a Regional Forest Priority Area and as a forest-coffee conservation site.
records.name: Yayu

records.country_title_en: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
records.introduction_en: The Isle of Wight has a strong tradition of environmental action with numerous projects and initiatives promoting environmental education and awareness, increased community engagement, and healthier lifestyles and diets. The island is also developing eco-tourism and working with universities and institutions to foster environmental innovation and attract new investment. It is testing new measures for climate change mitigation and adaptation.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Isle of Wight represents a unique assemblage of species. It is a nexus between the northernmost point for some species and the southernmost for others. For example, the Glanville fritillary butterfly is found in abundance on the island’s southern cliffs, yet is exceptionally rare elsewhere in Britain. The Isle of Wight has no endemic species, as the island’s isolation is relatively recent, about 7,000 years ago. Endemic sub-species or varieties may yet be found among the lower animals and plants. The island is home to species that occur nowhere else in Britain, most notably the early gentian. The Isle of Wight woodlands are unique in the UK for the co-existence of stable populations of the red squirrel (Sciurus vulgaris), hazel dormouse (Muscardinus avellanarius), Bechstein’s bat (Myotis bechsteinii) and barbastelle bat (Barbastella barbastellus). These occur in woodland that is not influenced by deer or the grey squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Isle of Wight
records.country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

records.country_title_en: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
records.introduction_en: North Devon Biosphere Reserve, in South West England, is centred on Braunton Burrows, the country’s largest sand-dune system. It follows the linked catchments of the Taw and Torridge to the sea, and includes Lundy Island, a national biodiversity hotspot. The reserve’s objectives are to conserve and restore connected land–river–sea systems while supporting a fair, low-carbon local economy. Priorities include raising public awareness, building skills and research capacity, and promoting sustainable practices across local industries.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: North Devon Biosphere Reserve links land, coast and sea in a continuous ecological gradient from the uplands of Dartmoor and Exmoor, along the rivers Taw and Torridge, through Atlantic oak woodland to the waters around Lundy Island. It includes Braunton Burrows, one of the most iconic dune systems in the Northern Hemisphere, long recognised as a reference site for research on dune morphology and ecology. The dunes support rare species such as the amber sandbowl snail (Catinella arenaria), recorded at only two sites in the UK. They also deliver vital ecosystem services: filtering water, storing carbon and supporting modest provisioning uses through controlled grazing, alongside the cultural benefits for walking, wildlife watching and landscape appreciation. Dartmoor and Exmoor hold some of southern England’s largest peat bogs, which serve as major carbon sinks and help to regulate downstream flows. The Mires Project has restored the area’s hydrology by blocking drainage grips to retain water in the peat, raising water tables and reducing peak flows in key rivers. Culm grasslands form the largest remaining tracts of purple moor-grass and rush pasture in western Europe, supporting species of conservation concern such as the marsh fritillary butterfly in damp grasslands. The Taw and Torridge rivers are a stronghold for recovering otter populations and feed the Taw–Torridge Estuary, a Site of Special Scientific Interest that hosts thousands of overwintering wildfowl along key western European migration routes.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: North Devon
records.country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

records.introduction_en: Dedoplistskaro Biosphere Reserve lies in eastern Georgia in Kakheti, set on the Iori Plateau between the Alazani River to the north and the Iori River to the south, close to the border with Azerbaijan. The landscape runs from uplands south of Dedoplistskaro at 1,001 metres down to 90 metres in the Eldari Lowland. Part of the Caucasus Biodiversity Hotspot, it is regionally important for arid and semi-arid ecosystems. The reserve’s purpose is to conserve connected dryland and riparian systems while supporting sustainable rural development, prioritising sustainable water use and stronger rangeland management.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: A dryland climate shapes a varied terrain of open steppe, semi-desert, forest-steppe and open arid woodlands. The ground is punctuated by badlands, terraces, ravines and karst-like forms, with a slightly more humid influence along the Alazani corridor. Pistachio (Pistacia mutica) and juniper (Juniperus foetidissima) woodlands stand beside tussock grasslands and scrub, and floodplain and gallery forests line the main rivers. The Alazani and Iori rivers link uplands to the Eldari Lowland, supporting riparian woods that stabilise soils, filter sediments and sustain biodiversity in a water-limited setting. The site supports high species richness for arid and semi-arid systems. More than 200 bird species are recorded locally, with the plains and low hills functioning as an important staging and wintering area on regional flyways. Wintering flocks of little bustard (Tetrax tetrax) are characteristic, with quail (Coturnix coturnix) frequent in semi-desert habitats. Wetlands and open waters attract pygmy cormorant (Phalacrocorax pygmaeus) and great egret (Egretta alba). The reserve is the focus of the national reintroduction of goitred gazelle (Gazella subgutturosa).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Dedoplistskaro

records.introduction_en: Named for the Alazani River and its two northern tributaries – the Tusheti Alazani and the Piriqita Alazani – the Three Alazani Rivers Biosphere Reserve lies in the Kakheti region of eastern Georgia. It runs from subnival ridges and high mountain slopes in Tusheti to lowland floodplains near Alaverdi. The site sits within the global Caucasus Biodiversity Hotspot, recognised for exceptional temperate forest diversity with high endemism. The reserve’s aim is to conserve vital linked ecosystems and the cultural landscapes they support, maintain traditions such as seasonal pastoralism and strengthen livelihoods through practical measures in farming, market development, research, monitoring and education.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set in the Greater Caucasus range, the reserve spans lowland floodplains near Alaverdi to peaks above 4,000 metres in the historic region of Tusheti. The elevation gradient brings together floodplain forests, river gorges and springs, montane and subalpine forests, shrub zones, alpine and subnival grasslands, and scree and nival areas with permanent snow cover. The landscape has exceptional endemism and species richness. Tusheti alone holds more than 1,000 vascular plants, including local endemics such as Aconitum tusheticum, Primula luteola and Rosa tushetica, with a high proportion of Georgian and Caucasian endemics. Snowfields, alpine meadows and small glaciers play a crucial role in the wider landscape, regulating seasonal flow into the Alazani River, helping to keep summer waters cool, sustaining riverine habitats and supporting fish and amphibians. The river corridor and its upland-to-lowland gradients support habitat connectivity for wide-ranging mammals and migratory birds. Faunal diversity across the reserve is high, with a remarkable 180 bird species recorded. Characteristic mountain ungulates include East Caucasian tur (Capra cylindricornis), bezoar goat (Capra aegagrus) and chamois (Rupicapra caucasica). The area supports two emblematic Caucasian galliforms, the black grouse (Tetrao mlokosiewiczi) and the snowcock (Tetraogallus caucasicus), alongside raptors such as the bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus) and golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Three Alazani Rivers

records.introduction_en: Situated in the Niger basin, this biosphere reserve is part of the Sudano-Guinean vegetation zone. It plays a central role in protecting primary open dry forests, which are believed to represent the last relicts in Guinea and probably in all western Africa.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Situated in the Niger basin, the reserve covers open dry forests, gallery forests along the Niger River and its tributaries, woodland and herbaceous savanna, ponds as well as agroforestry ecosystems. Among scientific projects undertaken in the biosphere reserve are species inventories, a rehabilitation project for chimpanzees, and the monitoring of the West African manatee (Trichechus senegalensis) and the endangered endemic catfish Arius gigas. An ecomuseum and a botanical garden provide environmental education within the biosphere reserve. The vegetation includes open dry forest with Isoberlinia doka, Khaya senegalensis, Cola cordifolia and Prosopis africana; gallery forests characterised by Alchornea cordifolia, Pterocarpus santalinoides and Nauclea pobeguinii; woodland savannah with Daniellia oliveri, Khaya senegalensis and Afzelia africana; woodland and shrubby savannah characterised by Parkia biglobosa, Vitellaria paradoxa and Pterocarpus erinaceus; grassland savannah with Andropogon gayanus, A. amplectens, A. subamplectens and Imperata cylindrica; and agroecosystems.
records.name: Haut Niger

records.introduction_en: The Massif du Ziama Biosphere Reserve lies on the border with Liberia in south-eastern Guinea, about 100 km from the city of N’Zérékoré.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The forest is dense, evergreen to semi-evergreen. There are two vegetation layers: a lower layer at 950–1,000 metres and an upper montane layer. Vegetation types include umbrophilic, mesophilic, semi-xerophilous, swamp, riparian and gallery forests. Important species include niangon, lovoa, entandrophragmas, dabema, Khaya, iroko, makoré, mamea, bako and popo. In 1999, the reserve hosted 1,306 plant species, of which 654 were trees, shrubs and lianas, and 62 were grasses. According to a survey in 1991–1994, Ziama contains 124 species of mammals, including elephants, monkeys, buffalo, dwarf hippopotamus, chimpanzees, ungulates and carnivores. There are also 31 bat species and 36 rodent species. Birds number 286 species out of the 347 recorded in the region. Reptiles include 54 species – 41 snakes, 10 lizards, two tortoises and one crocodile – and there are 30 species of amphibians. Ziama Forest is a refuge for several rare, vulnerable and threatened species. It is home to 22 mammal species protected under CITES. The forest is also one of the most important habitats for endemic species within the Upper Guinean forest block between Sierra Leone, Liberia and Côte d’Ivoire.
records.name: Massif du Ziama

records.introduction_en: One of the truly wild places in Guatemala is the east–west mountain range that runs through the country’s south-eastern highlands. The mountains encompass parts of the Baja Verapaz and Izabal departments at the eastern part of Guatemala City. Protection of the area is particularly important because it contains an estimated 60 per cent of Guatemala’s remaining cloud forest.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Owing to the topography and diversity of plant associations in the Sierra de las Minas Biosphere Reserve, there are places of notable scenic beauty. El Salto de Chilascó is one of the highest waterfalls in Central America, with a height of over 130 metres. It is located in the community of Santa Cruz, Chilascó, Salamá, Baja Verapaz. Another site of great beauty, and one of the most visited in the reserve, is the Angel Stone, located in the community of Los Albores, surrounded by cloud forest at an altitude of 2,400 metres. At this site, wildlife such as the quetzal, horned turkey and other large mammals can be observed, alongside striking landscapes. The biosphere reserve is also home to at least 885 species of birds, mammals, amphibians and reptiles. More than 17 evergreen tree species are endemic to the area. The region is considered an irreplaceable seed resource for reforestation and agroforestry throughout the tropics.
records.name: Sierra de las Minas

records.introduction_en: The Trifinio Fraternidad Transboundary Biosphere Reserve is a tri-national reserve spanning El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras. It is the first transboundary biosphere reserve in Central America and makes a major contribution to implementing the Mesoamerican Corridor. It includes key biodiversity areas such as Montecristo National Park and a variety of forest ecosystems. A key function of this mountain area is securing water supplies for local communities. It also plays an important role in regional development through coffee production, conifer-forest extraction and agrotourism. The reserve has received strong high-level political support, including from vice-ministers of the three countries, alongside the involvement of local communities in promoting sustainable development.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Trifinio region harbours rich biodiversity and is vital to the water supply of all three countries, as it is the source of Central America’s three largest rivers. Predominant ecosystems include cloud forest, subtropical dry forest and pine–oak forest. The area also contains complex wetlands, notably Lagunar Güija, an international Ramsar site and refuge for more than 45 globally threatened species. Fauna includes the white-nosed coati (Nasua narica), ocelot (Leopardus pardalis), Baird’s tapir (Tapirus bairdii), northern crested caracara (Caracara cheriway) and the endangered Geoffroy’s spider monkey (Ateles geoffroyi).
records.name: Trifinio Fraternidad

records.title_en: Cacique Lempira, Senor de las Montanas
records.introduction_en: The Cacique Lempira Señor de las Montañas Biosphere Reserve is in the west of the country and includes Montaña de Celaque National Park. The reserve contains cloud forest and mixed pine–oak forest. Part of the area is highland and includes Honduras’s highest mountain, Cerro Las Minas, at 2,849 m. Most of the population lives in the transition area and is rural, with agriculture representing 87 per cent of economic activity.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is home to over 940 plant species, 323 of which are of interpretative importance. Others are endemic, such as Oreopanax lempiranus, Miconia celaquensis, Molinadendron hondurense and Alfaroa hondurensis, as well as species endemic to the wider region. Faunal diversity includes 60 mammal species and 32 reptile species. Three reptiles are CITES-listed: the rattlesnake (Crotalus durissus), green iguana (Iguana iguana) and boa (Boa constrictor). There are 22 amphibian species; according to IUCN, five are endangered and five critically endangered. Three amphibians are endemic: Bolitoglossa celaque, Leptodactylus silvanimbus and Craugastor anciano. There are 269 bird species. Threatened species include the golden-cheeked warbler (Setophaga chrysoparia), highland guan (Penelopina nigra) and resplendent quetzal (Pharomachrus mocinno). The king vulture (Sarcoramphus papa) is listed in CITES Appendix II. These are the most studied taxa in the park. Within the core zone, Montaña de Celaque National Park is considered the most important protected area in western Honduras. It contains the country’s only cloud forest that integrates the continental watershed. The reserve also includes the nation’s highest point, Cerro Las Minas, which supplies water to communities in its area of influence.
records.name: Cacique Lempira, Senor de las Montanas

records.introduction_en: Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve, designated in 1980, spans tropical moist and tropical wet forest. It includes important coastal–marine areas and a variety of habitats rich in biodiversity.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Using Holdridge’s classification, the reserve comprises tropical moist forest and tropical wet forest. It includes important coastal–marine areas and diverse habitats, as well as mangroves, pine and teak forest associations, savannahs, wetlands, lagoons, coral reefs and cays. Most of Río Plátano is covered by rainforest, which harbours the reserve’s greatest biodiversity. Trees include mahogany, laurel, carapa and teocote pine (Pinus teocote). A total of 586 plant species have been identified, 23 of which are newly recorded for Honduran flora. The reserve also harbours 130 mammal species, 36 per cent of the country’s reptile species, 57 per cent of bird species and 70 per cent of fish species. Cultural diversity is significant, with Garifuna, Miskito, Tawahka and Pech communities living in the reserve. Annual rainfall ranges between 2,000 and 4,000 mm. The average annual temperature is 20–26 °C. Natural landscapes fall into three broad categories: coastal plains, high mountain lands and inland mountains. Ecoregions within the biosphere reserve include a wetland ecoregion with mangroves, lagoons, freshwater and saline marshland, seasonal creeks, swamp woodland and the coastal strip. Other ecoregions are the pine savannah, the Atlantic broad-leaved forest, the highland pine forest and the maritime zone.
records.name: Rio Plátano

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve lies a few kilometres from the Nicaraguan border in the department of Choluteca. It has rich biological diversity, including several endemic faunal species. The biosphere reserve contains 18 villages. Main economic activities include horticulture, fruit and coffee production, ornamental plant cultivation, livestock breeding and milk production. The area is also known for its saddlery products, including belts, harnesses and boots.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The climate has traditionally been described as tropical. However, due to widespread agricultural deforestation and higher altitude, up to 1,700 m above sea level, in many cases it can be more aptly described as temperate. There are several endemic faunal species, some present only in small populations. Mammals include the northern tamandua (Tamandua mexicana), white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) and white-faced monkey (Cebus capucinus). Significant avian diversity has been recorded, with 129 recognised groups. The highland guan (Penelopina nigra) and the red-tailed hawk are endangered. A total of 18 families of herpetofauna have also been observed. In terms of flora, the International Union for Conservation of Nature and national authorities have classified guaiacum trees (Guaiacum sanctum) as being under serious threat.
records.name: San Marcos de Colon

records.introduction_en: The Trifinio Fraternidad Transboundary Biosphere Reserve is a tri-national reserve spanning El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras. It is the first transboundary biosphere reserve in Central America and makes a major contribution to implementing the Mesoamerican Corridor. It includes key biodiversity areas such as Montecristo National Park and a variety of forest ecosystems. A key function of this mountain area is securing water supplies for local communities. It also plays an important role in regional development through coffee production, conifer-forest extraction and agrotourism. The reserve has received strong high-level political support, including from vice-ministers of the three countries, alongside the involvement of local communities in promoting sustainable development.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Trifinio region harbours rich biodiversity and is vital to the water supply of all three countries, as it is the source of Central America’s three largest rivers. Predominant ecosystems include cloud forest, subtropical dry forest and pine–oak forest. The area also contains complex wetlands, notably Lagunar Güija, an international Ramsar site and refuge for more than 45 globally threatened species. Fauna includes the white-nosed coati (Nasua narica), ocelot (Leopardus pardalis), Baird’s tapir (Tapirus bairdii), northern crested caracara (Caracara cheriway) and the endangered Geoffroy’s spider monkey (Ateles geoffroyi).
records.name: Trifinio Fraternidad

records.introduction_en: La Hotte Biosphere Reserve is in south-eastern Haiti and encompasses both terrestrial and marine areas. The region is considered a biodiversity hotspot due to a wide range of climates, from humid to subtropical dry. The reserve includes six mountain peaks, the highest reaching 2,347 m, as well as mangrove, coastal and marine ecosystems in the north at Iles Cayemites and in the south at Ile-à-Vache. Key economic activities are farming, agroforestry, fisheries, commerce and handicrafts.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The core area comprises 13 protected areas established to conserve ecosystems, landscapes, biodiversity and cultural values, and to support research and education. Peaks range from 1,992 m at Pic Grand Colline to 2,347 m at Pic Macaya, with coastal, marine and mangrove ecosystems in the north at Iles Cayemites and in the south at Ile-à-Vache. The area’s high diversity reflects climatic variation from humid to subtropical dry forest. Vegetation provides habitat for many animal species endemic to Hispaniola and to Haiti. Some groups, such as rain frogs (Eleutherodactylus), are endemic to the Massif de la Hotte. Within the karst forest, trees host numerous orchids (Lepanthes, Lepanthopsis) as well as bromeliads, lichens and bryophytes. Several freshwater and marine fish species occur in the reserve. In rivers and ponds, two species of tilapia (Cichlidae family), common carp (Cyprinus carpio) and the native Limia have been recorded. Marine species include the ball anemone (Condylactis gigantea), the rock-boring urchin (Echinometra lucunter) and octopus. Other species present include the Hispaniolan emerald (Chlorostilbon swainsonii), the spotted sandpiper (Actitis macularius) and the Hispaniolan boa (Epicrates striatus).
records.name: La Hotte

records.introduction_en: The Hungarian section of the Mura–Drava–Danube Biosphere Reserve lies in south-west Hungary, along the Croatian border. It is a classic lowland floodplain landscape shaped by wide river valleys, old riverbeds and oxbows that supports flagship species and rare plants. Ecologically, the area supports rich floodplain biodiversity and important migratory connectivity along the Danube–Drava corridor. The reserve’s key objectives are to restore a living floodplain and promote management that aligns conservation with local livelihoods.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve spans three riverine units: the Danube, the Drava and the Mura, each shaping distinct floodplain habitats and soils. Softwood willow and poplar galleries occupy the lower floodplain, forming on frequently flooded shallow gravel and sand bars, and islands. These stands provide tree hollows used by bats and nesting cavities for protected birds. On higher ground, hardwood oak, ash and elm galleries develop on older alluvial soils and support a well-developed shrub and herb layer. Cut-off former river branches, together with side branches and oxbows, host diverse aquatic and reedbed communities. They act as nurseries for fish and amphibians, provide key feeding and nesting areas for herons, storks and other waterbirds, and help maintain hydrological connectivity and migratory staging along the Danube and Drava corridor. Significant protected animal species include the wild cat (Felis silvestris), otter (Lutra lutra), beaver (Castor fiber), pond bat (Myotis dasycneme) and pygmy cormorant (Phalacrocorax pygmaeus). Several strictly protected plants find optimal conditions, such as the black hawthorn (Crataegus nigra) in the Gemenc and Béda floodplain and the German tamarisk (Myricaria germanica) on Drava gravel shoals, which persist only when the river is free to move gravel naturally, maintained through cross-border cooperation. Fritillaria meleagris, Peucedanum verticillare and western sub-Mediterranean elements such as Anemone trifolia and Dentaria trifolia occur in wet meadows and at forest edges, some at their northern range limits, underscoring the need for nature-friendly floodplain management.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mura Drava Danube

records.introduction_en: North-west of Budapest, bound by the andesite block of the Börzsöny and Visegrád Hills, the Danube flows through a narrow, meandering valley forming an almost U-shaped bend known as the Danube Bend. Bernard Newmann described this stretch as one of the grandest along the 2,000-mile river. The Pilis and Visegrád hill ranges on the west bank, once a royal hunting ground, were designated a Landscape Protection Area in 1978 to conserve the landscape and its abundant natural values. Owing to these values and the notable opportunities for environmental education, it was recognised as part of UNESCO’s International Network of Biosphere Reserves.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: A distinctive feature of this biosphere reserve is its diversity. The hill range, cut by valleys formed through tectonic forces and erosion, is composed of more than ten rock types, including Dachstein limestone and andesite tuff. On this varied surface, and according to relief and aspect, several plant and animal communities have formed. Over one hundred lakes and ponds occur within the reserve, including both natural and small artificial waterbodies ranging from 10 m² to 1 ha. The natural ponds were created by earthquakes, tectonic movements and mudslides, while the artificial ponds formed where river valleys were dammed. These ponds served as water reservoirs for wildlife and for grazing animals in the forests. Today, even the artificial ponds have a natural appearance, and their flora and fauna are valuable. They are especially important for herpetofauna and provide breeding sites for amphibians. Many have become silted; as part of a restoration programme, 14 small ponds were restored.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Pilis

records.introduction_en: Located in the Great Hungarian Plain, Hortobágy Biosphere Reserve is a vast, flat edaphic steppe landscape, the archetype of the Hungarian Puszta, recalling features of the Central Asian steppes in Central Europe. Hortobágy is not only a short-grass alkaline steppe but also includes marshes, fishponds, and small patches of forest and tree plantations. It is the most important bird migration site in the Carpathian Basin, and perhaps in continental Europe outside marine shores and estuaries. Many parts of the reserve are also designated as Ramsar sites.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The alkaline habitats, grasslands and marshes were historically influenced by the Tisza River, which meandered north of the area for 20,000–30,000 years and flooded it seasonally, though not every year. River regulation works, including cutting off meanders and building dikes, caused major changes to the landscape. A significant part of the alkaline marshes has dried or degraded since the nineteenth century.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Hortobágy

records.introduction_en: Located in the Western Ghats in southern India, the Agasthyamala Biosphere Reserve has peaks reaching 1,868 m above sea level. Consisting mostly of tropical forest, the site is home to 2,254 species of higher plants, including about 405 that are endemic. It is also a unique genetic reservoir of cultivated plants, particularly cardamom, jamun, nutmeg, pepper and plantain. Three wildlife sanctuaries, Shendurney, Peppara and Neyyar, are located within the site, as well as the Kalakad Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve. There are a number of tribal settlements in the biosphere reserve that rely largely on biological resources for sustenance, although recent projects have been set up to reduce dependence on the forests.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Agasthyamala Biosphere Reserve is located at the southernmost end of the Western Ghats and incorporates peaks reaching 1,868 m above sea level. It covers 3,500 km² and encompasses tropical forest ecosystems within the Tirunelveli and Kanniyakumari districts of Tamil Nadu and the Thiruvananthapuram and Kollam districts of Kerala. It hosts one of the most diverse ecosystems in peninsular India and constitutes an important biogeographical hotspot within the Western Ghats. The reserve hosts 2,254 species of higher plants, including about 405 endemics. It is also a unique genetic reservoir of cultivated plants, particularly cardamom, jamun, nutmeg, pepper and plantain. The reserve is home to about: 79 species of mammals, of which 20 are endemic; 88 species of reptiles, of which 45 are endemic; 45 species of amphibians, of which 30 are endemic; and 46 species of fishes, including 10 endemics. A total of 337 bird species have also been reported, of which 20 are endemic. The reserve includes three wildlife sanctuaries, Shendurney, Peppara and Neyyar, as well as the Kalakad Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Agasthyamala

records.introduction_en: Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve exemplifies the tropical forest biome and lies within the Western Ghats system, which represents the confluence of Afro-tropical and Indo-Malayan biotic zones. Biogeographically, the Western Ghats is one of the most important regions and a noted hotspot for speciation in the tropics. The biosphere reserve contains unique and threatened ecosystems, including a range of forest systems from seasonal rainforests in the low hills, to tropical montane forests and grasslands in the higher reaches, and moist deciduous through scrub to dry deciduous towards the plains in the eastern end. The region is noted for rich biodiversity. It houses about 3,500 species of flowering plants, of which 1,500 are endemic to the Western Ghats. The fauna consists of over 100 species of mammals, 550 species of birds, 30 species of reptiles and amphibians, 300 species of butterflies, a large number of invertebrates, and many more species that await discovery by scientists.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve harbours a wide spectrum of ecosystem types such as tropical evergreen forests, montane sholas and grasslands, semi-evergreen forests, moist deciduous forests, dry deciduous forests and thorn forests. Major parts of the core areas in Kerala and Tamil Nadu include evergreen, semi-evergreen, moist deciduous, montane sholas and grassland vegetation types. The core area in Karnataka contains mostly dry deciduous forests and a few patches of moist deciduous, semi-evergreen and scrub jungles. These ecosystems occur from hilly terrain to meadows extending from 300–2,670 m, and together they constitute excellent habitat for flora, fauna and microbial forms. The varied habitats of the biosphere reserve support a sizeable number of animal and plant species, including many endemics of special conservation relevance. Endemic plants include Rhododendron arboreum, Actinodaphne malabarica, Garcinia morella, Glochidion neilgherrensis, Garcinia gummi-gutta, Litsea bourdillonii, Michelia nilagirica, Mahonia leschenaultiana and Cinnamomum sulphuratum. Important faunal elements needing protection include the tiger (Panthera tigris), elephant (Elephas maximus), gaur (Bos gaurus), lion-tailed macaque (Macaca silenus), chital (Axis axis), sambar (Cervus unicolor), wild boar (Sus scrofa), barking deer (Muntiacus muntjak) and Nilgiri tahr.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Nilgiri

records.introduction_en: Located in the state of Sikkim, bordering Nepal to the west and Tibet, China, to the north-west, this biosphere reserve encompasses one of the highest ecosystems in the world, with elevations from 1,220 to 8,586 metres above sea level. It lies within one of the world’s 34 biodiversity hotspots. Vast natural forests support high species diversity with notable endemism. The main economic activities are agriculture and horticulture, along with animal husbandry, and fish, dairy and poultry farming.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Situated over the Himalayan trans-axial belt, the biosphere reserve features valleys with numerous ravines, deep gorges and gullies, as well as saddles, crests, knolls and river terraces. These landforms are mostly found in the lower mountain zones. At higher elevations, slopes give way to gentler alpine meadows, and several lakes of different sizes occur in this belt. Further upslope, important topographic features include rocky outcrops at the base of the Himalayas, glacial moraines, scarps and talons. There are 73 important lakes covering 3.34 km², embedded within seven watersheds. Glaciers, mountains and peaks occupy the highest parts of the reserve on a permanent basis. The biosphere reserve is a transboundary biodiversity hotspot conservation area. About 22 endemic and 22 rare and threatened plants occur here. The reserve has also yielded newly described plant taxa such as Myrmechis bakhimensis, Craniotome furcata and Cortiella gauri. Epiphytes and lianas are abundant. In addition, about 30 species of rhododendron are recorded, and there are over 42 confirmed mammal species belonging to 16 families.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Khangchendzonga

records.introduction_en: Almost the entire area of the Tadami Biosphere Reserve is mountainous at around 1,500 m above sea level, with a maximum altitude of 1,819.9 m and a minimum of 350 m. This excludes the basins of the Tadami River and its tributary, the Ina River. Steep massifs are found in the southern and western parts, while the northern mountains have slopes shaved by avalanches and exposed bedrock. In this complex topography, mosaic vegetation forms as plant communities adapt to each habitat. As the Tadami Biosphere Reserve lies within the Japan Sea climatic area, it has a humid subtropical climate.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Tadami Biosphere Reserve is located at the eastern edge of the Echigo Mountains, the western edge of Fukushima Prefecture, and the southern part of the Tohoku region in Honshu. Geographically, it consists of large-relief mountains of more than 600 m, middle-relief mountains of 400–600 m, low-relief mountains of 200–400 m, a gravel plateau and the floodplains of the Tadami and Ina River basins. The high mountains of Tadami are home to riparian forests and predominantly cool temperate deciduous broad-leaved forests, typically beech forest (Fagus crenata). The riparian forests occur in the basins of the Tadami and Ina Rivers, where the rare tree Salix hukaoana grows naturally across a total range of 50 km, in the largest numbers found in Japan. The growth of this tree depends on river disturbance from spring melts, which indicates that the basin’s river environment has been conserved in a highly natural state. As an enclosed mountainous region facing the winter monsoon, this biosphere reserve has some of the heaviest rainfall and snowfall in Japan. The annual average winter snow cover is 2.5 m. Steep, complex nivation landforms are found particularly in the north, resulting from heavy snowfall and green tuff bedrock of comparatively fragile nature. In response to steep topography, an oceanic climate and a complex landscape, a plant population has developed that is specifically adapted to these conditions. A landscape mosaic is composed of evergreen coniferous forest such as Pinus parviflora on the ridges, shrubs like Quercus mongolica on avalanche slopes, beech forest on relatively stable lower parts of slopes where debris and soil have been deposited by avalanches, and riparian forests like Japanese wingnut (Pterocarya rhoifolia) along the stream banks. … [truncated]
records.name: Tadami

records.introduction_en: Mount Hakusan Biosphere Reserve is located in central Japan and spans the prefectures of Toyama, Ishikawa, Fukui and Gifu. Mount Hakusan, at the centre of the biosphere reserve, is a volcano 2,702 metres above sea level with eight craters near its summit. Among mountains with alpine zones, Mount Hakusan is located at the westernmost point. Most people live in mountain villages in the transition areas. Japanese people have lived there since ancient times.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is dominated by Mount Hakusan, a volcano with eight craters near its summit. The area is characterised by lake and pond habitats. Senjaga Lake, in one of the summit craters, is frozen all year round. The park exhibits distinct altitudinal zonation of vegetation, ranging from warm temperate to alpine zones. Coniferous forests surround the base of the mountain, dominated by firs (Abies mariesii), pines (Pinus aristata) and Japanese cedar (Cryptomeria japonica) along the Tedori River. Deciduous forests and woodlands are also present. The alpine flora of the summits contains stands of creeping pine and is rich in species such as Anemone narcissiflora and Orchis aristata. Steep, non-woodland alpine scree slopes and areas of snow slip serve as refuges for distinctive ‘Altherbosa’ communities of tall herbaceous plants, especially in denuded forest areas. The rich mammal fauna includes a large population of Japanese macaque (Macaca fuscata), Asiatic black bear (Ursus thibetanus japonicus), Honshu sika deer (Cervus nippon aplodontus) and Japanese serow (Capricornis crispus). The avifauna includes golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos) and Hodgson’s hawk eagle (Nisaetus nipalensis).
records.name: Mount Hakusan

records.introduction_en: The Yakushima and Kuchinoerabu Jima Biosphere Reserve, situated 60 km south of Kyushu, is known for the Yaku cedar primeval forest. It encompasses the area inscribed on the World Heritage List (under the name ‘Yakushima’, inscribed in 1993) and now covers the entire island, as well as the island of Kuchinoerabu and the surrounding marine area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Yakushima is a round-shaped island with an area of 504 km2 and a circumference of 132 km, situated on the sea 60 km south-southwest of Cape Sata, the southernmost tip of Kyushu. Around the highest peak of Mount Miyanoura, the highest mountain in the Kyushu region at 1,936 m, in the centre of the island, there is a mountain range of seven mountains reaching 1,700 m and over, and more than 45 mountains reaching 1,000 m. There are coastal terraces along the coast from the north-east to the south, where gravel from the Alluvium era has accumulated. The Miyanoura, Anbo and Nagata rivers flow from the mountainous area and form Oko Waterfall, with a fall of 88 m, and Senpiro Waterfall, with a fall of 60 m. Due to these features, Yakushima was selected in 2007 by the selection committee of Japan’s top 100 sites of geological structures as one of the top 100 geological structure sites in Japan. Kuchinoerabu Jima is a gourd-shaped island with an area of 38 km2 and a circumference of 50 km, situated about 12 km west-northwest of Yakushima. A narrow part separates the island into the old and young volcano groups. Shin-dake and Furu-dake, with an elevation of 657 m, are both still active and form a unique volcanic landscape with many vents, craters and eruptive fissures. The coastline around the island features sea cliffs. As for mammals, 16 species are identified, including four endemic subspecies: Yakushima deer (Cervus nippon yakushimae), Yakushima macaque (Macaca fuscata yakui), Japanese white-toothed shrew (Crocidura dsinezumi umbrina) and Ryukyu flying fox (Pteropus dasymallus).
records.name: Yakushima and Kuchinoerabu Jima

records.introduction_en: The Cilento and Vallo di Diano biosphere reserve is in south-central Italy, bordering the Tyrrhenian Sea. It is characterised by low dolomite mountains with typical karst features such as sinkholes and caves. The coastline comprises cliffs, bays and sandy beaches, with sea caves and freshwater springs. Mediterranean sclerophyll vegetation is divided into many habitats according to altitude, ranging from dry coastal garrigue to holm oak woodlands, mixed forests of oak, hornbeam and alder, natural stands of European beech, and high-altitude grasslands. The fauna is notable for its birds, especially birds of prey. The cultural heritage is particularly rich, with traces of human occupation dating to Palaeolithic times and archaeological and historic vestiges of a succession of civilisations.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is in the Campania region, southern Italy, and includes the territory of the National Park of Cilento, Vallo di Diano and Alburni, its contiguous areas and marine protected areas. The coastline comprises cliffs, bays and sandy beaches, with sea caves and freshwater springs. One of the most interesting characteristics of this area is the high level of biological diversity, strongly related to variability, lithology, geomorphology and climate, which is little found in other parts of the peninsula. There are 28 sites of Community importance, including two marine sites recognised by the European Commission Habitats Directive, and eight Special Protection Areas recognised by the European Commission Birds Directive. Endangered or threatened animal species include the European otter (Lutra lutra), Corsican hare (Lepus corsicanus), Mediterranean horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus euryale), rock partridge (Alectoris graeca orlandoi) and Eleonora’s falcon (Falco eleonorae). The mountain landscape changes markedly: rocky, wooded upper slopes give way to the pre-Alpine thermal and environmental conditions of the middle and lower valley. Human presence increases as altitude decreases and as the valley widens in its lower part, with residential, commercial and productive settlements.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Cilento and Vallo di Diano

records.introduction_en: The Collemeluccio–Montedimezzo Biosphere Reserve is located in Isernia province in Molise, central Italy. It encompasses two forests that cover 637 ha in a sub-mountain area. Penna Mountain, at 1,277 metres above sea level, and Colle San Biagio border the area to the east and west. Of the two forests, Collemeluccio has smoother and lower reliefs, at 1,080 metres above sea level. The main habitats include silver fir forests, mixed forest of silver fir and turkey oak, turkey oak forest with coppices of hornbeam, ash, field maple and stone, and beech forests. Silvicultural intervention has been undertaken to replenish turkey oak stands. Small villages are spread across the biosphere reserve, with many people commuting to the town of Molise. The main economic activities are agriculture, breeding and traditional handicrafts. The area is also subject to tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The landscape is characterised by a sub-mountain range with a variety of reliefs and lacustrine and fluvial plains. The major rivers are the Sangro, which runs through the north-west of the reserve, the Trigno, which borders the Collemeluccio forest, both flowing to the Adriatic Sea, and the Vandra, which rises near the Montedimezzo forest and flows into the Volturno river basin, which drains to the Tyrrhenian Sea. There are more than five freshwater springs within the reserve. The main habitat of the biosphere reserve is forest cover, characterised by silver fir stands (70 per cent) and turkey oak stands (30 per cent) in Collemeluccio, and turkey oak stands (45 per cent) and beech stands (45 per cent) in Montedimezzo. In 2006, floristic relevés were conducted in the two core zones, recording 377 vascular plant entities, divided into 75 families and 240 genera. The Eurasiatic chorotype predominates (29 per cent), while Eurimediterranean, Oriental and Boreal chorotypes occur in significant numbers (approximately 14 per cent). In 2007, a survey recorded 37 bird species in the Montedimezzo forest and 32 species in the Collemeluccio forest. Among the vertebrates listed in the annexes of the EU Habitats Directive, the spectacled salamander (Salamandrina terdigitata), Italian stream frog (Rana italica), grey wolf (Canis lupus) and European polecat (Mustela putorius) were also recorded.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Collemeluccio-Montedimezzo Alto Molise

records.introduction_en: The Collina Po Biosphere Reserve is in the Piedmont region of northern Italy and covers the Turin stretch of the River Po with its main tributaries and the Collina Torinese hillside. The River Po is the main reservoir of biodiversity in the Turin plain, due in part to the numerous wetlands along its course. Its physical and geological characteristics have led to the formation of many gravelly shores, oxbows and riparian woods that host a variety of species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The River Po is the principal element of the biosphere reserve, with the foothill and high-plateau section running initially northwards as far as Chivasso, where the river turns east. The river is the main reservoir of biodiversity in the Turin plain, due in part to the many wetland areas along its course. The Turin Hills are characterised by sedimentary rocks of marine origin, which are fairly loose and easily eroded. These physical and geological characteristics have led to the formation of many gravelly shores, oxbows and riparian woods that host a variety of species. The territory is rich in fauna, including the Italian barbel (Barbus plebejus), the Eurasian badger (Meles meles), the greater horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus ferrumequinum) and the tessellated water snake (Natrix tessellata). There are 136 bird species, including the merlin (Falco columbarius), the tawny owl (Strix aluco) and the Eurasian spoonbill (Platalea leucorodia). The buffer zone and transition area contain eight Savoy residences belonging to the ‘Residences of the Royal House of Savoy’, which have been designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Collina Po

records.introduction_en: The Ledro Alps and Judicaria biosphere reserve is in the Trentino–Alto Adige region of northern Italy, between the Brenta Dolomites, one of the main constituents of the Dolomites World Heritage Site, and Lake Garda. The site is representative of the southern slopes of the central–eastern Alps. It comprises a variety of habitats, including alpine meadows, forests, grasslands and moorlands that alternate with traditional crops. Its location supports rich and varied biodiversity, creating a continuous north–south corridor between the protected areas of the Po Valley and the northern Alps. The area also includes two pile-dwelling settlements around Lake Ledro and Lake Carera–Fiavè, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The reserve is highly valued as a tourist destination, with tourism the main source of income for permanent residents. Agriculture is a principal economic activity, in particular viticulture, olive, fruit and vegetable growing, and animal husbandry.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve forms part of a corridor linking the Adamello Brenta Nature Park in the Trento Autonomous Province in the north and Upper Lake Garda Park in the Lombardia region to the south. The central and southernmost part of the area is characterised by steep rocky mountain slopes, mostly covered with broad-leaved or mixed woods and interrupted by pastureland or agricultural crops. Open areas predominate in the higher band or on the valley floor. The southern part features higher mountains, with conifer woods, above which extensive grasslands and the rocky pinnacles of the Dolomites offer spectacular scenery. Large carnivores such as the lynx (Lynx lynx) and brown bear (Ursus arctos) represent the top of the food chain in the reserve. In 1996, the Adamello Brenta Nature Park established the Life Ursus project to reintroduce the brown bear following a drop in numbers to near-extinction levels. Between 1999 and 2002, 10 brown bears were released. They adapted well to their new environment. Today, there are over 30 brown bears in the Central Alps. Reptiles, invertebrates and birds include the rock partridge (Alectoris graeca saxatilis), black woodpecker (Dryocopus martius), Eurasian pygmy owl (Glaucidium passerinum), white-clawed crayfish (Austropotamobius pallipes italicus), alpine newt (Triturus alpestris) and Aesculapian snake (Elaphe longissima).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Ledro Alps and Judicaria

records.introduction_en: The Monviso Biosphere Reserve is a glacial cirque between the Alpine mountains and the Mediterranean. Surrounded by river valleys and high-altitude lakes, the area enjoys a dry, sunny climate.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Monviso encompasses a mosaic of ecosystems, from the arid, rocky landscapes of the high altitudes of the Monviso massif (up to 3,841 m), to unusual forest ecosystems hosting, among others, Pinus cembra. The Alevè forest, extending along the western Alps, is the reserve’s most distinctive and intact area. Along the Po River a continuum of riparian environments can be followed from its springs at Pian del Re (2,020 m) to the municipality of Casalgrasso and downstream towards the Province of Torino, all shaped by the river’s permanent flow. Important ecosystems occur along the river and its small tributaries, hosting endemic species of conservation value. Notable fauna include Salamandra lanzai, Coronella austriaca, Parnassius apollo, Callimorpha quadripunctata, Tetrao tetrix and Mustela erminea. Noteworthy flora include Primula hirsuta, Veronica allionii and Juncus triglumis. The biosphere reserve contains areas recognised by international conservation frameworks such as Natura 2000 and Important Bird Areas.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Monviso

records.introduction_en: The Po Delta Biosphere Reserve is a delta plain in northern Italy, formed by the River Po and recent human activity. Created by the confluence of the river’s main branches, it comprises coastal dune systems and sand formations, lagoons, fishing ponds, marshes, fossil dunes, canals and coastal pine forests, as well as vast brackish wetlands and cultivated lands dominated by rice farming. These landscapes provide the area with a unique identity and a high level of biodiversity due to the extensive range of habitats. The reserve is an important tourist destination, and tourism together with agriculture and fish farming are the main economic activities of local communities.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Po Delta is the only delta in Italy and contains the largest national reserve of wetlands, whose waters flow through ancient coastal dunes before meeting the sea. The delta plays a major conservation role due to its diversity of environments. These include river branches and a dense secondary hydrographic network, coastal dune systems and sand formations, sandbars, lagoons, fishing ponds, marshes, fossil dunes, canals and coastal pine forests, in addition to vast and mainly brackish wetlands. The Po Delta hosts over 360 species of birds, including the purple heron (Ardea purpurea), spoonbill (Platalea leucorodia), glossy ibis (Plegadis falcinellus) and little egret (Egretta garzetta). It also supports a colony of pink flamingos (Phoenicopterus roseus) numbering over 10,000. The Cervo della Mesola is the only mammal to be found in the reserve, a red deer (Cervus elaphus) recognised as genetically distinct from other populations in Europe. The Po Delta Biosphere Reserve incorporates a UNESCO World Heritage Site, Ferrara, Città del Rinascimento e il suo Delta del Po, as well as three Ramsar Wetland Sites: Valli di Gorino e Territori Limitrofi, Valli Bertuzzi e Specchi d’Acque Limitrofi, and the Valli Residue del Comprensorio di Comacchio.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Po Delta

records.introduction_en: Sila Biosphere Reserve is in Calabria, a southern Italian region in the heart of the Mediterranean, and covers approximately 1,700 km². It includes Sila National Park (PNS). The Sila area is a large rectangular upland containing the main mountains of the Sila uplands in the central part of Calabria. The uplands form a mature erosion surface with soft-contoured mountains scattered with higher chains and peaks. From these, the region’s main rivers descend, including the Crati, Tacina, Neto, Trionto, Savuto and Corace. There are glacial moraines between 1,600 m and 1,750 m on Mount Botte Donato, as well as several springs, lakes and seasonal lakes. The plateau comprises many different landscapes, stretching across more than 400,000 ha of alluvial plains and valleys. The hilly, terraced terrain alternates with extensively flat areas and peaks that can reach nearly 2,000 m, where forest is the most predominant and distinctive element.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Sila’s landscape has been shaped by highly favourable ecological conditions. Sub-Mediterranean pine forests with endemic black pines are its major ecosystem type. Thanks to its morphological and geographical characteristics, Sila Biosphere Reserve hosts a wide variety of natural environments with different microclimates, depending on altitude and aspect. For this reason, the Sila Mountains include an extensive range of habitats. They provide a biodiversity reserve of great importance in the Mediterranean biogeographical region, rich in rare, local and endemic species. Sila hosts approximately 1,000 vascular plant species, of which 81 are endemic. It supports over 210 species of vertebrates, including 113 birds (82 nesting), 65 mammals, 16 reptiles, 12 amphibians and six fish. There is also a rich biodiversity of arthropods, estimated at over 15,000, with considerable local and regional endemism. Sila Biosphere Reserve is the only hotspot area in southern Europe, including the Apennines and Apuan Alps. The most important natural habitats include the sub-Mediterranean pine forests with endemic black pines and those in the deciduous Mediterranean forests. These feature the Apennine beech forests with Abies alba, beech forests with Abies nebrodensis, and the Apennine beech forests with Taxus and Ilex. In the Sila, these southern Apennine forest types cover the greatest area and have an excellent conservation status. Other major habitats and land-cover types include coniferous forests of the Mediterranean and Macaronesian mountains, herbaceous and alpine shrub vegetation, Mediterranean oak forests, and hygrophilous arboreal vegetation.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Sila

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is located on the Gulf of Naples and encompasses the active volcano Vesuvius, famous for its eruption in AD 79, which engulfed the town of Pompeii. The biosphere reserve includes the Vesuvius Park, which is protected, and a transition area that covers the surrounding coastline.The Archaeological Areas of Pompeii, Ercolano and Torre Annunziata are also inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. This area has been settled since antiquity and incorporates the town of Pompeii and the Vesuvian Villas, which were built by rich Neapolitan families in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.There is a long history of studies on the colonisation of lava by vegetation across different epochs. The traditional agricultural areas are diverse, with fruit, vines and flowers. The diversity of fauna is relatively poor however, the site acts as a resting and staging area for migratory birds. The local population practises agriculture, but traditional activities are declining. Measures are now being taken to renew interest in rural heritage and to develop cultural tourism and ecotourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Somma–Vesuvio volcanic complex is an important geological asset of continental Europe, with two morphologically distinguishable structures: the caldera of Mount Somma and the Gran Cono of Mount Vesuvius. Mount Somma has a very steep southern slope, while the northern slope is less steep and furrowed by numerous deep valleys that extend radially up the slopes. Mount Vesuvius has a typical cone shape, with a crater diameter of approximately 500 m and a depth of approximately 300 m. Although the park area forms part of a highly anthropised context and has assumed the typical characteristics of a biogeographic island, it is home to a very interesting wildlife community. The flora in the reserve is essentially Mediterranean, and numerous studies demonstrate the colonisation of the volcanic complex by more than 1,000 species, including extinct and recent species. Species of phytogeographical interest include the white birch (Betula pendula) and the Chinese ladder brake (Pteris vittata). The core and buffer areas of the reserve host numerous interesting species from a conservation and biogeographical perspective, and their biotic communities reflect the area’s peculiarities. The microfauna is particularly rich and interesting. In recent years, the establishment of the protected area has led to a significant increase in many species of birds and mammals, such as the buzzard (Buteo buteo), fox (Vulpes vulpes) and European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Somma-Vesuvio and Miglio d'Oro

records.introduction_en: The Tuscan Islands Biosphere Reserve is an archipelago in the Tyrrhenian Sea composed of seven main islands and a few isolated islets. It encompasses a wide range of geological, geomorphological and biological diversity representative of the Mediterranean region. The islands are covered by sclerophyllous evergreen forests, Mediterranean pine woods, maquis and scrub, and hardwood forests with deciduous oaks and chestnuts. The recent development of tourism has exerted strong pressure on the natural environment. As a result, certain terrestrial and marine areas, and some islands, now form part of a protected national park established to conserve rare and endemic species. People live permanently in the archipelago and depend mainly on services related to tourism, with relatively little employment in agriculture and fisheries. Projects are planned to introduce renewable energy resources and innovations in the agricultural sector, and to enhance the availability of water by means of alternative technologies. Current research focuses on geology and geomorphology, coral and fish distribution, monitoring of seawater quality and the restoration of populations of rare species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Located between the Tuscan coast and Corsica, the reserve consists of seven main islands (Gorgona, Capraia, Elba, Pianosa, Montecristo, Giglio and Giannutri) and a few smaller islands. It encompasses a wide range of geological, geomorphological and biological diversity representative of the Mediterranean region, including an assortment of sedimentary, metamorphic and igneous rocks, and a variety of landforms and processes. The main types of habitat are evergreen sclerophyll forests, Mediterranean pine woods and Mediterranean scrub, as well as chestnut and deciduous oak woods. Rare and endemic species on the islands include the peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus), the Mediterranean horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus euryale) and the red-rumped swallow (Cecropis daurica).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Tuscan Islands

records.introduction_en: The site is located in the eastern part of Lombardy. The area is characterised by typical Alpine and pre-Alpine valleys, ranging from valley-bottom landscapes to the high peaks of the Adamello group and the Adamello Glacier, and ending at Lake Iseo, one of Italy’s largest basins. The landscape features rivers and lakes, woods and forests, glaciers, meadows and prairies. Farming and animal husbandry in the region follow ancestral traditions.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is located in the eastern part of Lombardy and is one of the more extensive valleys of the central Alps. The area has typical Alpine and pre-Alpine valley characteristics, shaped by the great Adamello Glacier. The landscape ranges from typical valley-bottom areas to the heights of the Adamello group, and ends at Lake Iseo, one of the largest basins in Italy. The altitudinal range is from about 200 m above sea level in the valley bottom at Lake Sebino to 3,539 m above sea level at the Adamello summit. The predominant habitats of the reserve are inland waters, rivers and lakes, woods and forests, glaciers, meadows and prairies. The woodland ecosystem is the most represented. The Adamello Glacier is the largest in Italy. The mountain landscape changes markedly. The Alpine aspect, dominated by rocks, glaciers, snow areas and wooded mountainsides of the high valley, is influenced downslope by the pre-Alpine thermal and environmental conditions of the middle and lower valley.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Valle Camonica - Alto Sebino

records.introduction_en: The Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve is situated in the western Tien Shan Mountains on the southern spurs of the Chatkal Range in the west of Kyrgyzstan.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The main part of the area comprises a high mountain basin protected to the north, west and east by mountain ridges. The mountain lake Sary-Chelek is situated at about 2,000 m above sea level, with an area of 470 ha and a depth of 245 m. Owing to protection by the surrounding mountain ranges, winters are relatively mild and rich in snow, and summers are warm and wet. The elevation of the biosphere reserve ranges from 1,200 to 4,247 m above sea level. Main habitats comprise forests, meadows, steppes, rocks and screes, and some aquatic areas. The central and lower region is strongly dissected and covered by nut–fruit forests with walnut (Juglans regia), apple (Malus) and pear (Pyrus), and an understorey of Prunus divaricata, abelia (Abelia curumbosa), exochords (Exochorda) and juniper. This forest can grow here due to the favourable microclimate, a reflection of the local relief. Many of the fruits found in these forests have a high socio-economic value. Alpine forests include walnut, fir (Abies semenovii), spruce (Picea schrenkiana) and grape (Vitis silvestris), with meadows interspersed. There are tree–shrub communities of juniper (Juniperus), spruce and fir. Steppe habitats, rocks and screes, and water bodies are also present.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Sary-Chelek

records.introduction_en: The central Tien Shan mountain region around Issyk-Kul Lake is one of the last harmonious cultural landscapes in Central Asia, preserving near-natural habitats alongside traditional culture.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This mountain region, with Issyk-Kul Lake at its centre, is home to ecosystems of global importance and a wide variety of endemic species of wild fauna and flora. Issyk-Kul, 180 km long and 60 km wide, is the second-largest high-mountain lake in the world. Owing to its depth (up to 700 m), low salinity and warm springs, it does not freeze, even in winter. From the lakeshore, all major landscape types, from subtropical to tundra, occur in close succession. The fauna is highly diverse but unevenly distributed across landscapes, with 335 animal species recorded: 3 amphibians, 11 reptiles, 54 mammals and 267 birds. In total, 39 species are included in the Red Book of Kyrgyzstan. The government’s main objective is to develop ecologically sound land-use practices and economic activities in this area.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Issyk-Kul

records.introduction_en: The central part of Gwangneung Forest is a basin divided into east and west by the Bongseonsacheon stream at about 100 m above sea level, flowing southward. The basin is open to the north, while the other sides are enclosed by mountain peaks and ridges. Owing to this geography, winter air temperatures here are lower than in nearby areas. In the eastern part of the forest, Mount Jugyeop, the highest peak at 600 m, is linked by a gentle ridgeline to Mount Unak and the Gwangneung royal tomb at the southern end of the ridge.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The western part of the forest comprises Mount Soribong at 537 m, the second-highest peak, with three tributary ridgelines to the north, south and east. The eastern ridgeline forms a gentle decline that meets the Bongseonsacheon stream. The site formed around this eastern ridge, the central part of Gwangneung Forest, has fertile soil and is covered with old-growth deciduous broadleaf forest, assumed to be the climatic climax vegetation of the region.
records.name: Gwangneung forests

records.introduction_en: Mount Sorak lies on the east coast of the Korean Peninsula in the Taebaek mountain range, which consists of dissected granite and gneiss with rocky hills and ridges. It is the third-highest mountain in the country, with the main peak, Daecheongbong, at 1,708 metres above sea level.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The park contains virgin forests of the middle temperate zone and 1,292 species of flora. In the alpine region above 1,300 m, climatic factors such as wind, temperature and humidity have produced mixed forests of deciduous and evergreen needle-leaf trees. Pure forests occur in some parts of the park. Some 44 mammal species (including Korean goral, musk deer and otter), 109 bird species, 10 amphibians, 19 reptiles, 43 fishes and 1,683 insects have been recorded. Flagship species representing Seoraksan (Mount Sorak) are the Korean goral and the dwarf stone pine, which grows around Daecheongbong peak; the dwarf stone pine habitat is protected as a strict nature reserve. Seoraksan National Park has a lively and colourful ecosystem. Unique wildlife such as musk deer, Asiatic black bear and flying squirrel, and the pine tree in Seorakdong, are also protected as natural treasures.
records.name: Mount Sorak

records.introduction_en: Situated on the southern tip of the Korean Peninsula, the biosphere reserve includes terrestrial ecosystems surrounding Suncheon City, centred on Mount Mohusan and Mount Jogyesan, as well as coastal tidal-flat wetland ecosystems in Suncheonman Bay. The site’s biological resources include crustaceans, fish and shellfish, medicinal herbs, reed communities (Phragmites communis) and East Asian seepweed (Suaeda japonica). Inhabitants, including rural, fishing and mountain-dwelling communities, use ecosystem services in economic activities such as rice cultivation, medicinal herbs, and fruits including plums and persimmons.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Located on the southern tip of the Korean Peninsula, Suncheon Biosphere Reserve’s tidal flats and forests are rich in biodiversity. It is a significant wintering and stopover site for the endangered hooded crane (Grus monacha). It is also home to black-faced spoonbills (Platalea minor), white-tailed eagles (Haliaeetus albicilla) and leopard cats (Felix bengalensis), among others. Aquatic ecosystems are similarly diverse, featuring crustaceans such as the Japanese ghost crab (Macrophthalmus japonicus). The reserve’s ecological axis has two components: terrestrial ecosystems centred on Mount Jogyesan, and coastal tidal-flat wetlands in Suncheonman Bay. River ecosystems, such as the Isacheon and Haeryongcheon, act as corridors between terrestrial and coastal ecosystems, forming ecological networks.
records.name: Suncheon

records.introduction_en: Located at the southernmost tip of the Korean Peninsula, the Wando Archipelago Biosphere Reserve comprises 265 islands – 55 inhabited – with marine waters accounting for almost 90% of the site’s area. A warm, humid oceanic climate shapes warm-temperate forests on land and extensive intertidal and nearshore habitats at sea. The reserve’s principal objectives include conserving terrestrial and marine biodiversity, promoting sustainable development grounded in terrestrial and marine ecosystem services, and establishing participatory, community-led conservation and use.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Wando Archipelago Biosphere Reserve lies on the south-west coast of Jeollanam-do and encompasses habitats ranging from wetlands, salt marshes, and tidal flats to intertidal and nearshore coastal waters. A warm, humid oceanic climate—enhanced by the Haenam Peninsula blocking north-westerly winds—supports warm-temperate vegetation on land. Forests include temperate deciduous stands and evergreen broad-leaved forests with trees such as Quercus acuta and Castanopsis sieboldii.Wando is characterised by a rias coastline—drowned river valleys formed when rising seas inundated former river courses after the last Ice Age. This creates a deeply indented shore with large and small bays and underpins varied coastal landforms—bedrock shores, steep cliffs, sandy and pebble beaches, and extensive tidal flats—that support diverse marine life. The core zone serves as an important site for research and monitoring. Public institutions such as the Wando Arboretum and the Dadohaehaesang National Park Office conduct species-conservation and climate-adaptation studies on forest plants and track biome and climate trends, providing a scientific baseline for ecosystem management across the reserve.
records.name: Wando Archipelago

records.introduction_en: The Mount Chilbo Biosphere Reserve forms part of the Great Paektu Mountain Range, created on the eastern coast of the Korean Peninsula by fault movement and volcanic eruption during the late Neogene and early Quaternary period. The mountains range from 700 m to 1,103 m, creating a mid-altitudinal landscape. The Chilbo Stream flows through the Mount Chilbo Biosphere Reserve. Mount Chilbo holds significant cultural heritage, notably Kaesim Temple (built in 826) and ten other State Natural Monuments. The biosphere reserve covers 50,340 ha, with its highest elevation at 1,103 m above sea level and the lowest at 13 m. Primary protection targets include the Korean mushroom (Tricholoma matsutake) and its ecological environments.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Four ecosystem types occur in Mount Chilbo: forest, agriculture, freshwater and coastal. Biogeographically, the reserve belongs to the temperate deciduous forest ecosystem. Ravines and steep rocky cliffs in the coastal area create unique scenery with large and small waterfalls. Diverse natural landscapes, including dense forests, enhance the conservation value of the area. The soil is dark brown forest soil formed mainly from granite and basalt. Mount Chilbo has an inland climate in Inner Chilbo, a continental climate in Outer Chilbo and an oceanic climate in Sea Chilbo. With its natural beauty comes an altitudinal series of forest habitats: temperate coniferous forest, mixed forest and lowland pine-dominated forest. Recorded biodiversity includes 827 plant species and 274 vertebrate species (39 mammals, 192 birds, and 21 amphibians and reptiles). The reserve is important for conservation due to 16 endemic plant species, as well as 30 nationally and globally endangered plant and animal species. It has ten threatened plant species, including Celtis edulis, Phellodendron sachalinense and Exochorda serratifolia, and more than ten threatened animals, including Ursus thibetanus and Dryocopus martius. Mount Chilbo has abundant resources of medicinal plants, wild fruits and vegetables, notably the endemic Korean mushroom (Tricholoma matsutake).
records.name: Mount Chilbo

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve lies in the middle of the Great Paektu Mountain Range in the south-east of the country and includes adjacent marine areas to the east. Mount Kumgang is a forest-oriented ecosystem linked to coastal, agricultural and freshwater ecosystems. It is home to many endemic and rare species of global significance. The coastal area and natural lakes provide habitats for migratory birds along the East Asia–Australasian Flyway. The main economic activities are fishing, agriculture and forestry.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve has an intact altitudinal series of forest habitats, ranging from subalpine Ailanthus communities, subalpine coniferous and latifoliate forests, middle-elevation broadleaved forests, lowland coniferous and latifoliate forests, and lowland coniferous forests to swampy grasslands. Mount Kumgang has 1,228 species of higher plants in 533 genera and 146 families, including 67 fern species, 15 gymnosperms and 1,146 angiosperms. Genera represented by a single species number 291, 54.59 per cent of all genera in the area, and 14.4 per cent nationally, indicating a long floristic history and diverse habitats. Plants of commercial and academic significance include 112 endemic species, 46 threatened species, 318 medicinal herbs and 23 edible herb species.
records.name: Mount Kumgang

records.introduction_en: The Aksu-Zhabagly Biosphere Reserve is located in the north-west of Talasskiy Alatau and the south of Karatau in the West Tien Shan. It is home to 48 per cent of regional bird species, 72.5 per cent of vertebrates, 221 of 254 fungi species, 63 of 80 moss species, 15 of 17 vegetation types, and 114 of 180 plant formations found in the West Tien Shan. Approximately 2,500 insect species have been recorded in the reserve. The principal form of land use in the region is agriculture. Cereal crops such as wheat and barley are grown on rain-fed areas, and forage crops including corn, clover and alfalfa are grown on irrigated arable land. Local inhabitants breed cattle, sheep (South-Kazakh Merino), goats and horses (including trotters and the Donskaya breed), as well as poultry such as chicken and turkey.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve occupies the north-western edge of Talasskiy Alatau, the northern ridges and adjacent north-eastern slopes of the main Ugam ridge, and the southern part of Karatau in the West Tien Shan. The West Tien Shan mountain range acts as a barrier that catches moisture from the western transport of air masses, so the reserve’s ecosystems are more closely related to the natural systems of the Near East and the Mediterranean than to other ecosystems of the Tien Shan. Almost all landscape types and sub-types of the West Tien Shan are represented throughout the territory, except for deserts and gypsophilous subshrub communities, which occur at lower altitudes. The appearance of the West Tien Shan mountains is characterised by standing juniper forests that comprise three species of Central Asian junipers: Juniperus turcestanica, Juniperus zeravschanica and Juniperus semiglobosa. The reserve is also home to 221 of 254 fungi species, 63 of 80 moss species, 15 of 17 vegetation types and 114 of 180 plant formations of the West Tien Shan. The reserve provides a favourable environment for numerous faunal species, with 267 bird species recorded, including the Eurasian sparrowhawk (Accipiter nisus), white-throated robin (Irania gutturalis) and booted eagle (Hieraetus pennatus). Species in need of special protection include the saker falcon (Falco cherrug) and demoiselle crane (Anthropoides virgo). There are 52 species of mammals, including the brown bear (Ursus arctos), dhole (Cuon alpinus) and marbled polecat (Vormela peregusna). Two threatened species on the IUCN Red List occur here: the Menzbier’s marmot (Marmota menzbieri) and snow leopard (Panthera uncia). The snow leopard is the focus of large-scale activities by international conservation organisations across … [truncated]
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Aksu-Zhabagly

records.introduction_en: The Almaty Biosphere Reserve is located on the Zailiysky Alatau ridge, on the watershed of several river basins featuring a number of lakes. Its wild fruit forests, predominantly consisting of wild apple trees, are home to diverse fauna. It is a popular recreational area for city dwellers from the entire region. The biosphere reserve aims to develop eco-tourism, as well as sustainable animal husbandry and agriculture, which are major sources of income in the area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Almaty Biosphere Reserve is located on the northern and southern slopes of the Ile (Zailiysky) Alatau ridge, part of the Northern Tien Shan mountain system. The region hosts 960 plant species, including Iris albertii, Atraphaxis muschketowii, Oxytropis almaatensis, Pastinacopsis glacialis, and Cortusa semenovi.Mammal diversity is notable, with 39 species recorded, including the snow leopard (Panthera uncia), Tien Shan brown bear (Ursus arctos), Turkestan lynx (Lynx lynx), and stone marten (Martes foina).The impressive avifauna draws the eye skyward, with species such as golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos), bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus), black stork (Ciconia nigra), Barbary falcon (Falco pelegrinoides), sicklebill (Ibidorhyncha struthersii), and Himalayan vulture (Gyps himalayensis) soaring majestically above.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Almaty

records.introduction_en: This reserve comprises the Katunskiy Biosphere Reserve (Russian Federation, designated in 2000) and the Katon-Karagay Biosphere Reserve (Kazakhstan, designated in 2014). With a total area of over 1.5 million ha, the territory is used for livestock rearing and grazing, red deer farming, fodder production and apiculture. Tourism, hunting, fishing and the collection of non-timber forest products are also widespread.
