records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Great Altay Transboundary Biosphere Reserve forms part of the Altai–Sayan Ecoregion, which encompasses a wide variety of ecosystems. More than 200 protected areas of different legal status make up 16.5 per cent, about 17.6 million ha, of the ecoregion. Among other aims, the Great Altay Transboundary Biosphere Reserve focuses on conserving migratory species, especially ungulates and carnivores. For example, the snow leopard, an umbrella species for the high mountain areas of the Altai–Sayan Ecoregion, inhabits vast areas of this region, including parts of the Great Altay Transboundary Biosphere Reserve.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Katon-Karagay

records.introduction_en: Korgalzhyn was Kazakhstan’s first biosphere reserve. Situated in the north central part of Kazakhstan, the site is a complex of freshwater and saline lakes embedded in the dry steppe zone of Eurasia. Environmental degradation caused by previously unsustainable management practices are now being addressed through a number of pilot projects.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The territory is characterized by elevated plains, hills, and lake depressions, and experiences an extreme-continental climate. Korgalzhyn Biosphere Reserve is a natural complex of fresh and saline waters with coastal areas, featuring landscapes typical of the dry steppe zone of Eurasia. This makes it a critical wetland site for migratory waterbirds. The potential fodder reserves of just Lake Tengiz alone can support up to 15 million birds. The most northern nesting population of flamingo (Phoenicopterus roseus) is located here, with numbers reaching 50,000–60,000 birds in some years.For this reason, in 1974, the Tengiz–Korgalzhyn lakes, part of the Biosphere Reserve, were included on the Ramsar List of Internationally Important Wetlands. The reserve also supports globally threatened species, including the extremely rare steppe eagle (Aquila nipalensis), pallid harrier (Circus macrourus), Pallas’s sand grouse (Syrrhaptes paradoxus), demoiselle crane (Grus virgo), and great and little bustards (Otis tarda and Tetrax tetrax).Biodiversity in the reserve includes more than 500 plant species and over 1,400 species of water and terrestrial animals, comprising 42 mammal species, 14 fish species, and 344 bird species. Waterbirds of the Tengiz–Korgalzhyn lakes include 112 species, representing 87% of Kazakhstan’s total waterbird fauna. To date, more than 700 insect species have been recorded, although total species diversity may exceed 3,000. Over 60 rare species of plants and animals, listed in national Red Data Books, are present within the reserve.Korgalzhyn State Nature Reserve is also part of the UNESCO World Heritage site “Saryarka – Steppe and Lakes of Northern Kazakhstan.”
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Korgalzhyn

records.introduction_en: The Jabal Moussa Biosphere Reserve, overlooking the Mediterranean Sea to the west, is a mosaic of ecological systems that broadly represent the evergreen sclerophyllous broussailles and forests biogeographical region within a Mediterranean biome. A dominant feature is its steep, verdant mountainsides rising from a river lined with cool, aromatic sycamore trees, reaching summits of statue-like karstic rocks. The mountainous relief creates several eco-zones, promoting diversity that harbours many species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: From an aesthetic point of view, landscapes dominated by peaks and basins offer wide, far-reaching views. These are influenced not only by geographical position but also by the range of altitudes and the exposure of slopes in several directions. In the core area alone, 14 phytoecological groups and two agricultural types have been identified. In addition, Jabal Moussa is notable for having avoided uncontrolled urbanisation, the proliferation of roads and quarrying that have devastated other similar mountains.
records.name: Jabal Moussa

records.introduction_en: The Shouf Biosphere Reserve covers about 5 per cent of Lebanon’s total area. It extends along the ridge of the western chain of Mount Lebanon from Dahr el-Baidar in the north to Jezzine in the south. It overlooks the Bekaa Valley to the east and the Shouf Valley to the west. The mostly treeless summit of the Al-Shouf Cedar Nature Reserve forms the skyline of a large part of southern Lebanon.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: With some of the highest mountains in the Middle East, the region provides a wide range of ecosystem services, including a wild gene pool, freshwater storage, climate mitigation, hydrogeological balance, and aesthetic and recreational value. It hosts the largest stands of Lebanese cedars, one of the world’s great tree icons, as well as rich flora and many medicinal plants with high potential economic value. It is home to 520 plant species, including 25 internationally and nationally threatened species and 48 plants endemic to Lebanon. The area supports wildlife with good potential for restoration through reintroduction of charismatic species such as ibex, gazelle and vultures. It is a crossroads for bird migration, strategically located on routes between Europe, Africa and West Asia. Over 250 bird species are recorded in the biosphere reserve, many of which are observed at the Ammiq Wetland. With a surface area of 50,000 ha, the Shouf Biosphere Reserve is one of the largest protected areas in the Middle East and the eastern Mediterranean. It includes 620 ha of cedar forest.
records.name: Shouf

records.introduction_en: The Bundala Biosphere Reserve is Sri Lanka’s only coastal biosphere reserve. It presents a mosaic of ecosystems with a gradation of human interventions, from human-modified areas where people live and work, while contributing to sustainable development, to areas of high biodiversity value, including wetlands of global importance as a Ramsar site.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Bundala National Park, which forms the core zone, contains four brackish-water lagoons rich in wetland species, including two species of crocodile. The reserve has about 230 indigenous and migrant bird species, many of them wetland species. Habitat mapping in the reserve revealed ten main habitat types. The most important are the beach and seashore and sand-dune vegetation, scrubland, dry mixed evergreen forest, thorn forest, arid-zone forest, salt-marsh and lagoon-marsh vegetation, seasonal freshwater bodies, paddy, home gardens, and wetlands. There are also small areas of mangroves and some aquatic freshwater vegetation in tanks and seasonal water bodies.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Bundala

records.introduction_en: Matšeng Biosphere Reserve lies in Lesotho’s northern highlands, an area often referred to as the “Kingdom in the Sky”, for the elevation of the Maloti–Drakensberg mountain range. It forms part of a transfrontier conservation area, linking Lesotho and South Africa, safeguarding a montane landscape and the headwaters that feed Katse Dam. The landscape is defined by steep, high-altitude slopes, wetlands, waterfalls, rivers and gorges. The reserve’s objectives include protecting high-altitude grasslands, wetlands and woodlands, and the emblematic and endemic species they host. It also aims to strengthen community wellbeing through research-led stewardship, climate-resilient nature-based enterprises and locally developed, locally governed low-impact ecotourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set within the Maloti Mountain Range, the Matšeng Biosphere Reserve is a representative example of a minimally disturbed, natural system within the Drakensberg alti-montane grasslands and woodlands ecoregion, a highland belt stretching from Lesotho to South Africa, marked by endemism, distinct genetic diversity and striking natural features. The Maloti Mountains form a significant section of this ecoregion and are dominated by grasses including Merxmuellera, Themeda triandra and Festuca caprina. Within the reserve lie two protected areas: Tšehlanyane National Park and Bokong Nature Reserve. Tšehlanyane protects some of the last remaining indigenous woodlands in Lesotho, with fine examples of oldwood (Leucosidea sericea) conserved at its core, providing habitat for understorey plants unique to this area. The highland is also classified as an Endemic Bird Area of high priority. Notable fauna include the eland (Tragelaphus oryx), the endemic Maloti minnow (Pseudobarbus quathlambae), known locally as thoboshana, and the alpine endemic Drakensberg siskin (Crithagra symonsi). Abundant rainfall feeds rivers and wetlands that discharge into Katse Dam, supplying South Africa and downstream users. The wetlands provide regulating services, including water purification and flood control.
records.name: Matšeng

records.introduction_en: North Vidzeme Biosphere Reserve comprises 53 km of the Gulf of Riga coastline and borders Estonia to the north. It covers 474,447 ha, corresponding to the catchment basins of the Salaca, Svetupe and Vitrupe rivers. Lakes characterise the landscape, with more than sixty larger than 3 ha, as well as gentle, glacially formed hills and rolling plains.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The coastal area consists of sandy beaches, coastal meadows and stretches of bare rock. The site is important for conservation as it harbours raised bogs, wild rivers with wild Baltic salmon, coastal meadows traditionally maintained by grazing, and remnants of ancient broadleaf forest. Habitats include boreal coniferous and mixed forests, wetlands, raised bogs with open bog pools, fens and wet meadows, lakes and rivers, coastal dunes and the marine littoral area, alongside extensive agricultural and urban areas.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: North Vidzeme

records.introduction_en: Located in the south-west of the country, this biosphere reserve is a mosaic of terrestrial, coastal and marine ecosystems. It is considered a biodiversity hotspot due to vulnerable ecosystems, which include coral reefs, beaches, dunes, sea marshes, mangroves, gallery forest and littoral forest. The terrestrial part of the biosphere reserve is home to relatively few plant and animal species, with a high rate of endemism reaching 90 per cent. The main economic activities are agriculture, livestock farming and fishing.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Tsimanampesotse–Nosy Ve Androka Biosphere Reserve belongs to the intertropical marine biogeographic system of the south-west Indian Ocean. Five major Malagasy ecoregions are involved: the South Terrestrial Ecoregion, the Aquatic Ecoregion of the Southern Basins, the Aquatic Ecoregion of the West Basins, the Mozambique Channel Marine Ecoregion and the South Marine Ecoregion. The biosphere reserve comprises two national parks, Tsimanampesotse–Nosy Ve Androka and Aire Protégée d’Amoron’i Onilahy, with different structures. Tsimanampesotse National Park lies on the Mahafaly limestone plateau, with altitudes from 10 to 140 m. The backbone of the Mahafaly plateau is covered with forests. Red soils are favoured for peanut cultivation, and calcimorphous soils for maize. Characterised by a high endemism rate of about 90 per cent, the terrestrial flora and fauna are of great importance, with abundant genetic resources. Ecosystem services in the dry forests largely depend on diurnal lemurs and floristic plant species. In different xerophilous thickets, endemic plants such as Commiphora lamii and Rhigozum madagascariensis, and the threatened tortoise Astrochelys radiata, are key indicators for biodiversity conservation. Other species in the biosphere reserve include Tamarindus indica, Charadrius thoracicus, Typhleotris madagascariensis and T. mararybe.
records.name: Tsimanampesotse - Nosy Ve Androka

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve covers almost seven million hectares and encompasses a wide range of bioclimatic areas, from the humid Mediterranean zone to the hyper-arid Sahara. Its highly effective oasis systems protect the territory from desertification and support rich biodiversity. They also sustain local communities, who depend mostly on agriculture. The biosphere reserve also hosts the World Heritage site Ksar of Ait-Ben-Haddou, designated for its architectural and historic value.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Oasis du Sud Marocain consists of two ecoregions. The Mediterranean ecoregion features deserts and temperate grasslands, while the Saharan ecoregion in the north-east contains mixed mountain and highland systems. It has rich agrodiversity, including large areas with date palms, acacia forests and other high-altitude forests covered with Juniperus thurifera, J. phoenicea and Quercus rotundifolia. The biosphere reserve is the main place of endemism in North Africa. It is also home to most Moroccan species, including 63 per cent of the birds, 60 per cent of reptiles and 66 per cent of all mammals present in the country. For instance, the area is home to dorcas gazelle, Cuvier’s gazelle (Gazella cuvieri), Barbary sheep (Ammotragus lervia), houbara bustards (Chlamydotis undulata) and cobras (Naja haje).
records.name: Oasis du sud marocain

records.introduction_en: Located in the south of the country, this biosphere reserve encompasses the Prut River and floodplain lakes. Two-thirds of the surface of the area is occupied by Lake Beleu. A wetland area extends along the Prut River, covering a mosaic of water, meadow and forest ecosystems. The main economic activity is agriculture, which provides 90% of the inhabitants’ income.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: One of the natural wonders of the Republic of Moldova, the Lower Prut Nature Reserve protects the wetlands and riparian habitats around Lake Beleu and the Prut River. Around 200 bird species, 40 mammals and more than 300 plant species are recorded here, many listed in Moldova’s Red Book of endangered species. The reserve forms the entrance to the Danube Delta Biosphere Reserve, a labyrinth of water and land shared by Romania and Ukraine.Lower Prut is a patchwork of rivers and floodplains, with Lake Beleu – a relic of the Danube’s freshwater estuary – covering 628 ha, about two-thirds of the site. The lake supports high biodiversity, with over 27 fish species and nine amphibian species, including the ridge newt and green toad. Intact areas of the lake such as Cioroiu provide nesting habitat for endangered bird species, such as the small cormorant, yellow heron and white egret. Located on a major migratory flyway, the reserve serves as a nesting ground and an important stopover and wintering site. The territory is designated within the Natura 2000 network as both a Site of Community Importance (SCI) and a Special Protection Area (SPA).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Lower Prut

records.introduction_en: Indawgyi Lake is the largest freshwater lake in Myanmar. The site consists of a large open lake, floating vegetation, swamp forest and seasonally flooded grasslands. The hills surrounding the lake are covered by subtropical moist broadleaf forests that harbour threatened forest birds and mammals, including primates. The local population derives most of its income from farmlands bordering the lake.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Indawgyi Biosphere Reserve comprises Indawgyi Lake (12,000 ha), Southeast Asia’s third-largest lake, with surrounding wetlands and a largely intact watershed. The watershed is covered with subtropical moist broadleaf forests. Forests and wetlands of the Indawgyi Lake region provide habitat for endemic and globally threatened birds, fish, turtles, primates and other mammals. The area was designated as an Important Bird Area in 2004 and listed as a Key Biodiversity Area in the National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan, as noted by the Republic of the Union of Myanmar in 2011. Owing to its global biodiversity values, especially its outstanding importance for migratory birds, it has been nominated as a Ramsar site. More than 160 bird species have been recorded for the Indawgyi area. These include many globally threatened species, notably the slender-billed vulture (Gyps tenuirostris) and the white-rumped vulture (Gyps bengalensis). The biosphere reserve also holds important habitats for ungulates, such as seasonally flooded grassland that is critical for the endangered hog deer (Axis porcinus). The surrounding forests of the watershed are important habitat for globally threatened primates, in particular the eastern hoolock gibbon (Hoolock leuconedys) and Shortridge’s langur (Trachopithecus shortridgei).
records.name: Indawgyi

records.introduction_en: Situated in the south of Malawi, near the eastern border with Mozambique, the Lake Chilwa Wetland Biosphere Reserve is home to one of the world’s most diverse bird assemblages. Lake Chilwa, the country’s second-largest lake, was formed by tectonic processes. The lake functions as a shallow inland drainage basin. Its eastern side is composed of sandy soils, while the remaining soils are fine-grained clays. The Chilwa plain comprises seven agro-ecological zones defined by different soil groups. The reserve’s topography includes the Chilwa plains, open lake waters and mountainous areas such as Mount Zomba and Mount Mulanje. In 1997, the wetlands were designated a Ramsar site for their global significance as a major waterfowl habitat.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve lies within the tropical dry (deciduous) forest biogeographical region. Land cover includes marshes, swamps, open lake waters, five major rivers, islands, cultivated floodplains and grasslands. Lake Chilwa is a tropical, closed lake. Typically, one-third of the lake consists of open water, one-third of marshes and one-third of floodplains, although this varies seasonally. Dry (May–October) and wet (November–April) seasons lead to water-level fluctuations of up to one metre. Over the last century, the lake has dried out and refilled eight times. Forests within and around the reserve are among the oldest in Malawi. Typha swamps cover wetland areas, providing habitat and food for numerous species and playing a key role in nutrient cycling. However, seasonal burning of vegetation for hunting endangers particularly vulnerable species. Examples of fauna found in the reserve include the pink-backed pelican (Pelecanus rufescens), African rock python (Python sebae) and spot-tail tetra (Alestes imberi). Elegant grasshoppers (Zonocerus elegans) and creek rats (Pelomys fallax) are frequently consumed. The reserve is rich in birdlife, with 164 resident species, plus 41 Palaearctic and 14 intra-African migrant species that occur seasonally.
records.name: Lake Chilwa Wetland

records.introduction_en: The Mount Mulanje Biosphere Reserve is in the south-west of Malawi, near the border with Mozambique. Mount Mulanje lies halfway between mountain chains and upland areas that extend from the Ethiopian highlands to South Africa. It has rich biodiversity with a high level of endemism. The Mulanje cedar (Widdringtonia whytei) found in the reserve is considered the national tree of Malawi and is highly valued for its use in silviculture and its contribution to socio-economic development. Its protection and sustainable use are priorities. There are three main ethnic groups and several minorities living in the area. The main land-use activities are agriculture and pastoralism, selective logging, the extraction of medicinal plants and other non-timber forest products, as well as ecotourism. The mountain also carries important cultural significance, as ancestral spirits are believed to reside there. These sites are used as shrines for traditional rites.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Mount Mulanje Biosphere Reserve covers mountainous terrain measuring 26 km by 22 km, formed by an impressive geophysical syenitic intrusion that rises precipitously from the surrounding plains. Altitude ranges from 600 m above sea level to the highest point, Sapitwa Peak, at 3,002 m. A large section of the mountainside consists of a sheer rock face, interspersed with rainforest gorge valleys to the south and east, and dry brachystegia woodlands on the northern and western slopes. The Mulanje cedar (Widdringtonia whytei), recognised as Malawi’s national tree, is a key species of the mountain’s high cloud forests and is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List. The timber is highly prized for a variety of specialist purposes. However, illegal and unsustainable harvesting has led to diminishing forest cover, which is of particular concern in small cedar clusters. A number of taxa on Mount Mulanje are categorised as Endangered, Critically Endangered or Threatened. All are endemic and are pressured by human activities and climate change. These include the bar-throated apalis (Apalis thoracica flavigularis), stripe-cheeked greenbul (Andropadus milanjensis), Mulanje dwarf gecko (Lygodactylus bernardi bonsi), Mulanje forest chameleon (Nadzikambia mlanjensis) and cross-barred tree snake (Dipsadoboa flavida flavida).
records.name: Mount Mulanje

records.introduction_en: The Mwali Biosphere Reserve encompasses the entire land and marine territory of Moheli, the smallest of the islands of the Union of the Comoros, which is located in the Mozambique Channel ecoregion. Its location in this area gives it a high level of biological diversity and endemicity, with a continental shelf extending down to the 100m isobath, in the intertropical marine biogeographic region of the south-west Indian Ocean.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The main ecosystem types are the reef zone and its lagoon, marine phanerogams, mangrove formations, islets, seagrass beds, dry formations, wet formations, Lake Boundouni and permanent rivers. Since 2001, the Mwali Biosphere Reserve has been designated a marine park, a sanctuary for numerous species and ecosystems representative of the western Indian Ocean ecoregion. It is the first egg-laying site for the green turtle, an important breeding site for humpback whales and a refuge for the conservation of dugongs. This marine area was extended in 2015 with the creation of the Moheli National Park to preserve the island’s watersheds, which are equally rich in endemism. The park contains nesting grounds for the world’s largest bats, Pteropus livingstonii, endemic to the Comoros, as well as numerous species of endemic or regionally important birds and mammals, including mongo lemurs. The core areas of the biosphere reserve are uninhabited and cover the dry and humid forest cores as well as all the marine reserves of the national park.
records.name: Mwali

records.introduction_en: St. Mary’s Biosphere Reserve is located on the island of St. Kitts in the Leeward Islands chain of the Lesser Antilles. The reserve is an important site for biological diversity, comprising cloud forests, mangroves and coral reefs. It also includes the Brimstone Hill Fortress National Park World Heritage site, which is of particular historical, cultural and architectural significance. St. Mary’s is one of the first biosphere reserves of the Caribbean island countries and serves as an example of village participation in efforts to preserve the outstanding mosaic of natural and cultural landscape values.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: St. Mary’s is an important site for biological diversity, comprising cloud forests, mangroves and coral reefs. The reserve contains one of the most diverse natural communities on St. Kitts, encompassing the marine area and beaches near Canada, Keys and Cayon, and the surrounding tropical forests of the mountain ridgeline. Other physical features include long, narrow, forested ridges with deep valley ghauts, or seasonal streams, surrounded by rolling forested and agricultural hills. Many of the larger ghauts lead to sandy beaches and the Atlantic Ocean. The island remains seismically active and is composed almost exclusively of volcanic rocks of andesite or dacite mineralogy. Its geology is similar to that of other volcanic islands in the Lesser Antillean Archipelago. Newer volcanic rocks rest on a basement of older rocks, which are exposed only where newer deposits have been denuded. The sandy beach forms the primary nesting habitat of the leatherback sea turtle (Dermochelys coriacea). Conservation of this critically endangered species is a primary goal for the biosphere reserve. Bats are the only native terrestrial mammals to be found in the country today. Varieties include the pig-faced bat (Brachyphylla cavernarum), the fishing bat (Noctilio leporinus) and the velvety house bat (Molossus molossus). Other animals found in the reserve include the purple-throated carib (Eulampis jugularis), the Antillean crested hummingbird (Orthorhynchus cristatus) and lizardfish (Synodontidae). The biosphere reserve also includes the Brimstone Hill Fortress National Park World Heritage site.
records.name: St. Mary's

records.introduction_en: The largely mountainous Gangwon Eco-Peace Biosphere Reserve, located at the watershed of the Taebaek Mountain Range in northern Gangwon Province, borders the southern limit of the Demilitarized Zone to the north and reaches the east coast of the Korean Peninsula to the east. It is home to a wide range of rare and endangered flora and fauna. Development plans focus on ecotourism that draws on its ecological, cultural and social resources, as well as exploration of relics of the Korean War in the area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve forms part of the ecological backbone of the Korean Peninsula. It lies within two of the three core ecological axes designated by the Ministry of Environment –namely the Demilitarized Zone and Baekdu-daegan axes, which form the eastern and north–south ecological belts. The area contains a wide variety of environmental landscapes, ranging from flat areas in the west to mountainous areas in the east, and includes plains, grassland, farmland, rivers, high moors and mountains. It is an invaluable conservation site and a resource for academic research owing to its diverse landscapes and ecosystems. It also plays a crucial role as a stopover on East Asia’s bird migration route. Warm water erupts from a natural spring in Chuntong-ri, Cheorwon, during winter, helping to keep conditions mild year round. These factors make the region an excellent habitat for migratory birds, with as many as 126 species recorded. Wild animals documented in the area include 17 mammal species across 10 families, among them the Amur leopard cat (Prionailurus bengalensis euptailurus), a Category II endangered species designated by the Ministry of Environment, and the Siberian flying squirrel (Pteromys volans), designated Natural Monument No. 328 and a Category II endangered species. There are 61 fish species across nine orders and 17 families, including the cyprinid Hemibarbus mylodon (Natural Monument No. 259), the Korean bitterling (Acheilognathus lanceolatus), a Category II endangered species, and the Kumgang fat minnow (Rhynchocypris kumgangensis), which is endemic to the Korean Peninsula. Eighteen amphibian and reptile species across two orders and seven families are also present, including the Reeves’s turtle (Mauremys reevesii) and Russian rat snake (Elaphe s … [truncated]
records.name: Gangwon Eco-Peace

records.introduction_en: Jeju Island Biosphere Reserve is situated in the southern part of the Korean Peninsula and covers a lava plateau with a shield volcano at an elevation of 1,950 m above sea level. Located at the centre of the island, it comprises Mt Hallasan National Park, two stream corridors and three islets in its core area. A large number of species inhabit Jeju Island. The major industries are tourism, agriculture and stock farming.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Jeju is a volcanic island, formed approximately two million years ago. It embraces four major biogeographical ecosystems: alpine coniferous forest, temperate broadleaf forest, warm temperate evergreen lucidophyll forest and temperate grassland. The core area is protected as a national park and lies at the centre of Jeju Island. Many endangered plants and animals inhabit the reserve. A total of 134 taxa of Korean endemic plants exist here, 90 of which are Jeju endemic plants. Species on the island include the leopard cat (Prionailurus bengalensis), damselfish (Chromis notata) and the Jeju horse, a horse breed native to Jeju Island. The island is also home to endangered species such as the green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas japonica), black-faced spoonbill (Platalea minor) and Steller sea lion (Eumetopias jubatus). Jeju Island is the only place where all four internationally designated areas occur at the same location. These include Jeju Volcanic Island and Lava Tubes World Heritage Site, Jeju Island Biosphere Reserve, Jeju Island UNESCO Global Geopark and two Ramsar wetland sites: 1100 Altitude Wetland and Muljangori-Oreum Wetland.
records.name: Jeju Island

records.introduction_en: Located in the Chugaryeong Tectonic Valley, the Yeoncheon Imjin River Biosphere Reserve encompasses the entire county of Yeoncheon and the Imjin River basin. Its core area comprises forests and cultural heritage protection zones, with the Imjin River as its centrepiece. The river, largely untouched by humans, is home to Korean endemic fish such as Acheilognathus gracilis and Tanakia signifer, and mammals including water deer, otters and leopard cats.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Imjin River stands out for conservation. Topographical advantages, together with restrictions on civilian activities due to the heavy presence of military facilities nearby, have kept it largely undisturbed. The ecological value of its upper course is especially high because it benefits from double protection as both a military reservation and a water-source protection area. High water quality and broad rapids make it an ideal spawning site for natural monument and endangered fish such as Hemibarbus mylodon, Tanakia signifer and Gobiobotia brevibarba. It also supports Korean endemic fishes including Nipponocypris koreanus, Coreoleuciscus splendidus and Acheilognathus gracilis. Abundant wetlands along the river provide habitat for diverse wildlife. Notable species include water spiders, bean geese, greater white-fronted geese, eagles, golden eagles, otters and leopard cats.
records.name: Yeoncheon Imjin River

records.introduction_en: Mount Paektu Biosphere Reserve lies on the border with China, adjoining the Changbaishan Biosphere Reserve. Its northern boundary follows the international frontier: the Amnok (Yalu) River in the west, the Paektu massif across the central section, and the Tumen River in the east. The reserve is a high volcanic plateau and montane-forest landscape shaped by past eruptions, encompassing Lake Chon, the Samjiyon basin and the Rimyŏngsu waterfalls, a young yet ecologically stable mountain system of clear scientific value. The overarching aim of the reserve is to conserve intact forest ecosystems and associated historical sites, while delivering biodiversity protection and restoration, long-term research and education, and carefully managed nature-based tourism with local partners.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Mount Paektu lava plateau was formed by an initial volcanic eruption, with a subsequent eruption building Mount Paektu and Mount Potae above it. On the thick pumice layers of the first eruption, a larch forest ecosystem dominated by Larix olgensis established. On the main volcanic area formed by the second eruption, volcanic conifer forests developed, dominated by Picea and Abies. The elevational range creates strong habitat gradients that support high biodiversity. The flora includes numerous medicinal species used in traditional practice, notably Rhododendron chrysanthum, Rhodiola elongata and Angelica dahurica. Several taxa are rare or at risk, among them the tiger (Panthera tigris), dhole (Cuon alpinus) and grey wolf (Canis lupus), and threatened plants such as Rheum coreanum, Dasiphora mandshurica and Astragalus setsureianus, which are safeguarded within a designated plant reserve. Forest ecosystems deliver vital services for people and nature. These include flood regulation, clean drinking water, wildlife habitat, carbon storage, watershed protection and climate regulation, along with the provision of timber, food and medicinal plants. Larch and deodar are key to controlling soil erosion and supporting climate mitigation, while locally harvested herbs and other economically important species benefit nearby communities.
records.name: Mount Paektu

records.introduction_en: The Mount Kuwol Biosphere Reserve, on the west coast of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea and about 100 km south-east of Pyongyang, comprises a 954 m high mountain, adjacent coastal wetlands, lagoons, river estuaries and agricultural areas. Both the core area and the buffer zone form part of the Mount Kuwol Nature Reserve, designated in 1976.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve contains a range of ecosystems: forest in the core area, extensive agricultural land in the transition area, and wetlands along the coastline, rivers, streams and reservoirs. Habitats and land cover are therefore classified into three types: forest, farmland and wetland. The landscape features curious rocks, cliffs, peaks, valleys, waterfalls and ponds formed by long-term weathering and erosion. As a typical temperate forest area, it includes broad-leaved forest, coniferous forest and mixed broad-leaved–coniferous forest. The climate is temperate with four distinct seasons, influenced by a typical monsoon. Soils comprise five types: forest brown soil, alluvial soil, marshland soil, tidal land soil and paddy soil.
records.name: Mount Kuwol

records.introduction_en: The Mount Myohyang Biosphere Reserve covers the mountain areas of the Myohyang and Jokyuryong ranges on the left bank of the River Chongchon. The Myohyang Mountains debouch from Mount Rangrim and stretch north-east and south-west along the border of South Phyongan Province, linking Piro Peak (1,909 m) almost to Mount Sobak (2,014 m).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is bordered by a river or residential districts to the east, west and south, with the north connected to a mountain range that forms the ecological corridor. Elevations range from 100 m to 1,909 m. The landscape features granite–gneiss rock cliffs of the Cenozoic era formed by long-term erosion, as well as perennial streams fed by waterfalls. The Myohyang range runs along the River Chongchon in one direction and to the west in another, centred on Piro Peak. Soils are dark brown forest soils formed mainly from granite and granite–gneiss. The climate is continental with four distinct seasons; dry and rainy seasons are clearly marked, and a typical monsoon blows across the mountain.
records.name: Mount Myohyang

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve corresponds to the Altyn Emel State National Nature Park, one of the country’s protected areas and an important site for conserving the region’s biological diversity. It includes a large number of endemic plants. The site comprises deserts, riparian forests and floodplains of the Ili River, deciduous and spruce forests, as well as salt marshes. Residents live mainly from agriculture and cattle rearing, as well as ecotourism and recreational tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve lies in the central part of the Ili intermountain basin. According to natural physical and geographical zoning, the park area forms part of the Ili semidesert region of the Ili–Balkhash–Alakol desert depression. It is home to various mammals such as the muskrat, Turkmen kulan, Bukhara deer and the reintroduced Przewalski horse. The number of muskrats on the river floodplain and along the shores of the Kapchagai Reservoir is low due to sudden changes in water level. The number of kulans has exceeded 2,692. The Altyn Emel Biosphere Reserve also contains many rare and endangered animals, including two species of fish, two amphibians, one reptile, 11 mammals and 28 birds.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Altyn-Emel

records.introduction_en: Located in the most elevated part of the Central Kazakh Uplands, Burabay is best known for its many lakes. Fourteen of these cover a combined surface area of more than 100 km², and there are numerous smaller lakes. It is highly representative of the biodiversity of the forest–steppe Eurasian ecotone. In addition to agriculture and mining, the area has been a popular tourist destination since the establishment of the Shchuchinsk–Borovoye Resort Zone in 2005, owing to its proximity to densely populated regions in Kazakhstan and the Russian Federation and to good air, rail and road links.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The vegetation of the biosphere reserve is represented by six main types: forest, shrub, steppe, meadow, marsh and salt marsh. A significant area is occupied by pine forests (Pinus sylvestris), as well as birch–pine and pine–birch forests with Betula pendula and Betula pubescens. The vertebrate fauna includes 277 species belonging to 25 orders: 15 species and subspecies of fish, one species of amphibians, five species of reptiles, 209 species of birds and 47 species of mammals. This represents about 36 per cent of the total vertebrate fauna of Kazakhstan.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Burabay

records.introduction_en: Karatau is located in the central part of the Karatau ridge, a branch of the north-western Tien Shan, one of the world’s largest mountain ranges. With a total area of 151,800 ha, the reserve is an extremely important natural complex for the conservation of West Tien Shan biodiversity. By the number of its endemic species, Karatau ranks first among Central Asian regions. The regional economy is mostly based on cattle rearing, agriculture, ecotourism and recreational tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Karatau Biosphere Reserve lies in the central part of the Karatau ridge, a branch of the north-western Tien Shan, within South Kazakhstan region. It includes mountain arid and sub-arid ecosystems of the middle mountains of the Western Tien Shan. The area is characterised by flat tops and steep, deep canyons of temporary and permanent waterways, where rich tree–shrub and petrophyte vegetation with many relict and endemic elements is concentrated. Its flora has a high proportion of endemic species and subspecies, about 9 per cent of the total, due to the reserve’s relative isolation from other Tien Shan mountain systems, as it extends deep into the plains of the desert zone at the watershed of the Chu, Syrdarya and Talas rivers. One of the region’s most characteristic species is the Karatau goat (Ovis ammon nigrimontana).
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Karatau

records.introduction_en: Kolsai Kolderi lies on the northern Tien Shan mountain range in south-eastern Kazakhstan, mainly covering the Kungei Alatau range, with a smaller portion on the Trans-Ili Alatau range, from about 800 to 3,800 m. Broad uplands, jagged ridgelines and deep valleys frame a chain of lakes – Lower, Middle and Upper Kolsai, and Kaindy – formed by earthquake-triggered slides. The biosphere reserve conserves this full mountain–lake system and its Tien Shan endemics, safeguards glacier- and snow-fed headwaters and microclimate, restores forests and rangelands and supports low-impact livelihoods through zoning and managed nature-based tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Kolsai Kolderi presents a full mountain altitude sequence: shrub–grass steppes rise into a continuous belt of dark coniferous forest, then subalpine and alpine meadows, with bare rock and small glaciers at the highest elevations. Floristic richness is high, with over 500 vascular plant species, including numerous Tien Shan endemics. The reserve’s flagship tree is Schrenk’s spruce (Picea schrenkiana), a relict forming the core of the conifer belt with juniper, birch and aspen. Steppe and meadow communities host feather-grasses (Stipa), bluegrasses (Poa) and diverse forbs (non-woody flowering plants). Notable mammals include snow leopard (Panthera uncia), Tien Shan brown bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus) and Turkestan lynx (Lynx lynx isabellinus). Water shapes the system: snow and glacier melt drive the rivers and lakes, underpinning ecosystem processes and helping to stabilise the regional water balance and microclimate. The Shilik River is the largest river in the Northern Tien Shan, and originates from glaciers; its tributaries experience a prolonged spring–summer high-water period as meltwater descends from higher belts. Numerous cold groundwater springs emerge between roughly 1,540 and 2,850 m. Glaciers have retreated since the mid-twentieth century, increasing the number of moraine-dammed lakes and, with them, seasonal mudflow risk. Native fish diversity is naturally low in these cold, high-altitude waters. Some lakes now hold introduced rainbow trout.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Kolsai Kolderi

records.introduction_en: Located on the border of the Russian Federation, in the North-Eastern part of East Kazakhstan, the mountain-taiga forests of West Altai Biosphere Reserve are largely untouched. They include the only black taiga forests in the country, as well as Siberian and dark taiga. Wolverines and musk deer live in the biosphere reserve, which is on the seasonal migration routes of wild ungulates, such as elk, deer and wild boar. The local fauna includes more than 160 bird species, 129 of which nest in the region (black stork, golden eagle, peregrine falcon, gray crane, eagle owl). Mining and agriculture, mostly for wheat, potato, sunflower and beet crops, are the main economic activities in the biosphere reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The West Altai Biosphere Reserve in Kazakhstan is characterized by its mid-mountain taiga and high-mountain alpine landscapes within the steppe zone of temperate Eurasia. Distinctive features of the reserve include the alpine swamp complex Gulbische, the granite remnants of Linea Pillars, and the Big Turgusun River.West Altai supports a large variety of forest vegetation, including larch (Larix spp.) forests, dark coniferous mountain taiga, black taiga, cedar-larch mountain taiga, pine forests on granite (Pinus spp.), and spruce forests in river valleys (Picea spp.). Endemic flora in the region includes members of the families Salicaceae, Fabaceae, Scrophulariaceae, Ranunculaceae, Asteraceae, Rosaceae, Boraginaceae, and Poaceae.The reserve also hosts a diverse avifauna. Species such as black stork (Ciconia nigra), golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos), peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus), gray crane (Grus grus), and eagle owl (Bubo bubo) nest here. Seasonal migratory routes of elk (Alces alces), red deer (Cervus elaphus), roe deer (Capreolus capreolus), and wild boar (Sus scrofa) pass through the region, while taiga fauna such as wolverines (Gulo gulo) and musk deer (Moschus moschiferus) remain year-round.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: West Altai

records.introduction_en: Zhongar Biosphere Reserve lies on the northern slopes of the Zhetysu Alatau Range in south-eastern Kazakhstan. It incorporates the entire range of mountain ecosystems characteristic of Central Asia, spanning full altitudinal belts from lowland steppe and wild fruit forests to spruce stands, subalpine meadows and nival rock zones. The territory is of global importance as the location of the wild apple gene bank. The reserve’s core purpose is to conserve intact mountain ecosystems while supporting sustainable development in surrounding districts.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve protects a complete mountain gradient and the habitats that come with it: steppe grasslands, fruit woodlands, juniper thickets, Schrenk’s spruce forests, flower-rich subalpine turf and high rocky summits sustained by snow and glacial melt. Species richness is notable, with a strong share of endemics and many species listed in national Red Data Books as endangered or threatened. Wild fruit forests feature groves of Malus sieversii – the progenitor of cultivated apples worldwide – a genetic resource of global significance requiring dedicated protection. Avifauna spans steppe raptors, forest specialists and high-altitude breeders, reflecting the continuity of elevational habitats and likely migratory linkages across the range. Forests and alpine vegetation act as regional carbon stores and regulate water, with meltwater feeding rivers towards Lakes Balkhash, Sasykkol and Alakol. Under a sharply continental climate, these ecosystems buffer extremes, sustain downstream flows and provide a real-world setting to test and refine conservation approaches.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Zhongar

records.introduction_en: The Jabal Al Rihane Biosphere Reserve extends along the ridge of the southern Mount Lebanon chain, overlooking the Beqaa Valley to the east and the Mediterranean Sea to the west. Altitude ranges from 270 m in the south, where the Litani River forms a natural boundary, to 1,500 m in the north at Mzairaa, south of the villages of Jezzine and Niha.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is a mosaic of ecological systems broadly representing the evergreen sclerophyllous broussailles and forests biogeographic region within a Mediterranean biome. A dominant feature is the presence of many mountain peaks, including Jabal Safi (1,300 m), Jabal Sujud (1,200 m), Jabal Bir Kallab (1,360 m) and Jabal Bourqab (1,300 m). This mountainous relief gives rise to a number of eco-zones. From an aesthetic point of view, the landscape, dominated by peaks and basins, offers far-reaching views. Stands of old oak trees, more than 500 years old, are recognised as outstanding scenic landscapes.
records.name: Jabal Al Rihane

records.introduction_en: The Hurulu Biosphere Reserve primarily consists of tropical dry evergreen forest in Sri Lanka.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: A dry, monsoon-type climate prevails, with mean annual precipitation of 1,600 mm and a mean annual temperature of 27.3 °C. Dominant plant species are satinwood (Chloroxylon swietenia), palu (Manilkara hexandra) and the ebony tree (Diospyros ebenum). Among the most endangered animal species are the turtle (Testudo elegans), the Ceylon junglefowl (Gallus lafayettii), the elephant (Elephas maximus), the leopard (Panthera pardus) and the rusty-spotted cat (Felis rubiginosa).
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Hurulu

records.introduction_en: Sinharaja is the largest continuous evergreen rainforest remaining in the lowland wet zone of Sri Lanka.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Its importance for conservation is linked to its high endemism of flora and fauna. In 1971, 2,500 hectares of the Forest Reserve were transformed into an IUCN–IBP Strict Reserve with full protection for flora and fauna. In 1977, all timber exploitation in the entire forest was banned and, in 1978, it was designated as a MAB Biosphere Reserve.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Sinharaja

records.introduction_en: The Minett reserve in southern Luxembourg is the country’s first biosphere reserve and covers approximately one tenth of the country. It is home to the 80 km Red Rock Trail, named for its distinctive red surface and popular with hikers and cyclists. The reserve shares a border with France.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Minett Biosphere Reserve’s core area encompasses green valleys, sunny plateaux, extensive woodlands and striking cliffs. It combines its natural components with historical mines and urbanisation in a distinctive harmony. Watercourses and their immediate environments, including banks, wet meadows, reed beds and alluvial forests, form connecting corridors between distant biotopes and provide diverse habitats for many animal and plant species. The Minett region is one of Luxembourg’s most important wintering sites for bats, due to the extensive network of mine shafts and tunnels that remain from the mining era and shaped the landscape during exploitation. These sites lend themselves to swarming and wintering and are of both national and regional importance, with the region’s proximity to the border enabling transregional movements between bat populations.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Minett

records.introduction_en: The Ashaafean Biosphere Reserve lies in the municipality of Msallata, about 110 km south-east of Tripoli in Libya. Set in a mountainous landscape with varied topography under a Mediterranean climate, it contains biological values of regional, national and international importance, from endemic plants such as Linaria tarhunensis to notable fauna including the critically endangered Egyptian tortoise (Testudo kleinmanni). The reserve sits within a living cultural landscape shaped by ancient olive groves. The reserve aims to preserve this mountainous steppe environment while promoting sustainable local activities. Management seeks to foster sustainable economic and socio-cultural development by raising awareness among farmers and other land users, to ensure that agriculture and related activities remain ecologically sustainable.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve lies in a Mediterranean climate and includes mountains, valleys and small areas of plain. It spans dry woodlands and steppe grasslands that form an ecotone between the Mediterranean region to the north and the hyper-arid Sahara to the south. On the eastern extent of the Jabal Nefūsah Escarpment, Cenomanian dolomitic limestones with fertile clay-rich sediments shape cliffed slopes, rolling hills and dendritic wadis. This geodiversity underpins a mosaic of habitats, from local steppes dominated by esparto grass (Stipa tenacissima) to Aleppo pine (Pinus halepensis) woodlands, and sheltered valleys that allow deeper soils and more favourable microclimates for plant growth. Woody shrubs are a defining feature, many with aromatic or medicinal uses, including carob (Ceratonia siliqua), mastic (Pistacia lentiscus) and thyme (Thymus capitatus). Endemic plants such as Linaria tarhunensis and Amberboa libyca are key for genetic diversity, while ancient olives, local barley and wheat varieties play an important role for the area’s agricultural systems. Fauna of conservation concern include the striped hyena (Hyaena hyaena), Greek tortoise (Testudo graeca), houbara bustard (Chlamydotis undulata) and the critically endangered Egyptian tortoise (Testudo kleinmanni). Management priorities include tackling wildfire, curbing fuelwood collection and regulating the over-use of medicinal and aromatic plants to protect vegetation and soils.
records.name: Ashaafean

records.introduction_en: Situated on the western coast of Madagascar, the Belo-sur-Mer–Kirindy-Mite Biosphere Reserve comprises a watershed and a mosaic of rich but fragile ecosystems, including dry forests, thickets, thorn forests, savannahs, salty swampy depressions known as tannes, mangroves and coral reefs. The reef is a feeding area for spectacular marine megafauna, including the humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae), dolphins, dugong (Dugong dugon) and marine turtles. People in the area rely on these natural resources for their livelihoods and income. The site’s marine biodiversity, islands and two sacred saline lakes, home to the lesser flamingo (Phoenicopterus minor), are valuable assets for tourism. Aquaculture, pelagic fishing and salt production are also key areas of development.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area lies at the convergence of the western and southern Malagasy phytogeographical zones, resulting in high species diversity. It includes an upstream watershed together with downstream marine and coastal ecosystems. This terrestrial–marine landscape forms a diverse yet fragile mosaic of dry forests, thickets, thorn forests, savannahs, tannes, mangroves and coral reefs. Kirindy-Mite National Park lies within the core area and has the largest population of Adansonia grandidieri (about 500,000 trees), one of the seven Malagasy baobab species. Other common floral species include Madagascar rosewood (Dalbergia baronii), tamarind (Tamarindus indica) and Commiphora grandifolia. The reef is a feeding area for marine megafauna, notably the humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) and the dugong (Dugong dugon). The biosphere reserve also hosts several species endemic to Madagascar, including the fossa (Cryptoprocta ferox) and the narrow-striped mongoose (Mungotictis decemlineata), and supports endangered endemic species such as the Malagasy giant rat (Hypogeomys antimena), Madame Berthe’s mouse lemur (Microcebus berthae) and Verreaux’s sifaka (Propithecus verreauxi). The biosphere reserve also encompasses the Lacs arrière dunaires, designated as a Ramsar site.
records.name: Belo-sur-Mer - Kirindy-Mite

records.introduction_en: The Mananara Nord Biosphere Reserve comprises two major ecosystems, terrestrial and marine, both fundamental in providing food for the local population. The region has exceptional biological diversity with high rates of endemism. Since its designation in 1990, Mananara has served as a ‘multidisciplinary school’ of biodiversity preservation and socio-economic development, where managers, researchers and authorities work together on sustainable solutions.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Along the coast, the reserve features coral reefs with very rich biodiversity, including humpback whales, dolphins and turtles. Fishers have also reported the presence of vulnerable species such as the dugong (Dugong dugon). In the forest, the highest number of micro-mammals in the Eastern Ecoregion can be found, in particular a dozen lemur species, such as the aye-aye (Daubentonia madagascariensis). A recent study also recorded 77 bird species.
records.name: Mananara Nord

records.introduction_en: The Ohrid-Prespa Biosphere Reserve in North Macedonia joins with the Albanian biosphere reserve of the same name to form a transboundary biosphere reserve. The area combines water bodies with surrounding mountain reliefs, while flat areas mark the outer limits of the territories stretching across the two countries.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Ohrid–Prespa Transboundary Biosphere Reserve encompasses a significant range of ecological systems, from mountainous areas around the three lakes to temperate subtropical forests at lower altitudes around the water basins. Together, the Ohrid and Prespa lake system is one of the largest of its kind in Europe. Both lakes are of special value at national and international levels because of their geological and biological uniqueness. Lake Ohrid is famous for over two hundred endemic species, including diatoms, oligochaetes, leeches, poriferans, triclads, molluscs, ostracods and fish. Five of the endemic species are restricted to micro-ecosystems within the lake. Ten of the lake’s 17 fish species are endemic including the Ohrid trout (Salmo letnica) and Belvica acantolingua ohridana. There is also a unique, endemic forest community composed of Pinetum peuces, Paeonian Grecian juniper woods, Helleno-Moesian Quercus frainetto forests, and south-western Moesian fir beech forests. The Prespa region hosts original biotopes vital for preservation. These include extensive deciduous forests of Ostryo-Carpinion orientalis, evergreen box–juniper shrublands, evergreen coniferous forests consisting of 12 m-high Juniperus foetidissima and Juniperus excelsa, and the important endemic vegetation species of Ezerani. The protection of mammals is also crucial in the transboundary biosphere reserve. Notable species include the Balkan mole (Talpa stankovici), Balkan lynx (Lynx lynx martinoi), grey wolf (Canis lupus) and brown bear (Ursus arctos). The Balkan lynx is an exceptionally rare species of very high symbolic value. As for bird species, the Dalmatian pelican (Pelecanus crispus) is the reserve’s flagship species. In the Prespa region there are over 260 species of birds, … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Ohrid-Prespa

records.introduction_en: The Inlay Lake Biosphere Reserve is located in Taunggyi District, Southern Shan State. Inlay Lake is a freshwater lake and reportedly the second-largest inland lake in Myanmar. The Inlay Lake wetland ecosystem is home to 267 species of birds, of which 82 are wetland birds, and 43 species of freshwater fish, as well as otters and turtles. In addition, freshwater fish from the inland wetland constitute the major protein source for the people of Inlay. The reserve hosts diverse flora and fauna, and the lake is reported to be the nesting place for the globally endangered sarus crane (Grus antigone). Inlay Lake is also notable for the socio-cultural traditions of the local inhabitants, who have adapted their lifestyle and livelihoods to their biophysical environment. The majority earn their income from traditional methods of hydroponic farming, fishing and shifting cultivation. Farmers from one of the dominant ethnic groups in the Inlay Lake region, the Inthas, practise floating island agriculture, locally known as “Yechan”, a form of hydroponic farming.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Inlay Lake is a shallow lake located 884 metres above sea level in an elongated, flat-bottomed valley bordered by parallel mountains that rise to 1,500 metres and are covered by hill forest. The lake was formed more than 1.5 million years ago and is a remnant of a much more extensive series of lakes. These lakes formed as water dissolved limestone in the landscape, creating many limestone features such as caves, sinkholes, springs, spurs and intermittent streams. There are 29 streams in the watershed flowing into the lake, and Inlay Lake receives most run-off from four major sub-catchments containing 12 streams: Nanlet, Negya, Kalaw and Balu. The area consists of a network of freshwater wetlands and rivers and includes 527 species of medicinal plants, 11 species of bamboo, 184 species of orchids and 1,320 species of angiosperms (dicots). Fauna is diverse, and the lake is a nesting place for the globally endangered sarus crane (Grus antigone). Among the 16 endemic fish species, the Inlay carp (Cyprinus carpio intha) is culturally symbolic and important for consumption and household income. Species recorded include 267 bird species, 43 fish species, 10 reptile species, nine mammal species, three species of turtle, 75 species of butterfly and 20 species of snails. Notable examples include the monocled cobra (Naja kaouthia), pied kingfisher (Ceryle rudis), crested myna (Acridotheres cristatellus), large hawk-cuckoo (Hierococcyx sparverioides), large Indian civet (Viverra megaspila), Myanmar hare (Lepus peguensis) and golden jackal (Canis aureus).
records.name: Inlay Lake

records.introduction_en: The Baa Atoll Biosphere Reserve is in the central western Maldives in the Indian Ocean. The atoll lies just north of the Kashidhoo Kandhoo channel, which geographically divides the northern chain of atolls. It supports one of the largest groups of coral reefs in the Indian Ocean and acts as a stepping stone for the transport of planktonic larvae of reef organisms from the western and eastern Indian Ocean. The reserve is home to globally significant biodiversity across its numerous reefs and demonstrates a long history of human interaction with the environment.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Baa Atoll has a warm, humid tropical climate. The weather is dominated by two monsoon periods, a rainy monsoon from May to November and a dry monsoon from January to March. The dominant natural environment is marine, surrounded by deep ocean. Water depth varies considerably and includes lagoons ranging from 30–80 m, opening into the Indian Ocean. Channels running through the atoll may be 250–300 m deep. The lagoons enclose a variety of reef structures, including faros, micro-atolls, patch reefs and knolls. The main habitat types are coral reefs, islands, seagrass beds and mangroves. Coral reefs are the most important in terms of area and biodiversity. Maldivian coral reefs hold the richest diversity in the region and are the seventh largest in the world, accounting for about 5 per cent of the world’s reef area. The coral reefs support a high diversity of reef animals, including approximately 250 coral species, 1,200 reef and reef-associated fish species, marine turtles, manta rays (Manta birostris), whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) and seabirds. These also include threatened and endangered species such as the green turtle (Chelonia mydas), hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata), Napoleon wrasse (Cheilinus undulatus) and tawny nurse shark (Nebrius ferrugineus).
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Baa Atoll

records.introduction_en: Situated in the delta of the Senegal River, this transboundary biosphere reserve shows little variation in altitude. Its diversity derives from a vast hydrographic network divided into several basins. The landscape is very diverse and includes floodplains fed by water from the natural or artificial rising of the river, through hydraulic works, backwaters, lakes and the sea. Continental and coastal dunes slightly mark the relief. The floodplains are without vegetation in the dry season. The area’s conservation importance is evident in the great variety of protected areas designated here. Migratory birds find refuge in the delta, and more than 350 species have been recorded in the “Oiseaux du Djoudj” National Park, with a bird population of over 3 million from November to May.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The core areas of the biosphere reserve include national parks and nature reserves that are part of the national network of protected areas. These include the “Oiseaux du Djoudj” National Park in Senegal, which is also a World Heritage site and a Ramsar wetland, and the Diawaling National Park and the Chat TBoul Reserve in Mauritania, both Ramsar wetlands. The buffer zones are managed in accordance with their statutes, defined by the same texts as the core areas, except the Gandon Forest in Senegal, which is a community nature reserve. The transition area is public or state property and also includes private lands. In the delta, the agricultural landscape is dominated by irrigated rice farming and the cultivation of sugar cane. Livestock rearing, fishing and the harvesting of natural resources are also important human activities.
records.name: Delta du Fleuve Senegal

records.introduction_en: Located on the western side of the upper Bay of Fundy in New Brunswick, Canada, the area is renowned for its Acadian mixed wood forests, rugged coastline, extreme tidal ranges, salt marshes and tidal mudflats, as well as for its terrestrial and marine biodiversity. The area also has a rich cultural heritage that begins with the original Mi’kmaq Aboriginal inhabitants. The first settlers from France and other European countries during colonial times also influenced the shaping of the landscape, which is still evident today. The southern half of the area is one of the least developed on the east coast of North America, where steep, forested river valleys are deeply incised into the landscape, creating gorges with waterfalls, rapids and steep rock walls. Topographical elevations range from 30 m below sea level in the estuarine area to 400 m inland. At the head of the bay, a broad, gently undulating landscape features wide-ranging salt marshes along the coast.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The land area is defined by the watersheds and coastal areas that extend from St. Martin through to the Tantramar Marsh, which drains into the upper Bay of Fundy. The area is unique in its geological formations, terrestrial and marine ecosystems, cultural heritage, and its cross-section of rural communities and urban areas. The Bay of Fundy supports a wide diversity of plants and animals, and its scale enables a meaningful contribution to biodiversity conservation. Eight animal species are listed at risk, among them the bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus), Canada lynx (Lynx canadensis), eastern cougar (Puma concolor), harlequin duck (Histrionicus histrionicus) and peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Fundy

records.introduction_en: Located in Alberta in western Canada, this morainic landscape has characteristic boreal-zone features, including abundant wetlands, shallow lakes and rock formations, developed during the progressive retreat of glaciers about 12,000 years ago. Today, the biosphere comprises land modified by agriculture, mixed wood forests, grasslands and wetlands. The diversity of forest and upland habitats provides optimal conditions for bison, deer, elk and moose, supports diverse and abundant waterfowl, and sustains an abundant beaver population. Thirty-six plants and six plant communities within the moraine are considered sensitive due to limited distribution in the province.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Beaver Hills is a distinct geomorphological feature, a stagnant ice moraine that formed during the last glacial retreat. Earth and rock, deposited as the remnant ice blocks melted away, created a rolling landscape with distinctive ‘knob and kettle’ or hummocky terrain. Wetlands and shallow lakes fill the many depressions in these lands. Forests still cover much of the landscape, a result of limited development and past conservation action. The moraine is a disjunct area of the Dry Mixedwood Boreal Natural Subregion, which stretches across north-central Alberta. This southern extension forms an island totally enclosed by the Aspen Parkland Natural Subregion. It is characterised by aspen and balsam poplar forests with scattered patches of white spruce. Plant communities include a bog community consisting of Alaska birch (Betula neoalaskana) and common Labrador tea (Ledum groenlandicum), a native grassland community with western porcupine grass (Stipa curtiseta), a shrubland Saskatoon community (Amelanchier alnifolia) and two balsam poplar (Populus balsamifera) forest communities. The diverse habitats within the moraine support a broad assemblage of wildlife species. Out of a total of 439 wildlife species, the majority, 358 species, are birds. Mammals are the next most diverse group with 58 species. Due to the cold climate of central Alberta, only five amphibians, three reptiles and 15 butterflies (Lepidoptera) occur in the area. The diversity of forest and upland habitats provides optimal habitats for wood bison (Bison bison athabascae), plain bison (Bison bison bison), beaver (Castor canadensis), moose (Alces alces andersoni) and abundant waterfowl.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Beaver Hills

records.introduction_en: Bras d’Or Lake is in Nova Scotia and consists of a saltwater estuary watershed, an inland sea with three passages to the Atlantic Ocean. The Holocene transgression flooded a complex river–lake system of diverse geology, creating a small, deep inland sea with 12 significant watersheds that drain both highlands and lowlands. The terrestrial, marine and coastal habitats provide a home for human populations and rich biological diversity. The original settlers colonised the region following the retreat of glaciers. Today, their descendants make up the five Mi’kmaq populations that account for a significant proportion of the population occupying large areas of the watershed.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Bras d’Or Lake is an estuarine system located in the middle of Cape Breton Island. Cape Breton is a rugged and irregularly shaped island covering about 10,280 km2. It lies north-east of mainland Nova Scotia and is joined to the mainland by a 1.4 km causeway constructed in 1955. Differential erosion has resulted in steep hills around the lake and peninsulas within it. These features divide the estuarine ecosystem into five long, deep channels in the north half of the lake and a number of bays in the south. Along the west side of the watershed, steep hills rise abruptly to highland plateaux, the Cape Breton Highlands, at elevations of 250–300 m. Extensive wetland and bog deposits occur in the upper reaches of the watershed, specifically in the Cape Breton Highlands, the Boisdale Hills and the East Bay Hills. Large wetlands in the highland portions of the Middle River and Baddeck River serve to store and release water slowly to these major sub-watersheds within Bras d’Or Lake. The most common fish of the boreal group found in the area are cod (Gadus morhua), white hake (Urophycis tenuis) and winter skate (Raja ocellatus). Representatives of the Arctic-boreal group include alligatorfish (Aspidophoroides monopterygius) and daubed shanny (Lumpenus maculatus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Bras d'Or Lake

records.introduction_en: The Georgian Bay Biosphere Reserve comprises the largest island archipelago of the North American Great Lakes. Known locally as the Thirty Thousand Islands, it consists of a complex association of bays, inlets, sounds, islands and shoals along the edge of the Canadian Shield bedrock. Low-lying hills and ridges characterise the adjacent mainland. This topography supports a rich mosaic of forests, wetlands and rocky habitat types with associated biodiversity. The area is also noted for extraordinary scenic views, which attract large numbers of summer residents, cruising boaters and seasonal visitors.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The eastern coast of Georgian Bay has a complex topography and an extensive shoreline, along which lie numerous islands, deep coves, fjords and river mouths. It is thought to be the world’s largest freshwater archipelago. Habitats include open waters, sheltered bays, coastal wetlands, exposed bedrock shores, sandy and cobble beaches, riparian vegetation and upland boreal needleleaf forests on the mainland. Characteristic tree species include white spruce (Picea glauca), eastern white pine (Pinus strobus), white cedar (Thuja occidentalis) and red oak (Quercus rubra). The rich mosaic of interconnected habitats, combined with the inaccessibility of much of the area, supports and protects a high level of biodiversity. The reserve hosts over 100 species of animals and plants considered to be species at risk in Canada. These include reptiles such as the eastern massasauga rattlesnake (Sistrurus c. catenatus) and spotted turtle (Clemmys guttata). Larger mammals that range over broad areas include moose (Alces alces), black bear (Ursus americanus), river otter (Lontra canadensis) and snowshoe hare (Lepus americanus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Georgian Bay

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is located on the east coast of Vancouver Island in British Columbia. It is close to the Clayoquot Sound Biosphere Reserve, located on the other side of the island. Situated in the Coastal Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii) biogeoclimatic zone, the forests in the area were logged in the early 1900s. Today, second-growth trees are reaching harvestable size, which leads to pressures from the logging industries.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Mount Arrowsmith Biosphere Reserve includes the entire watershed draining the area. Management focuses on the maintenance of healthy aquatic, coastal estuarine and intertidal ecosystems. Because the health of these ecosystems is directly influenced by the integrity of streams and rivers flowing into them, these have been defined as the buffer zone. The area is under continuous urban development pressures. The biosphere reserve concept is believed to provide an ideal framework within which to address the complex problems facing Mount Arrowsmith today. The area is on the Pacific migratory bird flyway and includes critical migration and wintering habitats for many avian species. The endangered Vancouver Island marmot (Marmota vancouverensis) and Vancouver Island white-tailed ptarmigan (Lagopus leucura vancouverensis) occur in alpine habitats, and two endemic species of stickleback occur in one freshwater lake.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mount Arrowsmith

records.introduction_en: Redberry Lake Biosphere Reserve covers 112,200 ha in the province of Saskatchewan, south-west Canada. The regional landscape is composed of rolling prairie dotted with seasonal ponds and marshes, along with aspen and shrub groves. The core area is a saline lake with several islands. There are small patches of natural mixed prairie, which are very rare in this highly grazed and cultivated part of the prairies.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Redberry Lake is a closed basin in which water entering the lake does not pass out through downstream flows. The lake is a large kettle hole characterised by a central flat bottom. Gently shelving underwater slopes occur above depths of approximately 25 m. Water is shallowest in the south-west, south-east and north-east areas, and around the islands. There are small patches of natural mixed prairie, which are very rare in this highly grazed and cultivated part of the prairies. Major habitats and land cover types include typical prairie grasses such as wheat grass, fescue, oat grass and sedges, and forest dominated by aspen with shrubs such as silver willow and hawthorn. They also include a saline lake with rocky islands, farmland cultivated with wheat and barley, and pastureland. The reserve provides habitats for nine endangered, threatened or rare bird species, as well as over 180 other species, including the white-winged scoter (Melanitta fusca), California gull (Larus californicus), ring-billed gull (Larus delawarensis) and piping plovers (Charadrius melodus). A key research activity undertaken in the area is monitoring of American white pelican (Pelecanus erythrorhynchos) nesting sites.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Redberry Lake

records.introduction_en: The Southwest Nova Biosphere Reserve is located in the south-western portion of the peninsular Province of Nova Scotia in eastern Canada. The region is bound to the north by the Bay of Fundy, which has the world’s highest tides, and to the east by the North Atlantic Ocean. The majority of the terrestrial land base has been designated a biosphere reserve zone of cooperation comprising five counties, Annapolis, Digby, Queens, Shelburne and Yarmouth.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Southwest Nova represents the natural region of south-western Nova Scotia. The biosphere reserve includes major provincial landscapes that remain in a near-pristine condition, with intact ecosystem structures, processes and functions. Forests in the area are part of the Acadian Forest region, one of eight forest types in Canada. Tree species include red spruce, white spruce, white pine, eastern hemlock and larch, interspersed with red maple, red oak, sugar maple, white birch and white ash. Harvesting, fire, insects and storms all play major roles in influencing succession. While much of the biodiversity is typical of the boreal and mixed-wood forest, areas with warmer microclimates support southern-originating coastal plain flora and fauna, including water-pennywort (Hydrocotyle ranunculoides), Blanding’s turtle (Emydoidea blandingii), northern ribbon snake (Thamnophis sauritus septentrionalis) and southern flying squirrel (Glaucomys volans). The complex includes two large, protected areas, Kejimkujik National Park and National Historic Site, and the Tobeatic Wilderness Area, located in the core of the biosphere reserve and characterised by a high standard of biodiversity protection. Kejimkujik National Park has also served as a site for intensive research for several years because of its unique flora and fauna, and as an important national monitoring site for long-range transported air pollutants since 1977. Accordingly, there is strong collaboration among land users and local and regional educational institutions for environmental research and monitoring. Migratory bird sanctuaries exist along the coast in Queens and Shelburne counties, and the Bay of Fundy tidal flats provide critical migratory bird-feeding habitats for many species.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Southwest Nova

records.introduction_en: Waterton Biosphere Reserve is located at the extreme south-west of the Province of Alberta and encompasses some of the most spectacular and ecologically diverse landscapes in the Canadian Rocky Mountains and prairie grasslands. Together with Glacier Biosphere Reserve in neighbouring Montana, USA, it encompasses the Waterton–Glacier International Peace Park, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1995, and sits at the core of the Crown of the Continent, a large, relatively intact transboundary ecosystem in North America.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Alberta’s Rocky Mountain, Parkland and Grassland Natural Regions are all represented within Waterton Biosphere Reserve. Steep environmental gradients from the Continental Divide (2,910 m) to the prairies (960 m), the competing influences of Pacific maritime and Arctic continental air masses, and the varied aspects of the mountain terrain create a rich mosaic of habitats and associated flora and fauna. Several rare or threatened plant and animal species occur here. More than 1,000 vascular plant species, 182 bryophytes, 218 lichen species, 60 mammals, over 260 birds, 24 fish, and 10 reptiles and amphibians have been recorded within the ecologically diverse core area. All three subregions of the Rocky Mountain Natural Region are present. The Alpine Subregion (above 2,250 m) comprises treeless tundra with hardy, low-growing plants. Below this, the Subalpine Subregion (1,680–2,250 m) features distinctive krummholz (stunted, wind-shaped trees) at upper elevations, giving way to open forest with whitebark pine (Pinus albicaulis) and subalpine larch (Larix lyallii), and, in the lower subalpine, moist, cool Engelmann spruce (Picea engelmannii)–subalpine fir (Abies lasiocarpa) forest. The Montane Subregion (1,280–1,680 m), below the subalpine, comprises a mix of dry grasslands and relatively open stands of trembling aspen (Populus tremuloides) with conifers, typically Douglas fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), limber pine (Pinus flexilis) and lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta).
