Along the mountain foot lies a narrow band of the Foothills Parkland Subregion, with rough fescue (Festuca campestris) meadows intermingled with trembling aspen groves and a rich understorey of shrubs and forbs. Further east, this parkland transitions to the prairie grassland of the Foothills Fescue … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Waterton

records.introduction_en: The Albay Biosphere Reserve is at the southern end of Luzon Island in the Philippines. Terrestrial elevation culminates at 2,462 m, and the marine area reaches a depth of 223 m below sea level. The site has high conservation value, notably with 182 terrestrial plant species, 46 of which are endemic. Its marine and coastal ecosystems contain 12 mangrove species, 40 species of seaweed or macroalgae, and 10 species of seagrass. Five of the world’s seven marine turtle species are also found in Albay. Agriculture is the main source of income in the area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Albay Biosphere Reserve is in south-eastern Luzon in the Philippines. Its inland areas are mainly open habitats, grasslands and forests, while its coastline includes mangrove forest, urban centres and agricultural land. It is home to three mountains including Mt Mayon, the Philippines’ most active volcano, which rises to 2,462 m above sea level. The reserve contains 182 terrestrial plant species, 46 of which are endemic. It also hosts four endemic mammal species and 12 endemic bird species, including the famous Luzon bleeding heart (Gallicolumba luzonica). There are 17 species of amphibians, 13 of which are endemic, and 30 species of reptiles, 22 of which are endemic. In addition, Albay’s marine and coastal ecosystems are home to 62 plant species. These represent 62.5 per cent of all known species in the Philippines. Five of the world’s seven marine turtle species occur here. The diversity of seagrass, seaweed beds and mangrove forests is intrinsically linked with the diversity of faunal species found across the marine and coastal ecosystems, particularly in the marshlands or mangroves. The marine and coastal fauna encompasses 272 species, including 158 gastropod species, 15 bivalve species, 12 crustacean species, 13 echinoderm species, one sea slug species, 26 coral species and 42 fish species.
records.name: Albay

records.introduction_en: Straddling the Cameroon–Nigeria border within the Guinean Forests of West Africa, the Takamanda–Cross River Gorilla Biosphere Reserve protects one of the most critically endangered great apes on Earth.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Its mosaic of lowland rainforests, montane cloud forests and riparian corridors shelters approximately one-third of the entire global population of the Cross River gorilla, a subspecies whose survival depends on the ecological integrity of this forested landscape. Its mosaic of lowland rainforests, montane cloud forests and riparian corridors shelters approximately one-third of the entire global population of the Cross River gorilla, a subspecies whose survival depends on the ecological integrity of this forested landscape. The biosphere reserve also harbours the endangered drill monkey and Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzee, forest elephants, and over 950 plant species, many of them endemic.
records.name: Takamanda-Cross River Gorilla

records.introduction_en: The Dja Biosphere Reserve is located in the south of Cameroon and encompasses a variety of geographic and climatic zones that contribute to its high biodiversity. The area consists mainly of dense evergreen Congo rainforest and hosts a wide range of primate species. The Dja forest remains an important refuge for many plant and animal species, such as the moabi tree (Baillonella toxisperma). The harvesting of plants for domestic or pharmaceutical use constitutes a key source of income.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Dja Biosphere Reserve is located between the forests of southern Nigeria and the forests of the Congo Basin, encircled by the Dja river. The area’s relief is mainly flat and consists of a succession of round-topped hills. The biosphere reserve has a dense evergreen Congo rainforest dominated by the Sapotaceae family of flowering plants, including Afrostyrax lepidophyllus, Anopyxis klaineana and Anthonotha ferruginea, as well as swamps, old secondary forest around villages and Gilbertiodendron dewevrei forest. The richness and diversity of orchids is particularly noteworthy. The biosphere reserve hosts a rich diversity of fauna including 109 mammal species, 360 bird species and 61 fish species. It is also home to the world’s most important colony of grey-necked rockfowls (Picathartes oreas), with 50 active nests on the same rocky cliff. Important mammals in the reserve include the chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes), elephant (Loxodonta africana cyclotis), mantled guereza (Colobus guereza), leopard (Panthera pardus) and the critically endangered western lowland gorilla (Gorilla gorilla gorilla). The ECOFAC Programme (Conservation et utilisation rationnelle des Écosystèmes Forestiers d'Afrique Centrale – Conservation and rational use of Central African Forest Ecosystems) of the European Union, which began in 1993, supported studies on the plant and animal biodiversity of Dja. It has established an important training centre for capacity-building purposes and supplied equipment for the UNESCO MAB Project situated in Mékas village.
records.name: Dja

records.introduction_en: The fourth biosphere reserve to be designated in Cameroon, Doumba-Rey Biosphere Reserve is best known for its bird population and exceptionally diverse flora. Located in the transition area between savannahs and forests, the reserve plays an important role in carbon sequestration and hosts emblematic species, including elephants. There are some 60 villages in the biosphere reserve whose inhabitants are mainly Gbaya, Mboum and Mbéré peoples. The area is also used by Fulani and nomadic shepherds, engaged in pastoral activities, including sedentary and transhumant livestock breeding.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Due to its geographical location, straddling the boundaries of the North and Adamaoua regions, the Doumba-Rey Biosphere Reserve is a transitional zone with a fragile ecology that contains species from both forest and savannah ecosystems such as forest galleries, wooded savannah and shrub savannah. It plays an important role in carbon sequestration. A survey of the fauna revealed nearly 25 species of mammals divided into six orders, including the elephant (Loxodonta africana), the hippopotamus (Hippopotamus amphibius), the pangolin (Smutsia gigantea), the aardvark (Orycteropus afer), the Buffon’s kob (Kobus kob kob), the harnessed guib (Tragelaphus scriptus) and various carnivores. It is an important area for bird conservation, containing over 100 species, 10 of which are protected. In terms of plant life, the area abounds in exceptional diversity. The most abundant species include Anogeissus leiocarpus, Isoberlinia doka, Uapaca togoensis and Isoberlinia tomentosa.
records.name: Doumba-Rey

records.introduction_en: The Chréa Biosphere Reserve is located 50 km south-west of the capital, Algiers, along the northern and southern ridges of the Blida section of the Atlas Mountains.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The site plays a vital role in the area, notably as a water reservoir for large cities like Algiers, Blida and Médéa. It is also important from a conservation perspective, with rare and endangered ecosystems specific to the northern Atlas Mountains. The national park hosts 1,210 plant and animal species, such as the Atlas cedar (Cedrus atlantica) and the monkey (Macaca sylvanus).
records.name: Chrea

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is situated in the Djurdjura Mountains, at 800–2,300 m above sea level, on the Mediterranean coast in north-east Algeria. It is influenced by a Mediterranean climate, with a more continental climate in the south.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Depending on exposure and elevation, habitats include Mediterranean evergreen, deciduous and coniferous forests, as well as alpine meadows. Because of the marked climatic and topographic differences, the area is very rich in species diversity and hosts a number of endemic species. The M'Zaris Forest is habitat for the striped hyena (Hyaena hyaena). The relict species black pine (Pinus nigra) has been studied for its natural regeneration potential. Habitats include Mediterranean evergreen forests with oak, including Quercus ilex and Q. suber, and Mediterranean deciduous forests with Acer obtusatum, A. monspessulanum, A. campestre and Prunus avium. Mediterranean coniferous forests feature Cedrus atlantica, Pinus nigra, P. halepensis and Taxus baccata, and mountainous grasslands are characterised by Rumex acetosella, Scrophularia laevigata and Ononis aragonensis.
records.name: Djurdjura

records.introduction_en: El Kala Biosphere Reserve encompasses the largest national park in the north of Algeria, covering over 70,000 hectares.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The El Kala Biosphere Reserve is the last refuge of the Barbary red deer (Cervus elaphus barbarus) and is home to remarkable bird life, hosting more than 60,000 migratory birds every winter. While the El Mellah Lagoon has been listed an internationally important Ramsar wetland, lakes Tonga and Oubiara are also of international renown due to their support for vast biodiversity. The reserve is a mosaic of marine, dune, lake and forest ecosystems. Its marine strip is rich in corals, Posidonia meadows and fish.
records.name: El Kala

records.introduction_en: Spanning nearly 875,000 hectares at the crossroads of the Zagros Mountains and the Iranian Central Plateau, the Dalankuh–Qamishlou Biosphere Reserve encompasses a dramatic altitudinal range, from alpine peaks above 4,000 metres to semi-arid foothill steppes.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Its mountain pastures, rocky slopes, steppe grasslands and riparian habitats support the Persian leopard, wild goat, Isfahan ram and goitered gazelle, as well as an exceptional array of raptors including the golden eagle, imperial eagle and peregrine falcon.
records.name: Dalankuh-Qamishlou

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve covers part of the Kopet Dag mountain range along the Islamic Republic of Iran’s border with Turkmenistan. The ecological region of Kopet Dag is an important part of the Irano-Anatolian biodiversity hotspot. Its primary function is the conservation of many of the endangered species in this area. The main economic activities are agriculture and livestock.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Kopet Dag is a chain of mountains between the Balkans and the plateaus of Iran and Turan. It consists of two mountain ranges with a parallel extent. Together, they cover a large surface area. The northern range consists of the Kopet Dagh and Hezar Masjed mountains, and the southern range consists of the Golestan, Aladagh and Binaloud mountains. The Mashhad, Quchan, Shirvan, Bojnourd and Garmab plains are located between these two mountain ranges. These ranges join in the west. The Sarakhs Plain is located in the eastern part of the region, on the margin of the Turkmenistan Plain and the Karakum Desert. The Gorgan Plain is located on the eastern side of the Caspian Sea. Mountain forests and woodland cover most of the site, accounting for 79.6 per cent of the area. The mountain corridor has probably been a breeding centre in the area since the Pleistocene era. There are 169 important plant species and 52 major animal species occurring in the area, including many endemic species. Fauna and flora from Mesopotamia that have not been able to withstand droughts in adjacent low-altitude areas occur here. The varied biodiversity is directly involved in the provision of ecosystem services. For example, aromatic plants, including Ferula, are common food resources. Juniper woods (Juniperus) can be used as fuel. Bees and wild pollinating insects play a crucial role in agricultural crop pollination.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Kopet Dag

records.introduction_en: Located in the south-east of Iran, the Hamoun Biosphere Reserve includes both terrestrial and wetland ecosystems. It encompasses seven habitat types, ranging from desert and semi-desert areas to Hamoun Lake with its marshlands and watersheds. The three wetlands of the biosphere reserve are the most important in the region. The area is also a hotspot for migratory birds, with 183 species, and is home to 30 mammal species and 55 plant species. The cultural value of the site is heightened by important historical monuments and ancient temples, such as Mount Kooh Khajeh and Shahr-e-Soukhteh.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The natural borders of the biosphere reserve in the south are Mount Malek Siah and the ridge of Mount Malek Siah, which form the joint border between Afghanistan, Iran and Pakistan. Mount Chehel-dokhtaran and Mount Palang Kooh constitute the natural limits of the western part of the reserve at altitudes ranging from 1,500 m to 2,000 m. The reserve is located in the heart of the desert and semi-desert areas of Afghanistan and Iran. Lake Hamoun, a freshwater lake, encompasses marshlands, the watersheds of rivers, canebrakes, algae, insects and several fish species, especially during high-water periods. The reserve is also a hotspot for hundreds of migratory birds, especially wader and water species in eastern Iran. The area is of substantial ecological value due to the important role it plays in protecting landscapes, ecosystems, species and the genetic resources of the region. The region is home to 55 plant species belonging to 20 families, mostly Chenopodiaceae and Gramineae. Regarding fauna, the area hosts 30 mammal species belonging to 17 families, as well as 183 bird species and 44 reptile species belonging to nine families. There are seven amphibian species and 22 fish species belonging to four families. Examples include the striped hyena (Hyaena hyaena), the caracal (Felis caracal), the desert monitor (Varanus griseus) and the Dalmatian pelican (Pelecanus crispus). Lake Hamoun is the biggest freshwater lake located on Iran’s plateau and is internationally registered under the Ramsar Wetland Convention.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Hamoun

records.introduction_en: The Lake Oromeeh Biosphere Reserve is located at Lake Oromeeh in the north of Iran and forms part of the Caucasus–Iranian Highlands. Salt flats fringe the lakeshore, while the islands host pistachio forests and Artemisia steppe communities. Other habitats found in the reserve include wetlands, river estuaries, and sandy soils and coasts.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Lake Oromeeh Biosphere Reserve is one of the most important and valuable aquatic ecosystems in the country. The lake is surrounded by several freshwater wetlands, creating an area of high ecological significance. Lake Oromeeh is also the largest water body of its kind in the country and is listed as a Ramsar site for its unique natural and ecological values. Around 177 flora species have been identified around the reserve, and approximately 174 flora species are found on the islands. Among the major plant families around the lake are the Asteraceae family, which includes 33 species, and the Poaceae family, which includes 21 species. The lake and its surrounding wetlands constitute the main habitat for large algae populations, which play an important role in the lake’s food chain. For this reason, Lake Oromeeh is home to many migratory birds during the winter months. In addition, the islands provide habitats for a large number of breeding flamingos (Phoenicopterus roseus) and white pelicans (Pelecanus onocrotalus), while 11 aquatic bird species in the region are at risk of extinction. The southern islands also provide habitats for two endangered mammals, the Iranian fallow bear and the Armenian mouflon (Ovis orientalis gmelini).
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Lake Oromeeh

records.introduction_en: The Touran Biosphere Reserve is located in the Anatolian Iranian deserts, and comprises a variety of salt, gypsum, stone and sandy habitats. It covers clay lowlands and mountains, reaching altitudes of more than 2,200 m above sea level. Communities in the area depend mostly on agriculture, animal husbandry, horticulture and carpet sewing. Major human impacts on the ecosystem arise from overgrazing, especially by camels, illegal hunting and fuelwood harvesting.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Touran Biosphere Reserve is the largest complex of protected areas in Iran, covering around 1,459,506.2 hectares. The reserve lies to the south of Shahroud County in Semnan Province, with a smaller section situated to the south-east of Khorasan Province. The climate of the region is cold arid, as determined by the Ambrege method. The area encompasses mountains, ridges, plains, sand dunes and sand sheets. Wild mammals are currently the most important fauna in the reserve. Because mammals are strongly dependent on their environment, they are treated as indicators of their habitats. Forty-one mammal species live in the Touran area. Key species include the Asian cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus), the Iranian zebra (Equus hemionus) and the Turkestan sand cat (Felis margarita). Other key species include two birds, namely the Iranian ground jay (Podoces pleskei) and the houbara bustard (Chlamydotis undulata), as well as the monitor lizard (Varanus griseus).
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Touran

records.introduction_en: Located in Mongolia's South Gobi Province, the Tost Toson Bumbiin Nuruu Biosphere Reserve sits at a dramatic meeting of rugged mountain ranges and vast desert steppe. It is a landscape of extremes, where summer temperatures reach 40°C, and winters plunge to -35°C.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Connecting the Gobi Gurvansaikhan National Park and the Great Gobi Protected Area, it forms a critical wildlife corridor supporting one of the highest snow leopard densities in Mongolia, alongside ibex, argali, goitered gazelle and the Asiatic wild ass. Since 2008, a long-term ecological study has tracked the snow leopard population through camera traps and community-based monitoring, one of the most sustained research programmes on this elusive species anywhere in the world.
records.name: Tost, Toson Bumbiin Nuruu

records.introduction_en: Bogd Khan Uul Biosphere Reserve is located to the south of Ulanbaatar, in the southernmost forest steppe zone and the Khentei Mountain area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The northern slopes of the mountains are covered by dense coniferous forest, and the southern slopes by bare rocks. Among the most threatened animal species in the biosphere reserve are the musk deer (Moschus moschiferus), roe deer (Capreolus capreolus), sable (Martes zibellina) and Arctic hare (Lepus timidus). Nature conservation dates to the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, when Tooril Khan of the Khereid Aimag designated Bogd Khan as a holy mountain and prohibited logging and hunting.
records.name: Boghd Khan Uul

records.introduction_en: Situated in the eastern corner of Mongolia, this biosphere reserve covers a representative portion of one of the largest intact grassland ecosystems in the world. It lies on the Mongolian Plateau at an average altitude of about 800 m above sea level. Its main characteristic is rolling steppe that extends for more than 200 km along the Chinese border. The landscape is formed by gently rolling hills, with scattered mountains and sand dunes unique to the region.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area is rich in biodiversity, encompassing elements of the Siberian taiga and Manchurian flora and fauna, and is dominated by Central Asian steppes. Some of the largest remaining herds of Mongolian gazelle can be found in the region. These herds make up the largest remaining ungulate population in Asia. Dornod Mongol is home to several globally rare or threatened bird species and also hosts typical Central Asian fauna and flora in relatively natural settings compared with other Asian steppe ecosystems.
records.name: Dornod Mongol

records.introduction_en: The Hustai Nuruu Biosphere Reserve lies about 100 km south-west of Ulaanbaatar. It comprises mainly steppe ecosystems, with some taiga forests and alpine vegetation. The reserve aims to preserve threatened steppe and forest steppe ecosystems that elsewhere have been degraded by over-exploitation. It is also noted for the successful reintroduction of the endemic Przewalski’s horse (Equus przewalskii). This horse became extinct in the wild in the 1960s and now helps to restore the steppe ecosystem. As a flagship species, it also increases environmental awareness across Mongolia.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Habitats include steppe and mountain steppe characterised by Stipa krylovii, Cleistogenes squarrosa, Poa attenuata and Cymbaria dahurica, and mountainous steppe with Festuca lenensis, Chamaerhodos altaica and Orostachys spinosa. Forests are characterised by Betula platyphylla and Populus tremula. Floodplain and riverine forests include Salix ledebouriana, Agrostis mongolica and Poa subfastigiata. The landscape also features grazing areas and agricultural areas.
records.name: Hustai Nuruu

records.introduction_en: Khuvsgul Lake Biosphere Reserve lies in northern Mongolia and is named after Mongolia’s deepest and clearest lake, which holds the majority of Mongolia’s freshwater. The site comprises high mountain and taiga landscapes and has rich biodiversity, supporting a number of threatened species such as the Siberian ibex (Capra sibirica). The designation of the site as a biosphere reserve supports conservation of biodiversity and landscapes, sustainable development for local communities, and research and education within a long-term protected area framework.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve lies in a high-mountain landscape with rivers, wetlands and extensive uninhabited areas. Key ecosystems include floodplain meadows, dense taiga and forest-steppe. Khuvsgul Lake has been in its present form for seven to eight million years. Ninety-six rivers and streams flow in and a single river, the Eg River, flows out, so water exchange is very slow. Its waters support nine fish species, including lenok (Brachymystax lenok), Mongolian grayling (Thymallus nigrescens) and burbot (Lota lota). Surrounding habitats range from tundra to forest-steppe and support rare and emblematic mammals such as snow leopard (Panthera uncia), red deer (Cervus elaphus), reindeer (Rangifer tarandus) and Siberian ibex (Capra sibirica). Birdlife is abundant across mountains, forests and wetlands, with species of national conservation concern including the white-tailed eagle, osprey and whooper swan. The taiga and mountain slopes support diverse higher plants, medicinal species and lichens, with many taxa listed nationally for protection.
records.name: Khuvsgul Lake

records.introduction_en: Located in north-eastern Mongolia, in a transition zone between forest steppe and grassland ecosystems, the area is designated as a nature reserve. It protects low mountains, rolling hills and dry steppe ecosystems that are the habitat of the Mongolian gazelle and other wildlife. The Toson Khulstai Reserve spans two provinces, Dornod and Khentii. It includes parts of five soum units: Bayan Ovoo, Norovolin, Khulun Buir, Tsagaan Ovoo and Byantumen.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve aims to protect low mountains, rolling hills and dry steppe ecosystems that are the habitat of the Mongolian gazelle and other wildlife. Notable species include the globally endangered white-naped crane, the upland buzzard, the steppe eagle and the Siberian marmot. According to Udvardy’s biogeographical classification, published in 1975 by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources, Toson Khulstai Nature Reserve is included in the Mongolian–Manchurian Steppe of the Palaearctic Realm. The biome is temperate grassland.
records.name: Toson-Khulstai

records.introduction_en: Perched at the eastern tip of Timor Island, the Nino Konis Santana Biosphere Reserve is Timor-Leste's first, and a landmark designation for one of Southeast Asia's most ecologically significant landscapes. Sitting at the intersection of the Wallacea biodiversity hotspot and the Coral Triangle, it holds the country's largest remaining primary forest, coral reefs sheltering some 500 fish species. Lake Iralalaro, the most significant freshwater site in Timor-Leste and Nusa Tenggara, is home to 50 waterbird species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve harbours 168 bird species representing 87% of the Wallacean avifauna, including the critically endangered Yellow-crested Cockatoo, alongside the snake-necked turtle (believed extinct and rediscovered here) and endemic bats, four of which may be new to science.
records.name: Nino Konis Santana

records.introduction_en: Mao’er Mountain Biosphere Reserve features a mountain landscape of exceptional scenic beauty, with peaks reaching over 2,000 m above sea level.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Mao’er Mountain Biosphere Reserve is located in north-east Guilin in the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, with a total area of 17,008.5 ha. It targets the conservation of a primary subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest ecosystem, nationally protected flora and fauna, and the water conservation forest at the source of the Li River. Mao’er Mountain, the highest peak in the Nanling and in South China, is 2,141.5 m above sea level. Mao’er Mountain has dense forest vegetation, a well-developed surface water system, and high water–conservation capacity. It is the source of the Li, Zi and Xun rivers, and lies on the watershed between the Yangtze and Pearl River basins. The forest–marsh wetland within the subtropical evergreen–deciduous broad-leaved mixed forest at Bajiaotian, Mao’er Mountain, is unique. The reserve lies in the transition zone between maritime and continental climates and is characterised by a humid, mid-subtropical mountainous monsoon climate. It sits at the boundary between the middle- and south-subtropical zones. The vegetation is transitional between montane Castanopsis–Schima limestone forest and the Nanling Castanopsis–Altingia chinensis forest. Biogeographically, it falls within the subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest zone, specifically the eastern humid broad-leaved subzone and the southern sector of the mid-subtropical evergreen broad-leaved belt. Owing to topographic effects, the reserve supports diverse vegetation types with a well-developed altitudinal sequence, rich forest landscapes and numerous rare species. Notably, Fagus longipetiolata, Abies ziyuanensis, Tsuga chinensis, Tsuga longibracteata and Pinus kwangtungensis are well preserved here.
records.name: Mao'er mountains

records.introduction_en: Gaoligong Mountain is located in the Sichuan Highlands in the southern part of China. Its highest elevations exceed 4,000 metres, and this upper part of the mountain is designated as the core area. Evergreen broad-leaved forests, deciduous forests and bamboo woodlands are characteristic of the region. Because the area is difficult to reach, the forests and wildlife are well protected. The reserve is also known for its rich history and diverse national customs.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Mountains in the biosphere reserve have been subject to many orogenic cycles, including rises and falls, folding, faulting, denudation and planation. After planation at the beginning of the Cenozoic era, the mountains were uplifted again under the impact of the Himalayan orogenic cycle. The highest peak in the area, Gawagapu Peak, reaches 5,126 metres, and the lowest point is 600 metres at Nujiang. The mountainous region has a complex internal structure, including high mountains influenced by glaciers and tundra, a subalpine zone shaped by both water flow and glaciers, middle mountains influenced mainly by water flow, valley alluvial fans and terrace land along the valleys, as well as glacial and tundra landforms. The main habitat types in the reserve are forests, grasslands, rocky streams, rivers and lakes. Forest land covers 90.4 per cent of the total area. Abundant plant resources have been recorded here, including 4,897 species and varieties, and 1,196 genera in 256 families of higher plants. There are also 699 kinds of vertebrates, including 154 species of mammals, 419 species of birds, 21 species of amphibians, 56 species of reptiles and 49 species of fish, as well as 1,690 kinds of insects.
records.name: Gaoligong mountains

records.introduction_en: Huanglong Biosphere Reserve is situated in a mountainous area with peaks reaching up to 5,588 m above sea level. The area is recognised as a biodiversity hotspot, with part of it inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1992. Major wild animal species include the giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca), Rhinopithecus roxellanaand the leopard (Panthera pardus fusca). It is also scenically remarkable, with a system of some 3,400 travertine pools linked by travertine shoals, rapids and waterfalls. Reverence for the natural world among local communities, particularly among Tibetan people, has played an essential role in protecting the ecological environment and biodiversity in the reserve and surrounding areas.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve lies in the transition zone on the steep slope between two geomorphological units, the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau and the Sichuan Basin. Its eastern terrain tilts from north-west towards south-east, while its western part tilts from east to west. The reserve stands on the watershed between the Minjiang and Fujiang rivers, with fragmented terrain and substantial elevation changes. The maximum elevation is 5,588 m at Xuebaoding Peak, and the minimum is 1,700 m at the pass of Xigou Valley. The topography is characterised by numerous mountain peaks and deep canyons, broadly divided into three sectors: the Hongxingyan rock–glacial mountain sector, the Huanglong rocky sector shaped by karst water erosion, and the Xuebaoding Peak glacial mountain sector. The biosphere reserve is known for its distinctive karst landscape and abundant natural resources. Vegetation cover is about 89.9 per cent. There are 91 families, 241 genera and 520 species of vascular plants in the biosphere reserve. The giant panda, golden snub-nosed monkey (Rhinopithecus roxellana), Taxus chinensis and other nationally important protected wildlife have received effective protection, and the ecosystem has remained stable over the past decade.
records.name: Huanglong

records.introduction_en: Jinggangshan Nature Reserve was established in 1981 as a provincial nature reserve and was reclassified as a National Nature Reserve in 2000. It has been incorporated as a China Biosphere Reserve and a China National Forestry Demonstration Nature Reserve and is one of the 35 zones listed in the China National Biodiversity Conservation Strategy and Action Plan. The reserve hosts distinctive, biodiverse primary broadleaf forests that support various local development initiatives.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Jinggangshan Nature Reserve is located in south-west Jiangxi Province. It forms the northern part of Wangyangshan, which lies within the middle range of the Luoxiao Mountains and marks the boundary between Jiangxi and Hunan Province. The reserve contains the largest continuous area of primary broadleaf forest ecosystem in the subtropical zone at latitude 26° N. With many endemic species of fauna and flora, these broadleaf forests are the designated conservation targets of the nature reserve, which covers 29,053 ha. Air and water erosion, coupled with tectonic movements, shaped the current geological structure of Jinggangshan. The Neocathaysian tectonic system led to uplift in the Jiuling–Wangyangshan area, resulting in a topographic pattern of higher altitude in the south-west and lower altitude in the north and east. The landscape arose from a succession of shallow, drying seas. The geomorphology and topography are diverse, with four typical landscape types: mountain ridge, river valley, tectonic basin and karst. Jinggangshan is located in the centre of the eastern humid forests in the mid-subtropical zone. The vegetation is mid-subtropical, humid, broad-leaved evergreen forest. It is divided into sub-zones of southern China broad-leaved evergreen forest; Jinggangshan hill-land evergreen chinquapin forest; nanmu and “gill fungus” forest; and pine and fir forest. Jinggangshan has a large variety of habitats and micro-habitats for its diverse fauna and flora. Studies have recorded 3,415 species of higher plants, including 313 species of ferns. Jinggangshan has richer biodiversity than the eight adjacent individual mountains; its fern species are 2.1 times more diverse than in Europe. Vertebrate diversity has been recorded at 449 species, including 22 specie … [truncated]
records.name: Jinggangshan

records.introduction_en: Maolan Biosphere Reserve lies in southern Guizhou, close to the Guangxi border in south-west China. Here, one of the world’s best-preserved karst forests spreads across more than 20,000 hectares, with forest cover above 90%. Cone peaks and cockpit depressions hold clear streams, karst ponds and underground rivers, creating a landscape as hydrologically rich as it is visually striking. Ecologically, the site is a living repository of subtropical biodiversity, including many species found only on limestone. The reserve aims to protect the unique karst forest ecosystem and its diverse flora and fauna.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Maolan is celebrated for its well-preserved subtropical karst landscapes, featuring dense forests, limestone peaks, deep gorges, and an extensive network of caves and underground rivers. The main habitats of the reserve include subtropical evergreen broadleaf forest, subtropical evergreen and deciduous broadleaf mixed forest, agroecosystems including rice, rapeseed, sweet potato and medicinal plants, and forestry ecosystems. The fauna is rich, with many rare or endangered species, including forest musk deer (Moschus berezovskii) and rhesus monkey (Macaca mulatta). The area functions as a gene pool for southern China’s karst flora with over 1,000 recorded seed plant species including a notable concentration of limestone specialists and several taxa new to science. Hydrologically, Maolan’s forests regulate a striking two-layer groundwater system: a near-surface forest stagnant zone sustained by heavy rainfall and humid air, and deeper karst conduits that feed major underground rivers. This natural sponge moderates floods, maintains baseflows and sustains karst wetlands and springs. The system is both distinctive and fragile as forest loss quickly reduces infiltration, dries springs and accelerates erosion. Ongoing research, fixed monitoring sites and collaborations with universities focus on forest ecology, hydrogeology, cave biodiversity and species inventories, ensuring long-term evidence underpins management.
records.name: Maolan

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is located in south-east China. It has been a World Heritage site since 1990 and harbours a forest ecosystem almost unchanged since the last glacial period. Mount Huangshan has been a sanctuary for many ancient animal and plant species since the Quaternary glacial period. The area serves as an important germplasm bank and a hotspot for animal and plant biodiversity. This biosphere reserve is also an important water source for the Xin’An, Qing Yi and Qiupu river systems.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Unique geological, topographical and climatic conditions have created and protected the remarkable biodiversity of Mount Huangshan, and retains a well-preserved middle-subtropical, granite-mountain evergreen broad-leaved forest ecosystem. With a forest coverage rate as high as 90.51 per cent, a rich variety of plant communities and a complete vertical band spectrum, it is an important germplasm gene bank and one of the hotspots for animal and plant studies in the world. Due to the high mountains, ecological vertical differentiation is obvious, and biological species are extremely rich. There are as many as 2,385 types of higher plants, 417 vertebrates (38 fishes, 28 amphibians, 52 reptiles, 224 birds and 75 mammals), 175 species of butterflies and 138 species of spiders. There are 19 species of plants listed in the IUCN red list in the Mount Huangshan region. A total of 35 species are included in the CITES appendix. There are 20 species of animals listed in the IUCN red list, and 57 species are included in the CITES appendix. Among these species, there are also four endemic species of Mount Huangshan and eight endemic plant species of Mount Huangshan. In addition, due to the minor impact of the Quaternary glacial period, Mount Huangshan has become a sanctuary for many ancient animals and plants. It is one of the distribution centres for ancient relic species in East Asia and the world.
records.name: Mount Huangshan

records.introduction_en: Nanji Islands Biosphere Reserve, located in the south-eastern waters of Pingyang County, Zhejiang Province, consists of 52 islands, each more than 500 m2, as well as dozens of bare rocks, submerged reefs and surrounding coastal waters. Topography is dominated by low, rolling hills.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Because the islands are composed of different rocks, there are marked differences in basic features, landform morphology, vegetation distribution and other natural landscapes, including areas of granite and volcanic rock. The biosphere reserve offers diverse marine habitats that host many shellfish and algae species. Of the 403 identified shellfish species, 15 have been recorded only in Nanji waters. Shellfish and algae are intermittently distributed across tropical and temperate marine realms, which heightens the site’s importance for conservation and scientific research. These species are concentrated in the core areas. The geographical distribution fracture phenomenon reflects species resources are influenced by a wide range of factors. The Nanji Islands Reserve is a valuable platform for marine research and a source area for shellfish and algal resources.
records.name: Nanji Islands

records.introduction_en: The Shennongjia Biosphere Reserve lies on the eastern branch of the Dabashan Mountains, which link the Tibetan Plateau in western China with the Yangtze Plain in the east. The area spans a large elevation range, from 420 metres in the lowest valleys to 3,106 metres at the highest peak, and therefore supports a wide spectrum of vegetation zones. Forests are protected and, with numerous vascular plant species and a population of the golden snub-nosed monkey (Rhinopithecus roxellana), the reserve is considered a “Green Gene Pool of China”. Ecological tourism is the main economic sector in the reserve, and women are largely engaged in this work.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Shennongjia lies in the transition from the northern subtropics to the warm temperate zone, and from the Central China hills to the mountains of western China. It is a crossroads where a wide variety of species occur. Within the reserve, forests are vast and dense, river valleys are deep, and gullies and ravines are numerous. The terrain is complex and the climate varies markedly with altitude. These geographical and climatic conditions support a rich variety of species. According to available data, there are 3,239 species of vascular plants, including 275 varieties, in 1,027 genera and 236 families. Of these, 25 are national key protected species. There are also 493 vertebrate species and 4,143 insect species, 73 of which are under national key protection. In total, the reserve hosts a wide range of wildlife under prioritised protection, including 26 plant species and 73 animal species, as well as 42 endemic species. Located at the eastern fringe of the evergreen and deciduous oak-type China Armand pine region, its natural vegetation falls into six types: coniferous forest, broad-leaved forest, bamboo groves, shrubland, grassland and marsh. The flora has complex components and multiple origins. Shennongjia is also the easternmost habitat of the Sichuan golden monkey.
records.name: Shennongjia

records.introduction_en: Wuyishan Biosphere Reserve lies where Wuyishan City, Jianyang City and Guangze County meet in northern Fujian Province. The reserve was established to protect mid-subtropical forest ecosystems and rare and endangered fauna and flora. It is a mission-oriented nature reserve focused on biodiversity protection and management, scientific research, public outreach and education, and sustainable operation.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is in the north-west of Fujian Province, south-east China. The designated area includes a range of vegetation types that vary largely with elevation from about 200 to 2,158 metres above sea level. Evergreen broad-leaved forest is the most extensive and ecologically important type and includes some of the largest tracts of humid subtropical forest in the world. Habitats of special conservation interest include communities of Taxus chinensis and the middle-mountain dwarf forest. The reserve’s ecological function is reflected in its biodiversity and ecological processes. Wuyishan is regarded as one of the rare gene pools at this altitude globally. Its ecological landscape is diverse, with rivers and waterfalls, extensive forest plants, abundant birdlife and primates, striking hill and rock formations, marked climatic variation, ancient and valuable trees, rare flowers, a temple and a church, a museum and a bird-observation point. Forest covers 96.3 per cent of the area and provides a strong climate-regulating function that benefits residents and visitors. As the main ecosystem in the reserve, the forest also acts like a vast reservoir, providing about 1.7 billion cubic metres of water.
records.name: Wuyishan

records.introduction_en: Located in the extreme north-eastern part of the country, the Wudalianchi area is marked by relatively recent volcanism. A rich diversity of plants dating from the Tertiary period gives the site high conservation value. The reserve is an ideal research site for geology, seismology and geomorphology. It is also known for its rich heritage and cultural significance. Local authorities promote eco-tourism and “green food”, with high involvement of the local community. Young people and women are encouraged to participate in the development of the reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Located in the far north-east of China, Wudalianchi Biosphere Reserve is shaped by relatively recent volcanism. Within an area of about 1,060 km², it contains 14 volcanoes formed at different times, including historic eruptions in the early eighteenth century. Among these are Mount Laohei and Mount Huoshao (Huoshaoshan), which are among China’s youngest historically active volcanoes. The juxtaposition of older and more recently erupted volcanic areas makes the site well suited to studying primary succession and pioneer plant colonisation on barren substrates. The conservation value derives from a rich diversity of plants dating from the Tertiary period. To date, a total of 976 species of plants in 143 families and 428 genera have been recognised and verified. Rare species include Manchurian walnut (Juglans mandshurica), Northeast China ash (Fraxinus mandshurica), Orostachys malacophylla, Amur corktree (Phellodendron amurense) and wild soybean (Glycine soja). Eighty-nine families and 396 kinds of animals live here, including nationally rare species such as the great bustard (Otis tarda dybowskii) and red-crowned crane (Grus japonensis).
records.name: Wudalianchi

records.introduction_en: The Lower Paraná River Delta is an extensive wetland system. This type of ecosystem has attracted increasing interest due to recognition of its multiple functions. It is now also understood that these areas are highly sensitive to alterations. They are, and have long been, subject to various forms of human intervention that interfere with their functioning and place them at a high level of criticality.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is a freshwater tidal wetland; preserving the hydrological regime that underpins its main ecological characteristics is essential. As a growing delta, it is also necessary to preserve sedimentary dynamics to maintain natural geomorphological processes. Its connection to sea level, and the possible global trend of sea-level rise, makes the preservation of sites for long-term monitoring indispensable. Conservation here is also important given the Paraná Delta’s biogeographical uniqueness and ecological richness. This uniqueness stems from the movement of flora and fauna of subtropical lineage along the fluvial corridors of the Paraná and Uruguay rivers. These species coexist with elements from temperate latitudes, forming a typical deltaic pattern of communities and giving the area high species richness. In the area, both plant and animal species reach their southern distribution limits. This also highlights the importance of conserving genetic variation. The existence of a wide mosaic of environmental conditions, and therefore diverse habitat types, supports high faunal richness. Habitat-suitability analyses indicate favourable conditions for several fauna: marsh deer (Blastocerus dichotomus), giant otter (Lontra longicaudis), wild cat (Leopardus geoffroyi) and capybara (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris).
records.name: Delta del Paraná

records.introduction_en: The Laguna de Pozuelos Biosphere Reserve is part of the highlands of the Southern Central Andes. It lies within Dinerstein’s Arid Puna ecosystem, identified as a conservation priority.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is located in the extreme north of the Province of Jujuy at 3,600 m above sea level. Pozuelos is a typical high-Andean lagoon with shallow, brackish water and sparse vegetation. At its centre, the depth is about one metre. It lies on a broad high plateau, encircled by mountain ranges that define the basin. When full, the lagoon covers roughly 7,000 hectares. Its extent fluctuates with summer rainfall, and, beyond this seasonal cycle, prolonged droughts can cause it to dry out completely. Five main environments can be found within the biosphere reserve. These are the lagoon, the paleo-lagoon, the foothills and the volcanic relief, as well as the sierras, eastern and western, which include a main massif and river valleys. The Corporation for the Development of the Pozuelos Basin is promoting the comprehensive development of its inhabitants through plans and programmes aimed at making better use of natural resources, including llamas and sheep, while not neglecting the conservation function.
records.name: Laguna de Pozuelos

records.introduction_en: The Yungas Biosphere Reserve is located in northwestern Argentina, spanning the provinces of Jujuy and Salta. It covers a vast area dominated by Yungas (subtropical mountain forests) and is one of the largest biosphere reserves in the country.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Yungas Biosphere Reserve contains five core areas, covering 157,900 ha: Calilegua National Park, Baritú National Park, El Nogalar de los Toldos National Reserve, Potrero de Yala Provincial Park and Laguna de Pintascayo Provincial Park. The Yungas represent one of the most biodiverse natural systems in Argentina, home to nearly 50 per cent of the country's biodiversity. Its ecological importance lies in the broad national representation of species and a high level of endemism. Eighty-nine species of mammals have been recorded including the jaguar (Panthera onca), tapir (Tapirus terrestris), Andean deer (Hippocamelus antisensis) and ocelot (Leopardus pardalis). Other notable species are the giant otter (Lontra longicaudis), collared peccary (Tayassu pecari) and marmoset (Cebus apella). Some mammals are exclusive to the Yungas, such as the snout bat (Anoura caudifer), the red squirrel (Sciurus ignitus), the white-boned coendou (Coendou prehensilis) and the black-boned coendou (C. bicolor).
records.name: Las Yungas

records.introduction_en: Located in the semi-arid Chaco sub-region, the biosphere reserve shows a high level of natural environmental heterogeneity. This creates a complex mosaic of ecological systems representative of dry tropical forests in the region. The reserve experiences a continental-type climate with mild winters and warm summers. Rainfall is average to low and concentrated in spring and summer.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve belongs to the Chaco biogeographical region with tropical dry or deciduous forests. These include quebrachal forests dominated by Aspidosperma quebracho-blanco and Schinopsis lorentzii in the valleys, matorral scrublands and forests, flooded savannas, agricultural systems and grazed forests. Wetlands are also present, mostly along rivers, and provide a refuge for a wide range of species, including migratory birds. The protected environment of the reserve is representative of the woody ecosystems of the semi-arid Chaco, which until now have been poorly represented among protected areas in South America. Environmental heterogeneity ranges from abrasive pasture (aíbales-espartillales) to hardwood forests (quebrachales). The site contributes to the protection of endangered species, such as the tatú carreta (Priodontes maximus).
records.name: Riacho Teuquito

records.introduction_en: Located in the Province of Misiones, the Yabotí Biosphere Reserve is home to the richest biodiversity in Argentina. Its subtropical forests, with trees, bushes and bamboos, are a habitat for jaguars, tapirs and collared peccaries, among other endangered species. Within the biosphere reserve limits there are Guaraní villages, including one inside the Esmeralda core area. These communities have been actively engaged in sustainable development initiatives promoted by the biosphere reserve’s committee.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Yabotí has a subtropical forest climate with two main seasons: a tropical season with intense summer rains, and a subtropical season with less intense precipitation and cooler weather. While parts of the biosphere reserve have been affected by human activity in the past, they are undergoing recovery. This is demonstrated by the increasing presence of jaguars (Panthera onca), harpy eagles (Harpia harpyja) and tapirs (Tapirus terrestris), among other endangered species.
records.name: Yabotí

records.introduction_en: The site includes numerous islands and a coastline stretching over 120 km and comprises several important representative habitats of national and regional significance. These habitats include seagrass beds with three species, coral reef communities with more than 18 species, macroalgae outcrops with more than 15 species, and mangrove vegetation in monostands of Avicennia marina. Marawah Biosphere Reserve is also of global importance as a shelter and feeding ground for the vulnerable dugongs (Dugong dugon).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Marawah Marine Biosphere Reserve lies in the hot desert biome of the Middle East and Western Asia biogeographic region, combining characteristics from both the Arabian Desert and Palaearctic bioregions. The surficial geology of the reserve region comprises five mainly Quaternary deposits. These are sabkha, dune sands, dune sands with inter-dunal sabkha deposits, palaeodune deposits, and carbonate beach sand deposits. The reserve is significant for biological diversity conservation, since most of the marine and terrestrial species are present in the area. The total area represents about 4 per cent of the country. The habitats within the reserve are considered to be of national and regional importance. These habitats include seagrasses, mangrove, coral reefs, coastal sabkhas, rocky seashores, sandy seashores and rocky ridges. The site is of global importance as a shelter and feeding ground for dugongs. The area also provides crucial nursery and spawning grounds for a wide variety of fish species, and is regionally important as a foraging habitat for hawksbill and green turtles. Furthermore, the islands inside the protected area provide important nesting sites for hawksbill sea turtles and a number of migratory birds.
records.name: Marawah

records.introduction_en: The Mornington Peninsula and Western Port Biosphere Reserve includes the whole of Mornington Peninsula Shire and parts of the City of Frankston. It also covers coastal areas of the municipalities of Casey, Cardinia and Bass Coast, including Phillip Island and French Island. Western Port, also a Ramsar site, is a coastal embayment with extensive, relatively undisturbed mudflats and saltmarsh. It is internationally important as feeding and roosting habitat for summering waders. The site periodically supports more than 10,000 waders and more than 10,000 ducks and swans, as well as a rich invertebrate fauna of some 1,380 species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The coastline and hinterland of the Western Port catchment support some of Victoria’s most valuable natural areas. Western Port is representative of marine and coastal habitats, especially intertidal habitats, rarely found at this scale on the southern Australian coast. In addition to coastal wetlands, numerous inland swamps provide important habitat and support a wide range of native fauna. Many plants in the region show adaptation to subtle site differences, and significant genetic variation has been demonstrated in certain species from site to site. Unusual plant and animal communities also persist in remnant vegetation, large and small, and even limited sites have been recognised for botanical or zoological significance. Floristically unusual communities and rare plants still occur in the region; for example, over 60 orchid species and 10 eucalypt species are found on the Mornington Peninsula. Australia’s mammal fauna is distinctive. Many species are shy and nocturnal, which makes detection and population estimates difficult. Recorded mammals include the koala (Phascolarctos cinereus), wombat (Vombatus ursinus), eastern grey kangaroo (Macropus giganteus), swamp wallaby (Wallabia bicolor) and Australian fur seal (Arctocephalus pusillus). Almost 50 per cent of Victoria’s native terrestrial mammals have been recorded in the Western Port catchment. The site is also internationally important for birds, including the laughing kookaburra (Dacelo novaeguineae), Australian pelican (Pelecanus conspicillatus), royal spoonbill (Platalea regia), black falcon (Falco subniger) and orange-bellied parrot (Neophema chrysogaster).
records.name: Mornington Peninsula and Western Port

records.introduction_en: The Bia National Park and Bia Resource Reserve constitute the twin conservation area and represents the best example of transitional zone between moist evergreen and moist semideciduous forest types.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area is dominated by Celtis-Triplochiton associations, Teighemella heckelii and Entadrophragma angolense. The forest is actually very rich with biodiversity. Sixty-one species of mammals have been recorded. These include 9 primates amongst which are the Black and White Colobus, the Olive Colobus monkeys and chimpanzees; the area is one of the few areas in the country known to support the chimpanzees. The forest elephant and the highly threatened bongo are present. Over 200 species of birds have been recorded; they include the internationally endangered white-breasted guinea fowl. The National Park is almost a virgin forest with almost no human interference (apart from snail picking). It is only pristine rainforest and the finest example of its type remaining in Ghana today. However, the Resource Reserve has been opened up due to the past logging at the area and regeneration is taking place.
records.name: Bia

records.introduction_en: Situated in the West African savannah, this biosphere reserve presents a wide variety of natural landscapes including wetlands, gallery forests, dry clear forests, and tree and shrub savannahs. These are natural habitats for vulnerable and endangered species including the cheetah, elephant, lion, leopard and vulture. Agriculture is the main economic activity in Arly with cereal crops (millet and sorghum), peanuts and cotton, alongside livestock.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: A defining feature of the W Region biosphere reserve is its dry tropical forest climate with pronounced wet and dry seasons. The landscape forms a diverse patchwork of lateritic plateaus, valleys and floodplains cut by the Mékrou, Tapoa and other rivers, and dotted with seasonal and longer-lasting ponds.Periodic floods lay down alluvium – loose, often nutrient-rich sediment – that refreshes wetland habitats, while some ponds hold water into May, extending aquatic conditions late into the dry season. The reserve’s Ramsar-listed wetlands harbour high biodiversity value, sustaining fish populations by providing spawning and nursery areas, and serving as crucial dry-season refuges for terrestrial wildlife.Other key habitats in the reserve include elevated wooded savannas, home to extensive stands of baobab (Adansonia digitata). Shrub and herbaceous formations on the plateaus support antelope species, including duikers (Cephalophus spp.), roan antelope (Hippotragus equinus) and Damaliscus antelopes (Damaliscus spp.), and help protect soils and build organic matter on porous, low-fertility substrates.
records.name: W Region

records.introduction_en: Srébarna Lake is the last Danube riverside lake preserved in Bulgaria and a unique example of a type of wetland that used to be common. It is a freshwater lake that supports a rich diversity of plant and animal life, including species characteristic of the region as well as some that are rare. Some plant formations are typical for the wetland, including floating reedbeds and flooded willow woodlands.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Srébarna supports high and valuable biodiversity. A total of 1,166 genera have been recorded in the area, with 2,748 infrageneric taxa. A total of 243 bird species has been recorded, 57.5 per cent of the Bulgarian ornithofauna. Of these, 90 are Species of European Conservation Concern. There are 11 plant species listed in the Bulgarian Red Data Book. There are 27 amphibian and reptile species, and 23 species of fish, 18.1 per cent of Bulgarian freshwater fishes. There are 1,430 observed plant species. Srébarna is a biodiversity hotspot in Bulgaria and within the country’s portion of the Continental Biogeographical Region. The wetland is an important breeding, staging and wintering site for large numbers of birds. It is the only breeding site in Bulgaria for Pelecanus crispus, hosts a colony of Phalacrocorax pygmeus, and supports the largest breeding population of Aythya nyroca in the country. It is an important staging area for moulting Aythya nyroca and other rare and endangered wildfowl species in Bulgaria, including Anas strepera, Aythya ferina and Anas querquedula. During late autumn and in winter, it provides a staging site for geese species such as Anser albifrons, and it supports one of the largest concentrations of Anser anser in Bulgaria during this period. The lake provides a foraging area for the large Phalacrocorax carbo colony situated on a nearby Danube Island. In recent years, pelicans and pygmy cormorants have also fed in the lake. The wetland supports viable populations of a number of fish species, some of which are endangered in Bulgaria, including Pungitius platygaster, which here has one of the densest populations in the country. The site supports up to 52,355 waterbirds during migration and winter. This includes up to 50,550 Anser albifrons.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Srébarna

records.introduction_en: Situated in the West African savannah, the W Region Biosphere Reserve sits on an ancient massif above the Niger valley and is dissected by the Mékrou, Tapoa and Kourtiagou rivers linked to the Niger and Pendjari basins. The reserve presents a wide variety of natural landscapes from Ramsar-listed wetlands with aquatic meadows, to gallery forests, open dry woodlands and savannahs. As part of the W–Arly–Pendjari complex, a pioneering transboundary site in Africa, it underpins cross-border co-operation on conservation, development through community-involved resource management, and education and continuous monitoring.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: A defining feature of the W Region biosphere reserve is its dry tropical forest climate with pronounced wet and dry seasons. The landscape forms a diverse patchwork of lateritic plateaus, valleys and floodplains cut by the Mékrou, Tapoa and other rivers, and dotted with seasonal and longer-lasting ponds. Periodic floods lay down alluvium – loose, often nutrient-rich sediment – that refreshes wetland habitats, while some ponds hold water into May, extending aquatic conditions late into the dry season. The reserve’s Ramsar-listed wetlands harbour rich biodiversity, sustaining fish populations by providing spawning and nursery areas, and serving as crucial dry-season refuges for terrestrial wildlife. Other key habitats in the reserve include elevated wooded savannas, home to extensive stands of baobab (Adansonia digitata). Shrub and herbaceous formations on the plateaus support antelope species, including duikers (Cephalophus), roan antelope (Hippotragus equinus) and Damaliscus antelopes (Damaliscus), and help protect soils and build organic matter on porous, low-fertility substrates.
records.name: W Region

records.introduction_en: Located on the south-east coast of Sumatra, this biosphere reserve includes Berbak and Sembilang National Parks as well as two wildlife reserves. It contains undisturbed swamp-forest peat ecosystems, freshwater swamp forests and mangroves, and lowland forests surrounding riverbanks, with swamps reaching depths of up to 10 metres. Palm oil plantations, rubber, traditional agriculture, including rice and dry fields, and timber are the main economic activities.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The topography of the biosphere reserve is varied. While most of the land is flat, some is sloping (0–20 per cent), with an altitude of 0–140 m above sea level. The most typical topographic features are tree-dominated wetlands, including freshwater swamp forests, seasonally flooded forests and wooded swamps on inorganic soils, permanent freshwater lakes, such as large oxbow lakes, and intertidal forested wetlands with mangrove swamps, nipah swamps and tidal freshwater swamp forests. Permanent rivers, streams and creeks occur throughout the site. There are forested peatlands and peat swamp forests, man-made wetland areas, and lowland rainforest areas. With high biodiversity, the area is a suitable habitat for various flora and fauna of Sumatra as well as rare species. There are 23 palm species (Arecaceae), 250 bird species (including 22 migratory wader species), 13 reptile species, 60,000 ha of freshwater swamp and 1,500 ha of mangrove forest recorded. A large alluvial delta in the area serves as one of the most important habitats for migratory birds in the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, whose total number is about 0.5–1 million. Several protected species include Sumatran tiger (Panthera tigris sumatrae), Malayan tapir (Tapirus indicus), Malayan sun bear (Helarctos malayanus), saltwater crocodile (Crocodylus porosus), marble cat (Pardofelis marmorata) and leaf monkey (Presbytis rubicunda).
records.name: Berbak-Sembilang

records.introduction_en: Situated in West Java Province to the south of Jakarta, the Cibodas Biosphere Reserve exemplifies a humid tropical ecosystem under strong human pressure. The Gunung Gede–Pangrango National Park constitutes the core area and encompasses twin volcanoes and mountainous rainforests, including many species endemic to Java. The buffer zone comprises production forests, tea plantations and horticultural fields. The majority of the transition area is covered by irrigated rice fields and human settlements.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The core area consists of twin volcanoes: Mount Gede (2,958 m) and Mount Pangrango (3,109 m). A high saddle known as Kandang Badak, at 2,400 m above sea level, connects the two summits. The mountain slopes are very steep and are cut by rapidly flowing streams that carve deep valleys and long ridges. Generally, the core area is well drained. A few naturally occurring swamps, including Rawa Goyonggong, Rawa Denok and Situgunung, enrich the variety of habitats. Based on elevation and forest stratification, the vegetation is characterised by three ecosystem types: sub-montane, below 1,500 m above sea level; montane, 1,500–2,400 m; and sub-alpine, above 2,400 m. Mount Gede and Mount Pangrango have long played a significant role in conservation and in biological and ecological research, particularly botanical studies. In geological terms, both form part of recent mountain systems, with Mount Gede listed as an active volcano. The processes that led to the formation of these mountains began 3 million years ago and are still ongoing. This area also functions as an important hydrological catchment, providing water to approximately 20 million people. It is considered one of the wettest parts of Java, with rainfall ranging between 3,000 mm and 4,200 mm per year. More than 1,000 species of flora from 57 families can be found in the national park. The wild fauna includes 251 bird species, accounting for more than 50 per cent of bird species on Java. The park is also home to 110 mammal species, including the rare Javan gibbon (Hylobates moloch), more than 300 insect species, and around 75 reptile species. One bird species, the Javan hawk-eagle (Spizaetus bartelsi), was declared a national rare fauna symbol by Presidential Decree.
records.name: Cibodas

records.title_en: Betung Kerihun Danau Sentarum Kapuas Hulu
records.introduction_en: Located at the eastern tip of Kalimantan Barat Province on the island of Borneo, the biosphere reserve consists of the two national parks of Betung Kerihun and Danau Sentarum. It features unique lowland and montane tropical rainforests that are home to a great diversity of flora and fauna.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Betung Kerihun–Danau Sentarum Kapuas Hulu Biosphere Reserve is an area now experiencing continual erosion. It includes lowlands and basins, as well as lakes and swampy plains. In the highlands there are many narrow, elongated swamps surrounded by small hills. These swamps are continually inundated with water, especially during periods of heavy rainfall. The highlands are situated at higher elevations. There are 1,216 species of flora identified in Betung Kerihun National Park, comprising 418 genera and 110 families. Seventy-five species are endemic to Borneo, and 14 species were newly recorded. Faunal diversity is also very high, including 48 species of mammals, 17 species of primates, 301 species of birds, 103 species of herpetofauna, 112 species of fish and 170 species of insects. Danau Sentarum National Park is a habitat for approximately 794 species of trees and shrubs, orchids, about 147 species of mammals, 67 species of reptiles, 22 species of Indonesian amphibians, 311 species of birds and 266 species of fish.
records.name: Betung Kerihun Danau Sentarum Kapuas Hulu

records.introduction_en: The Bunaken Tangkoko Minahasa Biosphere Reserve in North Sulawesi is located in the heart of the Coral Triangle of the Indo-Pacific region in Indonesia. The biosphere reserve spans a total of 746,405.92 ha of terrestrial and marine habitats. The area encompasses a mosaic of ecological systems, including a coastal area with coral reefs and seagrass, mangrove and coastal forests, islands and terrestrial ecosystems. The biosphere reserve is home to over 130 species of mammals, including the Dian’s tarsier. The region profits from the production of cocoa, coffee, fisheries and ecotourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The core area of the Bunaken Tangkoko Minahasa Biosphere Reserve consists of five conservation areas: Bunaken Island National Park, Tangkoko Duasudara Nature Reserve, Batu Putih Nature Reserve, Gunung Lokon Nature Reserve, Manembe-Nembe Wildlife Reserve and Gunung Tumpa Forest Park. Bunaken National Marine Park represents Indonesia’s tropical sea ecosystem and is located at the centre of the marine and coastal biodiversity of the Indo-Pacific region. Mangroves in the Bunaken Island National Park are mostly located along the coasts of the small islands and Bunaken Island, where 34–46 mangrove species can be found, including Ceriops tagal, Rhizophora apiculata, Rhizophora mucronata, Bruguiera gymnorrhiza, Avicennia marina, Xylocarpus moluccensis, Sonneratia alba and Sonneratia caseolaris. Penyu hijau (Chelonia mydas) and Penyu sisik (Eretmochelys imbricata) are often seen when diving or snorkelling on reefs in the Bunaken National Park area. Mount Tumpa, one of the mountains in North Sulawesi Province, has a rich flora and fauna, including soil insects. It is a primary forest that is still intact and only slightly disturbed by human exploitation. Mount Lokon Nature Reserve has the unique ecosystem of the Mount Lokon area in the form of an active volcano area. It features mountain forests with active volcanoes and has two interesting caves. Primates found in this area are the Sulawesi black monkey or yaki (Macaca nigra), with a density of about two individuals per square kilometre, and the species of tangkasi (Tarsius spectrum). The squirrel or bajing (Prosciurillus leucomus) has a density of 6.83 per square kilometre. Other mammals are the kuskus (Phalanger) and the babi hutan (Sus celebensis). Based on research data, the diversity of diurnal birds includes … [truncated]
records.name: Bunaken Tangkoko Minahasa

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve and national park cover a vast area of tropical rainforest in northern Sumatra. Ecosystems include lowland evergreen dipterocarp forest, lower and upper montane rainforest, peat swamp forest, forest over limestone, sub-alpine meadows and heathlands, freshwater lakes and rivers, and sulphur mineral pools.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Gunung Leuser National Park is a rich yet vulnerable natural laboratory. According to MacKinnon and MacKinnon (1986), Gunung Leuser has the highest score for its conservation contribution to the Indo-Malaya conservation area. Leuser provides habitat for a wide range of fauna, including mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish and invertebrates. It has an extensive list of bird species, up to 380 species. Gunung Leuser is also home to 36 of 50 Sundaland endemic bird species. Almost 65 per cent of the 129 mammal species in Sumatra are recorded in this area. The ecosystem provides habitat for key fauna such as the Sumatran elephant (Elephas maximus sumatranus), tiger (Panthera tigris sumatrae), rhinoceros (Dicerorhinus sumatrensis) and orang-utan (Pongo abelii). The park is also habitat to the owa (lar gibbon, Hylobates lar) and the kedih (Presbytis thomasi). There are more than 4,000 plant species found in the park, including three of the 15 parasitic Rafflesia species. It is also a habitat for many medicinal plants (Brimacombe and Elliot, 1996). As a natural laboratory, Gunung Leuser is important for conservation, education, scientific research for local and foreign researchers, and ecotourism. The Orangutan Research Station in Ketambe, Southeast Aceh District, opened by Dr Herman D. Rijksen, remains an important site for researchers.
records.name: Gunung Leuser

records.introduction_en: Lore Lindu Biosphere Reserve and National Park comprise one of the largest remaining mountainous rainforests of Sulawesi. It is of high importance for biodiversity, culture and archaeology. Approximately 90 per cent of the area is montane forest above 1,000 m in altitude, representing most of Sulawesi’s unique mountain flora and fauna.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Lore Lindu National Park is one of Sulawesi’s important nature reserves and is home to a wide variety of flora and fauna. The park is located about 60 km south of Palu. It covers a large area that includes lowland and highland mountain forests, dense forests, flat fertile valleys, rivers, lakes and hot springs. The total area is 217,991.18 ha, with altitudes ranging from 200 to 2,610 m above sea level. The park, with its beautiful scenery, holds a great number of endemic flora and fauna. It lies within Wallacea, a transitional zone between Asia and Australia. The park also serves as a water reservoir for three main rivers in Central Sulawesi: the Lariang, Gumbasa and Palu. The rugged interior of the park is home to Sulawesi’s largest native animals, such as anoas, babirusas, tarsiers, Tonkean macaques, marsupials and Sulawesi’s largest carnivorous mammal, the civet. The park is home to at least five species of squirrels, and 31 of its 38 rat species are endemic. There are at least 55 species of bats and 267 species of birds, including maleo birds and red-knobbed hornbills. Thousands of interesting insect species can be seen around the park, including butterflies, which can be seen flying along the watercourse or drinking from puddles and mudbanks.
records.name: Lore Lindu

records.introduction_en: Siberut is the largest of the four Mentawai Islands situated off the west coast of Sumatra. It has been isolated from the Sumatra mainland and the Sunda Shelf for at least 500,000 years, resulting in an exceptionally high degree of endemism. Sixty-five per cent of the animals are thought to be endemic. Lowland dipterocarp rainforest is the principal ecosystem.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Siberut Island is isolated from the mainland Sunda Shelf by the Mentawai Strait, about 155 km from Padang, the capital city of West Sumatra Province. It covers five ecosystem types: primary dipterocarp forest, mixed primary forest, swamp forest, coastal forest and mangrove forest. The forest area is still relatively natural, with large trees. Sixty-five per cent of mammal species and fifteen per cent of fauna on Siberut are endemic at some taxonomic level, making the island, with its limited surface, unique in the world. Four primate species are found only in this reserve: the Kloss gibbon, also called the dwarf siamang (Hylobates klossii), the Mentawai macaque (Macaca pagensis), the Mentawaian leaf monkey (Presbytis potenziani siberu) and the pig-tailed snub-nosed monkey (Nasalis concolor siberu). About 134 bird species are found on Siberut, of which 19 are endemic. More than 31 mammal species and 864 plant species are also recorded in the park.
records.name: Siberut

records.introduction_en: Taka Bonerate–Kepulauan Selayar Biosphere Reserve is located in the south of Sulawesi, in South Sulawesi Province (Selayar Islands Regency). It covers a large marine area with small islands, numerous fringing reefs and atolls. Mangrove forests act as a barrier against strong sea waves and provide shelter and spawning grounds for various fish, as well as habitat for fauna such as birds. The mangroves include 22–26 species from 14 families, including Rhizophora stylosa and Ceriops tagal. Protected and threatened animals found at the site include softshell turtles (family Trionychidae), the green turtle (Chelonia mydas) and the napoleon fish (Cheilinus undulatus).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve lies between the Flores Sea, Java Sea and Banda Sea. It hosts the largest atoll in Southeast Asia and the third largest in the world. Coral reefs, mangroves, lagoons, sand dunes and seagrass are the main habitats. Coral reefs cover 91,382 ha and are a principal habitat for several species. Reef types found on the islands include atoll reefs (terumbu karang cincin), fringing reefs (terumbu karang tepi), barrier reefs (terumbu karang penghalang) and patch reefs (karang gosong). The reserve has high biodiversity, including several protected marine species such as the hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata), green turtle (Chelonia mydas), common dolphin (Delphinus delphis), napoleon fish (Cheilinus undulatus), sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) and short-finned pilot whale (Globicephala macrorhynchus). Between 22 and 26 mangrove species, belonging to 14 families, have been recorded. There are also 34 bird species: 12 land birds, 13 shorebirds and 9 seabirds.
records.name: Taka Bonerate-Kepulauan Selayar

records.introduction_en: The name Caatinga is a Tupi word meaning white forest or white vegetation: ‘caa’ meaning forest or vegetation, and ‘tinga’ meaning white. Caatinga is a xeric shrubland and thorn forest that consists primarily of small, thorny trees that shed their leaves seasonally. Cacti, thick-stemmed plants, thorny brush and arid-adapted grasses make up the ground layer. Many annual plants grow, flower and die during the brief rainy season.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Caatinga Biosphere Reserve is characterised by Caatinga vegetation, as well as deciduous forest during the drought period, the typical vegetation of the interior of north-eastern Brazil. Through the buffer and transition areas, the Caatinga Biosphere Reserve establishes ecological corridors among the diverse core areas, and it is also linked to the contiguous Mata Atlântica Biosphere Reserve and Cerrado Biosphere Reserve. Caatinga stands for the kind of vegetation that covers the greatest semiarid region in Northeast Brazil. The Caatinga Biosphere Reserve has been divided into six units. Unit I represents a Caatinga high forest characterised by a Tabebuia–Aspidosperma–Astronium–Cavanillesia association. Unit II varies from Caatinga middle or lower forest to open arboreal Caatinga. It presents four associations: Astronium–Schinopsis–Caesalpinia, Caesalpinia–Spondias–Bursera–Aspidosperma, Mimosa–Syagrus–Spondias–Cereus, and Cnidosculus–Bursera–Caesalpinia. Unit III represents a lower Caatinga forest and is characterised by a Pilosocereus–Poepiggia–Dalbergia–Piptadenia association. Unit IV occurs in low Caatinga and includes four associations: Caesalpinia–Aspidosperma–Jatropha, Caesalpinia–Aspidosperma, Mimosa–Caesalpinia–Aristida, and Aspidosperma–Pelosocereus. Unit V represents a type of bushy Caatinga and is characterised by a Calliandra–Pilosocereus association. Unit VI represents a Caatinga gallery forest and is characterised by a Copernicia–Geoffroea–Licania association. Land uses include dry farming, known locally as sequiro, agroecosystems, afforestation areas and pastureland.
records.name: Caatinga

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is characterised by the cerrado biome, including dense savanna woodlands known locally as cerrado, areas with twisted short trees and shrubs, and cerrado grasslands. It encompasses areas in the states of Tocantins, Maranhão and Piauí.
