records.ecological_characteristics_en: The upland grasslands of Chapada dos Veadeiros, as well as the Paraná valley wetlands, harbour unique species. Deciduous and semi-deciduous forests, with hardwoods prized for cattle fencing and construction, are a high priority for biodiversity conservation. Conservation in the Cerrado Biosphere Reserve emphasises restoring degraded habitats and creating ecological corridors to enhance landscape connectivity and protect these ecosystems.
records.name: Cerrado

records.introduction_en: The Espinhaço Mountain Range is the largest and most continuous Precambrian orogenic belt in Brazil and serves as a water divide between the São Francisco River basin and the basins that drain directly into the Atlantic Ocean. It extends in a north–south direction for approximately 1,200 km, from the Belo Horizonte region to the northern border of Bahia with Pernambuco and Piauí, with a width that varies from a few kilometres to over 100 km. Along the over 1,000 km of the cordillera, alternating elevations with peaks reaching up to 2,017 metres allow for great diversity in climate and rainfall conditions.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Above 500 m in the Espinhaço Range, the dominant vegetation is ‘rupestrian fields’, a unique mosaic of rocky grasslands and shrublands. This vegetation is predominantly composed of a continuous herbaceous stratum and small, sclerophyllous evergreen bushes. Although only a small number of areas have been intensively inventoried, it is estimated that there are approximately 3,000 plant species. About 30 per cent of the taxa are exclusive to the rupestrian fields, which would represent approximately 1,000 to 2,000 endemic species. A high level of endemism is also observed in the fauna: endemic birds, mammals, amphibians, reptiles and fishes have been recorded. The extent of the biosphere reserve, over 3,000,000 ha, and its biological, geomorphological and historical importance underpin the implementation of measures aimed at preserving this mountain complex. There are 16 protected areas, including national parks, state parks, state ecological stations and municipal natural parks, which form the core areas. In addition to natural values, there are cultural assets such as the colonial towns of Ouro Preto, Congonhas and Diamantina that are UNESCO World Heritage sites. Artistic and religious manifestations are kept alive along the entire length of the cordillera.
records.name: Espinhaço Range

records.introduction_en: The Pantanal Biosphere Reserve comprises the states of Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul and a small portion of Goiás. It covers the headwaters of the rivers that make up the Pantanal, one of the world’s most extensive wetland complexes, internationally known for its large bird, mammal, reptile, fish, insect and amphibian populations.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve includes both highlands and lowlands, from large lakes on the Bolivian border and broad floodplains and grasslands to highland cerrado in the Chapada dos Guimarães, Serra de Santa Bárbara and Urucum mountains. Summits reach 1,000 metres above sea level. Other notable ecosystems include seasonally flooded cerrado, highland grasslands and seasonally flooded grasslands, as well as cerradão (forest-like cerrado), deciduous forest, gallery forest and stands of buriti palm. Forest types influenced by neighbouring biomes also occur, notably Amazonian-type forest and Atlantic Forest–influenced forest. The Chaco and Chaco woodland are also present.
records.name: Pantanal

records.introduction_en: The Chamela-Cuixmala Biosphere Reserve is on the Pacific coast of the state of Jalisco, Mexico. It features mostly tropical dry forests over rolling hills, as well as lower wetlands and mangroves. Along the coast, coral reefs and refuge sites are home to several marine species. Together, these habitats support diverse flora and fauna, including a very high number of endemic species. Biologically, the region is among the most important in the country. With a combined area of 36,000 acres, the reserve hosts 70 species of mammals, 270 species of birds and over 1,200 plant species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Chamela-Cuixmala region lies on the coastal plain of the Sierra Madre del Sur, within the subprovinces of the Sierras of Jalisco and Colima. It is a predominantly mountainous region where the relief of the coastal plain is dominated by hills, interrupted by plains or floodplains of rivers or streams. The reserve encompasses a wide variety of landscapes, making it one of the most diverse and heterogeneous areas of the Pacific coast of the Americas. It features a very well conserved tropical dry forest, one of the world’s most threatened ecosystems. It also contributes to the conservation of insular ecosystems and beach zones that serve as nesting places for various turtle species. Chamela-Cuixmala is home to 68 species protected under Mexican legislation, including five species of sea turtles and the jaguar (Panthera onca).
records.name: Chamela-Cuixmala

records.introduction_en: Cumbres de Monterrey National Park is located in the province of the Sierra Madre Oriental and the sub-provinces of the Grand Sierra Plegada. The main ecosystems are coniferous forests, oak forests and scrub. It is considered a priority region and an important area for bird conservation because of its vicinity to the El Taray reserve, a parrot reserve in the mountains to the east. The area is important for ecosystem services, providing approximately 50 per cent of the water consumed in Monterrey and its metropolitan area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Vegetation includes bushes, crausicaule scrublands, pine woods and other types, supporting high biodiversity and endangered species such as the maroon-fronted parrot (Rhynchopsitta terrisi), the black bear (Ursus americanus) and the jaguar (Panthera onca). The biosphere reserve has boosted a recovery programme for their conservation. Near Greater Monterrey, the reserve is of extreme importance to the region due to its environmental services. It regulates the local climate and buffers natural phenomena. It caters to the region’s water needs, captures carbon dioxide, and protects biodiversity and ecosystems. However, the area is threatened by recent fires and by human activities.
records.name: Cumbres de Monterrey

records.introduction_en: The Berezinsky Biosphere Reserve is a representative example of the southern European taiga zone. It is located about 100 km north-east of Minsk on the edge of the watersheds between the Black Sea and the Baltic Sea. Berezinsky Biosphere Reserve is a patchwork of boreal coniferous and broad-leafed forests, lakes, watercourses, marshlands and flood plains, and it contains one of the largest undrained peat bogs in Eastern Europe, at 11,000 ha. Its populations of wolves, bears and bison, together with its rich bird life, attract many scientists.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Berezinsky Biosphere Reserve is situated in the temperate boreal-nemoral zone. Altitude ranges from 155–227 m above sea level. It lies on the flat watershed of the Baltic and Black Seas, in a low valley in the basin of the Berezina River. The landscape is a mosaic of coniferous and deciduous forests, lakes, peatlands, rivers, floodplains and small arable fields, with peatlands covering 60 per cent. The climate is temperate, continental and humid, with total annual precipitation of 690 mm. The Berezina is the main river in the reserve and flows through its territory for more than 110 km. There are seven small lakes in the reserve, covering about 2,000 ha in total. The flora comprises more than 2,000 species, including 804 species of vascular plants, of which 42 are rare in Belarus. The fauna includes 56 species of mammals, including Ursus arctos, Canis lupus and Alces alces, and 230 species of birds. All major ecosystem types are present, including forests, mires, water bodies and meadows. Forests are the main plant community: they cover 83.3 per cent of the territory and comprise four formation groups. Boreal coniferous forests of pine and spruce make up 56 per cent; deciduous mire forests of pubescent birch and black alder represent 34 per cent; deciduous secondary forests of white birch, aspen and grey alder make up 9 per cent; and broad-leaved forests of oak, lime and ash account for 1 per cent. The main ecological value lies in the richness of plant communities and fauna within a comparatively limited area, and their largely natural state.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Berezinsky

records.introduction_en: Pribuzhskoye-Polesie Biosphere Reserve lies in the south-west of Belarus in Brest and Malorita districts, the warmest part of the country. Its boundary follows the West Bug River to the west, the Belarus–Ukraine border to the south, district lines to the east, and the Brest forestry glades to the north. The reserve forms part of the West Polesie Transnational Biosphere Reserve spanning Belarus, Poland and Ukraine. The site is significant for its intact wetland–forest mosaic and for vital cross-border ecological connectivity. Its objectives focus on safeguarding the area’s natural conditions, enriching biological and landscape diversity, and maintaining traditional forms of land use where compatible with conservation.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve comprises a landscape of forest and wetlands in the western part of Polesie, a cross-border lowland region of Eastern Europe. Forest is the dominant cover and includes dry valley forests long shaped by human use. Wetlands are widespread and varied, from mires and bogs to extensive floodplain alder woods with Populus nigra. Floodplain willow groves with white willow (Salix alba) represent one of the most valuable riparian habitats in Belarus. Open habitats complete the mosaic with meadows and agroecosystems. The hydrological network underpins biodiversity and connectivity across the site. The Kopajuvka is a small river shared by Belarus, Poland and Ukraine that provides a crucial ecological link between the Shatsky Lakes and the Baltic Sea. Once channelled and sluiced, the river valley is now undergoing self-restoration, with meanders re-forming and floodplain processes returning. A steady distribution of beaver lodges along the riverbanks marks this successful rehabilitation. The area’s international importance for wetland conservation is underscored by its West Bug floodplain, which lies within the Bug River Ramsar site and supports many globally threatened species.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Pribuzhskoye-Polesie

records.introduction_en: Located in the north-west of the Republic of the Congo, about thirty kilometres east of the Gabon border, Odzala Kokoua is a nationally significant protected area. It brings together extensive lowland rainforest, swamp forest along the Mambili and upper Djoua, dry wooded savannas in the south and more than one hundred forest clearings that shape wildlife movements and foraging. This mosaic underpins exceptional biodiversity and delivers tangible local benefits. The reserve’s goals are to conserve these forests and savannas, support fair local livelihoods linked to conservation, and advance research and monitoring on gorillas, forest elephants and ecosystem change to guide management.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set in the north-western Congolian lowland forests ecoregion, the reserve forms one of Central Africa’s largest remaining blocks of intact lowland rainforest. Around 85% of the area is forest, with the remainder a mosaic of forest–savanna and open savanna. Within this landscape lie Congolian evergreen and semi-deciduous forests with dense Marantaceae understorey, swamp forests along the Mambili and upper Djoua, dry wooded savannas in the south, and more than one hundred forest clearings (bais) that shape wildlife movements and foraging. Ecologically, Odzala’s bais, wetland–alluvial systems and broad forest–savanna transitions underpin habitat connectivity, hydrological regulation and high species turnover. The site is recognised as an Important Bird Area and contributes to regional conservation through its mosaic of representative Central African ecosystems and the ecological processes they sustain. The flora is notable for first national records of the small tree Diospyros whitei and the orchids Brachycorythis lisowskii and Habenaria lisowskii. The reserve supports fauna of international significance, including the largest known population of western lowland gorillas and one of Congo’s two largest forest elephant (Loxodonta africana cyclotis) populations. Typical mammals include leopard (Panthera pardus), spotted hyena (Crocuta crocuta), forest (dwarf) buffalo (Syncerus caffer nanus) and great forest hog (Hylochoerus meinertzhageni).
records.name: Kokoua-Odzala

records.introduction_en: The Cinturón Andino Biosphere Reserve is located in the Macizo Colombiano, in the Andean chain of southern Colombia. It comprises three national parks: Cueva de los Guácharos National Park, Puracé National Park and Nevado del Huila National Park. Cueva de los Guácharos contains complex geological formations and caves carved by the Suazas River.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The terrain is steep and covered by humid and cloud forests. The biosphere reserve also includes the snowy peaks of Nevado del Huila, which rise to 5,750 metres above sea level. Vegetation ranges from sub-hygrophyte levels to snow levels and includes cloud forest and high barren plains. The park is especially rich in birds, such as the condor (Vultur gryphus), Colombia’s national emblem, and the Accipiter collaris. It also supports the mountain tapir, or danta (Tapirus pinchaque). The volcanic chain of Puracé National Park includes seven craters, sources of thermal waters, 30 lagoons and waterfalls, and the headwaters of the Magdalena, Cauca and Caquetá rivers, forming a fluvial star.
records.name: Cinturón Andino

records.introduction_en: The Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta Biosphere Reserve is in northern Colombia, not far from the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta Biosphere Reserve. Ciénaga Grande is one of the largest coastal wetlands in Latin America, comprising coral reefs and mangroves.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve includes Isla de Salamanca National Park and the Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta Flora and Fauna Sanctuary. It sits at the interface of fresh and brackish waters, shallow bays and deeper coastal waters, creating a mosaic of habitats that support high biodiversity. The alluvial prairies of recent origin within the Magdalena River’s primitive delta feature mud-bank formations, lagoons and channels with extensive mangrove stands, sawgrass marshes, and both flooded and non-flooded forests.
records.name: Seaflower

records.introduction_en: Located in the south-west of the Democratic Republic of Congo, about 120 km east of the Atlantic coast, Luki Biosphere Reserve represents the humid tropical rainforest ecosystem.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: At altitudes between 150 and 500 metres above sea level, many different habitats can be distinguished, including: primary forests with Gossweilerodendron balsamiferum, Gilletiodendron kisantuense and Terminalia superba; secondary forests with Terminalia superba; woody and herbaceous savannas; agroecosystems; and agroforestry systems. The plant resources of the area are used for both commercial purposes (palm oil, coffee and cacao) and traditional nutrition (banana, taro, manioc, rice, corn).
records.name: Luki

records.introduction_en: The Entlebuch Biosphere Reserve is located at the foot of the Alps in central Switzerland.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve covers reaches an altitude of 2,350 metres above sea level. Few regions in the country have natural and cultural landscapes that are as intact as those in Entlebuch. It includes peat bogs and raised bogs, alluvial and riverine forests, as well as complete cave systems, such as the Schrattenfluh and the Napf area.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Entlebuch

records.introduction_en: The Archipiélago de Juan Fernández Biosphere Reserve is situated 650 km off the Chilean coast in the Pacific Ocean. It includes the whole archipelago, comprising the islands of Robinson Crusoe, Alexander Selkirk and Santa Clara, and all islets in the area. The Juan Fernandez Archipelago is volcanic in origin, with steep, rugged mountain ranges and deep ravines.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This reserve is an insular ecosystem, characterised by 131 endemic plant species, representing 62 per cent of the native vascular flora. Remnants of the past include Lactoris fernandeziana and Thyrsopteris elegans, and ten endemic species: Cuminia, Dendroseris, Juania, Lactoris, Megalachne, Podophorus, Robinsonia, Selkirkia, Thyrsopteris and Yunquea. An outstanding characteristic of the Juan Fernández forests is that all recorded tree species occur only in the archipelago, meaning they are 100 per cent endemic. Fauna includes the Juan Fernandez firecrown (Sephanoides fernandensis), the Juan Fernandez tit-tyrant (Anairetes fernandezianus) and the Juan Fernandez fur seal (Arctocephalus philippii).
records.name: Archipiélago de Juan Fernández

records.title_en: Laguna San Rafael y el Guayaneco
records.introduction_en: Located in the Valdivian Forest and Chilean Nothofagus biogeographical region, Laguna San Rafael is an area of varied topography and great scenic beauty. It includes the Continental Patagonian Range with rivers and lakes, the Insular Patagonian Range, the Central Plain and the Patagonian Glaciers.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This biosphere reserve contains high ecosystem diversity. Of the ten plant formations in the Aysen Region, seven are found in the reserve: high-mountain deciduous shrubland, Aysen deciduous forest, Puyahuapi evergreen forest, Baker mixed evergreen forest, evergreen coastal shrubland, periglacial shrubland, Messier Channel peat bogs, and swampy evergreen shrubland. As most of the reserve is coastal, notable features include estuaries, mudflats, and coastal and beach lands. There is also a large area of other wetlands, including peatbogs, swamps, lakes, lagoons and rivers. The whole of the North Patagonia Ice Fields is included which cover over 400,000 ha with numerous glacier breakoffs. The well-known San Rafael is the main tourist attraction of the XI Aysen Region and one of the most outstanding glaciers in the country.
records.name: Laguna San Rafael y el Guayaneco

records.introduction_en: The Cabo de Hornos (Cape Horn) Biosphere Reserve represents a milestone for biodiversity conservation worldwide, as it includes an extensive area that covers the entire southern tip of Chile and the Americas, representing a treasure in terms of biological and cultural diversity. Here are the southernmost forests on the planet, at 55–56° S, which grow within a mosaic of pristine ecosystems. These include tundra formations and high Andean habitats, as well as glaciers, ice fields and Andean peaks. They also include permanent and intermittent watercourses, brown-kelp forests, fjords, channels, currents and intricate seabeds.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This biosphere reserve is part of the Magallanes sub-polar evergreen rainforest, also known as the sub-Antarctic, with a mosaic of contrasting ecosystems and unique characteristics on a global level. The most representative ecosystems are Magallanes sub-polar evergreen rainforests, sub-Antarctic Antarctic beech (Nothofagus antarctica) forests, deciduous lenga beech forests, mixed lenga beech and Magallanes Nothofagus dombeyi forests, high Andean habitats and the Magallanes tundra complex. Coastal and marine areas are representative of the sub-Antarctic region, which favours biodiversity. The sub-Antarctic ecoregion includes a great diversity of Chilean non-vascular flora and is a hotspot for bryophyte diversity on a global level, with over 300 hepatic species and over 450 species of moss. These 750 bryophyte species represent over 5 per cent of all bryophytes known worldwide.
records.name: Cabo de Hornos

records.introduction_en: The Lauca Biosphere Reserve is situated in the Puna biogeographic region in the northern part of Chile in the Andean chain. It is home to unique flora with endemic species, some of which are of great medicinal importance, as well as fauna that include vicuñas, guanacos, vizcachas, foxes, quirquinchos, pumas, tarucas, suris or ñandús, and a great variety of birds such as flamingos and guallatas. This is one of the areas with the greatest number of bird species described in Chile.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The following plant formations occur. Low ‘tolar’ scrubland is characterised by shrub-like, resinous plants with stunted growth, forming relatively dense scrub, with dominant plants reaching about one metre in height. High ‘queñoal’ scrubland comprises small trees up to five metres high on the mountain slopes. The humid ‘bofedal’ steppe occurs above 4,000 metres where running water is present. It includes an association of Oxychloe andina, characterised by its marshy cushion form. Pulvinate plants occur from 3,800 metres upwards and include Laretia compacta and Parastrephia quadrangularis. The principal species, Laretia, forms very compact cushions up to two metres in diameter and one metre high. The bofedales (high-Andean wetlands) are among the most important habitats, providing food and water for both wild and domestic animals. Native fauna is a major asset, contributing to ecological value and scenic interest. Birdlife is diverse, with nearly 150 species, representing about 30 per cent of the country’s total.
records.name: Lauca

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve includes Campana National Park and Lago Peñuelas National Reserve. The relief is gently undulating, with small hills and several gullies. The highest peaks are El Roble, at 2,222 metres above sea level, and La Campana, at 1,920 metres. The major vegetation type is scrubland with Looser (Cryptocarya alba), boldea fragran (Peumus boldus), and winter’s bark (Drimys winteri).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This biosphere reserve includes various ecosystems, all hosting endemic species. Hygrophyll forests are present in the lower parts of gullies and on humid slopes, with species such as Crinodendron patagua, Persea lingue, Dasyphyllum excelsum and Beilschmiedia miersii. Sclerophyll forests host Cryptocarya alba, boldo (Peumus boldus) and the soapbark tree (Quillaja saponaria). Deciduous forests include Nothofagus macrocarpa. Palm forests include the Chilean palm (Jubaea chilensis). Spiny shrub formations feature Acacia caven and Schinus polygamus. There is xerophyllous and Chusquea culeou shrubland, and highland steppe shrubland. There are also formations of large puyas, or “chaguales”, including Puya chilensis, Puya coerulea and Puya berteroniana. One body of water in the reserve forms an important wetland for migratory birds and occasional resident ones. A total of 125 species of aquatic, riparian and terrestrial birds have been recorded.
records.name: La Campana-Peñuelas

records.introduction_en: Torres del Paine lies between the Andes Mountains and the Patagonian steppe in southern Chile and opens towards the Pacific coast. It is an area of great scenic beauty, with many ridges, crags, glaciers, waterfalls, rivers, lakes and lagoons.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve comprises four well-defined ecological zones. Pre-Andean scrubland occurs on plains and plateau-like formations, where species are adapted to economising water under exposure to strong winds. The deciduous Magellanic forest includes all tree and shrub communities in the area, dominated by lenga (Nothofagus pumilio). The Patagonian steppe, also on plains and plateaux, has a cold semi-arid climate with up to 400 mm of annual rainfall; here, perennial medium- to low-height grasses grow in ditch-like depressions. The Andean desert corresponds to a zone where vegetation only develops up to 1.5 m in height with cover ranging from 30 per cent to 0 per cent due to extreme climatic conditions and altitude. Notable is the pre-Andean scrub association dominated by Mulinum spinosum. Parts of the flora are endemic to the reserve and to the Province of Última Esperanza, with Adesmia campestris rare and locally restricted.
records.name: Torres del Paine

records.introduction_en: Alto Bernesga Biosphere Reserve is one of three new units of a large-scale biosphere reserve that will encompass the entire Gran Cantabria mountain range.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The wealth and biodiversity in the Alto Bernesga Biosphere Reserve are exceptional because of its biogeographic position in the transition areas between dry Spain and humid Spain, that is, between the Mediterranean region and the Euro-Siberian or Atlantic region. The flora includes high mountain grasslands on crags, rocks and passes, oak groves, acidophilous Oro-Cantabrian beech trees, and Euro-Siberian riparian forests of willow and poplar trees. Endemic plant formations are present, notably the Sabina Albar forests and Oro-Cantabrian oak groves. In terms of fauna, special mention should be made of the birdlife, with endangered species such as the red kite, the Egyptian vulture, the peregrine hawk and the golden eagle. The chamois (Rupicapra rupicapra) is also an emblematic species of the region. In addition to a diversity of flora and fauna, the reserve is of great palaeontological value due to the Devonian seafloor fossil sites. This wealth makes Alto Bernesga highly attractive to researchers and students worldwide, who visit its unique sites; only three comparable sites exist elsewhere, and they are less accessible.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Alto de Bernesga

records.introduction_en: Área de Allariz Biosphere Reserve, in Galicia on the Iberian Peninsula in north-western Spain, is important for cultural values and sustainable land use, enabling conservation of local flora and fauna.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is of great biogeographical importance, because the local flora and fauna have been preserved in this border territory between two extensive ecological areas. These are the morpho-tectonic semi-endorheic depression with a flat base where the River Limia flows, and the mountain ridge to the north, characterised by the Allariz granitic massif, where the confined Arnoia River winds. Three ecologically valuable areas stand out. The veigas are enclaves of land on the banks of the Antela canal and the Limia River, with herbaceous and shrub vegetation. The touzas form a mosaic of meadows or croplands separated by patches of trees. The sebes are mixed stands of pedunculate and Pyrenean oak with considerable species diversity.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Área de Allariz

records.introduction_en: The Bardenas Reales Biosphere Reserve and Natural Park are located in northern Spain and comprises the Natural Reserve ‘Rincón del Bú’ and the Reserva Natural ‘Caídas de la Negra’.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: To the north lies the great plateau known as El Plano. La Blanca occupies the central area, a large depression where softer sedimentary rocks leave clay unprotected and give rise to spectacular and capricious erosive formations or badlands. La Negra is located to the south and comprises a group of horizontal tubular formations. The climate is characterised by extremes, with very cold winters giving way, with almost no transition into spring, to torrid summers. Rainfall is scant and irregular and is frequently torrential. The action of strong, dry winds, particularly strong, dry north-easterly winds known as cierzos, accentuates the aridity of the area. All this has made Las Bardenas into a true cold desert in the heart of Europe, where the conditions of the great central Asian steppes are reproduced. This is reflected in the Aralo-Caspian vegetation found here, where species of halophilous flora predominate. These species are adapted to living on saline soils in the depressions, giving way to Mediterranean forests of Aleppo pine in the more thermophilous areas of La Negra. In terms of fauna, the biosphere reserve hosts an abundance of birds of prey, such as the griffon vulture, the Egyptian vulture, the golden eagle and the peregrine falcon. There is also a great diversity of grassland birds, such as the great bustard, little bustard, Eurasian stone-curlew, black-bellied sandgrouse and the rare Dupont’s lark.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Bardenas Reales

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is located in the extreme south-east of the Iberian Peninsula, in the most arid part of Europe. It includes a marine zone to a depth of 60 m. Volcanic rocks characterise the landscape, and Mediterranean plant communities such as cornical (Periploca laevigata), tomillares in the Labiatae family, and halophytic matorral adapted to drought have high floristic diversity. These communities are considered a priority for conservation at European and Mediterranean levels.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Cabo de Gata Sierra is one of the main European volcanic mountain massifs. It stretches to the coast with cliffs over 100 m high, edged with salt flats and chains of fixed sand dunes. The coastal shelf is well conserved, with vast underwater meadows of Posidonia and benthic communities associated with the dimly lit rocky seabed. The climate is conditioned by the proximity of the Sahara Desert and the influence, during most of the year, of the Azores anticyclone. The result is high temperatures and scant, irregular rainfall. The biosphere reserve hosts an abundance of semi-arid plant formations with fan palms, the only autochthonous continental European palm tree, Pistacia lentiscus, Olea europaea sylvestris, and the Indian jujube (Ziziphus jujuba). Numerous endemic species specific to the zone occur together with many species characteristic of Saharan flora. In the dunes and sand flats, vegetation adapted to saline soils has developed, including European beach-grass, Salicornia and Arthrocnemetea. Regarding the fauna, the biosphere reserve is home to grassland birds such as the stone-curlew, the Tibetan sand-grouse and the black-bellied sandgrouse, and a diversity of aquatic birds present in the sandflats, such as the black-winged stilt, the pied avocet, the flamingo and the rare Audouin’s gull.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Cabo de Gata-Nijar

records.introduction_en: The Fuerteventura Biosphere Reserve is located on the oldest and second largest of the Canary Islands. The western coastline extends for more than 100 km and is free of human intervention. Unlike the other Canary Islands, the topography is characterised by U-shaped valleys and low mountains. The highest peak is Pico de la Zarza at 807 m in the south of the reserve. The island also contains a rich fossil record distributed across 50 palaeontological sites of global importance.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Due to the island’s proximity to the African continent, the climate is very arid, resulting in an almost complete lack of tree cover. However, the lack of abundant vegetation facilitates the observation of climate-change impacts and efforts to understand the development of geological features. Volcanic activity can be traced back more than 20 million years, with the formation of a mountain that exceeded 3,000 m in altitude. Today, the highest mountain on the island barely exceeds 800 m. The main habitat types in Fuerteventura are steppe, sea cliffs, and the largest desert and semi-desert in Europe. Despite its arid character, the island hosts a significant range of biodiversity. Zygophylletum fontanesii, a genus in the Zygophyllaceae family, and common greenshank (Tringa nebularia) are described as the most common species. Other noticeable species are olive (Olea europaea), Persian turpentine tree (Pistacia atlantica) and Pistacia lentiscus, a small tree of the pistachio genus. In addition, the biosphere reserve is home to approximately 644 species of vascular plants, representing one-third of all such species found in the Canary Islands. Fossils of extinct fauna provide historical evidence of rich diversity. Examples include sea snail (Strombus bobonius), dune shearwater (Puffinus holeae) and lava mouse (Malpaisomys insularis). Contemporary fauna of special interest includes common kestrel (Falco tinnunculus), yellow-legged gull (Larus michahellis) and Cory’s shearwater (Calonectris diomedea). A number of vulnerable animal species also live on Fuerteventura, including little shearwater (Puffinus assimilis) and Bulwer’s petrel (Bulweria bulwerii).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Fuerteventura

records.introduction_en: Sierra de Grazalema is located in the limestone massifs shared by the Andalusian provinces of Cádiz and Málaga. It has a typical karst morphology, which gives this protected natural area impressive geological phenomena. Its rainfall, among the highest in the Iberian Peninsula, is a determining factor for the great diversity of ecosystems present in this region and, therefore, its impressive biodiversity.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This protected natural space holds innumerable natural values related to its very high environmental diversity and resulting biodiversity. Its microclimate is extraordinarily rainy, exceeding 2,000 mm per year, as it is one of the first mountain barriers encountered by the humid fronts of the Atlantic. This gives rise to one of the most extensive forested patches in Spain. It contains a very representative sample of Spanish firs, a species endemic to the mountain ranges of Cádiz and Málaga. These are reminiscent of the firs that populated them during the glaciations. Alongside these stands, there is a dense Mediterranean forest of holm oaks, cork oaks and gall oaks. In addition to its intrinsic value, this forest is home to more than 130 species of birds, 44 species of mammals, 24 species of reptiles and 10 species of amphibians. With respect to its geological values, the karst modelling of this mountain range translates into an abundance of canyons, caves and chasms. Together with the exuberant vegetation, this produces an abrupt and beautiful topography.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Sierra de Grazalema

records.introduction_en: El Hierro is a volcanic island, the youngest and smallest of the Canary Archipelago. Situated in the Macaronesian biogeographical region, its vegetation includes coastal matorral, thermophilous juniper forest, evergreen woodlands and pine forest, as well as marine and coastal habitats. El Hierro has great biological diversity, at both ecosystem and species levels. In 2014, a hybrid hydro–wind electricity generation system made El Hierro the first energy self-sufficient island relying entirely on renewable energy sources.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: El Hierro is the most westerly and smallest island in the Canary Archipelago. It has abrupt landforms with steep slopes, and most of its coastline comprises cliffs. The mountains reach a maximum altitude of 1,501 m. The climate is conditioned by its proximity to the tropics and influenced by the trade winds. Combined with altitude, this gives rise to various climatic zones, with rainfall ranging from 150 mm in the southern coastal areas to 750 mm in the northern divide. The distribution of the main ecosystems is staggered. Coastal scrubland includes succulent plants such as different kinds of spurge. There are thermophile forests of Spanish juniper, evergreen laurel forests together with myrtle and tree heath, and, finally, the Canary pine grove. There are numerous endemic species of flora and fauna, among the latter the El Hierro giant lizard (Gallotia simonyi), once thought to be extinct. However, recently, residual populations have been found that have enabled its rehabilitation. Other endangered species are the white-tailed laurel pigeon, the European storm petrel (Hydrobates pelagicus) and Bulwer’s petrel (Bulweria bulwerii). The wealth of marine life is exceptional and much visited by divers from all over the world.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Isla de El Hierro

records.title_en: Las Sierras de Cazorla y Segura
records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve and natural park include the upper reaches of the Guadalquivir River, together with a vast reservoir built for hydroelectric power generation, and extensive mountains and forests. The landscape is a mosaic of peaks, valleys, rocky gorges and vertical cliffs, and displays many typical karst limestone features. The Sierras of Cazorla, Segura y las Villas are part of a great mountain massif. They are dominated by several peaks over 2,000 m, with Empanadas being the highest. The forests are particularly notable.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This is the largest protected area in Spain. It covers a series of limestone mountain lines in a north-east to south-west direction, where carbonate rocks, limestone and dolomite predominate, with great richness in fossils, and with interspersed marl and detritic levels, mainly sand. In addition to tectonic action, another major morphodynamic agent shaping these landforms is water, specifically its action on carbonate rocks. This has generated spectacular karst landscapes and gives rise to various rivers. For this reason, it represents an important reservoir of water resources, both surface and underground. It constitutes the headwaters of two important river basins, the Guadalquivir and the Segura, which provide refuges for flora from more northern latitudes. Its floristic catalogue amounts to some 2,228 species, among which there are more than 30 local endemisms. The diversity of habitats in this area favours the presence of more than 200 species of inventoried vertebrates, with certain local endemism such as the Valverde lizard (Algiroides marchi). Its wealth of fish, including trout, barbel and bogue, allows for 16 inland fishing reserves, 22 fishing refuges and a fish farm. Large herbivores constitute its most emblematic faunal group, with species such as deer, wild goats and wild boar. Birds of prey stand out for their abundance and richness. Notably, the bearded vulture reintroduction project, run at the Guadalentín captive breeding centre in the heart of the reserve, has successfully returned the species to the biosphere reserve since 2006.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Las Sierras de Cazorla y Segura

records.introduction_en: The Lanzarote Biosphere Reserve comprises the northernmost island of the Canary Archipelago, including the northern islets.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The island is relatively flat, with a maximum altitude of 670 m. It is of volcanic origin, with vast lava fields known as malpaís and a profusion of craters in Timanfaya National Park. There are also shallow seabeds that harbour a great wealth of biodiversity. The climate is dry subtropical, with trade winds and a mean annual rainfall of 115 mm. There are no permanent watercourses. The vegetation is xerophilous, adapted to storing and retaining humidity. There is a high number of endemic species. The island culture developed adaptations to trap and use scant and unpredictable rainfall. This includes agricultural techniques for sowing under ash and using volcanic sheet flows beneath inverted cones, forming unique landscapes such as those of the La Geria valley.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Lanzarote

records.introduction_en: Dehesas de Sierra Morena is located in the north-west of Andalusia and includes three Natural Parks: Aracena and Picos de Aroche in the province of Huelva, Sierra Norte de Sevilla, and Hornachuelos in the province of Córdoba.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This vast reserve forms a continuous area along the southern edge of the Iberian Plateau, where medium to low mountains alternate with some higher ranges. This internal fragmentation facilitates a diversity of habitats. Within this mosaic, the most representative ecosystem is the dehesa, a hollowed-out forest that occupies more than 50 per cent of the territory and features distinctive species such as cork oaks, holm oaks, chestnuts and gall oaks. Magnificent riverbanks with gallery forests, dotted with willows and ash trees, the chestnut forests, and the diversity of species in the noble scrub complete its landscapes. The high biodiversity of these varied landscapes includes emblematic Mediterranean fauna such as the Iberian lynx, the Spanish eagle and the Eurasian black vulture.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Las Dehesas de Sierra Morena

records.introduction_en: La Gomera is centrally located in the Canary Archipelago, surrounded by the islands of Tenerife, La Palma and El Hierro. It is one of the least populous islands, and tourism plays an increasingly important role.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The island of La Gomera has a surface area of 371 km² and a maximum height of 1,487 m at Alto de Garajonay. It has an exceptionally sharp relief organised in radial, deep ravines. Its physiography is the result of an ancient volcanic structure that has undergone intense freshwater and marine erosion. This weathering process has led to a central plateau at about 1,000 m in altitude and to its extensions along the divides between ravines. Humidity and clouds from the sea are often halted on this plateau, producing a “sea of clouds”. This effect generates high humidity that has favoured the existence of the most important area of the archipelago, Garajonay National Park. The park is also a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is noted for its laurisilva (laurel) forest, a habitat that has almost disappeared from southern Europe and North Africa. La Gomera has a total of 4,182 species, of which 1,063 are endemic to the Canary Islands and 268 are exclusive to La Gomera. Most of the endemic species are located in the central part of the island, especially in the laurisilva forest. Among the most representative plant species are laurisilva, Frankenia ericifolia, Astydamia latifolia, Limonium pectinatum, Reichardia ligulata and Zygophyllum fontanesii. The most representative animal species are the osprey (Pandion haliaetus), the common kestrel (Falco tinnunculus), the Barbary falcon (Falco pelegrinoides), the little shearwater (Puffinus assimilis) and the La Gomera giant lizard (Gallotia bravoana).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: La Gomera

records.introduction_en: Situated in central-western Spain, La Siberia Biosphere Reserve features major freshwater reservoirs along the Guadiana and Zújar rivers in a landscape of large plains and oak forests. To the north and north-east, it borders the region of Villuercas-Jara-Ibores, which has been designated a UNESCO Global Geopark. The reserve contains a wide variety of habitats that support highly diverse flora and fauna, including extensive plains and forest formations. Sustainable development plans to boost social and economic activity have been developed to curb emigration.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve lies in the north-east of the Province of Badajoz in the central-western part of Spain. Major freshwater reservoirs occur along the courses of the Guadiana and Zújar rivers, which traverse La Siberia. These reservoirs play an important role in supporting a wide variety of habitats that are home to diverse flora and fauna, including extensive plains and forest formations. The vegetation is characterised by the predominance of Quercus formations, including holm oak (Quercus ilex), cork oak (Quercus suber) and Portuguese oak (Quercus faginea). These landscapes also support organic livestock. The peat bogs are home to rare species such as Drosera rotundifolia and Pinguicula lusitanica. Shrub vegetation is also present, including kermes oak (Quercus coccifera) and strawberry tree (Arbutus unedo). Despite the great diversity and rich fauna, five species are in danger of extinction, 19 are vulnerable and 158 are on the List of Wild Species under a Special Protection Regime. Endangered mammals include the Iberian lynx (Lynx pardinus) and horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus ferrumequinum). Emblematic birds include the Iberian imperial eagle (Aquila adalberti), the golden kite (Milvus milvus), the black vulture (Aegypius monachus) and the black stork (Ciconia nigra). Notable reptiles include the ocellated lizard (Lacerta lepida), the Mediterranean pond turtle (Mauremys leprosa) and Lataste’s viper (Vipera latastei). The area includes the Embalse de Orellana Ramsar site. Of the total surface area of the reserve, 43.27 per cent forms part of the Natura 2000 Network.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: La Siberia

records.introduction_en: The La Palma Biosphere Reserve in the Canary Islands was extended and renamed in 2002, with the former Los Tiles Biosphere Reserve now constituting the core area. The biosphere reserve now encompasses the entire island, which contains a wide range of representative habitats, reflecting the transition from the coast up to the mountain peaks.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: La Palma, whose highest peak is Roque de los Muchachos at 2,426 m, is considered one of the highest islands in the world in relation to its surface area. It is a miniature continent that contains, staggered at different altitudes, all the representative ecosystems of the Macaronesian region, a biogeographical region grouping the archipelagos of the Canaries, Madeira and the Azores. The sequence begins with coastal Euphorbia obtusifolia and spurges, then gives way to thermophile forest. It subsequently transitions to monteverde vegetation, including laurel forests, tree heath and faya, which at greater altitudes are replaced by Canary pine. At the summit, the vegetation is dominated by Adenocarpus viscosus and scrubland. The laurel forests are especially noteworthy. They are associated with horizontal precipitation, caused by the condensation of coastal fogs driven by the humid trade winds. This permanent atmospheric humidity, characteristic of the Tertiary Era has enabled relict plants to survive. Forest function is also vital for aquifer replenishment, which is essential for the development of the island. Among the fauna are numerous endemic insect species and unique birds, such as Bolle’s laurel pigeon and the white-tailed laurel pigeon.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: La Palma

records.introduction_en: The Los Ancares Leoneses Biosphere Reserve is located in the extreme north-east of the Province of León. The reserve is named after the major Ancares River, which flows through the area. Other extensive rivers in the region are the Cúa, Burbia and Ancares. It belongs to two major hydrographic basins, the Cuenca Norte and Cuenca del Miño. Three sub-regions can be found within the reserve, namely Valle de Ancares, Valle de Fornela and Alto Burbia. The boundaries are marked by three mountains: the Sierra del Caurel in the west, the Sierra de los Ancares in the north-east and the Cordillera Cantábrica in the north. The highest peaks are found in the north-eastern and south-western parts of the reserve: Cuina at 1,998 metres, Miravalles at 1,996 metres, El Mostellar at 1,924 metres and Peñarrubia at 1,826 metres.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The major ecosystem types in the biosphere reserve are Atlantic mountains. Other habitat types include heathlands, meadows and shrublands. Characteristic flora species are Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) and sweet chestnut (Castanea sativa). Coniferous and deciduous forests occur throughout the reserve, with their distribution depending on the mountain level and the influences of the Atlantic and Mediterranean climate. The pygmy shrew (Sorex minutus), Daubenton’s bat (Myotis daubentonii) and the house sparrow (Passer domesticus) are common fauna species. The Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus) and Montagu’s harrier (Circus pygargus) are among the most endangered species in Spain. The reserve is home to endemic fauna, such as the broom hare (Lepus castroviejoi) and a distinctive form of grey partridge (Perdix perdix). It also supports endangered animals, including the brown bear (Ursus arctos).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Los Ancares Leoneses

records.introduction_en: The Macizo de Anaga Biosphere Reserve is located in the north-east of the island of Tenerife in the Canary Islands. Macizo de Anaga hosts significant faunal diversity, with reptiles, birds and fish, and in particular large numbers of invertebrates, with 1,900 species recorded. The reserve consists of four protected natural areas, a Rural Park and three Integral Natural Reserves, as well as areas that form part of the Natura 2000 network, including a Special Bird Protection Area and Special Areas of Conservation.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: From a geological point of view, the massif is one of the oldest areas on the island, with rocks dating back seven million to nine million years. Over this long period, the area has experienced cycles of volcanic and erosive activity, the result of which is a rich geological and geomorphological mosaic.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Macizo de Anaga

records.introduction_en: The largest and best-preserved Mediterranean forest worldwide is located in the region, which is surrounded by hills covered with oak forests and Mediterranean thicket, and dotted with rocks and streams. Rivers and reservoirs irrigate the riverside areas, resulting in rich and varied biodiversity. This site lies in the Province of Extremadura and is characterised by sclerophyllous Mediterranean forests and dehesas, a landscape modelled by human impacts through cattle raising and production of cork from cork oak trees. The landscape of the biosphere reserve is very representative of a Mediterranean agrosylvopastoral system.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The central area consists of a succession of sierras at an altitude of about 500 m, festooned with quartzite crests. The best representations of Mediterranean forest and shrubland, harbouring 90 per cent of the Mediterranean flora present in the Iberian Peninsula, are found on the slopes of these sierras, particularly on the shady sides. Towards the outer part, and coinciding with the transition zone, the terrain is less rugged and more accessible to humans. Here, dehesas take over from the Mediterranean forest. They are in an excellent state of conservation, together with other less representative ecosystems such as the riparian woodlands, irrigated land near the Tiétar River, and the orchards and smallholdings near the villages. The presence of endangered species, such as the lynx and the black stork, is noteworthy. However, the most emblematic species in the biosphere reserve are the numerous and large colonies of birds of prey, such as the exceptional Spanish imperial eagle (known as Adalberti’s eagle), and the colonies of the Eurasian black vulture.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Monfragüe

records.introduction_en: The Picos de Europa Biosphere Reserve encompasses some of the highest montane systems of the large Cantabrian Mountains range.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area was designated a national park in 1918 because its natural ecosystems were relatively undisturbed. Habitats include low coastal Atlantic forest and abundant beech forest with Fagus sylvatica, as well as oak woods with Quercus robur, Quercus patraea and Quercus pyrenaica. There are also small relict sclerophyllous and sub-sclerophyllous forests. The area is home to endangered species such as Ursus arctos, Canis lupus signatus and Tetrao urogallus.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Picos de Europa

records.introduction_en: The Redes Biosphere Reserve is the third biosphere reserve in the Cantabrian mountain range in the Province of Asturias. It is characterised by great biological and cultural diversity and is part of the effort to create a Gran Cantabrian Biosphere Reserve together with Somiedo and Muniellos, which would be the first biosphere reserve in Europe to cover an entire ‘ecoregion’. Redes comprises two areas characteristic of the Cantabrian Mountains: the karst limestone areas in the eastern regions, and the silica, quartzite, slate and sandstone areas in the west.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Redes is located on the northern slope of the eastern Cantabrian Cordillera in the upper basin of the Nalón, one of the rivers with the greatest discharge in northern Spain. The territory includes the whole of the Caso and Sobrescobio councils, with altitude variations ranging from the River Nalón at 350 m to 2,104 m at Pico Torres. The landforms are steep, with deep ravines and spectacular waterfalls such as those along the Ruta del Alba. The ecological importance of the biosphere reserve is noteworthy for its vast forest masses of autochthonous beech and oak, which are in a good state of conservation. This enables emblematic species to survive, such as the brown bear, the western capercaillie, the royal eagle, the Egyptian vulture and the middle spotted woodpecker. It is also important for its production of water resources that supply water to the whole central Asturian watershed.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Redes

records.introduction_en: Sierra del Rincón Biosphere Reserve lies in the north-eastern sector of the Community of Madrid. The relief is characterised by a mountain chain to the north, east and south. The eastern part also includes two valleys: the Hiruela Valley, delimited by summits with slopes descending towards the Jarama River, and the Puebla Valley, which constitutes a drainage river basin.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve harbours a variety of species of flora and fauna associated with its history of farming and stock raising. Its singularity arises from a mosaic of dehesas, rocky areas, scrubland, rural units and reforested woodlands. These are organised around four valley depressions of varying sizes: the Pradena–Montejo depression, and the valleys of Horcajuelo, La Hiruela and La Puebla. They are surrounded by mountainous belts such as the southern foothills of the Cebollera massif, and the Peña de la Cabra and La Hiruela sierras. The dehesas, clearly differentiated by their fences, are located on the lower slopes and in valley bottoms. They alternate with fenced fields and rural units. The reforested woodlands occupy the slopes, together with rocky outcrops and scrubland, while grasslands develop in the highlands. As a whole, the territory includes seven types of natural habitat. These are: mixed or single-species pine stands; shrubland formations, including piornal with rock-rose (Cistus) and broom; acidophilic scrubland with rock-rose (Cistus) and heath (Erica); oak groves; pastureland; rocky patches; beech forests, such as the unique Hayedo de Montejo; ash and holm oak forests; and riparian forest formations. Biodiversity is represented by numerous species of flora and fauna that confer high conservation value on the biosphere reserve territory. Many of these species are endangered and legally protected by international conventions and regional or national catalogues. Others are endemic species that are scarcely distributed in Mediterranean environments.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Sierra del Rincón

records.introduction_en: Terras do Miño, located in Galicia, is a traditional cultural landscape with many highly important natural habitats and terrace systems formed by erosion and accumulation, associated with specific sections of the Río Miño. The Miño river network drains south-west Galicia in the Iberian Hercynian Massif, underpinning the area’s geomorphology and shaping its ecological and cultural character.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The mountain landscapes of the Serra do Xistral and the riparian landscapes of the river and lagoon ecosystems of Parga–Ladra–Támoga are particularly noteworthy. A multitude of rivers and streams flow into the Miño, the territory’s veritable backbone. This hydrological network has given rise to many priority habitats of community interest in a good state of conservation. These include Galician–Portuguese oak groves, known locally as carballeiras and reboleiras, alluvial alder and birch forests, wetland scrub with gorse, Erica and broom, and semi-flooded grasslands with peculiar peat bogs with mosses and Sphagnum. Among the fauna, there is the permanent presence of the wolf, otter and river mussel. Owing to their extreme sensitivity to water pollution, these species indicate that the riparian ecosystems are in good condition. The river and lagoon ecosystems of Parga–Ladra–Támoga, together with the entirety of the mountain landscapes of the Serra do Xistral, have been proposed for inclusion in the Natura 2000 Network as Natural Protected Areas within the category of Specially Protected Natural Value Areas, according to the provisions of Law 9/2001 of 21 August of Conservación da Natureza.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Terras do Miño

records.title_en: Valles del Jubera, Leza, Cidacos y Alhama
records.introduction_en: The Valles del Leza, Jubera, Cidacos y Alhama Biosphere Reserve is in the south-east of the La Rioja region of Spain. This Mediterranean mountain area is drained by the Leza, Jubera, Cidacos and Alhama rivers. It is covered with forests of temperate-climate species and aromatic scrub, combined with a stony landscape.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This biosphere reserve is a mountain area in the south-east of the La Rioja region that belongs to the Iberian System range. Its highest mountain peaks reach around 1,600 metres. Although there are some important beech forests, such as the Santiago beech grove, the main forest species in this area is holm oak. It occurs in well-conserved forests and also in enclosed pastures. Gall oaks and boxwood also occur, surrounded by diverse Mediterranean scrubland. Next to the villages, the landscape becomes more humanised, and olive and fruit trees can be found. Rocky outcrops and river canyons are an ideal nesting habitat for Bonelli’s eagle, griffon vulture, Egyptian vulture, Eurasian eagle-owl, peregrine falcon and other species. This area also harbours emblematic species such as wildcats and otters, and large populations of ungulates including roe deer, red deer and wild boar. There are 180 palaeontological sites, well known to the scientific community and tourists, with well-preserved dinosaur tracks. Hot springs and medicinal waters flow through the territory and are marketed by spa companies. Some of these waters are sulphurous, and the sulphide-rich subsoil has enabled pyrite mining that is renowned worldwide.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Valles del Jubera, Leza, Cidacos y Alhama

records.introduction_en: La Amistad Biosphere Reserve and National Park lie in the foothills and mountains of the Cordillera de Talamanca, between the mountain ranges of Panama and Costa Rica.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Cordillera de Talamanca is the highest and wildest non-volcanic mountain range in Central America. It was formed by orogenic activity, creating the divide between the Pacific and Caribbean oceans. Of the 20 life zones of Costa Rica, at least eight occur in the park, ranging from lowland tropical wet rainforest to cloud and páramo forests. Most of the main crest lies within the montane rainforest life zone and is characterised by mixed oak forest, which contains the largest tracts of virgin forest in Costa Rica. On high peaks along the ridge over 3,000 metres above sea level, there are frequent stands of páramo, swamps and cold marshes. The páramo on Mount Kamuk contains the richest and most varied vegetation in the entire Talamanca Range. Signs of tapirs (Tapirus terrestris) are abundant near the Panamanian border. Puma (Puma concolor), ocelot (Leopardus pardalis), jaguar (Panthera onca), jaguarundi (Herpailurus yagouaroundi), Central American squirrel monkey (Saimiri oerstedii) and Geoffroy’s spider monkey (Ateles geoffroyi) are found within the biosphere reserve.
records.name: La Amistad

records.introduction_en: Savegre Biosphere Reserve is on the central Pacific coast of Costa Rica, 190 km from the capital, San José. It has rich biodiversity and is home to 20 per cent of the country’s total flora, 54 per cent of its mammals and 59 per cent of its birds. The main productive activities are agriculture and livestock. Ecotourism has increased significantly in recent years and has become a source of socio-economic growth in the region.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Savegre Biosphere Reserve borders La Amistad Biosphere Reserve to the north and east, and Cordillera Volcánica Central Biosphere Reserve to the north. It is the first and only reserve in the country to contain an important marine–coastal component. The site has high value in terms of ecosystems, biodiversity, water resources and connectivity. Owing to its varied topography and heterogeneous microclimates, it is one of the most biodiverse sites in the country. It is home to 20 per cent of the country’s total flora, 54 per cent of its mammals, 59 per cent of its birds and about 330 species of butterflies. The area comprises two zones with a high level of endemism in Costa Rica: the upper parts of the Cordillera de Talamanca and west of Panama, and the basal forests of the South Pacific. It contains 71 endemic plant species, including Passiflora gilbertiana, Bartlettina silvicola, Pseudima costarricense, Sarcaulus and Pitcairnia halophila, palm species such as Chamaedorea piscifolia and Chamaedorea incrustata, and trees including Matisia tinamastiana and Lacmellea zamorae.
records.name: Savegre

records.introduction_en: Situated on the southern coast of Cuba in Matanzas Province, the Ciénaga de Zapata Biosphere Reserve covers 628,171 ha. It is one of the largest and most important wetlands in the Caribbean region, with a marine southern boundary. Ciénaga de Zapata was designated a Ramsar site in 2001. This is a cluster biosphere reserve with several core areas of high conservation value located within Ciénaga de Zapata National Park.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve contains a wide diversity of ecosystems and land-cover types, including grasslands, mangrove forests, Ciénaga forest, semi-deciduous forest, evergreen coastal and sub-coastal forest, and coastal and sub-coastal matorral. Coral reefs and coastal lagoons are also present. The area supports the main populations of the Cuban crocodile (Crocodylus rhombifer), the American crocodile (Crocodylus acutus) and birds such as the American flamingo (Phoenicopterus ruber).
records.name: Ciénaga de Zapata

records.introduction_en: The Tonle Sap Biosphere Reserve is in the north-east of Cambodia. It includes Tonle Sap Lake, the most extensive freshwater lake in South-east Asia, which lies at the centre of the Tonle Sap Basin. The basin is bordered by the Dong Rek Mountains to the north, the Cardamom Mountains to the south-west, and small hills to the east that separate it from the Mekong River.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area comprises three habitats: Tonle Sap Lake in the centre, floodplains and freshwater swamps that surround the lake, and seasonally flooded rice fields and grasslands near two national roads that define the reserve’s outer boundary. During periods of rainfall, the Mekong River overflows and can expand the size of the lake by up to five times. Water levels in numerous streams around the lake also rise, creating a complex delta system that provides habitats for a variety of species with different characteristics. A Ramsar site is situated within Tonle Sap, known as the Boeung Chhmar and Associated River System and Floodplain. The richest vegetation in the reserve is found in the Stung Sen Core Area and river mouth, gallery forests, and the outer floodplains north of Bak Prea. Tall forests with unique biodiversity grow in the Stung Sen Core Area. The gallery forests endure rainfall periods that last six to eight months. Because of its short‑stature upland vegetation, the outer floodplain has higher diversity than the areas surrounding Tonle Sap Lake. Moreover, 80 per cent of the floodplains are covered by swamp scrubland. Two hundred higher plant species, many of which have adapted to the rainy and dry seasons, occur within the reserve. In addition, flooded forests provide a natural protective barrier for villages against inundation and soil erosion. Fish are the most species-rich vertebrate group in the biosphere reserve. The flooded forests, and the ecosystem more broadly, provide critical habitat for numerous plant and animal species. Common species include the long-tailed macaque (Macaca fascicularis) and the hairy-nosed otter (Lutra sumatrana). Vulnerable and endangered species include the masked finfoot (Heliopais personata) and the greater adjuta … [truncated]
records.name: Tonle Sap

records.introduction_en: This mostly marine biosphere reserve is home to several endemic species, including turtles and cetaceans, as well as an abundance of fish, seabirds and marine reptiles. One of the most arid places in the country, Maio features striking beaches which, alongside its festivals, craft markets and historic heritage, have attracted a growing number of tourists in recent years. Most of the island’s population make a living from maize, beans, melons and salt production, as well as tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Maio Biosphere Reserve encompasses the entire island and marine zone. It includes six main components: Maio Island Natural Park, Cimidor Lagoon Natural Reserve, Praia do Morro Natural Reserve, Casas Velhas Natural Reserve, the Barreiro and Figueira Protected Landscape, and the Salt Pan of Porto Inglês. Marine ecosystems host eight local endemic species of gastropods including Conus boavistensis, three species of turtles (Chelonia mydas, Eretmochelys imbricata and Caretta caretta) and cetaceans, as well as the lemon shark (Negaprion brevirostris) and tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier). On land, more than 256 species of fauna have been identified, including three endemic lizards (Chioninia spinalis mayensis, C. delalandii and Tarentola mayensis). Over 100 migratory bird species have also been recorded in the region.
records.name: Maio

records.introduction_en: Krkonoše/Karkonosze is a transboundary biosphere reserve in north-western Czechia and south-western Poland. The Krkonoše/Karkonosze Mountains form part of the Sudetes in north-eastern Bohemia, a mountain system shared by Czechia, Germany and Poland. The reserve represents a unique pocket of arctic nature in Central Europe and an extraordinary crossroads where arctic, alpine, lowland and mountain elements mingle within a relatively small territory. The area is known for high biodiversity across four altitudinal vegetation belts. Human activities have shaped nature and the landscape throughout the Krkonoše Mountains over the last four centuries. Today, it is a popular tourist destination for hikers and skiers, especially on the Czech side.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Krkonoše Mountains lie on the northern fringe of the Bohemian Massif. Two main ridges are connected by two summit etch plains. A steep tectonic slope forms the Polish side, while on the Czech side several parallel ranges, divided by river valleys, project from the main ridges. Several glacial lakes occur on the Polish side, and a complex of subarctic peat bogs is found on the summit plateau along both sides of the border. Four distinct altitudinal vegetation belts are recognised, from submontane in the foothills up through montane and subalpine to the alpine belt at the highest elevations. This habitat diversity supports rich biodiversity. Animal species include the alpine shrew (Sorex alpinus), western capercaillie (Tetrao urogallus), peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus) and lesser horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus hipposideros). The reserve contains two Ramsar sites: the subalpine peat bogs in the Karkonosze Mountains on the Polish side, and Krkonošská rašeliniště on the Czech side.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Krkonose

records.introduction_en: The Šumava Biosphere Reserve includes a substantial part of the north-east-facing Bohemian Forest, a large Hercynian mid-mountain range that straddles the border between the Czechia, Germany and Austria. The reserve lies adjacent to the Bayerischer Wald Biosphere Reserve in Germany.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Šumava is a flat or gently undulating region near the Austrian and Bavarian borders that has been shaped by human activity for more than ten centuries. The Šumava mountains form one of the most extensive forested areas in Central Europe. Primeval mountain forests, glacial lakes, peat bogs, rivers and canyons are the key landscape features. Forests cover approximately 65 per cent of the biosphere reserve, including flowering and acidophilous beech forests and mountain spruce forests, and the proportion within the Šumava–Bohemian Forest National Park is even higher at 83.8 per cent. Peat bogs are another important natural element. There are extensive plains at approximately 1,000 m above sea level in the Šumava Mountains, and large areas of these plains are used as meadows or pastures. Among wild animals, the northern birch mouse is notable. The Eurasian lynx has been successfully reintroduced. Wild birds include the capercaillie and black grouse. In the headwaters of the Blanice River lies the most important site for the river pearl mussel in Czechia.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Sumava

records.introduction_en: The Volga-Akhtuba Floodplain Biosphere Reserve, based on the existing nature park of the same name, is one of the most significant and unique natural territorial complexes in the south of Russia. It plays an outstanding role as an environmentally integrating and stabilising component, including for local climate regulation. It is practically the only site within the Volga valley that has preserved a natural hydraulic streamflow regime throughout the entire length of the Volga River from the source at Tver to the estuary.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Wetlands are landscapes of special value in the biosphere reserve, with typical plant communities and wildlife. They include extensive floodplain meadows and spawning grounds and serve as resting sites for migratory birds and habitats for nesting populations. The wetlands encompass a wide spectrum of water bodies and permanent and seasonal shallows, as well as waterlogged areas with a free water table that continuously or periodically covers the land surface. In all of these sites, water is the main factor that determines plant and animal living conditions and controls environmental status. In comparison with surrounding arid landscapes, the Volga–Akhtuba floodplain is distinguished by a mosaic, contrasting structure of versatile landscapes and an abundance and diversity of water bodies. There are about 3,000 water bodies, in contrast to the semi-desert landscapes of the North Caspian. The area includes high-yield floodplain meadows and valuable spawning grounds. It also features unique park-like oak groves with the English oak genotype and highly fertile soils formed by spring flood deposits washed from the extensive Volga basin. The productivity of floodplain agricultural lands is almost 20 times that of the surrounding landscapes. There is also an abundance of waterfowl.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Volga-Akhtuba Floodplain

records.introduction_en: Located in south-west Germany in the Saarland region, Bliesgau Biosphere Reserve has a wide variety of soils and microclimates. The reserve was created to encompass very contrasting landscapes, including its industrialised and densely populated north. In the mostly rural south, it features semi-arid grasslands as well as orchid- and woodruff–beech forests. These host the greatest density of Saarland’s habitat types and species of national and international importance.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Bliesgau Biosphere Reserve can be roughly divided into the Muschelkalk areas in the south, characterised by open land, and the more forested Buntsandstein areas in the north. The area is characterised less by spectacular, nationally endangered species than by many regionally typical species, such as the semi-collared flycatcher (Ficedula semitorquata) and the wildcat (Felis silvestris). At least eight orchid species present are at risk of extinction, notably Aceras anthropophorum and the pyramidal orchid (Anacamptis pyramidalis).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Bliesgau

records.introduction_en: Located in southern Germany, in the state of Baden-Württemberg, this biosphere reserve comprises low mountain ranges, silvicultural forests, low plains, mountain hay meadows and lowland moors. Seventy per cent of the area is forested. The region has retained a distinct cultural identity, with customs and handicrafts. Sustainable tourism is widely promoted.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Black Forest Biosphere Reserve is one of Central Europe’s most diverse low mountain ranges and is designated as a grassland-rich forest landscape. It has an exceptional vertical extent of over 1,000 m, ranging from 310 to 1,400 metres above sea level, corresponding to a climatic range from subalpine, snowy mountain conditions to a warm, fruit-growing climate. Around 70 per cent of the area is forested and about 25 per cent is extensively used for agriculture, mainly grazing. This traditional use has created a mosaic of open and wooded areas, resulting in high biodiversity. The largely glaciated landscape also features many special landforms, such as block slopes and valley walls, some left in a near-natural state. The fauna includes numerous species that are threatened at the European scale. Mammals include beaver (Castor fiber), lynx (Lynx lynx) and wildcat (Felis silvestris). The area also supports many bird species, including western capercaillie (Tetrao urogallus), citril finch (Carduelis/Spinus citrinella), Bonelli’s warbler (Phylloscopus bonelli), water pipit (Anthus spinoletta) and Eurasian tree pipit (Anthus trivialis).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Black Forest

records.introduction_en: Situated in the transitional area between Lower Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt in northern Germany, the Drömling Biosphere Reserve is an ecologically valuable and culturally significant landscape shaped by centuries of human intervention. Once an impenetrable marshland, it has been transformed through an extensive system of ditches and canals, earning it the name as the Land of a Thousand Ditches. Today, it stands as one of the largest peatland complexes in the region and plays a key role in the European Green Belt, a cross-border ecological corridor along the former inner-German border. Drömling serves as a living laboratory for sustainable regional development, climate resilience and ecosystem restoration.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Drömling landscape is nationally and internationally significant for its unique combination of water-bound ecosystems, transitional habitats, and centuries of human influence. With 40% of its soils classified as fen – peat-rich wetlands fed by groundwater – it represents the largest fen area in Saxony-Anhalt and one of the most extensive in northern Germany.A defining feature of the area is its intricate watercourse network, spanning more than 2,200 km and connecting the Weser and Elbe river catchments. This hydrological system underpins a wide range of ecological functions, from flood retention and water filtration, to carbon storage and habitat provision, and gives rise to an extraordinary richness of biotopes in a relatively confined area. It also supports source populations of Elbe beaver (Castor fiber albicus) and Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra), hosts the largest white stork (Ciconia ciconia) population west of the Elbe, and provides breeding habitat for meadow birds such as lapwing (Vanellus vanellus), snipe (Gallinago gallinago) and Eurasian curlew (Numenius arquata).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Drömling

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve lies in the low mountain ranges of the Rhön in central Germany. In contrast to other German low-mountain areas, the Rhön is known as the land of open vistas, representing an open cultural landscape shaped by human use over many centuries.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Naturally, the region would be covered by beech (Fagus sylvatica) forest. However, extensive farming and dairy cattle rearing have transformed forests mainly into montane and submontane humid grasslands on siliceous soils. Two bogs host numerous endangered animal and plant species. The region is also known for habitat suitable for black grouse (Tetrao tetrix). The Rhön was designated a biosphere reserve after German reunification, spanning three Länder. At that time, a framework management plan for the protection, maintenance and development of the Rhön Biosphere Reserve was prepared with the participation of all stakeholders.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Rhön

records.introduction_en: The Schaalsee Biosphere Reserve is in the Land of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern in northern Germany.
