records.ecological_characteristics_en: A defining feature of this relatively small area is its diverse landscape and variety of habitats. It is characterised by semi-natural ecosystems of woodland, bogs, lakes and dry sites. Lake Schaalsee itself formed as a glacial-tongue basin during the Weichsel glacial period. Owing to its physiographic conditions, the overlap of continental and Atlantic climatic influences, and decades without disturbance while it lay on the inner-German border until November 1989, the region contains a diverse range of near-natural ecosystems and is species-rich in both flora and fauna. Characteristic near-natural ecosystem types occur in its forests, raised bogs and lakes. The presence of Atlantic geo-elements, in the broad sense, makes the Schaalsee region a good example of the Central Baltic beech-wood area, representing temperate broadleaf forests and woodlands in northern Central Europe. Research focuses on monitoring Lake Schaalsee and the otter (Lutra lutra) population, as well as analysing visitor perception. The area is of special significance as a breeding, moulting, resting and overwintering ground for waterbirds and shorebirds. Owing to its high faunal value, most of the Schaalsee landscape has been designated a Special Protection Area (SPA) under the EU Birds Directive.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Schaalsee

records.introduction_en: The UNESCO Spreewald Biosphere Reserve, whose name means “forest along the River Spree”, is a unique landscape in Central Europe, situated about 100 km south-east of Berlin. Shaped during the last ice age, it forms a vast inland delta around the River Spree. The area comprises meadows, forests and fens, but its distinctive feature is more than 276 km of navigable channels. The channels, rivers and their surroundings provide habitat for many animal and plant species. Farmers continue the tradition of using the channels for fishing and transport, and many tourists explore the region on traditional Spree Forest punting boats (the Spreewaldkahn) or by canoe.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Overall, the network of channels, rivers and streams totals about 1,500 km. These waterways offer protected habitat for some 6,000 animal and plant species, including rare species such as fire-bellied toads, common snipe, beavers and otters. Dragonflies and grass snakes are characteristic of the delta’s landscape. The streams have also shaped the remaining floodplain. The Spreewald hosts many groundwater-dependent fens, other wetlands and marshes, alder forests, sedge meadows and wet meadows, which in turn support rare plants such as water chestnut, sundew and various orchids. In autumn, large numbers of waterfowl pause on their journey south, and sea eagles hunt. Lapwings and snipe breed in the area.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Spreewald

records.introduction_en: Located in the southernmost part of Germany, in the state of Baden-Württemberg, the Swabian Alb Biosphere Reserve is known for its high diversity. Elevations range from 328–872 m above sea level, and dense forests are interwoven with open areas. The area housed a military facility for over 110 years and is noted for its fruit-tree meadows and the Alb Escarpment with its valleys and creeks. Set within one of Germany’s most prosperous, industrial regions, the biosphere reserve forms part of a statewide sustainable development strategy that promotes ecotourism and sustainable agriculture and forestry projects.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: At the foothills of the German Alps, the Swabian Alb features a mosaic of forests, open rock formations, scree, unforested nutrient-poor calcareous grasslands and shrublands. It is also known for species-rich hay meadows and fruit-tree meadows, which provide breeding grounds for various birds, including endangered species such as honey buzzard (Pernis apivorus), middle spotted woodpecker (Leiopicus medius) and Bonelli’s warbler (Phylloscopus bonelli).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Swabian Alb

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve encompasses and protects the entire coast of Lower Saxony. Through its network with the neighbouring reserves in Hamburg and Schleswig-Holstein, it also covers the entire German Wadden Sea. This cooperation is part of the Trilateral Wadden Sea Cooperation, which strives for harmonised conservation of the Wadden Sea World Heritage site and for the sustainable development of the whole Wadden Sea Region. With the exception of very small border areas, the entire Wadden Sea of Lower Saxony lies within the biosphere reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: All typical habitats are almost entirely included in the protected area. These comprise tidal channels and inlets near the coast, the eulittoral tidal flats, salt meadows, dune habitats, and special biotopes such as the Schwimmendes Moor at the outer dyke and the heath-covered cliff that represents a natural, undisturbed transition between land and sea. Large sections are characterised by little or no human intervention, and around 45 per cent can develop freely as dynamic, self-organising ecosystems. Other areas are subject to some human influence, including coastal protection measures that limit natural dynamics, shrimp fisheries and tourism. Management measures in recent years have improved ecosystem protection in line with sustainability principles. Biomass is produced by bacteria, plants and animals that have evolved adaptations to the extreme ecological conditions of the tidal flats. The tidal flats support a high number of specialised species, with some 10,000 recorded in the biosphere reserve. The Wadden Sea is also of global significance for migratory birds using the East Atlantic Flyway: an estimated 10–12 million waders and waterbirds use the Wadden Sea twice a year, 1–3 million of them in the Lower Saxony sector. As the primary, and often only stopover point, the Wadden Sea is essential for birds to regain energy. Ecological connectivity along the flyway makes the area crucial for the survival and successful breeding of species thousands of kilometres away.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Waddensea of Lower Saxony

records.introduction_en: Moen (Møn) biosphere reserve comprises a series of islands and islets in the southern Baltic Sea. Its landscapes include woodlands, grasslands, pastures, wetlands, coastal areas, ponds and steep hills. The biosphere reserve includes a number of small villages, scattered farms and residential areas. The main activities are trade, agriculture, fisheries and tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Since the last ice released its grip on the area, post-glacial processes have modelled the landscape in the area. Elevated sea floor and beach ridges are characteristic landscape features. A combination of isostatic land rise after the last glaciation, and marine erosion and sediment transport from the coast further east, has shaped the landscape around Ulvshale and Nyord. The sea surrounding the biosphere area varies from brackish water in the west to more saline water in the east. The marine part of the biosphere area includes habitats such as coastal lagoons and stone reefs, as well as features such as mudflats and sand flats exposed at low tide. A variety of rare plants can be found, with up to 18 orchid species, red-listed birds such as the peregrine falcon and the red kite, and not less than 112 red-listed species of fungi, of which 11 species have not been found elsewhere in Denmark.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Moen

records.introduction_en: Following the Peace Accord between Peru and Ecuador in October 1998, the two countries strengthened their fraternal ties, trust and cooperation across various areas. This led, in June 2017, to UNESCO’s designation of the Bosques de Paz Transboundary Biosphere Reserve. It was the first in South America and the 17th worldwide. The area comprises the Northwest Amotapes–Manglares Biosphere Reserve, extended in March 2016 and located in the Tumbes and Piura regions of Peru, and the Bosque Seco Biosphere Reserve, located in the provinces of Loja and El Oro in Ecuador and created in June 2014.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The site includes the seasonally dry forests of Ecuador and Peru, which are significant as the core of one of the world’s most important areas for biological diversity: the Tumbesian endemism region. It spans coastal territories and the foothills of the Western Andes, reaching elevations of up to 3,080 m. This gives the reserve a biological diversity with a high degree of endemism. Within the biosphere reserve, 219 species of vascular plants have been recorded, 15 of which are endemic. In addition, approximately 800 bird species have been recorded (8 per cent of all species worldwide), of which 59 are endemic. The Tumbesian endemism region is one of the four most important avian endemism zones on the planet. Of the bird species restricted to this region, fifteen are threatened and their range is confined to less than 5 per cent of their original habitat. Likewise, 5 per cent of the endemic birds and 17.5 per cent of the region’s subspecies are found only in the dry forest. There are also 142 mammal species, 14 of them endemic. Species present include white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus), neotropical river otters (Lontra longicaudis), the American crocodile (Crocodylus acutus), howler monkeys (Alouatta palliata) and jaguars (Panthera onca).
records.name: Bosque Seco

records.introduction_en: Martinique is an island located in the volcanic arc of the Lesser Antilles, and is globally significant as part of the Caribbean biodiversity hotspot. The island combines striking mountainous landscapes with extensive coastal and marine environments, offering an exceptional range of natural habitats and high endemism. The Martinique Biosphere Reserve’s main purpose is to conserve and restore the island’s land–sea ecosystems while sustaining cultural identity through community-led stewardship. Management priorities include sustainable production and local consumption, responsible tourism, and a shift to renewable energy and public transport, underpinned by environmental education and applied research.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve covers the island’s entire land and marine area. The mountainous north holds the humid and montane forests of Montagne Pelée and the Pitons du Nord, designated “Forêts d’Exception”, while the south comprises mornes (the partially eroded cores of ancient volcanoes) and lowland plains. A rugged relief with steep slopes and a dense hydrographic network of 161 rivers meets an indented coastline of bays and coves. Offshore, three notable ecosystems coexist, supporting high landscape diversity and rich biodiversity: mangroves, seagrass beds and coral reefs. These coastal ecosystems form a natural defence for the island, dissipating wave energy, limiting coastal erosion, maintaining water clarity and serving as nurseries that sustain the island’s artisanal fisheries. Martinique forms part of the Caribbean biodiversity hotspot, one of the 35 globally, recognised for exceptional species richness under acute pressure. The island supports a number of globally threatened species including the Martinique Oriole (Icterus bonana). The Étang des Salines, a Ramsar-listed wetland, harbours unique biodiversity and provides resting, breeding and feeding areas for migratory birds, particularly shorebirds moving from North America towards the Guianas plateau. It also remains a site of memory linked to the island’s former saltworks.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Martinique

records.introduction_en: Situated in the delta of the Rhône River on France’s Mediterranean coast, the Camargue Biosphere Reserve is a mosaic of lagoons and one of Europe’s most important wetlands. Lying between river and sea, and on a migratory route between Europe and Africa, it is exceptionally rich in biodiversity with 272 recorded bird species. The area is designated as a Ramsar Wetland of International Importance. Habitats include freshwater and saline marshes, ponds, halophilous steppes, glasswort (Salicornia) grasslands known locally as “sansouires”, beaches, dunes and woodland.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Wetlands, saline steppes, beaches and dune systems are widespread. Humid depressions between dunes and numerous lagoons support floating and submerged vegetation. Mediterranean xerophilous grasslands occur alongside gallery forests dominated by Salix alba and Populus alba. There are also Carex communities and surrounding agroecosystems.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Camargue (delta du Rhône)

records.introduction_en: The Marais Audomarois Biosphere Reserve covers some 22,300 ha in northern France, including the city of art and history, Saint-Omer, and its wetland, a recognised Ramsar site.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Audomarois landscape owes its richness to its setting at the intersection of three natural regions: the coastal plain, the Flandre intérieure and the Artois hills. These varied landscapes host a wide range of flora and fauna. The main natural habitats are reedbeds, tall herb stands, peaty woods, meadows, ditches and rivers. Aquatic plants include flowering rush (Butomus umbellatus), greater spearwort (Ranunculus lingua) and marsh fern (Thelypteris palustris), alongside submerged and floating vegetation. These habitats enable many bird species to breed, feed and rest. Several threatened plants occur here, including water hemlock (Cicuta virosa), river water-dropwort (Oenanthe fluviatilis) and Stratiotes aloides. The area’s natural heritage is especially notable for the abundance and variety of waterbirds. Lying on major migration routes, the marsh provides food and essential stopover sites for species such as sedge warbler (Acrocephalus schoenobaenus), bluethroat (Luscinia svecica), Eurasian reed warbler (Acrocephalus scirpaceus) and the rare aquatic warbler (Acrocephalus paludicola). Reflecting this ecological value, the Audomarois marsh benefits from multiple protections, including Natura 2000 site status, National Nature Reserve, Regional Nature Reserve and Regional Nature Park designations. Since 2008, the wetland has also been listed as a Ramsar site of international importance.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Marais Audomarois Aa – Hem – Flandre

records.introduction_en: Set on the Lorraine slopes of the Vosges in north-eastern France, the Moselle Sud Biosphere Reserve protects a wetland–forest system with high biodiversity and a living cultural landscape shaped by extensive cattle and sheep farming, canals and nature-based tourism. Its importance is reflected in the Ramsar-listed Étang de Lindre (Lindre Pond) and a network of Natura 2000 sites. The biosphere reserve’s objectives are to conserve landscapes, ecosystems and species, to foster research and monitoring in partnership with nearby universities, and to support sustainable development rooted in local livelihoods and low-impact tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve comprises four complementary landscape units: the Vosges foothill forests to the east; the agricultural upper Sarre valley at its centre; the pond-dotted Pays des Étangs to the north-west; and the saline Seille headwaters to the west. On the Vosges piedmont, fir–beech forests hold characteristic mountain flora and fauna. The Sarre valley interweaves farmland, villages and river habitats. The Pays des Étangs comprises about 130 interconnected ponds. The Seille rises in salt-rich springs that give local ecosystems a rare, site-specific character in France. The pond network is of particular significance as a stronghold for biodiversity and an internationally important migratory stopover. The Étang de Lindre is a Ramsar site and supports some of the region’s richest birdlife, including goldeneye, osprey and white-tailed eagle, with large migratory gatherings of pochard and common crane. Ecologically, the many small ponds, pools and seasonally flooded meadows act as “spares” when larger ponds are temporarily drained for management, helping the wider wetland system absorb climatic swings. On the Vosges side, the Crête du Grossmann (Grossmann ridge) includes a State Biological Reserve managed by the National Forest Office and is also designated as a Natura 2000 Special Area of Conservation; the area supports long-term research and capercaillie habitat restoration. The massifs also support fox, roe deer, wild boar, wildcat, pine marten, stone marten and red deer.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Moselle Sud

records.country_title_en: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
records.introduction_en: Situated on the south-central Welsh coast in the estuary of the Dyfi River, this biosphere reserve represents saltmarshes and estuarine systems in the west of the United Kingdom. The estuary is one of the most important wildfowl and shorebird centres in Wales, and it also comprises a Ramsar site. Cors Fochno has a large expanse of primary raised mire and contains many invertebrate species, including some of national and international importance. Upstream along the Dyfi Valley are remnants of native oak woodland.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Dyfi is a glaciated catchment of predominantly hill land, with thin, acidic soils developed on lower Palaeozoic sedimentary strata. Broadleaf woodlands, typically dominated by sessile oak or ash, are a feature of the valley slopes and its many tributaries, although conifer plantations now dominate large areas. The bryophyte, lichen and fern communities of the shady, damp valley woods are particularly notable, with many Atlantic species. Several areas of upland moorland occur. They comprise mixtures of acid grassland, blanket bog and dwarf shrub heath, are often contiguous with larger upland areas, and support important bird populations. The Dyfi is a classic bar-built estuary and one of the foremost examples of a drying, sandy, nutrient-poor estuary. Important populations of migratory fish, birds and otters occur, along with extensive areas of saltmarsh of the Atlantic salt meadow type. The spit dune system of Ynyslas is an actively accreting system with good representation of dune community succession, including marram fore-dunes and humid dune slacks. The estuarine raised mire of Cors Fochno is one of the largest and best preserved active raised bogs in the United Kingdom. It is a key site for climate-related research and supports important assemblages of lower plants, invertebrates and birds.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Biosffer Dyfi
records.country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

records.country_title_en: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
records.introduction_en: The Brighton & Lewes Downs Biosphere Reserve is located on the south-east coast of England, forming a central unit of the hills of the South Downs National Park. It is centred on the Brighton chalk block that lies between the River Adur in the west and the River Ouse in the east. Chalk downland makes up the principal terrestrial landscape of the area, bounded at each end by the two river valleys. The coastline is dominated by impressive chalk cliffs in the east and urbanised plains in the west, running to the estuary of the River Adur at Shoreham. The area is nationally and internationally renowned for its arts and culture, distinctive settlements, independent mindset, and its links to the surrounding iconic English landscape of downland, white chalk cliffs and beaches.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Brighton & Lewes Downs Biosphere Reserve is found within the temperate broadleaf forest biome of the Palaearctic realm’s British Island province. It includes the following habitats: coastal chalk cliffs, subtidal chalk reef, freshwater wetland, shingle beaches, deciduous woodland, river estuaries and chalk grassland. Three distinct but interrelated environments make up the biosphere reserve area: rural, coastal and marine, and urban. The rural environment contains lowland chalk grassland, which is one of the richest wildlife habitats in the country. It is particularly important for its high botanical species diversity, with up to 40–50 vascular plant species per square metre. It also supports invertebrate communities, notably butterflies. Twenty species have a substantial proportion of their breeding populations within this habitat. Characteristic species include Phyteuma orbiculare, Decticus verrucivorus and Lysandra bellargus. The coastal and marine environments are made up of a moderately exposed coast and an inshore area of the English Channel, with cliffs providing nesting niches for birds such as Fulmarus glacialis. The discontinuous chalk ledge to the west of Brighton gives rise to a unique series of low, underwater, north-facing chalk cliffs. Biological records show over 300 marine species in the area. The area is home to 211 species that have been recorded on international conservation lists, such as the European eel (Anguilla anguilla), in addition to 1,052 local rare species, including the hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) and the yellowhammer (Emberiza citronella). Important local genetic varieties include the unique elm tree, Ulmus, as well as wild apple tree varieties. The domesticated breeds of South Downs sheep and rare Sussex cattle are also … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Living Coast
records.country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

records.country_title_en: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
records.introduction_en: Galloway and Southern Ayrshire Biosphere Reserve comprises a major biogeographic region represented by an upland massif centred on the Merrick and the rivers that flow from this upland through forests and farmland to the sea. Landscape mosaics in the area include uplands, moorlands, mires, woodlands and forests, farmland, river valleys, coast and shoreline. The biosphere reserve is working to demonstrate the importance of landscapes and ecosystems for the future of sustainable development in a region that is experiencing change in traditional livelihoods.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve forms a coherent biogeographic unit influenced by underlying geology, topography and river drainage systems, with a rugged mountainous core, an extensive periphery of forest, woodland, arable land and pasture, and a varied coastline. There are two predominant topographic regions: rolling uplands with prominent rounded hills punctuated with valleys, and lowlands of gently undulating topography with incised river valleys. In the north, the major geological and topographic feature is the Southern Uplands Fault, which marks the northern limit of the Southern Uplands and its contact with the Midland Valley of Scotland. The high ground has a variety of acidic habitats, predominantly heathland and mires, with patterned bogs at Silver Flowe that are unusual in Britain for their upland location. These habitats are valuable for the species they support, such as raptors, including the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos). They are also important carbon stores and contain some of the longest records of prehistory preserved in peat. The lower ground has a range of habitats including native broadleaved woodlands, fens, marshes, rush pasture, unimproved lowland grassland, raised and blanket mires, and moorland. There are extensive remnants of native woodlands in the wet hollows amongst the glacial landforms and in the river valleys. Riparian planting is predominantly of native species, and these provide important wildlife corridors. Wetlands in the river valleys and adjacent managed grasslands also provide overwintering roosts for geese and swans from the Arctic. The rivers are well stocked with trout and other native species, although invasive non-native species, such as the American signal crayfish (Pacifastacus leniusculus), have invaded some rivers.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Galloway and Southern Ayrshire
records.country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

records.country_title_en: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
records.introduction_en: Formerly known as Beinn Eighe, Wester Ross Biosphere Reserve is situated in the north-west of Scotland. It displays a suite of habitats primarily influenced by upland and oceanic factors. Most of Wester Ross is covered by open heathland, bare rock, scree and wet grassland, with scattered bogs and peatlands. Of national interest are two variants of dwarf shrub heath and a western variant of moss heath. Woodland, found below 300 m close to Loch Maree and in various isolated gorges, includes the best remaining examples of western pinewood in Britain, and also contains birch, holly, ivy, rowan, oak and juniper.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Wester Ross is dominated by wild, rugged mountains, remote glens and long, steep-sided straths, or valleys, which extend down to the sea. The area is characterised by isolated mountains such as Ben Mor Coigach, An Teallach, Slioch and Beinn Eighe. Fast-flowing rivers empty into sheltered bays and sea lochs, or inlets. The indented coastline is long, varied and beautiful, ranging from exposed headlands to well-sheltered sea lochs. The open coasts of Wester Ross are partly sheltered by the islands of Raasay and Skye in the south, and by the island chain of the Western Isles across the Minch. The seashores are predominantly rocky and covered with barnacles and seaweeds. An offshore rock in Outer Loch Torridon is the northern recorded limit for the spongy green seaweed, Codium adhaerens. Crofter’s wig, Ascophyllum nodosum, is a very distinctive form of the common egg or knotted wrack, which lives unattached on the shore in very sheltered corners. This endemic seaweed is only found in west coast sea lochs and nowhere else in the world. It is home to the largest remnant of ancient Caledonian forest in Wester Ross. Some of the Scots pine trees are about 400 years old. Its rugged slopes support one of the UK’s best tracts of prostrate juniper and moss heath. Rare lichens, liverworts and mosses flourish, from the mild, damp woodlands up to the highest peaks. Below the tree line, the pine marten (Martes martes), Scottish crossbill and northern emerald dragonfly make their home in the ancient pinewoods. Otters and black-throated divers can be seen where the slopes meet the waters of Loch Maree. The red deer (Cervus elaphus) is the largest native land mammal in the UK. It is found predominantly in open moorland habitats, which are characteristic of much of upland Scot … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Wester Ross
records.country: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

records.introduction_en: North Karelia Biosphere Reserve encompasses a rich natural landscape. It is home to over 2,000 lakes, as well as extensive forests that cover about 70 per cent of the region.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Magnificent landscapes include Koli National Park, a national treasure set on some of the oldest bedrock in the world. Forests cover roughly 70 per cent of North Karelia, and there are approximately 2,200 lakes. Lake Pielinen, one of the lakes within the biosphere reserve, is the fourth largest in Finland.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: North Karelia

records.introduction_en: The Utwe Biosphere Reserve is located in the south-west of Kosrae, a small mountainous volcanic island in the South Pacific. The biosphere reserve lies on the relatively flat and narrow coastal plain that extends from the foothills to the shore. Most of the island’s interior is rough and rugged. Mangrove swamps and coral reefs surround most of the island.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: According to the Division of Fisheries, over 335 species of fish have been recorded, as well as 180 coral species, including 13 soft corals and over 150 hard corals. Other ecosystem types in the biosphere reserve include tropical rainforest, wetland forest, seagrass beds and marine lakes. The wetland forest has different kinds of green ferns and harbours the only remaining stand of Ka trees (Terminalia carolinensis) in the world. Isolated by more than 300 nautical miles from its nearest neighbour, Kosrae has been little influenced by modern development and industry. However, as in other states within the Federated States of Micronesia, Kosrae’s marine resources are being depleted, and some marine species such as turtles, lobsters, corals and giant clams are endangered. The core area, which is mainly composed of mangrove and marine areas, has been designated with the main objective of protection. All human activities, including the harvesting of natural resources, are prohibited. The terrestrial buffer zone protects the core area against external pressures, and the marine buffer zone is protected as a no-take zone.
records.name: Utwe

records.introduction_en: Badiar Biosphere Reserve is in the north of Guinea and is adjacent to the Niokolo-Koba Biosphere Reserve in Senegal.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The main ecosystems form a mosaic of plain vegetation types: plateaux and hills; grassland and shrubland savannahs; woodland savannahs; open forests; gallery forests; and swampy grasslands. The biosphere reserve is characterised by herbaceous vegetation forming a grassy layer with a continuous upper stratum averaging 2 m in height. Dominant grasses include Andropogon and Pennisetum, with trees such as Mitragyna, Borassus aethiopum and Piliostigma thonningii. Fauna is rich and varied, including Cephalophus maxwellii, Cephalophus rufilatus, yellow-backed duiker (Cephalophus), Panthera leo, Canis aureus, Cercopithecus patas and Cercopithecus diana.
records.name: Badiar

records.introduction_en: The Nimba Massif lies on the border between Guinea, Liberia and Côte d’Ivoire. The Monts Nimba chain is notable for the beauty and originality of its landscapes and for a highly contrasting range of climatic influences shaped by its geography, topography and orientation. These factors, and others, explain the successive classification of the Nimba chain as a nature reserve in 1944, a biosphere reserve in 1980, a World Heritage Site in 1981, and placed on the List of World Heritage in Danger in 1992. The biodiversity of the plains, hills and forests of Nimba provides local people with food, energy, water, medicinal resources, shelter, agricultural land and other essential resources. It is considered a natural reservoir that can support economic development and local well-being.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Mont Nimba Biosphere Reserve hosts almost 85 per cent of Guinea’s recorded biological diversity, representing about 2,835 animal species: 107 mammals, 72 birds, 58 reptiles, 45 amphibians, 38 fish, 38 molluscs, 2,408 insects, 31 myriapods, 17 scorpions, 18 arachnids, 17 opiliones and 46 annelids. The Déré Forest contains vegetation of great botanical diversity that has been relatively well preserved. Many rare plant and animal species, endemic or having largely vanished from the Upper Guinea forest block due to clear-cutting and hunting, are found within the Mont Nimba Biosphere Reserve, aided by rugged topography and, in places, lateritic soils.
records.name: Mont Nimba

records.introduction_en: Located on the south-western coast of Crete, this biosphere reserve and national park lie in a mountainous limestone area famous for the deep, narrow Samaria Gorge. The area comprises high-altitude Mediterranean forest, including virgin stands of cypress (Cupressus sempervirens), as well as maquis and phrygana. Typical Mediterranean fauna includes the endemic wild goat (Capra aegagrus cretensis). As in much of the Mediterranean, the area was formerly subject to grazing and timber extraction. As of 1999, the designated biosphere reserve is uninhabited. The region around the gorge is culturally notable, with ancient ruins, churches and castles. Tourism is the main economic activity, though activities are restricted within the national park. There is a visitor centre at the gorge entrance.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Gorge of Samaria, at the southern edge of the Omalos plateau, dominates the biosphere reserve. This unique geological formation extends for about 16 km. Altitudes range from sea level to 2,134 metres. Twenty-two springs, numerous torrents, karstic caves and steep, near-vertical rocks combine to create a highly diverse geomorphological relief. Soils are generally poor, mainly terra rossa. The area includes high-altitude Mediterranean forest with cypress (Cupressus sempervirens), pine (Pinus brutia) and phrygana, including Pistacia and Cistus. Among the typical Mediterranean fauna, the endemic wild goat (Capra aegagrus cretensis) is well known, as is the Cretan badger (Meles meles arcalus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Gorge of Samaria

records.introduction_en: Bolama-Bijagós Biosphere Reserve is an archipelago of 88 islands located on the coast of Guinea-Bissau in western Africa. It was formed from the ancient delta of the Rio Geba and the Rio Grande.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Bijagós archipelago has a considerable diversity of fauna. The wealth of the natural environment is mainly linked to the presence of the sea and the existence of mangroves and mudflats. The terrestrial environment includes palm groves, littoral woodland savannahs and semi-dry forests. A great diversity of mammals, reptiles, birds and fish are to be found. The archipelago has been recognised as the most important site in Africa for the green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas) to lay their eggs, with nearly 10,000 adult females. Other protected or rare species are still relatively abundant, such as Crocodylus niloticus and Crocodylus tetraspis tetraspis, Hippopotamus amphibius, Trichechus senegalensis, Sousateuzsii and Tursiops truncatus. Every year the archipelago is visited by close on 800,000 Palaearctic waders and also nesting species of birds.
records.name: Bolama-Bijagos

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is located in the large mountain area of Mount Velebit on the Adriatic Sea. Altitudes range from sea level to 1,757 metres above sea level. The area is a 145 km long and 10–30 km wide stretch of karst landscape.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The maritime slope is barren karst, while woodlands cover the central mountain ranges and the Lika slope. Habitat diversity is very rich. It includes woodlands of Pinus halepensis, sub-Mediterranean shrub with Paliurus spina-christiand Carpinus orientalis, and beech (Fagus sylvatica) woods. There are also fir and beech woods (Abies alba) and pine woods of Pinus nigra. Subalpine beech woods and subalpine meadows are present as well.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Velebit Mountains

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve forms part of a transboundary reserve shared with Hungary, extending along the Drava, Mura, and Danube rivers. These rivers are divided by flood-prevention dykes into two zones: a natural inundation area and a flood-controlled area. The reserve provides an important setting for studying and comparing different approaches to floodplain management.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Most terrestrial habitats in the core area and buffer zone are covered by softwood or hardwood gallery forests, with extensive grasslands along the Drava River. The area contains a variety of wetland habitats, including some of the most threatened in Europe, such as alluvial forests and wet grasslands. It also features gravel and sand bars, islands, steep banks, oxbow lakes, backwaters, abandoned riverbeds and meanders. These habitats are bordered by riparian forests and arable land with scattered pastures, providing shelter for a great many species. Significant protected animal species include the wild cat (Felis silvestris), otter (Lutra lutra), beaver (Castor fiber), pond bat (Myotis dasycneme), pygmy cormorant (Phalacrocorax pygmeus), willow warbler (Phylloscopus trochilus), white-tailed eagle (Haliaeetus albicilla), little tern (Sterna albifrons), Danubian newt (Triturus dobrogicus), black-winged stilt (Himantopus himantopus), bittern (Botaurus stellaris), purple heron (Ardea purpurea), great white egret (Egretta alba) and black stork (Ciconia nigra). The unique wetland area of Kopacki Rit is also a Ramsar site and hosts more than 20,000 birds during the winter period. Recorded diversity in the area includes about 400 plant species, 400 invertebrate species, 44 fish species and 293 bird species, as well as 55 mammal species.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mura-Drava-Danube

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve includes La Selle in Haiti, designated in 2012, and Jaragua–Bahoruco–Enriquillo in the Dominican Republic, designated in 2002. The two reserves are linked ecologically across a political and administrative frontier. Their joint designation supports more coherent environmental management.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: On the Haitian side, the biosphere reserve is located in the Massif de la Selle, which contains Haiti’s highest peak, Pic la Selle (2,684 m), and the second most biodiverse region of the country after the Massif de la Hotte. These two mountain ranges form the southern peninsula of the island of Hispaniola, known for its high level of endemism. Most endemic species are flowering plants; around 16 per cent are endemic to this specific region. The Dominican side includes three biogeographic regions in the Caribbean: the Hoya del Lago Enriquillo, the Sierra de Bahoruco and the Procurrente de Barahona. It comprises a wide variety of natural ecosystems, from tropical highlands to karstic terraces with coastal and marine areas, islands and cays, with rich biodiversity and important regional endemism. The area has rich faunal diversity, including the brown pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) and the West Indian manatee (Trichechus manatus). Isla Beata and the Los Frailes cays host an enormous variety of marine birds, with some 107 bird species recorded. Some 67 reptile species are reported across the reserve. Geologically, the area has a wide variety of igneous and sedimentary rocks dating to the Late Jurassic, around 140 million years ago.
records.name: La Selle

records.introduction_en: The Kiskunság Biosphere Reserve and Kiskunság National Park are of priority importance for conserving biological diversity in the Pannonian Biogeographical Region. The biosphere reserve’s territory was designated a national park in 1975. Three parts of the reserve have been wetlands of international importance under the Ramsar Convention since 1979, 1997 and 2006. Since 2004, it has comprised several Natura 2000 sites under the EU Birds and Habitats Directives. Kolon-tó at Izsák has been a Biogenetic Reserve since 1995. Its diverse terrestrial and aquatic habitat mosaics support rich flora and fauna, including species that are otherwise endangered, threatened or rare in Hungary.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: About 80,000 ha of Kiskunság National Park are covered by sodic habitats. In the Danube–Tisza Interfluve, the extent of sodic habitats is the second largest in the Carpathian Basin; in terms of habitat variety and plant diversity, they rank first. The mosaic-like sodic areas of the Danube–Tisza Interfluve include all major Central European types of sodic habitats, represented in thousands of local variations. The fauna of the sodic lands is as distinctive as the flora. Sodic grasslands, with patches of open water, are home to terrestrial insects adapted to the sodic environment and the puszta. Frequent herbivorous insects include Dociostaurus brevicollis and the Moroccan locust (Dociostaurus maroccanus). The endemic Saragossa porosa kenderiensis also occurs here. Among typical sodic-nesting birds, the number of pied avocets (Recurvirostra avosetta) can exceed 100 pairs in a good year, and migratory groups can be over 200. Numbers of nesting black-winged stilts (Himantopus himantopus) and Kentish plovers (Charadrius alexandrinus) tend to be smaller but steady.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Kiskunság

records.introduction_en: The Dublin Bay Biosphere Reserve (formerly North Bull Island) comprises Dublin Bay, North Bull Island and adjacent land, including parts of Dublin, the capital city of Ireland. It contains one of the finest sand-dune systems in Ireland and is internationally important for its conservation value. The island hosts high-quality examples of several rare and threatened coastal habitats.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is significant for conservation because it supports well-developed saltmarshes and dune systems that display all stages of development, from the earliest phase of colonisation to stable and full maturity. The area is also important for nesting and wintering waterfowl. The major habitats and land-cover types include saltmarsh with glasswort (Salicornia dolichostachya and S. europaea), Puccinellia maritima and sea lavender (Limonium humile). There is a sand-dune complex with saltwort (Salsola kali), sea rocket (Cakile maritima) and sea couchgrass (Agropyron junceiforme), as well as beaches, a lagoonal sand flat, and lagoonal mudflats with algae such as Enteromorpha intestinalis, E. compressa and Ulva lactuca. The site qualifies for international importance because numbers of three species exceed the international threshold: light-bellied brent goose (Branta bernicla hrota), black-tailed godwit (Limosa limosa) and bar-tailed godwit (Limosa lapponica). Species such as grey heron (Ardea cinerea), goldeneye (Bucephala), red-breasted merganser (Mergus serrator) and greenshank (Tringa nebularia) are regular in winter in numbers of regional or local importance. North Bull Island and parts of the buffer zone in north Dublin include populations of the Irish mountain hare (Lepus timidus hibernicus), a uniquely Irish subspecies of a species of national and international importance. This hare is under severe pressure from recreational disturbance and illegal poaching. Dublin Bay Biosphere Reserve also contains three Ramsar sites: Sandymount Strand, North Bull Island and Baldoyle Bay.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Dublin Bay

records.introduction_en: Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve, located in the Himalayan Mountains in the northern part of the country, includes, as core areas, the Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers National Parks, which together form a single World Heritage site. Nanda Devi National Park has remained more or less intact because of its inaccessibility. The Valley of Flowers National Park is renowned for its meadows of endemic alpine flowers and outstanding natural beauty. Together they encompass a unique transition zone between the mountain ranges of the Zanskar and Great Himalaya.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve includes reserved forests, evam soyam (civil) forests, panchayat (community) forests, agricultural land, grassy slopes, alpine meadows (known locally as bugyals) and snow-covered areas. The alpine vegetation mainly comprises herbaceous species and scrub communities such as Rhododendron campanulatum, R. anthopogon and Salix denticulata. These meadows harbour a large number of rare and endangered, native and endemic species. The area has a large altitudinal range, 1,800–7,817 m and is dominated by the peak of Nanda Devi. The unique topography, climate, soil and biogeographical location of the biosphere reserve give rise to diverse habitats, communities and ecosystems, and a large number of ecologically and economically important species. Some 1,000 plant species, including lichens, fungi, bryophytes and pteridophytes, have been recorded. The percentage of native and endemic species is high compared to non-native species. Over 55 per cent of the species are native to the Himalaya, over 10 per cent are endemic, and 225 are near endemic. Among these plant resources, the inhabitants of the Pindari, Lata–Tolma–Malari and Valley of Flowers areas use 224 species for various purposes such as medicine, food and animal fodder. Seven endangered mammal species find refuge in the area, such as the snow leopard (Panthera uncia), Himalayan black bear (Selenarctos thibetanus), brown bear (Ursus arctos), musk deer (Moschus chrysogaster) and bharal, or blue sheep (Pseudois nayaur).
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Nanda Devi

records.introduction_en: The Nokrek Biosphere Reserve is located in the north-east of India on the Tura Range, which forms part of the Meghalaya Plateau, with an average altitude of 600 metres. The entire area is mountainous, and Nokrek is the highest peak of the Garo Hills at 1,412 metres. The north of the reserve has gently undulating hills, while steep slopes characterise the south. The biosphere reserve contains major rivers and streams that form a perennial catchment system. Examples include the Ganol, Dareng and Simsang rivers, with the Simsang the longest and largest. The Simsang originates in the north of the biosphere reserve. The Dareng originates from the southern peaks. The Ganol flows westward into the Brahmaputra River, which supplies water to numerous towns.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The tropical climate, characterised by high humidity, monsoon rains from April to October and high temperatures, provides ideal conditions for rich vegetation and varied biodiversity. Evergreen and semi-evergreen deciduous forests dominate the landscape, and 90 per cent of the Nokrek Biosphere Reserve is covered by evergreen forest. Some patches of bamboo forest occur at lower altitudes, and a remarkable variety of endemic Citrus also grows in the reserve, especially Indian wild orange (Citrus indica). Representative species include cotton tree (Bombax ceiba), hairy sterculia (Sterculia villosa) and golden shower tree (Cassia fistula). Highly vulnerable and threatened faunal species in Nokrek include the slow loris, the giant flying squirrel (Petaurista philippensis) and the pig-tailed macaque (Macaca leonina). The reserve is also home to other unique and endangered animals, such as tigers, leopards, elephants and hoolock gibbons. The latter are the most endangered apes in India and therefore receive special protection.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Nokrek

records.introduction_en: The Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve is located in the biogeographical region of the Deccan Peninsula and the biotic province of central India. The Satpura mountain ranges cross India from west to east, and Pachmarhi lies at their centre. The highest peak is Dhoopgarh at 1,352 m above sea level, while the Pachmarhi hills have steep slopes in the northern regions. The eastern boundary of the biosphere reserve follows a road with cultivation farms close to the Dudhi River, and the southern boundary borders the Tawa plateau.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Pachmarhi comprises three protection sites: the Bori Sanctuary, Satpura National Park and Pachmarhi Sanctuary, collectively known as the Satpura Tiger Reserve. The Pachmarhi Plateau is also called the Queen of Satpura because it contains valleys, marshes, streams and waterfalls, which together support unique and varied biodiversity. Forests represent approximately 63 per cent of the biosphere reserve’s area. Agricultural lands account for 30 per cent, wastelands for 2.18 per cent, water bodies for 5 per cent, and human settlement areas for 0.54 per cent. Teak (Tectona grandis) and sal (Shorea robusta) are the most common and distinctive flora in the forests. The major ecosystem types are tropical moist deciduous forests, tropical dry deciduous forests and Central Indian subtropical hill forests. The climate varies with elevation and is characterised by strong monsoons. More than 150 species of flora are used for medicinal purposes. In addition, 60 species of pteridophytes have been recorded, including 48 species of fern. Notable species include whisk fern (Psilotum triquetrum) and adder’s-tongue ferns (Ophioglossum nudicaule). The largest wild herbivores found in the reserve are gaur (Bos gaurus). Other rare and endangered species include bears, tigers and leopards, the giant squirrel (Ratufa indica) and the crested serpent eagle (Spilornis cheela). More than 50 mammal species, 254 bird species, 30 reptile species and 50 butterfly species live in the Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Pachmarhi

records.introduction_en: Located in north-east India, the Similipal Biosphere Reserve lies within two biogeographical regions: the Mahanadian east coastal region of the Oriental realm and the Chhotanagpur biotic province of the Deccan peninsular zone. Volcanic–sedimentary rocks occur in three concentric rings, accentuating the area’s geology. The highest peak in the Similipal hill range is Khairiburu at 1,168 m. Numerous waterfalls and perennial streams flow into major rivers, including the Budhabalang, Baitarani and Subarnarekha.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve contains the largest tract of sal tree (Shorea robusta) in India. Its tropical monsoon climate supports distinctive biodiversity, with 1,076 species of vascular plants, including 93 orchids, around 300 medicinal plants and 52 endangered flora. Two endemic orchids are Eria meghasaniensis and Tainia hookeriana. Other noteworthy flora includes beautyberry (Callicarpa arborea), cotton tree (Bombax ceiba) and mahua (Madhuca longifolia). Altogether, the reserve is home to 42 mammal species, 264 bird species, 39 reptiles and 12 amphibians, with approximately 52 fauna species considered endangered. Paradoxus jorandensis is cited as a valuable and possibly endemic species. The Bengal tiger (Panthera tigris tigris) and the Asiatic elephant (Elephas maximus) are also present in the reserve.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Similipal

records.introduction_en: Sunderban is the largest delta and mangrove forest in the world. The Indian Sunderban is bound on the west by the river Muriganga and on the east by the rivers Harinbhanga and Raimangal. Other major rivers flowing through this ecosystem are the Saptamukhi, Thakuran, Matla and Gosaba. Sunderban has an extremely rich diversity of aquatic and terrestrial flora and fauna, and its highly productive ecosystem acts as a natural fish nursery. Although the region lies south of the Tropic of Cancer, the temperature is equable due to its proximity to the sea. The average annual maximum temperature is around 35 °C. The average annual rainfall is 1,920 mm.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biogeography of Sunderban is unique, and the region harbours a rich diversity in terms of species, ecosystems and habitat types. This deltaic ecosystem, which is the single largest continuous area in the world for the threatened Bengal tiger and the largest contiguous mangrove patch on the globe along with Bangladesh, is very productive and well known for its high degree of specialisation. Sunderban has the largest mangal diversity on the planet, with 81 plant and 1,586 animal species. This biosphere reserve is located in the vast Ganges Delta, south of Calcutta and bordering Bangladesh in the east. It represents the largest mangal diversity in the world, with 81 mangal plant species, and it provides habitat for the threatened Royal Bengal tiger (Panthera tigris tigris). The core area, Sunderban National Park, has been designated a World Heritage site. Much of eastern India depends on fishery resources from Sunderban. More than 40 species of mammals, 163 species of birds, 56 species of reptiles, 165 species of fish, 23 species of molluscs, 15 species of prawns and 67 species of crabs have so far been reported in the biosphere reserve, such as the hawk eagle (Nisaetus) and the saltwater crocodile (Crocodylus porosus).
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Sunderban

records.introduction_en: The Kobushi Biosphere Reserve encompasses most of the Kanto Mountains, including the main Okuchichibu ridge of 20 peaks rising above 2,000 m. It is a watershed and source for major rivers, notably the Ara, Tama and Fuefuki, as well as the Chikuma, or Shinano, river. The biosphere reserve features a wealth of geological formations and rock types, with fauna that includes almost 40 per cent of Japan’s recorded butterfly species, 24 of which are endangered. The area has traditionally been a centre for the cultivation of grapes, persimmons, peaches and other delicacies collectively described as the “eight rare fruits of Koshu”.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Kobushi Biosphere Reserve is characterised by steeply sloping mountainous terrain that remains densely wooded up to the vicinity of the ridgeline, with less denuded and barren land than in the mountains of the Japanese Alps. Several conditions are conducive to forest establishment: there are few mountains higher than the tree line; debris is limited because there are few faults or fractures in the strata; and the soil is well developed, as bedrock on slope surfaces weathers into a variety of particle sizes. The climate also promotes forest growth, with relatively abundant rainfall, mainly during summer. The fauna inhabiting this diverse environment are as abundant as the flora. In addition to species at the top of the food chain, such as large mammals and raptors, a variety of other species can be seen, including those favouring frigid, warm, alpine and lowland climates. For example, the presence of 126 species of butterfly, just under 40 per cent of Japan’s approximately 320 species, has been confirmed, distributed from the subalpine zone to grasslands and semi-natural satochi-satoyama habitats. This figure includes 24 endangered species, making the area a treasure trove of rare species. In addition to large mammals such as the Asian black bear (Ursus thibetanus japonicus), Japanese deer (Cervus nippon) and Japanese serow (Capricornis crispus), which is a nationally designated special natural monument, raptors such as the mountain hawk eagle (Nisaetus nipalensis) and common buzzard (Buteo buteo) can be observed.
records.name: Kobushi

records.introduction_en: The Minami-Alps Biosphere Reserve includes a series of mountains above 3,000 m. It is one of Japan’s few high-rainfall areas, with a maximum elevation of 3,193 m above sea level and a lowest elevation of 180 m. Most of the site is forest, with areas characterised by alpine plant communities, including flower fields, and dense forest vegetation. This vast region shows marked environmental gradients and great biodiversity. The Minami-Alps Biosphere Reserve is home to festivals rich in ancient rites, with discoveries of relics from the Jomon Period, and folk arts that have been preserved and passed down. Inhabitants lived in regions closely connected to the mountains and engaged in hunting, fishing, gathering vegetables and agriculture. The biosphere reserve intends to strengthen existing interactions between the different regions. It aims to prevent the isolation of settlements in mountainous areas with steep slopes, maintain shared values across industry, education and cultural activities, promote the transmission of regional cultures to the next generation, and resolve local community issues jointly.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Minami-Alps Biosphere Reserve is flanked on two sides by rivers and lies within the Palaearctic region. The main habitats consist of the alpine vegetation region, with numerous endemic species such as Callianthemum hondoense, the subalpine coniferous forest region, the deciduous broad-leaved forest region, and the evergreen broad-leaved forest region. Land cover includes planted forests, agricultural land and residential areas. Except for planted forests, the vegetation is formed from natural and secondary vegetation. It includes both limited primeval environments and regenerated natural forests previously logged. Planted forests are mostly around settlements and supply wood products, typically conifers. They are widely distributed in the transition areas and have high market value. Hills in the subalpine zone contain planted forests of larch, Japanese cedar, Japanese cypress and Japanese red pine. The alpine zone above 2,600 m has communities of dwarf stone pines and various other alpine plant communities. By contrast, the lowlands are used for paddy fields, tea fields, deciduous orchards, other agricultural land and housing. Within the biosphere reserve there are many streams, rivers, lakes and other open water bodies in the Fuji, Oi and Tenryu river systems. The alpine zone has a relict, distinctive distribution of plants and animals that migrated south along the Japanese archipelago during the Ice Age. As the alpine zone of the Minami-Alps lies at the southern end, it is susceptible to global environmental change and many species are at risk. Even so, the mountain zone supports a diverse range of species. It features large, rare birds such as the rock ptarmigan and the golden eagle, as well as species endemic to Japan, including serow, Japanese dor … [truncated]
records.name: Minami Alps

records.title_en: Mount Odaigahara, Mount Omine and Osugidani
records.introduction_en: The Mount Odaigahara, Mount Omine and Osugidani Biosphere Reserve extends across the eastern part of the Kii Peninsula. The area includes several mountain ridges and the peaks of Mount Odaigahara, 1,695 metres above sea level, and Mount Omine, 1,719 metres. The biosphere reserve exhibits subtropical and temperate rainforests with evergreen and coniferous forests, temperate deciduous broadleaf forest, sub-alpine coniferous forest and conifer plantations.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area includes several mountain ridges and the peaks of Mount Odaigahara (1,695 metres) and Mount Omine (1,719 metres). Many of the valleys are deep, with waterfalls up to 200 metres, caused by geological uplift and the rejuvenation of rivers. There is a clear vertical zonation of vegetation from the warm-temperate zone to the sub-alpine zone. The biosphere reserve exhibits subtropical and temperate rainforests with evergreen and coniferous forests, temperate deciduous broadleaf forest, sub-alpine coniferous forest and conifer plantations. Large mammals such as the Asian black bear (Ursus thibetanus), Japanese serow (Capricornis crispus) and sika deer (Cervus nippon) have been recorded. There are also 102 bird species, including the red-flanked bluetail (Tarsiger cyanurus) and the Arctic warbler (Phylloscopus borealis). The Mount Omine range, which straddles the core area and the buffer zone, has been designated a World Cultural Heritage site, ‘Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range’, by UNESCO.
records.name: Mount Odaigahara, Mount Omine and Osugidani

records.introduction_en: This site, part of the Sobo–Katamuki–Okue mountain range, is characterised by steep mountains. Forests cover 85 per cent of this site. The use of forest resources, including wood production, shiitake mushroom cultivation and coal production, has remained sustainable. Owing to high forest biodiversity, research on fauna and flora in the mountain range has long been conducted, and the area has become an important base for biodiversity in the region.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: here are still many natural forests at high altitude in the Sobo–Katamuki–Okue mountain range, where a wide range of vegetation from warm temperate to cool temperate can be found depending on elevation. It is a precious area, home to many rare plants and animals with limited areas in which to live, such as the Japanese serow (a special natural monument) and the so-called Sohayaki group of plants, said to reveal the origins of the Japanese archipelago. These rare species are endangered, so their habitat requires protection.
records.name: Sobo, Katamuki and Okue

records.introduction_en: The Miramare and Trieste Coast Biosphere Reserve is situated about 7 km from the city of Trieste, on the Gulf of Trieste close to the Slovenian border. It takes the form of a rocky karst promontory with coastal cliffs and beaches. Marine habitats of special conservation interest include the tidal zone, which harbours many endemic species such as the brown alga (Fucus virsoides), and undisturbed cliffs with a diverse benthic fauna. Many tourists enjoy underwater tours or visit the castle and garden of the Habsburg family. The aim of the biosphere reserve is to maintain biological diversity in the marine environment surrounding Trieste through scientific research and monitoring. Environmental education for students and the public is also a major activity.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Miramare and Trieste Coast Biosphere Reserve is located in the coastal area of the Province of Trieste. It includes a portion of the coast of Trieste situated between the Miramare promontory and Sistiana Bay, and the surrounding marine area. The reserve is about 11 km in length, 1–1.5 km wide landwards, and about 1.85 km seawards. The landward landscape encompasses the Trieste Karst plateau, which slopes towards the sea, with traditional terraces shaped by dry stone walls and farmed with olive trees and vineyards. Karstic woodlands, together with grasslands and dry grasslands, ensure high biodiversity values. On the southern slopes, black pines grow in association with typical elements of the karstic woodland. The marine biotope is characterised by Zostera marina and Cymodocea nodosa meadows, with endemic species such as Fucus virsoides. The calcareous rocks at the edge of Miramare host a European shag (Phalacrocorax aristotelis) colony. Other species inhabiting the reserve include the yellow shore crab (Eriphia spinifrons), European lobster (Homarus gammarus), European sea bass (Dicentrarchus labrax) and the short-snouted seahorse (Hippocampus hippocampus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Miramare and Trieste Coast

records.introduction_en: The Valle del Ticino is a riverscape biosphere reserve located along the Ticino River in northern Italy, at the meeting point of the culturally rich regions of Lombardy and Piedmont. The reserve functions as an important ecological corridor within the urbanised and industrialised Po plain. The site encompasses a mosaic of ecosystems with large river habitats, wetlands, riparian woods and patches of primary plain forest, which covered the entire valley during Roman colonisation. The area also features a traditional rural landscape with semi-natural ecosystems, including paddy rice, cornfields, permanent grasslands and marcita (water meadows). People living in the biosphere reserve are mainly engaged in the services and industry sectors.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Valle del Ticino Biosphere Reserve encompasses the Ticino Valley from the watershed of Lake Maggiore and its rivers to the confluence with the River Po. It extends north to cover areas along the shores of Lake Maggiore in Piedmont, including Lagoni di Mercurago, Canneti di Dormelletto, Bosco Solivo and Fondo Toce. The area is one of the largest river parks in Europe. It retains a mosaic of natural ecosystems typical of large water bodies, as well as remnants of primary plain forest that covered the entire Po plain at the time of Roman colonisation. From an ecological and biogeographical standpoint, the Ticino River valley represents an extraordinary biological corridor running through the urbanised plain between the Alps and the Apennines. The rich diversity of animal and plant species in the Ticino Valley makes the reserve unique and exceptional, thanks to the well-preserved character of its natural environments and safeguarding actions across the territory. Several rare or area-specific species are worthy of preservation and require monitoring, including the European otter (Lutra lutra), the Aesculapian snake (Elaphe longissima), the Eurasian bittern (Botaurus stellaris) and the red-footed falcon (Falco vespertinus).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Ticino, Val Grande Verbano

records.introduction_en: Dana Biosphere Reserve has an area of 300 km². It covers a rugged landscape along the Great Rift Valley, including mountain ridges, plateaus and desert plains. The biosphere reserve encompasses Jordan’s four biogeographical zones: Mediterranean, Irano-Turanian, Saharo Arabian and Sudanian penetration. It is therefore home to the country’s most diverse nature. Several globally threatened species find refuge here, such as the Syrian serin (Serinus syriacus), the lesser kestrel (Falco naumanni), Blandford’s fox (Vulpes cana) and the Nubian ibex (Capra nubiana).
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve holds a relatively large representation of biodiversity. It includes 833 plant species, representing one-third of the country’s flora, including three species newly described to science. A total of 215 bird species have been recorded in Dana (about 50 per cent of Jordan’s birds) and 38 mammal species (also about 50 per cent of the country’s mammals). Dana Biosphere Reserve contains seven of the 13 vegetation types occurring in Jordan. These support many plants, birds and mammals. The reserve is characterised by four main biogeographical zones: Mediterranean, Irano-Turanian, Sudanian and Saharo Arabian. Altitudes range from 100 metres below sea level up to 1,500 metres above sea level. A system of wadis and mountains marks the site, extending from the tops of the Rift Valley mountains down to the desert lowlands of Wadi Araba.
records.name: Dana

records.introduction_en: Located at the foot of Kilimanjaro on the Kenyan side of the border, the Amboseli Biosphere Reserve contains a variety of ecological zones, including natural dry mountain forest, mountains, savannah rangelands, wetlands and swamps. These areas are home to a wide variety of species, including elephants, lions and giraffes. The biosphere reserve was part of the UNESCO–MAB project ‘Biosphere Reserves for Biodiversity Conservation and Sustainable Development in Anglophone Africa (BRAAF)’, which aimed to ensure the long-term conservation of biodiversity by involving the local population in its sustainable use.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Amboseli Biosphere Reserve is located in southern Kenya at the border with Tanzania. Its ecosystem consists of basement plains, saline plains with freshwater swamps, and the volcanic slopes of Kilimanjaro. The vegetation reflects the mainly semi-arid environment. In the past decade, populations of elephants, giraffes and lions have increased, while poaching cases registered in the biosphere reserve have declined. However, illegal harvesting of the African sandalwood tree (Osyris lanceolata) has risen. The plant’s essential oils are used in perfumes and cosmetics.
records.name: Amboseli

records.introduction_en: Situated on the equator about 180 km north of Nairobi, Mount Kenya is a solitary mountain of volcanic origin. A belt of moist afromontane forest from 1,800–3,200 metres above sea level gives way to a zone of tree-like heather at about 3,200 metres, and further up to moorlands and grasslands. Mount Kenya National Park was established in 1949 and became a biosphere reserve in 1978. In 1997, Mount Kenya National Park and adjacent forest reserves were inscribed on the World Heritage List. Mount Kenya is also important as a major water reservoir for its foothills and adjacent areas. Increasing conflicts over water resources provide the background for an assessment of the complex ecological and socio-economic dynamics of the highland–lowland system of Mount Kenya and the adjacent upper Euaso Ng’iro North Basin.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Vegetation includes afromontane forest, moorland and grassland. The biosphere reserve is a major water reservoir for adjacent areas. The major tree species and land cover types in the lower zones include Juniperus procera and Cassipourea malosana. Higher-altitude zones are dominated by bamboo, Arundinaria alpina, and a mosaic of bamboo and Podocarpus milanjianus. At higher altitudes, rainfall also supports Hagenia abyssinica and Hypericum revolutum, as well as grass and moorland. In areas with plentiful rainfall, especially on the windward side, giant camphor, Meru oak and other hardwoods thrive. Species found exclusively on Mount Kenya and rarely elsewhere include giant groundsel and giant lobelia. The biosphere reserve also hosts endemic wildlife such as the river frog, the side-striped chameleon, the marine viper, the king mole rat and the mole shrew. Other wildlife present includes giant forest hogs, leopards, eland, buffalo, duiker, an antelope species, and colobus monkeys.
records.name: Mount Kenya-Lewa

records.introduction_en: El Vizcaino is in the central part of the Baja California peninsula, in the Sebastian Volcano region between the Gulf of California and the Pacific Ocean. It contains a great abundance and variety of wild fauna and flora, including numerous species endemic to the Mesoamerican region and species that are endangered elsewhere. Protection of the site is justified by the exceptional value of its desert, mountain and coastal and marine ecosystems, which link the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of California. The reserve is also important for its fossil beds and numerous marine birds, including some under threat of extinction. The grey whale (Eschrichtius robustus) frequents the bay. The peninsula holds more than 400 prehistoric sites of importance, as well as petroglyphs, wall paintings and ancient ruined structures.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The diversity of physical and climatic environments has led to very rich wildlife, both in its forms and in its adaptation to this arid region, typical of what is known as the Sonora Desert, one of North America’s four deserts. In the terrestrial part of the reserve, 463 species of flora have been recorded, and 37 are known to be endemic to the geographical area in general. The greatest number of plant associations on the peninsula is concentrated in this region. Approximately 8.3 per cent of the flora is endemic to the geographical region of the El Vizcaino Desert. The biosphere reserve contains three subdivisions of the Sonora Desert. The sub-province Vizcaino Desert is the best represented, covering almost 95 per cent of the reserve. The sub-province Gulf Coast occupies a narrow strip along the eastern borders of the sierras to the east of the reserve, and the Magdalena Region covers only 1 per cent. Its lagoon complex is the grey whale’s calving and mating site, and it harbours healthy populations of Mexican bighorn sheep, mule deer, puma, coyote and 64 other species of mammals. It is also a refuge for 125 species of migratory birds and forms the transition zone between tropical and temperate climates.
records.name: El Vizcaino

records.introduction_en: La Michilía lies 75 km south of the city of Durango in the Sierra de Michis, a branch of the Sierra Madre Occidental. The Sierra de Michis consists of igneous rock from the Tertiary period. In the reserve, the topography shows a high degree of relief. There are several ephemeral streams and lagoons, as well as two permanent streams: the Laurel to the west and the Temascal to the south-east. Marshy meadows occur in the core area. Pine and holm oak forests cover most of the reserve. It covers 342,388 ha. Administratively, it spans the municipalities of Tlahualillo and Mapimí in the state of Durango, Jiménez in the state of Chihuahua, and Sierra Mojada in the state of Coahuila.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is located in one of the branches of the Western Sierra Madre. Its physiographic limits are two mountain chains, the Sierra Michis and the Sierra Urica. The area between these sierras has several plateaux and small hills separated by valleys and canyons of varying depth. There are five vegetation types in the reserve. Conifer forest includes Pinus, Quercus–Pinus, Pseudotsuga, Cupressusand Juniperus. Oak forest features Quercus. Other types are grasslands, xerophyllous shrubland, and aquatic and subaquatic vegetation. Its forests act as a catchment for two basins important to regional agriculture. The reserve hosts 770 species of vascular plants. The fauna is predominantly of Nearctic origin with North American affinities. The imperial woodpecker (Campephilus imperialis) used to occur in the area but is now extinct. The Mexican grey wolf (Canis lupus baileyi) and the American black bear (Ursus americanus) have been reintroduced in the reserve. Other notable vertebrates include the white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus), puma (Puma concolor), coyote (Canis latrans), wild turkey (Meleagris gallopavo), thick-billed parrot (Rhynchopsitta pachyrhyncha) and golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos).
records.name: La Michilía

records.introduction_en: Montebello lies between the physiographic region of the High Plain of Chiapas and the Gulf Coastal Plain, part of the physiographic province of the Sierras de Chiapas and Guatemala. The region corresponds to Miranda’s floristic regions termed the “central massif” and the plains and slopes north of the central massif. Its physiography ranges from small drainage features to large trenches, with large caves and cavities of varied shapes and dimensions.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Lagunas de Montebello National Park is in south-east Chiapas State, in the Sierra Madre de Chiapas physiographic province, on the border with Guatemala. Altitude is 1,500 m above sea level. The climate is temperate, with an annual average temperature of 23.6 °C. Summers are very rainy; average annual precipitation is 1,862 mm. Principal ecosystems represented in the park are coniferous forest, cloud forest, and aquatic and subaquatic vegetation. Montebello forms part of a hydrological basin that is a high priority for conservation and constitutes a wetland with 59 lakes of different colours. As an important terrestrial priority region, it also represents a significant Mesoamerican biological corridor and habitat for migratory and resident species, including at least 277 bird species, 65 mammal species and 35 reptile species. Vegetation is represented mainly by 208 tree species and 50 orchid species, with many epiphytes and ferns. A total of 106 species are recognised as endangered and 27 as endemic.
records.name: Lagunas de Montebello

records.introduction_en: The reserve is an area of high geological and ecological complexity and of human activity. It presents a high diversity of environments corresponding to nine vegetation types. It is of great relevance as the northern limit of rainforest on the American continent and a unique case in Mexico and North America, given the connection of different forest and rainforest types from the seacoast to the volcano summits. It is a key rainwater catchment, as it is among the rainiest areas of the country.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This biosphere reserve hosts significant ecosystem diversity and nine types of primary vegetation. It marks the northern limit of moist forest in the Americas and is unique in Mexico and North America for its continuity of forest types from the coast to the volcano tops. It is a catchment area, as it is one of the rainiest parts of the country. Within the reserve, 2,698 species of vascular plants and 877 vertebrate species have been identified, including 46 amphibians, 122 reptiles, 140 mammals and 569 birds, as well as 133 species of Odonata and 860 species of butterflies. Among the fauna, 21 species are endemic. It is a key area for birds migrating from North America: of the 569 bird species recorded, 223 are Nearctic and Neotropical migrants. The reserve contains endemic species as well as endangered species of fauna. Examples include Chironectes minimus, Vampyrum spectrum, Alouatta palliata, Ateles geoffroyii and Cyclopes didactylus. Among the birds are Jabiru mycteria, Cairina moschata, Sarcoramphus papa, Harpyhaliaetus solitarius, Harpia harpyja and Spizastur melanoleucus. The reserve also contains abundant ichthyofauna with endemic taxa such as Bramocharax caballeroi, Poecilia catemaconis, Poeciliopsis catemaco and Priapella olmecae.
records.name: Los Tuxtlas

records.introduction_en: Located in south-eastern Mexico on the north-eastern side of the Chiapas Highlands, the Nahá–Metzabok Biosphere Reserve forms part of the Lacandona Forest at the northern edge of the Selva Maya. Rugged karst ridges and canyoned valleys frame a compact diversity of ecosystems, from montane rainforest and cloud forest to pine–oak woodland and a network of natural lakes with seasonally flooded shorelines. Indigenous Maya–Lacandón, Tzeltal and Chol communities live within and around the reserve and draw on ancestral knowledge in land-use practices that align with careful use of forest and water. Guided by scientific research and monitoring, the reserve’s objectives are to restore ecological processes and secure sustainable management for community benefit.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Nahá–Metzabok lies in a humid tropical belt with marked altitudinal variation on a karst landscape. Strongly folded and faulted calcareous hills, oriented north-east to south-east, create a rugged topography of long, dissected ranges with large karst plateaux and narrow ravines. The combination of high moisture, elevation gradients and complex geomorphology drives abrupt changes in temperature, soils and water availability over short distances. This creates a compact mosaic of habitats: lowland tropical rainforest, montane cloud forest, oak forest on cooler slopes and ridges, and seasonally flooded ‘spiny’ forest fringing lakes and backwaters. The seasonally flooded spiny forest is characterised by logwood (Haematoxylum campechianum) and supports abundant epiphytes, including orchids and bromeliads.
