The reserve hosts hundreds of bird species, many of them North American winter migrants, and flagship mammals including jaguar, ocelot, margay, jaguarundi, northern tamandua, and both howler and spider monkeys. Tall humid forests regulate the local hydrological cycle as intact canopies intercept rain, leaf litter maintains thin but active soils, and karst basins store and slowly release water – sustaining streams, moderating floods and droughts, and underpinning downstream agriculture.
records.name: Naha-Metzabok

records.introduction_en: Located over the mouth of Yucatán’s largest groundwater basin, between the towns of Celestún and Maxcanú, the Ría Celestún Biosphere Reserve forms part of a vast wetland corridor in the west of the peninsula. Fresh water from underground aquifers surfaces here, making the reserve a unique example of a natural wetland in the area. Its mangroves, dunes and lowland rainforests hold substantial natural heritage, particularly for birds, and the area is a resting place for many migrating species. Although especially known for its pink flamingos, its pristine beaches, with waters ranging from turquoise to light blue, attract thousands of visitors every year.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve is notable for its diversity of environments, comprising interdependent ecosystems such as the shallow continental marine platform, coastal dunes, mangroves, lagoons, marshes and lowland rainforests. These habitats support almost 1,150 species of mammals, birds and plants. The area includes 304 resident and migratory bird species, notably coastal and marshland birds such as herons (Ardeidae), ducks (Anatidae) and gulls. Ría Celestún and Ría Lagartos are both important areas for the Caribbean flamingo (Phoenicopterus ruber ruber), which nests, feeds and reproduces here, with a population reaching 23,000 birds. Other bird species include the threatened plumbeous kite (Ictinia plumbea) and brent goose (Branta bernicla), the endangered Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata) and piping plover (Charadrius melodus). The beaches and lower dunes serve as nesting places for turtles, and various projects aim to protect these ecosystems.
records.name: Ría Celestún

records.introduction_en: Sian Ka’an Biosphere Reserve is the largest protected area in the Mexican Caribbean, and is a UNESCO World Heritage site. Located on the eastern coast of the Yucatán Peninsula, it is home to vast biodiversity, especially bird and marine species, in its tropical forests, mangroves, marshes and barrier reefs. In the language of the Maya peoples, Sian Ka’an means “origin of the sky”. Tulum, a beach resort, and the world-famous Maya ruins located within the biosphere reserve limits attract large numbers of tourists each year.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve has an undisturbed sea–land interface along a well-conserved coastline with tropical forests, mangroves and marshes. Its diverse tropical forests, savannahs, pristine wetlands and part of the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef provide habitat for remarkable flora and fauna, including charismatic mammals such as jaguars (Panthera onca), pumas (Puma concolor), ocelots (Leopardus pardalis) and tapirs (Tapirus bairdii). Among marine invertebrates, there are 84 coral species and 276 crustacean species. The site appears to be the location in Mexico with the greatest similarity to the Antilles. It is a nesting area for turtles and for sea and marshland birds, and is noted for distinctive life in underground, flooded galleries. It is also home to more than 300 bird species, 120 of which are migrants. The area is known for its cenotes, natural pits exposing groundwater, which host various communities, some endemic.
records.name: Sian Ka'an

records.introduction_en: The Sierra Gorda Biosphere Reserve is located in the state of Querétaro in northern Mexico. Its strategic biogeographical position between the Nearctic and the Mesoamerican Mountain regions makes Sierra Gorda one of the most ecologically rich and diverse places in Mexico. It comprises 14 vegetation types and is dominated by tropical sclerophyllous forest. The conservation of the ecosystems of Sierra Gorda is essential. They host a number of threatened species and serve as a refuge for migratory species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The rugged topography of this biosphere reserve, with altitudes ranging from 260 to 3,100 m above sea level, and rainfall fluctuating between 350 and 1,800 mm, together with its location at the convergence of the Nearctic, Neotropical and Mountain Mesoamerica realms, all contribute to a wide mosaic of habitats. The reserve harbours 15 types of vegetation. These include evergreen, sub-evergreen, subdeciduous and deciduous forests, and sub-montane shrubland and cloud forest. Oak, pine, juniper and fir forests are also present, as are alpine chaparral, temperate grasslands, xerophilous grassland, xerophilous scrubland and riparian gallery forest. The fauna and flora include 1,718 species of vascular plants and 124 species of macromycetes, in addition to 131 species of mammals, 363 species of birds, 72 species of reptiles and 23 species of amphibians. It is estimated that 30 per cent of Mexican daytime butterflies are present in this area, with approximately 600 species. The reserve is home to the jaguar, the Yucatán brown brocket, the Mexican black bear, the spider monkey and the otter. Notable birds include the great curassow, the crested guan, the bearded wood partridge (Dendrortyx barbatus), the military macaw (Ara militaris), the red-crowned amazon (Amazona viridigenalis), the toucan, the emerald toucanet and the American crocodile. It also hosts endemic species such as the Querétaro pocket gopher (Pappogeomys neglectus), the Autochton siermadriorbutterfly, and a great number of fish and troglobitic arthropods.
records.name: Sierra Gorda

records.introduction_en: Sierra de Huautla Biosphere Reserve, known as REBIOSH, is located in the Balsas basin and is a rich reservoir of species endemic to Mexico. Its rugged topography creates an altitudinal range from 700 to 2,240 m above sea level. The site presents a broad representation of ecosystems, notably low deciduous forest, gallery vegetation and pine–oak forest.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve lies in the basin of the River Balsas and is a rich reserve of Mexican endemic species. Its rugged topography gives rise to altitude variations from 700 to 2,240 m above sea level, with a wide representation of ecosystems. Low deciduous forests, gallery vegetation and pine–oak forests are noteworthy for their land cover. The low deciduous forests harbour a high percentage of life forms exclusive to Mexico, and the number of endemic species is higher than in other types of vegetation. A total of 939 species of native vascular plants have been recorded out of the 3,345 reported for the state of Morelos. Relict populations of 44 species of butterflies, representative of a warm, humid geological stage in this region, are found here. There are 71 species of mammals, 208 species of birds, 53 species of reptiles, 18 species of amphibians and 14 species of fish. Relevant fauna include the short-horned baronia (Baronia brevicornis), the beaded lizard (Heloderma horridum), the military macaw (Ara militaris), the rufous-backed robin (Turdus rufopalliatus), the Balsas screech owl (Otus seductus), the pileated flycatcher (Xenotriccus mexicanus), the puma (Puma concolor), the ocelot (Leopardus pardalis), the margay (Leopardus wiedii), the bobcat (Lynx rufus) and the jaguarundi (Herpailurus yagouaroundi). Various species of wildlife endemic to the Balsas basin, Mesoamerica and Mexico are represented in the Sierra de Huautla Biosphere Reserve: seven species of mammals, 34 species of birds, 28 species of reptiles and six species of amphibians.
records.name: Sierra de Huautla

records.introduction_en: Volcán Tacaná, on the border with Guatemala, is part of the Central American Core volcanic chain, known as the Nucleo Centroamericano. It contains fragile ecosystems rich in wild flora and fauna of cultural, scientific, economic and biological relevance. Its biodiversity and high endemism are especially evident in the high mountain ecosystems and landscapes, and in the volcanic edifice. This edifice has geophysical features of great scientific and aesthetic value that are representative of humid environments of Andean origin found in Mexico.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The region of Volcán Tacaná, in the core of Central America, is a rich reservoir of endemic species and species of Central and South American origin which, in Mexico, occur only in this area. The topography is rugged, with ecosystems of evergreen medium-altitude forests, cloud forests, and pine, oak and fir forests. It is the only place in the country where two ecosystems are represented: the tropical páramo and the chusqueal ecosystem. The Volcán Tacaná Biosphere Reserve harbours endemic flora such as Chasquea martinezi and endemic fauna including Cyllopsis, Limanopoda cinna and Dalla (Lepidoptera–Rhopalocera). The biota of the volcano also includes a significant number of charismatic or protected species, such as the canaco tree (Chiranthodendron derbianus) and the ornate hawk-eagle (Spizaetus ornatus). There are innumerable species of orchids and bromeliads. Biodiversity and endemism are particularly evident in the high mountain ecosystems and landscapes, and in the volcanic edifice. This edifice has geophysical features of great scientific and aesthetic value that are representative of humid environments of Andean origin in Mexico. Average annual rainfall can reach 2,000–5,000 mm, as in Soconusco.
records.name: Volcán Tacaná

records.introduction_en: This Russian biosphere reserve is located in the middle section of the Volga River, about 55 km south-west of the city of Nizhny Novgorod. Part of the biosphere reserve, the Kama–Bakaldino Mires, is designated as a Ramsar wetland and represents the largest peatland complex south of the northern taiga zone in Europe.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve comprises large areas of pine forests recovering from logging activities and fires since the 1970s. Some fragments of old growth have been preserved. Within the biosphere reserve, logging, poaching and peat extraction are restricted.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Nijegorodskoe Zavolje

records.introduction_en: Altaisky Biosphere Reserve is located in the Altai Mountains in south-central Russia. Established as a natural reserve in 1932, it includes mountains, taiga forests and steppes. A characteristic feature of the reserve’s landscapes is the abundance of lakes: 2,560 medium and small lakes, including about 1,200 of glacial origin. Swampy locations are found in intermontane depressions, river valleys and on smoothed slopes.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: There are more than 3,101 plant species in the reserve, of which more than 250 are Altai–Sayan endemics. Since the Altaisky reserve was established, 16 fish species, 2 amphibian species, 6 reptile species, 326 bird species and 70 mammal species have been recorded. As for mammals, the biosphere reserve is home to 70 species. The following species are included in the IUCN Red List: Uncia uncia, Ovis ammon ammon, Haliaeetus albicilla and Falco peregrinus.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Altaisky

records.introduction_en: This is a cluster biosphere reserve next to the border with Mongolia, 700 km south-east of Lake Baikal. Situated in the Mongolian–Manchurian Steppe biogeographic region, the area comprises vast steppes and pine forests at elevations ranging from 598 to 769 m above sea level.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The main habitat types are the wetlands of the Torey hollow, including open lake surfaces, nearshore areas overgrown with reeds, boggy meadows and shallow reed-filled waters in the deltas of the Uldza and Imalka rivers. There are also steppe sites of dry and genuine Dauria steppes, and small forest–steppe parts of the Tsasuchey pine forest. Crops and ploughlands occupy only small areas in the buffer zone of the reserve. Their extent changes depending on the climatic situation. At the beginning of a droughty period, the number of arable fields decreases markedly. Sodic lakes, such as Barun-Toney Lake, and wetlands lying in ancient tectonic depressions are of particular interest for birdlife. A total of 308 bird species have been identified, many of which are endangered. The climate is extremely continental, with winter temperatures falling to −40 °C and summers reaching +40 °C.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Daursky

records.introduction_en: The Khankaiskiy Biosphere Reserve lies in the Prikhankayskaya and Prisungachinskaya Lowlands in the central part of the Zapadno-Primorskaya Plain, close to the Chinese border. The terrain is mostly flat, but five ridges separated by wet depressions run along the eastern coast of Lake Khanka. These are former beach ridges of the lake.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Lake Khanka, which is shared between Russia and China, is one of the largest freshwater lakes in Eastern Asia. The biosphere reserve includes part of Lake Khanka and comprises open lowlands with meadows, wetlands, swamps and many small lakes. Also designated a Ramsar site, it is noted for its variety of bird and fish species. A total of 337 bird species have been recorded in the biosphere reserve, and the lake’s ichthyofauna has no analogue among other freshwater bodies in the Palaearctic, with 74 fish species. The unique ornithofauna of the Lake Khanka Basin was first described by N. M. Przhevalsky in 1869–1870. Japanese crane (Grus japonensis), white-naped crane (Grus vipio) and Far Eastern stork (Ciconia boyciana) are protected here in co-operation with other state nature reserves. The Prikhankayskaya Lowland is also the only nesting place in Russia of the reed parrotbill (Paradoxornis heudei) and the intermediate egret (Egretta intermedia). The swamps of the eastern shore of Lake Khanka are unique in the region for vegetation and wildlife. The flora consists of 680 species of vascular plants and 322 species of algae. Higher plants include heat-loving and ancient species such as Manchurian water-nut (Trapa manshurica), lotus lily (Nelumbo komarovii) and prickly water lily (Euryale ferox).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Khankaiskiy

records.introduction_en: Located at the heart of the Eurasian continent and known for its rich biodiversity, more than 80 per cent of this biosphere reserve is covered by mountain taiga. Sustainable forest management and agriculture, beekeeping and tourism are the main economic activities practised at the site.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Dark coniferous forests are represented by cedar and fir trees. They mostly form mixed stands across a large part of the area. Pure cedar or pure fir forests are rarely found. A small area is occupied by taiga cedar–larch forests. Dark coniferous birch forests occupy small areas in river valleys and on lower slopes. The fauna of the mountain taiga area is rich and includes 11 fish species, three amphibian species, three reptile species, 139 bird species and 50 mammal species.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Khakassky

records.introduction_en: Kizlyar Bay is one of the largest bays in the Caspian Sea and is also one of the largest migratory routes for birds in Eurasia. It represents a diversity of marine, coastal and desert-steppe ecosystems, including populations of threatened animals such as the Caspian seal, many species of birds and sturgeons. Livelihoods depend on fishing, land use including grazing and haymaking, hunting and tourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve ensures conservation of globally important natural complexes and objects of the north-western coast of the Caspian Sea. It includes three Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas (IBAs) of global significance: Nizhnekumskiye Floods, Kizlyar Bay and Tyuleny Island. There are also two potential Ramsar sites: Kizlyar Bay and Nizhnekumskiye Floods. The area supports populations of globally threatened animals, including the Caspian seal, many species of birds and sturgeons. The entire water area of the biosphere reserve lies within the boundaries of a special North Caspian Protected Fishery Zone, whose status is close to that of a nature sanctuary. Mammals of the reserve comprise 47 species, with five listed in the IUCN Red List and the Red Data Book of Russia. The north-eastern part of Kizlyar Bay and Tyuleny Island is greatly important for reproduction of the Caspian seal, the only endemic pinniped species of the Caspian Sea. Other rare species include the jungle cat, the Caucasian otter, the European mink and the marbled polecat. The biosphere reserve is highly valuable for the breeding, migration and wintering of more than 280 species of birds. Kizlyar Bay is a key part of one of the largest migratory routes of birds in Eurasia, connecting the European part of Russia, western Siberia and northern Kazakhstan with Transcaucasia, western Asia, the Near East and north and east Africa.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Kizlyar Bay

records.introduction_en: Kronotskiy Biosphere Reserve is situated in one of the remotest parts of the Russian Far East, on the Kamchatka Peninsula, the landmass that separates the Sea of Okhotsk from the Pacific Ocean.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area represents some of the most pristine parts of the Kamchatka Peninsula and contains a remarkable set of volcanoes, some of which are still active, as well as hot springs and geysers. The biosphere reserve has an elevation range from 0 to 3,528 m above sea level. Vegetation changes with elevation, from tundra to temperate broad-leaved forest, and includes coastal areas.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Kronotskiy

records.introduction_en: This reserve comprises the Katunskiy Biosphere Reserve (Russian Federation, designated in 2000) and the Katon-Karagay Biosphere Reserve (Kazakhstan, designated in 2014). With a total area of over 1.5 million ha, the territory is used for livestock rearing and grazing, red deer farming, fodder production and apiculture. Tourism, hunting, fishing and the collection of non-timber forest products are also widespread.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Great Altay Transboundary Biosphere Reserve forms part of the Altai–Sayan Ecoregion, which encompasses a wide variety of ecosystems. More than 200 protected areas of different legal status make up 16.5 per cent (about 17.6 million ha) of the ecoregion. Among other aims, the Great Altay Transboundary Biosphere Reserve focuses on conserving migratory species, especially ungulates and carnivores. For example, the snow leopard, an umbrella species for the high mountain areas of the Altai–Sayan Ecoregion, inhabits vast areas of this region, including parts of the Great Altay Transboundary Biosphere Reserve.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Katunsky

records.introduction_en: Facing the unfolding Siberian expanses to the north and shouldered by the Altai Mountains to the south, the Kuznetsky Alatau Ridge remains virtually unchanged since the last ice age. In these remote mountains, the biosphere reserve serves as a hub for social services, environmentally oriented small businesses, ecotourism and the revival of the local Indigenous culture.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: It encompasses mountains with Siberian fir and Siberian pine, and tundra and taiga ecosystems where Siberian forest reindeer, moose and brown bears live. Otters, minks, muskrats and beavers thrive on the shores of its rivers and lakes. The general appearance of the Kuznetsky Alatau relief is determined by the predominance of low-mountain watersheds, above which stand individual peaks, a plexus of mountains and asymmetric mountain ranges of the middle-mountain type. The interaction of a complex geological structure and neotectonic movements with river activity has led to significant dissection of the terrain.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Kuznetsky Alatau

records.introduction_en: Laplandskiy Biosphere Reserve is situated in the western part of the Kola Peninsula, about 120 km south of Murmansk and 120 km north of the Arctic Circle. It is an area of plains and mountains, with glaciated landforms and exposures of the Baltic Shield. There are permafrost patches in the mountains, but the climate is moderated by the influence of the Gulf Stream. Polar nights last 25 days and the “white nights” season lasts 100 days.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Forests of pine (Pinus sylvestris), spruce (Picea abies, P. obovata) and birch (Betula verrucosa, B. pubescens) cover more than half of the area. Another 28 per cent is covered with mountain tundra at elevations of about 300 to 450 metres above sea level. In between, there is a well-marked transition zone of birch woodland. Mires, rivers and lakes cover the rest of the biosphere reserve. Mammals in this region include the beaver (Castor fiber), lemming (Lemmus lemmus), brown bear (Ursus arctos) and pine marten (Martes martes).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Laplandskiy

records.introduction_en: Situated between the meandering Volga to the west and the steppes of Kazakhstan to the east, the biosphere reserve forms a crossroads of landscapes and cultures. At its centre lies Lake Baskunchak, known throughout Russia for its salt production, which stands out from the surrounding scrubland. The biosphere reserve is a landmark of the Caspian Depression and contains numerous archaeological and cultural monuments that attest to its position on the Silk Road.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: It is home to 230 bird species, including curly pelicans, long-legged buzzards and several species of eagles and falcons. It lies on migratory routes used by bird species protected under the Ramsar Convention. The mountainous semi-arid ecosystem also hosts 88 species of higher vascular plants, 12 species of reptiles, notably the endemic squeaky gecko (Alsophylax pipiens), more than 160 insect taxa and 113 species of arachnids. There are 46 species of mammals, including a relic population of the antelope Saiga tatarica, wild boar, elk and roe deer.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Mountain Great Bogdo

records.introduction_en: The reserve lies south-east of Moscow along the middle course of the Oka River, within the Meschera lowland. It sits at the junction of three biogeographic zones: the broad-leaved forest zone, which comprises the largest part, the taiga and the forest-steppe to the south.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve comprises a Ramsar site that covers an extensive floodplain of lowland rivers, lakes and forested peatlands, which provide habitat for many waterfowl and waders. Within the area there is a European bison breeding centre, established in 1959, and a crane breeding centre founded in 1979. New generations of European bison, about 300 individuals, and Siberian crane, around 80 individuals, from both centres will be released into nature.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Okskiy

records.introduction_en: The Prioksko-Terrasnyi Biosphere Reserve is in the southern part of the Moscow Region on the left bank of the Oka River, a right tributary of the Volga River. The core of the biosphere reserve comprises the natural complexes of the Prioksko-Terrasnyi State Nature Zapovednik, a state-protected nature reserve. Its unique feature is the combination of typical broad-leaved and mixed forests with old-growth steppe pine forests. These landscapes are formed on south-facing sands of a terrace located above the Oka River floodplain.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The core area of the biosphere reserve is the Prioksko-Terrasnyi State Nature Reserve, which combines typical broad-leaved and mixed forests with an old-growth steppe-influenced pine forest. Almost all types of plant communities of the Moscow Region are found in the biosphere reserve. They range from upland bogs to oak forests, from spruce forests to vast floodplain meadow. The Bison Breeding Centre, located in the biosphere reserve core area, was founded to save the largest European mammal, the European bison (Bison bonasus), from extinction. Today the bison nursery is used to create free-living bison populations. More than 600 calves have been born in the nursery during its existence. In the period 1999–2015, more than 116 animals were exported to create sustainable free-living bison populations.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Prioksko-Terrasnyi

records.introduction_en: The Sayano-Shushenskiy Biosphere Reserve is located in the Krasnoyarsk Territory of Siberia on the left bank of a large man-made reservoir, where the Yenisey valley cuts through the Western Sayan mountain range. The state natural biosphere reserve “Sayano-Shushensky” is a nature-protective, scientific and educational establishment of federal value. Its purpose is to preserve and study the natural course of processes and phenomena, the genetic fund of plant and animal life, and particular types and communities of plants and animals. It also aims to conserve the typical and unique ecological systems of the Western Sayan Mountains, the centre of the biogeographical province of the Altai–Sayans highland, relating to the biome of mixed mountain forests and the mountain systems of the Palaearctic area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Covering a vast area with an elevation range from 400 to 2,735 metres above sea level, the biosphere reserve contains a rich diversity of habitats. These include extensive coniferous and mixed forests, subalpine and alpine meadows, mountain tundra, mountain steppe, taiga, streams and marshlands. There is a marked difference in climate and soils between north- and south-facing slopes of the Sayan Mountains. The northern slopes, influenced by Atlantic air masses, are wetter, while the southern slopes are more continental due to Arctic influence.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Sayano-Shushenskiy

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve lies in the Manchurian–Japanese Mixed Forest biogeographical region in the far south-east of Russia. It comprises a complex system that includes the central eastern part of the Sikhote-Alin mountain ranges and marine areas of the Sea of Japan.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Main habitats of interest include pine–spruce woods with Rhododendron fauriei, meadow, birch and oak associations, steppe meadows and yew groves. Characteristic mammals include the critically endangered Amur tiger (Panthera tigris altaica), the Manchurian red deer (Cervus elaphus xanthopygus), the main prey of Amur tigers, the Himalayan black bear (Ursus thibetanus) and the brown bear (Ursus arctos). The presence of these species was one reason for the designation of the area as a World Heritage site.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Sikhote-Alin

records.introduction_en: The Voronezhsky Biosphere Reserve is located in two regions of the Russian Federation, the Lipetsk and Voronezh regions, and five municipalities: the Usmansky, Verhne-Khavsky, Ramonsky and Novousmansky municipal districts, and the Railway urban district of the city of Voronezh. Many rural settlements are located directly on the borders of the biosphere reserve. As a specially protected natural territory, Voronezh State Nature Zapovednik was established in 1923 to protect the beaver. Later, the Zapovednik became a complex reserve and now conserves natural complexes, including island pine forest, in the Russian forest-steppe zone. In 1985, the Zapovednik was declared a biosphere reserve by UNESCO. Within the Zapovednik, a core area and a buffer zone have been designated.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is a mixed forest with stands of pine (Pinus sylvestris), oak (Quercus robur) and lime (Tilia cordata), and floodplain forests of alder (Alnus glutinosa). Fifty-four mammal species are present, including Russian desman (Desmana moschata), beaver (Castor fiber), otter (Lutra lutra) and elk (Alces alces). The forest was heavily logged in the past. Today, reafforestation of riverbanks with willow (Salix) has enabled forest recovery and allowed the beaver population to increase. The Voronezhsky Biosphere Reserve experimental beaver breeding ground is an essential element of the reserve’s initiative for environmental education. It has been open to the public since it was founded. The first visitors could watch beavers kept in open enclosures on the bank of the Usman River from a viewing platform. Since the 2000s, the breeding ground has been regularly visited by tourist groups. In addition, TV segments and documentaries are regularly filmed at the beaver breeding ground.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Voronezhskiy

records.introduction_en: Puerto Galera Biosphere Reserve is situated on Mindoro Island, about 120 km south of Manila. It comprises the northern tip of Mindoro Island and is bound to the north by the Verde Island Passage, to the west by the Camarong River and to the east by the municipality of San Teodoro.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Ecosystems represented here include savannas and grasslands, dipterocarp forests, mossy forests, mangroves, coral reefs and coastal ecosystems, as well as agroforestry systems. A wide variety of endemic species are present, including the tamaraw (Bubalus mindorensis). The conservation of coral reefs has been recognised as one of the main tasks of the biosphere reserve. Healthy coral reefs are important for the conservation of biodiversity, the maintenance of traditional lifestyles and culture, tourism revenue, education and research.
records.name: Puerto Galera

records.introduction_en: Graciosa Island is part of the Central Group of the Azores Archipelago. With an area of 60.7 km² and 44 km of coastline, it is the second smallest island in the archipelago. It is also the flattest, with a highest point of 405 m.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Graciosa Island stands out for its relative dryness, associated with the absence of large reliefs. This translates into a relatively small number of habitats and species, mainly terrestrial flora and fauna. However, this apparent limitation is offset by high geodiversity, characterised by a wide variety of geological structures, forms and materials. The Furna do Enxofre, located inside the Natural Monument of Caldeira da Graciosa, is an imposing lava cave that contains the largest volcanic dome in Europe. There are also hot springs, the best known on the coast of Carapacho, which feed the existing thermal facilities known as Termas do Carapacho. With regard to biodiversity, the natural reserve of the islet of Praia, off Vila da Praia, is particularly noteworthy. It hosts one of the richest and most diverse colonies of seabirds in the Azores, as well as various other endemic species associated with its vegetation cover. This biodiversity hotspot is visited annually by eight rare and sensitive bird species that nest there, all included in Annex I of the EU Birds Directive. These include a Macaronesian endemic subspecies, Audubon’s shearwater (Puffinus lherminieri baroli), and a local endemism, Monteiro’s storm-petrel (Hydrobates monteiroi). Also noteworthy are two species of bats: Nyctalus azoreum, endemic to the Azores and one of the few species in the world with strong daytime activity, and Pipistrellus maderensis, endemic to Macaronesia, with its usual nocturnal activity.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Graciosa Island

records.introduction_en: Paúl do Boquilobo Biosphere Reserve in central Portugal comprises a natural freshwater wetland surrounded by marshes, which lie in a bend of the Almonda River. Floods from the Tejo River naturally inundate the site in winter, and part of it dries out when the water table is mechanically lowered in spring to create larger areas for cultivation. The site may also act as a flooding buffer zone that increases protection of adjoining farmland against erosion caused by winter floods. For many years this wetland has been a valuable sink for alluvial particles carried in by the Tejo River, creating rich cultivated areas that have contributed to the economic wealth of the area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The marshes have characteristic aquatic vegetation in permanently inundated areas. Lines of cottonwood (Populus), willow (Salix) and other trees form characteristic hedges around the wetland and offer excellent cover for breeding birds and other fauna. Three core areas are designated, including the densest willow growths. Sunflower and other fast-growing annuals are grown on fertile sediments around the marsh. The wetland, which is also a Ramsar site, is a very important wintering site for waterbirds in Portugal, with concentrations of ducks, pintail (Anas acuta), cattle egret (Bubulcus ibis), little egret (Egretta garzetta), black-crowned night-heron (Nycticorax nycticorax) and a growing population of the spoonbill (Platalea leucorodia).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Paúl do Boquilobo

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve, located in the archipelago of Madeira, combines terrestrial and marine areas. The terrestrial areas host more than 1,600 taxa with a high level of endemism, including 15 floral taxa that are exclusive to Porto Santo. The biosphere reserve is home to several species of marine reptiles and mammals, notably the rarest seal in the world, the Mediterranean monk seal (Monachus monachus), and the loggerhead sea turtle (Caretta caretta). Its marine biodiversity is yet to be fully catalogued. Tourism is the island’s most important economic sector.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The terrestrial biodiversity of the site includes more than 1,600 taxa with a high level of endemism. About 396, or 24 per cent, belong to various taxonomic groups such as fungi, lichens, plants (both non-vascular and vascular), and animals (both invertebrates and vertebrates). Some species have international, national or regional conservation status. The flora includes a large number of endemic vascular plants. Among the approximately 536 identified taxa, 15 are exclusive to Porto Santo, and the most recently described, Echium portosanctense, Pericallis menezesii and Sonchus parathalassius, are noteworthy. In addition, 28 are endemic to Madeira and 26 are endemic to Macaronesia.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Porto Santo

records.introduction_en: Situated at the southern tip of Viet Nam, the Mũi Cà Mau Biosphere Reserve comprises tropical wetlands and rainforests, and includes the offshore island groups of Hòn Khoai, Hòn Chuối, Hòn Đá Bạc, Hòn Buông. It brings together mangrove systems, peat swamp forests and associated marine–coastal habitats of high ecological value and global significance. The reserve’s objectives are to conserve and restore natural resources and forest cover, maintain biodiversity, strengthen climate resilience, and support sustainable livelihoods in the buffer zone, advancing a balanced relationship between people and nature.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The core area comprises three parts: strictly protected zones within Mũi Cà Mau National Park and U Minh Hạ National Park, and a coastal protection belt. The Mui Ca Mau Biosphere Reserve hosts rich and varied biodiversity across marine, mangrove and closed tropical rainforest ecosystems. Characteristic species include bui (Ilex cymosa), mop (Alstonia spathulata), melaleuca (Melaleuca cajeputi), three-leaved dau dau (Euodia lepta) and tram (Syzygium cinereum). Notable fauna include the lesser short-nosed fruit bat (Cynopterus brachyotis), crab-eating macaque (Macaca fascicularis), lesser adjutant (Leptoptilos javanicus), painted stork (Mycteria leucocephala) and spot-billed pelican (Pelecanus philippensis). Mũi Cà Mau National Park is Ramsar-listed and contains the largest remaining mangrove forests and intertidal mudflats on the Cà Mau Peninsula within the Indochina Mangroves biogeographic region. It is the only site in Viet Nam where two tidal regimes interact, driving sediment build-up that forms new mudflats and habitats. The park contributes to a coastal protected-forest corridor linking mangrove and Melaleuca forest (Melaleuca leucadendron) on alum-rich wetland, which maintains connectivity and resilience. The area supports species of global concern, including the critically endangered Batagur baska, and the endangered Lutra sumatrana and Platalea minor, and serves as an important stopover and wintering site for waterbirds. Mangroves also deliver vital ecosystem services, including coastal protection from erosion and storm surges, moderation of local climate, regulation of water flows and filtration of pollutants.
records.name: Mui Ca Mao

records.introduction_en: Dong Nai is the new name of the former Cat Tien Biosphere Reserve, which was designated in 2001. It is located in the Dong Nai province in the south-east of Viet Nam. In this region the plateaux of the central Vietnamese highlands give way to the Nam Bo Delta. The area includes typical landforms of the Truong Son Mountain range and the lowland rivers, streams, semi-plains, medium hills, relatively flat lands and scattered lakes, ponds and wetlands of the eastern Nam Bo Delta.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Cat Tien tropical forest ecosystem forms part of the Indo-Pacific biogeographical region. Typical forest types include evergreen broad-leaved forest, bamboo forest and other mixed forest. Cat Tien National Park provides protection for this continuous mosaic of forests. Within the park there is great variation in topography, from steep hill areas in the north to large lowland areas, wetlands, riverine areas and cultivated fields in the south. The area has been able to retain much of its original diversity due to the survival of areas of unmodified habitat and the suppression of hunting and other forms of disturbance. There are seven different habitat types and a total of 1,610 botanical species on five geographical landscapes. Of the known species, 31 are listed as rare and 23 are endemic to Cat Tien. The forest types and geographical sites function as habitats for unique tropical fauna, which include 259 bird species, 64 reptile species, 33 amphibian species and 99 fish species. These include endangered species such as white-shouldered ibis (Pseudibis davisoni), Indochinese tiger (Panthera tigris corbetti), Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) and the critically endangered Javan rhinoceros (Rhinoceros sondaicus annamiticus), one of the world’s rarest large mammals.
records.name: Dong Nai

records.introduction_en: Set in northern Viet Nam where the Red River meets the sea, the Red River Delta Biosphere Reserve brings together estuarine wetlands, mangroves, mudflats, beaches and seagrass beds. The area lies on a major flyway for migratory waterbirds and centres on Xuan Thuy National Park, designated under the Ramsar Convention. The reserve’s purpose is to conserve estuarine ecosystems and sustain the coastal cultural landscape while supporting livelihoods linked to fisheries and mangrove use.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: At the river mouth and along the coast, the reserve comprises estuaries, wetlands, mangroves, mudflats and seagrass beds under a tropical monsoon regime. Coastal landforms are shaped by river-borne and marine sediments, with mangrove root systems trapping alluvium and gradually raising the shoreline. Upper mudflats support young mangroves with reeds and other herbs. Lower, frequently inundated mudflats of fine sand or muddy clay provide feeding grounds and nursery habitat. Seasonal sand islands form at the river mouth and favour mangrove colonisation, and a network of tidal canals moves water and sediments. The reserve supports large seasonal congregations of waterbirds migrating from breeding grounds in northern Asia to wintering areas in the Indo-Malayan and Australian regions, including threatened species such as spoon-billed sandpiper (Calidris pygmaea), black-faced spoonbill (Platalea minor), Chinese egret (Egretta eulophotes) and Saunders’s gull (Chroicocephalus saundersi). Xuan Thuy National Park, at the core of the coastal wetlands, is recognised under the Ramsar Convention. Dominant mangroves include Kandelia candel and Sonneratia caseolaris. Mangroves, seagrass and mudflats buffer storm surges, reduce erosion and sustain productive fisheries across the delta.
records.name: Red River Delta

records.introduction_en: The Western Nghe An Biosphere Reserve is located in central Viet Nam, in a mountainous and remote area that is difficult to access. Its climate is strongly influenced by north-east and south-west monsoons. The topography of the surrounding Annamite mountain range also affects atmospheric circulation, resulting in significant climatic differences throughout the area. The region hosts some of the most diverse and rich flora and fauna in Viet Nam.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve has three core areas, including one national park and two nature reserves, covering almost all types of tropical rainforest and various habitats, including mountains, wetlands, rivers and others. An area of primary forest is located along the border with Laos. Recently, about 2,500 plant species have been reported. About 2,000 species, 74 per cent, belong to the category of phanerophytes. There are, at present, 130 species of large and small mammals. The area also supports 295 bird species, 54 species of amphibians and reptiles, 84 species of fish, and 39 species of bats found only in Viet Nam and north-east Thailand. In addition, there are 14 species of tortoises, 305 species of butterflies and thousands of species of other insects, including 68 valuable and rare species recorded in the Red Book of Viet Nam. There are 295 species of birds, including local and migratory birds, and 22 species considered to be globally threatened and endangered. Populations of the crested argus (Rheinardia ocellata), great hornbill (Buceros bicornis) and rufous-necked hornbill (Aceros nipalensis) are of global significance, while the lesser fish eagle (Ichthyophaga humilis) is of national significance. The reserve is also home to the Gong culture of the Central Highlands of Viet Nam, which is inscribed on the list of UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage.
records.name: Western Nghe An

records.introduction_en: The East Usambara Biosphere Reserve is part of the Eastern Arc Mountain range and covers the Tanga region. It falls under the jurisdiction of three districts: Korogwe, Muheza and Mkinga. Livelihoods in and around the East Usambara Biosphere Reserve stem from small-scale farming and cattle breeding.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is one of 34 biodiversity hotspots in the world, and with its array of endemic plants and animals it is often compared to the Galapagos Islands. The site contains both submontane rainforest and lowland wooded grassland. These rainforests secure the water supply for the surrounding local community, the Tanga city population and industrial use. The biosphere reserve is divided into three land management zones, each with a specific management plan aligned with the MAB programme. The core area is an extensive biodiversity research and training site that includes 14 protected forest reserves, such as Amani Nature Reserve, Nilo Nature Reserve and Amani Botanical Garden. It is characterised by high concentrations of flora and fauna, including many medicinal plants and 13 endangered bird species. The buffer zone features commercial forest plantations, patches of natural forest turned into village forest reserves by local communities, and tree crops. Finally, the transition area is home to sisal and tea plantations whilst providing a living environment to over 80 villages. With two ecosystem types, mountains and coastal forests, the East Usambara Biosphere Reserve features a variety of vegetation. These range from tropical evergreen forests, including Cephalosphaera usambarensis and Allanblankia stuhlmanii, to tropical submontane rainforests and savanna woodland with Combretum and Annona, as well as agroforestry, agroecosystems, grazing and urban areas.
records.name: East Usambara

records.introduction_en: The Jozani–Chwaka Bay Biosphere Reserve contains the only national park on the island of Zanzibar in Tanzania. Its landscape is a mosaic of mangroves, tropical forests and coral rag forests, as well as groundwater forests, salt marshes, and agricultural and residential areas. The site is a biodiversity hotspot, home to reef fish species, dolphins and 168 species of birds, including 30 species of global and regional importance. Of the site’s 291 known plant species, 21 are considered endangered. The inhabitants of the reserve live mainly from activities related to tourism, fishing, beekeeping, butterfly rearing and crab fattening.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area is virtually flat, with the exception of groundwater forest, which features moderate slopes on the western and eastern sides. The soil of the Jozani forest is rich, black and highly organic, but it ceases abruptly at the forest margin, giving way to broken coral rag with shallow pockets of light brown sandy soil. The landscape is a mosaic of mangroves, tropical forests and coral rag forests, groundwater forests, salt marshes, and agricultural and residential areas, making the area a biodiversity hotspot. Of the 291 plant species, which belong to 83 families, 21 are under threat or endangered. Several plant species are used for traditional medicines. The area is home to many faunal species, including the African civet (Civettictis civetta), mangrove kingfisher (Halcyon senegaloides) and African goshawk (Accipiter tachiro). It also hosts endangered endemic species such as the Kassina Jozani frog, Zanzibar red colobus (Piliocolobus kirkii), Aders’ duiker (Cephalophus adersi) and Zanzibar servaline genet (Genetta servalina archeri).
records.name: Jozani-Chwaka Bay

records.introduction_en: The Bañados del Este Biosphere Reserve includes protected areas such as Monumento Histórico y Parque Nacional Fortaleza de Santa Teresa, Parque Nacional y Reserva de Fauna y Flora de El Potrerillo de Santa Teresa, and Monumento Histórico Parque y Fuerte San Miguel. It also encompasses Refugio de Fauna Laguna Castillos, Reserva Forestal de Cabo Polonio y Aguas Dulces, Monumento Natural de Dunas y Costa Atlántica, and Parque Nacional Lacustre de las Lagunas de Rocha y Garzón. This ‘Eastern Wetlands’ region comprises a remarkable complex of ecosystems with high biological diversity and very rich wildlife.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Low hills on a rocky substratum also occur on the ocean coast, and several coastal lagoons are among the most remarkable features of the region. Most of these lagoons are separated from the sea by a narrow sand bar that regularly opens, allowing the entrance of seawater. The biosphere reserve is the only area in the country where Butia palms exist in almost pure associations, covering an area of almost 70,000 ha. At present, the palm is at risk of extinction because of ageing plants and the lack of regeneration, as buds are eaten by cattle. Dominant elements of the herbaceous community include Cyperaceae, Juncaceae and Gramineae, as well as Monte psamófilo and extensive stands of conifers. The indigenous fauna remains almost intact, except that the marsh deer (Blastocerus dichotomus) is now locally extinct.
records.name: Bañados del Este

records.introduction_en: Encompassing a mosaic of ecosystems ranging from lush tropical rainforests to marine areas along the Gulf of Urabá, the reserve covers 3,016 km², almost 40 per cent of which is marine. The archaeological park and museum are a tourist destination and tell the story of one of the first Spanish settlements on the American continent, Santa María La Antigua del Darién, founded in the early sixteenth century.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Within the vibrant Darién ecoregion, part of the Biogeographic Chocó, lies a biodiversity bridge that connects the fauna and flora of North and South America. Emblematic species include the harpy eagle (Harpia harpyja) and colourful poison dart frogs. The area also includes a portion of the Gulf of Urabá, considered a marine biodiversity hotspot. It encompasses a broad mosaic of ecosystems, including tropical rainforest biomes and marine and coastal ecosystems.
records.name: Darién Norte Chocoano

records.introduction_en: The Val d’Aran biosphere reserve is nestled at the western frontier of the Catalan Pyrenees, Catalonia’s only north-facing valley. Its unique position as a watershed between the Mediterranean and Atlantic realms gives rise to diverse climatic and biological landscapes. It is also a bastion of Occitan cultural and linguistic heritage.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Val d’Aran is the only north-facing valley in Catalonia and acts as a watershed between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic, resulting in different climatic and biological conditions. The landscape also includes mountainous peaks such as Tuc de Molières at 3,010 m and Besiberri Sud at 3,014 m, which form part of the main axis of the Pyrenees mountain range.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Val d'Aran

records.introduction_en: Located in the central north of Gyeongsangnam-do Province, the Changnyeong Biosphere Reserve spans 531 km² and includes habitats from the forests of Mount Hwawang to the Upo Wetland and surrounding croplands. It supports freshwater ecosystems, forest habitats and sustainable agriculture. Local agriculture includes onions and garlic alongside ecotourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Main habitats are forests within and around Mount Hwawang, cropland and wetlands including the Upo Wetland. Forests occupy the largest area, followed by paddy and dry fields, grassland and water bodies. The site encompasses freshwater wetlands and streams, a forest ecosystem with rich terrestrial biodiversity and an agricultural ecosystem based on sustainable practices. It is important for conserving species in the transition areas that link aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. Since 2008, the Upo Wetland has played a role in restoring the crested ibis (Nipponia nippon). In 2018, the Upo Wetland was recognised as a Ramsar Wetland City.
records.name: Changnyeong

records.introduction_en: Situated in western Mongolia, Khar Us Lake Biosphere Reserve occupies a vast depression within the Great Lake basin spanning 14,153 km² in Khovd Province. Its ecosystems include aquatic environments, deserts, high mountain terrain and steppe landscapes, each contributing to the region’s ecological richness. The biosphere reserve is a haven for rare and endangered species and also for cultural heritage, as it is home to diverse ethnic groups whose livelihoods revolve around sustainable animal husbandry. Efforts are under way to develop sustainable ecotourism, aligning with Khovd Province’s focus on heritage-based tourism for economic diversification. Local herders have formed community-based organisations to safeguard their pasturelands and wildlife, highlighting their dedication to conservation and sustainable livelihoods.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The site includes several primary ecosystems, such as aquatic environments, deserts, high mountain ecosystems, human-created areas and patch ecosystems. The steppe ecosystem comprises 59 per cent of the whole territory of the biosphere reserve. The site encompasses the Mankhan, Buyant, Myangad, Chandmani and Durgun soums of Khovd aimag (province) and Durvuljin soum (county), of Zawkhan aimag (province). Each area has a different protection regime that promotes nature conservation and the livelihoods and sustainable development of local communities, as mandated by Mongolian national legislation covering the environment, lakes, special protected areas and transition areas.
records.name: Khar Us Lake

records.introduction_en: In Ethiopia’s far southwest, along the border with South Sudan, the Anywaa Forest Biosphere Reserve safeguards a vital ecological corridor linking Gambella National Park, national forest priority areas, and wildlife reserves with neighbouring protected areas across the border, including Boma National Park. The biosphere reserve encompasses six major ecosystems—from moist Afromontane and transitional rainforests to riverine forests, wetlands, and wooded savannahs—making it a haven for biodiversity and cultural heritage alike.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Anywaa Biosphere Reserve protects a complex mosaic of six major ecosystems, including Moist Afromontane Forests, Transitional Rainforests, and Combretum-Terminalia woodlands. This diversity of landscapes shelters over 1,000 vascular plant species, around 40 of which are endemic. The reserve is a critical habitat for significant wildlife, including the Nile lechwe (Kobus megaceros), African elephant (Loxodonta africana), shoebill (Balaeniceps rex), and African wild dog (Lycaon pictus). Sustained by rivers contributing up to 40% of the Nile's flow, the biosphere reserve&'s waterways support more than 110 freshwater fish species.
records.name: Anywaa Forest

records.introduction_en: Nestled in the northernmost reaches of Jordan, the Yarmouk Biosphere Reserve protects a dramatic stretch of the Jordan Rift Valley where altitudes plunge from 450 metres to 150 metres below sea level. The biosphere reserve lies within the Yarmouk Basin, a landscape shaped by steep wadis, fertile terraces, and perennial streams. This topographic variety creates a mosaic of habitats that sustain high biodiversity while preserving cultural landscapes that have supported human life for centuries. Designated under the stewardship of the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature, the reserve aims to integrate conservation, sustainable development, and community participation.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve encompasses a range of Mediterranean and Rift Valley ecosystems defined by four main vegetation types: deciduous oak steppe, cultivated Aleppo pine forests, steppe vegetation, and aquatic plant communities. Three perennial watersheds—Wadi Al-Kursi, Wadi Al-Mantamra, and Wadi Ain Al-Sukar—feed into a network of valleys that serve as crucial wildlife corridors. These habitats support diverse plant and animal species, including regionally significant birds and mammals adapted to steep valleys and riverine systems. The intact core area conserves representative ecosystems that are essential for maintaining ecological connectivity and biodiversity within the northern Jordan Rift.
records.name: Yarmouk

records.introduction_en: Flowing freely from the Pindus Mountains in Greece to the Adriatic Sea, the Vjosa River and its valley form one of Europe’s last wild river systems. The biosphere reserve encompasses river channels, islands, and floodplains that are constantly reshaped by the river’s uninterrupted flow. This dynamic hydrology creates a unique mosaic of habitats, regulates water flows, stores carbon, mitigates floods, and supports the cultural traditions and livelihoods of communities along its banks. The biosphere reserve brings together core, buffer, and transition zones to safeguard ecological integrity while fostering sustainable development.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Vjosa Valley contains one of the most intact river ecosystems in Europe, with habitats including braided channels, gravel bars, riparian forests, wetlands, and coastal lagoons. It shelters more than 1,600 recorded species, many of them rare or endangered. Key species include the Albanian water frog (Pelophylax shqipericus), Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus), Dalmatian pelican (Pelecanus crispus), Adriatic sturgeon (Acipenser naccarii), European eel (Anguilla anguilla), Pindus stone loach (Oxynoemacheilus pindus), long-fingered bat (Myotis capaccinii), wild chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum), and Queen Olga’s snowdrop (Galanthus reginae-olgae). The Vjosa Delta and Narta Lagoon contain up to 18 Natura 2000 habitats and are critical stopover and wintering sites for migratory birds such as the greater flamingo (Phoenicopterus roseus) and Audouin’s gull (Larus audouinii). The river’s natural flow regime maintains dynamic geomorphological processes and high habitat heterogeneity, supporting exceptional biodiversity.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Vjosa Valley

records.introduction_en: The Omo Biosphere Reserve is situated about 135 km north-east of Lagos in southern Nigeria. The major habitats are dry evergreen mixed deciduous forests in the north and wet evergreen forests in the south. Plantations and agricultural land also occur within the area. The major economic activities are timber exploitation, fuelwood harvesting, cultivation of arable crops, hunting, fishing and the plantation of indigenous and exotic tree species, all of which take place in the transition area. Soil erosion and loss of biodiversity are the principal threats to the reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The predominantly ferruginous tropical soils of Omo are typical of soil varieties found in the intensively weathered areas of basement complex formations in the rainforest zone of south-western Nigeria. The river complex in the area has a network of rivulets, streams and small rivers that form several tributaries to major rivers in the area. These include large perennial rivers such as the River Oni along the border east of Omo and the north-western Oluwa. The forests in the reserve are mixed moist, semi-evergreen rainforest. The vegetation of the complex is classed as lowland rainforest, which typically contains many valuable timber trees. The area is extremely rich in species and has high levels of endemism. It also has the highest variety of butterflies in Africa, a large proportion of which are endemic. The main plant species of the area include Diospyros, Dracaena mannii, Khaya ivorensis and Cordia millenii. Among the animal species found in the reserve are chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes), pangolin (Manis tetradactyla), long-crested eagle (Lophaetus occipitalis), civet cat (Viverra civetta), white-throated monkey (Cercopithecus erythrogaster), African elephant (Loxodonta cyclotis) and the globally threatened yellow-casqued hornbill (Ceratogymna elata).
records.name: Omo

records.introduction_en: Nordhordland Biosphere Reserve is centrally located on the coast of western Norway and comprises the coastal landscape between Bergen and Sognefjorden. It stretches from the Atlantic Ocean in the west across the outer coastal archipelago, passing through hundreds of fjords and inlets, and ends in the mountains to the east at 1,300 m above sea level. Water is a central theme because it has shaped the region’s natural features and because people have long used lakes, rivers, fjords and the open ocean for hunting, fishing and transport. Nordhordland is also vital for the Norwegian economy, with large hydroelectric resources and oil and gas extracted from the seabed off the coast.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is characterised by a high diversity of ecosystems with associated flora and fauna. At its western edge lies the open archipelago, which protects the mainland from the open sea. The ecosystems here are linked to the Norwegian Trench and the Norwegian Continental Shelf. The sea contains clean, clear Atlantic water with a high salt content. In the ocean depths are deep-water corals, and further in are extensive kelp forests. In addition to Lindåsosane, a system of small, shallow fjords, three major fjords stand out: the national salmon fjords of the island of Osterøy, Masfjorden and Lurefjorden. The freshwater systems show high diversity in the rivers flowing from the mountains to the fjords, and largely depend on nutrients and organic material transported from the land by run-off and wind. Water quality and biological processes are therefore strongly influenced by bedrock, biological processes and human activity in the catchment. These river systems are especially important regionally and globally as spawning areas for Atlantic salmon.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Nordhordland

records.introduction_en: Located on Peru’s northern Pacific coast within the Ecuadorian dry forest belt, the Noroeste Amotapes–Manglares Biosphere Reserve brings together coastal mangroves and the western Andean foothills in a coastal–montane gradient. Best known for the Tumbes Mangroves, the largest mangrove complex in Peru, the reserve also conserves seasonally dry forests at the heart of the Tumbesian centre of endemism, a recognised biodiversity hotspot. The reserve aims to promote sustainable use of natural resources and cleaner production, while maintaining biological diversity as the productive base for improving people’s quality of life.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set across the Ecuadorian dry forest, tropical Pacific coastal landscapes and mangrove ecosystems, the Noroeste Amotapes–Manglares Biosphere Reserve presents a gradient of ecosystems from scrub and very dry forest, to dry and tropical submontane forest and mangroves. The reserve brings together three core protected areas: Cerros de Amotape National Park, Coto de Caza El Angolo and the Tumbes Mangroves Protected Area. Characteristic vegetation in the reserve includes ceibo (Ceiba trichistandra) and algarrobo (Prosopis pallida), while emblematic fauna includes american crocodile (Crocodylus acutus), green iguana (Iguana iguana), andean condor (Vultur gryphus) and peruvian thick-knee (Burhinus superciliaris). The Tumbes Mangroves Protected Area safeguards Peru’s largest mangrove forest. Five mangrove species occur here, including black, white and red mangroves, forming nursery and shelter habitats that underpin high bird, fish and reptile diversity. The reserve’s dry forests also stand out for their species richness and high endemism within a relatively small area. They are an important ecosystem, supporting fauna not found elsewhere on the Peruvian coast or in the highlands, including species characteristic of the Amazon region. They are also crucial, especially in the Cordillera de los Amotapes, for maintaining agricultural and livestock activity in the valleys, ensuring a sufficient and timely water supply.
records.name: Noroeste Amotapes-Manglares

records.introduction_en: Harbouring four emblematic Peruvian ecosystems with many species of high bio-ecological value and high levels of endemism, Bosques de Neblina–Selva Central lies in a transition area between the Andes and the Amazon forest. This contrast is evident in altitude, which ranges from 440–5,100 metres above sea level, and is reflected in its remarkable biological and cultural diversity. The area is paramount for the protection of important headwaters.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: While less than 10 per cent of the region’s biodiversity has been catalogued, Bosques de Neblina–Selva Central hosts various endemic and endangered species, such as the Andean bear (Tremarctos ornatus) and the Andean cock-of-the-rock (Rupicola peruvianus). The site shares its northern border with the Oxapampa-Ashaninka-Yanesha Biosphere Reserve, designated in 2010, ensuring a conservation corridor across the entire region. Among the most representative vegetation are Polylepis forests and the queen of the Andes (Puya raimondii), known for its giant flower spike. Fauna in the area includes the northern viscacha (Lagidium peruanum), Andean fox or culpeo (Lycalopex culpaeus), spectacled bear (Tremarctos ornatus), Andean white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus), taruca (Hippocamelus antisensis) and Andean condor (Vultur gryphus).
records.name: Bosques de Neblina - Selva Central

records.introduction_en: Located in the Central Cordillera, the Gran Pajatén Peruvian Biosphere Reserve is characterised by high altitudes and a pristine ecosystem. It incorporates the Río Abiseo National Park, which is inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List. The site is home to rainforest fauna and flora characteristic of this region of the Andes, and has a high level of endemism. It is the only place on Earth where the yellow-tailed woolly monkey (Lagothrix flavicauda), previously thought extinct, is found. Gran Pajatén also lends its name to an archaeological site in the Andean cloud forests of Peru, which provides a window into pre-Inca society. Main economic activities in the biosphere reserve are agriculture, notably cacao and coffee, livestock and mining.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Gran Pajatén biosphere reserve is located in Peru, nestled between the Andes and Amazon plains. Its territory covers 2,509,699 ha and comprises a diversity of natural habitats, notably dry forests and Yungas, tropical valleys along the eastern slope of the Andes Mountains characterised by a rainy, humid and warm climate. While the reserve reaches a maximum height of 4,650 metres above sea level, it contains important gold mines and rich water resources due to the presence of 150 lagoons that originate from glaciers. The Gran Pajatén biosphere reserve comprises around 5,000 flora species, of which 174 are Pteridophyta. The forests contain an abundance of Polylepis multifuga, endemic in Peru, and Andean palm trees. In addition, the biosphere reserve is home to 903 animal species, of which 27 are endemic. These include 181 mammal species, 409 bird species, 30 amphibian species, 14 fish species and 253 invertebrate species. Many fauna species native to Peru are in danger of extinction, especially the yellow-tailed woolly monkey (Lagothrix flavicauda), the San Martin titi monkey (Callicebus oenanthe) and the yellow-browed toucanet (Aulacorhynchus huallagae). An assessment undertaken by the biosphere reserve also found threats to other species, including the jaguar (Panthera onca), the spectacled bear (Tremarctos ornatus) and the taruca (Hippocamelus antisensis), a deer species native to South America.
records.name: Gran Pajatén

records.introduction_en: The East Carpathians Biosphere Reserve is a transboundary mountain reserve in Central Europe that encompasses areas of significant value for biodiversity conservation. It covers the western edge of the East Carpathians, stretching across Poland, Slovakia and Ukraine. The European mountain areas of the reserve are among the few that retain well-preserved native flora and fauna. In particular, the mixed Carpathian forest provides suitable conditions for large mammals such as the European bison (Bison bonasus). Population density varies, from vast wild spaces on the Polish side to relatively densely populated areas in the Ukrainian part, with cultivated valleys, hay meadows, pastures and deciduous forest. Forestry remains the main local economic activity.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The East Carpathians Biosphere Reserve is located in Western Bieszczady, the southern part of which is known as Bukovske Hills. Primeval forest fragments in this area have been preserved up to the present day. Large portions of the territory comprise forest and non-forest ecosystems, accompanied by numerous plant communities growing in semi-natural rural areas. Four distinct vegetation types are found within the biosphere reserve: beech forest (Fagetum sylvaticae), beech–fir forest (Fageto-Abietum), dwarf-shrublands with green alder (Alnetum viridis), and a belt of treeless poloniny, subalpine meadows dominated by Prata subalpina. The mixed Carpathian forest provides suitable conditions for large mammals such as the European brown bear (Ursus arctos), the European bison (Bison bonasus), the Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx) and the European wolf (Canis lupus). Over 100 species of birds live in the area, including the black stork (Ciconia nigra) and the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos). The reserve also contains several sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List, including the Wooden Tserkvas of the Carpathian Region in Poland and Ukraine, and the Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians in Slovakia and Ukraine.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: East Carpathians

records.introduction_en: Krkonoše/Karkonosze is a transboundary biosphere reserve in north-western Czechia and south-western Poland. The Krkonoše/Karkonosze Mountains form part of the Sudetes in north-eastern Bohemia, a mountain system shared by Czechia, Germany and Poland. The reserve represents a unique pocket of arctic nature in Central Europe and an extraordinary crossroads where arctic, alpine, lowland and mountain elements mingle within a relatively small territory. The area is known for high biodiversity across four altitudinal vegetation belts. Human activities have shaped nature and the landscape throughout the Krkonoše Mountains over the last four centuries. Today, it is a popular tourist destination for hikers and skiers, especially on the Czech side.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Krkonoše Mountains lie on the northern fringe of the Bohemian Massif. Two main ridges are connected by two summit etchplains. A steep tectonic slope forms the Polish side, while on the Czech side several parallel ranges, divided by river valleys, project from the main ridges. Several glacial lakes occur on the Polish side, and a complex of subarctic peat bogs is found on the summit plateau along both sides of the border. Four distinct altitudinal vegetation belts are recognised, from submontane in the foothills up through montane and subalpine to the alpine belt at the highest elevations. This habitat diversity supports rich biodiversity. Animal species include the alpine shrew (Sorex alpinus), western capercaillie (Tetrao urogallus), peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus) and lesser horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus hipposideros). The reserve contains two Ramsar sites: the subalpine peat bogs in the Karkonosze Mountains on the Polish side, and Krkonošská rašeliniště on the Czech side.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Krkonose / Karkonosze

records.introduction_en: The Masurian Lakes Biosphere Reserve is distinguished by extraordinary environmental and landscape values. It is dominated by forest and aquatic ecosystems. The picturesque landscape, which stands out among other parts of Poland, developed several tens of millennia ago as a result of the activity of the Scandinavian ice sheet. As it advanced and retreated, it formed the forested undulating hills and extensive plains seen today. Wetlands, rivers and lakes developed in depressions. In addition to large lakes surrounded by forests, the area features several tens of smaller lakes. Many of them are dystrophic lakes with accompanying peatland vegetation.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The rich mosaic of ecosystems provides favourable conditions for many rare, protected and relict species of vascular and cryptogam plants, lichens, fungi, and vertebrate and invertebrate animals. A total of 499 taxa recognised as valuable have been recorded in the area of the biosphere reserve so far. The group includes 271 taxa under strict legal protection in Poland, 138 under partial protection, 61 species from Polish Red Books and 192 taxa from Polish red lists. It also includes 75 species listed in Annex II of the Habitats Directive and Annex I of the Birds Directive, and 251 from the Global List of Endangered Species developed by the IUCN. The biosphere reserve also contributes to the preservation of genetic pools of native animal races. Since 1949, traditional stable breeding and reserve breeding of the Polish pony has been conducted. The animal is recognised as a unique environmental-breeding relic demonstrating Poland’s contribution to global breeding culture. Research conducted by the Field Station of the Polish Academy of Sciences in Popielno is also of high importance. It concerns the protection of Polish Red Cattle. This native race constitutes valuable material for ecological agriculture, in biological, landscape and ethnographic terms.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Masurian Lakes

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve is one of the largest forest complexes in north-western Poland. Within this forested area, there are a number of natural habitats in need of protection. These include pine and deciduous forests, heathlands, Lobelia lakes, dystrophic lakes with stonewort meadows, and peat bogs.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve contains ecological systems typical of the lowlands of Middle Europe. Many rare, relict and protected species occur here, including vascular plants such as trees, bushes, dwarf shrubs and herbaceous plants, as well as cryptogamic plants such as algae, lichens, mosses and liverworts. Fungi are also present, alongside diverse invertebrates and vertebrates. Many of these species are listed on the Polish Red Lists of endangered species. Recorded taxa include 10 algal species on the Red List, 149 lichens, 29 mosses and 136 vascular plants. In addition, 212 species appear on the local list, and 38 species are listed as extinct on the national and local lists. The fauna comprises 33 fungi, 2 cyclostomes, 11 fishes, 8 amphibians, 5 reptiles, 53 birds and 15 mammals.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Tuchola Forests

records.introduction_en: The Roztocze Transboundary Biosphere Reserve is located in the Roztocze region in Poland and Ukraine, a natural and cultural borderland near the European Union border. It lies in the immediate vicinity of Lviv in Ukraine and Zamość in Poland, cities inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Roztocze has potential for dynamic development because of its scenic location and rich natural and cultural heritage. The Ukrainian part, called Roztochya, was designated a biosphere reserve in 2011.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The varied relief and complex geological structure are reflected in the tremendous diversity of living nature. The area of the biosphere reserve is not homogeneous. Loess areas are located in the west and are characterised by the highest density of ravines per 1 km² in Poland. Tomaszów Roztocze, known as Roztocze Tomaszowskie, features limestone hills cut by river valleys in the southern marginal zone, forming deeply cut valleys with topographic thresholds. Rava Roztocze, known as Roztocze Rawskie, is an area of wooded hills, mineral waters and good weather, with many sunny days. Roztocze is an ecological corridor of European importance, a narrow land connection linking the Polish Highlands with Podolia, enabling the movement of plants and animals. As a result of this, and its location at the Carpathian arc, plant species of three geographical areas occur in this region. The region is an important natural boundary. The north-eastern limit of the geographical range of beech, fir, spruce and sycamore runs through the region. Heterogeneous forests are the main resources of the region, including in particular the Carpathian beech forest and fir forest. Mammals of Roztocze are represented by 66 species, including three considered extinct (one confirmed, two unconfirmed), and four alien invasive species. The most interesting mammals are bats, including the barbastelle, greater mouse-eared bat, Bechstein’s bat and Alcathoe bat, as well as fat dormouse, forest dormouse, lynx and wolf. The most important refugia of mammals in Roztocze are natural forests located mainly in protected areas. The avifauna of the region includes species of high nature conservation value such as ferruginous duck, black stork, honey buzzard, lesser spotted eagle, Ural owl, boreal owl, gre … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Roztocze

records.introduction_en: The original Big Thicket of Texas covered between 809,371 and 1,214,056 hectares, or 2–3 million acres, in what is now mapped as the Pineywoods and Coastal Marsh ecoregions of the state. People have called the Big Thicket an American ark and the biological crossroads of North America, as it has one of the most biologically diverse assemblages of species in the world.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is a transition zone where south-eastern swamps, eastern deciduous forests, central plains, pine savannas and dry sandhills meet. This diverse habitat allows an impressive array of species to coexist. These include approximately 1,320 species of vascular plants, 60 mammal species, 86 reptile and amphibian species, 34 species of freshwater mussels, nearly 1,800 invertebrate species in the order Lepidoptera (butterflies, moths and skippers), 97 fish species, at least 300 bird species and 400 species of mushrooms. Cactus and orchids, beech trees and bald cypress trees, azaleas and pine trees, roadrunners and alligators, and, historically, bison, jaguars and red wolves are all included in the array of species. Four of the five known types of carnivorous plants found in the United States are found in the Big Thicket. The abundant rainfall, 54 inches per year on average, and the long growing season, around 246 days, ensure that the vegetation and animal life thrive in this unique area of Texas.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Big Thicket

records.introduction_en: The Everglades National Park is a shallow basin tilted to the south-west and underlain by extensive Pleistocene limestones. The reserve includes Fort Jefferson National Monument, which consists of a group of seven coral reefs called the Dry Tortugas National Park. Three major banks, Pulaski, Loggerhead and Long Key, form a pseudo-atoll with a mud-bank type formation.
