records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve lies at the interface between temperate and subtropical America. It is also positioned between fresh and brackish water, shallow bays, deeper coastal waters and coral reefs, creating a complex of habitats that supports a high diversity of flora and fauna. The area of transition from freshwater, or glades, to saltwater, or mangrove, is highly productive and incubates great numbers of economically valuable crustaceans. Southern Florida vegetation is unique in the United States, but similar communities occur throughout the Caribbean and parts of tropical America. Habitats include freshwater and wet prairies characterised by islands of tropical hardwood trees, saltmarshes, mangrove forests, beach and dune complexes, brackish-water estuaries, cypress swamps, marine systems and coral reefs.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Everglades & Dry Tortugas

records.introduction_en: Hawaiian Islands Biosphere Reserve lies within Hawai‘i Volcanoes National Park and encompasses active volcanic landscapes centred on Mauna Loa and Kīlauea. Mauna Loa is a huge shield volcano that rises from roughly six kilometres below sea level, to 4,169 metres above. Kīlauea is among the world’s most active volcanoes, renowned for its historic lava lakes at Halemaʻumaʻu. The diversity of successional habitats across recent lava flows, together with elevational and rainfall gradients, supports high ecological and genetic diversity at landscape scale. The reserve’s objectives are to conserve unique volcanic ecosystems, support appropriate nature-based use, and enable research and education.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Much of the land surface is geologically young, roughly 1,500 years old, and shaped by recent lava flows that create a mosaic of soils, plant communities and successional stages across rainfall gradients from rainforest to desert. Five major ecosystem groupings occur: subalpine, montane seasonal, montane rain forest, submontane seasonal and coastal lowlands. Distinct vegetation types are recorded, from dense rainforest to sparsely vegetated lava, with some native species restricted to single valleys or slopes. The Ola‘a Forest tract, roughly 10,000 acres, retains one of the largest remaining stands of old-growth ōhi‘a and fern forest in the Hawaiian Islands. Fauna includes six species of migrant seabirds and a range of native and introduced birds. Protected species include the ‘io (Hawaiian hawk) and nēnē (Hawaiian goose). Native Hawaiian bats are the only land mammals. Endemic forest birds include four honeycreepers – ‘apapane, ‘i‘iwi, ‘amakihi and creeper – while small breeding populations of the endangered Hawaiian dark-rumped petrel have been documented near Mauna Loa’s southwest rift zone. Conservation priorities include safeguarding large areas of native vegetation and rare plants, and protecting habitats for these endangered and endemic species.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Hawaiian Islands

records.introduction_en: Situated in the Luquillo Mountains of north-eastern Puerto Rico, the Luquillo Experimental Forest Biosphere Reserve encompasses five subtropical life zones: moist, wet and rain forest, and lower montane wet and rain forest. It spans nearly 1,000 m in elevation, from 120 to 1,074 m above sea level, and measures 11,331 ha, as reported by Weaver in 2012 and the USDA Forest Service in 2016. The biosphere reserve is rich in biodiversity and is home to thousands of native species, including 150 fern species and 240 tree species, 23 of which are found only within the reserve, according to the USDA Forest Service in 2016.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The forests in the biosphere reserve are classified into four types. Vegetation in the lower elevations consists of the lower montane rain forest or the subtropical wet forests, dominated by the tabonuco tree (Dacryodes excelsa). The montane thicket, or lower montane forest, occupies the gentle slopes above 600 m elevation and is characterised by the Colorado tree (Cyrilla racemiflora). Sierra palm (Prestoea acuminata) is associated with unstable soils, and dwarf forests occupy the highest elevations.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Luquillo

records.introduction_en: Situated on the Olympic Peninsula on the north-west coast of Washington State, the Olympic Biosphere Reserve and National Park are known for ecosystem diversity. This includes rugged, glacier-capped mountains, a wild Pacific coast, and magnificent stands of old-growth forest and temperate rainforest.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Glacier-clad peaks interspersed with extensive alpine meadows are surrounded by an extensive old-growth forest, which includes the best example of intact and protected temperate rainforest in the Pacific Northwest. Characteristic trees are Sitka spruce (Picea sitchensis), western hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla) and western red cedar (Thuja plicata). Eleven major river systems drain the Olympic Mountains, offering some of the best habitats for anadromous fish species in the country. The area also includes 100 km of wilderness coastline, the longest undeveloped coast in the United States. It is rich in native and endemic animal and plant species, including critical populations of the endangered northern spotted owl (Strix occidentalis) and marbled murrelet (Brachyramphus marmoratus). The large coastal subspecies of Roosevelt elk (Cervus elaphus roosevelti) was first described in the Olympic Mountains, and its protection was an important reason for establishing the national park in 1938. The area is also designated as a World Heritage site.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Olympic

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve is situated in the Sonoran Desert in south-western Arizona, on the border with Mexico. Wide alluvial basins separated by steep mountain ranges characterise the area’s topography.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The area is a representative example of the predominantly desert scrub vegetation of the Sonoran Desert, including the organ pipe cactus (Stenocereus thurberi), a large cactus rarely found in the United States but common in Mexico. Three major plant associations of the Sonoran Desert are present: the Arizona upland with saguaro cactus (Carnegiea gigantea), paloverde (Cercidium) and organ pipe cactus; the California microphyll with creosote bush (Larrea tridentata) and bursage (Ambrosia); and floristic components normally associated with the Mexican Gulf coast association, notably elephant tree (Bursera microphylla) and senita cactus (Cereus thurberi). There are some desert riparian areas and relict oak woodlands. Forty-nine native mammals occur within the monument, including the endangered Sonoran pronghorn (Antilocapra americana sonoriensis).
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Sonoran Desert

records.introduction_en: The Southern Appalachian Biosphere Reserve is situated at the southern end of the Appalachian Mountains, a series of ancient ranges across six states. It includes the highland portions of northern Georgia, north-eastern Alabama, western South Carolina, eastern Tennessee, western North Carolina and south-western Virginia. In addition to the biosphere reserve units, which include Great Smoky Mountains National Park, Oak Ridge National Environmental Research Park, Coweeta Hydrological Laboratory, Mt. Mitchell State Park and Grandfather Mountain State Park, the region includes a variety of national and state parks, recreational and wildlife areas, national and state forests, an experimental forest, lands administered by the Tennessee Valley Authority and Cherokee Indian lands.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Southern Appalachian Mountains are a major North American biome. They are characterised by complex, interconnected landscapes with steep, terrain-driven biophysical gradients that have their origin in Pleistocene glacial history, as described by Bossu et al. (2013) and Kozak and Wiens (2010). The region contains about 80 species of amphibians and reptiles, 175 species of terrestrial birds, 65 species of mammals, 2,250 species of vascular plants and possibly as many as 25,000 species of invertebrates. At 1,812 m, Grandfather Mountain is the highest peak on the Blue Ridge Escarpment. Defined by sharp, rocky peaks, Grandfather Mountain supports excellent occurrences of many rare high-elevation community types and an exemplary assemblage of rare plant and animal species. Federally endangered plant species include spreading avens (Geum radiatum) and Roan Mountain bluet (Houstonia montana). Federally threatened plant species include Heller’s blazing-star (Liatris helleri) and Blue Ridge goldenrod (Solidago spithamaea). Federal species of concern include mountain bittercress (Cardamine clematitis), tall larkspur (Delphinium exaltatum), Carolina saxifrage (Saxifraga caroliniana), Gray’s lily (Lilium grayi) and the liverwort Sphenolobopsis pearsonii. Federally endangered animal species include the Virginia big-eared bat (Corynorhinus townsendii virginianus), the Carolina northern flying squirrel (Glaucomys sabrinus coloratus) and the spruce-fir moss spider (Microhexura montivaga). Federal species of concern among animals include the eastern small-footed myotis (Myotis leibii), Appalachian cottontail (Sylvilagus obscurus), Alleghany woodrat (Neotoma magister), southern water shrew (Sorex palustris punctulatus), Southern Appalachian northern saw-whet owl (Aegoliu … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Southern Appalachian

records.introduction_en: Mount Pietrosul Mare is the largest mountain complex in the Rodna Massif, which is situated to the north of the Eastern Carpathians. This biosphere reserve is very important from a biodiversity conservation perspective.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Habitats in the reserve are extremely diverse due to high elevation changes, from 900 to 2,300 metres above sea level. They include mountain forest ecosystems, as well as alpine meadows with many endemic and endangered species. There are forests of beech (Fagus sylvatica), spruce (Picea abies) and arolla pine (Pinus cembra). Alpine and subalpine pasture supports Carex curvula and Festuca airoides, with shrublands of Rhododendron kotschyi. Arcto-alpine habitats include species such as Cerastium alpinum, Silene acaulis and Atragene alpina. Circumpolar habitats feature Woodsia ilvensis, Diphasiastrum alpinum and Salix herbacea. Central European alpine habitats characteristic of the Rodna Massif include dwarf pine (Pinus mugo), green alder (Alnus viridis), Salix retusa and Callianthemum coriandrifolium. There are also lakes of glacial origin.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Rodnei Mountains

records.introduction_en: Chernomorskiy (meaning ‘Black Sea’) Biosphere Reserve is situated on the northern coast of the Black Sea, about 45 km south-west of the city of Kherson. It represents shallow coastal, estuarine and inland wetlands, as well as marshes, shallow coastal bays, dune systems, halophytic seaside steppe and forest-steppe, which were once common in this region.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: In the territory of the reserve, unique natural complexes are present. These include azonal sandy forest-steppe on the arenas of the lower Dnieper, seaside solonetzic desertified steppe, coastal and island complexes, and natural aquatic complexes of shallow-water bays and the Black Sea. A variety of ecological conditions has produced rich flora and fauna. More than 700 species of plants grow under natural conditions, and up to 3,000 species of invertebrate animals inhabit the reserve. A total of 457 species of vertebrate animals occur here: about 80 kinds of fish, five kinds of amphibians, nine reptiles, 306 birds and 53 species of terrestrial and aquatic mammals. More than 50 per cent of species are protected by the Bern Convention, included in the European Red List, and listed in the Red Book of Ukraine. The Black Sea Biosphere Reserve is one of the most interesting places for the protection of terrestrial nature in Europe, a standard of natural complexes of the south of Ukraine, a centre of endemism, and a place for preserving many rare and protected species of plants and animals.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Chernomorskiy

records.introduction_en: Dunaisky Biosphere Reserve lies in the Ukrainian sector of the Danube Delta on the Black Sea, close to the border with Romania. The area is one of the largest natural refuges in the Northern Black Sea region and is part of the Kilijska Delta Ramsar site, recognised for its rich bird and fish life along major Eurasian flyways. It is a constituent part of the Danube Delta Transboundary Biosphere Reserve, shared with Romania. The reserve’s priorities include renaturalising key areas, restoring more natural water regimes in its marshes, and guiding agriculture and animal husbandry toward environmentally friendly practices. Long-term monitoring, education and carefully managed access support these goals.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This is a dynamic delta shaped by moving channels, seasonal floods and the steady delivery of sediment to the sea. Shallow fresh waters and floodplains form the core of the landscape, dominated by extensive stands of common reed (Phragmites australis) and sedge communities that give way to open water with floating vegetation such as water chestnut (Trapa natans) and fringed water lily (Nymphoides peltata). Riverine forests and scrub develop along raised riverbanks and backwaters, creating shaded channels, nest sites and corridors used particularly by woodpeckers such as the great spotted woodpecker (Dendrocopos major). On the seaward edge, shallow coastal waters support migratory and commercial fish, including migratory sturgeons such as Russian sturgeon (Acipenser gueldenstaedtii), as well as Black Sea forms of anchovy (Engraulis encrasicolus) and shad (Alosa kessleri pontica). Sandy ridges, dunes and spits hold specialist plants such as Leymus sabulosus, Argusia sibirica, sand wormwood (Artemisia arenaria) and field wormwood (Artemisia campestris). The wetlands act as a large natural buffer that slows floods, filters water and traps sediment and carbon, reducing nutrient loads and helping to stabilise shorelines during storms. Open waters, reed beds and mudflats lie on important migration routes for waterbirds and provide breeding and wintering habitat at a European scale. Wild boar (Sus scrofa) and raccoon dog (Nyctereutes procyonoides) use the mosaic of islands, reed and riparian thickets, and the hydrological connectivity between river, lagoon and sea supports spawning and nursery grounds that underpin regional fisheries.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Dunaisky

records.introduction_en: Golija-Studenica Biosphere Reserve is situated in south-western Serbia and lies within the inner zone of the Dinaric mountain system. It covers a mountainous region and includes a mosaic of ecosystems, such as forests, shrubs and lakes.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The local population cleared parts of the forests over centuries and thus created species-rich pastures and meadows, which are still maintained today. In the area, many non-governmental organisations are interested in protecting the natural environment and implementing sustainable development principles. The establishment of a biosphere reserve aimed to allow these organisations to carry out their programmes and contribute to the functions of the Golija-Studenica Biosphere Reserve, based on a rich history of scientific research and observations.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Golija-Studenica

records.introduction_en: The Gishwati–Mukura Landscape is located in the Albertine Rift in the western part of Rwanda. This young national park is a global biodiversity hotspot, home to a variety of endemic and endangered species. After decades of poorly managed land use, the country has been carrying out a major restoration effort, moving towards socio-economic development based mostly on ecotourism.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Gishwati–Mukura Landscape is critical for protecting biodiversity. The reserve is recognised for two primate species, the eastern chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) and the golden monkey (Cercopithecus kandti), which are endemic and endangered. Other species such as the side-striped jackal (Canis adustus), a variety of bats and small mammals, inhabit this forest. Vegetation in the reserve includes three bryophytes that occur exclusively in the Gishwati Forest: Porella abyssinica, Leptoscyphus expansus and Cololejeunea parva.
records.name: Gishwati Mukura Landscape

records.introduction_en: Volcans Biosphere Reserve is located in north-western Rwanda on the border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda. It comprises five volcanoes: Karisimbi, Muhabura, Bisoke, Sabyinyo and Gahinga. The reserve covers 160 km² of rainforest and bamboo. It is home to 30 per cent of the global population of mountain gorillas (Gorilla beringei beringei). It supports 115 mammal species, 187 bird species, 27 reptile and amphibian species and 33 arthropod species. It has 13 orchid species protected by CITES and three endangered reptile species. It also has 245 plant species, 17 of which are threatened on the IUCN Red List.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: At the international level, the Volcans Biosphere Reserve forms part of the Albertine Rift, an important ecological system in eastern and central Africa. It is home to many fauna and flora species endemic to the subregion. It shelters one of the four great apes, the mountain gorilla, an endemic and endangered subspecies that lives only in two large forests: Bwindi Impenetrable National Park and the Virunga Mountains, of which the core area of the Volcans Biosphere Reserve is part. Mountain gorillas attract thousands of international tourists annually and have become a symbol of hope for Rwanda. Together with neighbouring protected areas, the biosphere reserve forms the Virunga Mountains, a unique transfrontier area and an early example of regional collaboration in the region. At the national level, it helps regulate climate and provides many other ecological services. Regional natural forests play an important role in regulating precipitation, and it rains three times more in the Virunga volcanoes than in surrounding areas. More than 300,000 people directly depend on water supply from the forest. Over the last three decades, habitat and ecosystem structure have been less impacted by human interventions due to institutional management efforts in collaboration with community conservation. For instance, the population of Gorilla beringei beringei, the most vulnerable species in this protected area, has increased in the last two decades.
records.name: Volcans

records.introduction_en: East Vättern Scarp Landscape is a distinct example of the landscape in the central part of southern Sweden. It is dominated by agricultural and forestry lands, with villages and settlements consisting of small farms and individual homes.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The East Vättern Scarp Landscape region is centrally located in southern Sweden, with habitats reflecting the country’s southern deciduous broadleaf forest region and the northern coniferous forest region. The biosphere reserve contains several deep lakes. Of these, Lake Vättern is Sweden’s largest cold-water lake and the fifth largest lake in Europe. Its total surface is 105,520 ha. The lake is home to 31 fish species, including the large salmonid Salvelinus umbla, which is also a key symbolic species of the East Vättern Scarp Landscape. It also supports great biodiversity across a wide range of organism groups. There are several glacial relict species in Lake Vättern, including a number of crustaceans and a few fish species, notably the grayling (Thymallus thymallus). These species have adapted to lake living after the last glacial period and post-glacial rebound. The insects along the shores of Lake Vättern are also notable and are more reminiscent of the rivers of northern Sweden than lakes in the south of the country. On a stretch of just a few kilometres there are four different hardiness zones and extensive biodiversity. Lake Vättern clearly influences the local climate, with cold springs but long, mild autumns. Because of this, several post-glacial warming relicts have been able to survive in the region and on the slopes down to Lake Vättern, which have an oceanic climate. For example, the only incidence in all Scandinavia of the symbolic species, the bulin snail (Ena montana), occurs in the ravine environments near the lake. Gisebo and Gränna are home to one of the country’s largest fruit-growing districts, which is not common at this latitude and altitude. Due to the central location of the East Vättern Scarp Landscape in the southern third of Sw … [truncated]
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: East Vättern Scarp Landscape

records.introduction_en: Straddling the Arctic Circle, the Vindelälven–Juhttátahkka Biosphere Reserve includes large parts of the Vindelfjällen nature reserve, one of the largest in Europe. The northern part of the biosphere reserve is mountainous, forests cover its central part, while the south is a coastal area. The area is home to two distinct cultural communities, Swedish and Sami, with rich cultural traditions. Activities in the biosphere reserve include mining, forestry and reindeer husbandry, which enjoys official protection as a traditional activity of public interest. The Sami Parliament is officially responsible for ensuring that Sami interests are defended in spatial planning. Samernas Riksförbund (SSR), the National Federation of Swedish Sami people, works more directly to support “samebys” on planning issues. The Sami Parliament has also drawn up an action plan for Sami livelihoods and culture to address climate change.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The entire landscape in the biosphere reserve has been sculpted by the inland ice sheet. The area includes a large number of habitats and types of land use, found either in a limited part of the area or in widely scattered locations. The mountains are often barren, inhospitable and demanding environments for vegetation, but their climate is stable throughout the year. However, in recent decades, mountain environments have been affected by ongoing climate change. The mountain heaths are home to low-growing alpine and subalpine vegetation that is normally impacted by long-term grazing. Reindeer are the dominant grazing species in the barren mountain region, but grazing by small rodents also affects mountain biotopes. Outbreaks of the autumnal moth are a prime disturbance in mountain birch forests. These forests stretch in a belt along the entire mountain chain and therefore constitute a relatively large and extensive forest type.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Vindelälven-Juhttátahkka

records.introduction_en: The region of the Saloum Delta is a remarkable testimony to the synergy between a natural environment with extensive biodiversity and a style of human development that is still present, albeit fragile. Located in the centre-west of the country, it is an interesting site for the conservation of biological diversity because the biosphere reserve is characterised by a great diversity of habitats, including savannah, mangrove, sandy islets, lagoons and shorelines. For instance, the region is home to a quarter of the world’s population of royal terns (Sterna maxima). Bird Island is also the world’s first wintering and breeding site for this endangered species.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This biosphere reserve and national park is situated in the delta of the seasonal Sine and Saloum rivers, about 150 km south‑east of Dakar. The biosphere reserve comprises 72,000 ha of marine areas, 23,000 ha of flooded areas and 85,000 ha of terrestrial islands. Mangroves are dominant, but sand dunes, open forest on sandy soils, coastal waters and sand islands also characterise the area. The mangrove is principally made up of four species: Rhizophora racemosa, R. mangle, R. harrisonii and Avicennia nitida. Estuarine habitat includes banks of intertidal sand and mudflats, thick mangrove dominated by Rhizophora racemosa, R. mangle, R. harrisonii and Avicennia nitida, open flat areas known locally as tanns, and islands with halophilic species such as Sesuvium portulacastrum, Philoxerus vermicularis and Paspalum vaginatum. There is also dry forest and sand dunes. The area is important bird habitat and is a site for breeding colonies of migratory waterbirds, including over 30,000 pairs of the royal tern (Sterna maxima).
records.name: Delta du Saloum

records.introduction_en: The biosphere reserve is located in the agro-ecological zone of Senegal called Ferlo. It is an area of low plateaux and alluvial plains formed by fossil valleys and temporary flows that join the Ferlo valley. The biosphere reserve is exploring options to diversify traditional livestock-rearing and subsistence farming livelihoods.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is part of the Senegal–Mauritania basin. The area has a tropical-Sahelian climate in the north and a Sudano-Sahelian climate in the south. Average rainfall ranges from 300 mm in the north to 600 mm in the south. The altitude rarely exceeds 50 m except at significant dune accumulations. The geological substrate consists almost entirely of sandstone and clay formations of the Continental Terminal, covered by Quaternary sands that create sand dunes 1–5 m thick. The biosphere reserve hosts relict plant and animal species of national, sub-regional and international importance. It has a rich and diverse fauna and is home to emblematic species such as the red-fronted gazelle (Gazella rufifrons), the golden jackal (Canis aureus), the spotted hyena (Crocuta crocuta), the oryx, the dorcas gazelle (Gazella dorcas) and the helmeted guinea fowl (Numida meleagris). Ferlo is currently the only refuge of the red-necked ostriches (Struthio camelus) in the Sahel. In terms of vegetation, Ferlo is characterised by a great diversity of ecosystems and vegetation types, which include savannah, shrub and herbaceous gallery forests along rivers, shrub-steppe, valleys, ponds and pastures.
records.name: Ferlo

records.introduction_en: The Škocjan Caves Biosphere Reserve encompasses the Škocjanske jame Regional Park, including the Škocjan Caves, designated both as a World Heritage Site and a Ramsar Wetland of International Importance. This site is a global reference for karst studies.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The specific underground ecosystems typical of karst are well known for geomorphological, geological and hydrological formations resulting from the limestone bedrock. The limestone is the main reason for the constant lack of running surface water in karst and the formation of caves. It has influenced how animals and plants have adapted, including the occurrence of rare and endemic species such as the cave salamander (Proteus anguinus), invertebrates and bats, as well as the rational use of water by farmers. The Škocjan Caves comprise a system of 11 interconnected underground caves, flat-floored valleys that extend over collapsed dolines, natural bridges and sinkholes. They are adorned with stalactites, stone curtains and broad rimstone pools. The biosphere reserve is important for demonstrating the rational use and management of water sources. Typical karst land is ecologically very vulnerable because of large underground pools of potable water. The biosphere reserve seeks to integrate and co-ordinate sustainable agricultural practices with the preservation of caves and local hydrological processes, controlling surface and subsurface pollution from fertilisers and wastewater.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: Škocjan Caves

records.introduction_en: Sakaerat Biosphere Reserve lies on the north-eastern flank of the Khao Khieo Massif, on the rim of the Korat Plateau, about 240 kilometres from Bangkok. Elevation ranges from roughly 250 to 760 metres across a tilted, gently dissected plateau, with intermittent streams that retain water locally through the dry season and drain to the Mun River. The reserve is regionally important for conserving Thailand’s upland forest mosaic, including dry dipterocarp forest now much reduced across the country, and for long-running field science that informs management. Current priorities are to maintain and restore key habitats, apply research and monitoring to guide decisions, deliver tightly managed educational camps and training, and support cooperative agriculture and low-impact tourism in the transition area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Set on the forested uplands of north-east Thailand, Sakaerat comprises dry evergreen, mixed deciduous and dry dipterocarp forest, with smaller areas of reforestation and bamboo. The core is dominated by dry evergreen and dry dipterocarp types, the latter a South-east Asian ecosystem now much reduced across Thailand and therefore a protection priority. Emblematic fauna include king cobra (Ophiophagus hannah) and Siamese fireback (Lophura diardi). The contiguous forest supports practical ecosystem services. Mature stands store carbon over long periods, while the structure of dry evergreen forest favours slower turnover of organic matter, helping to retain carbon. The biodiversity maintained within the core area supplies biological control agents such as predaceous mantids that help regulate crop pests in adjacent farmland, supporting a small cluster of organic farms on the southern edge of the reserve. Management focuses on maintaining habitat quality through non-invasive research in the core, routine ranger patrols to deter poaching, and community stewardship schemes that provide alternatives to extractive activities.
records.name: Sakaerat

records.introduction_en: The East Carpathians Biosphere Reserve is a transboundary mountain reserve in Central Europe that encompasses areas of significant value for biodiversity conservation. It covers the western edge of the East Carpathians, stretching across Poland, Slovakia and Ukraine. The European mountain areas of the reserve are among the few that retain well-preserved native flora and fauna. In particular, the mixed Carpathian forest provides suitable conditions for large mammals such as the European bison (Bison bonasus). Population density varies, from vast wild spaces on the Polish side to relatively densely populated areas in the Ukrainian part, with cultivated valleys, hay meadows, pastures and deciduous forest. Forestry remains the main local economic activity.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The East Carpathians Biosphere Reserve is located in Western Bieszczady, the southern part of which is known as Bukovske Hills. Primeval forest fragments in this area have been preserved up to the present day. Large portions of the territory comprise forest and non-forest ecosystems, accompanied by numerous plant communities growing in semi-natural rural areas. Four distinct vegetation types are found within the biosphere reserve: beech forest (Fagetum sylvaticae), beech–fir forest (Fageto-Abietum), dwarf-shrublands with green alder (Alnetum viridis), and a belt of treeless poloniny, subalpine meadows dominated by Prata subalpina. The mixed Carpathian forest provides suitable conditions for large mammals such as the European brown bear (Ursus arctos), the European bison (Bison bonasus), the Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx) and the European wolf (Canis lupus). Over 100 species of birds live in the area, including the black stork (Ciconia nigra) and the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos). The reserve also contains several sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List, including the Wooden Tserkvas of the Carpathian Region in Poland and Ukraine, and the Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians in Slovakia and Ukraine.
records.regional_network: Europe and North America Biosphere Reserve Network (EuroMAB)
records.name: East Carpathians

records.introduction_en: The Dinder National Park was established in 1935 and became a biosphere reserve in 1979. Situated along the border with Ethiopia, this biosphere reserve includes tropical savannah and grassland ecosystems. The whole biosphere reserve is considered a core area with rich flora and fauna.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Dinder Biosphere Reserve serves as a vital habitat for terrestrial migratory species that spend the dry season in the park. The park’s extensive wetlands also provide refuge for many migratory birds. The biosphere reserve is home to a variety of wildlife species. Key herbivores include tiang (Damaliscus lunatus tiang), reedbuck (Redunca redunca), waterbuck (Kobus ellipsiprymnus defassa), roan antelope (Hippotragus equinus), oribi (Ourebia ourebi), warthog (Phacochoerus aethiopicus) and cape buffalo (Syncerus caffer caffer). Other animals, such as baboon (Papio anubis), vervet monkey (Chlorocebus aethiopicus) and hussar monkey (Cercopithecus aethiops), are frequent. The greater kudu (Tragelaphus strepsiceros) and red-fronted gazelle (Gazella rufifrons) are restricted to certain locations.
records.name: Dinder

records.introduction_en: This reserve comprises the Al Dair massif, which contains dry savannah woodlands, forest ecosystems and a network of streams. It is one of the few remaining areas with rich biodiversity in the semi-arid region of North Kordofan. The site supports 112 plant species, most of which have medicinal and aromatic uses. There are also 220 species of birds and 22 species of mammals and reptiles.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: More than 112 plant species have been recorded in the biosphere reserve, including 95 species of medicinal and aromatic plants. The dominant plant species in the upper slopes and escarpments ecosystem are Boswellia papyrifera, Dichrostachys cinerea, Acacia tortilis, A. mellifera, A. etbaica, Terminalia, Anthephora hochstetteri and Combretum glutinosum. Most of these plants are very rare and endangered and are not found elsewhere in North Kordofan. There is a very special ecosystem named “Fawas”. A total of 20 fawas have been identified in the biosphere reserve. Although the exact number of wildlife species is yet to be determined, twenty-two mammalian species have been recorded on the mountain. The most prominent are greater kudu, baboons and hyrax, among others. The last count of wild animals during 2016 recorded 150 kudu and 1,000 keko. It has been observed that monkeys, baboons and reptiles have increased in numbers. With regard to vegetation, Gana trees and many other plant species have increased in abundance and density. About 220 species of birds are seen in the jebel.
records.name: Jebel El Dair

records.introduction_en: The island of Príncipe is one of three existing oceanic volcanic islands of the Gulf of Guinea. It is geologically the oldest of the group, formed 31 million years ago. The biosphere reserve includes the entire emerged area of the island of Príncipe and its islets Bom Bom, Boné do Jóquei, Mosteiros, Santana and Pedra da Galei, and the Tinhosas islands.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The island is characterised by gentle relief in the northern half and a mountain range in the southern half composed of several phonolitic peaks with altitudes between 500 and 948 metres. In this southern area there is a patch of primary rainforest. The difference in geomorphology and terrain between the two sides results in distinct bioclimates. This influences the distribution of the island’s main ecosystems, with lotic systems in the area of the massif and its valleys, and lentic systems in the northern plains. The biosphere reserve hosts great biodiversity in both terrestrial and marine ecosystems, with high rates of endemism in many groups of organisms, especially vascular plants, molluscs, insects, birds, reptiles and bats. It is part of the biodiversity hotspot of tropical forests of West Africa and contains a wide range of plant communities and habitats of high international importance, including primary tropical forests, forest shade, palm trees and lowland riparian habitats. Given its importance for the reproduction of sea turtles, seabirds and cetaceans, as well as for its coral reefs, it is an area of great international interest for the conservation of global biological diversity.
records.name: Island of Principe

records.introduction_en: Rising from the Gulf of Guinea, the Ilha de São Tomé Biosphere Reserve includes volcanic peaks, lush forests, coastal ecosystems, and fertile agricultural lands. At its core is the Obô Natural Park, encircled by buffer and transition areas that integrate marine islets, agro-forestry zones, and community landscapes. It forms part of the Congo Basin forest system, one of the planet’s most important ecological regions. Together with Príncipe Biosphere Reserve, it forms the first ever whole-country biosphere reserve.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve shelters around 1,200 plant species, with 148 endemics unique to the island. Its emblematic fauna include the dwarf ibis (Bostrychia bocagei, CR), the São Tomé shrew (Crocidura thomensis), and a wide diversity of endemic amphibians and reptiles. Four marine turtle species nest on its beaches, while marine buffer zones include islets such as Ilhéu das Cabras, Ilhéu Santana, and Ilhéu das Rolas, important for coral reefs, seabird colonies, and cetaceans.
records.name: Ilha de São Tomé

records.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve hosts important ecosystems and species, with highly diverse habitats including páramo-like montane forests, cloud forests, vegetation on volcanic lava flows and conifer forests.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Land cover includes forest plantations, coffee plantations, grassland and crops. There are 12 endangered plant species and 58 threatened species, as well as 12 endemic species among birds and other vertebrate groups. Recorded taxa include fungi, bromeliads, orchids, bryophytes, agaves and extremophile bacteria. Other ecosystems include wetlands of national importance: Lake Coatepeque, Laguna Verde and Laguna Las Ninfas. All feature aquatic vegetation and aquifer-recharge areas linked to ongoing volcanic activity. Almost 4,000 ha are set aside for conservation across the nine core zones. A further 39,500 ha of shade-grown coffee plantations interconnect the core zones, enabling the movement of flora and fauna and forming a fundamental part of the Mesoamerican Biological Corridor (MBC). The area is identified as a geographical unit in El Salvador’s Land-use Planning and Development Plan, though the reserve extends beyond the conservation area’s limits. A number of Indigenous communities live in the territory, maintaining their traditions and Indigenous languages.
records.name: Apaneca-Llamatepec

records.introduction_en: The Trifinio Fraternidad Transboundary Biosphere Reserve is a tri-national reserve spanning El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras. It is the first transboundary biosphere reserve in Central America and makes a major contribution to implementing the Mesoamerican Corridor. It includes key biodiversity areas such as Montecristo National Park and a variety of forest ecosystems. A key function of this mountain area is securing water supplies for local communities. It also plays an important role in regional development through coffee production, conifer-forest extraction and agrotourism. The reserve has received strong high-level political support, including from vice-ministers of the three countries, alongside the involvement of local communities in promoting sustainable development.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Trifinio region harbours rich biodiversity and is vital to the water supply of all three countries, as it is the source of Central America’s three largest rivers. Predominant ecosystems include cloud forest, subtropical dry forest and pine–oak forest. The area also contains complex wetlands, notably Lagunar Güija, an international Ramsar site and refuge for more than 45 globally threatened species. Fauna includes the white-nosed coati (Nasua narica), ocelot (Leopardus pardalis), Baird’s tapir (Tapirus bairdii), northern crested caracara (Caracara cheriway) and the endangered Geoffroy’s spider monkey (Ateles geoffroyi).
records.name: Trifinio Fraternidad

records.introduction_en: Two fundamental processes underpin landscape and ecosystem conservation here. The first is the presence of El Salvador’s largest mangrove expanse.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: This mangrove ecosystem is a global priority, representing 46.82 per cent of the Mangroves of the Dry North Pacific Coast in Mesoamerica, an ecoregion declared Critically Endangered by WWF in 2006. These ecosystems support innumerable natural processes essential to the environmental services provided to communities, and they sustain the livelihoods of most local residents.The second process is the conservation of two “sweet” forest ecosystems of major regional and national importance: evergreen broad-leaved forests and semi-deciduous mixed broad-leaved forests. The former provide habitat for El Salvador’s only remaining primate, the Geoffroy’s spider monkey (Ateles geoffroyi). Remnants of the most extensive and least fragmented semi-deciduous mixed broad-leaved forests are found within the Xiriualtique–Jiquilisco Biosphere Reserve. In total, 37 endangered species and 58 threatened species are conserved in the reserve.
records.name: Xiriualtique - Jiquilisco

records.introduction_en: Located near the border with Cameroon, Sena Oura is Chad’s first biosphere reserve. It covers 173,520 ha of some of the last intact Sudanian savannah in the country and is home to elephants, giant eland and giraffes. With fertile soils and favourable agroclimatic conditions, traditional agriculture, particularly livestock herding, underpins local livelihoods. Forestry also contributes to the economy, including non-timber forest products such as honey and shea butter.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The site’s ecosystems include watercourses, ponds and salt marshes, which provide specialised habitats for several groups of animal species. Sena Oura supports communities that include many rare or endangered species, notably Derby eland (Taurotragus derbianus), roan antelope (Hippotragus equinus), korrigum (Damaliscus korrigum), elephant (Loxodonta africana), giraffe (Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum) and large carnivores. An extensive cave network offers excellent habitats for bats across caves and rocky areas. Gallery forests, occurring mainly along watercourses, are dominated by Ficus congoensis, Mitragyna stipulosa, Diospyros mespiliformis and Celtis integrifolia.
records.name: Sena Oura

records.introduction_en: Stretching across the alluvial plain, and the delta and riverbank areas of the Mono River, this site comprises a mosaic of landscapes and ecosystems consisting mainly of mangroves, savannah, lagoons, floodplains and forests, including sacred forests. The reserve’s inhabitants are mostly engaged in small-scale agriculture of oil palm and coconut palms, pasture, forestry and fishing.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Recognised under the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, the Mono River delta on the Benin–Togo border supports diverse habitats including rivers, lakes, wetlands, savannah, gallery forest, mangroves and beaches, and a rich fauna including hippopotamuses, manatees, whales and many species of waterfowl. The biosphere reserve also has various species that are endemic to the Dahomey Gap, such as the white-throated guenon (Cercopithecus erythrogaster). Critically endangered species include the hawksbill sea turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata) and the leatherback sea turtle (Dermochelys coriacea).
records.name: Mono

records.introduction_en: The Oti-Kéran–Oti-Mandouri (OKM) complex has varied topography dominated by river basins and vast plains, which give rise to the different ecosystems in the area.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The main vegetation formations include Sudano-Guinean savannah with trees. Because of this vegetation, the complex supports varied fauna, rich mainly in savannah species.
records.name: Oti-Keran/Oti-Mandouri

records.introduction_en: The Repetek Reserve, located in the central part of the East Karakum Desert covers typical sand desert. Its landscape features arid, large, hummocky, ridged sand dunes and valley-like depressions. This is one of the hottest regions in Central Asia, and the climate is typical of southern extra-tropical deserts.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Repetek Biosphere State Reserve forms part of an Important Bird Area and is one of the oldest nature reserves in Turkmenistan. It is one of the few natural desert sites in Central Asia with large coverage of black saxaul. The site supports the most complete assemblage of bird species typical of the sand desert of the Karakum. In addition, the site supports stable populations of globally threatened mammals, such as the goitred gazelle (Gazella subgutturosa). There are 22 reptile species, two of which are included in the Red Book.
records.regional_network: South and Central Asia MAB Network (SACAM)
records.name: Repetek

records.introduction_en: Queen Elizabeth Biosphere Reserve and National Park straddle the equator in western Uganda. Covering an altitudinal range of 910 to 1,390 metres above sea level, it is composed of a wide range of ecosystems, including semi-deciduous tropical high forests, undulating savanna grasslands, Acacia savanna, tundra and wetlands. The area also includes partly saline lakes, which include Lake George, a Ramsar site, and Lake Edward.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The core area of the reserve supports a wide range of Uganda’s natural habitats and landforms, including grassy plains, distinctive savanna woodlands, tropical forest, wetlands, rivers, swamps, lakes and volcanic craters. The reserve has a greater biodiversity than any other protected area in Uganda. The core area is also used as a model for conservation education, research and monitoring of biodiversity trends. The vast savanna and forest animal species, and the scenic landforms, attract an increasing number of tourists to the reserve. Hence, the reserve contributes to the tourism industry, which is Uganda’s second leading income earner. Large herbivore species include hippopotamus, elephant, buffalo, Uganda kob, waterbuck and topi. Large carnivore species include lion, leopard and spotted hyena. The reserve is also inhabited by over 600 species of birds, both migrant and resident. The following are amongst the endangered wildlife species found in the reserve: chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes), the African elephant (Loxodonta africana), leopard (Panthera pardus) and the shoebill stork. The northern Queen Elizabeth lions (Panthera leo), although generally scheduled as Vulnerable in CITES, are at a high risk of extinction due to human–lion–livestock conflicts.
records.name: Queen Elizabeth

records.introduction_en: The Delta del Orinoco Biosphere Reserve was created by Decree No. 1,633 of 5 June 1991, published in Official Gazette No. 34,812 of 3 October 1991, and encompasses 1,125,000 ha, including the protected areas, buffer and transition areas. This represents about 31 per cent of Delta Amacuro State’s total surface. The terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems of the Delta del Orinoco are characterised by high biological diversity, with more than 2,000 plants and a very rich terrestrial and aquatic fauna comprising more than 151 mammal species, 464 bird species, 76 reptiles, 39 amphibians and 210 ichthyological species. Considerable numbers of terrestrial and aquatic invertebrates also inhabit this territory.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Delta del Orinoco is a highly dynamic and complex fluvial–marine sedimentary basin formed in the Holocene. Its sediments were deposited mainly by the main flow of the Orinoco River and, to a lesser degree, by surrounding geomorphological units, including flows from the San Juan River and other currents draining from the plains of La Mesa. It is embedded in a mosaic of mangroves, swamp forest, moist forest, plains and shallow-water aquatic ecosystems. A series of fluvial and tide channels, the latter in the coastal plain, divide the vegetation. Among its vegetation, dominant species include Machaerium lunatum and Montrichardia arborescens, as well as Ludwigia, Mikania congesta and Bignoniaceae climbers. Floating prairies occur, formed mainly by Eichhornia crassipes and Eichhornia azurea. In terms of fauna, the biosphere reserve is home to valuable vertebrates and invertebrates of taxonomic value. The invertebrates include numerous groups that are important sources for local consumption, such as molluscs represented by oyster (Crassostrea virginica), Melongena melongena and guarura (Pomacea ursus). Several crustaceans are present, represented by shrimps and crabs such as Macrobrachium carcinus, Macrobrachium surinamicum, Macrobrachium amazonicum, white shrimp (Litopenaeus schmitti) and titi shrimp (Xiphopenaeus kroyeri). Besides common species in the region, like Cairina moschata, the biosphere reserve is also home to various endemic species, such as Dasyprocta guamara, Picumnus nigropunctatus, Dendrocincla fuliginosa deltana and Anolis deltae.
records.name: Delta del Orinoco

records.introduction_en: The Socotra Archipelago is located off the Horn of Africa, at the crossroads between the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. It is recognized as a regional centre of biodiversity, with spectacular endemic species such as the dragon blood tree (Dracaena cinnabari). Socotra has a rich cultural heritage, including the unique Soqotri language. Isolated from the rest of the world, traditional land and sea uses changed little until the 1970s.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Socotra is globally important for biodiversity conservation because of its exceptionally rich and distinct flora and fauna. Thirty-seven per cent of Socotra’s plant species, 90 per cent of its reptile species and 95 per cent of its land snail species occur nowhere else in the world. Socotra is of particular importance to the Horn of Africa’s biodiversity hotspot and, as one of the most biodiversity-rich and distinct islands in the world, has been termed the “Galápagos of the Indian Ocean”. Socotra is particularly important for plant diversity. It has 825 plant species, of which 307, or 37 per cent, are endemic. Socotra has high importance for bird species, as underlined by BirdLife International’s identification of 22 Important Bird Areas on Socotra. Socotra also supports globally significant populations of other land and sea birds, including a number of threatened species. The marine life of Socotra is also very diverse, with 253 species of reef-building corals, 730 species of coastal fish and 300 species of crab, lobster and shrimp.
records.name: Socotra Archipelago

records.introduction_en: The Cape West Coast Biosphere Reserve is located on the south-western coast of South Africa, north of the Cape Town metropolitan area. It stretches between the Diep River mouth in the south and the Berg River in the north. The Langebaan Lagoon and Lower Berg River support a high diversity of wader bird species. The Lower Berg River provides the highest number of wader birds in South Africa. The area contains several urban areas, including the commuter town of Atlantis in the south and Saldanha Bay town and its industrial complex in the north.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve extends from the Diep River near Milnerton in the south to the Berg River in the north, and inland to the western watershed of the Koeberg–Dassenberg–Swartberg–Karringberg ranges. The biogeographical region comprises coastal plains on the seaward side of the Cape Fold Belt mountains. These plains form the interface between the coastline and the interior uplands and mountains. The primary wheat-growing areas and the fishing rimland fall within this region. The major ecosystem types include coastal plains, a marine-influenced fynbos area, marine areas and wetlands. The vegetation is characterised by dominant emergent shrublands. These include West Coast Renosterveld, with Elytropappus rhinocerotis shrublands, sand plain fynbos with Phylica cephalantha shrubland, and dune thicket strandveld with Euclea racemosa shrubland. The Cape West Coast Biosphere Reserve is located in the Cape Floristic Region, also known as the Cape Floral Kingdom. It is the smallest of the world’s six floral kingdoms. The region is notable for the richness of its plant species, which amount to about 8,700 species, and for high endemicity, with 68 per cent of plant species found only in the Cape Floral Kingdom. The unique West Coast Benguela marine system, with wind-induced upwellings of deep, cold, nutrient-enriched waters, ranks among the most productive ocean areas in the world. These enriched waters support large populations of diverse sea life, including Heaviside’s dolphin (Cephalorhynchus heavisidii), the southern right whale (Eubalaena australis) and the humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae). More than 240 bird species have been observed on the tidal flats of the Lower Berg River. Mammal species include the steenbok (Rhapicerus campestris), the Cape grey mongoose ( … [truncated]
records.name: Cape West Coast

records.introduction_en: The Gouritz Cluster Biosphere Reserve is in the southern part of South Africa. It is divided into four connected sectors that extend from sea level to 2,240 metres. This is the only place in the world where three recognised biodiversity hotspots converge, namely Fynbos, Succulent Karoo and Maputaland–Pondoland–Albany. The site is characterised by a high level of plant endemism, with 1,325 species, including 182 Succulent Karoo endemics and 92 Red List species, and by threatened invertebrates, including seven endemic species of the enigmatic beetle genus Colophon and 14 butterfly species. It provides a migratory route for large mammals such as the leopard (Panthera pardus) and serves as a nursery for marine species. Despite its rich biodiversity, the area faces deep-rooted socio-economic challenges, including high unemployment, widespread poverty, sprawling informal settlements with inadequate services, rising HIV rates and growing crime.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Due to its relatively large size, the biosphere reserve is subdivided into four sectors or clusters: Towerkop, Kammanassie, Langeberg and St Blaize. The landscape is marked by remarkable variety and transition. Along the shore, fine-grained sandy beaches and dunes alternate with wave-cut platforms and exposed headlands. Deeply incised river valleys cut into the coastal platform, terminating in estuaries and, in places, forming coastal lagoons. The Outeniqua and Langeberg mountains separate the coastal region from the Little Karoo and form a natural barrier between the southern Cape and the interior. Further inland, the Kammanassie, Kouga and Swartberg mountain ranges form the northern and eastern boundaries of the reserve. The Gouritz Cluster Biosphere Reserve is the only area in the world where three recognised biodiversity hotspots converge, namely Fynbos, Succulent Karoo and Maputaland–Pondoland–Albany. The entire domain falls within the Cape Floristic Region, the smallest yet one of the richest of the six floral kingdoms of the world. The reserve is rich in endemic plant species, with more than 670 species. Even the arid inland portion is rich in endemic species, with at least 400 plant species. In terms of fauna, the reserve plays an important role in conserving two unique and threatened populations of the Cape mountain zebra (Equus zebra zebra) and the bontebok (Damaliscus pygargus pygargus). Populations of leopard (Panthera pardus) are present in most of the mountainous areas. Threatened invertebrates include seven endemic species of the enigmatic beetle genus Colophon and 14 endemic butterfly species. The reserve includes three recognised UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the Swartberg Complex, Boosmansbos Nature Reserve and Baviaanskloof.
records.name: Gouritz Cluster

records.introduction_en: The Quiçama Biosphere Reserve spans across the provinces of Luanda, Icolo e Bengo, and Cuanza-Sul, covering municipalities such as Quiçama and Cabo Ledo. This region holds high conservation value, serving as a habitat for seabirds, marine turtle nesting sites, and threatened species like the African manatee and the savanna elephant. It is also home to endemic species, including the rare pink-flowered Tessmannia camoneana, reflecting the area’s rich genetic diversity. Stretching along 206 km of coastline, the reserve encompasses unique geological formations, mangroves, estuaries, sandy beaches, and lagoons, which not only sustain biodiversity but also provide crucial socio-economic benefits to surrounding communities. As part of its blue economy vision, Angola aims to balance ecological integrity with sustainable development, employment, and social well-being. The Quiçama Biosphere Reserve will advance these goals, integrating conservation with research, innovation, sustainable tourism, and community-based initiatives. The recognition of both marine and freshwater ecosystems, which provide food, income, and cultural value, underscores the importance of protecting biodiversity while ensuring the long-term resilience and prosperity of local populations.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: The Quiçama Biosphere Reserve encompasses a mosaic of ecosystems that give it exceptional ecological value. Terrestrial habitats range from arid coastal cliffs with aloes, succulents, and Euphorbia candelabrum to savannahs, gallery forests, mangroves, and wetlands dominated by papyrus. Despite limited endemic flora, the region hosts species of conservation importance, such as Tessmannia camoneana, alongside diverse mammalian fauna, including elephants, buffalo, hippopotamus, and the threatened African manatee. Birdlife is especially rich, with more than 200 recorded species, including globally threatened ones like the Cape Gannet and Damara Tern. The area also supports important reptile diversity, such as sea turtles, dwarf crocodiles, and locally endemic lizard and snake species. These ecosystems contribute to ecological integrity and highlight the reserve’s role in both biodiversity conservation and scientific research. Equally significant are the coastal and transitional ecosystems, including mangroves, estuaries, sandy beaches, and tidal plains, which sustain marine productivity and provide critical habitats. Mangroves in Mussulo, Cabo Ledo, and Longa support fisheries, stabilize coastlines, and shelter shrimp and crab populations vital to food webs. Estuaries of the Cuanza and Longa rivers serve as nurseries for fish, crustaceans, and migratory birds, while sandy beaches provide nesting grounds for five species of sea turtles and feeding sites for migratory birds. Inland, rivers and lakes harbor diverse fish, amphibians, and reptiles, supporting both ecological balance and community livelihoods. Together, these habitats form interconnected ecological corridors that reinforce biodiversity resilience and underline the global significance of the Biosphere Reserve.
records.name: Quiçama

records.introduction_en: The Bioko Island Biosphere Reserve is a highly diverse and ecologically significant area, encompassing lowland Guineo-Congolese rainforests, high-altitude Afro-montane forests, and rich endemic fauna, including endangered primates as well as distinctive birds and other mammals. Its vegetation is shaped by altitude, climate, and historical human activity. The Biosphere Reserve fulfills three core functions by combining: conservation, protecting species and habitats within the Luba Caldera Scientific Reserve and Pico Basilé National Park; sustainable development, promoting equitable economic growth, poverty reduction, cultural preservation, and ecotourism in Malabo, Luba, and surrounding communities; and logistical support, facilitating research, monitoring, education, and training through the National Institute of Forest Development and Management (INDEFOR) and the MAB National Committee. This integrated approach ensures the protection of biodiversity while fostering socio-economic resilience and environmental stewardship across the island.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Bioko Island hosts highly diverse and unique ecosystems, with vegetation ranging from lowland Guineo-Congolese rainforests to high-altitude Afro-montane forests. The island’s flora is dominated by secondary formations, with Polyscias africana as a key species across Afro-montane zones between 1,400 and 2,500 meters. These forests feature a mix of medium-sized trees, tree ferns, and shrubs, and their composition varies with altitude, anthropogenic influence, and historical disturbances such as fires. The terraced lowlands and mountainous central region create a range of microclimates, with annual rainfall from 1,200 mm in lower areas to over 11,000 mm in the southern Ureca region, shaping forest distribution and ecological dynamics. The island’s fauna is equally distinctive, including highly endangered and endemic primates such as the dril (Mandrillus leucophaeus) and the black colobus (Colobus satanas), as well as other mammals like Ogilby’s duiker and pangolins, which face threats from hunting. Bird species such as the Yellow-billed Turaco (Tauraco macrorhynchus), Giant Turaco (Corythaeola cristata), and Bald Turkey (Bycanistes albotibialis) are characteristic of the dense tropical forests of Equatorial Guinea. The combination of complex topography, high rainfall, and rich biodiversity makes Bioko’s ecosystems ecologically significant, supporting both unique species and critical habitats while presenting ongoing conservation challenges.
records.name: Isla de Bioko

records.introduction_en: Located on the southern slope of the Gissar Range in Tajikistan, the Romit Biosphere Reserve ranges from 1,200 to 3,192 m above sea level. Its triangular territory is defined by the Sorbo River to the west, the deep gorges of Ushruta and Vashruta to the north, and the Karateginsky Ridge to the southeast. The biosphere reserve encompasses a diverse mountain landscape that serves as a key ecological refuge and a living example of sustainable mountain resource management.
records.ecological_characteristics_en: Romit’s ecosystems form three distinct altitudinal zones: mountain steppe, mountain forest-steppe, and highlands. Each zone hosts unique plant communities and wildlife. The area shelters 32 mammal species, including the snow leopard (Panthera uncia), as well as other species listed in the Red Book of Tajikistan. Its varied landscapes support a rich assemblage of flora and fauna adapted to high-altitude environments, making it an important center for biodiversity conservation in the Gissar Range.
